# The commentary of Saint Thomas Aquinas on the books of Boethius's *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, with his exposition, happily begins.

<margin>P</margin> **"You must serve philosophy so that true freedom may befall you."** <note>original: "Philosophie seruias oportet vt tibi contingat vera libertas"</note>
These are the words of Seneca in his eighth letter to Lucilius, because philosophy is rightly called the science of truth, according to the second book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, a foundational text on the nature of reality</note>; and philosophy brings forth delights wonderful in their stability and purity, according to the tenth book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, discussing the highest human good</note>. And to many, philosophy has seemed a wonderful and divine thing, according to Aristotle’s *On the Heavens* <note>original: "de celo et mundo"</note>. Furthermore, no science is like philosophy, which clarifies the soul and causes it to take delight in this world, in both pursuit and righteousness, according to the *Book of the Apple and Death* <note>original: "libro de pomo et morte"; a popular medieval work falsely attributed to Aristotle, describing his final conversation before death</note>. And philosophy draws man from the obscurity of ignorance to knowledge, from the darkness of folly to the light of wisdom and the clarity of the intellect, according to that same book of Aristotle. Furthermore, philosophy liberates one from superstition and is not disturbed by the fear of death, according to Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and philosopher</note> in his book *On the Ends of Good and Evil* <note>original: "de finibus bonorum et malorum"</note>. Therefore, Seneca, considering these and similar conditions and the laudable effects of philosophy, exhorts us to the service of philosophy in the proposed proposition, saying thus:

**"You must serve philosophy."** This proposition can indeed be proved by many reasons. First, in this way: One must serve that through whose service true freedom occurs; but philosophy is such a thing; therefore. The major premise is known because freedom is the noblest condition which human nature desires and affects. The minor premise is evident through the same Seneca, who, after setting forth this proposition, "You must serve philosophy," adds, "so that true freedom may befall you," and after a few interjected words, says: To serve philosophy is itself freedom. 

It is proved second in this way: One must serve that which perfects the mind, arranges life, governs actions, demonstrates what should be done and what should be omitted, and without which no one is secure; philosophy is such a thing; therefore, etc. The major premise is known, for these conditions pertain to the perfection of man. The minor premise is declared by Seneca in his sixteenth letter to Lucilius, speaking of philosophy, where he says: **"It shapes and fashions the mind; it arranges life, governs actions, and demonstrates what should be omitted. It sits at the helm of those wandering astray and directs the course of those tossed by waves; but without it, no one is secure."** 

It is proved thirdly in this way: One must serve that which grants a great increase in the knowledge of the ultimate end; philosophy is such a thing; therefore, etc. The major premise is known because the knowledge of the ultimate end confers a great increase to life, according to the first book of the *Ethics*. The minor premise is declared: For the ultimate end of human life is happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>, the knowledge of which philosophy hands down. For Philosophy says, in the third book of *The Consolation*, in the second prose section, that happiness is a state perfected by the gathering together of all goods. And in the same third book, Philosophy shows in what true happiness consists and how it may be reached. 

It is proved fourthly: One must serve that which makes man equal to God; philosophy is such a thing; therefore, etc. The major premise is known of itself. The minor premise is evident through Seneca, in his forty-ninth letter to Lucilius, who says: **"For this philosophy promises me: that it will make me equal to God."** 

It is proved fifthly: One must serve that which is the mistress of all sciences, the nurse of all virtues, the highest consolation of fallen souls, which is the promise of the true light, and whose exhortation is righteous and most worthy by its own authority; philosophy is such a thing; therefore, etc. The major premise is known because one is reasonably served on account of these laudable conditions. The minor premise is declared: For philosophy is the mistress of all virtues, according to the first book of *The Consolation*, in the third prose section; she herself is the nurse of all virtues, in the second book of *The Consolation*, in the fourth prose section. She herself is the highest consolation—

It cites classical authorities like Seneca, Aristotle, and Cicero to define philosophy as the path to true freedom, happiness, and divine likeness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory "Proemium" or preface to the commentary. The previous page established philosophy as the science of truth and the source of true freedom. Here, the author addresses common objections to studying philosophy—such as the role of fate and the distraction of poverty—before transitioning to the formal analysis of Boethius’s text.</meta>

# Preface

...of fallen souls, in the first prose of the third book of *The Consolation*. It is the very medicine of the true light, in the first prose of the fourth book of *The Consolation*. And its exhortation is most worthy of its own authority, in the first prose of the fifth book of *The Consolation*. Thus, the declared proposition is clear, which says: **"You must serve philosophy."**

But you might ask: "What does philosophy profit me if fate exists? What does philosophy profit me if God is the ruler? What does philosophy profit me if chance commands?" To this, Seneca responds in his seventeenth letter <note>original: "xvij. epistula sua"; this is likely a reference to Seneca's *Moral Epistles to Lucilius*, specifically Letter 16, where he discusses these themes</note>: whether the fates bind us by an inexorable law, or whether God as the judge disposes all things for the universe, or whether chance mixes human actions without order—still, one must persist in philosophy. For philosophy has the duty to protect us. Indeed, it exhorts us to obey God willingly, to follow Him, to continually resist Fortune <note>the personified force of luck and change</note>, and to endure chance.

However, although all humans by nature desire to know, yet few—which is a cause for sorrow—are free for philosophy. This happens because many, having abandoned interior delights, flee toward the pleasures of the body. Yet it is not right for bodily pleasures to be more desirable than interior ones, because bodily pleasures hinder one from the <term>Highest Good</term> <note>original: "summo bono"; the ultimate state of happiness or union with the divine</note>, while interior ones lead toward it. Whence Boethius, in his treatise on the highest good, says: they ought to grieve who, being detained by sensual pleasures, abandon interior goods. For those surrendered to sensual goods do not attain the highest goods. Boethius, in the fourth prose of the fourth book of *The Consolation*, compares such sensual men to **bats** <note>original: "vespertilionibus"</note>, saying: "For they cannot lift their eyes, accustomed to the shadows, to the light of clear truth; they are like those birds whose sight the day does not illuminate but blinds."

And although sensual and common men do not magnify the name of philosophy but rather blaspheme it, nevertheless philosophy perseveres in its own dignity, as Seneca testifies in his twenty-third letter to Lucilius <note>Seneca, *Epistle* 13 or 23, discussing the endurance of virtue</note>: "Malice will never become so strong, nor will it ever rise so far against the virtues, that the name of philosophy does not remain sacred and venerable."

But you might say: "I am not able to philosophize because I am poor; if I had riches, I would give myself entirely to philosophy." And this seems reasonable, because nature by itself is not sufficient for contemplation, but it is necessary that food, drink, and other services exist beforehand; and for this reason, the priests in Egypt, having the necessities of life, began to philosophize out of wonder. This excuse on the grounds of poverty is not valid. Listen to Seneca in his seventeenth letter to Lucilius, who says: "There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy. For even hunger must be endured, which some have endured in sieges; and what other reward for their patience was there, except not to fall under the will of the enemy? How much more is it that which promises perpetual liberty—fear of no man—and that which frees the soul from madness." Indeed, riches have stood in the way of philosophizing for many. Poverty, however, is unencumbered and secure. "If you wish to be free for the mind, you must be poor, or like a poor man," because a healthy study cannot happen without the care of <term>fragility</term> <note>original: "cura fragilitatꝭ"; here referring to the humble management of one's mortal needs</note>; and "fragility" is voluntary poverty. These are the words of Seneca.

It is true, therefore, that necessities are required for philosophizing, but a few things suffice for a human. For it is not necessary for one who is to be happy to be the master of the land and sea, because nature is content with a few and very small things, as seen in the second book of *The Consolation*, fifth prose. Therefore, cast all things from you and strive toward philosophy with a great run and all your strength; thus says Seneca in his seventeenth letter to Lucilius. You must serve philosophy, therefore, so that true freedom may befall you, so that true security may happen for you, so that happiness may become known to you, so that you may become equal to God, and especially so that, placed in adversities and tribulations, you may be most truly comforted through her—following the example of Boethius, whom philosophy most sweetly comforted when he was relegated to exile, driven from all goods, stripped of dignities, and afflicted by many miseries. This consolation of philosophy is treated in the book of Boethius which is entitled *The Book of the Consolation of Philosophy*, which is our present intention.

Let these things suffice for the introduction to this book. But before we come to the literal text, five things must be premised: First, the cause of the work being undertaken... <note>The text cuts off as it begins to list the Aristotelian "four causes" (material, formal, efficient, and final) plus the title/subject</note>

<summary>This page concludes the preface by arguing that philosophy is essential for true freedom regardless of fate or poverty, using Seneca's Stoic advice to defend its pursuit. It establishes philosophy as a source of divine comfort, citing Boethius's own suffering in exile as the ultimate proof of its value.</summary>

# Preface

...of this book. Third, concerning the title of this book and its explanation. Fourth, concerning the reason for the title of the present book. Fifth, concerning the general summary and meaning of this book.

Regarding the first point, namely the reason the work was undertaken and why **Boetius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman statesman and philosopher</note> wrote this book, it should be known that **Boetius**, an eminent man and Roman consul, was of the Catholic faith. While disputing concerning the Catholic faith against two heretics—namely **Nestorius** and **Eutyches** <note>Nestorius and Eutyches held opposing heretical views on the nature of Christ; Nestorius emphasized the distinction between his human and divine natures, while Eutyches argued they were fused into one</note>—when there was no one else to resist them, **Boethius** defeated them in a public council, as is clear in his book *On the Two Natures in Christ*.

However, in the time of **Theodoric**, king of the Goths, when the same **Theodoric** wished to exercise his tyranny against the Romans and oppress any good men, **Boetius**, armed with virtue more than all others, resisted him. **Boetius**, out of a love for justice and exposing himself to danger, liberated those whom tyrannical rage had invaded. Yet when King **Theodoric** saw that only **Boetius** was resisting him, he pondered how he might destroy him. Since he could find no just cause against him, he fashioned two false accusations.

**He said** that **Boetius** had prevented an informer from delivering letters to him which contained an accusation against the Roman Senate, so that the Senate might be held guilty of treason. **Boethius** touches upon this cause in the fourth prose of this first book, saying:

> We are accused of having hindered an informer from bringing documents by which he might make the Senate guilty of treason.

Secondly, he accused **Boethius** of having sent certain letters to the Emperor in Constantinople through which he might restore the ancient liberty of the Romans. **Boethius** touches upon this cause in the same prose, saying:

> For what pertains to the falsely composed letters by which I am accused of having hoped for Roman liberty?

For these reasons, **Boethius** was accused by vile and infamous persons; he was judged guilty without a defense and was banished into exile to Pavia by King Theodoric. While placed in exile, **Boethius** reflected on his past prosperity and considered his present adversity. He composed this *Philosophical Consolation* against the mutability of Fortune so that no man placed in a similar state might despair, but might have a source of comfort. From these words, it is clear that the reason for undertaking the work is this: so that while **Boethius** was banished into exile, driven from all goods, and stripped of his dignities, he might defend himself philosophically, wishing to console any person placed in a similar state so they do not despair.

Second, we must consider the "causes" of this book. The <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The person or agent who brings something into being</note> was **Boethius**, who, in describing the material of this book, uses both prose and verse. In this, he imitated Marcianus Felix Capella, who used this style in writing *The Marriage of Mercury and Philology*, which is mentioned in the *Theodolus* <note>A popular medieval school text, the *Ecloga Theoduli*</note> where it is said:

> To that excellent offspring whom, through the love of Stilbon <note>original: "stilbonis"; a Greek name for the planet Mercury</note>, you have joined with the great ones above, as Capella bears witness.

Although this book by **Boethius** greatly excels the book of Marcianus both in the nobility of its subject matter and the privilege of its eloquence, for **Boethius** is considered no less than **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in prose nor **Virgil** in verse. **Boethius** uses prose in this book to set forth the arguments for consoling Boethius, proving that one must not grieve over the loss of temporal things. He uses delightful verse so that, while it is heard, sorrows may be surrendered to oblivion.

The <term>material cause</term> <note>The subject matter or substance of the work</note> of this book is philosophical consolation ordered toward the contempt of worldly things and the desire for the highest happiness; or, philosophical consolation persuading that no one should be puffed up in prosperity nor depressed in adversity. Or, otherwise, the material cause or subject of this book is the miserable state of **Boethius**, with philosophical consolation introduced over it.

The <term>formal cause</term> <note>The structure or internal arrangement</note> of the treatise of this book consists in its division, which will be seen later. The formal cause of the treatment, however, is Boethius’s mode of proceeding, which is a <term>dialogue</term>—that is, the speech of two people. For Boethius introduces two personae in this book: namely, himself, mourning his misery, and Philosophy, grieving with him and consoling him over his misery. And this is reasonable. For according to Saint **Gregory**: the true order of consolation is that when we wish to lift someone up from sorrow, first...

<meta>This page continues the "Proemium" or Preface to the commentary on Boethius. # Preface

...let us see how to harmonize with his grief. Therefore, the **formal cause** <note>In medieval philosophy, the "formal cause" refers to the structure or style of a work</note> is a **dialogue**. This is because in a certain part of this first book, **Philosophy** is introduced addressing **Fortune** himself, where a certain rhetorical figure occurs called **ethopoeia** <note>A rhetorical device where the author speaks in the voice of another person or character; original: "ethopoeia"</note>. Regarding this, the *Graecissimus* <note>A famous medieval grammatical poem by Eberhard of Béthune</note> says that it introduces others speaking through ethopoeia, as when **Fortune** speaks to **Boethius** himself. Alternatively, it can be said according to common usage that the formal cause of the treatment is fivefold: **definitive, divisive, probative, improbative,** and **expositive of examples**, as will be seen in the book.

The **final cause** <note>The "final cause" is the ultimate goal or purpose of the work</note> of this book is that, by knowing it, we may protect ourselves and any others placed in adversity and tribulation with philosophical consolation, and that we might not be puffed up in prosperity nor depressed in adversity.

Third, we must look at the **title** of this book and its explanation. It should be known that the title, according to **Remigius** <note>Remigius of Auxerre (c. 841–908), a Carolingian scholar</note> in his commentary on Donatus, is the key or the entrance to the following work. The word "title" (*titulus*) is said to come from **Titan**, which is the **Sun**; for just as the sun illuminates the world, so the title illuminates the book. The title is placed before the book for the completion of the work and the praise of the author. Thus, the title of the present book is as follows: *The book of the Consolation of Philosophy by the illustrious man Anicius Manlius Torquatus Severinus, former consul, Patrician, and Ordinary, begins.*

But it is asked why so many proper names are placed in the title. Some say that perhaps it was the custom of the Romans to thus record the names of their grandfathers and predecessors. Or, it can be said another way: many names are placed in the title for the sake of the honor and praise of **Boethius** himself. For according to **Seneca** in his book *On Clemency* addressed to Nero: "Many surnames are given for the sake of honor" <note>original: "Multa cognomia honori data sunt"</note>. Just as a common person does not wish to be noted by more than one name—because the more they are named, the more they are known, and the more they become base—so a respectable person wishes to be named by many names so that their fame may become better known and shine brighter to others. For every good thing brought into the common view shines more brightly.

This title is explained as follows: **Boethius** was called **Anicius** after a certain noble Roman of that name from whose family he descended. Or, he was called **Anicius** as if "invincible" <note>original: "inuictus" from "a" (without) and "vicos" (victory/conquest). The author is attempting a Greek etymology for Anicius from *a-niketos*</note>; for **Boethius** could never be conquered so as to be turned from justice to injustice, as he himself testifies in the fourth prose of this first book, saying: "No one has ever dragged me away from what is right to what is wrong" <note>original: "Numquam a iure ad iniuriam me quisque detraxit"</note>.

Secondly, **Boethius** was called **Manlius** because he was of the family of the Manlii, who were noble Romans.

Thirdly, **Boethius** was called **Torquatus** after a certain noble Roman of that name who, when entering into single combat with a certain man from Gaul, defeated him and took away the torque <note>A neck-ring or collar of twisted metal</note> he had on his neck. By reason of this, he was called **Torquatus**, and **Boethius** was of his family.

Fourthly, **Boethius** was called **Severinus** from "severity" (*severitate*). For he was severe when he opposed **Theodoric**, king of the Goths. Or, he was called **Severinus** as if "following the truth" (*sequens veritatem*); for in judgments, he could never be turned from the truth by either love or hatred.

Fifthly, **Boethius** was called **Ex-consul**, as if one of the consuls of the Romans, or "ex-consul" as being placed outside of the consulship which he previously held. Those who had already laid down the consulship were called "Ex-consulars"; and although they ceased from the honor of the consulship, they were nonetheless held in great reverence afterwards, more than others.

Sixthly, he was called **Patrician** after a most noble Roman of that name from whose family **Boethius** came. Or another way: noble Romans were called "Patricians" because they looked out for the republic just as a father (*pater*) does for a son, and their names were written in golden letters. Therefore, they were called "Fathers," and **Boethius** was one of their number, which is why he was called **Patrician**.

Seventhly, he was called **Ordinary** because he set the republic in order (*ordinavit*). Or otherwise, they were called "Ordinaries" who were of such great dignity that they were worthy of any rank or order (*ordine*), and such was **Boethius**.

By his eighth and proper name, he was called **Boethius**, which is interpreted as "helper" (*adiutor*), because he came to the aid of the poor in their necessity.

Fourth, we must look at the reason for the title of this book. This book is titled *On the Consolation of Philosophy*. Here it should be known that "philosophical consolation" is called a rational demonstration declaring what has been lost...

# First Meter
a 4

...it is not something to be grieved over, nor is it something whose possession should be celebrated. Because he treats this subject in the present book, it is titled accordingly. Fifth, we must look at the general summary of this entire book. Here it should be known that **Boethius** shows in this book that temporal goods are transitory and that total, true happiness <term>felicitas; the state of supreme well-being</term> does not consist entirely in them. Consequently, one should not grieve over their absence, nor rejoice in their presence, and no one should be puffed up in prosperity nor depressed in adversity. It is also shown in the present book what the **highest good** is, where it is located, and how one may reach it. It is also demonstrated that the good are always powerful and the wicked are always weak, and that the good never lack their rewards, nor the wicked their punishments. After this, it is shown what **divine providence** is, what **chance** is, what **fate** is, and what **free will** is. **Boethius** sets forth arguments by which he proves that free will cannot seem to stand with divine providence; he presents the false solutions of some and disproves them. Afterward, he shows the true solution, which he confirms with reasons. These and many other beautiful things are determined in this book, as will be clear in the following sections.

### The first book of Anicius Manlius Torquatus Severinus Boethius, Ordinary Patrician and former Consul, on the Consolation of Philosophy, begins happily.

## The first meter, in heroic elegiac verse.

<margin>The present book of Boethius is divided in its primary division into five parts. Second, it sets forth the five partial books it contains. In the first, he complains that he is subject to miseries.</margin>

<note>original: "Carmina qui quondam studio florente peregi / Flebilis heu mestos cogor inire modos." These are the famous opening lines of the Consolation.</note>

In the second book, he provides consoling remedies. In the third, he determines the nature of true happiness, where it is situated, and how one reaches it. In the fourth, he raises certain questions to **Philosophy** herself. In the fifth, he determines the nature of chance and divine providence. The first book begins here: *Songs...* The second book begins there: *After he [had finished] for a little while...* The third there: *She had now finished that song...* The fourth there: *When Philosophy [had spoken] these things...* The fifth there: *She had spoken, and the course of her speech...* What is dealt with and concerning what subject in each book will be clear in its own place. The first book is divided into three parts, because there are seven meters and six proses in this first book, which parts will be made clear. Moreover, what the subject matter and intention of each part are will similarly be made clear. It should be noted that the first meter of this first book is called **elegiac**. An **elegiac meter** is one that consists of one hexameter verse (that is, of six feet) and another pentameter (that is, of five feet). It is called "elegiac" from *eleys* <note>A medieval etymology deriving "elegy" from the Greek word for pity or misery; original: "eleys"</note>, which means misery; for an elegy is a misery. Indeed, the elegiac meter was invented for describing misery, although today some use it to describe other things. Hence **Horace** says: "At first, complaint was composed in unevenly coupled verses; afterwards, the sentiment of the granted prayer was included" <note>original: "Usibus impariter cinctis querimonia primum. Post hoc incusa est voci sententia compos." From Horace's Ars Poetica.</note>. However, who was the first inventor of such elegiac meter is doubted; hence **Horace** says: "Yet who first sent forth these small elegies, the grammarians dispute, and the case is still before the judge" <note>original: "Quis tamen exiguos elegos emiserit autor. Grammatici certant et adhuc sub iudice lis est." Also from Ars Poetica.</note>. This first meter is divided into four parts. First, **Boethius** laments the state of his misery resulting from the change [in his fortune]...

The second part begins at "the glory of the happy man" <note>original: "gloria felicis"</note>; the third part at "death is happy for the good" <note>original: "mors bonum felix"</note>; the fourth at "why [did you call] me happy?" <note>original: "quid me felicem"</note>. First, he does what was stated; second, he confirms his words at the phrase: "Behold, the tattered..." He says first: I, **Boethius**, who in a former time of prosperity, while my study was flourishing, completed—that is, composed—delightful and joyful poems. Now, in a time of tearful adversity—that is, worthy of being wept over—I am compelled to begin—that is, to start—sad measures—that is, three...

<margin>sad measures, that is, three...</margin>
...sorrowful meters concerning my misery. It should be noted, as was said before, that **Boethius** uses both prose and meter in this book. This is because such a style of writing was more suitable to his subject matter. For just as a healing potion that is bitter is taken more delightfully if it is mixed with some sweetness, so the arguments of **Philosophy** delivered in prose are more willingly received by **Boethius** if they are sweetened by the pleasantness of meter. Therefore, **Boethius** uses meter at one time and prose at another, because it is more delightful to use alternating forms. Hence **Avienus** says in his *Poetry*: "That which tastes good, a faulty frequency makes tasteless." 

Also note that **Boethius** begins his book with meter rather than prose, because the metrical style of writing was more common among the ancients than prose. Or perhaps because meter is more delightful than prose; thus, to better entice his listeners to his book, he uses meter at the beginning. 

Also note concerning the text that "songs" <term>carmina; poems or rhythmic verses</term> are called metrical writings measured by certain "feet" <note>The "foot" is the basic unit of rhythm in poetry, like a heartbeat</note> in one sense. In another sense, they are any sayings or writings, even in prose, which concern a delightful subject. **Boethius**, however, while his study was flourishing, mostly composed prose "songs" about delightful subjects. For he published certain philosophical "songs," some logical, and some theological, as is clear to anyone looking at his various books. But in a time of adversity, **Boethius** was compelled to compose sad metrical songs. 

Also note that **study** <term>studium</term> is the vigorous application of the mind to doing something with good will. I say "with good will" because wisdom will not enter into malevolent souls—so says **Solomon**. And the perfection of a disciple consists of three things according to **Boethius** in *On the Discipline of Scholars*: attention, teachability, and benevolence. For the possession of the good is impossible for one who desires knowledge but does not study as one ought—**Eustratius** in the first book of the *Ethics*. 

Also note that study is two-fold: flourishing and arid. Three things are required for flourishing study. First, youth is required, because young people are more perceptive than the elderly; the elderly, however, are more forgetful. Second, the possession of necessities is required, because nature is not sufficient in itself for contemplation, but it is necessary for requirements to exist—from the fourth book of the *Ethics*. Third, tranquility of mind is required, which happens through the calming of the passions, because a resting and settled soul becomes prudent—from the seventh book of the *Physics*. For where the passions dominate, the intellect is obscured. Therefore, **Boethius**, at the end of this first book, encouraging us to flee the passions, says: "Drive away joys, drive away fears, put hope to flight, and let no grief be present. The mind is cloudy and bound with chains where these things reign." Arid study, however, is that in which opposite conditions meet, namely: old age, lack of necessities, and mental disturbance. 

Note that the verses about misery are called "sad measures" <term>mesti modi</term>. They are called "measures" <term>modi</term> from "modulating" because they are modulated by poetic feet. And they are called "sad measures" by reason of their subject matter, because they concern a sad subject, namely adversity. Note that in the first two verses, an **antithesis**—that is, an opposition—is noted. For it says in the first verse "once I completed," which is contrasted in the second verse by "I am compelled."

"To enter" <note>original: "inire"</note> means "to begin." It should also be noted that **Boethius** reasonably laments his condition because of the transformation of his philosophical study, which has now been turned into the poetic study he is currently forced to use. For **Boethius** proposed to write down his grief in meter

and not to be consoled by philosophy. For philosophical study is the study of truth, because in the second book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Referring to Aristotle's work</note> it is rightly held that philosophy is called the science

<column-break/>

of truth. Poetic study, however, is the study of falsehood; for according to the proverb in the beginning of the *Metaphysics*, "poets tell many lies." Likewise, through philosophical study, happiness is acquired according to the *Ethics*. Through the poetic study of falsehood, however, comes [only] the certainty mentioned in the second book of the *Metaphysics*. **Behold, the tattered...** Here **Boethius** confirms his statement. He said that he was compelled to begin sad measures, and now he proves it. Second, he answers the reasoning there at the phrase: **At least no terror.** First, he says: I have rightly said that I am compelled to begin sad measures; behold the proof of this to the senses. For the **Camenae**—that is, the poetic Muses—"tattered," <note>original: "lacere"</note> meaning they tear at the minds of men, dictate to me the words to be written, namely metric songs and elegies. The verses of misery which the Muses dictate to me "moisten"—that is, they make wet—my "face"—that is, my countenance—with "true weeping." 

It should be noted that according to the poets, the Muses were imagined to be on Mount Helicon near the Caballine spring <note>The Hippocrene, or "Horse's Spring," created by Pegasus</note> of which **Persius** speaks at the beginning of his book, saying: "From the Caballine spring," etc. These Muses are imagined by poets to have provided the knowledge for composing metric songs. These poetic Muses were called **Camenae**, as if "singing pleasantly" <note>a medieval folk etymology: "canentes amene"</note>, because they greatly delight men by means of their meter. 

Note that these poetic Muses are called "tattered" <note>or "lacerating"</note> in an active sense because they tear at—that is, distract—the minds of men, subjecting them to various passions: now the passion of love, now of grief, as is clear through **Ovid**'s writings on love and through other poets. Or they are called "tattered" in a passive sense because of their poems, which are called "tattered" because they are not established with the firmness of reason. Here it should be noted that some songs are called "whole" <note>original: "integra"</note> and some "tattered" <note>original: "lacera"</note>. "Whole" songs are philosophical ones, mixed with no falsehood but established by the firmness of reason, and they strengthen the soul. "Tattered" songs are poetic ones that do not instruct or console a man but rather "tear"—that is, distract—the minds of men, now bringing pleasures back to a man’s memory, now grief, now other passions. 

Likewise, it should be noted that elegiac verses were primarily invented for the purpose of describing misery. And because the Muses dictated these verses to **Boethius**, through which he recalled his misery more than he was consoled by them, the elegies were the cause of "true weeping" for **Boethius**. 

Likewise, it should be noted that there are two kinds of weeping: flattering and true. Flattering weeping is that which is faked, such as the weeping of a mistress <note>original: "amasie"</note>. For if a lover says to his mistress, "You do not love me," she begins to weep so that she might hold him more firmly through her tears. But when she cannot extort any more coins from him, she says: "Go, boy, I never truly knew you." The other kind is true weeping, which proceeds from true sorrow of the heart and true piety; **Boethius** was moved to such weeping by the Muses dictating songs to him. 

Note that this word "elegy" <note>original: "elegi"</note> can be interpreted in two ways. In one way, it is taken as a nominative [plural], and then the sense is: "The elegies—that is, the verses of misery—moisten my face with tears." In another way, it is taken as a genitive [singular], and then the sense is: "The Muses moisten the face of the 'elegy'—that is, of the miserable man—with true weeping." For according to **Hugutio** <note>a 12th-century grammarian</note>, *elegus, -a, -um* means "miserable."

**At least no terror.** Here **Boethius** answers a silent question. Someone might ask: how do the Muses dictate songs for you to write when you have been banished into exile, since you entered there without any co-

# Book One.

...sent. To this, Boethius responds: although all my friends abandoned me in exile because of fear of the Emperor <note>original: "timorem imperialem"; referring to Theodoric the Great, who imprisoned Boethius</note>, nevertheless no imperial terror could conquer these Muses <note>the personifications of the arts and poetry</note> so as to prevent them from following our journey even into exile, dictating songs to us. It should be noted that although external goods can be taken from a person by force—such as by theft, robbery, or fire—knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note> cannot be taken away. For knowledge is not removed by violence, nor is it consumed by old age, nor diminished by sadness. Whence <margin><unclear>the part that says... will delight</unclear></margin> <margin><unclear>that in time... they console... not me...</unclear></margin>

**Seneca**, in his second letter to **Lucilius**, recounts that when **Stilbo** <note>original: "Stilbo"; likely referring to the philosopher Stilpo of Megara</note> came out of the fire alone after his homeland was captured and his children, wife, and other goods were lost, he was asked by **Demetrius** if he had lost everything. He replied, "I have lost nothing; all my goods are with me: justice, virtue, and prudence." And **Boethius** suggests this by saying that the Muses did not leave him. Whence <margin><unclear>what... of youth... through... in youth... glory...</unclear></margin> Also, **Alanus** in *The Complaint of Nature* <note>original: "alanus de planctu nature"; Alan of Lille, a 12th-century scholar</note> says of knowledge: "Above every possession flows a noble possession which, when scattered, is gathered; when given out, it returns; when made public, it receives an increase. Through it, a noble treasure is born in secret inner chambers, and the effect of eternal delight is acquired. This is the sun through which the mind casts out darkness from the eyes of the heart, the delicious paradise of the soul. This makes the mortal immortal and, by the authority of a divine transformation, turns a passing human into a god."

Note concerning this word "at least" <note>original: "saltim"</note>: at least three words can be pronounced with "tim" that ought to be pronounced with "tem." For we say *saltim* for *saltem* <note>at least</note>, *timpus* for *tempus* <note>time</note>, and *extrimplo* for *extemplo* <note>immediately</note>, which is against **Hugutio** <note>Hugutio of Pisa, a famous medieval grammarian</note> who says: "Three 'Tims' I detest: *extimplo*, *timpora*, *saltim*."

->**The glory <gloss>that is</gloss> of my once happy <gloss>prosperous</gloss> and green <gloss>that is, delightful</gloss> youth:**<-
->**Now console the fates of a mournful <gloss>that is, sad</gloss> old man. <gloss>that is, of old age</gloss>**<-

"The glory of a happy [youth]." Here **Boethius** laments his state regarding his physical decline. And first he proposes it in general, and second in particular. The second part begins "For she comes" <note>original: "venit enim"</note>. He says first: "Once the glory of happy (that is, prosperous) youth and the glory of green (that is, delightful) youth used to console me, but now the fates (that is, the events) of a mournful old man (that is, sad old age) console (that is, comfort) my [lot]." It is as if he were saying: "Previously I was consoled by sweet youth, but now I am consoled by sad old age." According to this sentiment, the text is explained thus: "The glory of happy youth (that is, prosperous youth) and green (that is, delightful) youth formerly—supply 'consoled me'—now the fates (that is, the events) of a mournful old man (that is, sad old age) console my [lot]."

It should be noted that commonly that text is explained otherwise by referring it to the poetic **Muses** <note>original: "Camene"</note> thus: The Muses, who once in the time of youth were the glory of a happy and green youth—which is said because young men used to be trained in the poetic art, in which those who progressed were glorified in the use of meters and rhythms—now however the Muses console my fates in the state of a mournful old man. Note here that "happy youth" is that which is adorned with external goods, of which goods **Aristotle** speaks near the beginning of the book *On Good Fortune*, saying: "Without external things, of which Fortune is the mistress, it does not happen that one is happy." But "green" (that is, delightful) youth is that which is decorated with the goods of nature, namely strength, beauty, and agility. Whence **Aristotle** in the *Ethics*: "He is not entirely happy who is ugly in appearance, or solitary, or lacking offspring." Note that **Boethius** represents in himself a state of misery when he says the "fates of a mournful old man" console him, since they least of all console a man, but rather disturb him. Also, when he says the poetic Muses console him, he likewise represents a state of misery, because the poetic Muses do not result in consolation for anyone, but rather in the nourishment of pain.

Item: regarding the meanings of "fate" <note>original: "fati"</note>, **Hugutio** provides two little verses, saying: "Constellation, death..."

that is, upon my head. Another sign of old age is that my skin, "loose" <note>original: "laxa," meaning slackened or hanging</note>, trembles on a "worn-out body" <note>original: "effecto," meaning the flesh is consumed and emptied</note>. Note that many evils and discomforts surround an old man: for his skin is shriveled, his heart is shaken, his lungs are weakened, his loins grow stiff, his back is bent, and his limbs tremble. Whence the poet said: "We wish for old age, but when it arrives, it is a bad arrival; it is hunchbacked, deaf, blind, and cranky." Because of this, Boethius says that old age has come to him with its own evils. Note concerning that part, "and grief [has ordered] its age": there are three causes of old age, namely: time <note>original: "etas"</note>, illness, and adversity. Old age brought on by time is natural; however, that brought on by illness or adversity is accidental <note>meaning situational or caused by outside factors</note>, which is the kind of old age Boethius had, having grown old due to a multitude of grief and sadness. It should be noted that Boethius's graying was "untimely." **Huguitio** <note>Huguitio of Pisa, a famous 12th-century grammarian and lexicographer</note> says "untimely" <note>original: "intempestivum"</note> is that which is unsuitable, inconvenient, useless, or out of season; whence that is called untimely which does not have a suitable time or is not fitting for the time. And because Boethius was young in age and yet had grown old from adversity, his graying was untimely. Note that in youths, the skin is thick because of the abundance of blood, from which flesh is generated; but because blood decreases in the elderly, their flesh also decreases, and thus their skin becomes loose. Regarding this word <term>effeto<note>worn-out, exhausted, or literally "past bearing"</note></term>, it is derived from pregnant women who, when they have given birth, are called *effecte*—that is, emptied of the fetus. Whence Huguitio says that a fetus is the offspring of a woman while still in the womb, and the word comes from *foveo* (to cherish/warm) because it is warmed there. From this comes *fetus, -a, -um*, meaning "full." From that comes *effetus*, meaning weak, as if without the strength of power or emptied of strength. From this also comes *fetosus*, meaning full of offspring; as in the Psalm: "Their sheep are fruitful" <note>original: "Oues eorum fetose"; a reference to Psalm 144:13</note>. The elderly can be called *effeti* as if "set outside of fruitfulness" because old age is not fit for producing offspring. "Happy is the death of men." Here Boethius laments his state regarding the duration of his miserable life. First, he establishes which death of men is happy and which is not, saying: That death is happy which does not "intrude"—that is, does not thrust itself into the "sweet years"—meaning prosperous times when it delights a person to live. Similarly, that death is happy which comes, when often called, to the "sorrowful"—meaning in years of sadness, for in years of adversity, the wretched are accustomed to call upon death. Then he shows which death is cruel, saying: "Alas, with a deaf ear..."—that is, a closed ear.

# Book One.

<margin>
...[cruel] death. It had almost submerged, that is, it had overwhelmed my head. He says that in a time of prosperity death always hastened to overwhelm me; but now because cloudy fortune—that is, adversity—has changed its deceitful face, impious—that is, my wretched life—protracts, that is, prolongs its delays...
</margin>

Cruel death <note>original: "saeva mors"</note>, that is, harsh death, turns away from <note>original: "avertit"</note>, that is, spurns, wretched men and refuses <note>original: "negat"</note>, that is, does not want to close their weeping eyes. It is as if he says: it is a cruel death that does not allow the wretched to die. And he says "weeping eyes," implying by this that in death the eyes of men are closed. And then Boethius laments the prolongations of his life, saying: While unfaithful fortune <note>original: "fortuna malefida"</note>, that is, treacherous fortune, favored me—that is, smiled upon me—with light <note>original: "levibus"</note>, that is, transitory goods, a sad hour [had nearly submerged my head].

<gloss>To death... do they grieve?</gloss>
### Alas, alas, with how deaf an ear she turns away from the wretched
### And cruel, she refuses to close weeping eyes
### While unfaithful fortune favored men with light things
### A sad hour had nearly submerged my head
### Now because she has changed her deceitful face to a cloudy one
### An impious life protracts unwelcome delays

...unwelcome [delays] of living, that is, hateful to me; because on account of misery Boethius himself was weary of living. Note that although according to common people and according to appearance this sentiment about a happy and cruel death seems true, yet according to the truth of the matter it is false. For death even in a time of prosperity can be good; for according to Seneca it is best to die when it is a delight to live <note>A Stoic perspective: dying at the peak of happiness prevents future suffering</note>. And in a time of adversity it can be bad, because adversity often leads to despair. Boethius, however, by representing the state of a wretched man, puts forth this sentiment as if it were true. 

It should be noted that death is compared either to the present life or the future life. In the first way, that death is called "happy" which flees in a time of prosperity and hastens in a time of adversity. But if death is compared to the future life, then it can be called good and bad in a time of prosperity and also adversity. For if death leads to glory <note>Heaven/Eternal life</note> it is called good; if to punishment, it is called bad. 

It should be noted according to Remigius <note>Remigius of Auxerre, a 9th-century scholar</note> in his commentary on Donatus <note>A standard Latin grammar textbook</note> that "Alas" <note>original: "heu"</note> is sometimes one syllable and sometimes two, as the necessity of the meter requires. Hence in this instance it is two syllables <note>pronounced "he-u"</note> when saying: "Alas, with how deaf an ear she turns away from the wretched." 

It should be noted that this verb "to turn away" <note>original: "avertor"</note> is sometimes passive, constructed with the ablative via a preposition, as when saying "I am turned away from you," which is the same as "I am removed." Sometimes it is a deponent verb <note>a verb with a passive form but active meaning</note> constructed with the accusative, as when saying "I turn away from you," and then it is the same as "I spurn you," and so it is taken in this context where death turns away—that is, spurns—the wretched. Hence the verse: "In the passive voice, *avertor* notes being removed; if it be deponent, *avertor* signifies to spurn." 

It should be noted Boethius calls fortune "unfaithful" <note>original: "malefida"</note> because she is deceptive. Whence Seneca says: "Adverse fortune has crushed no one except him whom favorable fortune deceived." And elsewhere Seneca says: "Fortune keeps faith with no one. She is not content to harm any man just once. Whomever she favors too much, she makes a fool." 

Note that the goods of fortune are called "light" <note>original: "levia"</note> because they are transitory. For they do not endure around a person, according to Seneca: "That is not yours which fortune made to be yours." For the good that she could give, she could also take away. 

It should be noted that Boethius calls fortune "cloudy" <note>original: "nubila"</note>, that is, dark or blind. For in ancient times fortune was depicted as blind, because she approaches and departs unexpectedly, or because she makes a man blind by exalting him in prosperity and depressing him in adversity. It should be noted that Boethius says fortune once changed her deceitful face toward him. For fortune was once depicted with a double face: the front part white, and the back part black. Prosperity was designated by the white; adversity by the black. Therefore fortune changed her deceitful face of prosperity toward Boethius; afterwards she showed him the face of adversity.

->Prose One of the First Book.<-

**Lo, while I in silence.** Here begins the first prose of this first book, in which Boethius introduces Philosophy <note>original: "phia"</note> consoling him over his misery. Where note that the desiring Boethius and Philosophy herself consoling him are nothing other than the mind willing to escape the oppression of sensuality and reason consoling him by the vigor of wisdom. It is divided thus: First, Boethius shows how Philosophy appeared to him; second, what she did regarding him, starting at: "Who, when she saw the poetic Muses." First, he describes the appearance of Philosophy regarding the time and place, and describes her disposition regarding her face, her sight, her color, her vigor, and her age. Second, he describes Philosophy regarding her external clothing. Third, regarding the ornaments and signs she carried in her hands, starting at: "Her garments were." Third, at: "And in her right hand indeed." He says first: "While I, Boethius, was revolving—that is, thinking—silently with myself these things which I said above in the metre, and was marking out—that is, describing—with the office of the pen a tearful complaint—that is, one provoking tears—a woman seemed to have stood above the crown—that is, above the head—in the manner of a very venerable face, with burning and piercing eyes—that is, clear beyond the common power of men—that is, beyond other men—who appeared in a vivid—that is, delightful—color. And she appeared to me as if of inexhaustible—that is, unconsumed—vigor, as if she herself were so full of life—that is, duration—that in no way would she be believed to be of our age. Her stature was of ambiguous—that is, doubtful—discernment—that is, recognition—because now—that is, sometimes—she restrained—that is, extended—herself to the common measure of men—that is, our length—and sometimes she seemed to strike—that is, touch—the high summit of the topmost crown—that is, the height of the head; and when she had lifted her head higher, she even penetrated the heaven itself by her length."

It should be noted that Boethius describes Philosophy appearing to him in the form of a woman because "Philosophy" among the Greeks and "Wisdom" <note>original: "sapientia"</note> among the Latins are of the feminine gender. Or, it is because just as a woman nourishes infants with milk, so philosophy nourishes the less perfect with easy doctrines. Or, it is because Boethius was sick, and a woman is more compassionate and more able to console the sick than a man. For according to Solomon: "Where there is no woman, there the sick man groans." <note>A medieval proverb often linked to the Book of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 36:25</note> Note that "to stand" means to hold oneself in an upright manner; and because philosophy raises a man to delight...

<header>Book One.</header>

...making the intellectual [faculties] cause the sensual ones to fall away. For this reason, she is described as having "stood." She is said to have stood "above the crown of the head" because philosophy exists in the intellectual soul, which has no physical organ in the crown of the head, for the intellectual soul is not the action of any bodily organ <note>The commentator is referencing the Aristotelian idea that while the senses use organs like the eyes or ears, the "intellect" is an immaterial power.</note>. Or, she is said to stand "above the crown" because she has descended from the heavenly hinge, as Boethius <note>original: "Boe."</note> says in the third prose of this first book.

It should be noted that Philosophy is said to be of a "venerable countenance" because she makes those who possess her worthy of respect. For according to Cicero <note>original: "Tulliu"</note>, only wisdom is that which deserves honors. Likewise, according to Cicero, reverence is a fitting and mature gravity which is obtained through philosophy; therefore, she is said to be of a venerable countenance. It should be noted that whatever is "burning" is "penetrating," and because through reason and intellect—which are the "eyes" of philosophy—we penetrate the innermost things and their quiddities <term>quiddities — from the Latin 'quidditas', meaning the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, philosophy is said to have appeared with "burning eyes." And because through philosophy we contemplate things that common and ordinary people do not contemplate, she is said to have had "piercing eyes" beyond the common...

# A woman of very venerable countenance, with burning eyes, piercing beyond the common power of men; with a vivid color and of inexhaustible vigor, although she was so full of years that she was by no means believed to be of our age. Her stature was of an ambiguous measure. For now she restricted herself to the common measure of men, but now she seemed to strike the sky with the summit of her crown. When she raised her head higher, she even penetrated the very heavens, frustrating the gaze of the men looking upon her.

...strength of men. It should be noted that "vivid color" is a natural, beautiful, and delightful color. Since philosophy is most beautiful in herself—being a marvelous and divine thing—and delightful because she brings wonderful pleasures, she is described as appearing in a "vivid color." Likewise, philosophy appeared with "inexhaustible vigor" because philosophy, being perpetual, cannot be exhausted. Or, she is of "inexhaustible vigor" because however much a person may know of philosophy, many more things still remain to be known. This is evident from the diversity of opinions in philosophy, where one destroys another. Also, because philosophy is eternal and had preceded Boethius himself, he says she was not "of his age."

It should be noted that there are three essential parts of philosophy according to the sixth book of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*: natural, mathematical, and divine. In terms of "natural philosophy," Philosophy is said to "restrict herself to the common measure of men" insofar as she treats natural things which are commonly known through the path of the senses, among which the nature of man is the highest point reached. However, Philosophy is said to "strike the sky" regarding "mathematics"—that is, regarding astronomy—insofar as she treats the movements and shapes of the stars. She is said to "penetrate the sky" regarding "metaphysics," insofar as she directs one toward the knowledge of God and separate substances <note>original: "substantiarum separatarum" — in medieval philosophy, these are beings existing without matter, such as angels or pure intellects</note>. And philosophy is said to "frustrate the gaze of men looking upon her" because we cannot have perfect knowledge of separate substances in this life. For as the eye of the night-owl <note>original: "nycticorax"</note> is to the light of the sun, so is our intellect to the things most manifest in nature, according to the second book of the *Metaphysics*.

"Her garments were of very fine threads..." Here Boethius describes Philosophy regarding her outward appearance: first, regarding the material of the garments; second, regarding the patterns on the garments.

¶ It should be noted that by Philosophy's garments are understood her essential parts and the liberal arts <term>liberal arts — the traditional core curriculum of medieval education, including grammar, logic, and rhetoric</term>. For just as a body is adorned with clothes, so is philosophy decorated with its parts. By the "thinnest threads" are understood philosophical precepts or philosophical propositions. For just as one thread in a garment is arranged around another, so is one proposition [set] next to another. These propositions are called "thinnest" because through them a person investigates subtle things. These kinds of precepts are also said to be of "subtle craftsmanship" by reason of the ornament of words and meanings found in them; and they are of "indestructible material" because, although they are poorly expressed by some, they nevertheless possess indestructible truth in themselves.

¶ It should be noted that by Philosophy's "hands," with which she had woven her garments, are understood the philosophers who wrote down the philosophical precepts. They are reasonably called "Philosophy's hands" because, unless they had been instructed in philosophical precepts, they would have been quite unable to express them.

# First Book

### Commentary on the Nature of Philosophy

[The author] has commented. Or, for this reason the garments of Philosophy were smoky: because Philosophy was handed down obscurely by the ancients—by Empedocles poetically, by Plato enigmatically, and by Aristotle under an obscurity of words. Note that there are two main parts of Philosophy: namely, the **practical** and the **theoretical**. Therefore, on Philosophy's garment, two letters were interwoven: <term>Π</term> <note>original: Pi, for Praxis</note> and <term>Θ</term> <note>original: Theta, for Theoria</note>. The <term>Π</term> was in the lower part of the garment and the <term>Θ</term> in the upper. By this, it is implied that practical philosophy is lower, while speculative philosophy is higher in the order of dignity.

By the middle steps which were between both letters, the "sciences of eloquence" are understood, which are: **grammar**, **logic**, and **rhetoric**. It should be noted that there is said to have been an ascent by steps from the practical to the speculative. By this, he implies that a person must first be sufficiently instructed in practical matters so that afterwards they may be able to ascend to contemplative things.
<margin>namely, to the contemplative things</margin>

**"And in her right hand indeed..."** Here Boethius describes Philosophy regarding the insignia and ornaments which she carried in her hands, saying that Philosophy's right hand carried **booklets**, while her left carried—that is, bore—a **scepter**, which is a royal rod. It should be noted that all the care and intention of a wise man is occupied either with the contemplations of wisdom, which are symbolized by the booklets, or with the government of the republic, which is symbolized by the scepter. And because the contemplation of wisdom is more powerful than the government of a republic, Philosophy is said to have the booklets in her right hand and the scepter in her left.

**"When she [saw] the poetic Muses..."** After Boethius shows how Philosophy appeared to him, he here shows what she did regarding him. First, he shows how she drove away the poetic Muses; second, he shows how he himself was stunned by this; third, how Philosophy approached his bedside and lamented his condition. The second part begins at "But I"; the third at "Then she."

He says first: "Which" (supply: Philosophy), "when" (for "after") "she saw the poetic Muses standing by our couch" (that is, the bed), because Boethius lay down like a sick man in bed. And when she saw the Muses dictating songs to my weeping, Philosophy herself was "moved for a moment" (that is, a little bit) and "inflamed" (that is, incensed) with "grim eyes" (that is, cruel or terrible eyes), and she said: "Who permitted these theatrical harlots" (that is, shadowy figures) "to approach this sick man, who would not only" (that is, not just) "fail to soothe" (that is, heal) "his pains with any remedies" (that is, medicines), "but" (for "but rather") "would nourish" (supply: his pains) "with sweet poisons." For these Muses are they who, with the "fruitless thorns of the passions" (that is, the emotions), "kill" (that is, destroy)...

Then that troupe, i.e., the crowd of Muses, having been rebuked, i.e., cleansed, being more sorrowful, i.e., sadder, cast down their face, i.e., inclined it toward the ground, that is, to the earth, and confessing their shame with a blush, gloomily left the threshold, i.e., the house in which Boethius lay. ---

For this reason, the poetic Muses were said to stand by Boethius's bed: because Boethius studied to write down his grief in verse. Also, Philosophy is said to be "somewhat moved" (to anger), by which it is implied that immoderate anger should not fall upon a wise man, for virtue consists in the moderation of passions. Whence, although to be angry is natural to man, yet to be angry when it is proper, and as it is proper, and as much as is proper, belongs to a virtuous and wise man. Whence Seneca: "What is more cruel than anger?" Similarly, in the book *On the Cardinal Virtues*: "Be slow to anger." Furthermore, an interrogation is sometimes made due to someone's ignorance, sometimes so that something may be proven from the response made, and sometimes for the sake of offering a rebuke—and in this last way, Philosophy asks, saying: "Who [has allowed] these stage-performing harlots <note>original: "scenicas meretriculas"</note> [to approach]?" 

Note that the poetic Muses are called "little harlots"; for just as a harlot entices a man by delighting him, conferring no benefit upon him, and mingles with anyone not out of love but for the hope of profit, so poets do not write for the love of knowledge but so that they may obtain some praise or reward. And they delight by means of the meter, conferring little utility but inducing various passions. Philosophy calls the Muses "stage-performing harlots" because poetic songs used to be recited on a "scena" <note>original: "scena"; stage</note>. Note here that a *scena* was called a shaded place in a theater where the persons reciting tragic or comic poems were hidden. Whence *scena* is interpreted as "shading" or "shadow." Or for this reason the poetic Muses are called "stage-like" <note>original: "scenice"</note>, i.e., shadowy, because they are the shadow of knowledge, not true knowledge, since they overshadow the minds of men. Also, a metrical description of grief does not heal the grief but rather increases it, because the consideration of misery is provocative of sadness. Everyone considers with diligence what they wish to write. Also, a metrical description is said to be "sweet poison" because it pleases and it harms: it pleases by reason of the meter, but harms because of the memory of grief. Also, affection is a vehement passion of the soul, twisting the soul and hindering the true judgment of reason. And they are...

# Book One

There are four passions of the soul: joy, grief, hope, and fear. These are called "unfruitful thorns" <note>The commentator uses the metaphor of thorns to show how emotions can "choke" the growth of rational thought, much like weeds in a field.</note> because they suffocate the harvest of reason, which consists of knowledge and virtue. Likewise, although one should grieve over any error, one should grieve more over the error of a wise man than that of a fool. This is because the error of a wise man corrupts others by his example; however, the error of a fool does not, because no one takes an example from a fool. For this reason, Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian.</note> said: "All bad examples have arisen from good things." Therefore, Philosophy says that one must grieve more for the error of Boethius than for that of any other profane person.

Furthermore, according to Huguitio <note>Huguitio of Pisa, a 12th-century grammarian often cited in medieval commentaries for etymologies.</note>, "fanum" is the same as "temple." Likewise, "profane" <note>original: "prophanus"</note> means "sacrilegious," as if to say "far from the temple" <note>original: "procul a fano"</note>. Anything that is not sacred is also called profane; hence all laypeople and the illiterate are called "profane" because they are far from the "temple of wisdom." Also, according to Huguitio, "work" <note>original: "opera"</note> is diligence in doing things, but the "work of philosophy" is the intention or labor toward learning something philosophical.

Furthermore, Elea <note>original: "eleys"</note> is a city in Greece where Aristotle studied; hence his studies are called "Eleatic." The Academy, however, was a city or villa where Plato studied, where his studies are called "Academic." Boethius was nurtured in both types of study. Philosophy also calls the Muses "Sirens." For just as the Sirens attract ships by the sweetness of their song, putting them in danger, so the Muses entice men (or the minds of men) by the delight of their meter, and they submerge and darken reason with some passion. Likewise, the fact that Philosophy alone expelled the assembly of the Muses signifies that one wise person, by his own virtue and wisdom, extinguishes the infinite errors of fools.

**"But I, whose vision..."** Here Boethius shows how he was stunned by the act of Philosophy, saying: **"But I,"** Boethius, **"whose vision"**—that is, my sight—**"plunged in tears, had grown dim"**—that is, had been darkened—**"so that I could not discern"**—that is, investigate—**"who this woman of such imperious authority"**—that is, power—**"might be, I was stunned"**—that is, I marveled—**"and with my gaze fixed"**—that is, inclined—**"toward the earth, I began in silence to wait for what she would do next"**—that is, consequently—**"concerning me."** It should be noted that because Boethius grieved for the loss of temporal things, his "vision"—that is, his reason and intellect—had grown dim, because he could not recognize Philosophy. Note also that although Boethius was stunned by the act of Philosophy, he nevertheless waited in silence to see what she would do next, thereby hinting that he was the kind of person who could receive consolation. For those who refuse to hear others, and do not submit once reason is heard, create for themselves a primary obstacle to consolation. **"Then she, drawing nearer..."** Here Boethius shows how Philosophy, approaching him, lamented his condition, saying: **"Then she,"** Philosophy, **"drawing nearer, sat on the furthest edge of my bed"**—that is, of my heart—**"and beholding my countenance, heavy"**—that is, weighed down—**"with grief and cast down"**—that is, inclined toward the ground—**"in sorrow,"** she complained in these following verses about the perturbation of our mind. Note that Philosophy is said to have sat on the "furthest part of the bed"—that is, of Boethius's heart. For since he was in sadness and grief on account of the loss of temporal things, he possessed little or no wisdom; and because his entire care was focused on lost earthly things, he is said to have had a "countenance cast down to the ground in sorrow."

It is also called a **tetrameter** <note>original: "tetrametrum," from the Greek "tetra" meaning four.</note> because of the number of its feet, as it contains four feet. <column-break/>

universally the disturbance of the minds of men; second, she specifically turns her lament toward Boethius himself, where it says: **"This mind, once..."** <note>original: "hic quondam."</note>
First, she says: **Alas, how**—that is, how much—**the mind** of man **is dull**—that is, obscured—**plunged into a headlong depth**—that is, into the care for temporal things which casts a man down. Such a mind, **having abandoned its own light**—that is, its capacity for contemplation—**tends**—that is, struggles—**to go into outer darkness**—that is, into external states of ignorance.
This happens to a man as often as the mind is **driven**—that is, tossed about—**by earthly winds**—that is, by worldly prosperities or chance events. Thus, **care**—that is, anxiety over temporal things—**harmful**—that is, damaging—**grows beyond measure**—that is, beyond all moderation.

Note that within us there is a twofold power: the **rational virtue** and the **sensual virtue**. <note>The commentator refers to the medieval psychological division between the "higher" rational mind and the "lower" animal senses.</note> The senses, however, always oppose reason, because the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. When sensuality overcomes reason, then man is in a bad state of governance and becomes beast-like. Hence **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> says in his commentary on the third book of *On the Soul*: "It is shameful for us to cast away the rule of the superior virtue and put on the rule of the inferior virtue, which we have in common with the beasts."
Therefore, it is written in the third book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note> in the old translation: we must strive and labor greatly so that our "desiring" virtue is subject to reason. For just as children live perversely if they are not forced to live rightly by their teachers, so the sensual appetite leads us to insolence unless it is constrained by the rule of reason. Most men, however, follow sensuality rather than reason, toiling for external goods and sensual delights, by which they are hindered from the contemplation and knowledge of the highest good. Therefore Philosophy, lamenting this, says in the meter: **Alas, how it is plunged into a headlong depth.**

Likewise, when the soul thrusts itself into the cares of temporal things, it is plunged deeply and becomes dull because it is deprived of the knowledge of things and of its Creator; being so deprived, it falls into **outer darkness**—that is, into external states of ignorance.
Regarding this, note that there are two kinds of ignorance. One is **natural**, which is found in the very young and the very old; this is called **internal ignorance** because it happens from a natural defect. The other is the ignorance caused by a man's **negligence** when he is preoccupied with external things; such is called **external ignorance** because it is outside of nature, according to which it is said that "all men by nature desire to know."
The first kind of ignorance, being natural, is not a vice; for no one blames those who are naturally unsightly, nor does anyone praise those who are naturally good. The second kind is a vice, since it comes from a man's negligence. Boethius speaks of this in the fifth prose of this second book: "For other living creatures, to be ignorant of themselves is nature; but for men, it comes as a vice."
Likewise, he mentions **harmful care**. Hence **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> says in his proverbs: "He has given himself a great share of disturbance who has infected himself with external things."
Likewise, reason and intellect are called the **light of man**, because they illuminate a man toward...

# Book One.

...knowledge of the creature and the creator. It is called, moreover, the proper light of man, because the human race alone lives by art and reason, as stated in the introduction to the **Metaphysics** <note>The commentator refers to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, which begins with the famous claim that "all men by nature desire to know."</note>. In this passage, "Once free with the sky open," Philosophy specifically turns herself to lamenting Boethius. First, she shows with how much contemplation Boethius once flourished. Second, she shows how, deprived of such contemplation, he now thinks only of earthly things (beginning at the line: "Now he lies exhausted"). 

Philosophy commends Boethius for three things: first, for his knowledge of **astronomy**; second, for **natural philosophy** (beginning at: **"Moreover, the causes"**); and third, for **metaphysics** (beginning at: **"Who willed the stable"**). 

First, she says that Boethius, once "free"—meaning released from the care of temporal things—was accustomed to travel through the "open sky" by means of his reason into the "ethereal paths," which refers to the movements of the celestial bodies. He himself "discerned," or rather gazed upon, the "lights," meaning the rays of the "rosy sun." He saw—meaning he observed with great desire—the stars...

...the stars, meaning the constellations of the "cold moon." And Boethius himself, as a "victor" over ignorance, held every star "grasped by numbers," meaning by certain calculations. He understood whatever "wandering star" <note>original: "stella erratica." In the ancient world, "erratic stars" were the planets, distinguished from the "fixed stars" because they appeared to move independently across the sky.</note> practices "wandering returns," now moving forward and now backward. A star is called "bent" because it is moved through various "circles" or orbits. 

It is because his soul was liberated from external cares that he was permitted to "philosophize." Indeed, certain arts are called **liberal arts** <note>The *artes liberales* included the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy).</note> because the "sons of free men"—that is, the nobility—who were liberated from temporal cares, used to devote their time to such arts. This is why Philosophy says that Boethius was "once free." 

Note that she says "with the sky open." Although a human being cannot physically reach the planets of heaven, he encompasses them through contemplation. <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term> <note>original: "hermogistus." A legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many philosophical and scientific works were attributed.</note> touches on this beautifully, saying: **"Man is a great miracle"** <note>original: "Magnum miraculum est homo." A famous quote from the *Asclepius*, a Hermetic text.</note>, a creature to be honored. Here, the intellectual soul passes into the nature of God as if it were God himself. By the nature of his soul, man is the master of the fish; he knows the race of demons; he cultivates the earth and mixes with the elements. With the sharpness of his mind, he descends into the depths of the sea. He measures the sky, which he sees as most high, with the sagacity of his soul. No gloom of the air confuses his mental intention, nor does the density of the earth hinder his work, nor the depth of the water obscure his sight.

Note that the sun appears "rosy" at its rising because of the vapors placed between our sight and the sun; for something white appears red when seen through smoke. Although vapors are also present at midday, the sun does not appear rosy then because those vapors are not thick, but are thinned by the sun's heat. 

Note that Philosophy calls the moon "cold." This is not to be understood "formally"—since all qualities like hot, cold, moist, and dry have no place in celestial bodies, as they do not receive foreign impressions—but the moon is called "cold" "virtually" or "effectively." This is because it produces cold and moisture in things here below. For this reason, nights when the moon is present are colder and more humid than during the great days. 

Note that the planets are said to have "wandering returns" because they move with a double motion: that of the "first movable" <note>The *primum mobile*, the outermost sphere in the geocentric model that carries all other spheres from east to west every 24 hours.</note> from east to west, and their own proper motion from west to east. Or, they are called wandering because they sometimes appear to us as "stationary," sometimes "retrograde," sometimes near, and sometimes somewhat distant. 

Note that a wandering star is called "bent," meaning moved through various orbits of circles, namely the **deferent** and the **epicycle** <note>The deferent and epicycle were geometric models used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain the complex, "looping" motions of planets.</note>. By reason of these circles, they are sometimes said to be progressing, sometimes retrograde, and sometimes stationary, as was said; this can be seen in the theory of the planets or astronomy. 

**Moreover, the causes.** Here she commends him regarding natural philosophy...
