at a determined time, such as twice in a natural day. Winds, however, are generated at undetermined times. **"Who turns the stable..." Here** Philosophy commends Boethius for his **metaphysics** <note>The study of the fundamental nature of reality and first causes.</note> and again for his **natural philosophy**, saying that Boethius was also accustomed to search out which spirit—that is, **intelligence** <note>In medieval cosmology, "Intelligences" were celestial beings or spiritual forces thought to move the heavenly spheres.</note>—turns the stable orb of the firmament with its daily motion. Or also why the star of the sun (or another star having a rising and setting) is about to fall into the Hesperian waves—that is, into the waters of the western sea—and rise again—that is, be born again—from a glowing sunrise—that is, from the splendid east. She says that Boethius was accustomed to inquire why the stars that seem to set in the west rise again in the east. Also, he was accustomed to search out who "tempers" the peaceful hours of spring—that is, the springtime—so that it adorns the earth with rosy flowers. Who "gave"—that is, ordained—that fertile autumn, in the full—that is, fruitful—year, should "flow in"—that is, exert its influence—with heavy grapes—that is, with filled clusters. He was also accustomed to "render"—that is, assign—various causes for "lurking nature"—that is, for natural things. Note that everything that is moved is moved by another, according to the seventh book of the **Physics** <note>Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book VII, which argues that whatever is in motion must be moved by something else.</note>. Therefore, the heaven is moved by another. Note, however, according to the Commentator on the twelfth book of the **Metaphysics**, that the heaven is moved by a twofold mover: by one "conjoined and appropriated" mover which is called an **Intelligence**, by which it is moved effectively; and by another "separate" mover which is **God**, by whom it is moved by reason of the final goal. Likewise, she says the celestial orb is "stable"; for although it is moved and changes location according to its parts, it does not change as a whole, and in this regard it is said to be stable—that is, immobile. Likewise, the cause why stars that set then rise again is nothing other than the circular motion of the **Primum Mobile** <note>The "First Moved" sphere, the outermost sphere in the geocentric model that carries all other spheres with it.</note>, which carries all stars with it, both fixed and wandering. Likewise, **Hesperus** is the star that follows the setting sun in the evening; from this star, the western sea is called the **Hesperian Sea**, because the sun and Hesperus appear to submerge themselves there. Not that it is actually so, but the common people think this way; for when the stars set, because of the interposition of the sea between the viewer and the stars, the stars appear to be submerged in the sea. Likewise, the springtime is called "peaceful" because it is suitable for human life. For the time of spring is hot and moist, in which life consists, according to the book **On Death and Life** <note>A reference to Aristotle’s *De Juventute et Senectute*, often titled *De Morte et Vita* in the Middle Ages.</note>. And therefore, at that time it produces flowers. For the matter of flowers is a subtle, watery moisture well-cooked by aerial heat. Therefore, because in spring the aerial heat and subtle watery moisture dominate (which require little digestion), flowers are produced in the spring, when the heat is tempered. Likewise, the vine...

...is carried to the side and makes a sound by driving the air; and because water is easily divisible, it easily gives way and is beaten back by the winds. Or it can be understood otherwise: for the ancients said that winds disturb the sea because winds are generated within the sea itself and do not exit, but create the flow of the sea. However, this opinion is not true, because the sea flows and ebbs...

### Second Prose of the first book.

Here begins the second prose of this first book, in which Philosophy investigates the disease of Boethius by certain signs; secondly, she consoles him so that he does not despair, the second part beginning at: *And when I was not...* **First**, **Philosophy** says: **Boethius**, I could complain much about the disturbance of your mind, but now it is rather the time for medicine than for complaint. Then indeed that woman, intent upon me with all her lights—that is, her eyes—said: "Are you not he who, once in the time of your youth, was nourished by our milk—that is, by easy instructions—and in a mature age was educated—that is, nourished—by our food—that is, by more difficult doctrines? You had emerged—that is, you had arrived—into the strength—that is, into the fortitude—of a manly soul. And yet, for certain, we had bestowed upon you such weapons—that is, instructions—which, unless you had first cast them away through forgetfulness, would have protected you with unconquered firmness." Philosophy says: "Do you recognize me? Why are you silent? Have you become quiet from shame—that is, modesty—or from astonishment?"

## **Boethius. And when [she saw me] not only silent but**

[sorrowful]. **Note** that silence sometimes comes from shame and sometimes from stupor. For when something is revealed to someone that they wished were hidden, they become bashful: their eyes are cast down, their face reddens and turns away, and their tongue is tied in speaking. **Note** that <term>stupor</term> in one sense is an abundant wonder of the mind, as in the phrase: *the Pope, the wonder of the world.* <note>original: "papa stupor mundi"; "stupor" here refers to a state of being struck with awe or amazement.</note> In another sense, it is an "alienation of the mind" <note>A state of being mentally "elsewhere" or losing one's faculties due to shock.</note>, and thus it is understood in this context and leads to silence. For since the movement of the tongue follows the patterns of the imagination, when the imagination is disturbed—as happens in the alienation of the mind—the tongue is hindered in speaking. Therefore Philosophy says: "Are you silent from shame or from stupor?" And because silence coming from stupor is worse than that caused by shame, since it is caused by some internal defect, Philosophy says: "I would rather you were silent from shame." 

**Note** that according to <term>Huguitione</term> <note>Huguccio of Pisa, a 12th-century scholar known for his dictionary of Latin derivations.</note>, shame (<term>pudor</term>) belongs to the body, but modesty (<term>pudicitia</term>) belongs to the mind. Shame is a bashfulness born from some circumstance that takes away memory or hinders the tongue. Stupor, however, is a state that takes away memory and hinders the tongue. And it is worse to be silent from stupor than from shame, because it is better to keep one's memory while not speaking than to speak while lacking memory. 

**Note** that Philosophy says she had Boethius "nourished on her milk." By the "nourishment of milk" is understood the <term>trivium</term>—namely grammar, logic, and rhetoric—in which youths are to be instructed step-by-step with easy lessons, just as a child is nourished with milk, which is a soft and easily digested food. But by that which she says—"you had grown into the strength of a manly spirit"—she refers to the <term>mathematical sciences</term> <note>This refers to the <term>quadrivium</term>: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy, considered more "solid food" for a mature mind.</note>, by which, as if by a more subtle science, a person is made of perfect age. 

**Note** that Philosophy bestowed "arms" upon Boethius—not physical arms, but spiritual ones. These are the intellectual virtues which <term>Aristotle</term> enumerates in the sixth book of the *Ethics*, and they are: intellect, wisdom, science, art, and prudence. And similarly the "cardinal virtues," which are four: prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude. And they are called "cardinal" <note>From the Latin "cardo," meaning hinge; these are the virtues upon which a moral life hinges.</note> because they claim a certain primacy for themselves over the matter they govern. Boethius threw away these arms when he clung to his sensory appetite for temporal things and was separated from the attention to celestial things. And of these arms the <term>Apostle</term> <note>Referring to St. Paul in his Letter to the Romans.</note> says: *Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, so that we may walk honestly as in the day.*

# Book One.

When Philosophy had seen me not only <gloss>that is, not just</gloss> silent but utterly <gloss>that is, totally</gloss> speechless and mute, she herself took notice. She placed her hand lightly upon my chest and said <gloss>that is, spoke</gloss>: "There is no danger regarding this man; he is suffering from <term>lethargy</term> <note>original: "letargum"; here used as a clinical term for spiritual amnesia</note>, <gloss>that is, the disease of forgetting</gloss>, a disease common to minds that have been deceived <gloss>that is, led astray</gloss>. although they have the power of the tongue for speaking. But one is called "speechless" or "mute" who not only does not speak but does not have the power of the tongue for speaking. <margin>It is the mark of a bad physician to despair of a sick person being cured.</margin> 
**Note** that "lethargy" is an infirmity caused by the oppression of the brain along with forgetting; it is joined to a continuous sleep, and thus lethargy is a disease that leads forgetfulness toward sleep. Thence, a "lethargic" person is a man who suffers from such a disease. The word is derived from <term>Lethe</term>, which is interpreted as "forgetfulness," and Lethe is a river of the underworld. Boethius, therefore, was suffering from lethargy <gloss>that is, the disease of forgetting</gloss> because if he had held the precepts of philosophy in his memory, he would never have grieved over the loss of temporal things. 

Likewise, she says lethargy is a disease of "deceived minds," because a mind is deceived when reason is bound due to a failure of the imagination (as in those with frantic madness) or due to a failure of memory (as in those with lethargy). **It should be noted** that man is composed of an <term>immortal soul</term> and a <term>mortal body</term>. But because Boethius was forgetful of the goods of the soul, he is said to have forgotten "himself"—not totally, but "for a little while"—because he still had a concern for earthly goods which pertain to the body. 

Likewise, through philosophy, a man has a perfect clarity of recognition. However, to recognize that which is known through philosophy, one must first recognize Philosophy herself. Therefore, Philosophy says, "he will easily remember himself if he recognizes us first." Likewise, by the "robes of philosophy gathered into a fold" are understood the philosophical precepts collected into one volume, just as in this book with which Philosophy herself consoles Boethius. **Note** that many conditions are required for a physician wishing to cure a sick person. First, that they look at the qualities and conditions [of the patient] and recognize the harmful <term>humors</term> <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—thought to control health and temperament</note>. Second, to [restore] him to speaking...

is called a dactylic hexameter meter <note>original: "metrum dactilicum exametrum"</note>. The second line, however, is Alemanian meter, named after its inventor; it is a tetrameter from the number of feet, dactylic from the dominant foot, and acatalectic because no syllable is added or missing. In this meter, Boethius declares through a certain simile how, once the obstacles were removed, he recovered the strength of his knowledge. The simile is as such: Just as clouds are generated when the North-West wind <note>original: "chorus"</note> blows, and through the placing of clouds

<margin>if there are four to <unclear>...</unclear> it is called <unclear>...</unclear> from <unclear>...</unclear> or <unclear>...</unclear> it is called <unclear>...</unclear></margin>

the sun and other stars are hidden from us: so when adversity is imminent, a person is affected by various passions which darken the intellect. And just as clouds are dissolved when the South wind <note>original: "austro"</note> blows and the sun’s rays return: so when adversity arrives, the passions are calmed by philosophical consolation and the intellect is illuminated. Therefore, the text says: *Then*, when Philosophy wiped my eyes, the *shadows* left me, once the *night*—that is, the darkness—was *shaken off*, and the *former strength* of knowledge *returned* to my *eyes* (that is, his vision), just as the sun *hides* (is concealed) when the *sidera* (the stars) are *gathered* (wrapped up) in a *headlong dance* (by such a wind), and the *pole* (the sky) *stood* (seemed to stand still) with *stormy rains* (cloudy rains), and *night* (darkness) is *poured from above* (from the clouds) upon the earth while the *stars* have *not yet* appeared in the sky. If *Boreas*, sent forth from his *Thracian cave* (from the Thracian region), *should strike* (drive away) this *night* (darkness) and *bring back* the *hidden day*, then *Phoebus* (the sun) *flashes out* (shines) and, *shaken* (strengthened) by his own light, *strikes* (hits) the eyes of men who marvel at the sudden light of the sun after the darkness. **Note** that Philosophy draws a person from the darkness of ignorance to the light of wisdom, according to the book *On the Apple* by Aristotle <note>The *Liber de Pomo* is a medieval work detailing the death of Aristotle, where he uses the scent of an apple to stay conscious while teaching about the soul</note> and also according to the metrist: "Art strengthens men and does not allow them to be evil." And therefore, when Philosophy dried Boethius’s eyes, the shadows of ignorance having been put to flight, the strength of his intelligence returned. **Note** that there are four principal winds that blow from the four parts of the world: namely, from the East, West, North, and South. Each of these has two side-winds, and thus there are twelve winds which are contained in these verses: "The East wind <note>original: subsolanus</note>, the South-East wind <note>vulturnus</note>, and the East-South-East wind <note>eurus</note> blow from the sunrise. And at midday the South wind <note>nothus</note>, the South-West wind <note>africus</note>, and the stormy South wind <note>auster</note> blow. From the West blow the North-West wind <note>circius</note>, the West wind <note>zephirus</note>, and the West-South-West wind <note>favonius</note>. But let the North-East wind <note>aquilo</note>, the North wind <note>boreas</note>, and the North-North-West wind <note>chorus</note> come from the North."

# Book One

<term>Boreas</term> <note>original: "boreas"; the North Wind in Greek mythology, associated with cold, clear air</note> is therefore the wind which, when it blows, clouds are generated and the stars are gathered together so that they are hidden by the clouds. Note that the pole is the star <note>the North Star, Polaris</note> that is always seen in the same place. But here "pole" is used for the <term>firmament</term> <note>the sphere of the heavens</note> as a part representing the whole through <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part of something refers to the whole</note>. Note that the pole—that is, the heaven—is said to "stand still" as if it were covered by <term>nimbose</term> <note>original: "nimbosis"; cloud-filled or stormy</note> rains, not because it actually stops, but because its movement is then not apparent to us. For we do not perceive the movement of the heaven except through the movement of some star; however, when the heaven is covered by dark clouds, no star can be seen. Note that according to <term>Huguccio</term> <note>Huguccio of Pisa, a 12th-century grammarian whose "Derivationes" was a standard reference for word origins</note>, a "nimbus" is a density of clouds arising from intemperance, and it is so named. Boethius here says "nimbose rains," meaning dense rains. The reason is that a thin rain does not block the sight of the stars. Note that Boreas is said to blow from the Thracian cave, because perhaps the region of Thrace is cavernous, and from those caverns, the wind is generated from dry vapors.

<margin>b</margin> **Not otherwise the clouds of sadness.** Here begins the third prose of the first book, in which Boethius shows how he recognized Philosophy. It is divided because first he shows how he recognized Philosophy and how he began to marvel at her presence, and how Philosophy responded to him. Second, Philosophy proves that the persecution of the wise by the common people is nothing new. The second part begins there: "Was it not so among the ancients?" He says first: "Not otherwise," meaning the clouds of my sadness being dissolved—that is, put to flight through the consolation of Philosophy. For just as clouds are dissolved by the blast of the North Wind, so I, Boethius, "drank in"—that is, looked at—the sky, which is to say, looking upward. And "I recovered my mind," meaning the vigor of reason, "to recognize the face of the healer," meaning the physician. "Therefore"—meaning for that reason—"when," that is, after I "brought back," that is, turned my eyes, and "fixed," that is, steadied my "gaze" upon her, I "looked back at my nurse, Philosophy," in whose <term>laribus</term> <note>original: "laribus"; literally the "hearths" or "homes" of the household gods, here interpreted as "schools"</note>—that is, schools—I had been occupied from "adolescence," meaning from my youth. And he inquired—that is, he said: "O teacher of all virtues, why"—meaning for what reason—"have you come, having glided down"—meaning having proceeded—"from the heavenly hinge"—that is, from the gate of heaven—"into these solitudes"—that is, the deserted places—"of our exile"—that is, our banishment? "Is it"—meaning could it be—"that you have come for this purpose: so that, being a defendant"—that is, as if you were guilty—"you might be harassed with me"—that is, be made manifest—"by false accusations?" That Philosophy "said"—that is, spoke: "O foster child"—that is, one nourished by me—"should I desert you?" As if she were saying: No. "Nor should I share"—that is, be divided from you—"by communicating the labor"—meaning sharing the labor and the "burden," which is the weight you have endured on account of the envy toward my name—meaning by reason of wisdom. "And yet surely it was not right"—that is, honorable—"for Philosophy to leave her path..."

—for just as a doctor brings health once the disease is driven away, so Philosophy, once ignorance is banished, grants the life of both worlds <note>this world and the afterlife</note>. For it is held in the *Book of the Apple* by Aristotle <note>original: "libro de pomo"; a medieval work falsely attributed to Aristotle depicting his deathbed conversation</note>: "He who finds philosophy finds life in both worlds." And elsewhere: "He who finds me finds life and shall draw salvation from the Lord" <note>a reference to Proverbs 8:35</note>. And therefore Boethius speaks of "the face of the one healing" <note>original: "faciem medicantis"</note>. It should be noted that Boethius did not just cast his eyes upon Philosophy, but "fixed his gaze" on her; by this it is implied that whoever wishes to philosophize must give themselves totally to Philosophy through continuous study and labor.

<margin>
<unclear>Usage of philosophy is of our nature, philosophy is not merely a virtue</unclear>
<unclear>Not through philosophy nor through virtue...</unclear>
</margin>

---

For just as one arriving swallow alone does not make a spring, nor does one warm day make a summer, so one single philosophical speculation does not make a philosopher. Note that the opportune time for philosophizing is the time of youth, which Boethius says he found, "in whose home <note>original: "laribus"; the Lares were Roman household gods, here representing the home or school</note> I had been observed since my youth." For the age of man is compared to wax; if it is too soft or too hard, it does not receive or retain the form of a seal. If, however, it is temperately soft or hard, it receives and retains the figure. In the same way, an age that is too tender, such as infancy, does not receive philosophical teaching, nor does an age that is too hard, such as extreme old age. But a temperate age, such as youth, easily understands and commits what is understood to memory. Note that by the "household gods" <note>original: "lares"</note> of Philosophy, they understand the various sects of philosophers, such as those of Aristotle and Plato, by whom Boethius was observed from his youth. And <term>Huguccio</term> <note>a 12th-century grammarian</note> says that "to be observed" <note>original: "obseruari"</note> is the same as "to dwell with" <note>original: "cōuersari"</note>. It should be noted that Philosophy is called the "teacher of all virtues" because she teaches all the moral virtues, as is clear from the *Ethics*. And I say "moral" because of the theological virtues, which are: Faith, Hope, and Charity. And Philosophy is said to have "descended from the high pole" because all wisdom is from the Lord God. For as it is written in the prologue of the book *On the Government of Princes* <note>original: "de regimine principum"</note>: It is God who pours the riches of his wisdom into souls; that is, he grants the grace of knowing to students, for whom nothing is difficult and without whom nothing is possible to be possessed. Note, as will appear later, that Boethius was falsely accused regarding composed letters and the interference of an informer, and that which wisdom performed was said to be done by magic arts. # Book One

Have you come so that you, along with me, might be driven about as a defendant by false accusations? Note: **Philosophy** <note>original: "phia"</note> touches upon three reasons why she ought not to have abandoned **Boethius** <note>original: "Boe."</note>. First, because a nurse ought not to abandon her foster-child. Second, because it is not fitting for one who suffers on behalf of another to be deserted by them. Third, because it is not fitting for Philosophy to abandon the innocent. **Boethius** was a foster-child of Philosophy; he himself was suffering injuries on account of Philosophy and was innocent. Therefore, etc. Note: according to Hugutio <note>A 12th-century grammarian often cited in medieval commentaries</note>, "I provoke" <note>original: "lacesso"</note> means when I desire to tear apart, or truly to afflict with injuries.

**Philosophy** <note>original: "philosophia"</note>—we have often fought a great struggle against the recklessness of folly, that is, against foolish and reckless men. And while that same Plato was living, his master, Socrates, unjustly earned the victory of death while I stood by him. Whose "inheritance"—that is, the inheritance of knowledge left to his disciples—when the Epicurean <note>Followers of Epicurus, often simplified in the Middle Ages as seekers of pleasure</note> crowd and the Stoics <note>Philosophers who emphasized virtue and endurance</note> and the others were endeavoring—that is, working—to go and seize it—that is, to snatch it, each for his own part—and when they themselves were dragging me, Philosophy, as a share of the loot, while I was crying out—that is, <term>contradicting</term> <note>original: "ꝑtradicẽtẽ"</note> them—and resisting, they tore my robe which I had woven with my own hands. And having taken away the scraps, they went away believing that I had yielded myself entirely to them. And because in those men there appeared certain traces of our habit—that is, of wisdom—the ignorance of the common people thought—that is, judged—them to be my associates—that is, my disciples. By the appearance of wisdom, it led some of them astray—that is, some by the error—that is, by the persecution—of the profane multitude—that is, the unlearned commoners—just as commoners are accustomed to subvert the learned. 

Note: because before the time of Plato, many wise men were persecuted by the common people, and in the time of Plato, Socrates his master perished on account of his wisdom. For he himself knew through his wisdom that there is one God; however, he rebuked others who worshipped many gods. Perceiving this, a leader of the Athenians named **Anytus** <note>Historical accuser of Socrates</note> forced him to drink poison in the name of the one God, and it did not harm him. Afterward, he forced him to drink poison in the name of many gods, and he perished. Note: after Socrates died, his disciples, who claimed the knowledge of Socrates for themselves as an inheritance, began to disagree about where their master Socrates had placed the "highest good." For some of his disciples, called Epicureans, said he had placed the highest good in pleasures. Others, like the Stoics, said he placed it in virtues. And each of them, for the defense...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Prose 3 of Book One of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*. Having listed the historical martyrs of philosophy, Lady Philosophy now explains why the "army of the wicked" should not be feared, using the metaphor of a spiritual citadel.</meta>

### Book One

The army of the wicked is innumerable. According to Solomon, the number of fools is infinite, and the perverse are difficult to correct. <note>original: "stultorum infinitus est numerus" — a reference to Ecclesiastes 1:15 in the Vulgate.</note> Note that the wicked are not ruled by the leader of reason, because reason pleads for the best things, while the wicked perform the worst. For they are led by the error of sensuality, following a beastly life, of whom it is said in the book of *Ethics*: <note>Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book I, where he discusses the "life of enjoyment" as being fit for cattle.</note> "There are some men who choose the life of cattle, similar to Sardanapalus." <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary Assyrian king often cited by ancient and medieval authors as the ultimate example of luxury and decadence.</note> And therefore Philosophy says that such people are not to be feared; because they are not ruled

<margin>
by reason, then their folly is easily dissipated. "Who if at any time against us": here Philosophy shows what must be done against the assault of the wicked by force. If an army of the wicked should press upon us—that is, persist—drawing up a battle line—that is, making war—against us wise ones, indeed for certain our leader—that is, Reason—draws together—that is, collects—her forces—that is, abundant sciences and virtues—into the citadel—that is, into the height of the contemplation of heavenly things. Truly, however, those wicked ones are occupied with plundering—that is, taking away—useless little baggage—that is, bodily riches—which are a burden and a weight of the body, sinking the soul.
</margin>

# ...they seemed most unlike them. Therefore there is nothing for you to wonder at if, in this sea of life <gloss>that is, the sea</gloss>, we are tossed by blowing storms <gloss>that is, tempests</gloss> and gales; for whom this is the greatest purpose: to displease the worst <gloss>that is, evil men</gloss>. Whose army, although it is an innumerable <gloss>that is, a multitude</gloss>, is nevertheless to be scorned because it is ruled by no leader <gloss>that is, reason</gloss>, but is hurried along and dragged by error alone, blindly and everywhere <gloss>that is, by a mad</gloss> and frantic <gloss>that is, distracted</gloss> impulse. Who, if at any time, drawing up a battle line <gloss>that is, war</gloss> against us, should press upon us <gloss>that is, as more powerful</gloss> and stronger, our leader indeed draws her forces together into a <gloss>that is, toward reason or a safe</gloss> citadel. They, truly, are occupied with plundering useless <gloss>that is, temporal things</gloss> little baggage. But we from above <gloss>that is, we mock them</gloss> laugh at them as they snatch up all the cheapest things, secure from all that mad up-

roar—that is, against the mad tumult of the wicked. For we are fortified by that rampart—that is, a protection—which it is not lawful for raging folly—that is, attacking us—to approach. 

It should be noted that Boethius here calls our <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: *ratio*</note> our "leader." Wherefore reason is defined thus: It is the habit directing every human action toward the ultimate and best end. Also note: by "citadel" he understands the height of the contemplation of heavenly things, and reason leads us to this. This is the ultimate good of human life which no one can take away. Note that "forces" <note>Latin: *copiae*</note> in this place are called the <term>sensory appetites</term> <note>Latin: *appetitus sensitivus* — the part of the soul that desires physical things</note>; and they are called *copiae* as if they were *cupiae* <note>A medieval etymological pun linking *copia* (abundance/forces) with *cupio* (to desire).</note> because they sometimes desire things against reason. Such forces reason ought to rule, and she must fortify herself with the rampart of humility and patience; then she will endure all attacks, adversities, and miseries with equanimity. She will not fear the temptations and harmful pleasures which the devil suggests, the flesh impels, and the world provokes. 

So says Marquardus. <note>Likely Marquard von Lindau (d. 1392), a Franciscan theologian whose works were widely used in the late Middle Ages.</note> Also note: he is deservedly to be laughed at who, having cast aside a greater and better good, chooses and is occupied with cheaper goods. But the wise choose the "goods of the soul," which are the greatest goods (according to the first book of the *Ethics*), while common people choose temporal goods, which are called the "cheapest of things" because they hinder a person from the knowledge of the Supreme Good. It should be noted that a citadel is a high building in which enemies fight; here, however, it is taken for the contemplation of heavenly things and the hope of future goods. For through these two, the wise [overcome] all the adversity of the wicked.

### Meter 4 of the First Book.
->Whoever is serene in a composed age.<-

Here begins the fourth meter of this first book, which is called the Valentinian meter after its inventor. <note>This refers to a specific classical meter consisting of dactylic and trochaic feet.</note> It consists of a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees; hence it can be called trochaic meter from the predominant foot. In this meter, Philosophy shows how a good person ought to behave so that the persecutions of the wicked do not prevail against them, and she declares this appropriately through certain similes. Secondly, she exclaims against those who fear tyrants. The second part begins there: "Why, oh wretched ones, so much..." <note>original: "Quid tantum miseri" – the start of the second half of this poem.</note>

---

She says first: Whoever is a person "serene"—that is, bright with virtue—in a "composed age"—that is, an ordered life—has "acted"—that is, trampled underfoot—"proud Fate"—that is, the outcome of temporal things. And whoever, "beholding"—that is, looking at—"either Fortune"—that is, the prosperous and the adverse—"upright"—that is, not bent—has been able to keep a "countenance"—that is, a mind—"unconquered," so that he is not conquered by prosperity through exalting himself, nor by adversity through being depressed. The "rage of the sea"—that is, the inundation of the sea—will not "move"—that is, disturb—that man, "stirring up"—that is, moving—from its "depths"—that is, from the bottom—the "churned-up tide"—that is, the churned-up boiling. For in the boiling of the sea, the water is turned through ebb and flow. She says as if to say: The force of the sea causing a boiling will not harm that man who does not exalt himself in prosperity nor is depressed in adversity. Nor will the "fire of Mount Vesuvius" harm such a man, as often as that mountain "twists out"—that is, emits—"smoke-producing fires" from its "broken chimneys"—that is, its caverns. She says as if to say: neither will wandering Vesuvius harm such a man with its fires. Nor will the "path of the burning thunderbolt," which is "used to"—that is, accustomed to—strike lofty towers, "move" that man. Note that Philosophy touches upon three things that do not harm a man who is constant in both kinds of fortune. The first is the "rage of the sea," by which the lustful are designated; for just as the sea grows hot and stinks from the sun and its own motion, so the lustful burn with their own desire, and when the lust is finished, they stink. Concerning whom the Scripture says: "The beasts have perished in their own dung." <note>A reference to Joel 1:17 in the Latin Vulgate, used here to moralize the natural imagery.</note> Such lustful people will not harm a man who is constant in both kinds of fortune.

The second thing he mentions is the fire of Mount Vesuvius, through which the greedy and the envious are signified. For just as the fire of Mount Vesuvius always burns, so the greedy always burn with the desire for external goods. And just as the fire, erupting at times, consumes the neighboring places, so the envious sometimes cause harm with words if they cannot do so with deeds; yet such envious people will not harm a constant man. The third thing he mentions is the lightning strike, through which the proud are understood. For just as lightning is generated on high, so the proud lift themselves up high.

And it seems a wondrous thing regarding the proud: that they wish to live with other humans and yet they cannot fly to heaven; such proud people will not harm a constant man. Others, through the rage of the sea, understand the envious; through fire, the angry; and through lightning, the proud, as has been said. Others, through the sea—which is noisy—understand greed; through fire, the pains of the body; and through lightning, the taking away of possessions.

Note that Vesuvius is a mountain of Italy, burning from within, which sometimes, when its caverns are ruptured, emits fire that consumes neighboring places. Note regarding this what Serenus <note>Likely referring to Serenus Sammonicus, a Roman physician and author.</note> says. Seneca says: "Such is the mind of the wise man as is the world above the moon; for such a world is always serene." <note>original: "superluminatus" – literally "above the lights" (the planets/moon), where the atmosphere was thought to be eternally calm.</note> And thus the mind of the wise man is always serene in either fortune. Whence Aristotle says in the *Ethics*: "The wise man knows well how to bear fortunes, because he holds himself like a square, without reproach." <margin>Ethics, Book 1</margin> <note>Aristotle uses the metaphor of a "square" (tetragōnos) to describe a person who is morally perfect and stable from every side, like a cube.</note> **Why do the wretched so much [at] fierce tyrants.** Here Philosophy exclaims against those who fear tyrants, saying: "Why (that is, for what reason) do wretched men wonder at, by fearing them, fierce tyrants raging without strength?" It is as if she says: tyrants are powerless, because they do not prevail unless a person subjects himself to them. And she adds: "Do not hope for anything" regarding temporal goods, "nor fear them" regarding adversities; then you will have "disarmed" (that is, weakened) the rage of the powerless tyrant. But whoever, being fearful, dreads the fear of temporal evils or desires temporal goods, such a person is not stable and "of his own right" (that is, of his own liberty). He has cast away the "shield" of security and, moved from the "place" of stability, he himself "weaves" (that is, composes) a "chain" of affections by which he may be dragged toward sadness and grief of mind. Note that earthly power extends to nothing except to the granting of temporal goods or to the taking of them away; and therefore no one is subject to earthly power except one who hopes for such goods or fears their removal. He, however, who neither fears nor hopes, is entirely above or outside earthly power. And consequently, earthly power can neither benefit nor harm him. Because of this, Philosophy exclaims against those wretched ones who, through hope of temporal goods or fear of their removal, subject themselves to earthly powers, saying: **Why do the wretched so much.** Note concerning that [line] **But whoever, trembling,** Seneca says in the *Book on the Cardinal Virtues*: "If magnanimity <note>original: "Magnanimitas" – greatness of soul, a key Stoic and Aristotelian virtue.</note> is within your soul, live intrepid and cheerful with great confidence; it belongs to a great soul not to waver but to stand firm and to await the end of life intrepidly. If you are magnanimous, you will never judge that an insult is being brought upon you by an enemy, but you will say: 'He has not harmed me, but he had the intention of knowing my mind.'" Note that a "tyrant" was once called a certain strong king, and it was said [to come] from *tiro* (that is, strength/fortitude); or that name is a cause appropriated for the worst rulers, and it is said from *tiro*...

Here Boethius responds to an objection; for Philosophy could object to him by saying: "What kind of reward ought you to have brought back, since you did not study for the sake of the common good, but for the sake of vain glory and your own utility?" To which objection Boethius responds, saying: "O Philosophy, you sanctioned—that is, confirmed—this opinion through the mouth of Plato: that republics are happy if wise men should rule them, or if it should happen to their rulers..."

### Prose Four.

...to study wisdom, and you confirmed by the mouth of that same Plato <note>original: "Platonis"</note> that it is necessary for republics to be governed by wise men, lest the rudders—that is, the governance—having been committed to the wicked—that is, the shameful citizens—should bring a plague and destruction—that is, ruin—upon the blood of good men. Therefore, I, following this authority—that is, the opinion—which I learned from you, Philosophy, during our secret leisure, desired—that is, took care—to transfer—that is, to bring—into action—that is, into the work of public administration—that is, for the common good.

---

<margin>to defend</margin>
...should rule. Or rather, that their rulers should study wisdom <gloss>pertain</gloss> <gloss>that is, whenever</gloss>. You, by the mouth of that same man, warned that this wisdom—<gloss>that is, taking up</gloss>—was a necessary cause for the republic, lest the rudders, if left to wicked and shameful citizens, should bring a plague and destruction upon men. Therefore, following this authority, I desired—<gloss>that is</gloss>—to transfer into the action of public administration what I had learned from you during our secret leisure. You and God, who has planted you <note>original: "inseruit," literally "grafted" or "sown"</note> in the minds of the wise, are my witnesses <note>original: "conscii," meaning those who share knowledge or witness</note> that no ambition brought me to the magistracy except the common desire of all good men. From this arose heavy and inexorable discords with the wicked; and for the sake of maintaining the right, which the freedom of conscience <note>original: "libertas conscientiae"</note> possesses, the offense of the powerful was always despised by me. How many times did I stand against Conigastus <note>a corrupt official under the Gothic King Theodoric</note> when he attacked the fortunes of every weak person...

<column-break/>

You, Philosophy, and God, who planted—that is, infused—you into the minds of the wise, are my witnesses—that is, my testifiers—that I brought no desire to the magistracy except the common desire of good men. It is as if he said: nothing moved me to hold office except utility. Because of this, there were for me heavy—that is, difficult—and inexorable—that is, unavoidable—discords with the wicked; and the offense of the powerful was always despised by me for the sake of protecting the right—that is, for defending justice—which the freedom of conscience possesses—that is, a free conscience, namely, to fear nothing while defending the right. Note: according to Plato, blessed is the republic whose master is a philosopher; woe to the nation whose master is a child <note>a common medieval reference to Ecclesiastes 10:16</note>; and

---

reasonably so, because philosophy and wisdom arrange one's life, rule one's actions, and demonstrate what should be done and what should be omitted. Whence Seneca says in his sixteenth letter: "If you wish to subject all things to yourself, subject yourself to reason. For you will rule many if reason rules you." And Aristotle in the prologue of the *Metaphysics* says: "It is the part of the wise man to rule and to order." From these things it is clear that the governance of the republic belongs to the wise; for this reason Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> says at the beginning of his *Rhetoric*: "The greatest benefits pertain to the republic if wisdom is present as the moderator and regulator of all things." Note that those who have already attained wisdom through study are called "zealots of wisdom" <note>original: "studiosi sapientie"</note>. However, those who are still acquiring wisdom by studying are said "to study wisdom." Note that Boethius calls study "secret leisure" <note>original: "secretum ocium"</note>, because in study a man is at leisure from exterior occupation; concerning which leisure without rest Seneca speaks in his sixty-seventh letter, saying: "No rest is peaceful except that which reason composes, and that is true tranquility in which the good mind unfolds." Note that God sends wisdom into the minds of the wise. This is written in the prologue of *On the Governance of Princes*: "It is God who pours the riches of his wisdom into the souls of the wise." Note that freedom of conscience means to fear nothing. As Macrobius says: "A free conscience has this specific quality: that if anyone possesses it, he fears no powerful person." Likewise, Seneca in his fourth book says: "The wise man, out of free will, fears nothing of the weakness of man because he possesses the security of God." And Seneca says in *On the Four Cardinal Virtues*: "To be just, it is not enough that you be innocent; if you are innocent..."

Note that every city or region which the Romans conquered, they made either <term>tributary</term>, or a <term>colony</term>, or a <term>province</term>. They made it "tributary" when, having left the inhabitants on the land, they compelled the men to pay a tribute. They made it a "colony" when, having expelled the inhabitants, they settled foreigners there to inhabit it. They made it a "province" when they put a certain Roman in charge of that land who, having collected the revenues, would send them to Rome; and the inhabitants of that land were called "provincials." Note: from these listed benefits it appears that Boethius did not hold office for his own profit but for the common good. ### Book the First.

I am not safe, as you will see later, even though I did not deserve to lose my security among the courtiers <note>original: *aulicos*, meaning those who lived in the royal court</note>, that is, the king’s intimates dwelling in the palace, because I opposed them for the love of justice. Note that one cause of Boethius’s distress was the frustration of his own merits: for the friendship and grace of those to whom he had granted many benefits was frustrated, and for whose sake he incurred much hatred and indignation. "But by whose informers were we struck down." Here Boethius touches upon his distress resulting from his unjust condemnation. First, he does this; second, he clears himself of certain charges brought against him. The second part begins at "Which to use..." First, he shows his unjust condemnation based on the accusation of vile persons. Second, based on the falsity of the crime imposed upon him. Third, based on the severity and perversity of the judge. The second part starts at "But for what crime," and the third at "And of whom one." First he says: "We were struck down," that is, struck down <note>original: *perculsi*, meaning to be smitten or terrified</note> by the accusing courtiers, one of whom was Basilius, who had been expelled from the king’s service because of his own malice. That man, being driven out and having taken money, was accepted to give a denunciation <note>original: *delatio*</note>, that is, an accusation of our name. The other two accusers of ours were Opilio and Gaudentius, whom King Theodoric, because of their innumerable frauds, had ordered to go into exile. When they refused to obey but defended themselves by entering churches <note>taking "sanctuary," a legal protection where criminals could not be seized within a church</note>, the king, when this was discovered <note>original: *compertum*, revealed to the king</note>, issued an edict <note>original: *edixit*, he commanded</note> that unless they departed from the city of Ravenna within a set time, they should be driven out and first branded on their foreheads <note>original: *signari in frontib⁹ cauterio*, a common punishment for those caught in fraud</note> just as evildoers are usually marked. And Boethius says that it seems this can be "added to" <note>original: *astrui*, or confirmed by</note> this severity: that on the very same day they were accusing us, their accusation was accepted. What then, O Philosophy, should be said? Did our "arts" <note>referring to his philosophical studies and virtuous way of life</note> deserve this? It is as if he were saying: surely these men were not justified because of our accusation. It is as if he said: indeed, Fortune should have been ashamed; even if Fortune was not ashamed of an innocent man being accused, yet the vileness of the accuser should have been a cause of shame for Fortune herself. Note this word *perculsus* <note>struck down</note>. Hugutio <note>Hugutio of Pisa, a medieval grammarian</note> says *pello, pellis*, *perculi* in the past tense and *perculsum* in the supine is the same as to strike or rather to terrify. But to strike...

<column-break/>

...would be more protective to be observed. "But by whose informers were we struck down?" One of whom, Basilius, having formerly been expelled from the king's service, was compelled by the necessity of foreign debt to denounce our name. As for Opilio and Gaudentius, when the royal judgment had decreed they go into exile for innumerable and manifold frauds, and they, refusing to obey, defended themselves by the protection of sacred buildings <note>referring to church sanctuary</note>, and when this became known to the king, he decreed that unless they departed from the city of Ravenna within the prescribed day, they should be driven out, marked with brands on their foreheads. What could be seen as added to this severity? And yet, on that very day, by the informing of these same men, the denunciation of our name was accepted. What then? Did our "arts" <note>his philosophical life and skills</note> deserve this? Or did the promised condemnation make those accusers just? Was Fortune not at all ashamed? If not for the innocence being accused, then the vileness of the accusers should have been a cause for shame.

### Fourth Prose.

It relates to the body, but to "strike" <note>original: *percellere*</note> relates to the soul. Note regarding this word "informers" <note>original: *deferentibus*</note>: that the word *defero* has three meanings. First, it is the same as to carry away <note>original: *deporto*</note>. From this comes "reporter" or "carrier." Second, it is the same as to honor. From this comes "honorer," one who shows honor. Third, it means to accuse. From this comes "accuser" <note>original: *delator*</note>, because he uncovers what was hidden; and this last way is how it is understood here. Hence the verse: *He accuses, he reports, he gives honors, and he carries things down.*

<margin>Boethius</margin>
**But you ask for the summary of the crime for which we <gloss>namely Boethius</gloss> are accused <gloss>namely Boethius</gloss>. We <gloss>namely Boethius</gloss> are said to have wished the Senate to be safe. You desire to know the manner. We are accused of having hindered an informer <note>a "delator" was a professional informant who profited from accusations</note> from bringing documents by which he might make the Senate guilty of treason <note>original: *lese maiestatis*, a crime against the dignity of the state or king</note>. What then, O teacher, do you judge? Shall we deny the charge so as not to be a source of shame to you? But I did want it, and I shall never cease to want it. We will confess. But the efforts of the informer to hinder us will cease. Or shall I call it a wicked thing <note>original: *nephas*</note> to have hoped for the safety of that order?**

<column-break/>

Note that for suitable witnesses, seven conditions are required, which are contained in these verses: Age, status, sex, discernment, reputation, and fortune; these things rule in witnesses if the matter requires it. First, age is required, because children cannot be witnesses. Second, a free status is required, therefore slaves cannot provide testimony. Third, the male sex is required, therefore women <note>this reflects the restrictive legal codes of the Middle Ages and Antiquity</note> cannot be witnesses. Fourth, discernment is required, therefore madmen and fools cannot testify. Fifth, reputation is required

<column-break/>

therefore infamous persons cannot testify. Sixth, fortune is required, for which reason the poor cannot testify. Seventh, faith is required, for which reason infidels cannot provide testimony. Among these conditions, two are considered "baser" <note>original: *viliores*</note>, namely poverty and infamy. Boethius, therefore, wishing to show that his condemnation was unjust based on the low quality of the accusing witnesses—for which reason they ought to have been rejected from giving testimony—says that in the first there was a defect of fortune, namely in Basilius. But in the other two, namely Opilio and Gaudentius, he says there was the vice of infamy. Note that nothing seems more severe or wicked than to admit base and damnable persons to testify against the innocent. As Seneca says in *On the Remedies of Fortuitous Events*: "A sentence can have no authority where he who is to be condemned speaks ill of you." "But you ask for the summary of the crime by which we are accused, the Senate, etc." Here Boethius shows the injustice of his condemnation, first from the falsity of the crime imposed upon him; second, from these words he draws a certain wonder <note>starting at "In which matter..."</note>. The first part is divided into two, according to the two things imposed upon Boethius, of which he excuses himself. The second part starts at "For concerning the composed..." The first thing imposed upon him was that he had hindered a certain messenger who was bringing an accusation of the Senate to the king, so that the Senate would be found guilty of treason. He says therefore in the text: O Philosophy, you perhaps ask for the "sum," that is, the sentence of the crime for which we are accused. We are said to have wanted to save the Senate: perhaps you desire to know by what manner. I say that we are accused, that is, argued to have hindered the informer from bringing documents, that is, letters, to the king by which he would make the Senate guilty of treason. What then, O teacher, do you judge, that is, decide? Shall we deny that crime so that we are not a shame to you? And yet I wanted to save the Senate, nor will I ever cease to want it. But the work, that is, the diligence of the informer in hindering this will cease, that is, it ought to cease, because it is not true that we hindered the informer of the letters. Is it not a wicked thing to desire the safety of that order, namely the Senate? As if to say: it is not a wicked thing. Truly, that Senate which consented to my condemnation has brought this about by its own decrees, namely...

We are bound to wish spiritual safety for everyone, even for the wicked, by reason of charity, through which even the wicked are to be loved, though not in their wickedness. But we are bound to wish temporal safety for all good people, and especially for friends. For friends who are sinning, we are bound to wish for their safety as long as they are curable, so that they may recover their lost virtue. But if, due to the magnitude of their malice, they are incurable, the friendship is dissolved and safety is not to be wished for. Also note that the "secret of conscience" is a virtue that is diminished when someone performs a virtuous work while boasting so that they may obtain fame and the praise of the people. Whence **Seneca** says: "Attend rather to conscience than to reputation." And **Macrobius** says: "The wise man places his glory in his conscience; the fool, however, in human praise." Whence **Isidore** says: "Whoever turns any good granted by God to their own praise undoubtedly causes virtue to pass into vice." **"And what person's manifest confession of a crime..."** Here Boethius shows himself to be perturbed by the severity and inflexibility of the judges, saying: What man’s manifest confession of a crime—that is, a sin—ever had judges so unified in severity that the error of human nature did not cause some of them to yield—that is, bend toward mercy—or that the condition of fortune—which is a chance event existing as uncertain for all mortals (meaning humans)—did not cause some of them to yield? If it were said that he wished to set fire...

**Note** that judges are sometimes moved to mercy for two reasons. First, because of the error of human nature, for the human mind is often deceived in judgment; since it does not know whether a person feels justly about a matter or not, and fearing God lest it judge unjustly, it is moved to mercy by sparing the accused. Second, judges are moved to mercy because of the outcome of fortune, which is uncertain for men. For what a judge condemns in another might easily happen to himself through fortune, and he ought to remember that. But neither of those causes moved the judges to pity Boethius; instead, they condemned him with one accord. 

**Note** that no one should be condemned, even for an enormous crime, unless they are present and convicted or have confessed the crime in court. Boethius, however, when he was condemned, was neither convicted nor had he confessed the crime; he was absent because he was in the school of Athens <note>Medieval commentators often believed Boethius was studying in Athens when he was accused, highlighting his status as a philosopher.</note>; therefore, he was unjustly condemned. 

**Note** that when Boethius was condemned, he was distant from the place of judgment by five hundred thousand paces, and since one thousand paces make one mile, he was a full five hundred miles away. 

**Note** that Boethius was condemned to proscription. Huguitio <note>Huguitio (Uguccione da Pisa) was a famous 12th-century grammarian who wrote a major dictionary.</note> says that **proscription** is a judicial sentence passed against someone whose name was deleted from the writing on the bronze tablet because of a crime. For it was a Roman custom that the names of the Senators, by whose counsel the city of Rome was ruled, were written in gold letters on a bronze tablet; hence they were called the "Conscript Fathers" <note>original: "patres conscripti"</note>. He is called "proscribed" <note>original: "proscriptus"</note> as if he were "placed far from the writing" <note>original: "procul a scriptura"</note>; and so Boethius was proscribed because his name was erased from the bronze tablet. "To darken these as if they were some wonder of crime..." Here Boethius clears himself of certain accusations. Second, he shows from where the reason for the accusation was taken.

The second part begins here: "But it is a crime." **Note** that it was charged against Boethius that he used the dark arts <note>original: "arte nigromantica," referring to necromancy or black magic</note> to sacrifice to demons in order to acquire high offices. "inner chamber"—that is, the wife of my house—and the assembly—that is, the multitude—of my most honorable friends, and my father-in-law Symmachus, a holy man and equally to be revered by his own deeds, defend me from all suspicion of this kind of crime. 

**Note** that it is the habit of the envious that when they cannot take away someone's integrity, they try at least to blacken it with some vice; and thus the reputation of Boethius was blackened by the vice of sacrilege. 

**Note** that "sacrilege" is the theft of a sacred thing, and a "sacrilegious man" is used to mean a wicked person. Also, sacrilege is the worship of demons or idols; hence "sacrilegious" means "idolater," and that is how it is understood in this context. 

**Note** that "ambitus," when the middle syllable is long, is the desire for honor. But "ambitus," when the middle syllable is short, means a circuit or going around. It is used in the first sense here. 

**Note** that philosophy repels all desire for external goods, as is written in the first book *On Plants*: that philosophy brings about three things—namely, the illumination of the mind, the desire for happiness, and contempt for the abundance of physical mass. 

**Note** that philosophy makes a human like God, not in a total similarity, but in a "participatory" way, so that a human participates in something of the divine condition, namely intelligence. Hence Seneca says: "This is what philosophy promises me: that it makes me equal to God." And elsewhere he says: "A man of contemplation is as if God is a guest in a human body." 

**Note** that sacrilege has no place under the eyes of philosophy, because philosophy itself disposes all things to be done and managed in the most orderly way, and does not permit a person to wander into devious paths. As Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> says in his book *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: philosophy frees one from superstition and does not allow one to be disturbed by the fear of death; and superstition is a vain religion and the worship of idols. 

**Note** that "inner chamber" <note>original: "penetral"</note> is a secret room, like a private interior place in a house or temple where treasures or other things are stored; it is used here for Boethius’s wife through a metaphor, putting the "container" for the "contained" because...

...she herself <note>Philosophy</note> used to dwell in the inner sanctuary. **Note** that Symmachus was a certain noble Roman and the father-in-law of Boethius, whose daughter Boethius had married, named Elpis <note>original: "Elphe"</note>. Boethius says this to this extent: because they were injured on account of Philosophy, they thus injured Philosophy more than him. **Note**: When Boethius was devoted to study, he fled the company of fools and sought secret places for the sake of study; therefore, they thought he was speaking with demons and sacrificing to them. **Note** that Boethius, because he was of a disturbed mind and in a state of misery, saw that the evil in this world were powerful and lived unpunished, while the good were powerless and lived unrewarded. <header>Book One</header>

Anapestic [meter] named from its predominant foot. An anapest is a foot contrary to the dactyl, consisting of two short syllables followed by a long one. This meter is "acatalectic" <note>original: 'acatbaleticum', referring to a verse that has a complete number of syllables in its final foot</note>, meaning it is without defect. In this meter, Boethius cries out against divine providence, marvelling that all things are ruled by God except for human actions—though this is actually false, it seemed so to Boethius in his disturbed state of mind. The text is divided as follows: first, he commends divine providence for its governance of celestial and terrestrial things; second, he mentions that human actions are not ruled by God; and third, he asks God to restore the affairs of men. The second part begins at "Your certain" <note>original: 'Tua certo'</note>; the third at "Whoever of things" <note>original: 'Quisquis rerum'</note>.

The first part is divided: first, he commends the rule of divine providence regarding celestial matters; second, he speaks more on terrestrial matters, beginning at "May your power temper the varied." First, he says: O founder <note>that is, creator</note> of the star-bearing <note>original: 'stelliferi', star-carrying</note> world, who, leaning <note>that is, joined</note> upon an eternal throne <note>that is, an eternal seat</note>, you turn <note>that is, you frequently rotate</note> the heights with a rapid whirl <note>that is, a swift motion</note>, and you compel the stars to suffer the law <note>that is, their due order</note>. Thus the moon itself now <note>that is, at certain times</note>, bright with a full horn as in a full moon, facing <note>that is, opposite to</note> all the flames <note>that is, lights</note> of her brother <note>that is, the sun</note>, this moon hides <note>that is, conceals</note> the lesser stars which are not seen during a full moon because of the greater light. And you compel her now <note>that is, sometimes</note>, so that the moon, being pale with a dark horn and being nearer to Phoebus <note>that is, the sun</note>, loses <note>that is, gives up</note> her lights <note>that is, her brightness</note>. It is as if he were saying: you make it so that the further the moon recedes from the sun, the more she is illuminated and obscures the lesser stars with her light; and the closer she approaches the sun, the more she is darkened. And you compel Hesperus <note>that is, the evening star</note>, which conducts chilling <note>that is, cold</note> actions in the night-time, during the twilight which is the first part of the night, following the sun. This same Hesperus, called Lucifer <note>the morning star, literally 'light-bringer'</note> in the morning, turning pale at the rising of Phoebus, again changes his accustomed reins <note>that is, his accustomed course</note>. For when he follows the sun in the evening, he precedes it in the morning. And you restrict the light <note>that is, the days</note> with a shorter delay in the time of frost <note>that is, winter</note> which makes the leaves fall <note>leaf-shedding</note>. And when the glowing summer comes, then you divide <note>that is, distinguish</note> the agile hours <note>that is, the short hours</note> of the night. It is as if he were saying: you make it so that in winter the nights are longer than the days, and in summer it is the opposite. 

Note that God is called the "founder of the star-bearing sphere" because the heavens and all nature depend upon Him, as stated in the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, Book XII (Lambda), which discusses the Unmoved Mover</note>. He is said to reside on an eternal throne because he is in the heavens, which are eternal. For the heavens are the place of the gods and spirits; all barbarians and Greeks, and whoever believe there are gods, attribute that place which is above to God, matching the immortal to the immortal—first the heavens and the world. And He is said to "turn the heavens with a rapid whirl." The motion of the firmament is called "rapid" because by its own motion it carries the other spheres along with it. Hence note that "to turn" <note>original: 'verso'</note> is a frequentative verb and signifies turning frequently. In this, it is implied that the heavens are always moved and will not cease. Because it says that it is not to be feared by those who measure that the heavens will stop. The reason is that the one moving the heavens moves them without fatigue and without pain, according to the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. Likewise, God is "leaning upon an eternal throne," that is, joined to the eternal heavens. Hence, God is in the universe in a threefold way: namely, essentially or presentially; sacramentally or mysteriously; and mercifully. Essentially or presentially in His true clarity in

God compels the stars to suffer his law, not by violence nor by forced motion (since nothing violent is perpetual), but he compels them by a voluntary arrangement to observe the law—that is, a determined movement—so that at their appointed time they rise and set. Note that the moon is by itself an opaque body, receiving light from the sun, and it is illuminated on that part which faces the sun. When, however, it is

<column-break/>

directly opposite the sun, as in a full moon, then with its own light it obscures the smaller stars because a greater light drowns out a lesser one. But when the moon is in that part of the sky where the sun is, as happens in a <term>conjunction</term> <note>When the moon and sun are aligned, resulting in a new moon</note>, then the upper part facing the sun is illuminated and the lower part facing us is darkened, and then we see nothing of the moon. But when it begins to move away from the sun, then the distant part begins to appear slightly to us, and then we say it is a new moon <note>original: "nouilunium"</note>; and the further it moves away, the more it appears illuminated to us. Note: Boethius says the sun is the brother of the moon because, according to the myths, Jupiter, lying with Latona, fathered from her two twins: namely, Phoebus, who is called the Sun, and Diana, who is called the Moon; and thus, according to the myths, the sun is the brother of the moon. Note: the star that follows the sun in the evening and precedes it in the morning has different names, as is clear from the verse: "Lucifer comes at dawn, Vesper and Hesperus are the same" <note>original: "Lucifer aurora venit vesperus hesperus idem"</note>. As to how it is possible that the same star follows the sun in the evening and precedes it in the morning, some say this does not happen in one and the same part of the year, but in different ones. For they say that in summer it follows the sun and in winter it precedes it. But this is against all authors, for it should happen in the same time of year. Others say that Mercury and Venus are stars of similar color and size, one of which follows the sun and the other precedes it, and thus it seems to be one star that follows and precedes; but this is not the case. Huguitio says that Venus is higher than the sun, speaking according to the ancient astrologers who placed Venus above the sun. When, therefore, it happens that Venus and the sun come to their setting together, because Venus is higher, it is seen longer in the evening than the sun. For the same reason, it is seen earlier in the morning, although they run their course equally fast. For distant rising things are seen sooner than near ones, and distant setting things are seen longer than near ones, even if they move at an equal pace. But modern astrologers have placed Venus below the sun. Others say it is one star that follows the sun at one time and precedes it at another; and they say, according to Ptolemy, that this star has an <term>epicycle</term> <note>original: "eclipticus," here describing a small circle on the circumference of a larger orbit</note> on whose circumference its body is carried. An epicycle is a small circle whose center is on the circumference of the carrying orbit. Now it is so that the epicycle of Venus is always with the sun, so that if a line were drawn from the center of the earth through the center of the Venusian epicycle to the firmament, the same line would pass through the center of the sun or would not be far from it. When Venus is carried around the circuit of the epicycle, sometimes it will be in the same line as the sun, sometimes it precedes, and sometimes it follows. Likewise, the stay of the sun above the horizon makes the day, since day is the movement of the sun over the earth; the stay of the sun below the horizon makes the night. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Boethius’s "Consolation of Philosophy," Book 1, Meter 5. The previous page discussed the movements of the sun and moon; here, the text transitions to the changing seasons and the winds, eventually moving into Boethius’s famous complaint that while nature follows divine law, human affairs seem governed by the whims of Fortune.</meta>

[The sun] stays longer in the summer time above the horizon and a shorter time below the horizon; therefore, summer days are longer than the nights. In winter, however, the opposite occurs, which is why winter days are shorter than the nights.

**"Your power tempers the varying year."** <note>original: "Tua vis varium temperat annum"</note>
Here Boethius commends the rule of divine providence specifically regarding earthly matters—that is, regarding the changing seasons of the year. O God, your power—which is to say your virtue—"tempers"—that is, orders—the "varying year," meaning the different seasons of the year, so that the **gentle Zephyr** <term>Zephyr: the Greek name for the West Wind, associated with the arrival of Spring</term>—that is, the spring wind—may "bring back"—that is, restore—the leaves which the breath of **Boreas** <term>Boreas: the North Wind, bringing cold and winter</term>—that is, the blast of the north wind—"takes away"—that is, destroys. 

And your power tempers things so that whatever seeds **Arcturus** (that star) <note>Arcturus is a bright star in the constellation Boötes, often associated with the transition to autumn</note> saw, **Sirius** <note>The "Dog Star," associated with the heat of midsummer</note>—that is, the Dog Star—"burns"—that is, ripens—those "high crops"—that is, tall crops—in the summer time. And he adds: nothing is left "loose"—that is, separated—from the **ancient law**—that is, the eternal law of divine providence; nothing leaves the work of its "proper station"—that is, the purpose for which it was established to perform.

Note that there are four seasons of the year: Spring, Winter, Autumn, and Summer. In the spring, a wind blows called the **Zephyr**, which is adjacent to the West Wind; and because its breath is light, it is called "gentle," and it produces green growth. In winter, and especially at the beginning, the blast of **Boreas** prevails, which is the wind adjacent to the North Wind, whose blast is strong and cold and destroys green things by stripping the trees.

Note that **Arcturus** is a star near the Greater Bear which marks the sowing of seeds, because at the time of its rising (when it rises with the sun), then the sowing happens, as in autumn. 

Note that **Sirius** is a star called by another name, the **Canicula** (Little Dog). It is called Sirius from *siren*, which means "drawn," because of the long stretch of heat; and it appears when the sun is in Cancer and is said to "burn" the crops—that is, to ripen them.

Note regarding Arcturus: see **Isidore** in his book *Etymologies*: Arcturus is a constellation placed behind the tail of the Greater Bear and rises in the autumn. **Vegetius** <note>A 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture and military matters</note> says that Arcturus rises after the Ides of September, twelve days before the Kalends of October. 

Likewise, Isidore says: The Canicula is a star and is called Sirius because in the summer months it is in the middle of the sky, and being joined with the sun, its heat is doubled; bodies are weakened and sweat; from this star, the **"dog days"** are named, in which medical purgations are troublesome.

**"You govern all with a fixed end."** <note>original: "Omnia certo fine gubernas"</note>
In this part, Boethius touches upon the fact that the actions of men do not seem to be ruled by divine providence; rather, he suggests they are abandoned to the governance of Fortune, saying: O God, you govern all things with a fixed end—that is, with a fixed order toward a goal—yet you "refuse"—that is, you scorn—to rule the actions of men alone. O Ruler God, you should rightly be "restrained"—that is, coerced—since **slippery Fortune**—that is, unstable Fortune—turns so many "turns"—that is, alternations—because she herself oppresses the **innocent**—that is, the guiltless—with a "harmful punishment" due to crime, though it belongs to the wicked man. And perverse morals—that is, men perverse in their habits—reside in...

...on a **lofty throne**, that is, a high place. ...harms them. Likewise, God governs all things toward a certain end. As the Commentator <note>Referring to Averroes, the influential medieval commentator on Aristotle</note> says in the tenth book of the *Metaphysics*: God is the measure and rule of all things and an infallibly true meter. But God is most wise because all wisdom proceeds from God; hence the Scripture says: "All wisdom is from the Lord." <note>Sirach 1:1</note> Note: Boethius saw in the world that the good are depressed and the wicked are exalted, even though it should rather be the opposite. Therefore, it seemed to him that the acts and operations of men were not ruled by God, but rather by **Fortune**, who humbles this one and exalts that one. Therefore, Boethius complains to God: **"Look upon all the wretched lands."** Here Boethius asks that God rule the acts of men and humans just as He rules the heaven, saying: "O whoever God you are, you who **bind**, that is, join, **covenants**, that is, the harmonies of things, **look upon the wretched lands**, that is, the humans dwelling on the earth. Therefore, you, O God, **compress**, that is, restrain, the **rapid floods**, that is, the great impulses of fortune. And by that **covenant**, that is, the governance by which you rule the immense heaven, you **make firm**, that is, strengthen, the **stable lands**, that is, humans stable on the earth." Note: Boethius says that man is not a cheap part of the world because it is written in the prologue of the book *On the Apple* by Aristotle: <term>On the Apple: A medieval pseudo-Aristotelian work (Liber de Pomo) concerning the soul</term> "Man is the most worthy of creatures, a likeness of all, made in the image of God." And in the second book *On the Soul*: <note>Aristotle's De Anima</note> that in a certain way the soul corresponds with all creatures. For it corresponds with angels in understanding, with beasts in sensing, with plants in growing, and with stones in existing. Note: Boethius compares **Fortune** to a **sea**, that is, the ocean. For just as a ship is tossed by the waves of the sea now on high and now into the deep, so a man is now raised up in prosperity by Fortune and now cast down in adversity.

...to drive you from your homeland would never have been right, that is, permitted for any [supply: of men]. For if you remember, that is, recall, of which homeland, that is, from what homeland you are a native, that is, born—not as [supply: just as] the city of the Athenians was once ruled by command, that is, by the scepter of a multitude, that is, of many rulers. There follows the Greek <note>Boethius quotes Homer’s *Iliad*: "One is the lord, one the king," applying it to God’s singular rule over the universe.</note> which means as much in Latin: namely, there is one Lord and one King, one and prince who rejoices in frequency, that is, in the frequent inhabitation of citizens, that is, inhabitants, and not in their expulsion. To be led, that is, guided by the reins, that is, the commands of this King, and to comply, that is, to obey justice, is the highest liberty. Or do you not know that most ancient law; that is, the statute of your city, that is, of right action, by which it is sanctioned, that is, confirmed, that it is not right, that is, does not pertain to it, to be an exile, that is, to suffer exile, whoever should prefer, that is, desire, to establish, that is, locate, his seat, that is, his habitation, in that city. For he who is contained, that is, comprehended, within the wall and fortification of that city, has no fear, that is, dread, that he deserves to be an exile; but whoever has ceased, that is, stopped, wanting to inhabit that city, equally ceases also to deserve, that is, to obtain merit.

**Note** that <term>delatrare: to bark</term> is properly of dogs. In this context, however, "to bark" is to speak against reason while grief is raging. And so **Boethius**, because he said the acts of men are not ruled by God, was speaking against reason; therefore he says he "barked." **Note** it is not for a wise person to be moved by those things said by an unwise person against reason, but he ought rather to instruct the beginner and console him. Therefore Philosophy was not moved by the complaints of **Boethius** but rather consoled him. **Note** Philosophy recognized **Boethius** to be wretched and an exile. Wretched is he whose mind follows the change of temporal things so that he is extolled in prosperity and depressed in adversity. An **exile** in this context is he, not who changes regions, but who acts against reason. **Note** that through tears it can be known that a person's reason is disturbed; but how much it is disturbed is not known except through the speech of the grieving one. Therefore Philosophy says: "by your tears I knew you were an exile, but how great the exile was I did not know."

Following Boethius’s emotional complaint about the injustice of his imprisonment, Lady Philosophy begins her "clinical" diagnosis of his mental state.
