# **Prose Five.**

...unless your own reasoning had revealed it to me. <note>original: "nisi tua ratio mihi prodidisset"</note> **Note:** He is truly driven from his homeland who loses his reason entirely. But he was only "away" in the sense that while he remains within the homeland, he retains his reason in some matters but loses it in others. **Boethius** was not driven far from his homeland because he had not lost all reason; for he believed all things are ruled by God, but in this he strayed: he did not think the actions of men were ruled by God. **Note** concerning the homeland of man, which is right reason. **Seneca** speaks of this in *On the Remedies of Chance*, saying: "Homeland is wherever a man is well." <note>Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher; this quote emphasizes that a wise person's true home is their internal state of mind.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>The Ruler</margin>
**...ruler <gloss>that is, the king</gloss> who rejoices in the multitude of his citizens <gloss>namely, the faithful</gloss> and not in their expulsion <gloss>that is, their removal through exile</gloss>. To be guided by his reins <gloss>namely, the commandments of God</gloss> and to obey his justice is the highest freedom. <term>highest freedom</term><note>A central Stoic and Christian paradox: true liberty is found in voluntary obedience to divine law, rather than doing whatever one wants.</note> Are you unaware of that most ancient law <gloss>namely, the divine law</gloss> of your city <gloss>namely, the city of reason</gloss> by which it is decreed that no one has the right to be an exile <gloss>that is, the permission to leave</gloss> who has chosen to establish his dwelling <gloss>namely, of virtue</gloss> within it? For he who is contained within its wall <gloss>namely, the commandments of God</gloss> and its fortification <gloss>namely, the grace of God</gloss> need have no fear of deserving to be an exile. But <gloss>but, that is, however</gloss> whoever should cease to want to inhabit it, equally ceases <gloss>that is, also</gloss> to deserve it. Therefore, it is not so much the look <gloss>that is, of this place of exile</gloss> of this place that moves me, as your own face <gloss>that is, your inner disposition</gloss>. Nor do I <gloss>namely, Philosophy</gloss> seek the walls of your library, adorned with ivory and glass <gloss>namely, of your seat</gloss>, as much as I seek the seat of your mind <gloss>namely, Philosophy seeking it</gloss>. In which I have placed not books, but that which [gives value] to books...**

<column-break/>

...is. Moreover, that which is "well" in a man is not in a physical place; it is in the man himself, in his power. If he is wise, he does not wander; if he is a fool, he is an exile. **Note:** No one expelled **Boethius** from the homeland of reason except himself; because Boethius exited the boundaries and limits of reason not by an outside force but by his own failing. **Note:** The city of the **Athenians** was ruled by the power of the multitude. For first, kings ruled it; then, as time passed, princes. Finally, for its governance, thirty-eight wise men were elected each year. But the homeland of reason is ruled by only one prince: namely, God, who is the rule of right reason. **Note:**

<margin>... <unclear>if any through the deed which he wills</unclear> / <unclear>God so that... </unclear> / <unclear>in the state... it happens at...</unclear></margin>

---

A man is said to originate from the homeland of reason insofar as his intellectual soul certainly originates from God by right reason. **Note:** A man remains in the homeland of reason insofar as he is subject to God and the divine law; and because God delights in the submission of his subjects, therefore He rejoices in the multitude of citizens and not in their expulsion. Moreover, someone is repelled from the homeland of reason by rebelling against God and receding from right reason. **Note:** He who obeys God is supremely free, because insofar as someone acts according to right reason, to that extent he is free. But by obeying God, a man acts most according to reason; therefore, such a one is most free. Whence **Seneca**, in his 56th letter, says: "You ask what freedom is. True freedom is to serve nothing except God, to bear prosperity and adversity with equal mind, and to regard Fortune as an equal." **Note:** No one exiles himself from the city of reason except through an affection for temporal things. Such an affection is voluntary, and therefore by will alone one exiles oneself from such a city. And because such an affection cannot occupy a man as long as he is within the limits of right reason—that is, within **Philosophy**—it is said "For he who [is contained] by its wall, etc." "Therefore, not so much [the look] of this place." Here Philosophy addresses certain unreasonable things said by **Boethius**, saying: "Since you strayed from the homeland of reason, therefore not so much"—that is, not only—"the face"—that is, the appearance of this place, namely exile—"as your face"—that is, the inner disposition of your mind—"moves me"—that is, disturbs me, Philosophy. And because he previously complained about the lack of his library of books, Philosophy, making little of this lack, says: "Neither do I, Philosophy, require"—that is, search for—"the walls of the library adorned"—that is, decorated—"with ivory"—that is, elephant bone—"as well as with glass"—that is, precious gems, etc.—"insofar as I, a suppliant, seek the seat"—that is, the tranquility—"of your mind, in which mind I have not placed..."

# To the sixth meter of the first book.

<margin>To the sixth meter of the first book.</margin>
> **When the heavy constellation of Cancer glows with the rays of Phoebus <gloss>the sun</gloss>. Then, he who entrusted generous seeds to the refusing furrows: Cheated...**

**When the heavy [constellation] with the rays of Phoebus.** Here begins the sixth meter of this first book, which is called a <term>Glyconic meter</term> <note>a classical verse form named after the poet Glycon</note> from its inventor; and <term>choriambic</term> <note>a metrical foot consisting of a long, two shorts, and a long syllable</note> from its predominant foot. A choriamb is a foot consisting of a long first and last syllable and two short middle ones. Wherefore the first foot of this meter is a <term>spondee</term> <note>two long syllables</note>. The second is a choriamb. The third is a <term>pyrrhic</term> <note>two short syllables</note>, which is a foot consisting of two shorts, and in its place an <term>iamb</term>—which consists of a short first and long last—is sometimes put. 

In this meter, Philosophy proves her statement by examples; for she says that for now strong remedies would not suit Boethius, but rather at another time. She proves, therefore, that all things require a determined time, and if they are done outside their proper time, they do not prosper. She proves this by three examples. Second, she touches on how the times which God has distinguished are not to be mixed, at the phrase "he marks the times" <note>original: "signat tpa"</note>. 

The first example concerns the seed which, if sown at an improper time, brings forth no fruit—as if someone were to sow in July or August. Wherefore the text says: "When" <note>original: "Cum"</note> (meaning whenever) "the heavy constellation of Cancer" <note>the zodiac sign associated with the height of summer</note> "glows"—that is, burns—with the "rays of Phoebus"—that is, the sun; "then"—that is, in that time—he who "entrusted"—that is, committed—"generous seeds"—that is, copious seeds—to the "refusing furrows"—that is, the hollows of the earth <insert>understand: refusing the hope of a harvest</insert>; such a man is "cheated"—that is, frustrated—in his "faith"—that is, in the benefit of "Ceres" <note>the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note>. Let him "go"—that is, approach—the "oaken trees"—that is, the oak—and "feed upon their fruits" <note>acorns, the food of animals or desperate men</note>. 

Then she provides the second example regarding flowers, which a man seeks in vain in the winter time, since their proper time is in the spring. Wherefore the text says: "You, about to pick"—that is, to gather—"violets, never seek"—that is, approach—the "purple grove"—that is, the flowery...

Note regarding what is said: "the whistling field." Augustine <note>original: "Augustio"</note> says that to whistle <note>original: "strideo strides" or "strido dis"</note> is to sound loudly or to strike teeth together or to gnash. **He marks the times with their own [traits].** Here Philosophy shows that the times which God has distinguished are not to be mixed, saying: God marks, that is, adorns the times, fitting them to their own duties. Nor does God himself allow the turns, that is, the alternations of the times, to be mixed, so that a time assigned to one duty should suit another—which turns of time he himself has restricted, that is, constrained. And she adds that just as someone is frustrated when seeking acorns from an oak tree at an improper time, so that which deserts the certain order by a headlong, that is, a hasty path, does not have happy endings, that is, a prosperous outcome. Likewise, by similarity, if Philosophy—having left behind the proper time—had administered medicines to Boethius, she might not have been prosperous in healing him. Note that through the proper order, things are preserved in their being and in their nature. And whatever falls away from order also falls away from being. Wherefore Boethius says in the second prose of the fourth book of this work: "For that is which retains its order and preserves its nature; but whatever falls away from this, leaves behind the being that is situated in its nature." Because of which, the proper order is to be observed in all things. Wherefore the poet says: "Order is the highest boundary in the art of the wise." Therefore Philosophy says: "that which by a headlong path..." Note: every agent in acting ought to set before himself a good end, because the agent is worthy by reason of a good end and is unworthy by reason of a bad end. Wherefore the poet: "Reward is not given after the beginnings for an example that is not good. Long..."

# Book One

You sang—that is <note>original: *i. [id est]*</note>, you said—this also a little while ago—that is, in the fifth meter of this first book. For you also deplored—that is, you lamented—only that human beings themselves were exempt—that is, lacking or not participating—in divine care—that is, divine providence. For you were not moved at all—that is, you did not doubt—concerning other creatures, that they were ruled by reason—that is, by the providence of God. Or "But oh!"—this is an interjection of wonder. I wonder vehemently that you, being placed—that is, situated—in such a healthy sentiment, are sick—that is, weak. "But"—that is, but we—"let us search more deeply"—that is, more profoundly. I do not know what it may be, but I suspect—that is, I am of the opinion—that something is missing from you.

<margin>Note that Boethius's infirmity was partly from a disordered affection, insofar as Boethius grieved over the loss of temporal things, and partly from a false estimation regarding two things. For he estimated that evil men were happy and powerful. Second, he estimated that men were not ruled by divine providence. Therefore, Philosophy searches for the radical <term>radical: from the Latin 'radix' meaning root</term> cause for which Boethius fell into these troubles.</margin>

<column-break/>

**Philosophy:** "So it is," she said. "For you even sang that a little while ago, and you lamented that humans alone were devoid of divine care. For concerning the rest, you were not moved to doubt that they were ruled by reason. But oh! I wonder greatly why you, established in such a healthy belief, are sick. **But** let us search more deeply; I suspect there is something missing—I know not what. **But** tell me: since you do not doubt that the world is ruled by God, by what rudders do you perceive it to be governed?" **Boethius:** "I recognize the meaning of your question," I said, "yet I cannot yet respond to the inquiries." **Philosophy:** "Was I right," she asked, "that something is missing, through which, as if through an opening in a strong wall, the disease of perturbations has crept into your mind?"

<column-break/>

Because the root of the whole sickness was ignorance of divine governance concerning humans, she first asks about the governance of the world. Note that Boethius hints at two reasons why the world is ruled by God. The first is: "Such certain things." Those things that are certain and determined are not ruled by chance and fortune, as the governance of such things would be uncertain. But the beings of this world are certain because they are produced by certain causes. She hints at the second reason: "Truly, to His own work," which is this: a thing caused is ruled by its cause. But God is the cause of the world, since the heavens and all nature depend on Him. Therefore, etc. Note that Philosophy reasonably marvels that Boethius, believing the world is ruled by God, thought humans were not ruled by Him. For Philosophy could argue thus: God rules the world according to you, Boethius. But humans are the principal part of the world, as you said before in the meter: "a part of so great a work." Therefore humans are ruled by God. "But tell me, since [you do not doubt] the world is ruled by God..." Here Philosophy asks about the circumstances of the world's governance. Second, because governed things are directed to their end, she asks secondly about the end of things. And because God's governance in truth also concerns humans, she asks thirdly about the knowledge of man. The second point begins: "But tell me." The third point begins: "But this also." First she says: "But O Boethius, tell me, since you do not doubt"—that is, you do not hesitate—"that the world is ruled"—that is, governed—"by God, do you also notice..."

<margin>Note that God does not rule the world with any external rudders, because then He would not be most self-sufficient. This will be clear in the second [book] of this work. Note that what a person scarcely understands, they do understand in some way, though with difficulty. Note that when the strength of the rampart of any fortification gapes open because of some breach made in it, then enemies enter the fortification. Similarly, when the fortification of reason, by which the mind is fortified like a rampart, gapes open because of a lack of some knowledge, then necessarily the disturbances of the emotions secretly enter the mind. "But tell me, do you remember." # Book One

...for whose sake other things are made. Because when the end <note>The "end" (*finis*) here means the ultimate purpose or goal.</note> is unknown, nothing is perfectly understood of those things which lead to that end; for all other things are regulated according to the requirements of the end. Note that when the beginning and the end coincide as one, just as in a circle the beginning and the end are the same, it then seems miraculous that the beginning is known while the end remains unknown. Since God is both the beginning and the end of all things, the knowledge of Him under the aspect of a "beginning" should also be known under the aspect of an "end." Moreover, that God is the beginning of all things is evident because from Him is derived the being and life of every individual—first of the heavens and the world. That He is the end of all things is evident because all things are made for His sake and are ordered toward Him. For in things consisting of art and nature, the lesser is always for the sake of the better; and God is the best of those things that exist in nature, according to the preamble of the *Metaphysics* <note>A reference to Aristotle’s work on the nature of existence.</note>. Note that although those who are disturbed may have some knowledge of things, they are nevertheless hindered from knowing perfectly. Therefore, although Boethius knew in some way that God was the beginning of things, because he was disturbed, he did not perfectly know the nature of this beginning, and thus he was ignorant that God is the end of all things. Note that "passion" is a movement of the desiring part of the soul under the imagination of good and evil, according to Eustratius <note>Eustratius of Nicaea, a 12th-century commentator on Aristotle’s *Ethics*.</note> in the second book of the *Ethics*. It is the nature of these passions that they can move men away from the stability of perfect knowledge, but they cannot totally uproot a person from all knowledge.

Boethius: "Is this what you are asking? Whether I know myself to be a rational and mortal animal? <note>This was the standard medieval definition of a human being, derived from Aristotle.</note> I know it, and I confess that this is what I am." Philosophy: "And do you know nothing else that you are?" Boethius: "Nothing." Philosophy: "Now I know," she said, "another—indeed the greatest—cause of your sickness: you have ceased to know who you yourself are."**

...they are hindered from knowing perfectly. It is the nature of these passions that they can move men away from the stability of perfect knowledge, but they cannot totally uproot him from all knowledge. 

**But I would also like you to answer this.** Here, Philosophy asks another question regarding the knowledge of human nature, saying: "But I would also like you to answer this, to give this response: do you remember—that is, do you know—that you are a man?" I, Boethius, said: "Why—that is, for what reason—should I not remember—that is, know?" And Philosophy asks further: "Therefore... could you set forth—that is, say—what a man is—that is, give the definition of a man?" Boethius responds: "Philosophy, are you asking me this—that is, whether I know myself to be a rational and mortal animal? I, Boethius, know and confess—that is, I admit—that I am that (supply: a rational and mortal animal)." Boethius says "nothing" (supply: further), and Philosophy said: "Now I know another cause—supply: besides the ignorance of divine providence—indeed the greatest cause of your sickness: you have ceased—that is, stopped—to know who you are." 

Note that although a man is mortal according to the body, he is not so according to the intellectual soul, which is the more dignified part of man. And because Boethius said he was nothing other than a "rational and mortal animal," he therefore sought nothing but mortal goods, over the loss of which he grieved. He did not care for the immortal part, namely the rational soul, whose immortal goods he should have desired. Therefore Philosophy says that Boethius does not know himself. Note that the greatest cause of a man's sickness is to be ignorant of himself. For Boethius says in the second book of this work, in the fifth prose, that the condition of human nature is such that it only excels other things when it knows itself. But when it ceases to know itself...

# Prose 6

<columns>2</columns>

If it should cease [to know itself], by that same nature it is reduced to something below a beast. For while it is natural for other living creatures to be ignorant of themselves, in humans it becomes a vice. And Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek philosopher and rhetorician</note> says in his work *On the Soul*: "What is more shameful than for the soul, while it is the knower of other things, to be ignorant of itself? If the soul is ignorant of itself, how can it be trusted as a reliable knower of other things?" He would say: in no way at all. Therefore, most fully... Here Philosophy, based on the words of Boethius, gathers all the causes of his entire infirmity.

<margin>that is</margin>
**Therefore, I have most fully found either the reason for your sickness or the approach for restoring your health. For because you are confounded by the forgetting of yourself, you have grieved that you are an exile and stripped of your own goods. Because you are truly ignorant of what the end goal of things is, you judge wicked and nefarious men to be powerful and happy. Because you have truly forgotten by what rudders the world is ruled, you think these shifts of fortune float along without a driver. These are great causes, leading not only to disease but even to death.**

<column-break/>

Philosophy says: "Therefore, I, Philosophy, have most fully—that is, most perfectly—found the reason (the cause) of your sickness (your infirmity), or I have found the approach (the access) for restoring your health (the recovery of your well-being)." She explains this: "Because you are confounded (confused) by the forgetting (the ignorance) of yourself, you have grieved that you are an exile and stripped (deprived) of your own goods (your riches). Because you are ignorant (you do not know) what the end goal of all things is, you judge (you think)

<column-break/>

that worthless (evil) and nefarious (iniquitous) men are powerful and happy. Because you have forgotten by what rudders (what systems of governance) the world itself is ruled, you estimate (you are of the opinion) that these shifts (these alterations) of fortune (of fortuitous events) float along (drift) without a driver." These are great causes, not only for disease, but they lead to death (the death or perdition of the soul). Note: a man who is ignorant of himself is placed outside the limits of right reason; such a person is said to be an "exile," as was seen before. Note: a man ignorant of himself, by thinking himself to be merely mortal, grieves over the loss of mortal things. Therefore Philosophy says: "Because you are confounded by forgetting, you grieved that you were an exile and stripped of your own goods." Note: a man is called powerful or powerless based on the pursuit or loss of the ultimate end (as seen in Book 4); because Boethius was ignorant of the ultimate end of things, he therefore thought the wicked were powerful. Note: Boethius was ignorant of the rudders by which the world is ruled; therefore he was ignorant that God disposes all things by His goodness, and thus he thought the shifts of fortune were without a driver.

But thanks be to the Author of health. Here Philosophy shows that Boethius is curable by providing the method for proceeding with his cure, saying: "Give thanks to the Author of health (of your well-being), because your nature (your natural vigor) has not yet entirely destitute (deserted) you. We, Philosophy, have the greatest kindling (the root) of your safety (your health): namely, the true opinion (the understanding) of the world's governance, which you believe..."

...the eyes, which are not able to penetrate the waves of the sea. Then it presents the third example: A "river"—that is, a stream—which "wanders"—that is, runs—"from high mountains," "it often stops"—that is, turns back—"by the obstacle"—that is, by the opposition—"of a loosened stone"—that is, a broken rock—"from the cliff"—that is, from the mountain. The analogy which Philosophy intends is this: Just as the stars accustomed to shine for us and illuminate the earth cease to do so because of the dark intervention of clouds, so the intellect and reason, which shine and illuminate man in the knowledge of truth, are hindered by the gloom of perturbations. Note that the analogy of the second example consists in this: just as the seawater remaining clear like glass allows the sight to penetrate it and see what is under the water, if it is disturbed by the wind, it then obstructs the sight. So the mind of a man at rest does not hinder the judgment of reason, but if it is moved and disturbed by the affection of temporal things, it immediately opposes reason, hindering its judgment. The analogy of the third example is this: Just as water running from high mountains proceeds freely on a straight path and is hindered from proceeding straight by the obstacle of a stone that falls from the mountain, so free reason, not hindered, judges correctly; but if reason is affected by the movements of the passions, it is hindered in its judgment and the knowledge of truth. Note that a "cliff" <note>original: "rupes"</note> is a stony mass or a stony mountain, while a "shard" <note>original: "sarx/sarum"</note> is a part broken off from the cliff, that is, from the mountain. "You also, if you wish." Here Philosophy exhorts to the flight from perturbations or affections of the mind, saying: if you wish to discern—that is, to see or judge—the true—that is, the truth...

# Book One

...by clear light, that is, by **true knowledge**. And if you also wish to grasp, that is, to reach the path—meaning the way of truth—by a straight track—meaning by the process of reason—then you must drive out, that is, repel, **joys** <gloss>supply: those which come from present goods</gloss> and drive out, that is, remove from yourself, **fear** <gloss>supply: concerning future evil</gloss>. Because <note>original: "q3" for "quia"</note> for "and," you must also put to flight **hope** <gloss>supply: which is for good fortune</gloss>, nor should **sorrow** be present <gloss>supply: which comes from the present loss of goods</gloss>. For the mind is cloudy, that is, dark or covered, and bound—meaning tied with reins or bonds—whenever these aforementioned things reign, that is, dominate within it: namely, joy for present goods, fear of future evil, hope for future good, and sorrow for present evil. 

**Note** that as was touched upon before, an **affection** <term>affection: a movement or "feeling" in the soul</term> is a movement of the sensitive part of the soul under a mental image <note>original: "fantasia"</note> of good or evil, affecting the mind and hindering the right judgment of reason. There are four such principal affections to which all others are reduced: namely, **joy**, **hope**, **fear**, and **sorrow**. Their classification is understood as follows: 

Every passion is either in respect to a good or an evil. If it is in respect to a **good**, this happens in two ways: either in respect to a present good, which is **joy**; or in respect to an absent good, which is **hope** for a future good. If, however, the passion is in respect to an **evil**, this also happens in two ways: either in respect to a present evil, which is **sorrow**; or in respect to an absent evil, which is **fear** of a future evil. 

**Note** that these passions are not to be driven out so that they simply do not exist in the human soul, for a person is scarcely ever found without them; rather, they are to be driven out so that they do not *rule* over the person. Therefore, it is the mark of a virtuous person to settle their passions so they do not dominate, because virtue consists in the moderation of the passions. If they reign and dominate in a person, they hinder the judgment of reason. Because of this, **Eustratius** <note>Eustratius of Nicaea, a 12th-century commentator on Aristotle's Ethics</note> says in his book on the *Ethics*: "It is necessary to struggle against the sensitive passions; if they prevail, they hinder the powers of the soul." 

**Note** that these passions and affections are harmful if they are directed toward earthly things; however, they can be meritorious and virtuous if they are directed toward their proper ends. Hence **Richard** <note>Richard of Saint Victor, a prominent 12th-century mystical theologian</note> says in his book *On the Twelve Patriarchs*: "We have ordered and true joy when we rejoice in true and eternal goods." Likewise, fear is virtuous if it is directed toward God, because it is written: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom* <note>Psalm 111:10; Proverbs 1:7</note>. And the same Richard says: "The first offspring of the virtues, without which no certainty can be held, is the fear of God." Likewise, hope, as the same Richard says, becomes "ordered" if it is born from the indulgence of forgiveness. Hence he says: "Truly and without doubt, the more frequently and vehemently someone is affected by sorrow for their internal guilt, the more certain and secure they become through hope for the indulgence of forgiveness." Similarly, sorrow is virtuous when it is done to lament a fault. Hence Richard says: "The more vehemently someone fears the punishment they deserved, the more bitterly they mourn the fault they committed."

---

->**Here ends the first book.**<-

<margin>After these things she was silent for a little while.</margin> This is the second book of Boethius on the **Consolation of Philosophy**, which continues from the preceding book in this manner: After Philosophy investigated the radical causes <note>The "root" or fundamental causes</note> of Boethius's infirmity in the first book, in this second book she proceeds to his cure. First, she applies light remedies to him; second, she applies stronger remedies in the following books. For Philosophy promised this method of healing to Boethius.

## First Prose of the Second Book.

After these things she was silent for a little while; and when she gathered my attention with a modest silence, she thus began. **Philosophy**: "If I have thoroughly known the causes and the state of your sickness, you are wasting away with affection <term>affection: a strong emotional pull or state of mind</term> and longing for your former fortune. That change alone, as you imagine it, has subverted the state of your mind.

<column-break/>

This book is divided into sixteen parts because there are eight prose sections and eight meters in this second book; these parts will become clear, and similarly, it will be seen what is dealt with in each part. The first prose is divided: First, it shows what Philosophy did after the aforementioned things and resumes one cause of Boethius's grief. Second, Philosophy sets forth a certain effect of Fortune. Third, she excuses herself from a certain matter. Fourth, she touches upon the opportunity for healing Boethius. Fifth, she proceeds to his light medicines. The second part begins at: *I understand*. The third at: *But as I think*. The fourth at: *But it is time*. The fifth at: *It is so, therefore, O Boethius*.

First she says: **After these things** <note>original: "Post hec"</note> which were said, Philosophy **was silent** <note>original: "obticuit"</note>, that is, she kept still **for a little while** <note>original: "paulisper"</note>, that is, for a small amount of time; **and when** <note>original: "atque ubi"</note>, that is, after she **gathered** <note>original: "collegit"</note>, meaning she understood, **my attention** <note>original: "attentionem meam"</note>, meaning my diligence, **with a modest silence** <note>original: "modesta taciturnitate"</note>, meaning a temperate stillness, she **began** <note>original: "exorsa est"</note>, meaning she started to speak **thus**, that is, in this way: **If** <note>original: "si"</note> because I have **known the causes** <note>original: "cognovi causas"</note>, that is, the radical reasons, **and also** <note>original: "que"</note> for "and," the **state** <note>original: "habitum"</note>, meaning the disposition of your **sickness** <note>original: "egritudinis"</note>, meaning your infirmity, **you**, Boethius, **are wasting away** <note>original: "tabescis"</note>, meaning you are saddened, by the **affection** <note>original: "affectu"</note> and **longing** for your **former fortune** which was once prosperous for you; **that fortune**, having been **changed** <note>original: "mutata"</note>, meaning varied in your eyes, **has subverted** <note>original: "pervertit"</note>, meaning changed, the **state** <note>original: "statum"</note>, meaning the disposition of **your mind** <note>original: "tui animi"</note>, just **as you imagine it for yourself**.

**Note** that Philosophy was silent after the aforementioned things so that Boethius might be better able to gather the words of Philosophy with a deliberate mind and answer her. For according to **Seneca** in his *Proverbs*: "To deliberate on useful things, delay is the safest path." Whatever must be done should be deliberated upon for a long time. Discuss once what you hear, and discuss the words you believe. Therefore, Philosophy was silent as if tired from the questions previously moved. Hence, Seneca in the book *On the Cardinal Virtues* says: "Do not always be in action; rather, at times give your mind a ruler, and let that rest be full of wisdom." 

**Note** what she says regarding "modest silence." Silence is twofold: one kind is **moderate**, the other is **superfluous**. Moderate silence is when one is silent when silence is required; of this, Seneca speaks in his *Proverbs*, saying: "Always hold a balance of voice and silence; yet in this, apply yourself more willingly so that you may listen more gladly than you speak. For he who knows not how to be silent, knows not how to speak." Superfluous silence is when one is silent when one ought to speak; of this, the Poet says: "For to have been too silent is harmful." 

**Note** that Boethius, in his state of misery, was not **magnanimous** <term>magnanimous: "great-souled," or possessing spiritual strength and courage</term> because he had a mind subverted by Fortune. For a magnanimous person is one whose constancy fights as a unified mind against the deformed assaults of Fortune, according to **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus</note> in the book of the *Ethics*. And Seneca, in his first letter to Lucilius, says: "I think the first argument of a composed mind is that it can stay still and dwell with itself." 

**Note** that Philosophy says Fortune has been "changed" regarding Boethius "as he imagines it." She says this because, according to the truth of the matter, Fortune had not changed regarding him, as Philosophy will prove below.

**I understand the many forms.** Here Philosophy sets forth the effect of Fortune, saying: **I understand**, that is...

For a square body, wherever it is thrown, stands firmly, just as the mind of a wise man remains constant whatever fortune is looming. **Note:** The rest of the soul occurs through the calming of the passions, which is caused by the ordering of reason with deliberation. ---

"Every sudden change of things does not happen without a conflict of minds." But it is time for you to drink something. Here Philosophy touches upon the opportunity for healing Boethius himself, saying: "But it is time"—that is, it is urgent—for you, Boethius, "to drink"—that is, to receive—and also to "taste something mild"—that is, easy—and also "pleasant"—that is, delightful—which, being light or delightful when "transmitted to the interior"—namely, of your soul—will "make a way for stronger draughts"—that is, for stronger remedies. She invites Rhetoric for the sake of its presence, in which she uses persuasive reasons adorned with rhetorical colors. She invites Music for the sake of the meter; for just as in music we use "rising and falling" <note>original: *arsis et thesis*. These refer to the upward and downward beats in music or poetic meter.</note>—that is, the harmonious raising and lowering of the voice—so similarly in meter we use raising when long syllables are lifted, and we use lowering when short syllables are depressed by a certain proportional harmony. **Note:** Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the preface to his *Rhetoric* that eloquence without wisdom can often be harmful, but never beneficial. Since, therefore, rhetoric is the science of speaking ornately, it does not benefit without wisdom. Therefore, Philosophy says that rhetoric then proceeds on the right path when it does not desert our laws, which are the laws and teachings of wisdom. "What is it then, O man?" Here Philosophy applies "gentle medicines" to Boethius. **Note:** "Gentle medicines" or remedies are called those arguments taken according to the common usage of men, persuading that one should not grieve over the adversity of fortune. But "stronger remedies" are the arguments that go against the common opinion of men, showing what the Supreme Good is and in what it consists.

# Book Two

Section 7: How one arrives at the truth, and how the evil are powerless and the good are powerful, and similar matters. First, therefore, Philosophy shows that one should not grieve for Fortune because she preserves her own nature regarding him; she demonstrates this with five persuasive reasons. She places the second reason at the point: **"if you approve"**; the third at: **"but whether"**; the fourth at: **"but if neither"**; and the fifth at: **"finally, with an even mind."** <note>original: *postremo aequo animo*. **Note:** An "enticement" <note>original: *illecebra*</note> is an illicit carnal delight enticing a man, though the term may be found used for any other delight. **Note:** Just as a beast, a small bird, or a fish is deceived by the hope of delight, so a man is fallaciously ensnared by the delight of Fortune's prosperity. Hence Seneca says in his 8th Epistle: "I cry out: avoid <note>original: *vitate*</note> whatever chance has given; stand suspicious and fearful toward every fortuitous good, for the beast and the fish are deceived by some enticing hope." 

**Note:** The delights of Fortune are false; for according to Saint Augustine, the prosperities of this world have true bitterness, false joy, certain pain, and uncertain pleasure. 

**Note:** Philosophy calls Fortune a "blind deity" <term>numen: a Latin word for a divinity or divine power</term>. Huguitio <note>A 12th-century grammarian often cited in medieval commentaries.</note> says that *numen* means God himself, or the power or majesty of God; but here it is taken for the goddess whom the ancients used to worship as Fortune. 

**Note:** Regarding the statement that Fortune is blind, Cicero <note>referred to here by his family name, Tullius.</note> says in the book *On Friendship*: "Fortune, like an ignorant physician, has blinded many; for because she is blind, she usually makes those blind whom she has embraced." 

**Note:** In ancient times, Fortune was depicted with a double face: bald and hairy. By her baldness, adversity was designated; by her hairiness, prosperity. Therefore Philosophy says: "you have discovered her ambiguous faces."

Note that **security** <term>security: here meaning *securitas*, a state of mental calm or freedom from care</term> delights a man most of all; for which reason it is to be sought. And **Boethius** will say later that the most unhappy kind of misfortune is to have been happy. **But if she can neither be retained by your will.** Here she posits the fourth reason, which is as follows: That which is a judgment of future misery is neither dear nor precious, nor consequently should one grieve for it. Fortune by wanting to impose a law of staying and leaving. **If you were to commit your sails to the winds.** Here she proves her statement through certain likenesses: namely, that Fortune is not in the power of man, saying: "If you were to commit the sails of a ship to the wind, you would be led not where your will sought (that is, desired), but where the blast of the wind drove you. If you trusted (that is, committed) seeds to the plowed fields (that is, the lands), you would weigh (that is, judge) the fruitful (that is, fertile) years and the sterile ones against each other," so that you would not have those years in your power. By a similar reasoning, you gave yourself to be guided [by Fortune]; it is necessary that you submit (that is, obey) the ways of your mistress. But (using *vero* for *sed*) you attempt (that is, labor) to hold back the force (that is, the course) of the turning wheel (that is, of movable Fortune), and you labor in vain. O most dull-witted (that is, most foolish) of all mortals, do you not know that if luck (that is, Fortune) begins to remain (that is, to be stable), then it ceases (that is, desists) to be luck? For just as it cannot simultaneously be true that someone is a human and is not rational, so it cannot simultaneously be true that something is Fortune and is not changeable. **Note** that just as one committing a sail to the wind is no longer in his own power to be led where he wishes, but is led according to the force of the wind; and just as one committing seeds to a field does not have it in his power that fertile or sterile years should result; so, by a similar reasoning, he who commits himself to Fortune does not have it in his power to have either prosperous or adverse Fortune. **Note** regarding this where it mentions the **turning wheel** <term>turning wheel: the *Rota Fortunae*, a common medieval symbol of the instability of worldly rank</term>, that in ancient times Fortune was depicted with a wheel for this reason: for in a wheel there are four different parts. One part is the highest; another the lowest; a third by which one descends from the top to the bottom; a fourth by which one ascends from the bottom to the top. Similarly, among men four variations are found. For some are in the highest prosperity, and such people are raised up on the wheel of Fortune. Others are in the highest adversity, and such people lie cast down beneath the wheel. A third group declines from prosperity into adversity, and such people descend from the summit of the wheel. A fourth group proceeds from adversity into prosperity, and such people ascend the wheel of Fortune. Hence, the one raised on the wheel of Fortune says: "I boast, having been raised up." The one descending says: "I descend, brought low." The one cast down says: "I am lowest on the axle of the wheels." The one ascending says: "I am chosen to be carried to the heights." <note>These four phrases—*Glorior elatus, Descendo mortificatus, Infimus axe rotarum, Lectus ad alta vehor*—were standard captions for the four figures usually drawn on a Wheel of Fortune.</note>

<summary>This page explains that Fortune is by definition changeable; to expect her to stay still is as illogical as expecting a sail to go against the wind. It introduces the famous imagery of the Wheel of Fortune, describing the four states of human life: rising, reigning, falling, and being without a kingdom.</summary>

# Book Two.

**Note** that nature does not grow accustomed to the contrary. For if a stone were thrown upward a thousand times, it does not "learn" to ascend, since its nature is to descend. Therefore, just as it would be most foolish for someone to labor to take away the nature of a thing, so it is foolish for one to labor to take away from Fortune its mutability—which is its very nature. Therefore Philosophy says, "O most dull-witted of all."

### First Meter of the Second Book.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>h</margin>ere, when she with proud right hand has turned her changes. This begins the first meter of this second book, which is called *yponauticum* <note>original: "yponauticum"; likely a medieval term for a "rowing song" or rhythmic meter</note> from its inventor, because the labor of sailors is lightened by the singing of this kind of meter. It is also called iambic meter from the predominant "foot" or beat. An iamb is a foot contrary to a trochee, consisting of a short first syllable and a long final one. It is called a "trimeter" meter: for although this meter has six feet, yet by counting

<column-break/>

### First Meter of Book Two.

## When she with proud right hand has turned her changes
## She is moved like the surging Euripus <note>A strait in Greece famous for its violent, shifting currents.</note>
## She, cruel, tramples kings once dreaded
## And, deceitful in face, lifts the lowly defeated.
## She neither hears soft prayers nor cares for wretched tears;
## Harsh, she mocks the groans she herself caused.
## Thus she plays, thus she proves her strength,
## And shows her followers a great marvel:
## If anyone is seen in one hour both prostrate and happy.

---

two feet as one measure <note>original: "metro"</note>, it will be a trimeter. In this meter, Philosophy describes the character of Fortune, saying: "This," namely Fortune, "has turned her changes," that is, the alternations of prosperity and adversity, "with a proud right hand." and when "she is moved like the surging Euripus," that is, like an overflowing sea, then "cruel Fortune," that is, bloody or harsh, "tramples," that is, crushes, "kings once dreaded," that is, feared. And she herself "lifts the lowly defeated"; she "neither hears soft prayers nor cares for the wretched," that is, the poor. And being "harsh," because she is not bent to the will of men, she "mocks," that is, derides, "spontaneously the groans of the wretched which she herself caused." "Thus she plays, thus she proves," that is, experiences, "her strength." She "shows her followers a great marvel," that is, a miracle, "if anyone is seen in one hour prostrate," that is, cast down by adversity, "and happy," that is, raised by prosperity. As if to say: Fortune seems to display a false—that is, a great miracle to men who gape at her goods—whenever someone is suddenly seen to change from adversity to prosperity and vice versa.

**Note** that Fortune is called "proud" because she fears no one, nor does she pay attention to the honesty or malice of anyone; and if she is called upon in the manner of the proud, she turns a deaf ear.

**Note** that "Euripus," according to some, is a whirlwind; and it is called Euripus as if it were a "rapid Eurus" <note>Eurus is the name of the East Wind</note>. According to others, however—and perhaps better—the Euripus is an arm or bay of the sea whose flow is uncertain, and because of the uncertainty of its course, ships are frequently endangered there. It is named from *eu*, which means "good," and *ripa*, meaning "bank," as if it were a "good bank" by way of contrast <note>This is a medieval linguistic device called "antiphrasis," where a thing is named by its opposite quality—like calling a dangerous shore "the good shore."</note>. Just as the course of the surging Euripus is uncertain, so too is the mutability of Fortune.

**Note** regarding the operation of Fortune, how she raises some and depresses others. Alanus <note>Alanus de Insulis (c. 1128–1202), a famous medieval theologian and poet.</note> speaks in the *Anticlaudianus*, saying: "She moves her headlong wheel and the labor of its motion / No rest closes it, nor do leisures stop the movement. / These she presses down, those she lifts; these she casts down, those she raises / And she forces men into various..."

## Prose Two of the Second Book.

<margin>
Note that a similarity of speech sometimes generates boredom; therefore, it is sometimes necessary to change the style. For this reason, Julius <note>likely the rhetorician Gaius Julius Victor</note> says in the fourth book of his Rhetoric: "the style in speaking ought to be changed so that satiety may easily be avoided by variety." Therefore, Philosophy here varies her speech through the introduction of a new person, using *prosopopeia* <term>prosopopeia: a rhetorical device where an abstract concept or an absent person is represented as speaking</term>, which figure is called "personification" by Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the famous Roman orator</note>. Therefore, Philosophy prepares Boethius for the introduction of Fortune, saying: "I would, however," etc.

**"I would, however, like to discuss a few things with you using the words of Fortune herself. You, therefore, consider whether justice demands it. Why do you, O human, bring me as a defendant in your daily complaints? What injury have we done to you? What goods of yours have we taken away? Contend with me before any judge you like regarding the possession of riches and dignities. When nature brought you forth naked from your mother’s womb, I received you as one destitute of all things; I cherished you with my riches; and—which now makes you impatient with us—I educated you with a leaning toward indulgent favor. And I surrounded you with the abundance and splendor of all things that are under my law. Now it pleases me to withdraw my hand: you should give thanks as one who has used things belonging to another. You have no right of complaint, as if you had lost your own things entirely."**

**Law** it is for the sea now to be smooth and calm with a level surface; now to grow rough with gales and waves.

Note that when Croesus, King of the Lydians, was about to fight against the King of the Persians, he consulted Apollo concerning the success of the battle; Apollo responded to him with this little verse: <note>original: "Cresus perdet alim transgressus plurima regna"</note> "Croesus, having crossed the Halys, shall destroy many kingdoms." The <term>Halys</term> is a certain river. Croesus understood the verse to mean that he, having crossed the Halys, would destroy (that is, demolish) many kingdoms belonging to Cyrus. But Apollo intended it thus: Croesus, having crossed the Halys, would destroy (that is, lose) many of his own kingdoms. And this is what happened; for when he had crossed the Halys, he was defeated by Cyrus and placed in the fire. But such a great downpour of rain occurred that the fire was extinguished and he escaped. Concerning this, when he was boasting greatly, his daughter named Fausta said: "Wait for the final day, before which no one should boast." <note>This echoes the famous warning of Solon to Croesus: "Count no man happy until he is dead."</note> Indeed, one night Croesus saw in a dream that he was atop a tall tree, where Jupiter watered him and Phoebus dried him. When he related this dream to his daughter, she replied: "You will be captured by Cyrus and suspended on a cross, where Jupiter (that is, the rain) will water you, and Phoebus (that is, the sun) will dry you." Which ultimately came to pass. From this, the mutability of Fortune can be weighed. Note that Paullus, the Roman consul, was sent to fight against the King of the Persians who was the proudest of men. When he had defeated him, considering his past prosperity and present adversity, he was moved by pity and wept over him and released him; from this, the mutability of Fortune is similarly weighed. Note that <term>tragedy</term> is a song censuring vices, beginning in prosperity and ending in adversity. It is named from <term>tragos</term> in Greek, which is <term>hircus</term> (goat) in Latin, and <term>odos</term> (song); because the singer of this poem was rewarded with a goat. Or as the tragic poets say, they look upon the ancient deeds and crimes of wicked kings in a mournful song before the people.

...the great citadels of Carthage, and **Scipio** <note>Scipio Aemilianus, the Roman general who destroyed Carthage</note>: but many are the Romans of another fate. These examples of others teach you, and your own deeds will teach you.

### The Second Meter of the Second Book.

**If as many as the sea churns up with rapid gusts.** This is the second meter of this second book, which is called "Asclepiadean" from its inventor, and "Choriambic" from its predominant rhythmic foot. What a "choriambic" foot is has been discussed before. That meter consists of a first spondee, two choriambs, and a pyrrhic or an iamb. This is the same meter as that hymn: **The glorious joys of the merits of the Saints.** The second part of the meter is called Pherecratean <note>original: 'ferragratium'</note> from its inventor, consisting of a first spondee, a second dactyl, and a third spondee or trochee. In this meter, therefore, Fortune complains about the insatiable greed of men, saying: If Plenty (that is, Fortune, whom the pagans called the goddess of abundance) should pour out so much wealth for men from a full horn as the sands the sea (that is, the ocean) churns (that is, rolls), driven (that is, moved) by rapid gusts (that is, impetuous winds); and if she poured out as much wealth as the stars that shine in the sky, produced (that is, risen) on starry nights, and Abundance herself does not pull back her hand by taking wealth away—using "hardly" <note>original: 'haud'</note> for "not"—the human race does not for that reason cease to weep (that is, by weeping to set forth) wretched complaints. And although God is lavish (that is, rich with much gold, pouring out much gold in the manner of a prodigal), and God himself willingly receives the prayers of men and honors the greedy (that is, those full of desire) with bright honors, if things already sought (that is, acquired) and...

### ¶ The Third Prose of the Second Book.

...[discusses]. Greed involves a desire for money which no wise person has ever craved. For it, coming with evils, once imbued, harms both the body and the manly spirit. For it, remaining insatiable, is diminished neither by abundance nor by lack. And in the same place he says: "What is it that many are driven by a desire for money, whose minds are so disturbed that they are not far from madness?" And Seneca says in letter 75: "Greed never has a greater evil except that it is ungrateful." And in letter 74, he compares the greedy to dogs, saying: "Have you seen a dog, sent by its master, catching pieces of bread or meat with an open mouth? Whatever it catches, it immediately swallows whole and always gapes in hope of the next piece." The same thing happens to us: whatever Fortune holds out to us as we wait, we let go of it without any satisfaction and immediately rise up to seize another's [wealth]. 

¶ Note: he who believes himself in need is not rich but poor, because Seneca says in the first letter: "Not he who has little, but he who desires more, is poor." For what does it matter how much lies in his chest or how much in his granaries, if he hangs over another's gaping mouth? <note>original: "alieno hiatu imminet" — a metaphor for eyeing someone else's property greedily</note> 

¶ Note that riches do not take away greed but increase it. Whence Seneca says in the seventeenth letter: "Let whatever the wealthy have possessed be gathered in you; let Fortune advance you beyond the private limit of money; let her cover you in gold, clothe you in purple, hide the earth with marbles; let statues and paintings be added, and whatever any art has labored over—you will [not] cease to desire greater things than these." Whence Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> [says]: "Meanwhile, as long as the money-bags swell with full coin, the love of money grows as much as the money itself grows."

### Third Prose.

<margin>b</margin>
**If, therefore, Fortune [spoke] for herself with you.** Here begins the third prose of this second book, in which Philosophy proves to Boethius that he ought not to complain about Fortune because she has bestowed many good things upon him. First, Philosophy inquires what he thinks of Fortune’s arguments. Second, she enumerates the goods of Fortune bestowed upon him, beginning at the words: *But nevertheless.* First, Philosophy shows that Boethius has nothing to say against Fortune. Second, Boethius responds. Third, Philosophy approves of his response, as will be seen. She says first: if Fortune spo—

**“If, therefore, Fortune were to speak with you on her own behalf in these words, you would surely have nothing to mutter against her. But if there is anything by which you might legally defend your complaint, you must bring it forward. We shall give you the opportunity to speak.” Boethius: Then I said, “These things are indeed beautiful, and smoothed over with the honey-sweetness of rhetoric and music; they delight only as long as they are heard. But for the wretched, the feeling of their evils is deeper. And so, when these sounds stop ringing in the ears, an ingrained sorrow weighs down the mind.” Philosophy: “And so it is,” she said. “For these are not yet the remedies for your disease.”**

<column-break/>

—ke with you in these words on her own behalf, you surely would not have anything to mutter against her <note>original: "hisceres"; literally 'to gape' or 'open the mouth'</note>—that is, you would not have a way to open your mouth to answer Fortune. And if there is anything by which you might legally defend your complaint, it is necessary—that is, required—that you bring it forward. We shall give you a place to speak. Then Boethius responds: "Those things which Fortune said are indeed beautiful, and they are smoothed over"—that is, softened with honey—"that is, with the delight of the sweetness of rhetoric"—namely, as far as the prose is concerned—"and of the sweetness of music"—namely, as far as the

---

meter—"and they only delight my mind as long as they are heard. But the sense"—that is, the perception—"of evils is deeper"—that is, more profound for the wretched than those words can reach. It is as if he says: though the words of Fortune delight me on the surface, they do not reach the depth of my pain. "And so"—that is, therefore—"when these words of Fortune have ceased"—that is, stopped—"to ring in my ears, an ingrained sorrow"—that is, one that has been let in—"weighs down my mind." Then Philosophy approves of Boethius's response, saying: "It is so. For these words of Fortune are not yet the remedies for your disease, but they are certain soothing applications"—that is, liniments—"against the healing"—that is, against the curing—"of a stubborn pain. For the remedies that penetrate"—that is, send themselves into the depth of your disturbances—"by expelling the root cause of your disease: these I will provide"—that is, apply—"when the time is right." 

Note that Boethius had nothing to say against the words of Fortune because she speaks the truth, and one must not speak against the truth. For all things harmonize with the truth, and the truth bears witness to itself, according to Aristotle <note>A reference to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*</note>. Note that *hiscere* <term>hiscere: to open the mouth to speak</term> is an inchoative verb <note>A verb expressing the beginning of an action</note> and is produced through syncopation, for regularly it should be said as *hiasco*; hence *hiscere* is to begin a "hiatus" or opening when someone opens their mouth. Note that *oblitus* <note>meaning 'forgotten'</note> with the second syllable long is the participle of the verb *obliviscor* (to forget). But *oblitus* with the second syllable short comes from the verb *oblino* (to smear), and *oblitus* is the same as "stained" or "smeared." Hence the verse: *The one who forgets is "oblitus" [forgotten], while "oblitus" is stained.*

# Book Two

Note regarding the statement that **ingrained sorrow weighs down the mind.** It happens to no one to not grieve over misfortune unless the mind is greatly elevated above fortune. As Seneca says in his 65th letter <note>original: "lxv. epl'a"; the quote is actually from Seneca’s 63rd Letter to Lucilius</note>: "I do not want you to grieve more, but I dare to encourage you, as a man, to stand tall so that you do not grieve." Such firmness of mind belongs to no one except those elevated far above fortune. And he adds: "Let us act so that the memory of those we have lost becomes pleasant to us. No one returns willingly to that which cannot be thought of without torment." Note that through the sweetness of rhetoric and music, Boethius has not yet been restored to virtue and wisdom; his sorrow weighing down his mind proves this. For **virtue and wisdom** suppress grief and sorrow. Whence Seneca says in the same 65th letter: "Just as the brightness of the sun obscures small lights, so wisdom and virtue, by their own greatness, crush and overwhelm pains, sorrows, and injuries."

**Nevertheless, do not wish to be considered wretched.** Here, Philosophy enumerates the "goods of Fortune" bestowed upon Boethius, by reason of which he ought not to consider himself miserable. First, she lists past goods that made him happy; later, in the fourth prose, she will list the goods that show him to be happy in the present. First, then, Philosophy describes his past happiness. Second, she excludes a certain objection (beginning at the words: *What if for that reason*). First, she lists certain common goods; second, more special ones (beginning at: *Moreover, it is pleasing*). First she says: "O Boethius, if you wish to consider yourself wretched, have you perhaps forgotten the number and measure of your happiness?" **I pass over**—that is, I move past—the fact that when you were **desolated**—that is, deprived of parents, both father and mother—the **care of the greatest men**—that is, the highest Romans—took you in. And you, **chosen**—that is, selected from among others—into **affinity with the princes of the city**, began to be **dear before you were a kinsman**, which is the most precious kind of relationship. Who will not proclaim you most happy with such **splendor of your fathers-in-law**, with such **modesty of your spouse**—that is, your wife—and with the **opportunity**—that is, the timely happiness—of **male offspring**? It is as if she says: there is no one who would not judge you happy in these things.

Note that there are three kinds of kinship:
1. That which is contracted from genealogy; in such a kinship, someone is called both a kinsman and "dear" at the same time, for a brother is both dear and a kinsman to a brother.
2. The kinship contracted from marriage, which is called **affinity**; in such kinship, someone is usually made a kinsman before they are made "dear."
3. The kinship contracted from **good character and virtues**; this is the most precious kind of kinship. In this type, someone is made **dear before they are made a kinsman**. Thus, Boethius was first made "dear" to the Roman princes by reason of his virtue before he became their kinsman by entering into marriage with them. Note that Philosophy says Boethius was—

<column-break/>

### —but there are still some gentle applications <term>fomenta</term> <note>These are "soothing applications" or "warm compresses," used here as a metaphor for light psychological comforts before the "stronger medicine" of hard philosophy is applied.</note> for a pain that is still stubborn <note>original: "contumacis"</note> against treatment. For those things that penetrate deep within, I shall remove when the time is right. **But nevertheless, lest you wish to be thought wretched: have you forgotten the number and measure of your happiness? I pass over how, when you were orphaned, the care of the greatest men took you in; and how you were chosen for affinity with the princes of the city, which is the most precious kind of kinship, you began to be dear before you were a kinsman. Who would not proclaim you most happy with such splendor of your fathers-in-law...**

# Prose 3

...happy in the brilliance of his **fathers-in-law** <note>original: "socerorum"</note> in the plural, even though he did not have more than one father-in-law, for a "father-in-law" is the man whose daughter someone marries, and it is not recorded that Boethius had two wives. Regarding this, it can be said that the term is used broadly here, not only for the wife’s father, but also for a brother-in-law who can also broadly be called a father-in-law. Therefore, she speaks of "fathers-in-law" in the plural. Note that Philosophy says Boethius was happy for three reasons: from the integrity of his fathers-in-law, from the modesty of his wife, and from the benefit...

...of his wife’s modesty: when she shall also proclaim the benefit of male offspring. **I pass over—for it pleases me to pass over common things—the dignities taken up in youth that are denied to the old; it delights me to come to the singular peak of your happiness. If any fruit of mortal things has any weight of blessedness, can the memory of that light be erased by any mass of encroaching evils, however great? When you saw your two children, both consuls, escorted from your home amid the gathering of the fathers** <note>The "fathers" refers to the Roman Senators</note> **and the enthusiasm of the common people; when, with them sitting in the curule chairs** <term>curule: an ivory folding seat that was a symbol of high magisterial power in Rome</term> **in the assembly, you, as an orator of royal praise, earned the glory of genius and eloquence: when**

<column-break/>

...of male offspring, that is, his own sons. **I pass over—for it pleases me to pass over common things.** Here, Philosophy enumerates certain spiritual goods for which Boethius should not consider himself wretched, and she says: "I pass over," that is, I wish to move past, "because I choose to pass over common goods, and it delights me to come to the special peak of your happiness," namely the honors taken up in youth which are denied to the old. And she adds: **If any fruit of mortal things has any weight of blessedness**, that is, if a man ought to be called happy because of some temporal good, **can the memory of that light**, that is, of your happiness which she now mentions, **be erased by any mass**, that is, by any weight of encroaching evils? What she says is: it cannot be erased. And what is that happiness? **When you saw your children**, that is, your sons, **together as consuls**, that is, elected as joint consuls, **escorted**, that is, led from your house amid the **gathering**, that is, the diligence of the fathers <note>the elders or senators</note> and amid the **enthusiasm**, that is, the joy of the common people. And **when you, with those same sons of yours sitting in the curule chairs**, that is, the judicial seats, **as an orator**, that is, a speaker of royal praise, earned the glory of genius and eloquence. When you, standing between them in the circus <note>The public arena where games were held</note>, that is, in the movement between the two consuls (your sons), satisfied the expectation of the surrounding multitude with a triumphal largesse, that is, a victory celebration. As I believe, you "gave words to," that is, deceived, Fortune, while she caressed you and cherished you as her own delight. You carried off a gift that she had never granted to any, that is, to any private person, that is, an outsider. **Do you wish to cast a count**, that is, a calculation, **with Fortune?** Now Fortune herself has first stung you with **envious eyes**, that is, jealous ones. If you consider the number and measure of the happy and the sad things, that is, of prosperity and adversity, you still cannot deny that you are happy.

---

Note that Philosophy, by saying "I pass over" and previously saying "I am silent," uses a certain rhetorical color called **occupatio** <term>occupatio: also known as praeteritio, a device where a speaker emphasizes a point by claiming to pass over it</term>. It is defined thus by Cicero <note>original: "tullio"</note>: "Occupatio occurs when we say we are passing over, or do not know, or do not wish to say that which we are nevertheless saying most emphatically." Note that it was formerly the Roman custom not to confer any dignity on anyone before thirty years of age, except for singular merit or integrity, or for the evident utility of the public state. Boethius, however, was elected consul in his youth, before the age of thirty. And this, Philosophy calls "common happiness."

# Book Two

...not because this was commonly granted to everyone, but because it happened not only to Boethius, but to a few others. For Tully <note>original: "Tullius," referring to the Roman statesman and author Cicero</note> relates in his *Book on Friendship* that Scipio was made consul twice before the age of thirty; similarly, Germanicus was made consul as a young man before thirty. But she touches upon the singular happiness of Boethius, saying: *When [you saw] the two consuls together.* Note that according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, an influential early medieval encyclopedist</note> in the book of *Etymologies*, there were "curule" seats <term>curule: an ivory folding chair used by high-ranking Roman magistrates as a symbol of their authority</term> in which the magistrates sat to deliver judgments.

And they are called "curule" from "chariot" <note>original: "currus"</note>, because the judges sat in such a chariot in which they were carried, so that they might more quickly deliver judgments to the people.
Note that it was the custom among the Romans in the election of consuls to deliver a speech to the people concerning the praises of the kings and those elected to the magistracy; and if he spoke well, he achieved glory from it. Boethius made a speech of this kind at the election of his sons as consuls.

<column-break/>

**...in the circus, standing between your two sons as consuls, you satisfied the expectation of the surrounding multitude with a triumphal largesse. You gave, as I think, words to Fortune while she caressed you, while she cherished you as her own darling. You took away an abundance of gifts such as she had never before entrusted to any private citizen. Do you wish, therefore, to settle the account with Fortune? Now, for the first time, she has grazed you with a jealous eye. If you were to consider the number and the measure of things happy or sad, you could not yet deny that you are fortunate.**

<column-break/>

...and from that his glory was doubled. And because a similar speech was accustomed to be made in triumphs in praise of those who had obtained victory, he therefore calls this kind of speech a "triumphal largesse." Note that he who promises some good and does not fulfill it "gives words" <note>original: "dat verba," a Latin idiom meaning to deceive or cheat</note> and not the actual thing, and thus he deceives. Therefore, Philosophy says, "you gave words to Fortune," that is, deceptions, by promising her some good because she so cherished you. Note that "calculus" <term>calculus: literally a small stone or pebble used by the ancients for counting or calculating accounts</term> in one sense is a small stone which does not hurt when stepped on. And because the ancients used such stones in computing, therefore "to calculate" or "to settle the account" <note>original: "calculum ponere"</note> is used for computing or for making a reckoning. Therefore Philosophy says, "Do you wish to settle the account with Fortune?" as if she were saying: you ought not to complain, for if you compute with her, she herself will find you much more happy than miserable.

*But if for that reason you [think] yourself [unfortunate]...* Here Philosophy excludes a certain objection. Someone might say: "these aforementioned goods do not make me happy because they are transitory." Philosophy excludes this objection, saying: *But if you do not estimate yourself fortunate*—that is, happy—because those things which then seemed joyful have gone away, you also should not estimate yourself miserable because those things which are now believed—that is, seen—to be gloomy are also passing away. *Have you come for the first time into this scene*—that is, the shadow of life—*sudden*—that is, unforeseen—and *a guest*—that is, a stranger—so that you ignore what goes on in this life? Or *do you think*—that is, do you judge—that there is any constancy in human affairs when the swift hour of death often dissolves man himself? For even if there is any faith in the permanence of the things of chance—though it be rare—yet the last day of life is a certain death for Fortune, even for a Fortune that remains. Therefore, what do you think *it matters*—that is, what is the difference—whether you desert that Fortune by dying, or it deserts you by fleeing? It is as if she were saying: it matters nothing as far as the inconstancy of Fortune is concerned; whether Fortune deserts the man or is deserted, it is manifest that it cannot remain.

<meta>This page concludes the prose discussion of Fortune’s fleeting nature and begins the commentary on the third meter of Book Two. It transitions from the historical examples of Boethius’s past successes to a philosophical argument on why earthly happiness cannot last, using celestial and natural metaphors to illustrate the inevitability of change.</meta>

Metrum 3.

¶ Note that in human affairs there is no constancy, the reason for which is: in that which is born <note>original: "genitum," referring to created or biological things</note>, there is no constancy, because nothing is born that is not also corruptible and non-permanent. But human things are born and produced; therefore, etc. It should be noted that the prosperity of fortune is not durable because adversity quickly puts it to flight. Whence Geoffrey <note>original: "Gaufredus," referring to Geoffrey of Vinsauf, a famous 13th-century medieval poet and rhetorician</note> in his *Poetic Art* says:
"Do not trust your riches if for a short time they shine upon you; for soon the clouds will be the closure of the serene sky." <note>original: "Dib⁹ ne crede tuis..." a common medieval cautionary verse about the fragility of peace</note>

**But if for this reason you do not consider yourself fortunate—because those things which then seemed happy have passed away—there is no reason why you should think yourself wretched; for the things which now seem sorrowful are also passing by. Did you come into this scene of life now for the first time as a guest? Do you think there is any constancy in human affairs, when a swift hour often dissolves man himself? For even if faith in remaining is rare for fortuitous things, the last day of life is nevertheless a kind of death even for a remaining fortune. What, therefore, do you think it matters whether you desert her by dying, or she deserts you by fleeing?**

# The Third Meter of the Second Book.

**When Apollo <note>original: "pheb⁹" (Phoebus), a title for the sun god</note> in the heavens with his rosy chariot begins to scatter the light, the star, dulled by the pressing flames, grows pale and loses its white countenance. When the grove, by the breath of the warm West Wind <note>original: "zephiri" (Zephyr)</note>, grows red with spring roses...**

[This meter is] trochaic <term>trochaic: a poetic meter consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one</term> from its dominant foot. But the second meter is called Glyconic <term>Glyconic: a form of Greek and Latin lyric meter</term> from its inventor, and Choriambic from its dominant foot. In this meter, Philosophy declares the mutability of worldly things by three examples. The first example is of the celestial bodies: while the sun shines in the sky, the light of the other stars is then obscured. Behold the change of the stars regarding their light, which nonetheless appeared before in the nighttime; but while the sun shines for us, it does not appear. Whence she says in the text "When Phoebus"—that is, the sun—"began to scatter"—that is, to send forth—"light with rosy chariots"—that is, in a rosy chariot—"the star dulled"—that is, obscured by the "flames"—that is, the lights of the sun "pressing upon it"—"it grows pale"—that is, it becomes pale according to its "white countenance." The second example is in the things born of the earth: when the West Wind blows, the earth is adorned with flowers, but when the South Wind <note>original: "austro" (Auster)</note> blows, the flowers fail. Behold the change in the things born of the earth...

<column-break/>

...the day, and twilight brings the nights <note>original: "inducuntqz crepuscula noctes"</note>. For which reason, no faith should be placed in fortuitous things. Note that Philosophy touches upon one reason and truth why fortune is not constant, which is this: man is not constant; therefore, neither is fortune. The premise is evident because the swift hour of death often dissolves men. The conclusion is proved by this: because fortune has no existence except regarding man, since it is found among those acting with a purpose (according to the second book of the *Physics* <note>original: "secūdo phisicorū," referring to Aristotle's *Physics*, where he discusses the nature of chance and luck</note>). Therefore, Philosophy says it makes no difference regarding the inconstancy of fortune whether fortune abandons man by fleeing, or man abandons it by dying; in whatever way it happens, she is always inconstant and non-permanent.

What kind of things the goods of fortune are is clear from this: because it is manifest and established—that is, stabilized—by eternal law—that is, divine law—that nothing born remains—that is, continues immutably. Note that the poets attribute a <term>quadriga</term> <note>A four-horse chariot</note> to the sun, which is named from the number of four horses. For the poets imagine the course of the sun to be pulled by four horses because of the four different states of the sun. For the sun when rising is red; at the third hour, shining; at the midday hour, burning; but at the evening hour, it is lukewarm. To the moon, however, they attribute a <term>biga</term> <note>A two-horse chariot</note> because of two properties of the moon; for the moon is naturally cold and humid. Note regarding this that it says "trust in fortuitous goods." Seneca says in the book *On the Consolation to Helvia* <note>The manuscript reads "filij elye," likely a scribal corruption of "Helviae," Seneca's mother</note>: "I never trusted fortune, who, when she seemed to act in peace with me, placed all those things which she most indulgently conferred upon me—money, honors, favor—in such a place from which she could take them back without disturbing me. I kept a great interval between myself and her; thus she neither took them away nor sent them out. Adverse fortune has crushed no one except him whom favorable fortune deceived. Fortune fears the brave; she terrifies the cowardly. She can take away wealth, but she cannot steal the soul." Note that Philosophy calls the goods of fortune "fleeting" <note>original: "caduca"</note>. This is what Seneca says in his 78th Epistle: "Because those things over which fortune exercises dominion are her own, just as money and honors; they are weak, fluid, mortal, and their states are uncertain."

Note that it says "nothing born is constant." Seneca says in the previously cited Epistle: "Because mortal things are diminished, they fall, they desert, they decrease, they are exhausted; thus in those things, because the cause is uncertain, there is inequality; but the nature of divine things is one." <margin>The fourth prose of the second book.</margin>

# Second Book

The punishment of a false opinion exists in the mind, not in the reality. Therefore, the misfortune of Boethius was not to be blamed on things, because it did not exist in them, but was to be blamed on his own false opinion.
