<meta>This page continues Philosophy’s argument that Boethius remains fortunate despite his exile. Having established that Boethius’s most precious "anchors"—his family—are safe, Philosophy now transitions into a broader philosophical critique of "well-composed happiness," arguing that no one is ever perfectly satisfied with their lot in life.</meta>

# Book Two

Note that just as death is the most bitter of all things because it cuts off everything and devours everything—and though some judge themselves not to fear death—nevertheless, according to Seneca in *Remedies for Fortuitous Events*: Life is the sweetest of all things. For all things desire to exist and to live; therefore everyone naturally strives to save their life because nothing is dearer. If, therefore, Boethius still possesses goods that are dearer than life <note>referring to his family mentioned on the previous page</note>, he ought not to consider himself miserable, but rather happy. Note that Philosophy calls friends <margin>an anchor is made of iron</margin> "anchors." For just as a ship is held fast by an anchor when a storm presses in and is saved from danger, so a man is lifted up by faithful friends when the adversity of fortune looms, so that he does not succumb to misfortune. For faithful friends hold back a man tossed by the impulse of fortune so that he is not totally cast down from his stability. Note that according to Hugutio <note>Hugutio of Pisa, a 12th-century grammarian often cited in medieval schoolbooks</note>, *suppetere* means to supply or to superabound; but *pigere* means to be lazy, or to repent, or to be burdened, or to be offended.

## <margin>concerning fortune</margin> <gloss>as Philosophy says</gloss> For who is <gloss>that is, abundantly</gloss> of such well-composed <gloss>so that he is in prosperity</gloss> happiness that he does not <gloss>as if no one</gloss> <gloss>in some matter</gloss> in some part <gloss>that is, discord</gloss> quarrel with the quality <gloss>that is, the disposition</gloss> of his status? <gloss>that is, miserable</gloss> For the condition of human <gloss>of riches</gloss> goods is an anxious thing, which either <gloss>namely, occurs</gloss> never comes in its entirety or never remains forever. <gloss>namely, to one man</gloss> To this man <gloss>money abounds</gloss> wealth overflows: <margin>poverty</margin> but his <gloss>that is, noble birth</gloss> degenerate blood <note>original: "degener sanguis," meaning low-born or lacking family prestige</note> is a <gloss>that is, a source of shame</gloss> disgrace. <gloss>namely, another man</gloss> This man's <gloss>high birth</gloss> nobility makes him <gloss>bright</gloss> famous: <margin>poverty</margin> but <gloss>poverty</gloss> the distress <gloss>of domestic affairs</gloss> of his family estate <gloss>that is, restricted</gloss> hemmed in, would rather he be unknown. <gloss>namely, a third man</gloss> That man, <gloss>with riches and nobility</gloss> overflowing with both, <gloss>without a wife</gloss> laments <gloss>that is, weeps for</gloss> a single life. <gloss>namely, a fourth man</gloss> That man is happy in his <gloss>with a wife</gloss> marriage: but <gloss>that is, lacking</gloss> bereaved <gloss>that is, of sons</gloss> of children.

For who is of such well-composed happiness? Here Philosophy proves that happiness cannot happen to anyone in its entirety. Secondly, she shows that the happier someone is, the more they are prostrated by a lighter adversity. Thirdly, she concludes from this that fortuitous <note>depending on chance or luck</note> happiness is bitter and miserable. Fourthly, she rails against men. The second point starts at: "Add that the happiest..." The third at: "To many..." The fourth at: "Why therefore, O mortals..." First, she says, who is the man of such well-composed happiness—that is, so abundantly happy—that he does not "quarrel," that is, disagree in some part with the "quality," that is, with the disposition of his status, which is his fortune? It is as if she were saying: no one is so happy. Because the "condition," that is, the status of human goods, is an "anxious thing," that is, a miserable thing that never comes to a man in its entirety, or never remains forever. Then she declares why it does not come to a man in its entirety: because to "this man," that is, to some man, wealth "overflows," meaning money abounds, but something else is lacking to him, because "degenerate blood," meaning lack of nobility, is a "disgrace" to him. However, "this man"—that is, another man—is made "famous" by his nobility, but being "hemmed in by the distress of his family estate," meaning poverty, he would "rather," that is, he would prefer, to be unknown. "That man"—that is, another person—is "overflowing," that is, surrounded by "both," meaning both riches and nobility; yet he "laments a single life," that is, a chaste life, because perhaps he cannot take a wife. "That man"—that is, another—is "happy in his marriage," namely by having a wife, but "bereaved," meaning lacking "children," that is, offspring, he "nourishes," that is, gathers wealth for a foreign heir. Another, however, having been gladdened by offspring, "sorrowfully weeps," that is, groans, for the "faults," that is, for the crimes of his son or daughter. Therefore, no one easily agrees with the condition of their fortune. For there is in every single man something that he, being inexperienced, does not know, or having experienced it, he shrinks from; and thus he quarrels with the quality of his status. Note that there is no man so happy that he does not find some condition in himself which he would wish not to have. Because of this, the condition of human goods is miserable.

# Fourth Prose

Because total happiness never comes to a human being, for while someone can despise all things, no one can possess all things. And one line of reasoning is drawn from the text: the condition of human goods does not result in total happiness for someone whose status is displeasing in some respect. But no one is found so happy that their status does not displease them in some matter, as the text declares; therefore, etc. Likewise, blood of a servile condition is called "degenerate" <note>original: *degener*</note> because humans are naturally free, but through servitude, they "degenerate" from their true nature.

**He nourishes his wealth for a stranger heir. Another, though delighted by his offspring, weeps in sorrow at the crimes of a son or daughter. Therefore, no one easily agrees with the condition of their fortune. For in each individual there is something which the inexperienced would not know, but the experienced would shudder at. Add to this that the sense of every most fortunate person is most delicate; and unless all things are available at their beck and call, being unaccustomed to any adversity, they are cast down by even the smallest inconveniences. So small are the things that take away the height of happiness from the most fortunate.**

[He] is cast down by adversity; comparing Boethius to others, Philosophy says: Add to the aforesaid that the "sense" <note>referring to emotional sensitivity or perception</note> of any most fortunate man is most delicate—that is, most impatient—unless all things are at his beck and call (that is, <unclear>ready</unclear>), he will be insolent—that is, impatient of all adversity—and is cast down from his happiness by even the smallest adversities. For those things are very small (that is, truly tiny) which take away (that is, carry off) the summit (that is, the perfection) of happiness from the most fortunate. ¶ Boethius, you conjecture (that is, you think) that there are many who would consider themselves close to heaven (that is, to God) if even the smallest part of the remains (that is, the tiny portions) of your fortune fell to them. ¶ This place which you call exile is home <note>original: *patria*, meaning homeland or fatherland</note> to those inhabiting it (that is, the residents); and so in their judgment, it pertains to happiness universally. Therefore, concerning fortuitous things, she concludes: nothing is miserable except when you think it so (that is, unless you judge it so by the reputation of your own mind). And on the other hand (that is, by the opposite), every lot is blessed by equanimity (that is, by the patience of a tolerant mind). ¶ Who is so happy that, when he has given his hands to impatience (that is, when he has become impatient), he does not wish to change his state? As if to say: no one is so happy.

Note that perhaps someone might say that no man is pleased with his status if he lacks great fortune; however, the lack of a small good does not prevent satisfaction with one's status or keep a man from being totally happy. Philosophy excludes this, saying: The happier someone is, the more delicate <note>in the sense of being "thin-skinned" or easily upset</note> they are. And the more delicate they are, the more they are burdened by the lack of a small good, and thus it takes away the fulfillment of happiness from the most fortunate. It should be noted that one and the same thing is judged by one to pertain to misery and by another to happiness. # Book Two

A person overflowing with the gifts of fortune, if something in his state displeases him, he wishes for his status to be changed and praises the status of another. Whence the retired soldier praises the merchant’s life; conversely, the merchant, having experienced the perils of the sea, praises military service. Similarly, the lawyers praise the farmers, and the farmers praise the city-dwellers. Similarly, an example is clear in Boethius’s *The Discipline of Scholars* <note>original: *de scolarium disciplina*; a medieval pedagogical text formerly attributed to Boethius</note> concerning the "son of inconstancy" who, feeling dissatisfaction with one status, was always assuming another and another.

Whence Seneca says in his 9th Epistle: "He is miserable who does not judge himself blessed." <note>original: *Miser est qui se beatum non iudicat*</note> Even if he should rule the world, he is not happy who does not think himself to be happy. **With how many bitternesses.** Here, Philosophy shows that accidental happiness is bitter and miserable, saying: "The sweetness of human happiness is sprinkled—that is, mixed—with many bitternesses," which, even if it seems pleasant to the person enjoying it, yet cannot be held back so that a person may have it when they wish. That is, it cannot be retained according to a human's will. The major premise is noted because the highest good is proper to man. ### Poem 4 of the Second Book

It is manifest that happiness based on luck is finished—that is, terminated—by the death of a human. It cannot be doubted that if this fortuitous happiness is able to bring—that is, give—blessedness, then the whole race of mortals—that is, humanity—would fall into misery at the end of death. But if we know many—namely the saints—have sought the fruit of blessedness not only through death but even through pains and punishments, in what way—that is, by what means—can the present life (supplemented, let us say, by being adorned with lucky goods) make people happy, when that life, once passed—that is, ended—does not make them miserable? It is as if she were saying: "In no way." Note: that whose presence is the cause of happiness, its absence is the cause of misery and unhappiness. This can be seen most clearly from this simile: just as a sailor, by his presence, is the cause of the ship's safety, so his absence is the cause of its peril. This is from the second book of the *Physics*. <note>Aristotle's *Physics*, where he discusses causes and accidents.</note> Therefore, if lucky goods were the cause of blessedness by their presence, they would be the cause of misery by their absence. However, since at a person’s death lucky goods leave the person by fleeing, and the person leaves them by dying, every person after death would be miserable and unhappy—which is false. For many attain blessedness after death. And because perhaps someone might say that when a person dies, their soul dies too—and thus a person would attain no blessedness after death—Philosophy excludes this by saying to Boethius: "You are that same man who has been persuaded by many demonstrations that the souls of humans are immortal." Note that all laws <note>The "laws" here refers to the consensus of philosophical and religious traditions.</note> agree on this: that the intellectual soul of a human is immortal. For it is separated from other things as the perpetual is from the corruptible, according to the second book of *On the Soul*. <note>Aristotle's *De Anima*.</note> And this is reasonable: because the intellectual soul, being immaterial, is not drawn out from the potentiality of matter but comes from outside—namely, from God. For according to Blessed Augustine, the soul is infused by being created and created by being infused. <note>original: "creando infunditur et infundendo creatur." A famous theological summary of "Creationism" (the idea that God creates each soul individually at conception) vs. "Traducianism."</note> Because of this, since the removal of matter is the cause of perpetuity through the commentary...

He says, therefore, in the text: "Whosoever, being a cautious man, wishes to place a lasting seat," that is, a firm dwelling, "and himself being stable, nor wishes to be overthrown," that is, cast down, "by the sounding blasts of the East wind," which is that specific wind. "And whoever cares to scorn the sea threatening with waves," that is, the surging sea, "he should avoid the peak," that is, the summit of a high mountain, "and avoid the thirsty sands," that is, dry ones. Then he assigns the reason why the peak of a high mountain should be avoided in building: because that peak of a high mountain is "vexed," that is, infested, by the "unruly South wind," <note>original: "auster protervus"</note> that is, a violent wind. Then he assigns the reason why the sands should be avoided: because these sands, being "loose," that is, disconnected by dryness, "refuse to bear," that is, do not wish to carry, a "hanging weight," that is, an unstable weight. "You, therefore, fleeing the dangerous lot," that is, the outcome, "of a pleasant seat," that is, a pleasant dwelling, "and being certain, remember to fix," that is, to stabilize, "your house on a humble rock," that is, a low-lying stone. Although the wind, "mixing the levels," that is, rolling the seas, "thunders," that is, rages with "ruins," that is, with ruinous blasts: you, happy, "established in the strength," that is, the firmness, "of a safe wall," <note>original: "geti valli" – likely referring to a fortified enclosure or rampart</note> that is, a fortification, "and you, serene," that is, tranquil, "will lead," that is, spend, "your age," that is, your life, "laughing," that is, mocking and holding as nothing, "the wraths," that is, the persecutions, "of the air," that is, of the breeze or the raging wind. Note that every virtue is corrupted by excess, since virtue consists in the middle. For virtue is a "deliberative habit consisting in a mean, determined by right reason." <note>This is a classic Aristotelian definition of virtue from the Nicomachean Ethics.</note> Therefore, all excess is to be avoided as a vice. Philosophy teaches us to avoid excessive prosperity, which she designates by the "peak of a high mountain"; such prosperity is often attacked by the envy and power of the great, which is designated by the driving wind. She also teaches us to avoid excessive poverty, which she designates as the "thirsty sand"; such poverty refuses to bear the lack of necessities, which is designated by the "hanging weight." For indigence weighs a person down.

### Prose five of the second book.

**B**ut since the reasons now into you... <note>The commentator repeats the opening of the prose to begin the analysis.</note> Here begins the fifth prose of this second book, in which Philosophy provides remedies that are more moving to Boethius, to show that the goods of Fortune are to be despised and that one should grieve less over their loss. These remedies are arguments taken from the loss of particular goods of Fortune, namely: riches, power, and glory. And first, she shows this regarding riches—that they are not to be greatly desired—by putting forward one general argument regarding all goods of Fortune. Second, she places arguments specifically about riches at the point starting "riches." First, she intends this line of reasoning: No one ought to greatly desire that which cannot be his own and which, considered in itself, is worthless. But all goods of Fortune are of this kind, for they are changeable and therefore cannot be a person's own property, and when considered in themselves, they become cheap. Therefore, etc. Hence she says in the text: *since the soothing applications*—that is, the medicines—*of my reasons are sinking into you.* Because I see that you are gradually coming to despise Fortune, I think I must use somewhat stronger reasons—that is, more moving ones. *Come now* <note>original: "age"</note> is an adverb of encouragement. For even if the gifts of Fortune were not *fleeting*—that is, happening by chance—and *momentary*—that is, transitory like a passing moment—what is in them that could ever *become yours* or, when *examined* and considered in itself, not *become cheap*? She means to say: nothing. Note that the goods of Fortune are fleeting and transitory, because Seneca says in his 76th letter: *All the goods of Fortune come to us, but they do not stick to us.* And if they are brought to us without any [effort] of our own...

# Book Two

They depart in weeping. And it is clear that if things are mutable <note>subject to change</note>, they are not a man's own true goods. For according to the same Seneca: *Call nothing your own that can be changed.* <note>original: "Nihil proprium dicas quod mutari potest"</note> Note that the goods of fortune, when considered in themselves, become worthless. As John Chrysostom says: *The goods of fortune grow old and are consumed in themselves, or are snatched away by strangers through deceit, violence, or false accusation.* <note>original: "Bona fortune in seipsis veterascunt..."</note> **Are riches precious by your nature or by their own?** Here Philosophy <note>The personification of Lady Philosophy from Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy</note> sets forth arguments regarding riches in particular, showing why they are not to be greatly desired.

Secondly, she proves this generally regarding riches at the point: *But what...* The first part is divided into five sections according to the five kinds of riches which she proves are not much to be desired: namely, money, gems, possessions, clothing, and servants. First, she shows her purpose regarding money; second, regarding gems at *Or does the beauty of gems...*; third, regarding possessions at *Do you...*; fourth, regarding clothing at *Now indeed...*; fifth, regarding servants at *Or indeed...*

<column-break/>

<insert>
**Are riches precious by your nature or by their own? Which of these is more excellent: gold or a great heap of money? But these shine better by being spent than by being hoarded. Indeed, avarice always makes men hateful, while generosity makes them famous. If that which is transferred to another cannot remain with anyone, then money is only precious when, having been transferred to others by the practice of giving, it ceases to be possessed.**
</insert>

---

First, by two arguments, she proves that riches are not much to be desired. The second argument begins at *But the same...* The first argument is as follows: Those things are not much to be desired which are precious neither by their own nature nor by the nature of the user. Riches are of this sort, therefore, etc. The major premise is well-known, because nothing is desired unless it is good and precious. The minor premise is explained: riches are not good by their own nature, because they do not make the person to whom they come good. Nor are they good on the part of the user, because they do not benefit the one who keeps them—for that would simply make a man a miser—nor are they good in the act of being distributed, for in that act they leave the man. For the text says: *Riches are either precious by their own nature or by the nature of you who use them.* And which of these is "rather," that is, more precious? Is it gold or the power of heaped-up money, that is, gathered together? But certainly these riches are not precious by being preserved, because they "shine better" by being poured out, that is, distributed, than by being hoarded, that is, retained. Indeed, avarice <term>Avarice: the greedy hoarding of wealth</term>, which heaps up money, always makes men hateful; and generosity <term>Largitas: the virtue of liberal giving</term>, which pours out money, makes them "bright," that is, honorable. She adds that if that which is transferred to another cannot remain with anyone, then money is precious—speaking ironically—only when it ceases to be possessed by being transferred to others through the use of giving.

It should be noted that a thing is "good" in two ways: either by its own nature or by the nature of the user. That is called good by its own nature which has within itself the source of its goodness, and it makes whoever receives it good, such as right reason, peace, and similar things. But that is called good on the part of the user which, if someone uses it properly, some good results from it. Hence, note according to Saint Bernard: *Only the error of men makes gold and silver be thought precious, when they are nothing but red and white earth.* <note>original: "terra rubea et alba"</note> Note that Seneca, in his eighty-eighth epistle, proving that riches are not good, argues thus: *That which is good makes men good. Riches do not make men good; therefore, riches are not good.* Likewise, that which can happen to the most contemptible and foulest person is not a "good." But riches happen both to the pimp and the gladiator trainer <note>original: "lenoni et laniste"</note>.

Drawing on Boethius, Seneca, and St. Bernard, the text concludes that riches do not possess inherent goodness because they do not improve the character of the possessor.</summary>

# Prose 5

->**[The Text of Boethius]**<-

**Why are you carried away by empty joys? Why do you embrace external goods as if they were your own? Fortune will never make those things yours which the nature of things has made foreign to you. Indeed, the fruits of the earth are undoubtedly intended for the nourishment of living beings. But if you wish to satisfy what is sufficient for nature's need, there is no reason to seek the abundance of Fortune. For nature is content with a few things, and the smallest at that. If you wish to burden her satiety with superfluities, whatever you pour in will become either unpleasant or harmful. Now, do you think it is beautiful to shine in varied garments? If their appearance is pleasing to the eye, I shall admire either the nature of the material or the skill of the craftsman.**

<column-break/>

[The Commentary]
...is content. If you wish to urge its satiety—<gloss>that is, to compel it</gloss>—with superfluous food and drink, that which you have poured into the belly will become either superfluous or unpleasant—<gloss>that is, sad</gloss>—or it will become harmful—<gloss>that is, dangerous</gloss>. <note>The commentator is explaining the physiological and moral dangers of gluttony.</note> From the text, such a reason can be formed: If that which seems more likely to be present is not present, then neither is that which is less likely. But it seems more likely that a human should glory in the beauty of the heavens and the stars; yet he ought not, because none of these things belong to him. Therefore, he much less ought to glory in the beauty of fields and other possessions. 

Note that nature is not to be burdened with superfluities but is to be nourished with a few things, because she is content with little. Whence Seneca says in his 16th Epistle: *If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if you live according to opinion, you will never be rich.* <note>original: "Si ad naturam vixeris nunquam eris pauper..."</note> Nature desires little, but opinion desires the immense. And the Blessed Augustine says: *Food should be taken like medicine.* And Gregory says: *While the belly is distended by excessive satiety, the sting of lust is awakened.* 

Furthermore, Aristotle, in a certain letter to Alexander, says: *He who exceeds the proper measure in fullness or in emptiness will not be able to escape the fury of sickness and the troubles of infirmities.* Therefore, he who seeks to conquer and refuses a burden for the sake of his own pleasure should not add eating upon eating; for every incontinent person is voluntarily ill, as stated in the *Ethics*. 

And it is added: I have heard of Hippocrates that he maintained diets for which he endured bodily weakness. His disciple said to him, "Distinguished teacher, if you were willing to eat well, you would not endure such weakness of body." To whom Hippocrates replied: *I eat so that I may live; I do not live so that I may eat.* <note>A famous ancient maxim often attributed to Socrates or Hippocrates.</note> Whence Aristotle says in the same place: *Nourishment is to be sought for the sake of endurance, not endurance for the sake of nourishment.* 

It follows: I have known many who reduced their food and, abstaining from their appetites and sparing their gluttony, lived temperately through diets; they were of the healthiest body, longest life, and good appetite. 

**Now, do you think it is beautiful.** Here Philosophy shows that one should not rejoice in the beauty of clothes as if it were one's own good; and she argues thus: One should not rejoice in a beauty that is not the beauty of the human being. But the beauty of clothes is not the beauty of the human; it is the beauty of the clothes themselves; therefore, etc. Whence she says in the text: *Now you think it is beautiful*—that is, to be ascribed to your own beauty—*to shine in varied garments.* It is as if she said: you ought not to think this. If the appearance—that is, the beauty—of these clothes is pleasing—that is, delightful—to the eye, I will admire the nature of the material of the clothes, or I will admire the skill—that is, the subtlety—of the craftsman forming the garment, but nothing [of yours]...

<sig>g 2</sig>

# Book Two.

Note that the splendor of outward appearance does not make a person better unless the inner character of the mind shines within them. <note>The author uses the word *habitus*, which refers to both clothing and a settled state of character.</note> Whence Seneca says: No one calls a sword good because its belt is gilded and its scabbard is inlaid with gems. Rather, a sword is good because it cuts well and has a sharp edge, and its point is good because it is capable of piercing any defense. Whence these verses: "If golden nobility clothes an earthen pot, it does not follow that the pot is any less made of clay." Likewise, the poet says: "Bind your head with laurel, cover your body with gems and gold; if you were a boor before, you will remain a boor still."

**Does a long line of servants make you happy?**
Here the author shows that one should not boast about a multitude of servants as if they were a primary good. He argues thus: Servants are either wicked in their morals—and thus they are harmful—or they are well-behaved, in which case their virtue has nothing to do with you, because this integrity belongs to the servants and not to you. Whence he says in the text: "Does a long line of servants make you happy?" <note>original: "An vero te longus ordo famulorum facit esse felicem."</note> As if to say: if servants are vicious in character, then they are a "pernicious burden," that is, a dangerous weight upon the house itself, and they are a fiercely hostile burden to the master himself. But if they are honest, "in what way"—that is, by what means—"shall the integrity of another be counted" among your riches? As if to say: in no way at all.

And then he concludes regarding all the aforementioned things, saying: From all these things it is "clearly shown"—that is, openly demonstrated—that none of these things which you count among your goods is actually your own good. If there is no "desirable beauty" in them (supply: which can be credited to you), "what is it"—that is, why is it—that you grieve over their loss or rejoice in their retention? But if the aforementioned things are beautiful—that is, because of their own nature—"what does that matter to you?" As if to say: nothing. For these things, "separated"—that is, divided—from your wealth, would have been pleasing on their own. For they are not precious because they have come into your riches; rather, because they seemed precious to you, you preferred to number them among your riches.

<column-break/>

**Does a long line of servants make you happy? If they are wicked in morals, they are a ruinous burden to the house and fiercely hostile to the master himself. But if they are honest, in what way shall the integrity of another be counted among your riches? From all these things, it is clearly shown that none of these things which you count among your goods is your own good. If there is no desirable beauty in them, why is it that you grieve when they are lost or rejoice when they are kept? For if they are beautiful by nature, what does that matter to you? For these things would have been pleasing even if separated from your wealth. For they are not precious because they came into your riches; but because they seemed precious, you preferred to count them among your riches.**

---

Note that servants who are wicked in morals are "household enemies" to the master and the entire house. Concerning these, it will be said later in the third book of this work, in the fifth prose: "There is no plague more effective at doing harm than a household enemy." <note>original: "familiaris inimicus." This is a famous quote from Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy.</note> And if they sometimes seem to be friends, this is by reason of utility, not by reason of virtue. Seneca speaks of these in *On Remedies*: "Flies follow carcasses, wolves follow the flock, ants follow the grain; that crowd follows the prey, not the man." Likewise, Seneca in his 41st Epistle: "In a man, that which is his own is to be praised. If he has a handsome household and a beautiful house, if he sows much, if he is much revered—none of these things are in him, but around him. Praise in him that which is his own, which can neither be taken away nor snatched away." <note>Seneca emphasizes that true worth is internal and cannot be lost through external misfortune.</note>

It draws heavily on Boethius and Seneca to distinguish between what a person truly owns (their virtue) and what is merely "around" them.</summary>

# Prose 5

-> g 3 <-

Why then [do you strive] with such a clamor for Fortune? Here Philosophy shows generally that riches are not to be greatly desired; and she does this by three arguments. She places the second there: "Is it so then?" and the third there: "But I deny." The first argument is this: Those things are not much to be desired through which a person does not attain the goals for which they are sought; but through riches, a person does not attain the goals for which riches are sought. For riches are sought for the sake of escaping want, which—

**Why then do you seek to banish want with such a clamor for Fortune? I believe you seek abundance. And yet, this turns out the opposite for you. # Book Two.

->**Second Column (Main Text)**<-

**And while other creatures are indeed content with their own traits, you—who are like God in your mind—seek the ornaments of your excellent nature from the lowest things. Nor do you understand how great an injury you do to your Creator. He willed the human race to stand above all earthly things, yet you thrust your dignity down below the lowest of matters. For if every good is more precious than the thing to which it belongs, then when you judge the cheapest of things to be your "goods," you submit yourselves to them by your own estimation. This indeed happens not without merit. For this is the condition of human nature: that it excels other things only when it knows itself. Yet that same nature is reduced below the beasts if it ceases to know itself. For while it is natural for other animals to be ignorant of themselves, in humans, it becomes a vice.**

->**First and Third Columns (Commentary)**<-

placed <gloss>that is, placed apart from you</gloss>. As if to say: "On the contrary, the good is within you if you are willing to consider it." Nor do you understand how much injury you do to your Creator <insert>namely, by perverting the order established by Him</insert>. For He, the Creator, willed the human race to stand before <gloss>that is, to excel</gloss> all earthly things. But you thrust your dignity down below even the lowest of things. This is proved in this way: For every good is more precious than that which possesses the good; since you judge the most worthless of things—such as the goods of Fortune—to be your own goods, you submit <gloss>that is, subject</gloss> yourselves to them by your own estimation <gloss>that is, opinion</gloss>. And this happens to man not without merit, for that is the condition of human nature: that it excels other things only when it knows itself. Yet that same human nature is reduced below the beasts if it ceases to know itself. For to other animals, it is nature to be ignorant of themselves, but in humans, it comes <gloss>that is, proceeds</gloss> from vice.

<note>The commentator is drawing on Aristotle's Ethics here.</note> Note that the proper good is implanted in man, which is right reason <term>recta ratio: the capacity to think and act in accordance with the highest truth</term> which always prays for the best things. In the action and contemplation of this reason, happiness consists; because the wise man is the most happy (according to the 10th book of the *Ethics*). And the man who cares for his intellect is seen to be most beloved by God in that same place. Therefore, the good of man is not to be sought in external things. Note that man is like God in mind and reason; because according to Seneca, reason is nothing other than a part of the divine spirit immersed in a human body. And the same says that a righteous mind is like a god dwelling as a guest in a human body. And the same says in his 6th book: "Learn rather to extol the mind into the immense; for the mind is a noble and generous thing." Note that a man who does not honor himself is worse than a beast. Whence Boethius, in his treatise on the highest good, citing the Commentator, says: "Woe to you men who are counted in the number of beasts, not recognizing the divine that is within you, by which you ascend to higher things and are like unto God." And he adds: he calls the "divine" in man the intellect and reason. Note that nothing prevents one and the same thing from being...

Meter 5 of the second book.
"Happy, too happy, was the former age." Here begins the fifth meter of this second book, which is called *pentitachum* from its inventor, and *anapestichum* from its predominating foot <term>anapest: a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables followed by one long one</term>. ->Happy, too happy, was the former age<-

->Not ruined by sluggish luxury, and accustomed<-
->To break long fasts with the easy acorn. Nor with Bacchus...<-

In this meter, Philosophy commends the first age <note>The "Golden Age" of classical mythology, a time of primordial peace and simplicity.</note> which was without the desire for riches, while lamenting the present age in which greed dominates and reigns. First, therefore, she commends the age of the ancients; second, she laments our own age (at the point where it says: *Would that now...*). First she says: The former age was exceedingly happy, content with "faithful fields" (that is, faithful agriculture), nor was it "ruined" (that is, depraved) by "sluggish luxury" (that is, heavy excess). That age was accustomed to "break" (that is, remove) a "long" (that is, late) fast with the "easy acorn" (that is, humble fruit). Nor did that age "know how" (that is, had the knowledge) to "confound" (that is, mix) the "gifts of Bacchus" (that is, wines) with clear honey to make <term>mead: a drink made of fermented honey and water</term> as is done now. Nor did they know how to "dye" (that is, dip) "shining fleeces" (that is, white wool) with "Tyrian poison" (that is, the blood of shellfish, a great abundance of which is found at Tyre to make the color purple). The grass gave them healthful sleep; for they did not sleep in ivory beds but on the grass. And the "gliding river" (that is, flowing water) gave them drink. And the "pine" (that is, that tallest tree) gave them "shadows" (that is, shady dwellings), for they did not live in houses or in elaborate buildings. Not yet did any "guest" (stranger) "cut" (that is, divide by sailing) the "heights" (that is, the deep sea), because there was as yet no use of ships; nor had they seen "new shores" (that is, foreign lands) with "merchandise gathered from everywhere," because each man remained in his own fatherland. Then, in that age, the "savage trumpets" were silent (that is, the tubes or horns calling men to war, called *classica* from *calo*, which means "I call"). Nor had "blood spilled by bitter hatreds" "stained" (that is, soaked) "horrid arms," because then there was no use of weapons. For why would "hostile fury" wish to "move arms first" when it saw "savage wounds" and yet saw "no rewards of blood"? For there was nothing for which they might fight. # Meter V

Good and simple people were content with little; they ate acorns, drank water, and did not cultivate vineyards. The poets called this the **Golden Age**, and it existed under Saturn; of this, Boethius <note>original: "B."</note> speaks in the text. The second age was called **Silver**, which was under Jupiter, when more cunning men invented agriculture and began to inhabit houses and plant vineyards. They called the third age **Bronze**, in which men, on account of their own concern for possessions,

> **knew not the heavy gifts <note>referring to luxury</note>. Nor did they mix clear honey with liquid wine. began to drive others away and give themselves over to a certain degree of malice. The fourth age they called **Iron**, when the malice and avarice of men abounded to such an extent that neither faith nor justice remained on earth; we are in this age, which Boethius laments at the end. Note regarding what he says about **"idle luxury"** <note>original: "inerti luxu"</note> that idleness and leisure are the causes of luxury. # Book Two

Note that Etna is a mountain in Sicily which frequently blazes with fires; human greed and desire are similar to it, for they are insatiable and never fully extinguished. <note>The author compares the volcanic eruptions of Mount Etna to the destructive nature of human passion.</note> Whence the title in the book *On the Ends of Good and Evil* <note>original: "de finibus bonorum et malorum" by Cicero</note> says: The desires of men are insatiable, overturning not only individuals but entire families. **Prose 6 of the Second Book.** "What then [shall I say] of dignities..." This is the sixth prose of this second book, in which Philosophy shows that high offices and powers are not to be greatly desired. And first, she proves her intent regarding dignity and power together; second, regarding power separately, at the point "But what..."; third, again regarding dignity and power together, at "To these..." First, she intends this reason: Those things are not much to be desired which, when they come to the wicked, make them worse, and do not make the good better. But high offices and powers are of this sort, as she declares in the text. Therefore, etc. Whence she speaks thus: "What shall I discuss"—that is, say—"concerning dignities and powers, which you, ignorant"—that is, unaware—"of true dignity and power, equal to the heavens"—that is, you compare them to the highest good.

# Prose 6

The second example concerns Regulus. <note>Marcus Atilius Regulus, a Roman general and consul famous for his integrity during the First Punic War.</note> Regulus was a Roman consul who, when he waged many wars against the Carthaginians, captured many of them; but eventually, he was captured by them. From this, it is clear that whatever anyone can do to another, he can also suffer that same thing from another. Whence Cato says: *The victor is conquered by the vanquished.* <note>original: "Victorem a victo rē."</note> And consequently, there is no human power that can prevent this. Hence it says in the text: What is there that anyone can do to another which he might not have to endure himself?

**...that he was slaughtered. Regulus had cast many of the Carthaginians** <note>original: "penoꝝ" (Poenorum), referring to the Phoenician/Punic ancestors of Carthage.</note> **captured in war into chains; but soon he himself offered his hands to the chains of the victors. Do you therefore think there is any power in that man who cannot prevent another from being able to do to him what he himself can do to another? Furthermore: If there were any natural or inherent good within these dignities and powers, they would never fall to the most wicked men.** For contrary things do not usually associate with one another; nature rejects the joining of opposites. **Thus, since there is no doubt that the most wicked men often enjoy these dignities,** it is also clear that things which allow themselves to cling to the worst of men are not good by their own nature.

Second, she shows the false naming of these "goods," at the point: *Concerning which also that...* The reasoning she intends is this: That which is naturally good in itself cannot be joined to the worst people. But dignities and powers come to the worst people; therefore, etc. The major premise is declared in the text. Whence it says: if there were any natural or inherent good in these dignities and powers, they would never fall to the most wicked. For opposites are not accustomed to be associated with each other, because nature rejects that contrary things be joined, that is, that they stand together. Since, therefore, there is no doubt that the most wicked very often "enjoy," that is, use, these dignities, it is also clear—that is, manifest—that these things are not good by their own nature if they allow themselves to "cling to," that is, remain with, the worst men. Finally, the same concerning all fortune. Here Philosophy shows that the same is concluded by itself concerning all accidental goods, saying: Finally (that is, in the end), it is permitted to conclude this same thing concerning all fortune, in which nothing is to be sought (that is, desired), and it is manifest that nothing of natural goodness (that is, innate goodness) exists within it, because fortune does not always join itself to the good, and it does not make those to whom it is joined good. Note that the "good" of fortune does not make that thing good to which it is added, just as music makes a musician and virtue makes a virtuous person. But because fortune does not make the wicked to whom it comes good, it is clear that no natural goodness is in it. However, how the wicked make the wicked good <note>The commentator likely means how the badness of the wicked is revealed or how they might be corrected.</note> will be clear in the fourth book of this work, in the sixth prose.

---

->The sixth meter of the second book.<-

"We know how many ruins he caused." This is the sixth meter of this second book, which is called Sapphic from its inventor <note>Sappho, the Greek lyric poet.</note>, and Trochaic from its dominant foot. It is a single syllable <note>The commentator is discussing the meter's structure</note>; each verse contains eleven syllables. It is "acatalectic," because no syllable is lacking for the perfection of the meter. In this meter, Philosophy declares by example that dignities and powers coming to the wicked do not make them good. She declares this through Nero, who, the more powerful he was, the worse he became. Philosophy touches upon four wickednesses of Nero in this meter. The first is that he set fire to the city of Rome, which burned for seven days and seven nights, so that by the spectacle of that fire he might know how great the fire had been when Troy was captured and burned. The second evil is that Nero killed a large part of the Senate without any cause. The third is that he killed his own brother so that he alone might rule more securely. The fourth is that he caused his mother to be killed so that he might see the place of the womb in which he had lain. Therefore, the text says: "We know how many ruins" (that is, how many dangers) Nero caused, "the city" (supply: Rome) "being burned" (that is, set on fire) and "the fathers" (that is, the senators) "being slaughtered" (that is, killed). For Nero, once "wild" (that is, cruel), after his "brother was slain," was himself also "wet with the poured-out gore of his mother." And describing her blood...

Note that according to Aristotle in the fifth book of the *Ethics*: "High office reveals the man." For the malice or the virtue of a man is shown in his leadership, just as is evident in Nero, whose malice and cruelty appeared in the empire of his dignity. Because of this, the same Aristotle says: "Injustice is most cruel when it possesses weapons." And in the seventh book of the *Ethics* he also says: "It is similar, therefore, to compare injustice to an unjust man; for he is ten thousand times worse than a beast." For an evil man will certainly do more evils than a beast. Note that besides these evils of Nero which are touched upon in the text, he perpetrated many more. For Philosophy says in the fifth prose of the third book of this work: "Nero forced Seneca, his familiar teacher, to choose the manner of his own death." And because Nero was the most cruel of men, Seneca wrote a certain little book to him entitled *The Book on Clemency*, in which he urges him to flee from cruelty and to practice mercy; which book begins thus: "I have determined to write to you, Nero Caesar, concerning clemency."

# Prose VII.

<margin>b</margin>

**Then I said, "You know..."** Here begins the seventh prose of this second book, in which Philosophy shows that worldly glory is not to be greatly desired. First, she introduces Boethius confessing that he did not greatly desire the aforementioned things—namely, powers and dignities—except insofar as they are the "matter" <note>original: *materia*; the raw material or means through which action is possible</note> for performing tasks. Second, Philosophy shows that since glory is a meager good, it is not to be greatly desired. The second part begins at: "But she [replied]."

And first: **"Then,"** meaning at that time, **"I,"** Boethius, **"said: O Philosophy, you know that ambition,"** meaning the desire for mortal things, **"which you spoke of, has dominated us too much. But we desired the matter for performing tasks so that our silent virtue,"** meaning virtue not put into practice, **"would not grow old within us."**

Note that in a wise person, the desire for temporal things does not dominate, because Philosophy brings about a contempt for shifting abundance. From the *Book of Plants*: And **Socrates**, when he went to Athens for study, threw a great weight of gold into the sea, saying: "I will drown you, lest I be drowned by you." <note>A common medieval anecdote illustrating the philosopher's rejection of wealth to avoid spiritual ruin.</note>

Note that the "matter for performing tasks" consists of those things without which affairs cannot be properly conducted. These are three: **wisdom, authority, and power.** For without wisdom, a thing is not conducted properly, as is evident in itself. Also, the task to be performed is adorned by authority, because an authentic man is heard more willingly and believed more easily. By **power**, indeed, the evil are suppressed and the good are exalted. Desiring this "matter," Boethius sought power and dignities.

->**Then I said: "You yourself know that the ambition for mortal things has dominated us too much. But we desired the matter for performing tasks, so that our silent virtue would not grow old." ¶ But she replied: "Yet this is the one thing that can entice minds that are indeed excellent by nature, but not yet brought to the finishing touch of the perfection of virtues: namely, the desire for glory and the fame of the best merits toward the commonwealth."**<-

Note that Boethius sought the "matter" of dignity and power for this reason: lest his **silent virtue grow old**, meaning lest his virtue remain silent while he reached old age, with no one speaking or writing anything in praise of his virtue. For virtue "grows old in silence" when one does nothing for which others might speak, and when nothing is written concerning his good deeds. For virtue perfects the one who possesses it; it renders their work praiseworthy.

**"But she replied: 'Yet this is the one thing...'"** Here Philosophy shows that worldly glory is not to be desired. First, she premises that the desire for glory entices many. Second, she proves it to be meager and empty, at the point: "The whole circuit of the earth..." <note>Referring to the next section of the text where she discusses the smallness of the world compared to the universe.</note>

First, she speaks thus: since Boethius sometimes sought dignities and powers lest his virtue grow old in silence, it seems he sought these things for the sake of praise and glory. Therefore Philosophy says: **"this is the one thing,"** namely the desire for glory and the fame of the best merits toward the **commonwealth** <note>original: *rempublicam*; the state or public good</note>, which fame is accustomed to entice the minds of men who are **excellent by nature**, but **not yet** brought to the **finishing touch** <note>original: *extremam manum*; literally 'the final hand,' a metaphor for the final polish or completion of a work</note> of the perfection of virtues. Consider from what follows how this fame and glory is meager and empty of all "weight," meaning significance.

Note that the desire for vain glory entices and delights many. Whence **Seneca** says in his 62nd Epistle: "This especially hinders us: that we are quickly satisfied with ourselves. If we find someone who calls us good men, or prudent, or holy, we are not content with a modest amount of praise. Whatever flattery shamelessly heaps upon us, we take as our due. We agree with those who affirm we are the best and wisest, even when we know they are often lying; we indulge ourselves so much that we wish to be praised for the very thing in which we act most contrary."

Note that the goodness of the mind is twofold: namely, **natural** and **acquired**. Natural goodness is that according to which someone naturally...

# Book Two

There are those who are pious, mild, sober, and chaste; but this goodness, if it is not corrected by virtue and wisdom, quickly lifts a man up toward empty glory. There is another kind of goodness acquired through the exercise of virtues and knowledge, which does not allow a man to be puffed up by vain glory, because the wise man places his reward in his conscience, while the fool places it in praise, according to Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (c. 400 AD), a Roman provincial whose commentary on Cicero's "Dream of Scipio" was a standard medieval textbook for cosmology and ethics.</note>. Therefore, Philosophy says that the desire for glory entices minds that are naturally excellent but not yet perfected by the virtues. Note that "fame" is the frequent praise of great merits in the republic, but "glory" is clear recognition accompanied by praise; or, glory is a widely spreading proclamation—that is, an announcement.

In this passage, Philosophy shows that worldly glory is meager and not to be greatly desired. First, she shows this by considering the space in which it is spread. Second, she shows it by the diversity of nations to which it is not spread. Third, she shows the same by the diversity of customs, because of which people judge the same thing in opposite ways. Fourth, she shows—

### Since this glory is meager and void of all weight, consider it thus: You have learned from astrological demonstrations <note>original: "astrologicis demonstrationibus"; in this period, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to mean the study of the stars.</note> that the entire circuit of the earth holds the ratio of a mere point compared to the space of the heavens. That is, if it were compared to the magnitude of the celestial globe, it would be judged to have no space at all. Of this so tiny region in the world, barely a fourth part is inhabited by living beings known to us, as you have learned from Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian geographer and astronomer whose "Almagest" and "Geography" defined the medieval understanding of the universe.</note> who proved this. First, she intends this reasoning: The breadth of fame consists in the breadth of the earth over which it spreads. But the earth is not broad over which the spreading of fame occurs, as is declared in the text. Therefore, fame cannot be spread widely and is entirely meager and not to be greatly desired. As she says in the text: *You have accepted*—that is, you have learned from astrological demonstrations—that the *entire circuit of the earth*—that is, the space of the earth—*obtains*—that is, has—the *ratio of a point* compared to the *space of the heavens*—that is, to the magnitude of the sky. You will explain this further by saying: if the earth is brought forward—that is, compared—to the magnitude of the celestial globe, it is judged to have *no space at all*. Of this *so tiny region*—that is, the earth—in the world, *barely a fourth part* is that which is *inhabited* by living beings known to us, as you learned from Ptolemy proving this. If you subtract in your thought from this fourth part of the earth how much the seas and marshes *press upon*—that is, occupy—and the parched land remains—that is, a wide region stretched out in thirst—that is, dryness—then there is scarcely left for men a *most narrow area*—that is, a very tight place for living.

In this, therefore, in a certain *minimum point of a point*—that is, in a tiny portion of the earth—you men, *hemmed in and shut off*, think about spreading your fame and making your name known—that is, exalting your name or fame—and this is done uselessly. For what can glory have that is *ample and magnificent* when it is *confined by such narrow and meager limits*—that is, boundaries? She means to say: it has nothing magnificent.

Note that the earth, in respect to the heavens, is of no sensible quantity, but stands like a point in respect to the circumference of the heavens themselves. This is because the horizon, which limits our sight, divides the heavens into two equal halves, which would not be the case if the earth had any significant size in comparison to the heavens. Likewise, if the earth were of any sensible size compared to the heavens, then the stars would not always appear to us to be of the same size. This is clearly false, because in the part where the earth was more bulging and closer to the sky, the stars would appear larger, and in the opposite part, smaller. Likewise, the smallest fixed star visible to the eye is larger than the whole earth. If, therefore, such a star appears so small to us situated on the earth—

Note that the Caucasus is a certain mountain situated in the northern part, to which the fame of the Roman city had not reached, although to the Parthians and other neighboring nations the fame of the Romans was "formidable"—that is, to be feared. *What of the fact that diverse...* Here he shows that worldly glory is meager on account of the diversity of customs, because of which the same thing is judged in contrary ways among different people. "Whoever seeks only with a headlong mind." Here begins the seventh meter of this second book, which is called Archilochian from its inventor, and iambic from its predominating foot; it consists of a first verse of three measures and a second of two. In this meter, Philosophy <note>The personification of Wisdom in Boethius's work</note> teaches how glory is to be despised by considering the vastness of the heavens and the narrowness of the earth, saying: "Whoever seeks," that is, desires with a headlong mind "only glory," and believes that to be the "highest," that is, the chief thing among things to be desired; let him "behold," that is, consider the "regions of the heavens," that is, the open parts of the sky. And let him behold the "narrow site of the earth," that is, the cramped space of the earth in comparison to the heavens. He will "be ashamed" of his "increased name," that is, his increased fame, which is "not able to fill the brief circuit," that is, the small space of the earth. And then she exclaims, saying: "O," because of this I wonder "why," that is, for what reason, do the "proud desire," that is, wish in vain to "lift," that is, extol their "necks" from the "mortal yoke," that is, mortal fame. For although "fame traveling" and "diffused," that is, passing through "remote peoples," may "unfold its tongues," that is, through the tongues of the people; and although your "great house," that is, your noble parentage or family, "may shine with bright titles," that is, praises; nevertheless "death despises high glory," and death "alike," that is, at the same time, "wraps the humble head," that is, the wretched man, and the "high," that is, the noble or the rich. And death "makes the lowest equal to the highest" by sparing no one. Which she declares, saying: "Where now do the bones of faithful Fabricius remain? What is Brutus or rigid Cato?" <note>Fabricius, Brutus, and Cato were famous figures of Roman virtue</note> as if to say: what remains of their glory?

# Book Two

Then there. That indeed. ¶ First she says: O Boethius, from what has been said it is clear that fortune is to be despised; but lest you think that I wage—that is, conduct—an inexorable—that is, implacable—war against fortune, you should know that sometimes it happens that fortune herself is not entirely without merit regarding men, in that some good comes to men through her. This occurs when fortune reveals herself by manifesting her own falsehood; when she uncovers her face through her adversity; when she confesses her true character through her instability.

And Philosophy adds: perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying, because it is a marvel what I desire—that is, long—to say, and therefore I can hardly explain the meaning in words. For I reckon—that is, I am of the opinion—that adverse fortune profits men more than prosperous fortune. <note>This is the central paradox of this section: that "bad luck" is actually better for the soul than "good luck."</note> Note that whenever there appears to be a contradiction in a saying, it seems a marvelous thing to say. To say that adverse fortune profits men seems to be a kind of contradiction in terms, for being adverse to someone and being profitable to them are mutually repugnant. Therefore Philosophy says: It is a marvel what I long to say, namely that adverse fortune profits more than prosperous. For the latter always [deceives] with the appearance of happiness.

**But lest you think I wage an inexorable war against Fortune, there are times when she, though she deceives, deserves well of men: namely, when she reveals herself, uncovers her face, and confesses her true character. Perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying. It is a marvel what I long to say, and for that reason I can hardly explain the meaning in words: for I reckon that adverse fortune profits men more than prosperous fortune. For the latter, always wearing the appearance of happiness, lies when she seems alluring. The former is always truthful when she demonstrates her instability through change. The one deceives; the other instructs. The one binds the minds of those enjoying her with a false appearance of goods; the other frees them by the knowledge of fragile happiness. Therefore, you may see that the former is windy...**

Here Philosophy proves her intent—that adverse fortune is better than prosperous—by three arguments. The second begins at "finally," the third at "or this." First, she says that prosperous fortune always lies when she seems—that is, appears—alluring with the appearance of happiness—that is, prosperity. But this—that is, adverse fortune—is always truthful when she demonstrates herself to be unstable by her own change. For she shows herself to be exactly as she is, and thus men are not deceived by her. But that one—namely prosperous fortune—deceives those who trust in her. This adverse fortune, however, instructs a man by showing that one should not trust in prosperous fortune because of its mutability. That prosperous fortune binds—namely by deceiving—the minds of men enjoying her with a false appearance of goods; this adverse fortune absolves—that is, sets free—the minds of men through the knowledge of fragile—that is, transitory—happiness. And then she summarizes the effects of each fortune, saying: Therefore you see that prosperous fortune is windy—that is, proud; flowing—that is, prodigal; and ignorant of herself. For men in continuous prosperity do not know themselves. This adverse fortune you see as sober and succinct—that is, humble, not proud—and prudent through the exercise of adversity. Note that from this text three arguments can be formed which...

# Prose 8

### That adverse fortune is better than prosperous fortune.

The first reason is this: Good fortune, under the appearance of happy circumstances, deceives the one possessing it; but adverse fortune does not deceive, for it is truthful, showing itself to be exactly what it is. Therefore, adversity is better than prosperity. The second reason is: prosperous fortune binds the minds of men with lying goods, but adversity frees the minds from false happiness. Therefore, it is better. The third reason: prosperous fortune renders men

flowing and always ignorant of themselves. This <note>referring to adversity</note> [renders them] sober, prepared, and prudent through the very exercise of its hardship. Finally, while "happy" fortune draws those who wander away from the true good with its charms, adversity for the most part leads them back to true goods, pulling them back as if with a hook. Or do you think this should be valued among the least of things: that this harsh, this horrible fortune has uncovered for you the minds of your faithful friends? This has separated for you the certain faces of your companions from the ambiguous ones. In departing, she took away her own [followers] and left you yours. At what price would you have bought this when you were "whole" and, as it seemed to you, fortunate? Cease now to seek your lost wealth; you have found friends, which is the most precious kind of riches.

<column-break/>

ignorant of themselves, but adversity makes men wise. Therefore, it is better than prosperity. Finally, "happy" [fortune leads away] from the true good. Here Philosophy sets forth the second reason, which is such: Whichever fortune draws one toward the investigation of the true good is better than that which draws one away from the true good. But adverse fortune is of this kind, therefore etc. Whence she says in the text: "Finally, happy," that is, prosperous fortune, with its charms draws those who are "straying," that is, wandering from the true good. This adverse fortune for the most part pulls them back with a "hook," that is, a grappling iron, leading them back to true goods. Note that because prosperous fortune seems to be close to happiness—because without the goods of fortune one

---

cannot happen to be happy, and [this is] concerning good fortune—therefore, with its charms, it draws the sensual man away from the true good, which consists in the contemplation of God. Adversity, however, because it shows that prosperous fortune is changeable, leads the man back to the true good, which is immutable. "Or do you think this should be valued among the least..." Here Philosophy sets forth the final reasons, which are such: That fortune is better through which true friends are recognized; but adverse fortune is such; therefore, etc. Whence she says in the text: "Or do you perhaps think this should be valued among the least goods," that this adverse fortune has "uncovered," that is, shown to you, the "minds," that is, the hearts of faithful friends? As if to say: that is a good among the greatest of goods. And this [adversity] has "separated," that is, distinguished for you, certain friends and the "ambiguous faces" of your "associates," that is, of friends. As if to say: harsh fortune taught you to discern between true and false friends, because prosperous fortune, in departing from you, "took away her own," that is, those who were friends by reason of prosperity, and "left yours," the friends who loved you, not for your possessions. "At what price," that is, for how much, would you have bought this when you were "whole," that is, established in the integrity of fortune, when you seemed to yourself fortunate and could have known your true friends? "Now cease," that is, stop seeking "wealth," that is, lost riches, because you have found true friends, who are the most precious kind of riches. Note that in adversity false friends flee, but in a time of prosperity they remain.

<summary>Lady Philosophy argues that misfortune is superior to prosperity because it reveals the truth, fosters wisdom, and distinguishes true friends from those who only love wealth. She concludes that the discovery of loyal friends is a treasure more valuable than the riches Boethius has lost.</summary>

# Book Two

Hence Seneca says in his *Book on Remedies*: "Those whom you believe to be happy are followed by many, just as flies follow honey, wolves follow carcasses, and ants follow grain; that crowd follows the prey, not the man." <note>original: "Quos tu felices credis..." Seneca the Younger was a Stoic philosopher often cited in medieval texts for his moral wisdom.</note> Note that adverse fortune reveals faithful friends. Whence Seneca says in his 20th Epistle: "The crowd of your household will cease to feed you when it is no longer fed by you; and what you could not know through your own benefit, you shall know through poverty. Poverty will retain true friends; whoever followed not you, but something else, departs. For this one reason, however, poverty is to be loved: it shows by whom you are loved." Where the poor Henry <note>Likely referring to Henricus Septimellensis, a 12th-century poet known for his elegies on the fluctuations of Fortune.</note> says: "Bad luck prevails in this alone: it shows one's friends; it shows both the way of the good and the way of the evil." Likewise the poet: "In happy times friends are not known; in a miserable lot, true affection is revealed." Likewise elsewhere: "When you are happy, you will count many friends; if the times become cloudy, you will be alone." Likewise Tobias: "A venal friend wavers toward the wealthy, but flees the needy; let love be fashioned so that it resonates as true." <note>A common medieval sentiment regarding "fair-weather friends."</note> Note that a faithful friend is the most precious kind of wealth, because a friend—according to the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>—is "another self," that is, friends have the same "wills and won'ts." For no one chooses to live without friends, even if he possesses all other goods. And Seneca in his Epistles says: "The wise man, even if he is content with himself, nevertheless wishes to have a friend for no other reason than to practice friendship, lest so great a virtue lie hidden." And Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> in his book *On Duties* says: "Honors, riches, and dignities are never to be placed above friendship."

### The Eighth Meter of the Second Book

**q** *That the world with stable faith.* Here begins the eighth and final meter of this second book, which is called *Glyconic* after its inventor, and *Amphimacrus* from its predominating "foot" <note>A "foot" is a unit of poetic rhythm.</note>. An *Amphimacrus* is an ancient foot consisting of a long first and last syllable and two short middle syllables; it is named from *amphi*, which means "around," and *macros*, meaning "long," as if having a long syllable on either side. In this meter, Philosophy commends Love, from which she says that friends are the most precious kind of riches. First, she commends divine love. Second, she shows how human nature preserves friendship (at the point: *This sacred...*). She does the first part as stated. Second, she shows that if divine love were removed, all things would be corrupted (at the point: *If he should drop the reins...*). First she says: Divine Love, ruling the lands and the sea and commanding—that is, frequently governing—the heavens, that love binds this sequence, that is, the harmony of things. For the world, with stable faith, varies its harmonious changes, that is, the alternations of the seasons of the year, and of night and day. And because the "struggling seeds"—that is, the contrary elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which were thought to be in constant conflict.</note>—hold a perpetual covenant, that is, a harmony, lest one totally destroy the other. Because Phoebus—that is, the sun—in his golden chariot brings forth—that is, produces—the rosy day, meaning the bright day. This same love causes Phoebe—that is, the moon—to rule, or preside over, the nights, which nights Hesperus—the evening star—has led, or brought in. And it causes the greedy sea to restrain its waves within a fixed boundary—that is, a determined limit—lest it be permitted to extend itself, that is...

...to extend wide boundaries across the wandering lands, that is, across the ample earth; <note>original: "latos terminos vagis terrenis"</note> add: by totally covering the earth. Note that Cicero, speaking on friendship, says: friendship is a virtue moving higher things toward the protection of lower things, and lower things toward the submission to higher things. For if friendship is removed, all joy is taken away from life. Note that he calls the elements "seeds" <note>original: "semia" for "semina"</note> because from them, as if from seeds, the elements are produced; for just as a seed is the beginning of fruit, so the elements are the beginnings

**If Love should let go of these reins,**
**Whatever now loves in return**
**Would wage continuous war.**
**And those things which now with allied faith**
**Urge on their beautiful motions:**
**Would strive to shatter the world's machine.**

**Joined together by a treaty.**

of mixed bodies. And he speaks of the "clashing elements" <note>original: "elementa pugnantia"</note> because of their contrariety; for some are hot, some cold, some moist, and some dry. These elements, through the ordering of divine love, maintain a close treaty, because the weight of the lower things does not take away the lightness of the higher things, nor vice versa, and they do not totally destroy one another at once. **If Love should let go of these reins.** Here he shows that if divine love were withdrawn, all things would be destroyed, saying: If

this divine love should let go of the reins—that is, the law of governing things—whatever now loves in return—that is, whatever is in harmony—would immediately wage war. And the elements themselves would strive—that is, struggle—to shatter—that is, destroy—the machine, namely the worldly structure, which they now urge on with allied faith—that is, a harmonious treaty—in beautiful motions—that is, making them move in an orderly fashion. Note that when love and harmony are removed, all things are dissolved. Hence Alan of Lille, in the *Anticlaudianus*, speaking in the person of Love and Harmony, says: "If the world had once observed, or would still observe, my rights, my laws, my treaties of love, you would not touch these chains, and the world would not groan under disasters." <note>original: "Si mea iura meas leges..."</note> **This Love also holds holy peoples.** Here Philosophy shows how through love she preserves and reconciles human friendship, saying: this love contains—that is, preserves—holy—that is, virtuous—peoples joined by a treaty, namely of friendship. And this love binds the sacred—that is, the sacrament—of marriage with the chaste loves of husband and wife. And this love dictates its laws—that is, imposes the law of friendship—on faithful companions. And because these things proceed from divine love as if from their own source, he therefore adds: O happy race of men (add: I say) if love (namely divine love) by which heaven is ruled, should rule your minds (add: by causing in them the harmony of friendship). Note that love dictates laws to faithful companions. Seneca, in his third letter, suggests the laws of friends and companions, saying: "Think for a long time whether someone should be received by you as a friend. But when it has pleased you for it to happen, admit him with your whole heart. Speak as boldly with him as with yourself. Indeed, live in such a way that you commit nothing to yourself unless it is something you could also commit to your friend. Mix all your cares and all your thoughts with your friend if you consider him faithful. For there are some who tell everyone things that should only be committed to friends; others dread the awareness of even their dearest ones, trusting no one. Neither should be done. For both are a vice: both trusting everyone and trusting no one." <note>original: "Diu cogita an aliquis..."</note> Note regarding the aforesaid that friendship properly so-called is found only in rational beings, and as such, friendship is the shared will for good things between certain people. But in a broad sense, friendship is also in irrational things, and as such, friendship is the harmony of diverse things with one another.

# Book Three

She had now ended her song. This is the third book of **Boethius on the Consolation of Philosophy** and it continues from the preceding books in this manner: After Philosophy in the first book examined the causes of Boethius’s grief, and in the second book applied easy remedies to him, in the present book and those following, Philosophy applies **Boethius’s** more serious remedies. Just as

<column-break/>

she applies more serious remedies—arguments proving, contrary to the common opinion of men, that true happiness does not consist in external goods—by showing in what true happiness is situated and how one may arrive at it. And this book is divided into twenty-four parts because there are twelve prose sections and twelve meters in this book. These parts will become clear in the progress of the book; likewise, who is speaking and what is determined in each of these parts will be made clear.

<column-break/>

## The First Prose of the Third Book.

->She had now ended her song, when the sweetness of the poem left me eager to hear more and struck with wonder, with my ears still strained. Therefore, a little while after, I said: "O supreme comfort of weary minds, how much you have refreshed me, whether by the weight of your thoughts or even by the delight of your singing! So much so, that I do not think myself unequal to the blows of Fortune hereafter."<-

---

The first prose of this third book is divided into three parts. First, **Boethius** shows how he spoke to Philosophy after the aforementioned things. Second, he sets down Philosophy’s response. Third, **Boethius** directs a certain petition to her. The second part begins at "Then she," and the third at "Then I." He says first: now that Philosophy had ended her song <note>original: "cantum"</note>, that is, the meter which was concerning the commendation of divine love and friendship. And when I, Boethius, had been enticed by the sweetness of the meter to listen with eagerness and wonder to the words of Philosophy with ears strained, I said: "O Philosophy, you who are the supreme comfort of weary minds, how much you have refreshed me with your prose and meters, so much so that I can now well resist the assaults of Fortune." And therefore he says: "The remedies which you previously said were serious, I do not fear, but I wait diligently to hear them." Note that Boethius calls the meter a "song" <note>original: "cantum"</note>. For just as in a song there is a rising and falling of the voice, so similarly in a meter, by reason of the quantity of short and long syllables, a certain rising and falling is observed. Because by reason of a long quantity a rising occurs, and by reason of a short quantity a falling occurs. Also, because meter is more subtle and more delightful than prose, it therefore soothes the soul. Whence the author of poetry compares meter to a young lady, saying: "Meter comes with a face like a young lady with combed hair, shining cheeks, a slender body, and excellent form." Therefore **Boethius** says "the sweetness of the poem," that is, of the meter. Likewise, a man ought to be eager and wondering regarding philosophy. Eager, according to what Seneca says in his 17th Epistle: "Cast away all those things if you are wise, or rather so that you may be wise, and hasten toward philosophy with a great run and with all your strength." Also, a man ought to be wondering, that is, admiring philosophy, because it is a wonderful and divine thing according to Aristotle in the beginning of his book *On the Universe* <note>original: "De Mundo"</note>; and philosophy brings wonderful delights, according to the 10th book of the *Ethics*. Likewise, "weary minds" are those oppressed by heavy care or some adversity. For these, philosophy is the supreme comfort, because she herself persuades one toward magnanimity <note>The virtue of being "great-souled" and rising above petty troubles.</note>, with which a man ought to constantly battle against the adversities of Fortune. Likewise, through philosophy, a man can well resist the blows of Fortune, because in the 1st book of the *Ethics*, Aristotle says: "The wise man knows well how to bear fortunes and conducts himself without blame, just as..."

Rather, they are only certain likenesses of true happiness, just as the phantasms of dreams are likenesses of things. **Note** that he calls exterior goods "images of true happiness." For just as an image is a thing that imitates and is not the thing itself, so exterior goods seem to express the form of true happiness, but true happiness...
