**The First Meter of the Third Book**

This is the first meter of this third book, which is called a choriambic meter after its inventor, or dactylic from its predominating foot <note>A "foot" is a unit of poetic rhythm; the commentator is analyzing the technical structure of the verse</note>, and the first verse of this meter is hypercatalectic, because after the first foot one syllable remains extra, namely "re" in this word *serere* [to sow]. And because Philosophy previously said

---

that it must first be shown what false happiness is, and afterwards what is true, therefore Philosophy in this meter commends this order through four examples. The first is that whoever wants to sow a good field must first root out the harmful weeds so that the field may bear fruit well; similarly, someone wishing to know true happiness must first root out the false. Whence it says in the text: *He who wishes to sow a noble field*, that is, a distinguished one, *first clears the lands*, that is, the fields, *of thickets*, that is, of roots which prevent the seed from growing, and he *cuts back*, that is, prunes away, *the fern*, that is, the useless weed, *with a sickle*, that is, a scythe, *so that the new grain*, <note>original: "Ceres," the Roman goddess of agriculture, used here to mean grain</note> *may go forth*, that is, progress, *heavy*, that is, burdened, *with fruit*. The second example is just as by tasting something bitter, honey appears sweeter; so through the knowledge of false happiness, true happiness is better recognized. Whence it says in the text: *The labor of the bees is more sweet*, that is, more pleasant, *if a foul taste first occupies*, that is, infects, *the mouth*. The third example is just as after a cloudy time, serenity is more pleasing; so after the knowledge of false happiness, the knowledge of true happiness is more pleasing. Whence it says in the text: *When*, that is, after, *the South Wind*, <note>original: "Nothus," the Greek name for the moist south wind</note> that is, the southern wind, *ceases to give forth rain-bearing sounds*, that is, blasts bringing on rains, *then the stars shine more pleasingly*, that is, more delightfully. The fourth example is just as the beautiful day follows the darkness of night, so the knowledge of true happiness follows the knowledge of false happiness. Whence it says in the text: *When*, that is, after, *the Morning Star*, <note>original: "Lucifer," literally the "Light-Bringer"</note> that is, the morning star, *has driven away*, that is, bound, *the darkness of night, then the beautiful day drives*, that is, leads, *the rosy horses* of the sun. Then she applies the examples to the purpose, saying: You first ought to consider false goods, and once they are rooted out, you ought to recognize the true goods in which happiness consists. Whence it says in the text: *You also, looking first*, that is, regarding, *false goods, begin to withdraw your neck from the yoke*, that is, from the yoke of false happiness; *thereafter*, that is, afterwards, *true goods shall enter*, that is, enter into, your mind. Note that just as vices must first be rooted out and afterwards virtues planted, so a field must first be purged and afterwards sown. Whence Tobias says: "With thorns and briars the fallow lands must be purged, so that the seed may be able to bear fruit in the fields." Note that "thicket" <note>original: "fructer"</note> according to Britto <note>A reference to William Britto, a 13th-century grammarian</note> is a density of twigs.

### Second Prose of the Third Book

**When she had lowered her gaze for a little while.** This is the second prose of this third book in which Philosophy posits diverse opinions concerning false happiness. And first, Boethius shows how Philosophy behaved after the aforementioned things. Second, Philosophy shows that all men strive to arrive at blessedness, which she herself defines. Third, she shows that men are often led away from true happiness by diverse errors. Fourth, she posits opinions concerning happiness. The second part begins at "The care of mortals"; the third at "To use this"; the fourth at "Of whom indeed." First: After Philosophy promised the order of proceeding from false happiness to the true, then she herself "lowered her gaze for a little while," that is, with eyes inclined and withdrawn as if into the "narrow," that is, the noble seat of her mind, she thus "began," that is, commenced to speak. Note that the inclination of the head is a sign of subtle imagination; because of which, those imagining subtly and profoundly incline the head. And sometimes they do not see things declared before their eyes. Therefore, Philosophy, wishing to speculate subtly concerning happiness—the speculation of which is difficult—having inclined her gaze, betook herself into the noble speculation of her mind. "The care of all mortals." Here Philosophy shows that all men strive to arrive at the one end of blessedness, which blessedness she herself both defines and describes thus: "All care," that is, the solicitude of mortals, that is, of men, which care the labor of manifold pursuits exercises; for some study in literature, some in merchantry, and so with others. That care proceeds by a "diverse path," that is, by a diverse mode of living; yet it strives to arrive at the one end of blessedness. Moreover, that which men strive to arrive at is such a good that, once it is obtained, one can desire nothing further. Which, indeed, is the supreme of all goods, containing within itself all goods; for if anything were "away from it," that is, lacking, it could not be the supreme good, because it would leave something "extrinsic," that is, outside that good, which could be desired. And these things having been said, she concludes the definition of blessedness, saying: "It is clear," that is, manifest, that blessedness is a state perfected by the gathering of all goods. Note that the knowledge of the ultimate end brings a great increase to...

->Begin to withdraw your neck from the yoke.<-
->Henceforth let true things enter the mind.<-

## Second Prose of the Third Book.

**WHEN** she had lowered her gaze for a little while and, as if received into the narrow seat of her mind, she thus began: "The care of all mortals, which the labor of manifold pursuits exercises, proceeds indeed by a diverse path, but nevertheless strives to arrive at the one end of blessedness. That, moreover, is the good which, once obtained, one can desire nothing further. Which is indeed the supreme of all goods, containing all goods within itself."

life in the first book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics</note>, because according to the requirements of the end, all other things are moderated, according to the *Lincolnian* <note>Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, a famous medieval commentator</note> in the first book of the *Posteriors*. Therefore, philosophy hands down to us the knowledge of the ultimate end, that is, blessedness. For the end is not more desirable than those things which exist for the sake of the end, as is clear through Aristotle in the third book of the *Topics*. Likewise, in the same place: that whose end is good is itself also good. Likewise, all things are to be named from their end. Whence the poet says:
> If the end is good, then the whole is praiseworthy.

<margin>concerning the end</margin>
# Which, if anything were lacking from it, could not be the highest good; since it would leave something outside of itself that could be desired. It is clear, therefore, that blessedness is a state made perfect by the gathering together of all goods. This state, as we have said, all mortals strive to attain by diverse paths. For there is naturally inserted into the minds of men a desire for the true good, but wandering error leads them toward false things.

Note: the "end" in practical matters <term>agibilibus: things to be done</term> holds itself just as the "principle" <term>principium: starting point or axiom</term> does in theoretical matters. Therefore, just as our intellect naturally adheres to first principles, so our appetite naturally adheres to the ultimate end, which is the highest good. Note that the "end" is twofold: namely, the end *by which* and the end *for the sake of which* all things are done. For that one is unique, such as God or blessedness; and this end is desired by all under one rationale, insofar as the good satisfies the appetite of man. However, the end *by which* is the operation <note>the action or work</note> by which men strive to attain the end *for the sake of which*; and such an end is not one, just as there is not one single operation for all people. Therefore the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says that the care of men proceeds by a diverse path to follow the ultimate end.

Note: that toward which all men strive to arrive is the good; because the good is that which all things desire (from the first book of the *Ethics*).
<margin>Blessedness</margin>
Note: because blessedness has the character of the ultimate end, it is such a good that, once obtained, nothing further is desired; it is the highest good. For it is of the nature of the "end" to be the last, and beyond that which is last, there is nothing. Therefore, it is also necessary that it be the highest good; because if, after obtaining it, some good were still lacking to it, it would not be the highest good. Such a thing is blessedness. Note: because blessedness is the best, most beautiful, and most delightful good, therefore blessedness is a perfect state by the gathering of all goods, containing in itself all goods. For if any good were lacking to it, it would not be the highest good. "This state, as we have said..." In this part, Philosophy shows that men are led away from true happiness by various errors, saying: this state of blessedness, as we have said, all mortals strive to attain by a diverse path, that is, by a different way; because the desire, that is, the appetite for the true good, is naturally inserted into the minds of men. But blessedness is the true good, because it is the highest good. However, wandering error leads men toward false goods.

Note: because blessedness gathers in itself all goods, therefore the desire for it is naturally inserted in men. Here, however, it should be known that blessedness "containing all goods" can be understood in two ways. In one way, *formally*; in this way it does not contain all goods, because happiness formally and essentially can exist without exterior goods, such as without riches and other goods. In another way, it is understood to contain them *virtually*, so that blessedness excels all goods, and in this way it is true. Note: that Philosophy here uses a certain figure of speech called an *epitheton* <note>an epithet or descriptive term</note> by saying "wandering error." For there is no error which is not wandering. Whence the poet:
> It becomes an epithet if you say "bitter wars."

Note: since the human mind naturally desires the true good, it never tends toward a false good except insofar as that false good is estimated to be a true good. Such an estimation, however, is a wandering error; therefore, wandering error leads to false things.

# Book Three.

->**Of these, some believe the highest good is to lack nothing.**<- This is where Philosophy sets forth various opinions regarding happiness, showing first how men were led toward false goods through error; second, she shows that they placed their blessedness in such goods; third, she shows that their natural intention was actually tending toward true blessedness. The second point begins at "To all of whom," and the third at "But the efforts of men." First, she shows how men erred regarding false goods by establishing them as their end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of life</note>. Second, she shows how certain ends were exchanged for one another. Third, she reduces other matters of chance to the aforementioned points. The second begins at "There are also," and the third at "In these, therefore." First, she says: "Of these," supply "men," who are led toward false goods; some are led to believe the highest good is to lack nothing, and they labor so that they may flow with—that is, abound in—riches, placing all sufficiency in wealth, and in this they were in error. Others, truly judging the highest good to be that which is most worthy of veneration—that is, honor—strive to be revered by their fellow citizens once they have obtained honors, thinking that true dignity consists in temporal honors, and in this they were in error.

<column-break/>

**Of these, some indeed, believing the highest good is to lack nothing, labor so that they may abound in riches. Others, however, judging the good to be that which is most worthy of veneration, strive to be revered by their citizens once honors have been obtained. There are those who establish the highest good in supreme power: these either wish to rule themselves or endeavor to stay close to those who rule. But to those for whom fame seems the best thing, these hasten to spread a glorious name through the arts of either war or peace. Most, however, measure the fruit of the good by joy and gladness; these think it most happy to overflow with pleasure.**

<column-break/>

And in this they were in error. There are others who establish the highest good in supreme power; these endeavor to rule or to stay close to those ruling as their counselors or familiars, thinking through this that they are truly powerful, and in this they are deceived. To those for whom "clarity"—that is, fame—seems to be the best good, they hasten to "propagate"—that is, to spread—a "glorious name"—that is, a beautiful reputation—through "arts"—that is, the pursuits of war (such as military men) or the arts of peace (such as the wise men of the world), believing that through this they acquire immortal glory; and they are deceived by this. "Most"—that is, many—"measure"—that is, gauge—the fruit of the good by joy and gladness; these "think"—that is, estimate—it "most happy" to "overflow"—that is, abound—in "pleasure"—that is, bodily delight—estimating that true joy consists in this, which is erroneous. 

Note that there are five things in which those erring from the true good have placed true happiness: namely, **riches, honors, powers, glory, and pleasures.** The sufficiency of these is understood as follows: since the "end" of a blessed man has the character of a "good," the end is diversified according to the diversity of the good. There is, moreover, a threefold good: the **useful**, the **pleasant**, and the **virtuous** <note>original: "bonum honestum," often translated as the "moral" or "noble" good</note>. Those who intended the "useful" good placed happiness in riches. But those who intended the "pleasant" good placed it in pleasures, and in those they placed their end and happiness. However, those who intended the "virtuous" good were diversified because the virtuous good is a good according to reason. Reason, moreover, is twofold: namely, **speculative** and **practical**. They did not speak of the virtuous good which consists in speculation <note>The contemplative life or theoretical study</note>, because such a good is hidden; rather, they placed happiness in the virtuous good which is the good of practical reason. Such a good, therefore, either consists in the opinion of men...

# Prose 2

Thus is glory; or rather, it consists in the exercise of a real act, and this is twofold. Either it consists in the exercise of one's own act toward others, and thus it is power; or it consists in the exercise of the acts of others toward oneself, and thus it is honor. There are also those who [exchange] their ends. In this part, he shows how certain people exchange these aforementioned ends, and he says: There are also some who exchange the ends and final causes for one another—that is, mutually—desiring one for the sake of the other. For some desire riches and pleasures for the sake of power.

**There are also those who exchange the ends and causes of these things for one another, such as those who desire riches for the sake of power and pleasures, or those who seek power either for the sake of money or for the sake of spreading their name. In these, therefore, and in other such things, the intention of human acts and wishes is occupied; just as nobility and popular favor seem to acquire a certain renown. Wives and children are sought for the sake of delight; but the most sacred kind of friends is not counted among the goods of fortune, but among the goods of virtue; but the rest are taken up either for the sake of power or for the sake of pleasure.**

<margin>
And there are others who seek power—that is, desire it—for the sake of money—that is, for riches—or for the sake of spreading their name—that is, for the sake of expanding their fame. Now, according to Aristotle in the third book of the *Ethics*: "As each person is, so the end appears to him." Therefore, according to the different disposition of men, different ends are chosen. Moreover, a thing is chosen for the sake of some end through which someone seems to be able to attain that end. Since, therefore, those placing the end in riches thought it was more possible to attain riches through power, they themselves desired power for the sake of riches, and
</margin>

conversely, those to whom it seemed they could attain power through riches desired riches for the sake of power; and thus they placed an exchange of these ends with one another. *In these, therefore, and in other such things.* Here Philosophy reduces all the "goods of fortune" <note>External worldly goods like wealth or status, as opposed to internal virtues.</note> in which men place happiness to the five aforementioned categories. And she says: In these five goods and other such things—namely, those reducible to the aforementioned—the intention of human acts and wishes—that is, desires—is occupied. And she demonstrates by example how other things are reduced to them: namely, nobility and popular favor, which seem to acquire a certain renown—that is, glory—therefore (it follows) they are reduced to glory. Wives and children—that is, offspring—are those things which are desired for the sake of delight—that is, for the sake of pleasure—therefore they are reduced to pleasure. But the most sacred kind of friends is not counted among the goods of fortune, but is counted in virtue. But the rest which fall under external fortune are taken up either for the sake of power, such as the administration of offices, or are taken up for the sake of delight, such as the practice of games. But the goods of the body are readily referred—that is, reduced—to the higher goods: because strength and size, which are signs of bodily fortitude, seem to provide excellence—that is, power—and thus they are reduced to power. So beauty and speed seem to provide celebrity—that is, glory—to which they are reduced. Health, however, seems to confer pleasure, to which it is reduced. And thus all the goods of fortune are reduced to the five aforementioned categories. Note that the lack of any good increases the desire for that good; therefore, according to the varying needs of men, their desire varies. Whence Aristotle in the first book of the *Ethics* says that the sick man [desires] health, the beggar riches; but those conscious of their own ignorance admire those who have something great above them. According to the different disposition of men, therefore, happiness was placed in different goods of fortune, which nevertheless [fall] under the aforementioned...

# Book Three.

They include five types of goods. Although friends bring joy, they are not to be counted among the goods of fortune. For since friendship is a virtue <note>original: "virtus"</note>, it follows that friends are acquired through virtue. That which is acquired through virtue is preserved through virtue, and such a thing cannot be a "good of fortune" <note>meaning a matter of random luck or external wealth</note>. Likewise, friendship founded upon the honest good is most holy and is numbered among the virtues; but friendship founded upon the useful and the delightful good is accidental. In all these things, they seek only happiness. In this part, Philosophy proves that all the aforementioned people sought happiness in these goods. She says: To all those desiring the aforementioned goods, it is clear—that is, manifest—that they themselves desire happiness. For that good which anyone seeks—that is, desires—above all others, he judges to be the Supreme Good <note>original: "summum bonum"</note>. But we define the Supreme Good to be happiness <note>original: "beatitudinem"</note>; therefore, that state which anyone desires above all others, he judges to be the good state—that is, happiness. And then she gathers the goods of false happiness, saying: You have before your eyes the proposed form of human happiness: namely, riches, honors, power, glory, and pleasures. Considering these, Epicurus <note>The ancient Greek philosopher often associated with the pursuit of pleasure</note> determined that pleasure was the Supreme Good because all other things seemed to bring—that is, to give—joy to the soul.

<column-break/>

Now truly, it is easy to see how the goods of the body relate to the higher things. For strength and great size seem to provide capability; health seems to provide Pleasure. In all these things, it is clear that only happiness is desired. For what anyone seeks above all else, he judges to be the Supreme Good. But we define the Supreme Good to be happiness. Therefore, he judges that state to be happy which he desires above all others. You have, therefore, before your eyes the proposed form of human happiness: riches, honors, power, glory, and pleasures. Considering these alone, a certain Epicurus consequently determined for himself that the Supreme Good was Pleasure, because all other things seem to bring joy to the soul. But I shall return to the pursuits of men, whose minds, even if with a clouded memory...

---

Not that everyone seeking the aforementioned goods was seeking happiness [directly]. For whatever someone chooses above other things seems to him to be the Supreme Good. But if someone chooses riches above all else, then riches seemed to him to be the Supreme Good; another chooses honors, and so with the others; therefore, all the aforementioned were seeking happiness. Not that the aforementioned goods are seen to provide some joy, since all things seem to be ordered toward joy as if toward an end; and because in pleasures there is the greatest joy, therefore the Epicureans placed happiness in pleasures. "But to the [pursuits] of men": here Philosophy shows that although men err in the aforementioned manner, nevertheless their intention is always carried toward true happiness. Secondly, she shows from where this arises. First, she sets forth her intent. Second, she declares it. First, she says: I return to the pursuits—that is, to the intentions—of men, whose mind, however, through a clouded—that is, obscured—memory (supplemented by the desire for present goods), nevertheless always seeks again the Supreme Good through a natural inclination. But the soul is ignorant of how it may seek it again, just like a drunkard who is ignorant of which path—that is, which way—he may return home. Note: just as a drunkard knows he has a home, but because of a defect of reason he does not know how to return to it, so men in some way know and recognize the Supreme Good in a general sense, and are naturally inclined toward it as if toward the principle from which they proceeded; but intoxicated by the love of temporal goods, they do not know how they may reach it. For do they not seem to err?

Therefore, the "Good" is what men seek through diverse pursuits, that is, through different intentions. Note that from this entire text one primary argument can be formed: namely, that those seeking the aforementioned goods are actually seeking happiness <note>Latin: *beatitudo*</note>. The reasoning is this: those who strive for sufficiency, reverence, power, celebrity, and joy are striving for happiness. But those desiring the aforementioned goods—namely riches, dignities, kingdoms, glory, and pleasures—strive for sufficiency, re-

verence, and so on for the others; therefore, they strive for happiness. The major premise is well-known, because sufficiency and reverence are properties of happiness which are most perfectly united in happiness; therefore, those seeking the properties of happiness are striving for happiness itself. The minor premise is clear from the text. Note that those seeking riches for the sake of sufficiency were seeking the Supreme Good in this through a natural appetite, because in the Supreme Good there is true sufficiency; and in this they were not erring. For happiness is not anxious or sad, nor is it subject to pains and troubles. This amounts to saying that even in the smallest things, that which is delightful to have and enjoy is sought. And these are the things that men wish to obtain, and for that reason they desire riches, dignities, kingdoms, glory, and pleasures: because through these they believe sufficiency, reverence, power, celebrity, and joy will come to them. It is the "Good," therefore, that men seek with such diverse pursuits, in which it is easily shown how great the force of nature is.

could come to them through riches. Similarly, those seeking dignities for the sake of reverence were seeking happiness by a natural intention, because happiness is most worthy of reverence. But because they thought supreme reverence would come to them through temporal dignities, they erred in this. And the same is understood for the others. *In which how great it is.* Here Philosophy <note>Referring to Lady Philosophy, the personified guide in Boethius's work</note> shows from where this comes: that although the intentions of men are diverse, they nevertheless aim at happiness. She shows that this comes from the force of natural inclination, which can be taken away from no one. And she says: *In which*—namely, in the appetite for the good or happiness—*it is easily shown how great the force of nature is.* Although there are various and disagreeing—that is, discordant—opinions of men concerning the Supreme Good, yet men "pro-feel"—that is, they agree—in loving, which means diligently desiring, the end goal of the Good, which is happiness. Note that without the end goal itself erring, the actions tending toward that end can be diversified. For if there were a diversity of ends because of the diversity of actions, one would not arrive at a single end, but would proceed into infinity regarding ends. This is proven false in the second book of the *Metaphysics*. And this is true concerning the "final cause" <note>The ultimate purpose for which something exists</note> for the sake of which all things are made: that it is one, and not concerning the end as it was previously seen. Therefore, although the opinions and pursuits of men are diverse, they nevertheless agree in desiring one end: namely, happiness.

### The Second Meter of the Third Book.

<margin>q</margin> **H**ow the powerful force of nature bends the reins. Here begins the second meter of this third book, which is called "Pindaric" after its inventor, and "Anapestic" from its dominating foot <note>A poetic meter consisting of two short syllables followed by one long one</note>. It is a dimeter consisting of four feet, of which two constitute one meter. In this meter, Philosophy had previously said that the force of nature works so that the intention of men always tends toward the good. Therefore, here she commends the force of nature, showing that the force of nature is so great that however much a thing is led away by habit or violence to something that is outside its nature, yet when left to itself, it always returns to that which is in it according to nature. She promises her intention, and secondly manifests her purpose. There she says: *Who.* First she says: it pleases me, Philosophy, to bring forth—that is, to manifest—with a musical song—that is, a sonorous one—with slow strings—that is, sounding in the mind of the heart—how great the reins—that is, the natural inclinations—powerful nature bends—that is, rules—by which laws provident nature preserves—that is, protects—the immense orb; and by which laws nature binds each thing with an unbreakable bond.

-> **Meter 2** <-

First, there is **creative nature** <note>original: "natura naturans," referring to God as the source of all</note> such as God, upon whom the heavens and all nature depend. Another is nature that is **both creating and created** <note>original: "natura naturans et naturata simul"</note> such as the heavens, which is called "created nature" insofar as it depends on God, and is called "creating nature" insofar as it influences these lower natures. ## The Second Meter of the Third Book.

### How many reins powerful Nature turns, with what laws she, provident, preserves the immense world, and how she binds and constrains each thing with an unbreakable bond—it is my pleasure to declare this with the pliant strings of the lute in a clear song. Although the beautiful lions of Carthage <note>original: "Poeni," referring to the Carthaginians/Libyans</note> wear chains and take food offered by hand, and fear their grim master, accustomed to bearing his lashes...

<column-break/>

...indicates he is evil. In this context, the speech of Philosophy can be understood as referring to nature in the third sense mentioned, although some explain it as nature in the first sense. Likewise, he calls the "laws of nature" the determinations and natural properties of each thing established for it by God. **"Although the beautiful lions of Carthage."** Here Philosophy manifests her proposition through four examples. Secondly, she concludes generally that it is the same in all other things where she says "they seek again." The first part is divided into four parts according to the four examples which will be made clear. The first is about quadrupeds, such as lions, which, although through a certain habituation they become domestic so that they—

<column-break/>

—seem to be pitiable in fearing their master; yet if they are greatly offended, their natural cruelty returns so that they tear their master with their teeth. Whence it is said in the text: *Which lions of Carthage* (that is, Libyan) *carry* (that is, bear) *beautiful bonds* (that is, chains on the neck) *and take* (that is, receive) *food given* (that is, offered) *to them by the hands of their master, and although they fear the grim* (that is, cruel) *master, these lions being accustomed to bear* (that is, endure) *the lashes of the master: but if blood has stained* (that is, moistened) *the bristling mouths* (that is, the necks) *of the lions because of excessive lashes, then the dormant spirits of the lions* (that is, their behavior) *return to their natural cruelty, and the lions remember themselves* (that is, their nature) *with a heavy roar* (that is, a great growl). They themselves weary* (that is, loosen) *their necks by undoing the knots* (that is, breaking the chains) *and their first tamer* (that is, that master) *receives* (that is, takes) *the torn* (that is, mangled) *furious rages with a bloody tooth* (namely, of the lion). Now, according to Isidore in the book of *Etymologies*, the "Poeni" are the Carthaginian people. Carthage is a city of Libya, which is why the lions of Libya are called "Poeni" lions, and these types of Libyan lions are more easily tamed. Now, however much lions are tamed and led away from their cruelty by habituation, if they are then touched by gore or blood, they return to their natural cruelty. **"Which sings."** Here he places the second example, which is about birds, and it is such: A small bird, captured and domesticated against its nature, however much it is cherished by the delights of men; yet when the opportunity arises, it returns to its wild state. Whence it is said in the text: *The talkative bird which sings on high branches, if it is captured and shut in the hollow of a cave* (that is, a small house, understood so that it stays there for the solace of men). Although the playful care of men provides it with cups smeared (that is, coated) with honey and provides large feasts with sweet zeal; yet if that bird, leaping from its narrow roof (that is, from its narrow little house), sees the pleasing shadows of the groves, it tramples those very foods with its feet, and being sad that it was detained, it seeks the woods and whispers with a sweet voice (that is, sings) in the woods. Now, nature does not become accustomed to its opposite; for if a stone were thrown upward a hundred thousand times, it does not become accustomed to ascending upward. For although by some custom or violence nature can be hindered for a time...

# Book Three

...yet it is always inclined toward its own proper work.
**Driven by certain powerful forces.** Here the commentator provides a third example regarding vegetation, specifically a growing branch, which is as follows: Although a small branch held upright may be bent down by force, yet when released to its own nature, it raises itself upward. Hence the text says: *A branch once driven*—that is, compelled—*by powerful forces*—supply: of a person bending it—*bends its top downward, but if the hand bending it lets go, it looks toward*—that is, regards—*heaven with an upright tip.* It is as if he were saying: once the violence of the bender is removed, the branch returns to its natural straightness. <note>This imagery illustrates the "Natural Law" where objects seek their inherent state once external pressure is removed.</note> **Note** that although the nature of inanimate things does not easily grow accustomed to the contrary, yet in rational humans, habituation or custom achieves much. For although someone may be of a "bad complexion" <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) which determined temperament.</note>, yet through use and habit, they are made capable and the complexion is changed. Hence **Seneca** says: *Custom is a second nature.*

**Phoebus falls into the Hesperian waves.**
Here Philosophy proves her intent by providing a fourth example regarding celestial bodies, which is this: The Sun, moved from the east to the west, falls into the Hesperian <note>Western</note> sea, but by a natural inclination, it returns to the east beneath our hemisphere. Hence the text says: *Phoebus*—that is, the Sun—*falls into the Hesperian*—that is, western—*waves, but by a secret path*—that is, a hidden way, namely beneath the earth—*he turns his chariot again*—that is, once more—*to his accustomed rising*—that is, to the eastern regions. Note that Boethius speaks here in the manner of the poets, who used to say the sun in the evening descended into the western sea so that it might be washed there from the filth and dust with which it was stained while being in our hemisphere. But this is not true; for thus...

<column-break/>

...more. **If blood has stained their bristling mouths, their former spirits return; with a heavy roar they remember their true selves. They loosen their necks from the released knots, and the tamer, first to be torn by a bloody tooth, is the first to soak up their rabid wrath.** <note>This refers to a lion returning to its wild nature after tasting blood.</note> **The bird that chatters on high branches is shut in the hollow of a cage. To this bird, the playful care of men may minister cups smeared with honey and large feasts with sweet devotion. Yet if, leaping within the narrow roof, it sees the pleasing shadows of the woods, it tramples the scattered food with its feet. Mournful, it seeks only the woods; it whispers of the woods with a sweet voice.** **A branch once driven by powerful forces bends its top downward. If the hand bending it lets go, it looks toward heaven with an upright tip. Phoebus falls into the Hesperian waves, but by a secret path he turns his chariot again to his accustomed rising. All things seek their own proper returns, and each rejoices in its own homecoming. Nor does any order handed down remain, unless it has joined its end to its beginning, and made the circle of itself stable.**

A human being, however, makes a stable circle of themselves by proceeding from God as if from their beginning; they pass through temporal things in which they do not stop, but pass on toward God as if toward their end through the contemplation of the mind.

# Book Three

Consider then, O Boethius, whether men are able to reach their destined end—that is, blessedness <note>Latin: *beatitudo*; the state of supreme happiness or well-being</note>—through those things by which they think they will obtain it. For if money or honors and the rest bring something of such a kind that nothing good seems to be lacking, then let us admit that some people become happy by the acquisition of these goods. But if they are not able to effect—that is, to do—what they promise, and if they lack many goods, is it not clearly—that is, manifestly—the case that a false

<margin>
appearance of blessedness is detected in them. It is as if she said: Note that the principle of all things, which is God, is true blessedness, as will later be clear. Such a principle is known as if through dreaming, and one arrives at it with difficulty; for we do not know Him perfectly in our present state, because our intellect relates to Him as the eye of an owl relates to the light of the sun (from the second book of the *Metaphysics* <note>A reference to Aristotle's work</note>). Also, one arrives at such blessedness with difficulty. Whence Alan of Lille says in the *Anticlaudianus*: "Access to this is difficult and the retreat is easy. The approach is open to few, the fall to all. Scarcely anyone is able to cross; everyone is able to turn away from that path; which offers rewards to few, but is closed to many. It is too narrow for the one entering, but wide for ruin."
</margin>

# Because if they are neither able to effect what they promise and they lack many goods, is it not clearly a false appearance of blessedness that is detected in them?

# First, therefore, I ask you yourself, who a little while ago were flowing with riches: among those most abundant wealths, was your mind never confounded by anxiety conceived from some injury? **Boethius.**

# And yet, I said, I cannot remember ever having been of such a free mind that something was not always troubling me. **Philosophy.**

"First, therefore, I ask you yourself..." Here Philosophy proves her intent: that these goods do not effect what they promise, and consequently, there is a false blessedness in them. And first she shows this regarding riches; afterwards the same regarding other goods. First, therefore, she proves that riches do not confer the sufficiency <term>sufficiency: the state of needing nothing else</term> which they seem to promise and for which they are desired. Second, she proves that riches confer indigence <term>indigence: a state of extreme poverty or lack</term>. Third, she proves that they do not take away indigence. The second point begins at: "And yet, I said, I cannot remember..." The third point begins at: "But what manner..."

First, she intends this line of reasoning: True happiness does not consist in those things which do not render a man self-sufficient. But riches are of this kind. Therefore, etc. The major premise is noted because happiness is the most sufficient good, lacking nothing. She declares the minor premise in the text, and Philosophy proceeds in a "didactic" manner—that is, by questioning and answering. And she says thus: "First, therefore, I ask you yourself, Boethius, who a little while ago were flowing with—that is, abounding in—riches: was your mind never confounded by anxiety—that is, sadness—conceived from some injury amidst your most abundant wealth?" And Boethius responded.

# Meter 3.

Whether wealth mitigates hunger, the rich man will still thirst and hunger. And while nature has its limits, for greed, nothing is enough. Therefore, if riches cannot remove—that is, repel—want, but instead create want, what is it? That is, how can it be that you believe they provide—that is, give—sufficiency? As if to say: it should in no way be believed. Note that all want is either a want of nature or of greed. The want of nature can be satisfied by very little, because nature

<margin>
is content with few and minimal things. <note>original: "paucis minimisq[ue] contenta est"</note> Whence, for the sake of nature, one ought not to seek great riches, nor can the want of nature be removed through riches, just as nature itself cannot be changed. But the want of greed is that which can in no way be filled; and thus riches cannot remove them; rather, they increase it more. As it is said: The greedy man will not be filled with money. Note that riches not only do not bring about sufficiency, but they do not even bring about wisdom; as Seneca says: "What use are many riches to a fool, as long as he cannot become wise through them?" <note>A reference to Seneca’s Epistles on the uselessness of external goods for the soul.</note>

The third meter of the third book:
Though the rich man flows with gold
</margin>

---

## I pass over the fact that nature requires very little, while for greed nothing is enough. Therefore, if riches can neither remove want and instead create their own: what is it that makes you believe they provide sufficiency?

### The Third Meter of the Third Book

->Though the rich man, in a swirling whirlpool of gold,<-
->Should amass wealth that will never satisfy his greed,<-
->And should deck his neck with pearls from the Red Sea's shore,<-
->And plow his rich fields with a hundred oxen,<-
->Yet biting care does not desert him while he lives,<-
->Nor do his fleeting riches accompany him when he is dead.<-

---

### The Fourth Prose of the Third Book.

"Whirlpool." <note>original: "gurgite"</note> This is the third meter of this third book, which is called Archilochian <term>Archilochian: a verse form named after the Greek poet Archilochus</term> from its inventor. It is iambic from the predominating foot, to which is joined an elegiac meter, in which meter the prose-writer <note>Boethius</note> inveighs against the greedy, whom the anxiety of riches afflicts in the present life and abandons in death. And he says: "What greedy rich man, in a flowing—that is, abounding—whirlpool of gold—that is, a multitude—amasses—that is, gathers—wealth that will not fill his desire?" And: "What rich man burdens—that is, weighs down—his neck with pearls—that is, precious gems—of the Red Sea shore—that is, the Red Sea, because gems are gathered on the shore of the Red Sea?" And: "What man cleaves—that is, divides by plowing—rich fields—that is, fertile lands—with a hundred oxen—that is, with a hundred oxen—yet biting care—that is, anxiety—does not desert him while he survives—that is, while living—and fleeting riches, which pass away easily, do not accompany him when he is deceased—that is, dead." 

Now concerning the literal meaning: a "whirlpool" <note>original: "gurges"</note> according to Huguitio <note>Huguitio of Pisa, a 12th-century grammarian</note> and Isidore in the book *Etymologies* <note>Isidore of Seville's 7th-century encyclopedia</note> is a high—that is, deep—place in a river; and in this context, it signifies an abundance and affluence of gold. Likewise, according to Huguitio, "pearl" <note>original: "bacca"</note> spelled with a double 'c' is found to be used for the fruit of the olive or laurel or for any fruit; however, it is sometimes found for a precious gem, and so it is taken here. Likewise, the greedy rich man is oppressed by a double evil: in the present life he is always anxious, and after death nothing of his riches accompanies him. Of this rich man, Alanus speaks in the book *The Complaint of Nature* <note>Alanus de Insulis, a 12th-century theologian</note> saying: "So that he may give various courses of coins to his purses, the rich man imposes fasts upon his own belly." Likewise: "The rich man's eyes feast on silver, but his belly is forced to play the philosopher." <note>Meaning the stomach must endure hunger while the eyes stare at useless wealth.</note>

->The Fourth Prose of the Third Book.<-

### Book Three

->**On Dignities**<-

This is the fourth part of this third book in which Philosophy proves that temporal dignities <note>High offices or positions of power</note> do not bestow the honor and reverence they seem to promise, and consequently, true happiness is not found in them. First, she proposes that dignities make a person honorable; second, she refutes that idea at the point beginning "Is there such power..."

First, she says: "But dignities make the man to whom they come honorable and reverend." Note that **honor** is the showing of reverence to someone as a testimony to their virtue, as understood from the fourth book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>. Or otherwise: **Honor** is a sign of an opinion of benefit, as **Aristotle** says in the book of *Rhetoric*. For when we believe we can be benefited by someone, we honor them. But **reverence** is a fitting and mature gravity, according to **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>.

"Is there such power in magistracies..." Here Philosophy refutes the proposition in four ways: namely, that dignities do not bestow honor and reverence. First, because they often fall to the wicked. Second, because through dignities, the vices of the wicked become known. Third, because they become cheapened in the opinion of men. Fourth, because they cease to shine with the changing of times. The second point begins at "In which..."; the third at "And so that you may recognize..."; the fourth at "But this among..." First, she says:

<column-break/>

**"Dignities make the one to whom they come honorable and reverend. Is there such power in magistracies that they may plant virtues in the minds of those using them and drive out vices? On the contrary, they are not accustomed to banish wickedness, but rather to make it illustrious <note>original: 'illustrare'; here meaning to make visible or highlight</note>. Thus it happens that we are indignant that they have often fallen to the most wicked men. Whence Catullus <note>The Roman poet</note>, although he saw Nonius sitting in the curule chair <note>A chair of high office</note>, nevertheless called him a 'tumor' <note>original: 'strumam'; literally a scrofulous swelling</note>. Do you see how much disgrace dignities add to evil men? Indeed, their unworthiness would be less apparent if they were not brightened by any honors. Could you yourself finally be led by so many dangers that you would think to hold a magistracy with Decoratus, when you perceived in him the mind of a most wicked buffoon and informer? For we cannot judge those worthy of reverence because of honors whom we judge unworthy of the honors themselves. But if you saw someone endowed with wisdom..."**

***

"Is there such power" — "Is there" stands for "Is there truly such virtue in magistracies (that is, in dignities) that they plant virtues in the minds of those using them, so that they drive out vices?" She speaks as if to say "No." Whence she adds: "On the contrary" — meaning certainly — dignities are not accustomed to put to flight wickedness, but rather to "illustrate" it, that is, to make it manifest. "Thus it happens" — that is, because of this — that we are indignant that they have very often fallen to the most wicked men. Whence **Catullus**, who was a wise and virtuous man, calls **Nonius**, who was a vicious man, a "tumor," even though he saw him sitting in the **curule** — that is, in the judicial seat of dignity. You see, therefore, how much disgrace dignities add to evil men, and they manifest them to be contemptible to good people. "Indeed" — meaning certainly — their unworthiness (that is, their malice) will be less evident if they do not "shine" (that is, become bright) with any honors. Boethius, could you be led (that is, attached) by so many dangers that you would hold office with **Decoratus** <note>A corrupt official under Theodoric</note> — that is, such a man...

<summary>This page examines why political office and high status do not bring true honor, arguing that power often highlights a person's flaws rather than granting them virtue. It uses the historical examples of Catullus's disdain for Nonius and the corruption of Decoratus to illustrate that the wicked are made more contemptible by the offices they hold.</summary>

# Fourth Prose

->Would you hold office if, while in it, you had to look upon the mind of a most wicked scoundrel and informer? That is to say: No.<-

Can we judge those worthy of reverence because of honors—that is, because of high offices—whom we judge unworthy of those very honors? That is to say: No. And if you saw someone endowed with wisdom, even if he held no high office, could you fail to consider him worthy of reverence for the wisdom with which he was endowed? That is to say: You could not judge him unworthy of his wisdom and virtue; because a proper dignity

<column-break/>

inheres in virtue, which virtue pours into those to whom it has been joined. And because popular honors cannot do this, it is clear—that is, manifest—that they do not possess their own beauty—that is, true dignity. <note>The commentator is distinguishing between "dignitas" as a political office and "dignitas" as an inherent quality of worth.</note> **Note:** From the text, such a reasoning can be formed: That which, when coming to someone, does not confer honor, and when not coming, does not take it away, does not make that person truly honorable. But high offices do not confer honor upon those to whom they come, nor do they take it away if they do not come; therefore [they do not make one honorable]. The minor premise is proved because honor follows virtue, according to the fourth book of the *Ethics* <note>A reference to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>. Whence we judge a vicious

---

man worthy of no honor, in whatever high office he may be; but we judge only the virtuous man worthy, even if he is not in office. Since, therefore, temporal offices neither confer virtues nor take away vices, it is manifest that they do not make one honorable. **Note:** Catullus <note>original: "catulus", likely referring to the Roman poet Catullus</note> was a wise and virtuous man who, out of indignation of soul, called Nonius—who was sitting in a curule chair <note>The seat of high Roman magistrates</note>—a "tumor" <term>struma: a scrofulous swelling or tumor</term> because dignity had been conferred upon such a malicious man. A tumor is a collection of humors in the neck; under this likeness, he called him a tumor because he had a collection of vices in his breast.

---

**Note:** That King Theodoric <note>The Ostrogothic King who imprisoned Boethius</note> wished to violently push a certain man named Decoratus into a magistracy so that he might rule the republic together with **Boethius**. **Boethius**, detesting his wickedness, refused to be associated with him; because of this, **Boethius** was afflicted with many injuries by King Theodoric. **Note:** That a "scoundrel" <term>scurra: a buffoon or parasite</term> according to Huguitio <note>A 12th-century grammarian</note> is the same as a lecher or a vain-speaker; properly, however, he is called one who follows a court for the sake of food. **Note:** That virtue makes a man reverend and noble, not office. For **Seneca** says in his 44th Letter: Virtue did not receive Plato as a noble and reverend man, but made him so. For who is generous, virtuous, and worthy, except he who is well-disposed toward virtue? A hall full of famous images and coins does not make men noble, but the mind and virtue rising above fortune. **In which that.** Here **Philosophy** proves by a second way that offices do not make men noble and honorable: because they manifest the vices of the wicked. In which, namely, because office comes to them, it is the more to be noticed; for if someone is more abject—that is, viler—the more he is despised by the many, since office cannot make the wicked reverend, it rather makes those whom it displays to the many more despicable. **But** this is not **with impunity**; that is, the office does not make these things unpunished, because the wicked return the favor to the office, which they defile by their own thinking.

# Book Three

That is to say: just as high office stains the wicked because it makes their malice manifest, so conversely, the wicked stain their offices. **Note** that through high offices, the vices of the wicked become known, because "leadership reveals the man" <note>A common medieval proverb: *principatus virum ostendit*</note>. Since vice makes a man contemptible, temporal dignity coming to the wicked makes them even more despised. Hence the poet Juvenal says: "Every vice of the soul carries with it a shame that is more conspicuous in proportion to the rank of the person who sins" <note>Juvenal, Satire 8.140-141</note>. And Seneca says: "High office held by the unworthy is a place of disgrace."

And so that you may recognize that true reverence, here Philosophy proves by a third way that high offices do not make one venerable, because they become worthless in the opinion of men. For those who hold offices are honored by their own people, yet among foreigners they are not cared for, such as by those who belong to another diocese <note>In this context, a "diocese" refers to a secular administrative district or territory</note>. Hence it is said: "And so that you may certainly know that true reverence—which is true happiness—cannot happen to any man through these shadowy dignities," that is, transitory things like a shadow. Gather the argument thus: if any man who has served, that is, used, a multiple consulship—that is, a high office—should happen to come...

<column-break/>

**For the wicked return the favor to the offices they hold, which they stain with their own contagion. And so that you may recognize that true reverence cannot be attained through these shadowy dignities, consider it thus: If a man who has held the consulship many times should happen to travel among barbarian nations, would that honor make him venerable to the barbarians? But if this were a natural gift inherent to high offices, they would in no way cease from their function in any nation whatsoever. Just as fire, in every part of the earth, never ceases to be hot. But since it is not their own inherent power, but the deceptive opinion of men that attaches this to them...**

...perhaps among barbarian nations, that is, foreign peoples, does the consulship of good men make him venerable to the barbarians? The answer is no. But certainly, if making one revered were a natural gift of these offices, it would in no way cease from its function in any place among any people, just as fire everywhere on earth never ceases to be hot, that is, to burn. But since the deceptive opinion of men, and not their own power, attaches this quality of making one revered to them, they vanish immediately when they come to those who do not judge them to be dignities, such as barbarian or foreign nations. **Note** that a thing is not stripped of its own proper operation; for since operation is the end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the Aristotelian purpose or goal of a thing's existence</note> of that which possesses the operation (according to the second book of *On the Heavens and the World*), a thing stripped of its operation would be stripped of its purpose, and thus would exist in vain. Therefore, if making one revered were the natural operation of high offices, they would make a man revered among all peoples. But we see that offices which make someone revered among their own people do not make him revered among foreigners.

But this is true among foreign nations. Here Philosophy proves by a fourth way, which is taken from the fact that offices become base through the change of time. For what was once a great dignity is considered as nothing in modern times. Hence she says: "But what I have said is true among foreign nations; yet even among those where these offices originated, they do not last forever." But certainly, for the Prefecture was once a great power among the Romans, but now it is an empty name and a census—that is, the high status of the Senatorial rank is now a heavy burden, which was once a great dignity. And if anyone...

# Fourth Meter

In former times, whoever took care of the food supply <note>original: "annonam"</note> for the people was called the Prefect of the Grain; he was held in great esteem. Now, what is more dejected than that prefecture? It is as if to say: nothing. For as we said a little while ago, it possesses no inherent beauty of its own, but rather receives its splendor from the opinion of those who use it, and then loses it again. And then he concludes by saying: Therefore, if dignities cannot make men worthy of reverence (as is clear from the first path); if they become foul by contagion, that is, by the wicked vice of those who hold them (as is clear from the second path); if they cease

**to shine due to the changing of times (as the fourth path teaches); if they become cheap in the estimation of foreign nations (as is clear from the third path); what is there of desirable beauty that they have in themselves, let alone what they might provide to others? It is as if to say: they have no beauty in themselves, and therefore cannot provide it to others.**

**They vanish immediately when they come to those who do not consider those dignities to be of value. But this is among foreign nations. Among those where they originated, do they endure forever? By no means. Even the Prefecture, once a great power, is now an empty name and a heavy burden on the senatorial census. If anyone once cared for the people's grain supply, he was considered great. Now, what is more dejected than that prefecture? For as we said a little while ago: because it has no inherent beauty, it receives splendor from the opinion of those using it, and then loses it. If, therefore, dignities cannot make men worthy of reverence; if they become foul by the contagion of the wicked; if they cease to shine by the change of times; if they become cheap by the estimation of nations: what is there of desirable beauty that they have in themselves, let alone what they might provide to others?**

### The fourth meter of the third book.

> **Though the proud man adorned himself**
> **In Tyrian purple <note>A costly violet-blue dye from Tyre, a symbol of imperial power.</note> and snowy pearls,**
> **Yet he lived hated by all—**
> **Nero, in his raging luxury.**
> **But this wicked man once gave...**

<margin>q</margin>
"Though the proud man in Tyrian purple." Here begins the fourth meter of this third book, which is called a "Valentian" meter from its inventor, "dactylic" from its dominant foot, and "tetrameter" from the number of feet. In this meter, Boethius confirms by example that dignities do not make one truly worthy of reverence, and consequently, happiness is not to be sought in them. For dignities came to Nero, who was the worst of men, and were bestowed by him upon others. Whence he says in the text: "What proud man?" Nero, of raging luxury, "adorned himself," that is, decorated himself, in "Tyrian purple," that is, pure

<column-break/>

**Note that the Prefecture was formerly a great dignity among the Romans. He was called the Prefect who presided over the other magistrates and surpassed all dignities in the Roman city. However, after Julius Caesar had seized the Empire, such dignity was transferred to the Emperor and its power was diminished, so that the name of that office remained without the reality. Likewise, the Senatorial dignity was great among the Romans, because the office of the Senators was formerly honorable—namely, to consult usefully for the Republic—but afterwards the Senators were compelled to serve the will of the Prince to the detriment of the Republic.**

# Book Three

<margin>Note the description of Nero’s raging luxury. For the Bishop of Lincoln <note>Robert Grosseteste, a famous 13th-century scholar and bishop</note>, named Scultus, relates that Nero, traveling through all the theaters of Italy and Greece, dressed in various finery, was often seen to have surpassed the lute-players, tragedians, and charioteers. He was driven by such great lusts that he seemed to have abstained neither from his mother nor his sister out of reverence for blood relation. He took a man as a wife, and was himself received as a wife by a man. He was of such unbridled luxury that he fished with golden nets which were drawn out by purple ropes, and they washed him with cold and hot ointments which cost no less than a thousand talents. And nevertheless, this same Nero, though so vicious, obtained the imperial dignity; indeed, he even bestowed dignities upon others.</margin>

...clothed in pure Tyrian purple <note>original: "sanguine tyri" - literally 'blood of Tyre,' the source of the most expensive ancient dye</note> and adorned with snowy little stones—that is, white pearls—yet he himself flourished while being hateful to all. That is, he was odious, for the wicked Nero gave to the venerable fathers—that is, the respected senators—the curule chairs <note>term: curules - the ivory folding chairs used by high-ranking Roman magistrates as a symbol of power</note>. These were undignified honors because they were given by an unworthy man. Who, therefore, would think—that is, judge—those honors to be blessed which miserable—that is, wicked and vicious—men bestow? The answer is: no one.

->The Fifth Prose of the Third Book.<-

**Can it be that kingdoms and the intimacy of kings have the power to make a man potent?**
**Why not, when their happiness lasts forever? And yet, antiquity is full of examples—as is the present age—of kings who have exchanged their happiness for calamity.**
**O, what a brilliant power this is, which is found to be not even effective enough for its own preservation! For if this power of kingdoms is the author of blessedness, would it not diminish happiness and bring in misery if it were lacking in any part?**
**But however far human empires may extend, there must necessarily be many nations left behind over whom each king does not rule.**

---

<margin>a</margin> This is the fifth prose of this third book, in which Philosophy shows that kingship and the intimacy of kings do not confer the true power which they promise and for which they are desired. And first, she shows that true power is not in those who rule; second, that it is not in the associates of kings (at the point: "For what should I say..."). That true power—and consequently blessedness—is not in rulers is proved in four ways: first, from the shortness of the duration of their rule; second, from the smallness of its extent; third, from the attachment of fear; and fourth, from the lack of security. The second point begins at "But if this..."; the third at "A strong outburst..."; the fourth at "And yet they would wish...". First, she proposes the intent by way of a question: "Do kingdoms and the intimacy of kings have the power to make one potent?" And she responds ironically: "Why not?"—meaning, why would they not make one potent since their happiness (that is, their power) lasts forever? This is added because it never actually happens. Wherefore she adds: "But certainly antiquity is full of examples, and even the present age, of kings who have changed their happiness for calamity." And she adds: "O, what a brilliant power," speaking ironically, "which is not even found effective enough for its own preservation." Note...

# Fifth Prose

No happiness lasts forever, at least not temporal happiness. This was shown previously by the ancient example of Croesus, King of the Lydians <note>Croesus was a king of Lydia (modern Turkey) famous for his wealth, whose downfall became a classic warning against pride.</note>. This is also clear from the examples of those who lived in the time of Boethius, such as the Roman Emperors who were frequently changed in their own times, oppressed now by wars, now by treachery, or cast down in some other way. Geoffrey <note>Geoffrey of Vinsauf, a medieval poet and rhetorician.</note> testifies to the same in his *Poetria*, saying: "This one thing you can know for certain: no power can be lasting; if you wish for examples, look to those who came before."

->Fifth Prose<-

**But in that part where power ceases to make men blessed, there enters that impotence which makes them wretched. In this way, therefore, it is necessary that a greater portion of misery resides within kings: a tyrant, having experienced the dangers of his own lot, likened the fear of his reign to a sword hanging over a man's head.** <note>This refers to the famous story of the Sword of Damocles.</note> **What then is this power, which cannot drive away the bites of anxiety nor avoid the stings of fear? And yet they themselves would wish to live in security, but they cannot. Hence they boast of their power; but do you judge a man powerful whom you see wishing for what he cannot achieve?**

<column-break/>

Look upon the fortunes of those who came before. Flourishing prosperity overturned ancient Athens. If this power of kingdoms—here he shows that royal power is not true power nor the source of happiness because of the smallness of its reach. He says: if this power of kingdoms is the author, that is, the cause of happiness, then surely if royal power is lacking in any part, it must diminish happiness and bring in misery. He speaks thus: but although human empires are spread far and wide, it is still necessary that many nations are left over which each king does not rule. For it cannot be that one man rules over all. But in that part where

power ceases to make men blessed, in that part enters the impotence that makes them wretched. Therefore, in this way, it is necessary for there to be a greater portion of misery than happiness in kings, since they are powerless in the greater part of the world. Note that if royal power makes one blessed, then where there is a lack of royal power, there will be a lack of happiness. Since, therefore, there are more nations over which the power of one king does not extend than those subject to his power, it follows that the king will be wretched in the greater part and not blessed. Therefore, true happiness does not consist in royal power. "Having experienced his lot"—here he shows that there is no true power in those who rule because of the fear attached to it, using an example. He says: a certain tyrant, namely Dionysius <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse, a Greek tyrant of Sicily.</note>, having experienced his lot—that is, how anxious the fear of dangers was—demonstrated it by the likeness of a sword hanging over a man's head. What then is this power that cannot drive away the "bites," that is, the gnawing of anxieties, nor avoid the "stings," that is, the prods of fear? He means to say such power is meager, that is, small. Note that Dionysius was a certain king who, when asked by one of his courtiers <note>Damocles, though not named here, is the courtier in the traditional legend.</note> why he was always sad when he seemed to have a blessed life, wishing to show him the cause of his sadness, ordered him to be placed among lavish feasts and ordered a sharp sword to be hung over his head by a thin thread. That man, seeing the sword, was terrified and could neither feast nor be joyful. Dionysius said to him: "Such is my life which you thought was blessed; for I always foresee death looming over me." Consider, therefore, how he who never ceases to fear can be happy. "And yet they themselves"—here Philosophy shows the same thing by a fourth reason taken from the lack of security, saying: "And yet, for certain, these kings would wish to live in security, but they cannot."

### Book Three

From this point, it follows that those who boast of their power cannot be secure, which is a mistake. This is proven when Philosophy asks: "Do you judge <note>original: 'censes'</note> him to be powerful who you see wishes to accomplish what he cannot?" The implied answer is: he is not powerful. "Do you judge him powerful who surrounds his flank with a bodyguard <note>original: 'satellite'—referring to armed attendants or henchmen</note>; who fears those whom he himself terrifies more than they fear him; who, in order to appear powerful, is placed in the hands of his servants?" The implied answer is: he is not powerful.

<margin>
**Note:** From the text, the following logic can be formed: That which does not make a person secure does not make them truly blessed. But temporal power is of this sort; therefore, etc. The conclusion is well-known: the greater the power, the less the security. **Note** that kings cannot be secure because they cannot help but dread imminent dangers. Indeed, Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman historian</note> tells of the aforementioned Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Elder, Tyrant of Syracuse</note> that he so feared barbers' razors that he taught his daughters how to trim beards. When they grew older, he ordered them to singe off his beard and hair with glowing coals, and he built his bedroom over a wide trench, into which he withdrew by a wooden bridge, because he feared his bodyguards and foreigners. "For why should I speak of the friends of kings?" **Here Philosophy speaks.**
</margin>

<column-break/>

**"Do you judge him powerful who surrounds his flank with a bodyguard? Who fears those whom he terrifies more than they fear him? Who, in order to appear powerful, is placed in the hands of his servants? For why should I speak of the favorites of kings, when I show that kingdoms themselves are full of such weakness? The power of kings often casts them down, sometimes while it is still intact, and often when it falls. Nero forced Seneca, his friend and teacher, to choose the manner of his own death. Antoninus <note>The Emperor Caracalla</note> exposed Papinian <note>A famous Roman jurist</note>, who had long been powerful among the courtiers, to the swords of the soldiers. Yet both of them wished to renounce their power. Of these, Seneca even attempted to hand over his wealth to Nero and withdraw himself into retirement; but while the very weight of their greatness dragged them down as they were about to fall, neither achieved what he desired."**

---

She shows that true power does not consist in being a royal favorite. Secondly, she excludes a certain objection. She proves, therefore, that friendship with kings does not make one truly powerful, since such friendship cannot be retained at will, and even when retained, it frequently turns into harm. She says, therefore: "For why should I speak" (that is, tell) of the favorites of kings, when I show that the kingdoms themselves are of great weakness? Namely, that the royal power, while still "intact" (that is, healthy), often casts down the favorites; and the royal power itself, when "fallen," also casts them down. 

How royal power destroys its own favorites while still intact is shown through examples. Nero forced Seneca, his friend and "teacher" (that is, master), to the choice of selecting his own death. The Emperor Antoninus exposed Papinian, his favorite who had long been powerful among the "courtiers" (those of the palace), to the swords of the soldiers. When both Seneca and Papinian wanted to renounce their power because of the cruelty of the princes, they wished to withdraw from them. Of these two, Seneca tried to hand over his riches to Nero to appease him and wanted to betake himself to "leisure" (that is, into a solitary life). But while the "weight" (that is, the greatness of power) drags down those who are "about to fall" (that is, destined to ruin), neither achieved what he wanted. What kind of power is this, then, which those who possess it dread; which, when you wish to have it, you are not safe, and when you wish to set it down, you cannot?

# Meter 5

you cannot avoid these double dangers, as was evident in the cases of Seneca and Papinian. <note>Seneca was the advisor to Nero, and Papinian was a jurist under Caracalla; both were forced to die by the emperors they served.</note>

What then is this power which those who possess it so greatly fear? A power which you are not safe while you wish to hold it, and which you cannot avoid when you desire to lay it down. Or are friends a safeguard—those whom fortune, rather than virtue, brings together? But him whom prosperity has made a friend, misfortune will make an enemy. Indeed, what plague is more effective for doing harm than a familiar enemy? <note>original: "familiaris inimicus," referring to a close associate or "frenemy" who knows one's secrets.</note>

<column-break/>

Note: Nero pretended to fear his teacher Seneca after he became Emperor, just as he had in his childhood. Therefore, he commanded him to choose his own manner of death, because he could no longer live. Seneca, having satisfied himself with food and drink, had a vein opened and died by drinking from a poisoned ring. For the ancients, the powerful and noble, used to carry poison under the gemstone of a ring, so that if any adversity befell them, they might flee to death.

Likewise, Antonius <note>Referring to the Emperor Caracalla (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus).</note> acting as Emperor, played the tyrant against his own people; he caused Papinian, his close friend who had long been powerful among the courtiers, to be killed by the swords of soldiers. From these examples it is clear how royal power, while intact, often strikes down its own associates. How royal power, when it has fallen, strikes down its associates is clear from this: for when associates imitate royal powers, it is necessary that when that power fails, the associates themselves also fail. "Or are they a safeguard." Here Philosophy excludes objections. For someone might say that a man can be preserved in his power through friends. Where some perish because of a lack of power, this is due to a defect of friends. Philosophy excludes this, saying that this cannot be true of friends who are joined by fortune. Regarding friends joined by virtue, we should not speak here, since they are not counted among the "goods of fortune" of which she speaks here. Whence she says in the text: "Or are friends a safeguard" (that is, a help) "whom fortune, not virtue, brings together?" As if to say: No. She proves this by an argument from opposites: Him whom prosperity (that is, fortune) made a friend, misfortune will make an enemy. Indeed, what plague is more effective for harming than a familiar enemy? As if to say: none, because we cannot guard against the enmity of such a person since our secrets are known to him through familiarity. Note that Seneca speaks of "sophistical" <note>False or deceptive</note> friends in his 9th Letter: "He who is taken up for the sake of utility will please only as long as he is useful. A crowd of friends surrounds those who flourish, but around the ruined there is solitude." Whence the poet says: "For love sought for a price sits with the gift; as long as the giving lasts, the friend lasts." Another poet: "While fortune thunders, she scares away fleeing friends. For who loves those whom a true storm does not test?" And another poet: "While the west wind blew, I was accompanied by many friends; but the north wind's blast puts them all to flight." And Horace: "Ants never go to empty granaries; no friend will go to lost wealth." Because a familiar enemy hurts much, the poet says: "A domestic enemy, as you know, hurts more in all things; and the matter itself shows how he does harm."

**"He who would wish to be powerful."** Here begins the fifth meter.

### Book Three

Therefore, he who wishes to be powerful must tame his fierce passions—that is, his cruel ones, because through cruelty a man is made like unto wild beasts—nor should he submit his neck, conquered by lust, to the reins of desire <note>original: "libidine concupiscentie"</note>—that is, to vicious impulses. Even though the Indian land <note>India was often used by medieval writers to represent the furthest edge of the known world to the East.</note> trembles at your laws from afar—that is, though your power extends even to the Indies—and though furthest Thule <note>A mythical or remote northern land, likely Iceland or the Shetlands, representing the northernmost limit of the world.</note> serves you, which is an island beyond Britain where the sun makes the summer solstice and proceeds no further—nevertheless, if you are unable to drive away black cares—that is, dark anxieties—and put to flight wretched complaints arising from the adversity of fortune, then that is no true power.

Note that he is truly powerful who subjects his sensuality to reason. Whence Seneca says: *If you wish to subject all things to yourself, subject yourself to reason.* For you find all things if reason finds you. And Aristotle in the third book of the *Ethics* says: *Just as a child ought to live according to the precepts of a teacher <note>term: "pedagogi" - a tutor or guide for a child</note>, so it is necessary for the desiring part of the soul to harmonize with reason.* Likewise Seneca: *He rules a great empire who governs himself.* He is stronger who conquers his own desire than he who subjects an enemy, for it is most difficult to conquer oneself. And Solomon says: *Stronger is the conqueror of the soul than the conqueror of a city.*

<column-break/>

**Nor let him submit his neck, conquered by lust,**
**To the reins of the seat of desire.**
**For though the distant Indian land**
**Trembles at your laws, and furthest Thule serves you,**
**Yet to be unable to drive away black cares**
**And put to flight wretched complaints**
**Is not power.**

# Prose Six of the Third Book.

**Truly, how deceitful and how foul is glory.**
**Whence not without justice the tragic poet exclaims:**
**"O glory, for thousands of mortals you are nothing else**
**than a great inflation of the ears."** <note>A metaphor for empty rumors or vanity that fills the ears but has no substance.</note>
**For many have often carried off a great name**
**based on the false opinions of the common people;**
**than which, what can be imagined more foul?**
**For those who are falsely praised...**
