# Prose Six of the Third Book.

<margin>g</margin>
"Truly, how deceitful is glory." This is the sixth prose of this third book, in which Philosophy shows that worldly glory does not belong to true happiness <note>term: "beatitudinem" - the state of supreme blessedness or the highest good</note> nor does it make one truly happy. And first, she shows this regarding the glory of one's own virtue; second, regarding the glory that comes from nobility of blood, at the point beginning "Now indeed." First, she shows her intent regarding glory that comes from the praise of false virtue. Second, regarding glory that proceeds from true merits, at the point "which if even." First, she intends this reasoning: That which is deceitful does not belong to happiness nor make one happy; but glory falsely acquired is deceitful; therefore, etc. Whence she says in the text: "Truly, how deceitful and how foul glory is," it is understood to be "sufficiently evident." That it is deceitful she proves by the authority of a certain poet who composed tragedies, saying: "Whence a certain tragic poet exclaims," and she places his authority in Greek <note>original: "in greco" - referring to a quote from Euripides used by Boethius</note> which sounds thus in English: *O glory, among thousands of men you are nothing else than a great inflation of the ears.* This she makes manifest, saying: "For many have carried off a great name"—that is, glory—"that is, they have falsely received it through the false opinions of the common people." And she shows that this kind of glory is foul, saying: "Than which"—namely, what was just said, to have glory by false opinions—"what can be imagined more foul?"

# Prose VI.

<note>original: "Prosa. vi."</note>

...can be estimated. It is as if to say: nothing. For those who are falsely proclaimed—that is, praised—must necessarily blush at their own praises. Note that according to Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</note> glory is frequent fame accompanied by praise. And it is twofold: vain and true. Vain glory is that which comes into being without anyone being aware of the truth. True glory is that which does not come into being without such awareness. Fame, however, is the knowledge of someone not only nearby but also in remote places. Note that fame induces false glory.

<margin>
False glory leads to shame. For shame is the cause of a loss of reputation arising from some shameful act committed. When, however, someone knows themselves to have acquired glory falsely, then they fear this being manifested; from which manifestation they fall into a loss of reputation and modesty. Even if these praises were sought by merits: Here Philosophy proves that glory acquired by merits does not pertain to happiness <term>beatitudo: the state of supreme spiritual blessedness or well-being</term>, intending such a reason: That which is of no concern to the wise man does not pertain to happiness. But even concerning glory acquired by merits, there is no concern for the wise man. Therefore, etc. The major premise is noted.
</margin>

**...it is necessary that they blush at their own praises. Even if these praises were sought by merits: what, however, could they add to the conscience of the wise man, who measures his own good not by popular rumor but by the truth of his conscience? But if this very thing—to have spread one's name—seems beautiful, it follows that it must be judged foul not to have extended it. But since, as I discussed a little while ago, it is necessary that there be many nations to which the fame of one man cannot reach, it happens that he whom you estimate to be glorious appears inglorious throughout the greatest part of the earth. Among these things, truly, I do not consider popular favor even worthy of mention...**

For the wise man cares most for happiness, since he is most happy <note>referring to Aristotle's Ethics</note>. The minor premise is placed in the text saying: Namely, that those praises looking toward glory, although they may be sought by merits, what nevertheless do they add to the conscience of the wise man who measures his good not by the rumor of the people but by the truth of his conscience? It is as if to say: nothing. Secondly, he says the same through an argument from opposites: That if it is beautiful to have spread one's name, therefore it is miserable not to have spread one's name. But since for a great part of the earth it is necessary that the name has not been spread, it is necessary for the greater part to be miserable. He says therefore: That if this very thing seems beautiful—namely to have spread, that is, to have divulged the name, that is, the glory—it follows that it is judged foul not to have extended the name. But as I discussed a little while ago, it is necessary that there be many nations to which the fame of one man cannot reach. It happens—that is, it occurs—that for the greatest part of the earth, he appears inglorious whom you estimate to be glorious. And because someone might say it suffices for happiness that a man be glorious among his own people by having the favor of the people, Philosophy says: among these goods which are in virtuous operation, I do not think popular favor worthy of mention, which neither proceeds from the judgment of right reason nor ever remains firm. Note that the wise man has no care for glory. As Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist writer</note> says: The wise man places his fruit in his conscience; the fool, however, in glory. And Seneca says: Attend to conscience rather than fame; but many fear fame, while few fear conscience. Note that popular fame does not proceed from the right judgment of reason.

<summary>Lady Philosophy argues that worldly glory is meaningless because it is often based on false praise and is geographically limited. She asserts that a wise person should value the internal truth of their conscience over the fickle and localized opinions of the public.</summary>

# Book Three

For the common people follow the inclination of their senses more than the judgment of reason. Nor does their fame last forever, because the reputation granted by the public varies according to the diverse passions of the crowd. Hence, the common folk judge according to their desires rather than the truth of the matter. In this regard, they are like birds whose sight is illuminated by the night and blinded by the day. From the fourth prose of this fourth book: <note>original: "ex quarto huius p̃sa quarta"</note> "Now indeed, how empty, how futile." Here he proves that the glory proceeding from nobility of blood does not belong to true happiness. First, he shows the vanity of this kind of glory; second, he shows what good there may be in nobility at the section beginning "But if there is anything." <note>original: "qd si quid"</note> He says first:

<columns>2</columns>

Now indeed, who does not see how empty and how futile—that is, how fleeting—is the name of nobility? As if to say: it is manifest that nobility, if it refers to renown <note>original: "claritudinē"</note>—that is, to glory—is foreign to those who boast of being noble. He proves this through the definition of nobility, saying: "For nobility seems to be a certain praise coming from the merits of parents." Because if proclamation—that is, praise—creates renown, it is necessary that those who are proclaimed—that is, praised—are the ones who are renowned. These, however, are your parents, not you. Therefore, if you do not have your own renown which comes from your own praise, the renown of another does not make you "splendid"—that is, glorious.

<column-break/>

**...I think it worthy of no regard, as it neither proceeds from true judgment, nor does it ever remain firm. Now indeed, who does not see how empty and how futile the name of nobility is? If it is referred to renown, it belongs to another. For nobility seems to be a certain praise coming from the merits of parents. Because if proclamation creates renown, it is necessary that those who are proclaimed are the ones who are renowned. Therefore, if you do not have your own, the renown of another does not make you splendid. But if there is anything good in nobility, I judge it to be this alone: that a necessity seems imposed upon the noble so that they do not degenerate from the virtue of their ancestors.**

<columns>1</columns>

->The Sixth Meter of the Third Book.<-

It should be noted that nobility of blood is an empty and futile name, because nothing truly ennobles a person except virtue. Hence, Alan of Lille <note>A 12th-century theologian and poet</note> says in his book *The Complaint of Nature*: "What is nobility to you, or the famous name of ancestors, if you yourself have been made a slave to your own vices?" Likewise, a person is noble if they shine with virtue. "He alone is degenerate who is pleased by an evil life." And "Poor Henry" <note>likely referring to the poet Hartmann von Aue's work or a similar moralizing text</note> says: "Not a distinguished race, nor the famous name of ancestors, but integrity flourishes with true nobility." And Seneca says: "No one is better than another unless he has a more upright mind and is more suited to the good arts." 

"But if there is anything [good] in nobility": Here he shows what kind of good is in nobility, saying: "If there is any good in nobility, I judge it to be only this: that a necessity seems imposed upon the noble lest they degenerate from the virtue of their ancestors"—that is, their progenitors—"namely, through vicious habits." For it is better to descend from an ignoble father and be well-mannered than to descend from a noble one and degenerate through vice. It should be noted that one must not boast of nobility, because Seneca says: "If you are beautiful, praise nature; if you are noble, praise your parents; if you are virtuous and wise, praise yourself; if you are rich, praise fortune; if you are powerful, wait a little while and you will be nothing." It should be noted, according to Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, that the best inheritance passed from fathers to children, surpassing all patrimony, is the glory of virtues and the honor of great deeds.

->The Sixth Meter of the Third Book.<-

### Meter 6

The entire race of men. This is the sixth meter of this third book, which is called **Alemanic** after its inventor, **Dactylic** from its predominant foot, and **Trimeter** from the number of feet. It is **hypercatalectic** because one syllable remains in excess. In this meter, Philosophy proves that all men are noble, except for the wicked. Oh, the entire race of men on earth, of whatever condition they may be, rises from a similar origin, because according to the soul,

**The entire race of men on earth**
**Rises from a similar origin. One**
**Is the Father of things. One who provides**
**For all. He gave to Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> his rays. He gave**
**Also horns to the Moon. He gave men to the**
**Earth, and stars to the sky. He enclosed**
**Within limbs the souls sought from that**
**High seat. Therefore, a noble seed**
**Produced all mortals. Why do you**
**Clamor about your lineage and ancestors? If**
**You look to your beginnings and to**
**God your Author, no one stands forth**
**As base-born, unless, fostering worse things**
**Through vices, he deserts his own origin.**

<column-break/>

all are from one Creator. For one is the Father of things—that is, one noble Creator, understand—who provides for all, understand, by governing them. That one Father gave to Phoebus his rays; he gave to the Moon her horns; he gave men to the earth—that is, to inhabit the earth. He gave stars to the sky for its adornment. This Father enclosed souls within limbs—understand, bodily limbs—souls, I say, "sought"—that is, received—from the "high seat," meaning in heaven. Therefore, a "noble seed"—that is, a noble beginning—produced—that is, brought forth—all mortals, meaning men. O men, why—that is, to what end—do you "clamor"—that is, boast with noise—of your

---

->Prose Seven of the Third Book<-

lineage and your ancestors? For if you "look to"—that is, consider—God the Author and your "beginnings," no one stands forth as "base-born" <term>degener: literally 'falling away from one's race'</term> and ignoble, unless "fostering"—that is, giving labor to—worse things by his vices, he "deserts his own origin"—that is, God, from whom he proceeded. Note that all men, in that respect by which they are men, are equally noble. Since nobility is a certain excellence contracted from one's origin, the nobility of a man ought chiefly to be regarded from that part by which he is a man: namely, from the part of the soul. Since, therefore, in all men there is the same origin of the soul—because all souls are from God—all men are equally noble. Only those are ignoble who degenerate from their origin. Moreover, the soul was produced from its origin by God and is similar to God; therefore, only those degenerate from nobility who, by vicious habits, defile the likeness of God which they contracted from their origin. <margin>Note: "souls sought from that high seat"</margin> Here he speaks in the **Platonic manner**, for Plato wished all souls to have been created at once in heaven so that they might later be sent into bodies. This is not true <note>The commentator here corrects Boethius/Plato with the medieval Church's view of 'Creationism'—that God creates each soul at the moment of conception</note>; rather, souls are created in the bodies. Therefore, he speaks in the Platonic manner when he says God enclosed souls received in heaven within the members of the body; more will be seen concerning this in the ninth meter of this third book. <margin>Note</margin> that of all men there is one origin, because they are created by God, whom we all call Father, and all souls are from God. Therefore, no one is more noble than another according to creation, though perhaps they are according to natural talent. For only those are ignoble who degenerate from their genealogy when they depart from virtues and adhere to vices.

# Book Three
<note>original: "Liber tertius"</note>

But what shall I say of bodily pleasures? This is the seventh section of this third book, in which Philosophy demonstrates that happiness does not consist in pleasure. First, she shows this regarding pleasure in general. Second, she addresses a certain pleasure specifically. The second part begins at the phrase: "Indeed, the most honorable..." She proves the first point in two ways.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The second point is established by two arguments. The second begins at: "Which, if they could..." First, she intends this line of reasoning: Happiness does not consist in those things which are followed by many disadvantages; but many disadvantages follow from pleasures, as she declares in the text, saying: "What shall I say of bodily pleasures, the desire for which—that is, the longing—is full of anxiety?" For a person is anxious when they lack what they desire. "Satiety, however"—that is, the fullness of pleasures—"is full of repentance," meaning punishment or regret. Since, therefore, anxiety and repentance are joined to pleasures, happiness does not consist in them. And she adds: "How many diseases those pleasures, and how intolerable..."
</margin>

**What, then, shall I say of bodily pleasures? The desire for them is indeed full of anxiety, while the fulfillment of them is full of repentance. What great diseases, what intolerable pains—as if they were a kind of fruit of wickedness—do they typically bring to the bodies of those who enjoy them! I do not know what joy the movement of these pleasures contains. But anyone who wishes to remember their own lusts will understand that the endings of pleasures are sad. If these pleasures were able to produce happiness, there is no reason why cattle should not also be called happy, since their entire aim is directed toward...**

<column-break/>

...intolerable pains they are accustomed to bring to the bodies of those enjoying them, as if a certain fruit of wickedness—this is sufficiently clear. I do not know what joy—that is, delight—the movement of these pleasures—that is, the emotional impulse—contains. However, whoever wishes to remember their own lusts—that is, their pleasures—will themselves understand—that is, recognize—that the exits—that is, the ends—of pleasures are sad.

<note>The following sections provide "Notae" or scholarly observations common in medieval commentaries to explain the ethical implications of the text.</note>

Note that pleasure is twofold: namely, intellectual and bodily. The first is to be pursued—namely, the intellectual—because it consists in contemplation, making the soul blessed. The second is to be fled because it consists in sensual delight, mortifying the body. Hence Seneca says in his 51st <note>The text says 52nd, but it refers to Letter 51 to Lucilius</note> Epistle: "Uproat pleasures especially, which embrace us in the manner of bandits so that they may strangle us." Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> says: "Pleasure hinders all counsel and, so to speak, binds the eyes of the mind; it is the enemy of reason and wishes to have no commerce with virtue."

Note that pleasure is full of repentance. For Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman historian</note> relates that when the philosopher Demosthenes sought the love of the courtesan Thais, she asked for a hundred talents <note>a massive sum of money</note> to grant her consent. Demosthenes, looking up to heaven, replied: "I will not buy such great repentance at such a high price." For he knew that repentance inseparably follows pleasure.

Note that pleasures bring many diseases. As Seneca says in a certain epistle: "Many dishes have made many diseases." And Aristotle maintains in the *Ethics* that those laboring in the passions of lust and gluttony <note>term: <term>crapula</term> (excessive drinking or gluttony leading to a hangover/sickness)</note> are greatly transformed in their bodies. Indeed, gluttony kills more than the sword. **"Which, if they could [produce] happiness..."** Here Philosophy proves the conclusion previously stated by another method, by leading the argument to an absurdity. The reasoning is this: if happiness consisted in pleasures, it would follow that cattle were happy. Which is...

The father, seeing he could not escape, killed himself. Also, a father is anxious about good sons because of his intense love for them and their promotion; if any adversity happens to them, the father considers himself unhappy. And from this it is clear that conjugal pleasure has anxiety annexed to it.

# Book Three

This is a dimeter <note>original: "dimetrum"</note>, that is, a verse of four feet. It is "catalectic" because it lacks a syllable; for after three feet, one syllable remains from the fourth foot. In this meter, Philosophy shows what evil follows all pleasure. For all pleasure, besides the anxiety attached to it, is transitory, which she confirms through a certain example, saying: "Every pleasure has this which I shall say," because pleasure acts—that is, it goads those enjoying it—with stings, which are punishments. And it is like the stings of flying bees: where, after the bee has poured out its pleasing honey, it flees and strikes the smitten hearts with a sting of too-tenacious a bite. This means the joy of pleasure is exceedingly transitory, but the anxiety it brings is exceedingly great in measure. It should be noted that although all bodily pleasure delights at first and afterwards pricks in the manner of bees, this is especially found in sexual pleasure <note>original: "voluptate venerea"</note>. Regarding its flight, Aristotle urges Alexander, saying: "O merciful Emperor, do not incline yourself too much to intercourse, for intercourse is a certain property of pigs. of the flying ones: **Where it has poured out its pleasing honey, it flees and strikes the smitten hearts with a bite too tenacious.**

<column-break/>

you practice the vice of beasts and the acts of brutes?" Believe me without doubt that intercourse is the destruction of the body, the shortening of life, the corruption of virtues, the transgression of the law, and it generates feminine manners. Furthermore, how sexual delight is to be fled is taught by Alan of Lille <note>original: "Alanus"</note> in *The Complaint of Nature*, saying: "If you wish to flee Venus <note>referring to sexual desire</note>, flee the places, the times, and the life; for place and time provide the fodder for it." And "Poor Henry" <note>Henry of Settimello, a 12th-century poet</note>, speaking of love, says: "You should proscribe it, therefore, with swords and clubs; and by fleeing, put to flight that which only flight puts to flight."

# Prose VIII.

...and should cast it away as a contemptible slave of a most vile and fragile thing, namely the body.
It should be noted that a person seeking money falls into the evil of violence, because every moneyed person is prone to violence, according to the first book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>. But one seeking honors and dignities will supplicate others by humbling himself; yet Seneca says in his *Book of Benefits*: "It is a troublesome and burdensome word to say 'I beg' with a downcast face." Similarly, in man, the goods of reason are much more to be praised than the goods of the body. 

Note that the goods of the body, such as magnitude, strength, and agility, are not to be greatly admired, because Seneca says: "Great things are not carried out by magnitude and bodily velocity, but by virtue." Whence Cato says: "He prevails by counsel to whom nature denied strength." Likewise, Seneca: "Excellence of genius can lie hidden under any skin." # Book Three

The elephant <note>original: "barrus"</note> is so named because its voice is called a "barrit." Its teeth are ivory. Its snout is called a "proboscis." Truly, the brightness of form. Here Philosophy shows her intent regarding the beauty of form, adding that it is a meager good because it is transitory and because it is only superficial. And she says "truly," but through "brightness," that is, beauty of form. "As rapid as it is," that is, how swift. It is quickly passing and is "more fleeting," that is, more unstable than the changeability of spring flowers; as if to say, this is evident enough. Wherefore, if men used lynx-like eyes, as Aristotle says, so that their sight penetrated obstacles—namely, bodies—would not that body of Alcibiades <note>An Athenian statesman known for his extraordinary physical beauty</note>, most beautiful on the surface, seem most foul once the entrails were inspected? "Truly the brightness of form, how rapid it is: how swift, and more fleeting than the changeability of spring flowers. For an acute fever, according to physicians, sometimes kills on the third day. And then he briefly gathers the aforementioned points, saying: "From all of which it is permitted to reduce to a sum," namely that these aforementioned goods cannot provide those things which they "promise," that is, offer; nor are they "perfected by the gathering of all goods," nor do they bring one to happiness like "paths," that is, ways; nor do they themselves make people blessed.

# Meter 8.

Note that Alcibiades <note>A famous Athenian statesman known for his beauty; here used in a common medieval anecdote about the deceptive nature of physical appearance.</note> was a most beautiful woman <note>original: "mulier fuit pulcherrima" - the commentator mistakenly identifies the historical Alcibiades as female, a common error in some medieval glosses</note> whom certain disciples of Aristotle, upon seeing her, told Aristotle to come and see. ...as if certain paths lead toward happiness, yet they do not make people blessed themselves.

### The eighth meter of the third book.

**Alas, how ignorance leads wretched men astray**
**Upon a wandering path:**
**You do not seek for gold upon the green-leaved tree**
**Nor gather jewels from the vine;**
**You do not hide your nets upon the mountain heights**
**To enrich your feasts with fish;**
**Nor if you choose to hunt the nimble mountain goat**
**Do you seek the Tyrrhenian waves.**
**Indeed, men even know the hidden depths of the sea**
**Beneath the crashing waves;**
**They know which water is more fertile with snowy gems**
**Or with the blushing purple dye;**
**They know as well which shores provide the tender fish**
**Or the sharp-spined sea urchins.**
**But where the Good they long for lies concealed,**
**In blindness they endure not to know;**
**And that which transcends the star-bearing heavens**
**They seek submerged within the earth.**

<column-break/>

The eighth meter of the third book.
This is the eighth meter of this third book, of which the first verse is called Asclepiadean meter <note>A complex classical poetic meter named after the poet Asclepiades.</note> after its inventor; it is also called Choriambic from its predominating foot. The second verse is called Archilochian meter after its inventor; it is also called Iambic from its predominating foot. In this meter, Philosophy laments the error of men who are clever in seeking the smallest goods, but in seeking the Highest Good are led away by ignorance. First she does this, and secondly she prays that men, weary of false goods, may return to the true Good; the second part begins at "What worthy thing..." <note>Referring to the next section of the poem.</note> She says therefore: "Alas" is an interjection of one grieving, and it is two syllables here for the sake of the meter. She says that ignorance leads wretched men away by a wandering path, that is, a transverse way—supply "away from the true Good." You men do not seek gold on a green tree, nor do you pluck gems from a vine. You do not hide—that is, you do not conceal—nets for the capture of fish on high mountains so that you may enrich your feasts with fish. And

---

if it pleases you to hunt goats, you do not seek—that is, you do not go to—the Tyrrhenian shallows, which is the Tyrrhenian Sea in Italy. Furthermore, for certain, men know—that is, they have learned—the hidden recesses themselves, meaning those concealed by the waves of the sea. Also, men know which wave is more fertile—that is, more abundant—with snowy gems, meaning pearls. Or which wave is more fertile with blushing purple—that is, the shellfish from whose blood the purple dye is made. And men know which shores offer tender fish or sharp urchins <note>original: "echinis" - sea urchins</note>—that is, such fish. But where—that is, in what place—the Good lies hidden, namely the beatific Good which they desire, they do not endure to know, being blind; and that Good which has gone beyond the star-bearing pole, men—diverted by the blindness of ignorance—seek in the ground, that is, they look for it in the earth. Third, she shows what true happiness is (the second part begins at "For that which..."; the third part at "You have therefore, she says, the form"). First, she says: "Thus far"—that is, up to this point—let it suffice to have shown the form of deceitful—that is, false—happiness, which if you look at clearly—that is, consider—the order is—that is, it remains—to show "next"—that is, afterwards—what true happiness is. And Boethius says: "I see that neither sufficiency can happen through wealth, nor power through kingdoms, nor reverence through dignities, nor glory through celebrity, nor joy through pleasures," though they seem to promise these things; and thus false happiness is in them. And Philosophy says: "Have you grasped the reasons why that is so?" And Boethius says: "I see and look"—that is, I recognize—"through a narrow chink"—as if to say: I do not see those causes fully, but imperfectly—"but I would prefer to know more clearly from you." And Philosophy says: "Indeed, certainly the reason"—that is, the cause of false happiness—"is very ready at hand." Note that false happiness is called "deceitful" because it does not fulfill what it promises; for riches promise sufficiency and dignities promise reverence, which they do not provide, as is clear from what was said before. Note that the knowledge of false happiness is useful, because the knowledge of evil is expedient <note>i.e., helpful for avoiding it</note>.

# Prose IX.

This is for caution, according to Alan of Lille in *The Complaint of Nature* <note>original: "alanū de planctu nature"; Alan of Lille was a 12th-century theologian who used personification allegory similar to Boethius</note>, because evil is not avoided unless it is known, and because the knowledge of evil leads to the knowledge of good through its opposite. Therefore, Philosophy wishes first to assign the causes of false happiness and then to show what true happiness is. **Because that which is simple...** Here Philosophy identifies the causes of false happiness and, explaining it, shows that self-sufficiency, power, reverence, glory, and joy are one in reality. Secondly, she shows how men [separate] these...

"For that which is simple and undivided by nature, human error separates; and it carries it away from the true and perfect toward the false and imperfect. Or do you think that which lacks nothing stands in need of power?" **Boethius:** "Not at all," I said. **Philosophy:** "You are certainly right. For if there is anything which in any respect is of a weaker strength, in this it must necessarily need the protection of another." **Boethius:** "So it is," I said. **Philosophy:** "Therefore, the nature of self-sufficiency and power is one and the same." **Boethius:** "So it seems." **Philosophy:** "But do you think that a thing of this kind is to be despised, or on the contrary, is it most worthy of the veneration of all things?" **Boethius:** "But this," I said, "cannot even be doubted." **Philosophy:** "Let us therefore add reverence to self-sufficiency and power, so that we may judge these three to be one." **Boethius:** "Let us add them, if indeed we wish to acknowledge the truth."

<column-break/>

...separate them from one another. The second part begins there: **"This therefore which is one..."** First, she says that the cause of false happiness is that human error separates—that is, divides—that which is simple and undivided by nature. And human error carries it away from the true and perfect good to the false and imperfect good. And then she declares this cause, showing that reverence, power, and all the others are one and the same in reality. And first she shows that power is the same as self-sufficiency, saying: "Or do you think that which lacks nothing stands in need of power?" And he responded, **Boethius:** "Not at all," I said. **Philosophy** approves, saying: "You respond rightly; for if there is anything that is of a weaker strength—that is, of feeble power—in any matter, it is necessary that it should need the protection of another." And **Boethius** says: "So it is," I said. Philosophy therefore concludes, saying: "Therefore, the nature of self-sufficiency and power is one and the same." And **Boethius** says: "So it seems." Then she shows that dignity <note>referring to 'reverentia' or 'veneratio'</note> is the same as the aforementioned, saying: "Since a thing of this kind is self-sufficient and powerful, do you think it should be despised as if unworthy? Or on the contrary, not despised, but most worthy of all veneration?" **Boethius** responded: "It cannot be doubted that this is most worthy of all veneration." And Philosophy: "Let us therefore add reverence to self-sufficiency and power, so that we may judge these three to be one." And **Boethius** says: "Let us add them, therefore, if we wish to acknowledge the truth." It should be noted that power is the same as self-sufficiency; for it involves a contradiction that something should be all-sufficient in such a way that it lacks nothing, yet lacks power. If it lacked power in respect to any possibility, it would not be entirely self-sufficient. It should be noted that in whomever exists the highest self-sufficiency and the highest power, in the same also exists the highest reverence. For insofar as something has the character of a principle <term>principle: a source or fundamental origin</term>, to that extent it is worthy of reverence, just as children revere fathers because they are the principle of their being, and servants their masters because they are the principles...

<sig>k 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: principles</meta>

# Book Three.

The motives of servants in following a command through authority, and we revere virtuous men because they are the principles governing political life. Power, moreover, signifies the nature of a principle, whence that which is most powerful is the greatest principle, and therefore such a thing is most worthy of reverence. **What then,** she says. Here she shows that glory and joy are annexed to the aforementioned things, saying: **What then do you judge? That which is most self-sufficient, most powerful, and most worthy of reverence—is this obscure and ignoble, or is it most illustrious with all celebrity?** <note>original: "celebritate," referring to being widely honored or renowned.</note> that is, glory. Boethius responds: **I confess that it is most celebrated,** i.e., most glorious, as it is. Then Philosophy concludes, saying: **It follows, therefore, that we must admit that renown** <note>original: "claritudinem," brilliance or fame.</note> i.e., glory, **differs in no way from the three previous qualities.** And Boethius says: **It follows, I say.** Then she shows the same regarding joy. She says: **That which lacks nothing from outside, and which can do all things by its own strength, which is revered and illustrious—is this not also most joyful?** Boethius responds: **I cannot imagine from where any sorrow could creep into such a being,** i.e., enter. Then Philosophy concludes, saying: **If the previous points remain true, it is necessary that this being be full of joy; and by the same concessions, it is necessary that the names of self-sufficiency, power, renown, reverence, and joy be diverse, but that their substance differs in no way.** Granting this, Boethius says: **It is necessary, I say.**

<column-break/>

**"What then,"** she said, **"do you think this is obscure and ignoble, or is it most illustrious with all celebrity? Consider indeed: that which was granted to lack nothing, to be most powerful, and most worthy of honor—would it lack renown, which it could not provide for itself, and for that reason appear in some part abject?"** Boethius: **"I cannot say so; for as this being is [the others], so also I confess it to be most celebrated."** Philosophy: **"It follows, therefore, that we must admit that renown differs in no way from the three previous qualities."** Boethius: **"It follows," I said.** Philosophy: **"That which lacks nothing external, which can do all things by its own strength, which is illustrious and revered—is it not certain that this is also most joyful?"** Boethius: **"But from where any sorrow could creep into such a being, I cannot even imagine. Therefore, it must be confessed to be full of joy, if indeed the previous points remain."** Philosophy: **"And yet this also is necessary by the same arguments: that the names of self-sufficiency, power, renown, reverence, and joy are indeed diverse, but in no way does their substance differ."** Boethius: **"It is necessary," I said.**

---

It should be noted that all creatures are compared to God as an effect to its cause. And because the knowledge of any cause shines back in its effect, it is necessary to have knowledge of God himself through his effect, and knowledge with praise; because the effect of God represents Him under the aspect of goodness and perfection, which is the matter of praise. Since, therefore, glory is "clear knowledge with praise," it is necessary that the principle of all things—which is most self-sufficient, most powerful, and most worthy of reverence—is also most glorious. It should be noted that to the most self-sufficient being, no good is lacking; and such a being has the appetite <note>In medieval philosophy, "appetitus" refers to a natural inclination or striving toward a good.</note> at rest in the good attained, which is joy. Therefore, the most self-sufficient good is also the most joyful.

The commentary explains that we know God's nature as the "Supreme Good" by observing these perfections reflected in His creation.</summary>

# Prose 9

It must be noted that all these things—**sufficiency, power, reverence, glory, and joy**—are one in substance. Let it not be thought that they are one in substance like a collection of different things; for then there would be a composition within it, which is contrary to the nature of the most powerful and most worthy being, because simpler things are more worthy than composite ones. But this will be made clearer later. Therefore, regarding this which is one, Philosophy here shows how men divide that which is essentially a unity. Secondly, she raises a doubt.

**Philosophy:** "Therefore, that which is a **one** and a **simple nature**, the wickedness of men divides; and while they attempt to obtain a part of a thing that lacks parts, they achieve neither a portion (which does not exist) nor the thing itself which they least desire."
**Boethius:** "In what way, and how?"
**Philosophy:** "He who seeks riches," she says, "to escape poverty, labors not for power; he prefers to be cheap and obscure, and even withdraws from himself many natural pleasures so that he does not lose the money he has prepared. But in this way, even **sufficiency** does not happen for him whom strength deserts, whom trouble stings, whom worthlessness casts down, and whom obscurity hides."
"He, however, who desires only to be able <note>original: "posse," referring to power or capability</note>, scatters his wealth, despises pleasures and honor that lacks power, and thinks nothing of glory."

<column-break/>

**Commentary:** Here she first shows how men divide that which is one. She says: That which is one and a simple nature is "disparted"—that is, divided—by human wickedness, meaning the wicked error of men seeking one thing without the others. And while men strive—that is, labor—to obtain a part of a thing that lacks parts, the man attains no "portion"—that is, a part—nor the whole thing itself which he affects and seeks.
**Boethius:** "In what way do men divide these things?"
**Philosophy** says: He who seeks riches for the sake of fleeing penury—that is, for the sake of sufficiency—yet labors [not] for power but prefers—that is, wishes more—to be "cheap"—that is, unworthy—and "obscure"—that is, inglorious—and thus cares nothing for dignity and glory.

---

Such a man even withdraws many natural pleasures from himself lest he lose the money he has "prepared"—that is, earned. But in this way, even sufficiency does not happen for him whom "strength"—that is, power—deserts; whom trouble stings; whom "worthlessness"—that is, [lack of] reverence—casts down; whom "obscurity"—that is, infamy—hides. (The implied answer is: No, he does not find it).
Then she shows the same regarding power, saying: He who truly desires only "to be able"—that is, power—he "profligates"—that is, scatters—his wealth, despises pleasures and honor lacking power, and thinks nothing of glory. But you see how many things such a man lacks! For it happens sometimes that such a person lacks necessities, is bitten by anxieties, and when he cannot drive these away, he even ceases to be "powerful," which was the very thing he most sought.
Similarly, one may reason regarding the other three: namely, honors, glory, and pleasures, just as with the previous two. For since each of these, when perfectly understood, is the same as the others (as has been declared), whoever seeks any of these without the others does not grasp that which he desires.
**It must be noted:** He who seeks a part of an indivisible thing will find neither a part nor the thing itself whose part he seeks, because in the nature of things, an indivisible thing has no parts. Since, therefore, the predicted five—sufficiency, reverence, etc.—are one and indivisible in reality, though they differ in name, he who seeks one without the other will not find it. It must be noted that these five are found...

<summary>Lady Philosophy explains that the five attributes of happiness (sufficiency, power, respect, glory, and joy) are actually a single, simple substance. She argues that human error fails to find happiness because people try to pursue these attributes individually rather than as a unified whole.</summary>

### Book Three.

In sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses</note> in which these five qualities exist in an imperfect and diminished way, one is found without the other. However, insofar as they are received according to a perfect and highest being—as they are found in blessedness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>—they are the same thing indivisibly, and one is not found without the other. For the highest self-sufficiency is blessedness; the highest reverence is blessedness; the highest power is blessedness; and so it is with the others. It should be noted that because man naturally desires blessedness, he sometimes desires each of the aforementioned five things insofar as they relate to blessedness. This occurs according to perfection, insofar as they are the same as blessedness. And because blessedness, since it is God, is indivisible, all five aforementioned things are indivisibly one. From this it is clear that because men seek these things according to their imperfect state in sensible things, and yet desire them according to perfection, men do not attain what they desire through them. "What then," I said. Here Philosophy raises a doubt because it has already been said that a man, by seeking each of these things separately, is frustrated in his search for blessedness. It can therefore be doubted whether by seeking all of them together, blessedness might be found. Therefore, Boethius says in the text: "What then," I said, as if to say: although blessedness is not

# Book Three.

In temporal things there is no true sufficiency, but only a likeness of it. Perfect **sufficiency**, however, includes all the other four <note>The five attributes of happiness: sufficiency, power, honor, fame, and joy</note>. And each of those other four, when perfect, includes the others. Therefore, that which is one perfect thing grants all; but that which grants all makes one truly perfect. Therefore he says: "That which can truly confer one [of these], that I recognize to be blessedness." Also, "I assent" <note>original: "assentior"</note> is a deponent verb and signifies the same as the neutral verb "I agree" <note>original: "assentio"</note>.

Because therefore the true—here **Philosophy** shows in what true happiness is established. And first she touches upon the order of this part in relation to the preceding ones, and teaches that divine aid must be implored so that you may know in what true blessedness consists. First, Philosophy says: "Boethius, since you have recognized what that true blessedness is, and you have recognized those things which falsely claim to be blessedness, it now remains for you to learn from where you may seek that true blessedness." And Boethius says: "That is what I have already been vehemently expecting from you for a long time." And Philosophy says:

<column-break/>

"Since therefore you have recognized what that true [blessedness] is, and what things falsely claim to be blessedness, it now remains that you should learn from where you may seek this true one." **Boethius**: "That indeed," I said, "is what I have already been vehemently expecting for a long time." **Philosophy**: "But since, as it pleases our **Plato** in the *Timaeus* <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue where he states that one should always invoke the gods at the start of any undertaking</note>, divine protection ought to be implored even in the smallest matters, what do you think must be done now so that we may deserve to find the seat of that highest good?" **Boethius**: "I say we must invoke the Father of all things, for if He is passed over, no beginning is rightly established." **Philosophy**: "Rightly said," she spoke; and at the same time she began to sing in this way.

### The ninth meter of the third book.

Since divine aid ought to be implored in the smallest matters, as it pleases our Plato in the *Timaeus*, what do you think should be done now—supply: "in so arduous a business." **Boethius** answers: "I think"—supply: "we must invoke"—the Father of all things, namely God, without whom no beginning is rightly established. Philosophy approves of this, saying: "You judge rightly." And at the same time, without interval, Philosophy sang in this way; that is, she proposed the invocation of God in a metrical melody. <margin>☞</margin> Note that in all things divine aid is to be implored, because it is God who pours the riches of His wisdom into the souls of the wise; He grants to students the grace of understanding, for whom nothing is difficult and without whom it is impossible to possess anything. So it is written in the prologue of *The Governance of Rulers* <note>De Regimine Principum</note>: "Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," as another Scripture says <note>James 1:17</note>. And **Blessed Augustine** says: "No one is so learned, no one so taught, that they do not require heavenly illumination." And **Blessed Gregory**: "Unless He be within who teaches, the tongue of the teacher labors in vain." Therefore Philosophy, wishing to show in what true blessedness consists, invokes divine aid, without which no beginning is rightly established.

# Meter IX

The lives of these men—that is, illustrious men—were described in this meter. It is called "dactylic" from its predominant foot, and "hexameter" from the number of feet, as it consists of six feet. In this meter, Philosophy invokes divine aid to show where true happiness lies and how one may reach it. First, Philosophy seeks to gain God’s favor by praising Him in many ways; second, she expresses her petition at the point beginning "Grant, O Father."

<margin>
Grant, O Father. Regarding the first part, it should be known that three things are required for a petition to be heard: First, the power to grant it; second, the will; third, the knowledge. Concerning the first two, it is discussed in the fourth prose of this book.
</margin>

## You who govern the world with everlasting reason:
## Sower of the earth and sky, who commands time to flow
## From eternity: remaining stable Yourself, You grant all things motion.

Second: There are two things in which every effect of human acts consists—will and power—and if either is missing, nothing can be accomplished. Regarding knowledge, it is clear that without it, nothing is done rationally. Therefore, wishing to show that God is able and knows how to hear her petition, Philosophy shows Him to be powerful through His governance of the world, the creation of heaven and earth, and the production of time. Second, she shows Him to be willing or benevolent through His goodness and mercy by which He produced all things. Third, she shows Him to be wise through the production of certain specific dispositions. The second part begins "Whom no external [causes]"; the third begins "You [bind the elements] by numbers."

First she says: O Father, who governs the world with everlasting reason—that is, by Your everlasting providence—You who are the sower—that is, the creator—of the lands and the sky, who commands time to go—that is, to proceed—from eternity <note>original: "ab euo"</note>—that is, from Your everlasting duration. You, remaining stable—that is, immutable—grant—that is, cause—all things to be moved.

It should be noted that this entire text from "O You who [govern] with everlasting" up to the part "Grant, O Father" should be read with suspense <note>as a long introductory invocation</note> and can be understood here as a vocative, an expression of wonder, or a prayer. It should be noted that "to govern" is to order things toward their proper end, which pertains to divine goodness. Moreover, the First Cause <note>a philosophical term for God</note> rules all things without being mixed with them, by flowing into them the virtue of life and goodness, according to the author of the *Book of Causes* <note>a widely cited medieval Neoplatonic text</note>.

It should be noted that "the world," according to Aristotle in his book *On the Heavens and the World*, is the constitution of heaven and earth and the natures within them; God governs this world with everlasting reason—that is, His everlasting providence, which is not transitory like human providence but remains for infinite duration. It should be noted that just as someone is called a "sower" <note>original: "sator"</note> who casts the seeds of plants and trees, so God is called a sower insofar as He created and produced heaven and earth. By "heaven and earth," the elements in between are also understood. He says "of the lands" <note>original: "terrarum"</note> using the plural number for the singular through antithesis.

It should be noted that "time" is a successive duration, since it is the "number of motion"—that is, the measurement of motion according to "before" and "after"—from the fourth book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's Physics</note>, which duration proceeds from eternity <note>original: "euo"</note>. Here it must be noted that "eternity" <note>aevum</note> is a duration remaining all at once, having no succession or mutability attached to it; it is the same as eternity <note>aeternitas</note>, which is the proper duration of God, by which God is the cause of time. For just as God, through His being, is the cause of every being, and through His goodness is the cause of every good, so through His duration He is the cause of every duration. It should be noted that God is "stable"—that is, immutable—because He is moved by no type of motion: not by generation or corruption, since He is unbegotten and incorruptible; nor...

God, however, is not necessitated by an efficient cause in the first way—namely, by the necessity of violence—since nothing is more powerful than He; nor by necessity in the second way, since He receives nothing from another. Nor is He necessitated by the necessity of a goal <term>final cause: the purpose or "end" for which something is done</term>, because He is not necessitated by another as if by a goal; rather, everything is compared to Him as the imperfect to the perfect, because He Himself is the Good...

It should be noted that the elements have a numerical proportion among themselves. For just as two square numbers agree in one proportional middle, so two elements contrary in two qualities agree in one middle element proportional to both. For example: a square number is one that results from the multiplication of itself by itself, such as saying "twice two" or "thrice three." Twice two is four, and thrice three is nine. We might take a proportional middle number, namely six, which exceeds four by the same proportion that it is exceeded by nine. For just as nine contains six and a half-part of six [9 = 6 + 3], so six contains four and a half-part of four [6 = 4 + 2]. It is similar in the elements; for fire and water are opposites in two qualities. Fire is hot and dry, while water is cold and moist. They are joined by one middle, namely air, which agrees with fire in heat and with water in moisture. It is the same for air and earth with respect to water. According to this meaning, the text is explained thus: You bind the elements by numbers, that is, by numerical proportions, so that...

# Book Three

->**Cold things** <note>original: *frigoza*</note>, that is, waters which are cold, are joined to **flames**, that is, fires which are hot, through one middle element which is **air**. And **dry things**, that is, lands which are dry, are joined to **liquids**, that is, parts of the air which are moist, through the middle element which is **water**.<-

**"You, connecting the Soul of triple nature that moves all things."** <note>A famous line from Boethius's poem addressed to God.</note> Here, Philosophy demonstrates wisdom through the production of the **World Soul** <term>World Soul: *Anima Mundi*, a concept describing a spirit that animates the entire universe</term>. Regarding this, it should be noted that this text is commonly explained according to the intention of **Plato** in his *Timaeus*. But because that explanation is extremely difficult and of little use, I shall pass over it and provide an easy explanation which follows the mind of **Aristotle**. For the sake of clarity, it must be noted that by "Soul

<column-break/>

**Connecting the soul through harmonious members, you release it. Which, when divided, has gathered its motion into two circles: it travels to return into itself, and circles the profound Mind, and turns the heavens in a similar image.**

<column-break/>

of the World," we here understand the **Intelligence** <term>Intelligence: a celestial being or force responsible for moving the stars and planets</term> moving the celestial sphere, which through its motion flows its power into lower things. And this Intelligence is said to be "middle" between God and the human soul. For just as it is exceeded by God in dignity and perfection, so it exceeds our own soul. It should be noted that the Intelligence of this world is said to be of a "triple nature" because of the three operations it possesses: namely, moving the celestial sphere, understanding God, and understanding itself. 

It should be noted that the celestial spheres are called "harmonious members" of the Intelligence because through them, as if through organs and instruments, the Intelligence flows into lower things. For although the Intelligence moves primarily for its own sake, it moves secondarily for the sake of lower things. With these premises, the text will be clear. 

Wherefore he says: **You, O God, connecting the Soul of the world** (that is, the Intelligence which is middle between God and the human soul, of a triple nature, meaning triple operation, moving all lower things through that influence), **you release it** (that is, you distinguish it) **through harmonious members** (that is, through the corresponding celestial spheres). **Which soul, when divided** (that is, divided in its operations), **has gathered** (that is, impressed) **motion into two circles** (namely, into the circle of the "First Mover" and the circle of the planets). **It travels, reflected back into itself** (namely, by understanding itself, which is one operation), **and it circles the profound Mind** (that is, the Divine Mind, by understanding God, which is another operation), **and it turns** (that is, moves) **the heavens in a similar image** (that is, by its intellection, which is its third operation). 

Note further: although the celestial bodies are diverse, yet by reason of the unity of their order they can be called "one body." Similarly, although the Intelligences are diverse, they can be called "one Intelligence" because of the unity of order in the operation of moving. Therefore, he speaks of "Soul" in the singular, and not "souls."

**"You, with like causes, [produce] souls and lesser lives."** Here Philosophy commends the wisdom of God from the creation of our souls, saying: O Father, you bring forth (that is, produce) the souls of men and **lesser lives** (that is, the souls of brute animals and plants) by the same causes with which you produced the World Soul. Namely, you, **fitting the sublime** (that is, the rational souls of men) **to light chariots** (that is, the celestial stars), **you sow them in heaven and earth** (that is, into earthly bodies). These souls, having turned back, **you make to return to you** by the **fire** (that is, by returning love/charity) and by a **kindly law** (that is, by your divine order). 

Note that the souls of beasts and plants are called "lesser lives" in respect to the soul of man, because they do not have as many or as perfect operations of life as the souls of men do.

# Meter 9

Note that by "swift chariots," according to the intentions of the Platonists, he understands the stars that are matched to the souls' courses. For the Platonists said that God created all souls at once and sowed them in heaven, assigning them to matching stars from which they later slipped down into bodies. This opinion—namely, that all souls were created at once—is not valid; rather, they are created anew every day and infused into the bodies created for them. <note>The commentator is correcting Plato's "pre-existence of souls" theory to align with the medieval Christian view of "creationism," where God creates a new soul for every new body.</note> It is said, however, that the soul is

### You [God] convey souls and lesser lives 
### by matching causes, and fitting them 
### to swift chariots, You sow them 
### in heaven and earth; which, by a 
### kindly law, You make to return, 
### turned back toward You by a 
### returning fire. Grant, O Father, 
### to my mind to ascend to Your 
### august throne. Grant me to 
### survey the fountain of good; 
### grant that, having found the light, 
### I may fix the clear vision of my 
### soul upon You. Scatter the mists 
### and the weights of this earthly mass.

<column-break/>

sown in the heavens because of the celestial powers from which every soul draws its cycle toward the body. Although the soul is produced by God within the body, nevertheless the union depends, on the part of the bodily dispositions, upon celestial power. Therefore, he says it is "sown in heaven and earth" because souls are not fitted to bodies except through the mediation of celestial power. <note>This refers to the medieval belief in astrology/cosmology where the stars influence the physical temperament of the body the soul inhabits.</note> Hence, in the second book of the *Physics*: "Man and the sun generate man." <note>original: "hominē generat et sol" — a standard Aristotelian citation meaning human reproduction is aided by the sun's heat/energy.</note>

<column-break/>

Note that God fits the created souls to "swift chariots," that is, to matching stars. This can be understood in this way: because the created soul has a parity and likeness with a star. For just as a star is the nobler part of its sphere and is perpetual, so the rational soul, being perpetual, is the nobler part of man. Or it can be understood thus: that God fits created souls to "swift chariots," that is, to reason and intellect, which are called the "courses" of the soul because they lead man to the knowledge of things. He "sows" these souls in heaven and earth because the soul, through reason and intellect, has knowledge of both celestial and earthly things. 

Note that by "returning fire," he understands the warmth of charity <note>term: charity (caritas) — in this context, the divine love that draws the soul back to God.</note> which makes a man who has turned away from God through vices return to Him through virtues. For unless a man loves God, he does not seek Him; unless he seeks, he will not find; unless he finds, he will not return to Him. 

**Grant, O Father, to my mind to ascend to Your august throne.** After Philosophy has gained the benevolence of God by praising Him in many ways, she here expresses her petition, saying: "O Father, You who do all the aforesaid things, grant—that is, concede—to the human mind to ascend to the august throne," that is, the noble seat of the Highest Good. "Grant me to survey," that is, to find by investigating, "the fountain of good," which is God, the source of all good. "Grant that, having found the light"—that is, having previously obtained knowledge—"I may fix in You," namely through love, "the clear vision," that is, the bright insights "of the soul," meaning of the reason and intellect. 

"O Father, scatter"—that is, disperse—"the mists," meaning the obscurities, "and the weights of this earthly mass," meaning the weight of earthly love. "And shine forth"—that is, be radiant with Your splendor—for You are the "serenity" by which (supply: "all things") are illuminated. You are the "tranquil rest" for (supply: "pious minds"). "To discern You"—that is, to see You—is the "end" (supply: "of all things"). You exist as the same; You are the "beginning" because You are the origin of all things. You are the "carrier" because You carry us through grace to where we cannot arrive by nature. You are the "leader," leading us from the error of ignorance to the truth of wisdom. You are the "path," since You are the Way and the Truth, and through You one arrives at You. You are the "boundary" beyond which nothing is sought, since You are the highest and perfect good. Note that the seat of the Highest Good is called "august" <note>original: "angusta" — the commentator interprets the Latin word for 'narrow' or 'lofty' as 'subtle' or 'refined'.</note>, that is, subtle.

### Prose ten of the third book.

<margin>
Prose 10 of the third book.
"Since therefore what is of the imperfect..." This is the tenth prose of this third book, in which Philosophy shows where true happiness is established. First, by continuing the argument, she proves that perfect happiness exists in the nature of things. Second, she shows in what true happiness consists, at the point: "But in what way..." First she says: "O Boethius, since you have seen in the preceding sections what the form of imperfect good is and what the form of perfect good is, now I think it must be demonstrated where this perfection of felicity—that is, perfect happiness—is established. In investigating this, I judge that this must first be inquired: whether any such perfect good, as you defined a little while ago (namely in the eighth prose), can exist in the nature of things, lest a hollow—that is, vain—image (a mental appearance) deceive us apart from the truth of the underlying thing (the existing reality)." But it cannot be denied that perfect good and perfect happiness exist in the nature of things, and that this good is like the fountain of all goods. And then she proves it to be so by this reasoning: In whatever genus one finds the imperfect, in that same genus one finds the perfect. But in the genus of things, one finds imperfect good and imperfect happiness, as...
</margin>

Since, therefore, you have seen what the form of the imperfect good is, and also what the form of the perfect good is, I now think it should be demonstrated where this perfection of happiness is established. In this matter, I think we must first inquire whether any good of the sort you defined a little while ago can exist in the nature of things, lest a hollow image of thought deceive us contrary to the truth of the actual subject. But that it does exist, and that it is, as it were, the fountain of all goods, cannot be denied. For everything that is said to be imperfect is held to be imperfect by the diminution of the perfect...

# Tenth Prose.

It is evident from what has preceded. Therefore, in the nature of things, there must be a "perfect good" and "perfect happiness." Philosophy treats this reasoning in the text and says: Everything that is said to be imperfect is held to be so by a diminution, that is, by a lack of the perfect. From this it follows that if in any category there is seen to be something imperfect, it is necessary that in that same category there is something perfect. For indeed, if perfection were removed or set aside,

it is so held. From which it happens that if in any category something appears to be imperfect, it is necessary that in that same category there is also something perfect. For if perfection were taken away, one could not even imagine from where that which is held to be imperfect could have emerged. For the nature of things did not take its beginning from diminished and incomplete things, but proceeding from the whole and the absolute, it glides down into these outer and weakened states. But if, as we demonstrated a little while ago, there is a certain fragile happiness of an imperfect good, it cannot be doubted that there is some solid and perfect happiness. **Boethius: Most firmly, I said, and most truly has this been concluded. Philosophy: But in what way, she said,**

<column-break/>

one cannot even imagine from where that which is held to be imperfect could have emerged, that is, have its being. For nature did not take its beginning from the diminished and the incomplete, that is, from the imperfect; but nature, proceeding from the whole and the absolute, that is, from the perfect, glides down into these extremes, that is, the lower and "effected" things, <note>original: "effecta" - here meaning things that are merely results or consequences rather than primary causes</note> that is, the fruitless. And from this, the "major premise" of the argument is taken: in whatever category something imperfect is found, in that same category the perfect is found. Then she adds the "minor premise," saying: just as we demonstrated a little while ago, there is a happiness of a fragile and imperfect good. And she sets down the conclusion, saying: therefore,

---

it cannot be doubted that there is some solid and perfect happiness. Granting this, Boethius says it is most firmly and truly concluded. It should be noted that in temporal and sensible <note>perceptible by the senses</note> things, there cannot be the highest and perfect good. And because there are many who do not think there are any goods besides sensible ones, Philosophy—before she shows where the perfect good is located—first proves that it exists, lest anyone think there is no perfect good in the nature of things. It should be noted that the "subject matter" is that about which speech and knowledge are held; but when we think of a thing that does not exist, then that thought is empty, deceiving us apart from the truth of the subject matter. Lest such a thought be seen as the knowledge of the highest good, she therefore first proves that it exists in the nature of things. It should be noted that the imperfect cannot be the principle <note>the starting point or origin</note> of things, because the perfect is prior to the imperfect, and nothing is prior to the principle. From this it follows that where there is the imperfect, there the perfect is to be found. It should be noted that one arrives at a certain perfection from which nature, beginning, progresses toward later, imperfect things—such as these lower things which are called "extremes" and the final "effects" of causes, not being causes to other lower things. # Book Three.

->He shows that perfect happiness is established in God.<- Secondly, he shows in what manner it exists in God, at the point where he says, "But I ask." First, he sets forth a well-known proposition. Second, from that he proves his intent at the point, "In this way truly." First he speaks: It has already been proved that there is such a thing as a perfect good. But as to where it dwells—that is, in what that perfect good resides—consider it thus. And then he adds the proposition: Every common conception of human minds proves—that is, concedes—that **God is the good ruler of all things.** And that God is a certain "good" he proves by this: because nothing better than God can be imagined. For who doubts that that thing is good, than which nothing is better? As if to say: no one.

<margin>It should be noted that all concede God to be the ruler of all things. This is stated because the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who held a dualistic view of the universe.</note> posited that there were two principles of things: one good, the other evil. Therefore, lest anyone by this occasion should deny that God is good, he proves this from the fact that nothing can be imagined better than God.</margin>

Wherefore Saint Augustine says in his book *On Christian Doctrine*: "All who know the Latin language, when the sound of the word 'God' touches their ears, are moved to think of a certain most excellent and immortal nature." For God is thought of in such a way that He is something than which nothing is better. "In this way truly, reason demonstrates that God is good," etc. Here he proves his intent—that happiness or the perfect good is located in God—by such a reason: Perfect good is true happiness. But in God is the perfect good. Therefore, in God is true happiness. Wherefore he says in the text: This reason demonstrates that God is good so as to convince—that is, to lead infallibly to the conclusion—that the perfect good is in Him. For unless God were such—namely, the perfect good—He could not be the ruler of all things. For if He were not the perfect good, there would be something more excellent than Him possessing the perfect good, because all perfect things are clear—that is, are manifest—to be prior to those that are less whole (that is, less perfect). Therefore, lest the reasoning proceed into infinity <note>The "infinite regress" argument: logic must stop at a first cause or highest point.</note>, it must be confessed that the highest God is most full of the highest and perfect good. And thus the minor premise of the reason is clear: namely, that in God is the perfect good. Now he proves the major premise, saying: "But we have granted"—that is, we proved in the ninth prose—"that the perfect good is true happiness." Therefore, it remains to conclude that it is necessary for true happiness to be located in the highest God. To which Boethius, consenting, says: "I accept"—that is, I concede—"nor is there anything that can in any way be contradicted."

<column-break/>

Consider it thus: that God, the ruler of all things, is good, is proved by the common conception of human minds. For since nothing better than God can be imagined, who doubts that that thing than which nothing is better, is good? In this way truly, reason demonstrates that God is good, so as to convince us that the perfect good also exists in Him. For unless He were such, He could not be the ruler of all things. For there would be something more excellent than Him, possessing the perfect good, which would seem to be prior and more ancient than Him. For all perfect things are clearly prior to those less whole. Wherefore, lest the reason proceed into infinity, it must be confessed that the highest God is [full] of the highest and perfect good.

# Tenth Prose

->**The Tenth Prose**<-

It must be noted that if God were not the perfect good but an imperfect one, the argument would proceed into infinity. The reasoning follows: God is either the perfect good or imperfect. If He is perfect, our proposition is proven. If He is imperfect, then there must be something prior to Him, since the perfect is prior to the imperfect <note>In medieval logic, "prior" means more fundamental or superior in the chain of being</note>. That prior thing is then either a perfect good or an imperfect one. If it is perfect, that shall be God, and the proposition is proven. If it is imperfect, there will again be something prior to it, since the perfect is prior to the imperfect.

<column-break/>

Again, it is asked of that prior thing: is it a perfect good or an imperfect one? And so one would proceed into infinity, or it must be granted that God is the perfect good. The text hints at this when it says: "Lest the reasoning proceed into infinity."

**Philosophy:** "But I ask you," she says. Here Philosophy shows the manner in which true happiness exists in God: it is not in God as something distinct from Him (like an accidental quality attached to a subject), but it is identical with Him. She proves this with four arguments. The second begins at "Finally," the third at "For altogether," and the fourth at "Look," she says. First, she sets forth her intention with a certain division of points, the parts of which she tests, saying:

**Boethius:** "I ask you, see that you prove it holily"—that is, firmly and inviolably—"that we have said the highest God is most full of the highest good." And Boethius asks, "In what way?" (implying: how is this proven?). Then Philosophy sets out the division, saying:

"Do you presume"—that is, do you think—"that this Father of all things has received from the outside <note>original: "extrinsecus"</note> that highest good with which He is said to be full? Or do you presume He possesses that good by nature from Himself, yet in such a way that you think the substance of God (who possesses it) and the substance of happiness (which is possessed) are two different things?"

Then she refutes these parts. First, she shows that God did not receive the highest good from the outside, saying: "For if you think the good which is in God is received from the outside, then you could"—that is, you would be able to—"estimate that the good which gave the gift is more excellent"—that is, better—"than the one who received it (namely, God)." This is false, because we confess Him to be the most excellent of all things. Then she proves that the perfect good is not in God naturally as something differing from His own substance...

<column-break/>

...to be most full. "But we have established that true happiness is the perfect good. Therefore, it is necessary that true happiness is located in the highest God."

**Boethius:** "I accept it," I said, "nor is there anything that can be contradicted in any way."

**Philosophy:** "But I ask you," she said, "see how holily and inviolably you prove what we said: that the highest God is most full of the highest good."

**Boethius:** "In what way?" he asked.

**Philosophy:** "Lest you presume that this Father of all things has either received from the outside that highest good with which He is said to be full, or that He has it naturally in such a way that you imagine the substance of God who possesses it and the happiness possessed to be diverse. For if you think it was accepted from the outside, you could consider that which gave it to be more excellent than that which received it. But it is most worthily confessed that He is the most excellent of all things. But if it is in Him by nature, yet diverse in definition <note>meaning they are logically distinct even if joined</note>—since we are speaking of God, the Prince of things—let him who can imagine who it was that joined these diverse things together. Finally, that which..."

<summary>Lady Philosophy argues that God and the Highest Good are identical, as God cannot receive goodness from an external source nor be composed of separate parts. She uses a logical proof to show that if God were not the perfect good, an infinite regress of "better" beings would occur.</summary>

# Book Three

saying: not if by nature—that is, through nature—the Supreme Good is in God. But if it were different from Him in its essential definition, let him who can imagine who it was that joined these diverse things together (namely, God and the Supreme Good). <note>original: "ratione quiditatiua" - a scholastic term referring to the 'whatness' or essence of a thing.</note> This is to say: one cannot grant that there is anyone prior to God who could join these diverse elements. It should be noted that the reasoning which Philosophy puts forward is this: The Supreme Good which is in God is either received from the outside or is in Him naturally. If from the outside, then something would be more excellent and noble than God, because the giver of the Supreme Good is more excellent than the receiver of it. If, however, it is in God naturally, it is either as the same as Himself or as something different from Himself. If it is the same as Himself, the proposition is proven; if it is different from Himself, there would be something prior that joined these diverse things. But to imagine such things is difficult. **Finally, that which from any...** Here Philosophy posits a second reason why the Supreme Good in God does not differ from Him, and the reasoning is such: That which is different from another is not that from which it is different. Therefore, if the Supreme Good were different from God, God would not be the Supreme Good, which is a wicked thing to say. <note>original: "nephas" - a religious or moral crime; unspeakable.</note> Hence she says in the text: Finally, that which is different from any thing, that is not the thing from which it is seen to be different. Therefore, that which by its nature is different from the Supreme Good, that is not the Supreme Good. If, therefore, the Supreme Good were in God in such a way that it was by nature different from Him, it follows that God would not be the Supreme Good—which is a wicked thing to think concerning God, than whom it is certain nothing is more excellent. Note: if anything in God were different from Himself, God would be a composite being and not of a simple essence, which is false. <note>The "simplicity of God" is a core medieval concept: God has no parts and is identical to His attributes.</note> Likewise, that which is in God and different from Him is either an "accident" or a part of Him. It is not an accident, because God is not the subject of any accident. <note><term>accident</term>: a quality that can change without changing the essence of a thing, like hair color.</note> If it is a part of Him, since a part precedes the whole, something would be prior to God, which is false. **For entirely of no thing the nature...** Here Philosophy posits a third reason, which is such: That which is the principle of all things is formally the Supreme Good, because the Supreme Good cannot be a derived thing. But God is the principle of all things; therefore, He is formally the Supreme Good. Moreover, the Supreme Good is happiness; therefore, God is formally the highest happiness. Hence she says in the text: Generally, the nature of no thing could be better than its own principle. Therefore, that which is the principle of all things, such as God, I would conclude by the truest reasoning to be the Supreme Good in its substance—that is, by its own substance. Assenting to this, Boethius says: "It has been most fully concluded." But it has been granted that the Supreme Good is happiness.

<column-break/>

...is different from any thing, that is not the thing from which it is understood to be different; therefore, that which is different from the Supreme Good by its nature, that is not the Supreme Good. It is a wicked thing to think this of God, than whom it is certain nothing is more excellent. For entirely the nature of no thing can exist as better than its own principle. Therefore, I would conclude by the truest reasoning that what is the principle of all things is also, in its own substance, the Supreme Good. **Boethius:** "Most rightly," I said. **Philosophy:** "But it has been granted that the Supreme Good is happiness." **Boethius:** "It is so," I said. **Philosophy:** "Therefore," she said, "it is necessary to confess that God is happiness itself." **Boethius:** "I cannot," I said, "refuse the previous propositions, and I perceive that this is a necessary consequence drawn from them."

<summary>This page provides a logical proof that God and the Supreme Good (and thus Happiness) are identical, arguing that God cannot be a composite being or secondary to any prior cause. It concludes that since God is the "principle" or source of all things, He must be the essence of goodness itself.</summary>
