# Tenth Prose
## Book 3, Section 2

Boethius says: "It is so," he says. Philosophy therefore concludes: "Therefore it is necessary to confess that God is [Happiness] itself." Boethius: "I cannot contradict this," that is, I cannot resist the prior propositions, that is, the premises. "I perceive that this follows as a consequence of those," that is, from those points. <note>The commentator is explaining the logical flow of the syllogism.</note> Note that the principle of all things is the supreme good substantially. For if something other than the principle were the supreme good substantially, like something created from a principle, it would follow that the created thing is more noble than its [principle].

**Philosophy: "Look," she said, "whether this same point might also be more firmly proven from this: that two supreme goods which are different from one another cannot exist. For it is clear that of goods which differ, one is not what the other is; wherefore neither can be perfect when one is lacking to the other. But it is manifest that that which is not perfect is not the supreme. In no way, therefore, can those things which are supreme goods be different. And yet we have gathered that both happiness and God are the supreme good; wherefore it is necessary that the supreme divinity itself be the supreme happiness." Boethius: "Nothing," I said, "can be concluded more true in reality, nor more firm in reasoning, nor more worthy of God." Philosophy: "Above these things, therefore," she said, "just as geometers are accustomed to bring forth something after their propositions are demonstrated, which they call 'porisms' <note>original: "porismata"; a Greek term for a deduction or corollary</note>, so I too shall give you a 'corollary' <note>original: "correlarium"; a gift or extra deduction</note>."**

[The commentary continues:] It is more firmly proven that there cannot be two supreme goods that are different from one another. It is "clear," that is, manifest, that of goods which differ, one is not the other. Wherefore, since one is lacking to the other, neither can be perfect, since the "perfect" is that to which nothing is lacking. But it is manifest that that which is not perfect is not the supreme good. Therefore, in no way can those things which are supreme goods be different. But we have gathered that God and happiness are the supreme good. Wherefore it is necessary that the very nature which is divinity, that is, the nature of God, be the supreme happiness. Boethius, approving this, says: "Nothing is truer than this, nor can anything be concluded more firmly by reasoning, nor more worthily of God." Note from the fourth book of the *Topics* <note>Referring to Aristotle's "Topics," a handbook on logic and dialectic</note> that what is said by way of "superabundance" <term>superabundantia: a logical term for a quality that exists in the highest possible degree</term> belongs to one alone. Since, therefore, the "supreme good" is spoken of by way of superabundance, there shall not be two supreme goods. Likewise, if there were two supreme goods, they would either be of the same species or differ in species. If they are of the same species, they will be equally perfect and one [will be the same as the other].

If happiness differed from God, since both God and happiness are the supreme good, there would be two supreme goods of which one would not be the other. ### Book Three

every blessed person is a god. Commending this conclusion, Boethius says: "And this is beautiful," I said—namely, that which you have just concluded—"and precious, whether you prefer it to be called a porisma or a corollary." It should be noted that "every blessed person is a god" is proved from the text thus: Men become blessed by the attainment of happiness. But happiness is divinity. Therefore, men become blessed by the attainment of divinity. But by the attainment of divinity, one is made a god. Therefore, every blessed person is a god. Or it can be argued thus: By the attainment of divinity, one is made a god; by the attainment of divinity, one is made blessed, since divinity is the same as happiness; therefore, every blessed person is a god. Note that according to Huguitio <note>Hugutio of Pisa, a 12th-century grammarian</note>, a "porus" is a subtle opening in the body through which sweat emanates. From this comes "porisma," that is, an opening or illumination of the sense. Those rules which geometricians propose to demonstrate something are also called "porismata" because they open and illuminate the mind of the reader; and he cites Boethius in this book regarding this name "porisma." It should also be noted according to the same Huguitio that from "corona" (crown) comes "coronarium," which is a reward for victory or a prize of war or contest—namely, a crown or something else—or a "coronarium" is that by which someone deserves honor or obtains a crown. He also cites Boethius in this place regarding this name "coronarium," but we commonly call it a "corollary" <note>original: "correlarium"</note>, and a corollary is a conclusion following from premises. Note that someone might say: "If every blessed person is a god, since there are many blessed people, there will be many gods." Boethius responds that there is one God naturally and essentially; but participatively—namely, by the participation of virtue and immortality—there can be many gods. Hence the Psalmist says: "I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High" <note>Psalm 82:6</note>. Likewise, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> suggests in the 12th book of the *Metaphysics*, where he concludes: "A plurality of rulers is not good; let there be one ruler," namely according to nature and essence. Therefore Seneca says: A man of hope...

# Book Three

You propose this for investigation, but I desire to hear what you determine—<gloss>that is, how you define the questions by resolving them.</gloss> It should be noted that the question which Philosophy moves is this: whether the aforementioned five—namely sufficiency, respect, and the rest—constitute happiness like different members <note>Latin: *membra*, referring to limbs or parts of a body</note> of one body, or whether they are all the same and are referred to some one thing, namely to the Good, which is the reason for desiring all these things. She asks whether these are in happiness as diverse things or related to one thing, namely to the Good, by reason of which they are desired. ### The Tenth Meter of the Third Book.

# Book Three

-> I assent, I said. <-

This is the eleventh prose of this third book, in which Philosophy leads Boethius into the knowledge of certain things which he previously confessed he was ignorant of: namely, what is the end <note>Latin: *finis*, meaning the ultimate goal or purpose</note> of all things and by what rudders the world is governed. First, she leads him into the knowledge of the first point; second, into the second point in the following prose. First, Philosophy investigates the definition of the Good; second, from this, she shows what the end of all things is (at the point: *And those things too much*). First, those things which were previously discussed are set forth; second, Philosophy approaches the main proposition (at the point: *Did we not, she said*). First, Boethius, agreeing with what was said before, says: **I assent, I said**, namely to the things already spoken. For all things stand true by the firmest reasons because they are demonstrative. And Philosophy says: **At what price, namely, will you value it if you should learn what the Good itself is?** Boethius responds: **At an infinite price**, namely, I will value it if it should likewise happen to me to know God, who is the Good. Philosophy says: **But I shall certainly lay this open by a most true reason.** Let them remain—that is, let them be granted now—only those things which were concluded a little while ago. And Boethius says: **They shall remain** without any contradiction.

<column-break/>

**I assent, I said; for all things, bound together by the firmest reasons, stand fast.**
**Philosophy:** Then she said: **At what price will you value it if you should learn what the Good itself is?**
**Boethius:** **At an infinite price, I said, if it should likewise happen to me to know God also, who is the Good.**
**Philosophy:** **But I shall lay this open, she said, by a most true reason; only let those things which were concluded a little while ago remain.**
**Boethius:** **They shall remain, I said.**
**Philosophy:** **Did we not, she said, demonstrate that those things which are sought by the many are not true and perfect goods for the reason that they differ from one another? And since one was absent from the other, it could not bring a full and absolute good. But then the True Good comes to be when they are gathered into one form and, as it were,**

---

in their own truth. It should be noted that to prove any conclusion, it is necessary for the principles to remain in their own truth and be granted; for if they were denied, the conclusion could not be deduced from them. Therefore, Philosophy, wishing to conclude what the Good is from those things which were concluded as if from principles, says she wishes to do this while those things which were proved remain. And Boethius says that they shall remain in their own truth. **Did we not, she said, demonstrate those things.** Here Philosophy approaches her intent by showing what the Good is, and she intends to prove this conclusion: **The Good is that which all things desire.** She proves this by such a reason: **The One and the Good are the same.** But all things desire to be one. Therefore, all things desire the Good.

Regarding this reasoning, she proceeds thus: first, she proves the major premise; second, the minor; third, having resumed the major, she brings in the conclusion. The second part is at: *Do you know therefore*; the third is at: *Is there therefore*. She proves the major premise—that the One and the Good are the same—by way of a question. And first she asks, saying: **Did we not demonstrate above in the ninth prose that those things which are sought by the many—namely, sufficiency, reverence, and power—are not true and perfect goods for the reason that they differ from one another?** (Add: in the way they are sought).

# Tenth Prose

->The Tenth Prose<-

...by many, and since if one were absent it could not provide the other, a full and absolute good would be one that lacks nothing. We have previously demonstrated that the one true good is created when all things are gathered into a single form and efficacy of blessedness <note>Latin: *beatitudo*</note>—that is, into a single efficient cause, namely God. Because the same thing, insofar as it is the same, is born to produce the same result. Boethius, granting this, says: "I cannot deny it." # Book Three

Is it not therefore so? In the third place, having taken up the major premise again, she concludes her intent. There she says: First, therefore, declaring the major premise—that everything remains as long as it is one—she says: "You know, O Boethius, that everything that exists remains and subsists as long as it is one; and when it ceases to be one, it likewise happens to be dissolved and to perish." Boethius asks: "In what way?" Philosophy declares this by an example, saying: "In animals this is evident; when the soul and the body come together into one and remain one, that 'one' is called an animal. But when this unity is dissolved by the separation of both soul and body, it is clear—that is, manifest—that the animal perishes and is no longer an animal." She posits another example: "The human body itself, as long as it remains in one form by the joining of the limbs, then the human species is seen—that is, beheld. But if the parts of the body, distributed and segregated—that is, separated from one another—should pull apart the unity, the body ceases to be what it had been. In the same way, to one running through all other things, it will undoubtedly be clear that each thing subsists—that is, remains—while it is one; but when it ceases to be one, it is seen to perish." And Boethius says: "Indeed, it seems no different to me when considering many things." <note>The commentator notes that some might argue being and unity are not the same because "evil people exist but are not one." He refutes this by referencing Book 4, arguing that evil people do not truly "exist" in a simple sense, just as a dead man is not truly a man.</note> "Is it not therefore..." Here Philosophy proves or declares the minor premise, namely that all things desire to be and to remain; and first she shows this, and secondly she proves it.

<column-break/>

For the substance of those things is the same whose natural inclination is not diverse.
Boethius: "I cannot deny it," you say. ¶ Philosophy: "Do you know then," she says, "that everything that exists remains and subsists as long as it is one, but perishes and is dissolved as soon as it ceases to be one?" # Preface

<margin>Note: Boethius does not doubt that animals desire to be and remain, for which he suggests reasons. That which labors to protect its health and avoid death desires to be and remain; but every animal is of this kind, therefore, etc. But whether it is so in vegetables and inanimate things, of this he doubts. The reason for doubt may be that in such things, operations are not so clearly serving the natural appetite for remaining as in animals, which move to perceive nourishment and other things pertaining to the conservation of life.</margin>

Philosophy shows that all things desire to exist and to remain. First, she demonstrates this; second, she proves that such a desire is natural. Second part there: "Nor now do we..." First, she shows the intent in animals; second, in vegetables; third, in inanimate things. The second part there: "And yet it is..." The third there: "For even..." First, Boethius says: Is there anything which, being naturally uncorrupted, would desire to arrive at its destruction—that is, at death and corruption—having abandoned the desire for subsisting? He responds to this:

If you consider animals which have a nature—that is, an <term>appetite</term><note>Latin: *appetitus*; here meaning a natural drive or instinctual leaning toward a goal</note> of willing (that is, pursuing) and nilling (that is, fleeing) something—I find nothing which casts aside the intention of remaining (supply: in the nature of things) and hastens of its own accord (that is, voluntarily) to destruction, with no external causes compelling it. For every animal labors to protect its safety and avoids death and ruin. But I am utterly in doubt as to what you think regarding herbs and trees, and what regarding inanimate things altogether: (supply: whether such things desire to exist and remain).

**Boethius:** "If I consider animals," I said, "which have some nature of willing and nilling, I find nothing which, with no external forces compelling it, would cast away the intention of remaining and hasten voluntarily to its end. For every animal labors to protect its safety, but avoids death and ruin. But what I should think regarding herbs and trees, and regarding inanimate things altogether, I am utterly in doubt."

**Philosophy:** "And yet there is no reason why you should be able to hesitate about this, when you look upon herbs and trees; first, they grow in places suitable to them, where, as far as their nature allows, they cannot quickly wither and die. For some indeed rise in the fields, others on mountains; marshes nourish some, others cling to rocks."

<margin>Here Philosophy proves that vegetables, such as herbs and trees, desire to exist and remain. And she proves this in four ways, as will be evident. First, from the quality of their locations: because they are born in such places where they can be preserved in being for a longer time. Whence she says: 'And yet for certain...' Boethius, there is no reason you should be able to hesitate (that is, doubt) about this, whether inanimate and vegetable things desire to be."</margin>

### Book Three

There are certain herbs called tamarisks <note>original: "merica"</note> which, if anyone attempts to transplant them to high places, they wither away. But nature gives to each thing that which is suitable to it, and labors so that they do not perish as long as they are able to remain. **Note:** Location is the principle of generation because it saves and preserves that which is placed within it, and through its mediation, celestial virtue flows into the thing located there. Since, therefore, vegetables such as herbs and plants require determined places in which they are saved, and in others they wither, it is clear that they themselves desire to exist and to remain. What shall I say of the fact that all things, as if into the earth— Here philosophy proves the same point by another sign taken from the manner of the situation of their parts according to their suitability for the attraction of nourishment, by which their being is preserved. And she says: what do you judge from this, that all herbs and trees draw nourishment through their roots, as if with their mouths submerged in the earth, and spread nourishment through themselves via the marrow <note>The "medulla" or pith of the plant</note>, through the wood, and through the bark? This is for no other reason than the desire for remaining. Then she posits another sign taken from the disposition of the parts to prove an external lesson, saying: What do you judge from this, that the most noble part, such as the marrow, is always hidden away—that is, located in the interior seat, meaning the middle of the plant—while on the outside it is held by a certain firmness of wood? The last part, however—that is, the exterior bark—as if "suffering evil" <note>meaning: capable of enduring hardship</note>, is opposed as a defender against the intemperance of the sky, that is, the air. Then she posits another sign taken from the propagation of seed, which is ordained for the conservation of nature in another similar in species, since the same individual cannot remain in number. And she says: Now indeed, how great is the diligence of nature so that all things are propagated by multiplied seed! Consider that all seeds—who does not know them to be like certain "machines," that is, instruments of remaining, not only for a time, but even for remaining forever "generically," that is, by successive generation. It is as if to say: there is no one to whom these things are not evident. It should be noted that the roots of plants are similar to a mouth since they have the same function—namely, to draw nourishment. Plants have roots fixed in the earth because they draw moisture and nourishment from the earth, which is first diffused into the marrow, then into the wood, then into the bark. The marrow is the softest part in the middle of the plant or tree, not able to endure the intemperance of heat and cold. Therefore—

<column-break/>

—while others are fertile, there are sterile sands which, if anyone tries to transfer them to other places, they wither. But nature gives to each what is suitable and labors lest they perish while they are able to remain. What shall I say of the fact that all things, as if with their mouths submerged in the earth, draw nourishment by their roots, and spread it through the marrow, the wood, and the bark? What of the fact that the most noble part, such as the marrow, is always hidden in the interior seat, while outside it is protected by a certain firmness of wood, and the outermost bark is opposed to the intemperance of the sky as a defender capable of enduring hardship? Now indeed, how great is the diligence of nature that all things are propagated by multiplied seed; all of which are intended not only for remaining for a time, but also for remaining "generically" as if forever, just as—

# Prose 11

Nature has placed the pith <note>original: "ipsam" referring to the medulla or life-force</note> in the middle, surrounded by the strength of the wood; the wood, moreover, is surrounded by the outer bark as a defender against the inclemency of the weather. It should be noted that because individual plants cannot remain the same in number <note>i.e., an individual plant eventually dies</note>, nature produces seeds in them so that through their propagation they may remain the same in species—that is, in something similar to themselves. Even those things which are believed to be inanimate <note>without a soul or life-force</note>—here Philosophy proves that even inanimate things desire to exist.

---

Who does not know that these are like certain machines? Even those things which are believed to be inanimate, do they not each desire what belongs to them by a similar reasoning? For why does lightness carry flames upward, while weight presses the earth downward, if not because these locations and motions are suitable to each of them? Furthermore, whatever is agreeable to a thing, that thing preserves; just as those things which are hostile to it destroy it. Thus, things that are hard, like stones, adhere most tenaciously to their parts and resist so that they are not easily dissolved. Those things which are liquid, like air and water, easily yield to those things dividing them, but they quickly slip back into those parts from which they were cut off. Fire, however, flees all division. Nor are we now speaking of the voluntary movements of a knowing soul—

<column-break/>

—by two signs. First, from their natural inclination toward a location. And she speaks thus: Even those things which are believed to be inanimate, such as stone, air, and fire, do they not desire—that is, seek after—that which is their own? That is, all inanimate things seek what is harmonious with their nature, by a similar reasoning for the sake of the preservation of their being. This is shown thus: Why does lightness carry—that is, move—flames upward, and weight—that is, gravity—press the earth downward? For no other reason than that these locations and motions are suitable to each individual thing for the salvation of their being. And she adds: Furthermore, that which is agreeable—that is, fitting—to each thing, that thing preserves in its being; just as those things which are hostile—that is, contrary—destroy it.

---

Secondly, she proves the same through another sign taken from the preservation of a natural property of this kind, which is continuity, which any natural thing strives to preserve. Whence she says: Now, those things which are hard, like stones, adhere to their most tenacious—that is, firmest—parts and resist through their hardness so that they are not easily dissolved. Those which are liquid—that is, soft—like air and water, easily yield to those dividing them but quickly slip back—that is, return—to those parts from which they were severed. But fire flees all division. Note that this last point, that fire flees all division, is explained in two ways. First, thus: something is "cut" when its parts are separated from one another so that they do not meet at any point. But the parts of fire cannot be cut in this way without always meeting in some point, as is most evident in the fire that is a flame. It is explained in another way: that fire flees all division because, on account of the vehemence of its action, it destroys the very thing that ought to cut it, and by igniting it, converts it into its own nature. *Nor are we now...* Here Philosophy posits that the desire for being is not a voluntary appetite, but a natural one. And she says:

# Book Three

<column-break/>

->**The Primary Text**<-

...but we are treating here of natural intent. Just as it is that we digest the food we have taken without thinking about it, and as we draw breath in our sleep without knowing it. For even in living beings, the love of remaining <note>original: "amor manendi"; the drive for self-preservation</note> does not come from the soul's volitions, but rather comes from the principles of nature. For often, when causes compel it, the will embraces death, which nature dreads. Conversely, the work of procreation—by which alone the endurance of mortal things lasts—which nature always desires, the will sometimes restrains. Therefore, this charity toward oneself <note>original: "sui caritas"; natural self-love or instinct for survival</note> proceeds not from animal motion <note>conscious movement or desire</note> but from natural intent. For divine providence has given to the things created by it this greatest cause for remaining: that they desire to remain naturally as long as they can. Wherefore there is nothing that you can in any way doubt: that all things which exist naturally seek the constancy of remaining and avoid destruction. **Boethius:** I confess, I said, that I now perceive without doubt [those things which previously seemed uncertain].

<column-break/>

<margin>We have not treated now of the voluntary motions of a knowing soul, but of natural intent, just as it is natural that we pass through (that is, digest) the food we have taken without thinking, and that in sleep we draw spirit (that is, we breathe) without knowing. For love (that is, the appetite for remaining, meaning to subsist) in animals does not come from volitions—add: "as you suppose," because you previously posited that the appetite for remaining was only in animals. But it comes from the principles of nature, because nature is found as much in animated things as in inanimate things.</margin>

<margin>Furthermore, he proves in two ways that the appetite for remaining is not from the will. First, he proves this because the will often embraces death, which takes away the existence of the individual; whence he says: **the will often embraces death**, for nature shrinks back from it (that is, abhors it) due to compelling causes, namely extrinsic ones, as is evident in the case of the martyrs.</margin>

<margin>Secondly, he proves the same from this: that the will sometimes restrains the operation that preserves the existence of the species, saying **conversely** (that is, through the opposite) to **that work of begetting** by which alone the **duration** (that is, the permanence) of mortal things lasts. That which nature desires, the will sometimes coerces, as is evident in those who are continent <note>those practicing celibacy or self-restraint</note>. Therefore this **charity** (that is, the appetite for remaining) does not proceed from animal motion but from natural intent which God implanted in nature.</margin>

<margin>For divine providence gave to the things created by itself this greatest cause of remaining, so that they naturally desire to remain as long as they can. Wherefore there is nothing that you can (that is, are able to) doubt: that all things which exist naturally desire the constancy of remaining and avoid destruction. Which Boethius, conceding, says: **I confess, I said, now that I perceive**—**undoubtedly** (that is, without hesitation)—things which recently seemed uncertain (namely, that vegetables and inanimate things naturally desire the permanence of being).</margin>

# Book Three

I rejoice because you have fixed your gaze—that is, you have reached a mark, meaning a mental recognition—upon the "middle truth." By this, she means the perfect truth which stands in the center. But this has now become clear to you, though you said you were ignorant of it a little while ago <note>referring back to Book 1, Prose 6</note>. And Boethius asks, "What is that?" Philosophy replies that it is the end <term>finis: the ultimate goal or purpose</term> of all things. She adds: for that is the end of all things which is desired by all; and since we have gathered that this is "the Good" (as is clear from the definition of the good), we must confess that the Good is the end of all things.

<margin>
It should be noted that by the "knowledge of the middle truth," she understands divine knowledge. For just as a point is the center of a circle from which all lines are drawn, so God is the center of truth from which all truth proceeds. Note also that all things seek their own end, since the end is the perfection of a thing, and a thing deprived of its end exists in vain. Since, therefore, it is in the nature of an "end" to be good—for those who take away the end take away nature itself, according to the second book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's Metaphysics</note>—therefore the end of all things is the Good.
</margin>

### "And that," she said, "I rejoice in greatly. For, my pupil, you have fixed in your mind the very mark of the middle truth. But in this, that which you said you were ignorant of a moment ago has become clear to you." "What?" I asked. "What the end of all things is," she said. "For that is surely what is desired by all. Since we have concluded that this is the Good, we must confess that the Good is the end of all things."

## The Eleventh Meter of the Third Book.

<margin>Meter 11 of the third book.</margin>

### Whoever searches for the truth with a profound mind,
### And wishes not to be deceived by any stray paths,
### Let him turn the light of his inner vision back upon himself.
### Let him force his long wanderings to bend into a circle,
### And let him teach his soul that whatever it labors for outside...

<margin>
q
</margin>
"Whoever with a profound mind." This is the eleventh meter of this third book, which is called Glyconic after its inventor, and Iambic from its predominating foot. In this meter, Philosophy shows how we can know the good and the true and arrive at the knowledge of things. Since Boethius previously confessed that he now knows what he was formerly ignorant of, she first shows the way by which we can arrive at the knowledge of truth. Secondly, she assigns the cause of it (at the phrase "Not all..."). She says first: "Whoever investigates"—that is, wishes to search out—the truth with a "profound mind"—that is, a subtle one—and "desires not to be deceived by any stray paths"—that is, by false opinions which make one deviate from the truth—let him "turn back upon himself"—that is, exercise within himself—the "light"—that is, the speculation—of his "inner vision"—that is, of reason and the interior intellect. And let him "force"—that is, lead back—his "long wanderings"—that is, the operations of the soul proceeding from the soul—"bending those movements into a circle"—that is, returning to the soul. And whatever the soul "labors for"—that is, works at by speculating—"outside"—that is, concerning external things—let it teach the soul, having been "drawn back"—that is, returned to itself—to "possess it in its own treasures"—that is, the powers which are memory and intellect. And then that which the "dark cloud"—that is, the obscurity of ignorance—"has long covered"—that is, hidden—"will shine"—that is, appear—"more clearly than Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> himself." It is as if she says that what was obscure for a long time will appear lucid to the intellect. Note that he who wishes to know the truth should direct his reason and intellect toward the external thing itself and its properties; and if anything...

# Meter 11
<margin>n 2</margin>

One should not judge immediately based on what is perceived from these things, but should return into oneself by deliberating whether it is so or not. For often that which is not good seems to be good, and that which is seems not to be. Indeed, one must not judge without deliberation that which has not been proven by long consideration. Therefore, Philosophy <note>The personification of Lady Philosophy in Boethius's text.</note> says that he should turn the light of his inner sight back into himself. It should be noted that a "circle" is a line drawn around returning to the same point; therefore, to "bend long movements into a circle" is when the power of the soul proceeds from the soul toward the object itself,

**To possess treasures hidden within oneself**
**That which the dark cloud of error has long obscured**
**Will shine more clearly than Phoebus <note>The sun</note> himself.**
**For the body, bringing in its forgetful mass,**
**Has not driven all light from the mind;**
**The seed of Truth surely clings within,**
**Which is awakened by the fanning of learning.**
**For why, when asked, do you judge right things of your own accord,**
**Unless the fuel lived submerged deep in your heart?**
**But if the muse of Plato sounds the truth,**
**Whatever each man learns, he remembers, though having forgotten.**

<column-break/>

diverts, and returns to the soul by deliberating whether it is so or not according to what it has recognized. *For the body... has not driven all light from the mind*, etc. Here Philosophy assigns the cause of what has been said: namely, why we are able to know the truth. For the body "bringing in"—that is, introducing—a "forgetful mass"—that is, a heaviness by which a man becomes forgetful—has not driven "all light"—that is, the knowledge of truth—from the "mind"—that is, out of the mind. Because the habit of first principles remains in the mind. And she adds "surely"—that is, for certain—the "seed"—that is, the principle of truth—"clings"—that is, remains "within"—that is, internally in the soul—which is "awakened by the fanning"—that is, the exercising—of "learning." 

That the seed of truth is in the soul is proven by this: that an ignorant boy, when he responds correctly to questions, such as whether "duality" is an even or odd number <note>A reference to the slave boy experiment in Plato's *Meno*</note>. Whence she says, "For why, when asked"—that is, interrogated—"do you judge"—that is, judge or respond—to "right things of your own accord"—that is, voluntarily—unless the "fuel"—that is, the root of truth—"submerged"—that is, hidden—"lived deep in your heart"—that is, in the profound mind. And she adds that if the "muse"—that is, the wisdom—of Plato "sounds the truth," that which each man learns, he "remembers, though having forgotten"—that is, having been oblivious. 

It should be noted that it is attributed to Plato that he wished souls to have known all things before they were joined to bodies; but once joined to bodies, they surrendered all things to oblivion; but through study and the exercise of wisdom, they recovered them. Therefore, he wished that "to know" is nothing other than a certain "recollection of old things." Philosophy seems to speak here with this intention. But it should not be said that knowing happens through reminiscence; rather, knowledge is acquired anew through discovery or teaching. It is true that our intellect naturally holds itself in the recognition of first principles. Whence Linconiensis <note>Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln (c. 1175–1253), a major medieval scholar.</note> says in the *First Posterior Analytics*: "Not only the voice of the teacher sounding outwardly, nor the letter seen, teaches; but these two move and awaken." The true teacher, however, is He who illuminates the mind within and shows the truth. 

It should be noted that just as health is sometimes caused by an intrinsic principle, namely from the heart, and sometimes by an interior and exterior principle, such as by a physician and the heart—but it is never caused by an exterior principle without the interior—so knowledge is sometimes acquired from an interior principle, such as from the agent intellect (as is evident in those possessing knowledge through discovery), and sometimes it is acquired from an interior and exterior principle together, such as from a teacher and the agent intellect. However, it is never acquired from an exterior principle without the interior.

Then I said: "I strongly agree with Plato <note>original: "platoni... assentior." # Prose 12.

That is to say, he joined together, which is understood to be God. Indeed, the order of nature would not proceed so certainly, nor would it unfold such ordered movements—that is, movements regulated by places, times, efficiency, spaces, and qualities—unless there were One who, remaining Himself immovable, disposed these variations of change. Whatever this is by which created things remain and are moved, I call it by the name common to all: **God**. <note>The commentator here is glossing Boethius’s text, emphasizing that the stability of the laws of physics and time requires an unchanging "Prime Mover."</note> Note that Boethius hints at three reasons why

<column-break/>

"A little while ago," she said, "you thought it was hardly to be doubted that this world is ruled by God." **Boethius:** "I do not think it is doubtful now," I said, "nor do I think I shall ever doubt it." **Philosophy:** "I will briefly explain the reasons by which I reach this conclusion. This world, made of such diverse and contrary parts, would never have come together into one form unless there were One who joined such diverse things. Once joined, the very diversity of their natures, being discordant with one another, would tear them apart and divide them, unless there were One to hold together what He has woven. Indeed, the order of nature would not proceed so certainly, nor would it unfold such ordered movements in places, times, efficiency, spaces, and qualities, unless there were One who, remaining Himself, disposed these varieties of mutations." **Boethius:** "Whatever this is by which created things remain and are moved, I call it by the name common to all: **God**." **Philosophy:** Then she said, "Since you feel this way, I have but a small [task remaining]..."

<column-break/>

the world is ruled by God. The **first** reason is taken from the joining of diverse things, which is as follows: Diverse and contrary things do not unite with one another by themselves. Since, therefore, the world is united from contrary parts—such as from the elements <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which were thought to have opposing qualities (hot/cold, dry/wet).</note>—it is necessary that there be someone uniting them, and this is God. Therefore, the world is ruled by God. She touches on this reason at the words: *this world*. The **second** reason is taken from the preservation of contrary things joined together, which is as follows: Diverse and contrary things, by the property of their own nature, dissociate from one another unless they are preserved by someone; but the parts of the world are diverse and contrary, therefore etc. She touches on this reason at the words: *Once joined*. The **third** reason is taken from the ordered arrangement of movements, which is as follows: Nothing moves with certainty and regularity according to the arrangement of place, time, efficiency,

<column-break/>

space, and quality, unless there is one rectifier and regulator. But the movements of those things which are in the world function regularly according to the five aforementioned things. Therefore, it is necessary to posit a rectifying and regulating power, which is God. Therefore, the world is ruled by God. She touches on this reason at the words: *Indeed, the order*. It should be noted that regular movements occur in the world in **places**, regarding the approach and distancing of the sun in the oblique circle <note>The ecliptic or the sun's apparent path.</note>. They also occur in **times**, regarding the variation of day and night. They occur in **efficiency**, because the moon effects the increase and decrease of fluids <note>original: "humidorum" - referring to the humors or bodily fluids and tides</note> according to its waxing and waning, and effects the ebb and flow of the sea. Ordered movements also occur in **spaces**, because the moon and other planets are sometimes distant from the sun and from each other by greater or lesser spaces. They also occur in **qualities**, because in summer it causes heat, and in winter, cold. *Then she said, "Since you feel this way..."* Here, Philosophy, having assumed that the world is ruled by God, proves that it is ruled by Him through His goodness; and she says: "Boethius, since you feel that the world is ruled by God, I think there remains for me a small task," that is, a small labor.

The conclusion which Philosophy brings forward is that evil is nothing. The reasoning for the conclusion is: God can do everything that exists since He is omnipotent; but God cannot do evil; therefore evil is nothing. And if you should say: "If evil is nothing, when a man is damned for evil, he is damned for nothing," it must be said that evil signifies a defect of good, not negatively but privatively <note>A "negative" absence is like a stone not having sight; a "privative" absence is like a human being blind—the lack of a quality that *ought* to be there.</note>. And therefore evil is a defect of the good that ought to be in the power of man to have. And if he does not have that good when he ought to have it, he is therefore damned. An example is given: Someone is bound to pay a hundred pounds, and if he does not pay, he will be imprisoned. It is certain that "not paying" is not a thing, but a "nothing" (an absence); yet a person is not said to be imprisoned for "nothing" in the simple sense, but because there was a "nothing" where there "ought to have been something." 

"Are you playing with me?" Here Boethius moves a philosophical question. Secondly, Philosophy solves it at the point "Then she..." First, Boethius, marveling at the connection and convolution of the reasons which Philosophy has used, asks whether this turning of arguments is from a delusion of Philosophy or proceeds from the nature of the thing. Briefly he recollects those reasons and says: "Philosophy, you play with me," that is, you delude me, "weaving a labyrinth," that is, making a difficult labor with arguments by making circular reasons, from which labyrinth you exit by the same part you entered. "You fold together a wonderful circle of divine simplicity," that is, you make a marvelous circulation of reason regarding the divine simplicity. And then he briefly recollects the reasons, saying: "You, starting a little while ago from happiness..."

# Prose 12
## .xii.

In this meter, after Philosophy has shown what true happiness is and where it is situated, she now exhorts us to persevere in the contemplation of that happiness. First, she states that he is happy who, having left behind earthly things, devotes himself to divine contemplation. Second, she shows what hinders this kind of contemplation. **Once, the poet [mourning] the death of his wife.** Here he shows what hinders the contemplation of divine things: namely, the affection for earthly things. He declares this through a certain fable which is as follows: Orpheus, the son of Calliope, was a lyre-player who played with such sweetness of the lyre that he attracted not only men but even brute animals; and he charmed them to such an extent that they set aside their natural impulses. He made the forests run and the rivers stand still. He had a wife named Eurydice; when the shepherd Aristaeus wished to love her, she fled through the meadows and, having stepped on a certain serpent, she died and descended to the underworld. Orpheus, wishing to bring her back from the underworld, began to appease the gods above with his lyre. But when he did not succeed, he descended to the underworld and so soothed the infernal gods that his wife was granted to him on such a condition: that before he left the underworld, he should not turn his gaze backward to look at his wife. However, when Orpheus had almost exited, led by love, he looked back and thus lost his wife. **Note** according to Aristotle in the second book of the *Metaphysics* and the commentator in the third book of *On the Heavens and the World*: Not everyone receives the truth in the same way. This is partly due to different customs, partly due to different natures, and partly due to a lack of instruction in logic. Hence, some receive the truth through the method of demonstration, some through the method of authority, and some through the method of fables. Therefore, so that Philosophy may satisfy such people, she sometimes uses demonstrations, sometimes authorities, and sometimes intersperses fables, as in the present case. 

**It should be noted** that Orpheus is called a "prophet" <term>vates: a poet-prophet</term> because he composed songs; he is called *vates* either from the "vigor of the mind" <note>Latin: *vi mentis*</note> or from "seeing" <note>Latin: *video*</note>. 

**It should be noted** that "Taenara" <note>The underworld</note> are so called as if they were "lamentable things" from *threnus*, which is a lamentation. *Taenarus* in the singular is the name of a certain mountain in which there is said to be a path to hell. In the plural, *Taenara* signifies infernal places, as Hugutio <note>A 12th-century grammarian</note> says. Commonly, however, this name is found written without the "r" in the first syllable and is called *Tenara* or *Tenarus*, as in the *Doctrinale*: "Tenarus is hell." However, Hugutio writes it all with the "r," as *Trenarus* and *Trenara*. Hence, perhaps by the fault of scribes, the "r" is sometimes withdrawn. 

**The triple-headed one is amazed by the new [song].** Here he shows how Orpheus appeased the monsters of hell, saying: The gatekeeper of hell, who is called Cerberus (as if he were a "devourer of flesh"), that triple-headed one, meaning having three dog-heads, was captivated by the new song, that is, a melody previously unheard. And he is amazed, that is—

# Book Three

distributed the punishment. That beloved one <note>referring to Pluto/Hades</note> said: let us give the man his wife. It should be noted that love cannot be restrained by law. For out of intense love, a person often transgresses the law, and love is stronger for fulfilling something than the law is for restraining it. Therefore he says: *Who gives a law to lovers? Love is a greater law unto itself.* <note>original: "quis legem dat amantibus. maior lex est sibi." A famous quote from Boethius's poem.</note> This is to say: why is a law of love given to lovers when love itself is a harsh law? This fable concerns you. Here, Philosophy, applying the fable to her purpose, exhorts us to avoid the impediment to the contemplation of the highest good <term>summum bonum: the ultimate goal of human existence, identified here with God</term>, and says: O humans, whoever you are who seek—that is, wish—to lead your mind—that is, the contemplation of the mind—into the heavenly day—that is, into the heavenly brightness—this fable just told concerns you, because it was introduced for your instruction.

<column-break/>

**Love is its own law. Alas, near the boundaries of the night, Orpheus saw his Eurydice, lost her, and killed her <note>metaphorically, by causing her second death</note>. This fable concerns you: whoever seeks to lead your mind into the heavenly day. For whoever, conquered, shall turn his eyes toward the Tartarean cave <note>the abyss of the underworld</note>, whatever excellence he carries with him, he loses it while he looks upon the depths.**

<column-break/>

For he who, conquered by the affection for earthly things, turns the lights—that is, the eyes of reason and intellect—into the Tartarean cave—that is, into earthly things which lead to the earthly depths—whatever excellence—that is, good—he carries by his labor, he loses it while he looks upon the depths—that is, while he intends toward earthly and temporal things which are the lowest. Note that concupiscence <note>strong worldly desire</note> and the affection for earthly things hinder the contemplation of the highest good. Whence Boethius, in his treatise on the highest good, says: Inordinate concupiscence hinders many from the highest good. For we see some follow laziness; some follow sensual delights; some follow the desires for gold and silver, except for a few men to be honored by Philosophy, who despise the desires of the senses and follow the desires of the intellect. And near the end of the same treatise he says: the philosopher is greatly delighted in the First Principle <note>God as the source of all things</note> in the contemplation of His goodness, and this alone is the right delight. For this is the life of philosophers, without which no one lives a right life. And he adds: I call a "philosopher" every human living by the order of nature, tending toward the heights and finishing a life that acquires the ultimate end and the best of human life, which is God, glorious and blessed forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>b</margin> **When Philosophy [had sung] these things with dignity of countenance.** Here begins the fourth book of the Consolation of Philosophy, of which this is the first prose, in which Philosophy assigns the reasons why evils are permitted in the kingdom of God since the ruler of all things is good, namely God. And she proves that the good are always powerful and the wicked are powerless; and just as vices are never without punishment, so virtues are never without reward. She also proves that all fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, is for the benefit of the good, but for the destruction of the wicked. She also proves that all things which are done by God are done rightly, and many other things as will be made clear. And this book is divided into fourteen parts because there are seven proses and seven meters in this fourth book, which will be made clear in the process. First, therefore, Boethius shows how [he interrupted] the intention of Philosophy...

### The first prose of the fourth book.

**When Philosophy** had sung these things, having preserved the dignity of her countenance and the gravity of her expression lightly and sweetly, then I, not yet having entirely forgotten my deep-seated sorrow, interrupted her as she was preparing to say something further. And I said: "O herald of the true light <note>original: "Veri preuia luminis"</note>, those things which your speech has poured forth until now...

<column-break/>

...all fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, is for the benefit of the good, but for the destruction of the wicked. She also proves that all things which are done by God are done rightly, and many other things as will be made clear. And this book is divided into fourteen parts because there are seven proses and seven meters in this fourth book, which will be made clear in the process. First, therefore, Boethius shows how [he interrupted] the intention of Philosophy...

---

...while she was still preparing to say more, by proposing the causes of his grief. Second, Philosophy promises him a perfect cure. Third, she gives the method of curing him. The second part begins at "Then although it were." The third begins at "And since." And fourth, she follows through on the intention of curing him in the following prose, at "Then I." First, he shows how he interrupted the intention of Philosophy, who wished to speak more. Second, he proves the causes of his grief; the second part begins at "But this is the cause." First, he says that when Philosophy had "sung," that is, chanted these things, namely the aforementioned, having "lightly" (that is, delightfully) and "sweetly" (that is, gently) preserved the "dignity" (that is, the reverence) of her "countenance" (namely her own) and the "gravity of her expression" (that is, of her speech). "Then" (that is, after this) "I" (namely Boethius), "not yet" (that is, not until now) "entirely" (that is, altogether) "forgetful" of my "deep-seated sorrow" (that is, internal grief), I, Boethius, "interrupted" the "intention" (that is, the purpose) of Philosophy, who was "preparing" (that is, intending) to say something further. And "I say": "O herald" (that is, the precursor) "of the true light" (that is, of perfect knowledge), namely those things which "your speech" (that is, your discourse) "poured forth" (that is, spoke) "until now" (that is, up to this fourth book), "were evident" (that is, were made manifest) and "invincible" (that is, irrefutable). "Then" (at one time) by "divine speculation" (that is, holy contemplation), "then" (at another time) by her own self, "then" (at another time) by "your reasons" (that is, demonstrations). And "those things" (namely the aforementioned) which were "recently forgotten by me" (at one time on account of the grief of the injury <note>The commentator refers to Boethius's imprisonment and eventual execution</note> which I suffered from Theodoric, King of the Goths) yet you did not speak of them "altogether" (that is, entirely) as "unknown" (that is, ignored) "until now." Note that "dignity" is an honest and commanding authority. Also, Philosophy is said to be "grave of expression," that is, of stable speech, because philosophical discourses are established by the firmness of reasons. # Book Three

->**The Speech of Philosophy**<-

<gloss>Here she responds</gloss> These things have been made clear both by the contemplation of divine nature and by your own invincible arguments. And although I had recently forgotten these things due to the pain of the injustice I suffered, they were not entirely unknown to me before now. But this itself is the greatest cause of our sorrow: that since a good Governor of the world <note>referring to God</note> exists, it is possible for evils to exist at all, or for them to pass by unpunished. Consider for yourself how worthy of wonder this alone is; but to this, another even greater thing is joined. For while wickedness rules and flourishes, virtue not only lacks its rewards, but is even trodden under the feet of the wicked and suffers punishment in the place of crimes. That such things happen in the kingdom of a God who knows all things, can do all things, but wills only good things: no one can sufficiently wonder at nor complain of this. **Philosophy.**

<column-break/>

Boethius, as if greedy to know certain things of which ignorance kept him in sorrow, interrupted the intention of Philosophy as she wished to say more. It should be noted that Philosophy is called the "guide of the true light" because she clarifies the soul and draws it from the obscurity of ignorance to the light of wisdom and the clarity of the intellect, according to the *Book of the Apple* by Aristotle <note>original: "ex libzo de pomo Aristotel." This refers to the *Liber de Pomo*, a medieval work falsely attributed to Aristotle describing his deathbed conversation.</note>. Or, she is called the guide of the true light because through her, as if through a path, a person arrives at the knowledge of the true light, which is God. For it is written in the *Book of the Apple* that through philosophy a person knows their Creator, who made all things from nothing; who is the beginner of all things begun and the Principle of all principles. And in the same place it is written that it was necessary for philosophy to be sent to instruct the ignorant and those who did not know their Creator.

**But this itself is the greatest.** Here Boethius proposes the causes of his sorrow, saying: "But this itself is the cause of our sorrow, and the greatest cause: that since the Ruler of things—namely, the good God—exists, either evils can exist at all or they pass by unpunished." If no other inconvenience followed, consider how much wonder this deserves. "But" is used for "and," to which another thing to be wondered at is joined: "For" is used for "because," while wickedness—that is, wicked men—is commanding (ordering) and flourishing (thriving), virtue—that is, the virtuous person—not only lacks rewards, but virtue itself, having been cast down, is trodden under the feet (the power) of the wicked (the evil). And virtue itself "pays the penalty"—that is, suffers punishments—in the place of crimes (in the place of the vicious). That these aforementioned things are permitted to happen in the kingdom (the world) of God, who knows all and is powerful over all, but wills and intends only good things: no one can sufficiently wonder or make a complaint.

Note that evils happen in the world; it is evident because reason always prays for the good. Since, therefore, the wicked are not ruled by the judgment of right reason but are conquered by the passions of anger and lust, they fail to achieve the good. Likewise, excess and deficiency belong to the category of evils, while virtue consists in the middle <note>A reference to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean."</note>. Since, therefore, in most things there is excess and deficiency, it is clear that evils exist in the world. Since, however, all...

That is, the circular motion of the celestial bodies, God existing as the glittering judge <note>original: "coruscus arbiter"</note>—that is, the splendid judge of things.

<margin>
It should be noted that he says fire grows hot by the motion of heaven. From this, it seems that heat is not a proper and essential quality of fire, since it is owed to the motion of heaven. But it must be said that a place is not only the cause of preserving what is located within it, but also of all the accidents naturally following from it. Therefore, because heaven is the place of fire, it is not only the cause of the fire itself but also of the heat following that fire. And because the proper disposition of heaven, through which it possesses heat above all things, is its motion, he therefore says fire grows hot by the motion of heaven, not excluding by this that heat is an essential quality of fire.
</margin>

# Second Prose

The goodness of the good is now shown from the fragility of the evil. It should be noted that Philosophy bases her statement—that if the good are powerful, the evil are powerless—upon a topical consideration <note>A "topical consideration" refers to a method of logical argumentation based on Aristotle's "Topics."</note> of "if the proposition holds in the proposition, the opposite holds in the opposite." For example, if health is good, then sickness is bad. She says she wishes to proceed by both paths, proving the powerlessness of the evil from the power of the good, and

<margin>
One who concludes through the "argument from contraries" would have a probable argument but not a necessary one. Therefore, she wishes to prove both parts and conclude the remainder from each. There are two ways Philosophy proves her intent here: first, by reasons; second, she excludes a certain doubt at the point "But they can"; third, she confirms the main intent by the authority of Plato at "From all of which." First, she proves the good are always powerful and the evil powerless by two reasons. Second, to show the same, she heaps up brief reasons at "But since you." The first is divided into two according to the reasons; the second begins at "Again, she said." First, she sets forth two things necessary for the first reason; second, she argues from these at "All men therefore." First, she sets forth one necessary thing, then another at "You remember..."
</margin>

the fragility of the evil becomes clear, and the weakness of the good is noted. But so that the faith in our opinion may be more abundant, I shall proceed by either path, confirming the propositions now from this side, now from that. There are two things upon which the effect of all human acts depends: namely, will and power. If either of these is missing, there is nothing that can be achieved. For if the will is lacking, one does not even attempt what he does not want; and if power is absent, the will is in vain. Thus it happens that if you see someone wishing to obtain something which he by no means obtains, you cannot doubt that the ability to get what he wanted was lacking. Boethius said: "It is clear, and can in no way be denied." Philosophy asked: "But if you see someone has achieved what he wanted, would you doubt that he was also able to do it?" Boethius: "Not at all." Philosophy: "In that which a man is able to do, he is judged strong; but in that which he is not able to do, he must be considered weak."

This she declares: for if the will is lacking, no effect is produced because no one attempts what he does not want. Then Philosophy concludes as if it were manifest from what was said, saying: "That which anyone is able to do, in that he is 'valid'—that is, powerful; but what he cannot do, in that he must be 'censured'—that is, [considered weak]."

Likewise, Philosophy asks, "Do you not recall that happiness is the Good itself, and in that way the Good is desired by all when happiness is sought," that is, desired. Boethius responds: "I do not 'recall' it because I hold it fixed in my memory." It should be noted that "to recall" <note>original: "recordari"</note> is to bring something back to the memory which has slipped away through forgetfulness. And because the fact that happiness is the highest good <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> had not departed from the mind of Boethius, but always remained as a habit, he therefore says he does not "recall" it but holds it as if fixed in his memory. "Therefore all men." Here Philosophy argues from what has been said, proving that the good are powerful and the evil are powerless by such reasoning: Whoever attains what they will are powerful, and those who do not attain what they will are powerless, from the first preamble. But the good attain what they will, namely the highest good; the evil, although they may will it, do not attain it, because if the evil attained the highest good they would not be evil. Therefore the good are powerful and the evil are powerless. Whence it says in the text: "All men, good and evil, strive to reach the Good with an indistinguishable intention," that is, an undivided intention. Boethius says: "That follows."

It should be noted that from the text such an argument is formed: when two people intend toward some goal, the one who achieves that goal through a natural function is powerful, and the one who does not achieve that goal through a natural function is powerless. But both the good and the bad naturally tend toward happiness; the good achieve it through a natural function, namely virtue, but the wicked do not. Therefore, the good are powerful, but the wicked are powerless. It should be noted regarding the last part that doctors usually take prognostic signs of health from the sick person when the patient raises themselves up and strives by themselves toward a stronger remedy. ### Brief arguments to demonstrate the proposition.
There are four arguments. The second begins at "I shall consider"; the third at "In which matter"; the fourth at "For why." First, she says: But since I perceive you are most ready to understand, I will heap up—that is, put together—frequent arguments. **And this, as doctors are accustomed to hope, is a sign of a nature now upright and resisting. But since I perceive you to be most ready to understand, I will heap up frequent arguments. For you see how great an infirmity of vicious men lies open, who cannot even reach that to which their natural intention leads and almost compels them. And what if they were deserted by this so great and almost invincible help of preceding nature? Consider indeed how great an impotence possesses wicked men; for they do not seek light or playful rewards which they are unable to follow and obtain, but they fail regarding the very summit and peak of things. Nor does the effect of that which they alone strive for day and night happen for those wretched ones. In which matter the strength of the good is eminent. For just as you would judge a man to be most powerful in walking who, proceeding on foot, was able to reach that place beyond which no further path lay open for walking, so...**

<column-break/>

...and what should be judged concerning those evil ones if they were deserted by this help of nature, which is so great and almost joined <note>original: "pene iuncto," likely a variant of "invicto" or "invincible"</note> before all things? From this it is argued thus: the greatest impotence is to fail from that which nature intends. But the wicked do this. Therefore, the wicked are impotent. **It should be noted** that she says "almost invincible" because the natural appetite for the good has no resisting contrary by which it may be conquered; nevertheless, through ignorance and the error of vices, it is perverted and thus in some way conquered, though not directly. **Consider indeed how great.** Here Philosophy places the second argument and says: consider from these things which I shall say how great an

impotence possesses wicked men. Nor does the effect of the good happen to those wretched ones in this—that is, because of this—which they themselves strive for—that is, labor to acquire—day and night—that is, transitory and temporal goods. **Note** that from the text such an argument is formed: the greater that is from which someone fails, the greater is his failure <note>original: "effectus," here used ironically or to mean the result of his actions</note> and he falls into greater impotence. But that from which the wicked fail is not something vile and small, but is the Supreme Good. Therefore, the impotence of the wicked is the greatest.

The reason she intends, in short, is this: When the wicked, having abandoned virtue, decline into vices, they either know that it is good to adhere to virtue or they do not know. If they do not know, they sin through ignorance. But nothing is more powerless than ignorance; therefore the wicked sinning through ignorance are powerless. If, however, they know it is good to adhere to virtue and yet decline into vices, they either abandon the good willingly or they do not. If they do not do so willingly, but are drawn by the lust of their passions and turn toward vices, it follows that they are powerless, because it is a great [lack of] power to be unable to resist the passions. If, however, they knowingly and willingly abandon the good, it follows that they are not only powerless, but that they altogether cease to be. For since every nature has an instinctual order of this kind toward an end, insofar as something stops following the order toward that end, to that extent it fails in its nature, and consequently in the very "being" of that nature. She presents this reason in the text and says: "For why, having abandoned virtue, do the wicked follow vices?" Is it not because of "ignorance"—that is, from an ignorance of the good? Or do they "knowingly and willingly" desert the good and turn aside to vices by will and knowledge? But in this way, they not only cease to be powerful, but they altogether cease to exist. For this she assigns a reason: for those who abandon the common end of all things that exist—namely God, who is Being itself—likewise cease to be.

# Second Prose

<margin>
God cannot do evil. Therefore, the ability to do evil proves weakness rather than power. To this is added: here he proves the same thing in a third way, saying that all power is to be counted among things to be sought, and all things to be sought (that is, desired) are referred to the Good, as if to a certain summit—that is, to the perfection of their nature. But the possibility (that is, the power) of committing a crime (that is, doing evil) cannot be referred to the Good. Therefore, it is not to be sought. However, all true power is to be sought. It is clear, therefore, that the "power" of the wicked is not power. Note that the argument can be formed from the text thus: Every power that is a power of nature is to be desired and is referred to the Good. Therefore, the power of evil is not power. From all of which, he concludes the principal conclusion regarding the power of the good and the weakness of the wicked, confirming it by the authority of Plato, saying: from these things already declared, the power of the good and the infirmity of the wicked appear beyond doubt. And it is clear that the sentence of Plato is true: that only the wise...
</margin>

"They can do evil; I wish they could not," says Boethius. Therefore, Philosophy argues: Since, therefore, only he who is capable of good can do all things, while those powerful in evil cannot do all things, it is manifest that those who can do evil have less power. <note>The argument here is that "power" is defined by the ability to achieve what one actually desires (the Good). Since evil is a lack of good, the ability to do evil is a lack of power.</note> It should be noted that the ability to do evil proves impotence rather than power. For if it proved power, then it would be attributed to the most omnipotent being, namely God, which is false. Hence it can be argued from the text thus: God can do all things and cannot do evil.

"Who would think that men can do all things?" **Boethius:** "No one, unless he be insane." **Philosophy:** "And yet, these same men can do evil." **Boethius:** "I wish indeed," I said, "that they could not." **Philosophy:** "Since, therefore, only the one capable of good can do all things, while those powerful in evil cannot do all things, it is manifest that those who can do evil have less power. To this is added that we have shown that all power is to be numbered among things to be sought, and all things to be sought are referred to the Good, as if to a certain summit of their nature. But the possibility of committing a crime cannot be referred to the Good. Therefore, it is not to be sought. And yet, all true power is to be sought. It is clear, therefore, that the possibility of the wicked is not power. From all these things, the power of the good and the undeniable weakness of the wicked appear manifest. It is clear that the opinion of Plato <note>A reference to Plato's *Gorgias*, where Socrates argues that tyrants do what they *see fit* but not what they *will*, because everyone wills the Good.</note> is true: that only the wise are able to do what they desire, while the wicked indeed perform what pleases them—that is, what satisfies their lust—but they cannot fulfill what they truly desire (by their rational appetite). For they do what pleases them while they think that through those things in which they delight, they will attain the Good which they desire; but they do not attain it at all, because shameful deeds do not lead to happiness."

# Book Four

For any desire—that is, lust—seeks out what it wants while people think they will obtain the good they desire through the things in which they take delight. But they do not achieve it at all, because shameful acts—that is, vices or vicious men—do not arrive at blessedness. It should be noted that desire is a rational appetite, whereas lust <note>original: "libitum"</note> pertains to the sensual appetite. Therefore, although the wicked may affect a desire for blessedness through their rational appetite, they nevertheless do whatever they please by following their sensitive appetite; thus, they do not reach blessedness. The wise, however, who despise sensual pleasures and strive for intellectual ones, are those who perfect their soul through the knowledge of their Creator, who made being out of nothing, as is written in the *Book of the Apple* <note>A medieval philosophical work, *Liber de Pomo*, falsely attributed to Aristotle, depicting his deathbed conversations.</note>. The soul shall not be saddened nor troubled when it departs from the body, as is written in that same book.

### Second Meter of the Fourth Book

Second Meter of the fourth book. "Those whom you see sitting on high." This is the second meter of this fourth book. And it is a mixed meter.

> **Those kings whom you see sitting on the high**
> **summit of the throne, shining in bright**
> **purple, hedged about by grim arms: threatening**

The first part of the meter is called "Almanic" after its inventor, and is called "Trochaic" from its predominating foot <term>Trochee: a metrical foot consisting of a long syllable followed by a short one</term>. The second part is called "Pherecratean" after its inventor, and "Spondaic" from its predominating foot <term>Spondee: a metrical foot consisting of two long syllables</term>. In this meter, Philosophy shows how the power of the wicked is to be considered, especially in those where it seems greatest, such as kings and princes. She begins the construction of the argument in the seventh verse: If anyone should pull away—that is, remove through consideration and intellect—the coverings—that is, the veils of empty outward worship—from these proud kings. These are the kings you see sitting on the high summit—that is, the height of the throne or chair. You see them shining, bright in purple; hedged—that is, surrounded—by grim arms—that is, arms that cause sorrow. I say these kings are threatening—that is, imposing threats upon the wretched—with a fierce countenance—that is, a cruel look—panting—that is, eager or hurrying—with the rage of the seat <note>likely a scribal error for "cordis" (heart)</note>—that is, the cruelty of death. He will soon see such "masters" bearing within—that is, in the soul—tight chains—that is, the bonds of vices. This is made manifest by what follows: for on one side lust—that is, concupiscence—tosses—that is, casts down—the hearts of such tyrants with greedy poisons. On the other side, anger lashes—that is, punishes—their minds; anger, I say, raising waves—that is, disturbances. Or grief wearies them, being captured by some misfortune, or slippery hope—that is, vain hope—torments them. Therefore, when you perceive one head—that is, one prince—bearing—that is, enduring—so many tyrants—that is, tyrannizing passions—he himself, oppressed by these wicked masters—that is, ruling vices—does not do what he desires.

Note that the intention of Philosophy is to say: if anyone could penetrate with their sight the hearts of princes—whom they see sitting on high thrones, adorned with bright garments, having terrifying weapons, and looking upon the wretched with a fierce face—they would immediately recognize by sight that these men are bound by many unbreakable chains: the passions of anger, hope, and fear. And being thus bound by passions, they do not...

Second she shows what that reward is, at the point: "But of what reward?" She proves the first by two reasons; she places the second there: "Finally." The first reason is such: Every thing for the sake of which something is done is the reward of that thing which is done. But all things are made and done for the sake of the Good. Therefore, the Good is the reward of all things that are done. But the Good cannot be separated from the good [people], for then they would no longer be good. Therefore, rewards are never lacking for the good. Whence she says in the text: "Of the things that are done"—that is, performed—that for the sake of which each thing is done—that is, performed—that seems not unjustly to be the reward of that thing. However much, therefore, the wicked may rage against the good, the crown <note>original: "corona"; a metaphor for the prize of victory</note>—that is, the reward—shall not fall from the wise man, nor shall it wither. That is, it shall not be diminished because the wickedness of others does not pluck away—that is, does not take away—the proper glory from upright souls. For if the good rejoiced in a reward received from the outside, someone else could take this away from them, or at least the one who had bestowed it.

But because his own uprightness confers that reward upon each person, then anyone will lack his reward only when he ceases to be upright. It should be noted that it was the custom among the Romans to run in a stadium—that is, in a certain space which they called a stadium—and he who came more quickly to the goal carried off the prize, namely a crown or something else, just as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:24</note> says: *Do you not know that those who run in a stadium all run, but one receives the prize? It should be noted that Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), the author of "The Consolation of Philosophy"</note> cannot lack a reward, because that by which a man is named "good" is virtue or virtuous operation. For according to Aristotle in the second book of the *Ethics*: *Every virtue will certainly be a habit from which a man becomes good.* Because of this, the dignity of virtue is the reward of those operating virtuously. It should be noted that however much the wicked rage, the crown shall not fall from the wise man. It should be noted that in this deduction, Philosophy does not take happiness to mean the state which the good will have after this life, but rather the state of happiness such as can be had in this life, which a man attains through the virtues. Hence, he who is essentially good is essentially happy and a god; and he who is not essentially good (that is, only by participation) is also here happy and a god by participation. <note>The commentator distinguishes between being "essentially" divine (God) and being divine by "participation" (virtuous humans sharing in God's nature).</note>

Therefore, just as for the virtuous their own virtue is their reward, so for the wicked their own wickedness is their punishment. It should be noted that whenever contrary qualities belong to contrary subjects, if the quality of one subject is shown to be present, then by the logic of opposites, the quality of the other subject is likewise assigned. Since, therefore, good and evil are different subjects, and reward and punishment are different qualities: if it is shown that the good do not lack a reward, it is shown that the wicked do not lack punishments. The reasoning is as follows: Punishment does not have the character of punishment except from the fact that it is a certain evil. # Third Prose

Everything is distinguished according to its nobility or lack thereof; for it is not possible to accept two species as equally perfect, but one is always worthier than the other. Therefore, it is necessary that every being which is not a human must be either above humanity or below humanity. Evil men, however, as has been proven, cease to be human through their wickedness. Therefore, it is necessary that the wicked be either above or below men. Since only uprightness <note>Latin: probitas; refers to moral integrity or virtue</note> carries a man above human nature, namely to the nature of the gods, it follows

**that when you see a man transformed by vices, you can no longer judge him to be a human. One who burns with greed, a violent plunderer of others' wealth: you would say he is like a wolf. One who is fierce and restless, exercising his tongue in lawsuits: he is comparable to a dog. The hidden plotter, who rejoices in having stolen through fraud: let him be equated to little foxes. One who rages with immoderate anger: let him be believed to carry the soul of a lion. The fearful and fleeing man, who dreads things not to be feared: let him be held similar to a deer. The sluggish and stupid man is numb: he lives as a donkey. The light and inconstant man changes his pursuits: he differs in no way from the birds. He who is immersed in foul and unclean lusts: he is held by the pleasure of a filthy sow. Thus it happens that he who, having deserted uprightness, has ceased to be a man—since he cannot pass into a divine condition—is turned into a beast.**
