It should be noted that there is a twofold cognitive power in us, namely the intellect and the senses. The intellect is something divine within us, through which we ascend to higher things and are similar to God. The senses, however, insofar as they do not obey reason, are something brutal within us, through which we are reduced below human nature and are made similar to beasts. Therefore Boethius says in his treatise on the highest good: "Woe to you men who are counted among the number of beasts, not recognizing the divine which is within you, through which you ascend to higher things and..."

### And herbs lacking power,
### Which, though they may change the limbs,
### Are not able to change the hearts. Within is the vigor of men,
### Hidden in a secret citadel. These poisons

<column-break/>

which it suffers. It must be noted that the transformation of a man into a beast while the rational soul remains is not possible in reality <note>original: "secundum rem"</note>. For if it were possible, it would be possible either according to a substantial change or an accidental one. It is not according to a substantial change, because through such a change a new substantial form is introduced; and thus two substantial forms differing in species—such as the form of a wolf and a man—would inform the same body at the same time, which is false. Nor is it possible according to the accidents

<column-break/>

proper to the matter, which dispose it toward a specific form. Because it is impossible for matter, according to one and the same disposition, to be proportioned to different forms. Therefore, it is entirely impossible for the intellectual soul to be united to matter disposed for the form of a wolf. Therefore, the transformation spoken of here, if it is possible, will only be according to the individual accidents arising from external causes, just as it is seen to have happened to King Nebuchadnezzar <note>The Babylonian king described in the Book of Daniel.</note>, of whom we read in Daniel that he was cast out from men and ate hay like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven until his hair grew like the likeness of eagles and his nails like the claws of birds. And because transformation according to such accidents leads to a distinct representation of the human species through the deformity of the figure, it can thus be said that a transformation into a beast was made while the soul remained. Others say that a transformation of this kind is not possible in reality, but according to a certain phantasmal appearance. Hence, it does not seem reasonable that Nebuchadnezzar transferred himself to the beasts eating hay, except that, agitated by a certain mania and phantasmal appearance, he considered himself a beast or a wild animal; because of which he was cast out from the company of men and lived with wild beasts. **Oh, too light a hand.** Here he shows that the transformation of the mind through vices is worse than the transformation of the body, because the mind is more noble than the whole body. And he says: I say the hand of Circe—that is, her power—is too light—that is, weak. Nor do I say her herbs are powerful, because although they are able to turn the limbs of the body, they are not able to turn the hearts. For within is the vigor of men, stored—that is, hidden—in a secret citadel—that is, hidden in the mind. But these dire poisons—that is, the vices—more powerfully drag men away from themselves...

# Book Four.

They pass through thoroughly, that is, they pass across and are not harmful to the body; or they are, that is, they cause a person to rage with a wound of the mind. <note>The commentator is explaining that while physical poisons harm the body, the "poisons" of vice affect the soul.</note> It should be noted that because the soul is nobler and more excellent than the body, a transformation occurring in the soul from virtues to vices while the human body remains is worse than a transformation of the human body into the appearance of a beast while the soul remains unchanged. For if the soul is unchanged, even granted that the body is transformed, the human is still called human by reason of the soul. But if the human body remains and the soul is transformed, then the human is no longer called human except equivocally <note>meaning "in name only," like a painting of a man is not a man</note>. Therefore, the transformation of the soul is worse than the transformation of the body while the soul remains unchanged.

# Fourth Prose

The wicked are more miserable when they accomplish what they desire than when they are unable to do so. Second, it shows that in this life nothing is long-lasting in comparison to eternal life. Third, it expresses wonder. **Boethius** <note>The author and narrator</note> on a certain point. The second part begins at "For neither." The third at "Then I." First, she <note>Lady Philosophy</note> says it is necessary for the evil to be more miserable when they have accomplished their desires than if they cannot fulfill them, which perhaps seems incredible to someone. The proof of this is:

-> For it is necessary that the wicked be more unhappy when they have accomplished their desires than if they cannot fulfill those things they desire. For if it is a misery to have willed evil, it is a more wretched thing to have had the power to do it, without which the effect of the miserable will would languish. Therefore, since there is a misery attached to each of these three misfortunes, it is necessary that those whom you see willing, being able, and accomplishing a crime are burdened by a triple weight. **Boethius:** I agree, I said, but I vehemently hope that they may soon lack this misfortune by being deprived of the possibility of committing a crime. **Philosophy:** They shall lack it, she said, more swiftly perhaps than you might wish, or than they themselves think they shall be rid of it. For there is nothing within such brief boundaries of life so late that an immortal soul should think it a long time to wait, especially since their great hope and the high engine of their crimes is often [destroyed] by a sudden and unexpected [end]. <-

<column-break/>

If it is miserable to have willed evil, it is more miserable to have had the power, without which—namely the power—the effect of the miserable will would languish, that is, fail. Therefore, since there is a misery for each of the three—namely the will, the power, and the accomplishment—it is necessary that they be burdened by a triple misfortune, that is, an evil, whom you see willing a crime, being able to commit a crime, and accomplishing a crime. **Boethius** says: "I agree," that is, I consent; "and I vehemently hope" that the evil, deprived of the possibility of committing a crime, may soon lack this misfortune. And **Philosophy** says: "They shall lack it," I say, "more swiftly," that is, sooner than you perhaps might wish—that is, than you are able to wish—or than they themselves think they shall lack it. It should be noted that **Philosophy** says that the power to do evil is worse than the will to do evil. **Boethius** <note>The commentator here notes a potential contradiction</note> says this seems false, because the power to sin is not an evil, but the will to sin is.

---

Wherefore according to **Seneca**: "All sin is in the action; every action is voluntary; therefore every sin is voluntary." <note>original: "Omne peccatum in actione; omnis actio est voluntaria; ergo omne peccatum est voluntarium."</note> For this reason also **Augustine** says: "Take away the will and there will be no hell." <note>original: "Tolle voluntatem et infernus non erit."</note> Therefore it is worse to will evil than to have the power for evil. The contrary is said here. To this it must be said that if "power" and "will" are considered in themselves and absolutely, then it is worse to will evil than to have the power. If, however, "power" is taken as following a bad will and serving it so that the bad will may be accomplished in an external work, then in this way the power is worse than the will, because without such power the effect of the will would languish—that is, its work would not be accomplished externally. Just as in the stated manner it is worse to have the power for evil than the will, so it is worse to accomplish the evil than to have the power. Thus, each of these three—willing, being able, and accomplishing—adds some evil over the preceding one. "For neither is there anything": here **Philosophy**, because **Boethius** hoped the wicked would sooner lack the power of committing crime, proves that in this life nothing is long-lasting or enduring in comparison to eternal life, saying: "For neither is there anything late," that is, slow or durable, "within such brief boundaries," that is, limits of the present life, "which an immortal soul should think" to wait for, that is, to remain, for a long time. The "great hope" of these evil men which they have concerning the longevity of life, and the "high engine," that is, the great power of their crimes, is often destroyed without [warning].

->which is known to be eternal.<-

The misery of the wicked would be eternal if it were not ended by death. It should be noted that opposites must be judged in opposite ways, since the causes of opposites are themselves opposite. Therefore, just as in good things that which lasts longer is better, so in evil things that which lasts longer is worse. Thus, since malice makes the wicked wretched, their misery would be infinite if they endured forever in life. But because death terminates their malice, it therefore diminishes their misery and unhappiness. **Then I.** Here Philosophy notes the amazement of Boethius at the deduction of Philosophy, saying: **O Philosophy, your inference is wonderful and difficult to grant** <note>original: "concessu difficilis"</note> **by which it is proven that the misery of the wicked is diminished by death.** <unclear>Here</unclear> I recognize that this agrees entirely with those things granted before. **you judge.** That is, that the aforementioned inference is believed with difficulty. But he who thinks it hard (that is, difficult) to approach the conclusion by granting it, it is right that he himself demonstrate that some falsehood preceded it in the premises, or show that the combination of propositions is not effective for a necessary conclusion. Otherwise, if the preceding points are granted, there is nothing to complain about (that is, to protest) regarding the inference; hence it is necessary to grant it, however hard it may seem. It should be noted that if one does not consent to a conclusion, this is either because of a fault in the matter or a fault in the form. A fault in the matter occurs if any of the premises are false. A fault in the form occurs if there is not a proper proportion of the propositions in respect to the conclusion, involving some fallacy. If, however, none of these occur, [the conclusion follows] by necessity.

# Fourth Prose:

The conclusion follows from the premises. For this too which I shall say—here Philosophy proves that the wicked are more wretched if they are not punished than if they are punished. Second, she resolves a certain doubt. Third, she provides a summary of the aforementioned points. The second part begins at "But I ask." The third begins at "This indeed so far." First, she sets forth the conclusion she intends to prove, excluding certain methods of proof by which the conclusion could be demonstrated. Second, she posits another method of proof from those.

"What is it then?" I asked. **Philosophy:** "The wicked," she said, "are happier when they pay the penalty of their crimes than if no penalty of justice restrained them. And I am not now striving for that which might come to someone's mind—that wicked morals are corrected by vengeance and brought back to the right path by the terror of punishment, or that they serve as an example to others to avoid blameworthy acts—but in another way I think the wicked are more wretched when unpunished, even if no account of correction and no respect for the example is considered." **Boethius:** "And what other way will there be besides these?" **Philosophy:** "Did we not grant that the good are happy, but the wicked are wretched?" **Boethius:** "It is so," I said. **Philosophy:** "If, therefore, some good is added to someone's misery, is he not happier than the one whose misery is pure and solitary, without the mixture of any good?"

<column-break/>

At the section "And those." First, she says: "This too which I shall say seems no less wonderful, but it seems equally necessary to be concluded from those things which have been assumed." And Boethius asks: "What then is this?" Philosophy says: "I say that the wicked are happier <note>The Latin 'feliciores' here is used in the sense of 'better off' or 'less wretched' within the context of the argument.</note> paying their penalties than if no penalty of justice restrained—that is, punished—them. But I am not striving—that is, I do not intend now—that it should come to someone's mind that wicked morals—that is, men of wicked character—are corrected by vengeance—that is, punishment—and by the terror of punishment they are led back to the right. And I do not intend that the punishment of the wicked be an example to other men for avoiding blameworthy things—that is, evils. But besides these two causes, there is another besides the aforementioned why I think the wicked are happier when punished, even if no

---

account of correction and no respect for the example is held." And Boethius asks: "What other way will there be besides these?" It should be noted that there are two causes for which it seems better for the wicked to be punished than unpunished. One is that through punishments the wicked are corrected and recover from evil. The second cause is that others, through fear of the punishment of the wicked, turn away from evil; and thus the punishment of the wicked is an example to others for fleeing evil. Although these two causes are true, nevertheless Philosophy does not intend to assign them here, but another cause besides these. "And those." Here Philosophy posits another way besides the aforementioned for proving that the wicked unpunished are more wretched than the punished. Second, she declares a certain assumption in the proof, at the point "But to be punished." First, she resumes what was proved above in the third prose, saying: "Did we not grant that the good are happy, but the wicked are wretched?" Boethius says: "It is so." And Philosophy: "If some good is added to someone's misery, is he not happier than the one whose misery is pure and solitary without the mixture of any good?" Boethius says: "So it seems." Further, Philosophy asks: "If to that same wretched man who lacks all goods, another evil were annexed, should he not be judged more wretched than the one whose misfortune—that is, evil—is relieved—that is, tempered—by the participation of a good?" Boethius says: "Why not?"—that is, why [should it not be so]?

<summary>Lady Philosophy argues the counter-intuitive point that the wicked are more miserable when they escape punishment, because punishment itself is a form of justice (a good) that mitigates their total wretchedness.</summary>

# Book Four.

Therefore, Philosophy says that when the wicked are punished, they have something of good attached to them: namely, the punishment itself, which is good by reason of justice. And when these same wicked men lack punishment, a further evil is present in them: namely, impunity itself, which you have admitted is an evil by merit—that is, by the law of iniquity. Boethius says: I cannot deny it. Therefore, Philosophy concludes that the wicked are much more unhappy when gifted—that is, provided—with unjust impunity (which is an evil impunity) than when punished with a just vengeance (that is, a penalty). <note>Philosophy argues that justice is a "good," so adding justice to a bad person makes them slightly better off than a bad person with no justice at all.</note> It should be noted that the argument which Philosophy intends is this: when the justice of man is added to malice, something of good is added, and he is happier than one to whom nothing of good is added to his malice. But when a wicked man is punished, something of good is added to his malice, namely the penalty, which is good by reason of justice. However, when he is not punished, something of evil is added to his malice, namely impunity, which is evil. Therefore, a punished wicked man is happier than an unpunished one. But it is just for the wicked to be punished. Here Philosophy declares a certain assumption in the proof: namely, that the punishment of the wicked is good and that impunity is evil, saying: it is manifest that for the wicked to be punished is just, and for the unjust to slip away—that is, to escape unpunished—is unjust. Boethius says: Who would deny that? Philosophy adds: No one will ever deny that everything which is just is good, and conversely—that is, by the opposite—it is clear (manifest) that what is unjust is evil. I, Boethius, said: these things as stated follow from those which were concluded a little while ago. It should be noted that Philosophy implies a double

<column-break/>

reasoning. B: So it seems to me. P: What if to that same miserable person, who lacks all goods, there were further annexed some evil besides those things by which he is already miserable? Should he not be judged much more unhappy than the one whose misfortune is relieved by the participation of some good? B: Why not? I said. P: Therefore, the wicked, when they are punished, have something of good annexed to them, namely the punishment itself, which is good by reason of justice; and when the same person lacks punishment, there is in him something of another evil, impunity itself, which you have confessed to be an evil by the merit of iniquity. B: I cannot deny it. P: Therefore, the wicked are much more unhappy when granted an unjust impunity than when punished by a just vengeance. P: But, she said, neither will anyone deny this: that everything which is just is good, and conversely, it is clear that what is unjust is evil. reasoning. The first is this: the punishment of the wicked is just; but what is just is good; therefore the punishment of the wicked is good. # Book Four.

->**The Commentary**<-

<column-break/>

->**The Text of Boethius**<-

This section responds to common opinion. The second part begins at "What then." First, he says: "O Philosophy, when I consider your inquiries—that is, your arguments—I think nothing truer could be said." But if I return to the judgments of common men, it seems otherwise. For who is there to whom these words of yours would not only seem unbelievable, but even unworthy of being heard? Philosophy replies: "It is so, because common people are unable to lift their eyes—which are accustomed to the darkness of their passions—to the light of clear truth, so that they might see the truth by the judgment of right reason." They are like birds—namely, night-owls and screech-owls—whose sight is illuminated by night and blinded by day. For as long as common people do not look at the order of things (which is like light) but look only at their own affects—that is, their desires (which are like darkness)—they think the lack of punishment for crimes or the freedom to do evil is a form of happiness; however, this is not so. 

See, however, what the eternal law—that is, divine providence—establishes: if you conform your soul to better things (namely, virtues), you have no need for an external judge to award a prize, because you have added yourself to the more excellent things, and consequently, you have become <note>Boethius often uses "becoming God" to describe the soul's participation in divinity through virtue.</note> divine. But if you turn your efforts toward worse things (vices), do not seek an avenger outside yourself, for you have thrust yourself into inferior things, and consequently, you have become a beast. 

He explains this with a simile: just as if you look at the ground and the sky by turns—now the sky, now the earth—even if external judgments cease, you yourself, by the mere logic of seeing, seem to be now in the mud (the earth) and now among the stars (the heaven). In the same way, even if all external things cease, by the very logic of acting well or poorly, you attain reward or punishment, as divine justice ordains this. But the common crowd does not perceive these things for the reason mentioned above. 

<note>The commentator adds a scientific note here.</note> Note that because the nature of sight requires an illuminated medium, according to common nature, the sight of the owl and screech-owl ought to see better in the day than in the night; yet the opposite happens to them. "When I consider your arguments," I said, "I think nothing truer could be said. But if I return to the judgments of men, who is there to whom these things would not only seem unbelievable, but even unworthy of being heard?" 

"It is so," she said. "For they cannot lift eyes accustomed to darkness to the light of clear truth; they are like those birds whose sight the night illuminates and the day blinds. For while they look not at the order of things, but at their own passions, they think the freedom to commit crimes or the lack of punishment is happiness. 

But see what the eternal law decrees: if you conform your soul to better things, you have no need of a judge to bring a reward; you have joined yourself to the more excellent things. If you turn your efforts toward worse things, do not seek an avenger outside yourself; you have thrust yourself into inferior things. Just as if you look at the filthy ground and the sky by turns, with all external things ceasing, by the very logic of seeing, you are now in the mud, now among the stars..."

# Book Four.

->The second syllogism <note>A syllogism is a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two assumed premises.</note> is this: the more someone is deserving of punishment, the more miserable they are. If, therefore, we judge those who are sick in body to be least worthy of hatred, but rather of compassion, then much more should we not pursue with hatred, but rather pity, those whose minds are overcome by wickedness. In malice, you will be more atrocious—that is, more cruel—than any bodily ailment. It should be noted that the wise ought not to hate the wicked, because Seneca says to Lucilius: <note>referring to Seneca’s "Moral Letters to Lucilius"</note> the wise should have the same affection toward the wicked as a doctor has toward his sick patients, whom he strives to treat not with hatred but with a remedy; for he does not disdain to look upon the remains of the sick nor even their <unclear>filth</unclear>.

<margin>
**The Meter of Book 4, Section 4.**
"Why does it please you to stir up such great movements?" Here begins the fourth meter of this fourth book, which is called "Valentian" after its inventor. The second line is called a pentameter or elegiac. In this, Philosophy exclaims against men who, through hatred, lead themselves to death by the movements of war. "What does it help," that is, what utility is there, "to stir up such great movements," namely of hatred? And why does it please you "to solicit fate," that is, death, "by your own hand?" He means to say there is no utility in it. The reasoning here is this: that if you seek death—that is, if you desire it either for yourselves or for others—it approaches of its own accord and does not delay—that is, it does not slow down—its "winged," or swift, horses. It is also a marvel that men, whom the lion, tiger, bear, and boar attack with their teeth, are the same men who...
</margin>

who among us, unless he be most foolish, would hate them? Indeed, to hate the wicked is devoid of reason. For just as a weakness of the body is a disease, so vice is like a sickness of the soul. Since we judge those sick in body to be least worthy of hatred but rather of compassion, much more are those whose minds are overcome by a wickedness more atrocious than any bodily ailment not to be pursued, but pitied.

**Is it because their characters differ and disagree**
**That they move unjust battle lines and fierce wars,**
**And wish to perish by the weapons of another?**
**The reasoning for such cruelty is not just enough.**
**To return a fit reward for these merits:**
**Love the good by right, and have pity on the wicked.**

---

...these same men attack—that is, invade—each other with the sword so that they kill one another. And Philosophy asks whether men move "unjust battle lines and fierce wars" and "wish to perish by the weapons of another"—that is, by mutual arrows—because their characters "differ and disagree"—that is, are in discord. Certainly, that reasoning for cruelty is not just enough. Do you wish, therefore, to "return"—that is, bring back—a "fit reward"—that is, a vicissitude—to the merits of both the good and the bad? Love the good and pity the wicked. It should be noted that he says death does not delay its "horses." By the "horses of death" are understood the partial dispositions of a period <note>term: *periodus* — a fixed lifespan or cycle</note> through which a human tends toward death. For every human has a certain and determined period of their life, because the forms of all things are virtually contained in their limits—that is, in the celestial bodies—as is evident in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption* <note>referring to Aristotle's scientific treatise</note>. It should also be noted that Philosophy here does not exclude the permission to wage a *just* war, but rather an *unjust* one, as he says "unjust battle lines."

# Fifth Prose.

->**The Fifth Prose of the Fourth Book.**<-

### Prose five of the fourth book.

**"From this I see,"** I said, "what either happiness or misery is established in the very merits of the upright and the wicked. But in this common, popular fortune, I perceive nothing of good or evil within it. For no wise man would rather be an exile, destitute, and disgraced, rather than being powerful in wealth, revered in honor, strong in power, and flourishing while remaining in his own city. For in this way, the office of the wise man is exercised more clearly and with greater witness when the happiness of those ruling is somehow poured out upon the peoples they touch. Especially since prison, the law, and the other torments of legal punishments are rather owed to harmful citizens, for whose sake they were even established. Why then..."

<column-break/>

**"From this I see."** This is the fifth prose of this fourth book: because Boethius was previously complaining that evils happen to the good and goods to the evil. Because of this, he even considered that the turns of these fortunes did not come from the order of divine providence, but from chance. Therefore, Philosophy <note>Lady Philosophy, the personified guide in the text</note> consoles Boethius by assigning the causes why evils happen to the good and goods to the evil. And first, Boethius expresses his grief in this: that the turns of fortune seem to be disposed in a confused and disordered way. Second, Philosophy assigns the cause of this appearance. Third, she consoles him by assigning the causes of the aforementioned things. The second part begins at "Nor is it a wonder." The third at "So, she said." First, Boethius premises certain things; second, he expresses the cause of his grief at "Especially since." First, he says, "I see from this," that is, from what has been said, what happiness is established in the merits of the upright—namely, becoming gods—and what misery is established in the merits of the wicked—namely, being transformed into beasts. "I perceive this," that is, I judge that there is "nothing," meaning something, of good or evil in this fortune

<columns>1</columns>

popular, that is, in the prosperity of fortune. Which he proves: for no wise man wants more to be an exile, destitute, and disgraced—that is, unsound—rather than powerful in wealth, revered in honor, and strong in power, and to flourish remaining in his own city. For just as through such goods of fortune the office of the wise man is exercised more clearly and with more witness—that is, with greater testimony, because such men are believed more—when the happiness of the rulers "is poured out," that is, flows down into the "touching," that is, neighboring, peoples. **Note** that in fortuitous goods <note>goods gained by chance or luck</note> there is something of good: because the wise man himself more readily exercises the office of governing subjects. For those who excel others in riches, power, and fame are more fit to rule the republic, because they are more fit to help the oppressed, to suppress the wicked, to protect the good, and to fight off enemies. And so, for the wise man who handles the business of the republic, power and abundance of riches are necessary. However, for the wise man who devotes himself to contemplation, riches are burdensome because he carries too much anxiety from them. "Especially since prison, the law, and the rest of the legal torments." Here Boethius expresses the cause of his grief and wonder, saying: since the law and prison, etc., the torments of legal punishments, ought to be owed to "harmful," that is, evil citizens, for whose sake they were established, I greatly wonder why these torments are "turned about," that is, changed in a contrary way...

The commentary explains that while spiritual virtue is the highest good, material fortune still has practical utility for governing a state.</summary>

It should be noted that a thing is a "marvel" when its cause is not known; for this reason, many marvel at an eclipse of the sun because they are ignorant of the cause. And because **Boethius** was ignorant of the cause of this conclusion—why bad things happen to the good and good things to the wicked—he therefore marveled at this, and the cause of his amazement was ignorance of the disposition of divine providence.

Since the more distant stars traverse a larger circle in the same amount of time that the closer stars traverse a smaller one—because both circles revolve once in a natural day—it is clear by the definition of speed and slowness that the stars closer to the pole move more slowly and the more distant ones more quickly. Surely—that is, for certain—then those things cease to be seen as wonders which previously, while ignorance remained, were seen as wonders. Note that the priests in Egypt began to wonder because of their sightings; seeing, for instance, eclipses of the sun and moon and being ignorant of the causes, they wondered at the entering causes; once these were found, they had knowledge of those eclipses, because to know is to recognize the cause of a thing. Therefore, when the cause is known, the thing is recognized, and by this means wonder ceases.

Otherwise, it is explained that in changeable things there is a triple disposition. One is that by which they pass from non-being to being through generations; regarding this, she says: *the generation of all things.* Or things remain in existence for some time after they are generated; regarding those, she says: *And every progression of changeable natures.* Or things proceed from being to non-being through corruptions; regarding those, she says: *And whatever is moved in any way.*

# Prose VI.

According to which things depend upon the divine will and power; and in this sense, Fate is conceded to be something that exists. Therefore, **Providence** is the divine ordering or disposition existing in the divine mind, by which all lower things are foreseen according to the state of their nature. **Fate**, however, is the divine disposition existing in changeable things, by which individual things are bound to their own ranks, as will become more clearly evident. Here he sets forth the difference—

**That these are different will easily be clear if anyone perceives the force of both in their mind. For Providence is that very divine reason established in the supreme ruler of all things, which disposes all things. But Fate is the disposition inherent in changeable things, through which Providence binds each thing to its own orders. For Providence embraces all things equally, however diverse, however infinite. But Fate arranges individual things distributed in motion, places, forms, and times, so that this unfolding of temporal order is united in the view of the divine mind.**

**Fate is the disposition inherent in changeable things**—that is, temporal things—**through which disposition Providence binds each thing to its own orders.** Then he explains these definitions from the properties of each, intending that Providence embraces all things at once. But it is manifest that all things are nowhere "at once" except in the divine mind; therefore, it is necessary that Providence be the reason existing in the divine mind. To Fate, however, belongs the fact that those things subject to Fate are distributed through places and times. Thus, the "fatal" order <note>The "fatal order" refers to the sequence of events as they happen in the physical world, governed by Fate.</note> carries a certain temporal succession. Such succession, however, exists only in changeable things themselves; wherefore it is necessary that Fate be in changeable things. Whence he says in the text: **For Providence embraces all things equally, however diverse and infinite; but Fate divides individual things distributed in motion, places, forms, and times.** This means, namely, that this temporal unfolding which belongs to Fate, when united in the view of the divine mind, is Providence. But that same unity, when divided and unfolded by times which imply succession, is called Fate. It should be noted that because he said earlier that the definition of things to be done, as it is in the divine intellect, is called Providence, but as it relates to changeable things is called Fate, it might seem to someone that Fate and Providence signify the same thing under different aspects. Therefore, Philosophy <note>Referring to Lady Philosophy, the personification who speaks in Boethius's text.</note>, excluding this, shows that they are really distinguished by providing the definition of each. # Book Four.

In the definition of fate, it is understood as an order, and that order is said to be inherent in changeable things—distinguished from the order which is in the Divine Reason itself, which we call providence. According to this order, divine providence binds each thing to its own arrangements: namely, that some things happen at one time and others at another; some earlier, others later. Although these are diverse, he shows here that although fate and providence differ, one nevertheless depends on the other, saying:

Although these are diverse, yet one depends on the other; namely, fate depends on providence. For the fatal order proceeds from the simplicity of providence, as he declares by a likeness, saying: Just as a craftsman—for instance, a builder—perceiving the form of the thing to be made (such as a house) in his mind, that is, looking forward, moves or produces the effect of the work. And that which he had foreseen in his mind simply and as a whole—namely, the form of the house with its parts all at once—he leads through temporal sequences toward the effect. First the foun-

providence may be. But the same unification, when distributed and unfolded in time, is called fate. Although these are diverse, one nevertheless hangs upon the other. Just as a craftsman, perceiving the form of the thing to be made in his mind, sets the effect of the work in motion, and that which he had foreseen simply and all at once, he carries out through temporal sequences; so God, by providence, disposes what is to be done in a singular and stable manner, but by fate, He administers these very things He has disposed in a manifold and temporal way. In this way, God by His providence disposes all things to be done singularly <note>meaning: simply and stably</note>, but by fate—that is, through fate—He administers those things He disposes temporally. It should be noted that divine providence has its being in the First Cause <note>term: First Cause (the ultimate source of all existence, i.e., God)</note>, but fate exists in the things caused. Likewise, divine providence has a single motion because it exists in a single simplicity, namely in the Divine Mind; but fate has a motion of plurality because it exists in many caused things. Likewise, fate depends on divine providence as an effect on its cause, but not the other way around. For just as the form of a manufactured thing depends on the form persisting in the mind of the craftsman and not vice versa, so fate depends on divine providence, but not vice versa. *Whether, therefore, by serving.* Here he posits various opinions concerning fate and says: Whether fate is exercised by certain divine spirits serving divine providence, or by the soul, or by the whole of serving nature; whether it is exercised by the motions of the celestial bodies, or by angelic power, or by the cunning of demons; whether by some of these or all of them—this is uncertain. However, this much is certain: that divine providence is the immobile and simple form of things to be done, but fate is the mobile disposition and temporal order of those things which the Divine Simplicity disposes to be produced. It should be noted that fate is the temporal disposition of things in which those things foreseen by God are brought to effect through the mediation of secondary causes <note>term: secondary causes (created beings or natural forces that act as instruments of God's will)</note>, concerning which causes there were various opinions which Boethius touches upon in the text, but [he settles] none.

This much is clear: that the immobile and simple form of things to be done is Providence; but Fate is the mobile connection and temporal order of those things which the Divine Simplicity has disposed to be done. Thus it happens that all things subject to Fate are also subject to Providence, to which Fate itself is also subject. However, some things placed under Providence surpass the chain of Fate. Those things which are close to the primary Divinity and are immobile exceed the order of fatal mutability. It should be noted that because Fate depends on Providence as an effect on its cause, it is necessary that those things depending on Fate also depend on Providence; but not vice versa, because the effect is not equal to its cause. Providence belongs to the Divine Intellect, but Fate belongs to those things carried out in created beings.

# Book Four.

<image-desc>A large, faint watermark is visible on the left side of the page, depicting a heraldic shield containing a rearing horse.</image-desc>

For as the example of the spheres <note>original: "orbium"</note> declares here, he explains that conclusion by showing how certain things are more subject to fate, some less, and some exceed fate entirely. Secondly, from what has been said, he concludes the relationship of fate to providence through certain similarities. Therefore, he says first: just as among spheres—that is, circles turning or moving themselves around the same hinge <note>original: "cardinem," referring to an axis or pivot point</note>—the one which is closer to the axis approaches the simplicity of the middle (the axis or center) because it moves with a slower motion. Thus, it approaches more closely the immobility of the axis. This circle, in respect to the outer one, acts as a center around which the outer one turns. Whence he adds that it is like a certain hinge—that is, the center of the other spheres located outside it, around which they revolve. Just as the nave <note>the central block of a wheel</note> in a wheel clings to the axle and is like a hinge around which the rims and spokes revolve. But the outermost—that is, the last outer sphere—rotated with a greater circumference, is spread out over larger spaces the further it departs from the middle indivisibility of the point (the center). If anything, however, connects itself to that middle, it is gathered into the simplicity—that is, the immobility—of the axis, and ceases to be spread out and flow through a great space. In a similar way, that which departs further from the First Mind <note>God or the Divine Intellect</note>, such as corruptible creatures, is entangled in the greater bonds of fate; and a thing is free from fate to the extent that it approaches closer to that hinge of things, namely God. For if it clings to the firmness of the Supernal Mind, it surpasses the necessity of fate. It should be noted that the more beings are near to the First Cause, the less changeable they are; and the more remote, the more changeable. Philosophy declares this by the example of different circles drawn from the same center, in which the circle further from the center is larger and moves more swiftly because it traverses a greater space in an equal time. However, the one closer to the center is smaller and moves more slowly, traversing less space. The middle circles behave in a middle fashion. And there is an excellent comparison of the center of the circle to the Creator; for just as the center is indivisible and many circles can proceed from it, so the Creator, being one and indivisible, creates and governs infinite things.

<column-break/>

## For as among spheres turning themselves around the same hinge, the one which is innermost approaches the simplicity of the middle, and exists as a kind of hinge for the others located outside, around which they may turn; but the outermost, rotated in a greater circumference, the further it departs from the middle indivisibility of the point, the more it is unfolded through larger spaces. But if anything connects and joins itself to that middle, it is constrained into simplicity, and ceases to spread and flow away. By a similar reasoning, that which departs further from the First Mind is entangled in greater knots of fate. And a thing is free from fate to the extent that it seeks to be near that hinge of things. But if it should cling to the firmness of the Supernal Mind, lacking motion, it also surpasses the necessity of fate. # Prose VI.

Therefore, it is as follows. Here, Philosophy <note>original: "P." for Philosophia</note> concludes the relationship of fate to divine providence through certain similarities, and says the series of fate is thus—that is, it relates to the simple stability of divine providence just as reasoning relates to the intellect. Wherein it should be known that what the intellect understands in simple truth, reasoning apprehends by way of discourse and succession. Also, fate relates to providence just as that which is being born relates to that

### which is, to eternity time, to the center point the circle; so is the moving series of fate to the stable simplicity of providence. That series moves the heavens and the stars, balances the elements among themselves, and transforms them by alternate exchange. The same renews all things that are born and die through similar progressions of offspring and seeds. This also binds the acts and fortunes of men in an indissoluble connection of causes; since these proceed from the immobile beginnings of providence, it is necessary that they also be immutable. For in this way things are best governed: if the simplicity remaining in the divine mind produces an unswerving order of causes. But here, this order [governs] things that are changeable and otherwise

<column-break/>

which exists. Wherein it should be known that what is being born is in a certain state of flux and motion, but that which is actually brought forth exists in a certain permanence. Also, fate relates to providence as time relates to eternity. Wherein it should be known that in time there is a succession of parts—present, past, and future—but eternity is without succession, existing all at once. Likewise, fate relates to providence as the circle relates to the center point. Wherein it should be known that the circle is extended and divided into parts, being mobile; but the point is immobile and indivisible, because according to the first book of Euclid: A point is that which

<column-break/>

<note>The following text continues from the second column and spans the full width of the page.</note>

has no part. "That series [moves] the heavens and the stars." Here Philosophy shows what those things are which are disposed by fate. Secondly, she concludes that those things which seem confused to the human intellect are, in divine governance, ordered reasonably (at the section beginning "Whereby it happens"). First, she says: that series of fate of which we spoke moves the heavens and the stars, balances the elements against one another lest they totally destroy themselves, and transforms them by alternate exchange so that from water comes air and vice versa. And the same series of fate renews all things being born and dying—that is, moving things—through similar progressions of offspring (regarding animals) and seeds (regarding vegetables). And fate also binds, by an indissoluble connection of causes, the acts (that is, the operations) and the fortunes of men. Since all these things proceed from the origins of divine providence, it is necessary for them to be immutable. For in this way things are best managed—that is, governed—if the simplicity remaining in the divine mind produces (that is, unfolds) an unswerving (that is, immutable) order of causes. Moreover, this order of divine providence restrains, by its own immutability, things that are changeable and which would otherwise flow blindly (that is, by chance). It should be noted that fate is considered in two ways: In one way as it exists in secondary causes, the order and disposition of which is called "fate"; and in this way fate is mobile and the things subject to fate are mobile. In the other way, fate is considered according to how it depends upon providence.

# Book Four

Divine <term>Providence</term><note>The timeless, overarching plan of God.</note> is entirely immobile; and thus <term>Fate</term><note>The execution of Providence within time and change.</note> derives its immobility from it. In this way, even fated things are, according to their substance, immobile. It should be noted that if anything could deviate from the order of Providence, then Divine Providence would fail in its effect, and this would result in the impotence of the Ruler. And if you say: "If all things are subject to Divine Providence, then all things happen by necessity," it must be said that this is not so. For God foresees things exactly as they are to be in the future: some He foresees 

will happen by necessity, and others contingently <note>meaning they could happen otherwise, depending on free will or chance</note>. This will be seen more clearly in the fifth book of this work. From this, Philosophy shows here that those things which appear confused in the world are, in the divine government, well-ordered, saying: "From this, Divine Providence has established an inevitable order for things." It follows that even if we are least able to perceive this order of things, and all things seem to us confused and disturbed, nevertheless its own method—that is, the proper order of Divine Providence—disposes all things, directing them toward the good. For there is nothing that exists for the sake of evil, not even by the wicked themselves, whom a perverse error turns aside while they are seeking the good, as was demonstrated before. Much less

<column-break/>

does it [Providence] restrain flowing things by its own immutability. "From which it happens that although to you—who are least able to consider this order—all things seem confused and disturbed, nevertheless its own method, directing all things toward the good, disposes them. For there is nothing which is done for the sake of evil, not even by the wicked themselves, whom (as has been most abundantly demonstrated) a perverse error turns aside while they are seeking the good; much less does the order proceeding from the hinge of the Supreme Good deflect anyone from its own beginning." 

"But," you will ask, "what confusion can be more unjust than that both adversity and prosperity happen to the good, and both desired and hateful things happen to the wicked?" Do men live with such integrity of mind that those whom they judge to be honest or wicked must necessarily be as they think? Yet in this, the judgments of men conflict, so that those whom some [judge worthy of] reward...

<note>The text below the column break provides a commentary on the passage above.</note>

That is, much less is the **fated order**—proceeding from the "hinge of the Supreme Good" (that is, from God Himself)—deflected from its "beginning" (that is, from God, who is the end and the beginning of all things). It should be noted that she says the wicked do nothing for the sake of evil, the opposite of which seems obvious. For many wicked people kill themselves. It must be said that no one acts with a view toward evil, because all things desire the good. If, however, someone works evil, this happens under a **fantasy of the good**. For someone existing in great anxiety estimates it to be a "good" to flee that anxiety; and considering nothing else, he follows this estimation by killing himself. Such a person, while depriving himself of the good, is led by a fantasy of the good, because at that moment he thinks it is a good to escape anxiety by the loss of life. "But," you will ask, "what confusion can be more unjust?" Here Philosophy solves the question of why good things happen to the evil and evil things to the good. First, she shows this in general; second, more specifically [at the passage] "But suppose someone..." First, she assigns the cause of the aforementioned event to the **defective judgment of men**; second, to the contrary judgments of God and men.

<summary>Philosophy explains that while the world appears chaotic, all events are directed toward the Good by Divine Providence. She argues that even the wicked seek the "good," though they are misled by a false perception of what is beneficial.</summary>

# Prose VI.

It has been said. Secondly, she explains herself through a simile at the point: *For it is not a dissimilar...* First, she says: "O Boethius, you will ask what consultation could be more unjust than that prosperity should sometimes happen to the good and adversity at other times, since prosperity should always happen to the good; and conversely, that for the evil, things desired should sometimes occur and things hateful at others, since hateful things should always happen to the evil." Philosophy says: "Do men live with such <note>original: "degunt id est vivunt"</note>

<column-break/>

integrity—that is, with such sound judgment of mind—that it is necessary for those to be virtuous or wicked whom they themselves have judged to be so? And yet, certainly in this matter the judgments of men conflict—that is, they are contradictory—so that those whom some deem worthy of reward, others deem worthy of punishment. But let us grant that someone could discern the good and the bad. Could he then gaze upon that inward temperament—that is, the interior condition and quality of souls—just as is usually said of bodies? As if to say: I speak of souls according to how men are accustomed to speak of bodies. It should be noted that because of the defective

---

judgment of men, it happens that they judge those to be good who are evil, and vice versa. If, therefore, they judge the evil to be good, and if evils happen to them, they think evils are happening to the good. And if to the good, whom they judge to be evil, good things happen, they think good things are happening to the evil. And therefore they also often think the good are being oppressed when the evil are oppressed (judging the evil to be good), and they think the evil are being exalted when the good are exalted (judging the good to be evil). *For it is not a dissimilar miracle.* Here Philosophy explains herself through a simile, saying: This miracle is not dissimilar—indeed, it is very similar to the point—to someone who does not know why sweet things suit some healthy bodies and bitter things suit others. Also to someone who does not know why some sick people are helped by light medicines and others by sharp <note>or "harsh"</note> ones. Although this seems wonderful to the ignorant, the physician does not wonder at it, for he knows the manner and temperament of health and sickness. Just as, similarly, although man is ignorant of what suits the good and the evil, nevertheless God, who is the searcher of hearts, knows these things, seeing that sometimes adversity suits the good and sometimes prosperity suits the evil. Therefore, He distributes to them accordingly. And this is what she adds, applying the simile to the soul, saying: "For what else is judged to be the health of souls but virtue <note>original: "probitas"</note>? What else is the sickness of souls but vice? And who else is the preserver of the good and the driver-away of evils but God, the ruler and physician?"

<summary>Lady Philosophy uses a medical analogy to explain why the "medicine" of fortune (prosperity or adversity) is distributed by God in ways that seem mysterious to flawed human judgment. She argues that only the Divine Physician truly understands the internal temperament of the soul and what it requires for its health.</summary>

### Book Four.

The judge of minds <note>original: "dicator mentium"</note>. Who, when He looks out from the high watchtower of providence, recognizes what is suitable for each person, and what He has recognized as suitable, He provides. From this—that is, from what has been said—comes that remarkable miracle of the fatal order <note>the "fatal order" refers to the unfolding of Fate as directed by God's Providence</note>; that is, it is that which men marvel at in the order of fate when it is carried out by God. That is, it is something at which those who are ignorant are amazed, or rather, they marvel. It should be noted that there is a good comparison between bodily health and sickness in relation to a doctor, and the virtue and vice of souls in relation to God. For just as a doctor, knowing the causes of health and sickness, knows what is suitable for the healthy and the sick while others are ignorant and marveling, so God, knowing the quality of souls, knows what is suitable for the good and what for the wicked, and He grants to each what is suitable for them. Sometimes He gives prosperity to the wicked and adversity to the good, at which the ignorant are amazed. It should be noted that a "watchtower" <note>original: "specula"</note> is called a high place fit for looking around. # Prose 6.

In your opinion, there is a perverse confusion. It should be noted that Cato of Utica <note>Cato the Younger (95–46 BCE), a Roman statesman famous for his stoic integrity.</note>, on account of his wisdom and virtue, held the greatest authority among the people. However, when Julius Caesar fought against Pompey, Cato judged Pompey’s cause to be the just one, aligning himself with the defeated side. Others, however, judged Julius to be just, aligning themselves with the victorious side. From this, it is clear that gods and men judged the same matter in contrary ways. <note>original: "victrix causa deis placuit, sed victa Catoni" — The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.</note>

**...confusion. But suppose there is someone so well-behaved that divine and human judgment agree alike concerning him. Yet, he is weak in strength of mind; if any adversity should befall him, he might perhaps cease to cherish the innocence through which he could not retain his good fortune. Therefore, the wise dispensation spares him whom adversity might make worse, lest he who is not suited for struggle should suffer.**
**There is another who is perfect in all virtues, holy and close to God. To touch such a man with any adversities, Providence deems a crime...**

<column-break/>

...the wise who followed Cato. **But if someone.** Here, Philosophy <note>The personification of Wisdom in Boethius's dialogue.</note> assigns specific causes for why prosperity and adversity happen indifferently to the good and the bad. Secondly, she excuses herself from a more extensive treatment of these causes. She declares her intent first regarding the good, and secondly regarding the evil. First, she assigns causes why evils do not happen to some good people; secondly, why evils sometimes do happen to them.

---

There, **To others, a mixture.** First, she shows why evils do not happen to the good; second, why good things sometimes happen to them. First, she assigns two causes why evils do not happen to the good. The first cause is the weakness of mind of a good person who, if adversity came to him, would become worse. Hence, the text says: **if there be.** That is, let us suppose someone is so well-mannered that divine and human judgment agree about him; perhaps he is weak in mind, not able to resist adversities. If something adverse should happen to him, he might perhaps cease to cherish innocence—that is, to practice virtue—through which he could not retain his fortune. This is because he would blame his innocence for the loss of his prosperity. We read of a similar case regarding Job, whom his wife reproached, saying: "Do you still persist in your simplicity? Curse God and die!" <note>A reference to Job 2:9.</note> Therefore, the wise dispensation—that is, the providence of God—spares him whom adversity could make worse, nor does it allow him to labor in adversity when it is not fitting. It should be noted that some good people are so feeble in mind that they would be changed by a small temptation of adversity; seeing this, God spares them lest He cast them down through adversity. Hence the Apostle says: "God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able." <note>1 Corinthians 10:13.</note> **There is another perfect in all virtues.** Here she assigns another cause why evils do not come to certain good people, saying: There is another man who is "absolute"—that is, perfected in all virtues—and holy and close to God. Divine providence judges it a "nefas"—that is, a crime or a great wrong—for this man to be touched by any adversities, to such an extent that He does not even allow him to be shaken by bodily diseases. This she confirms by the authority of a certain philosopher more excellent than herself, whose authority she places in...

# Book Four.

In Greek, this means as much as "the virtues have built the body of the holy man" in Latin—that is to say, by preserving him from adversity. <note>The commentator is glossing a Greek concept mentioned in the text of Boethius, likely referring to the idea that a holy person's character protects them.</note> Note that the second reason why adversity does not come to some is their excellent holiness. It should be noted why Philosophy says, "someone more excellent than me says," since nothing is more excellent than Philosophy. It must be said that the text should be explained thus: for a certain philosopher, more excellent than other philosophers, says this *through* me (Philosophy). **It often happens.** Here he shows why good things often happen to the good, saying: It happens, that is, it occurs in reality often, that the highest conduct of affairs—that is, the leadership of managing things—is deferred, that is, granted to the upright. This is not only for the benefit of good men, but so that the overflowing wickedness—that is, the abounding evil—of the wicked may be blunted, that is, checked or repressed. Then he assigns the reason why evils sometimes happen to the good, saying: To others—that is, to the good—God distributes certain "mixed" things—that is, sometimes good and sometimes evil—according to the quality of their souls. <column-break/>

...judges with providence, to such an extent that He does not even allow them to be shaken by bodily diseases. For as someone even more excellent than me said:

**"The virtues have built the bodies of the holy man."** <note>original: "Vir autem sacerdotalis..." This is a reference to a Neoplatonic or Hermetic idea that a truly holy person's physical form is composed of their virtues.</note> **It often happens that the highest conduct of affairs is deferred to the good, so that overflowing wickedness may be blunted. To others He distributes certain mixed things according to the quality of their souls. Some He bites back lest they grow soft through long-lasting happiness. Others He allows to be shaken by hardships so that they may confirm the virtues of the mind through the use and exercise of patience. Others fear more than is fair that which they are able to bear. Some have purchased the venerable name of the world at the glorious price of death.**

---

...bites back with adversities lest they "grow soft"—that is, become proud—through long-lasting happiness, which is prosperity. Other good people He allows to be shaken—that is, vexed—by hardships—that is, adversities—so that He may confirm the virtues of their minds through the use and exercise of patience, as is evident in the case of Job. <note>A reference to the biblical figure Job, tested by God with extreme suffering.</note> Others fear more than is fair that which they are actually able to bear; just as Thomas dreaded entering India, saying: "Lord, send me wherever you wish except to the Indians." <note>A reference to the tradition of St. Thomas the Apostle's reluctance to missionize India.</note> Others despise more than is fair that which they cannot bear, because by presuming, they look down on temptations which they are nevertheless unable to carry; such as Saint Peter, who said: "Even if it were necessary for me to die with you, I will not deny you," yet who denied Christ at the temptation and accusation of a servant girl. Both of these He leads—that is, He tests—with sorrowful things—that is, adversities—as a trial of themselves, that is, for the recognition of themselves, so that they may know what they can and cannot do.

He plunges other wicked men into deserved ruin—that is, misery—and adds that to certain wicked people the right of punishing is permitted—that is, granted power—so that it may be a cause of exercise in virtues and patience for the good, and a cause of punishment for the wicked. Note that happiness plunges some into the ruin of adversity. Whence Peter of Samaria says: "Rolling fortune promotes the unjust so that those she made climb headlong, she may rotate to the depths. For the swollen tower falls with a heavier ruin, and the tall cypress strikes the ground more heavily." <note>A common medieval poetic trope regarding the "Wheel of Fortune."</note> And it should be noted that the good are exercised in virtues and patience through adversities. Whence the same "Poor Henry" <note>referring to the poet Henry of Settimello</note> says: "It is fitting for a harsh nature to bear harsh things in the mind; the grape tastes better when fully matured; one passes through excessive heat to reach cool waters. And so, through opposites, man seeks sweet things." For as to the upright and the wicked: here he solves a certain objection, and secondly inserts a certain conclusion there: "from which often..." First he says: Someone might say, "You said that the right of punishing is granted to the wicked so they may be a cause of punishment to other wicked men. This does not seem true, because a wicked man does not punish a wicked man since they are alike." Philosophy solves this, saying: Just as there is no treaty—that is, concord—between the upright and the wicked, because they are always opposed to one another, so the wicked themselves cannot agree among themselves. Why not? That is, why would it not be so, since any wicked men disagree with themselves, their vices tearing apart—that is, distracting—their own consciences? And often the wicked do things which, once they have done them, they decree—that is, judge—ought not to have been done.

<summary>This page explains Boethius's arguments for why God allows the wicked to prosper: to prevent them from committing crimes out of poverty, to encourage them to reform out of fear of losing wealth, or to use them as instruments to test the virtuous.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the nature of evil and divine providence, specifically addressing how God utilizes the actions of the wicked to bring about good ends.</meta>

-># Prose VI.<-

It should be noted that a person is good to the extent that they maintain an order toward the ultimate end, which end is the supreme good. And because all good people maintain that end in their order, therefore all good people, in that they are good, agree with one another. Evil people, however, because they [fail to] preserve this order and disagree with themselves, cannot mutually agree with one another, etc. From which that supreme [providence] often... Here he introduces a certain conclusion, saying: From this, the wicked punish the wicked.

**For just as there is no treaty between the virtuous and the wicked, so the wicked cannot agree among themselves. Why should they not, when they disagree with themselves, their consciences being torn apart by vices, and they often do things which, once performed, they decide should not have been done? From this, that supreme providence has often brought forth a remarkable miracle: that the wicked make other wicked people good. For while some see themselves suffering injustices from the worst of men, burning with hatred for those harmful people, they return to the fruit of virtue while they strive to be unlike those whom they hated. For it is only the divine power to which even evil things are good, when by using them competently it draws out the effect of some good. For order indeed embraces all things: so that whatever has departed from the assigned reasoning of its order, although it falls back into another order, nothing in the realm of providence is left to chance. God, the strongest in the world, has completed all things when he foresees and looks forth upon all ages.**

<column-break/>

From this, divine providence has brought forth a remarkable miracle, namely that the wicked make the wicked good. This he explains: For while certain wicked people seem to suffer injustices from the worst of men, they themselves, burning—that is, glowing—with hatred for those more harmful—that is, for their losses—return to the fruit of virtue—that is, to usefulness—while such people strive to be unlike those wicked ones whom they hated. And he adds that only the divine power is such to which evil things are good—that is, they yield toward the good, as when a wicked person makes a wicked person good. Whence he adds: Because God, by using the wicked competently, draws out the effect of some good. For the fatal order <note>The "fatal order" refers to *fatum* or Fate, the temporal unfolding of God's eternal plan.</note> embraces all things: so that what departs from the assigned reason of order—namely the wicked—falls back into another order—namely of the good—lest in the kingdom of God's providence anything be allowed to temerity—that is, to disorder. And he places an authority in Greek <note>original: "Fortissimus in mundo deus cuncta peregit" - likely a Latin rendering of a Greek poetic fragment or Homeric sentiment.</note> which signifies as much as:

---

God, the strongest in the world, rules all things. It should be noted that the good proceeding from the malice of the wicked is not to be imputed to the wicked themselves, but only to the divine power which knows how to make good out of evil; and although God directs evil toward good by His intention and power, a human is not therefore without fault who does that evil with an evil intention. It should be noted that there is one order that is natural, and another order provided by God. The natural order is that we love God and our neighbor. The provided order is the temporal disposition of things which is called Fate; and although we often abandon the natural order by loving something more than God or by hating our neighbor, nevertheless you will never escape the order provided by God, which never happens otherwise than God foresees. And if anything recedes from the natural order, it falls back into another.

<summary>This text explores the Boethian concept of how Divine Providence maintains order even through the chaos of human wickedness, explaining that God can use the cruelty of the wicked to reform others. It distinguishes between the "natural order" of moral law and the "provided order" of Fate which encompasses all outcomes.</summary>

# Book Four.

Just as if something is evil in relation to mercy, it is good in comparison to justice; thus, within the kingdom of divine providence, nothing is left to chance—that is, to disorder. Nor is it right for man <note>original: "phas est hoī" (fas est homini)</note>. Here, Philosophy excuses herself from a more extensive investigation of causes, saying: "For it is not right for human genius to comprehend, nor for speech to explain, all the mechanisms—that is, the causes or arrangements—of divine work." Let it suffice only to have perceived this: that God, the producer <note>original: "proditor," used here in the sense of one who brings forth</note> of all natures, disposes all things, directing them toward the good. And all things that He has produced, He hastens to retain in His own likeness—that is, in goodness. He Himself eliminates—that is, excludes—through the series—that is, through the order—of fatal necessity, all evil from the boundaries of His commonwealth—that is, the world. Thus it happens that while evils are believed to abound on earth, if you look at the disposing providence, you would perceive that there is no evil anywhere. Then she invites Boethius to poetic consolation, saying: "I see that you are burdened by the weight of this question, which is difficult, and weary from the length of the discourse, you await some sweetness of song. Therefore, receive a draught of poetic sweetness, by which, being refreshed—that is, restored—you may strive more firmly toward further things."

<column-break/>

For it is not right for man to comprehend all the mechanisms of divine work by genius, nor to explain them in speech; let it suffice to have perceived only this: that God, the producer of all natures, likewise disposes all things by directing them toward the good. While He hastens to retain those things which He has brought forth in His own likeness, He eliminates all evil from the borders of His commonwealth through the series of fatal necessity. Thus it follows that those things which are believed to abound on earth—if you look upon the disposing providence—you would realize that there is no evil anywhere. But I see that for a long time now, burdened by the weight of the question and fatigued by the length of the reasoning, you await some sweetness of song. Receive, therefore, a draught by which, being refreshed, you may strive more firmly toward further things.

---

->The Sixth Meter of the Fourth Book.<-

Note that she says evil is nowhere to be found in comparison to divine providence, because evil is not any nature nor any thing. For every nature and thing seeks its own perfection. Since, however, that which is desirable has the character of "the good," if evil were a nature or a thing seeking perfection, evil would be good. It should be noted that there is no evil simply and totally in the world that does not, in comparison to divine providence, have the character of good. Hence, it is expedient for many defects to happen in the universe lest many good things be taken away. For if the air were not corrupted, fire would not be preserved; nor would the life of the lion be preserved unless the lamb or the donkey were killed. Neither would justice nor patience be praised if there were no iniquity. From this it is clear that many things are evil in comparison to us, which, in comparison to divine providence—disposing all things according to what best suits the universe—are good.

->The Sixth Meter of the Fourth Book.<-

<summary>Lady Philosophy explains that while evil appears to exist from a human perspective, it is non-existent within God's providential order, where even destruction serves a greater purpose. She concludes by offering a poem to refresh Boethius's weary mind before continuing their difficult investigation.</summary>

# Meter VI

->**If you wish to discern the laws of the high Thunderer.**<- This is the sixth meter of this fourth book, which according to some is called Adonic; according to others, it is Archilochian tetrameter from its inventor, and dactylic from its predominant foot. In this, the poetry commends divine providence in the arrangement of things: first, regarding the things governed by divine arrangement; second, regarding God the ruler, at the point: *Meanwhile He sits.*

If you wish to discern the pure
laws of the high Thunderer <note>original: "tonantis"; a poetic epithet for God, referring to Jupiter's role as the one who thunders</note>
with a skillful mind, behold the
heights of the highest heaven. There, by a just covenant of things,
the stars preserve their ancient peace. The
sun, stirred by its ruddy fire, does not
hinder the cold axis of Phoebe <note>The Moon</note>. Nor does the Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Major</note>, which
at the highest peak of the world
turns its rapid paths,
ever wash in the western deep.
Though seeing other stars submerged,
it never desires to dip its flame
in the ocean. Always with
equal changes of time, Hesperus <note>The Evening Star</note> announces the late
shadows, and as Lucifer <note>The Morning Star</note> he brings back the nourishing day.
Thus he restores the alternate courses. Thus
alternate love banishes discordant war
from the star-bearing shores. This concord tempers in equal measure—

<column-break/>

First, he commends divine providence in the government of celestial bodies; second,
in the government of the elements;
third, in the government of the seasons;
fourth, in the government of things that are
born and pass away <note>original: "generabilium et corruptibilium"</note>. The second part begins at: *this concord tempers*; the third at: *for these reasons*; the fourth at: *this tempering*. First,
he says: if you, being skillful—that is, wise—wish to discern with a pure mind the laws—that is, the regimes by which the world is ruled—of the high Thunderer—that is, of God—behold the heights, that is, the altitudes of the highest heaven. There the stars preserve their ancient peace—that is, the ancient concord which divine providence instilled in them by a just covenant.

<column-break/>

And the sun, stirred—that is, moved—by its ruddy fire—that is, its heat—does not hinder the cold axis of Phoebe—that is, the moon. Nor does the Bear, which turns its rapid motions around the North Pole, ever wash in the western deep—that is, the western sea—nor desire to dip—that is, submerge—its flames in the ocean—that is, the sea—while seeing other stars submerged in the sea. And he speaks in the common manner; for the common people believe that the stars, when they set, descend into the sea. And Vesper—that is, Venus—always at equal intervals of time announces the late shadows of night; and the same Venus, existing as Lucifer, brings back the nourishing—that is, bright—day. Thus eternal love, proceeding from divine providence, restores the alternate courses of the stars. Thus—that is, through such mutual concord—discordant war is exiled—that is, expelled—from the star-bearing shores—that is, from the celestial regions which carry the stars. It should be noted regarding this word *solers* <note>skillful/clever</note> that according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, an influential medieval encyclopedist</note>, it is interpreted as if "accustomed in art" or "useful," and thus it should be written with a double 'l'. But according to Hugutio <note>Huguccio of Pisa, a 12th-century grammarian</note>, it comes from *solon*, which is "all" or "much," and *ars* (art), as if "all or much in art," and thus it should be written with a single 'l'. It should be noted that God is named "The Thunderer" more from the storm of thundering than from any other storm, because a greater horror is struck into the minds of men by it than by any other; wherefore by the storm of thundering, men are more induced to reconsider divine power. Note that the Bear, having seven stars around the North Pole, never sets in its motion but always appears to us, although other stars rise and set for us. Regarding Venus, however, which follows the sun by night and is called Lucifer when it precedes the sun in the morning, this was seen in the first meter of the second book.

# Book Four.

This harmony tempers with equal measures. Here Philosophy commends the governance of divine providence over the elements, saying: this harmony, proceeding from divine providence, tempers the elements in equal ways so that the moist, fighting—that is, contrary—elements yield to the dry in turns, i.e., vice versa: so that sometimes the moist prevail and sometimes the dry; and so that the colds—that is, the cold elements—join in faith—that is, harmony—with the flames—that is, the hot elements—lest one totally destroy the other.

And this harmony causes the
hanging fire to rise into the
heights—that is, to move up-
ward—and the earths, heavy with
weight, to settle—that is, to reside
downward. Then she com-

breathes out scents in the spring itself—
that is, in the time of spring—suddenly—
that is, as it grows warm. The glow-

grain <note>original: "cererem," referring to Ceres, the goddess of grain</note>—that is, the crops.

<column-break/>

**The elements [tempered] in ways so that the moist**
**yield to the dry in turns. May the colds join**
**in faith with the flames. May the hanging fire**
**rise into the heights and the earths, heavy with weight,**
**settle. By these same causes, in the warming spring,**
**the flower-bearing year breathes out scents. The glowing**
**summer dries the grain. Heavy autumn returns**
**with fruits. The down-flowing rain waters the**
**winter. This tempering nourishes and brings**
