**The same [tempering], seizing them, hides and carries them away,**
**submerging what has risen in a final death.**

---

Autumn returns—that is, it comes back—heavy—that is, burdened—with fruits. The down-flowing rain waters the winter. Then she commends the governance of God concerning things that can be generated and corrupted, saying: This tempering—that is, the tempered disposition of divine providence—nourishes and brings forth whatever breathes life in the world—that is, whatever lives—and the same tempering, seizing those things which it made, hides—that is, conceals—and carries them away, namely from being, submerging what has risen—that is, what was produced—in a final death—that is, ultimate death. It should be noted, according to the Commentator <note>Likely referring to Averroes, the famous commentator on Aristotle</note> in the eighth book of the *Physics*: The first ancient [cause] does nothing without the second ancient [cause]—that is, the heavens. Therefore, the First Cause <note>God</note> works the generation and corruption of the elements and of all things in the world, and the distinction of the seasons, by means of the celestial bodies. Whence in the book *On the Apple* <note>A medieval work falsely attributed to Aristotle</note> it is written that the Creator of all things by His wisdom prepared the spheres, and in each sphere bright stars, and gave to them the power of signifying in this world, of making good and evil, death and life. And the stars move according to the power given to them by the Creator, according to His desire and will, in ascending and descending, now from the east to the west, now from the west to the east, without contradiction. And all stars are like servants obeying a master, and their course and motion is not from themselves nor by their own power, but it is the Creator who makes them move. Meanwhile the high Founder sits. Here she commends divine providence on the part of the Ruler, saying: Meanwhile, while things are thus carried out, the high Founder—that is, the supreme Creator of things, God—sits—that is, He remains immutably in Himself—ruling all, He turns—that is, moderates—the reins of things—that is, the bridles—existing as King through the wisdom of governance, Lord through the power of creation, the fountain of all goodness and the origin of all, and He Himself is a law to none, binding all things, and a wise arbiter—that is, a judge of the equal.

# Meter VI

Giving to all according to justice, namely God, who ruling all things, stirs up <note>original: "concitat," meaning to incite or set in motion</note>—that is, rouses—beings to go—that is, to proceed into existence—by motion. He halts them—that is, makes them remain in themselves—drawing all things back from non-existence. And He Himself, through grace, steadies the wandering—that is, those things unstable by nature. For unless God, calling back their straight strokes—that is, their straight progress which is from being toward non-being—should compel them—that is, lead them back—even into bent orbits—that is, into certain circular paths—those things

<margin>which the stable order of divine providence contains, having been broken apart—that is, separated from their source, which is God—would grow faint—that is, fail and come to nothing. This source is the common love for all beings, and all things seek again—that is, desire—to be held—that is, preserved—by the end of the good: because things cannot otherwise endure—that is, be made perpetual in being—unless, with love turned back, they flow back—that is, return—to the cause—that is, to the First Cause which gave them being through creation.</margin>

**Meanwhile the high Creator sits,**
**And ruling, guides the reins of things;**
**King and Lord, Source and Origin, Law and wise**
**Judge of equity. And those things which He stirs with motion**
**To go, He halts, drawing them back and steadying the wandering.**
**For unless, calling back the straight strokes,**
**He compelled them again into bent orbits, those things which now**
**A stable order contains, broken from their source,**
**Would grow faint. This is the continuous love for all;**
**They seek to be held by the end of the good.**
**Because they cannot otherwise endure,**
**Unless, with love turned back again,**
**They flow back to the Cause which gave them being.**

---

->Prose Seven of the Fourth Book.<-

It should be noted that beings are ruled by God through a certain circulation <note>The concept of "circulatio" refers to the Neoplatonic cycle of procession from and return to the Divine source.</note> according to which they are, in a certain way, made perpetual in being. For example: God has so disposed things that from a seed comes a plant, and conversely, from the plant a seed is produced. So in the generation of the elements, a certain circle is made while fire is generated from air, and again air from fire. Likewise, in rational creatures who proceed from God by the production of nature, there is again a reflection back to God Himself through the leading back of grace: so that nothing remains in things as existing and perfect except through a certain circulation. And Philosophy hints at this in the text. It should be noted that the end toward which all things tend by nature and desire is the highest good itself, which is God. Rational creatures follow after this end through the operation of the intellect and will; but irrational creatures attain it only through the fact that they represent Him through a certain participation in being: and therefore [everything] tends toward its ultimate end by the same desire, and she hints at this in the text when she says: "this is the common love for all."

->Prose Seven of the Fourth Book.<-

**Now therefore you see. This is the seventh and last prose of this fourth book, in which**
**Philosophy draws a certain conclusion from the premises. And first**
**she does this. Second, she adds a certain exhortation. The second part is there:**
**"Wherefore," she says. First, she posits the intended conclusion. Second, she com-**
**pares it to the opinion of the common people. The second part is there: "But it." First she says: "Do you see now..."**

# Book Four.

Boethius asks what follows from all these things we have said. Boethius says: "What is it?" and Philosophy answers: "That all fortune is entirely good." Boethius says: "And how can this be?" To which Philosophy replies: "Pay attention; since all fortune—whether pleasant or harsh—is granted for the sake of rewarding or testing the good, or for the sake of punishing or correcting the wicked, it is clear that all fortune is good, as it is established to be either just (such as that which punishes the bad and rewards the good) or useful (such as that which exercises the good and corrects the bad)." Boethius says: "This reasoning is very true; and if you consider the Providence which you taught a little while ago, and Fate, then this sentiment is confirmed by firm strengths," <note>original: "firmis viribus"</note> that is, by firm reasons.

### Do you now see what follows from all these things we have discussed? Boethius: "What is it?" Philosophy: "That all fortune is entirely good." Boethius: "And how can that be?" Philosophy: "Pay attention; since all fortune, whether pleasant or harsh, is granted for the purpose of rewarding or exercising the good, or for punishing and correcting the wicked, all fortune is good because it is established as being either just or useful." Boethius: "The reasoning is indeed very true. And if we consider the Providence or Fate you taught just now, the sentiment is true with firm strength. But if it pleases you, let us number this among those things you recently labeled as 'paradoxical' <note>original: "inopinabiles" — literally 'unexpected' or 'contrary to common opinion'</note>." Philosophy: "And why?" Boethius: "Because common human speech frequently asserts that the fortune of certain people is bad." Philosophy: "Do you wish then..."

It should be noted that since, according to divine Providence, prosperity and adversity happen to both the good and the bad—prosperity to the good for the sake of reward and adversity for the sake of exercise in the virtues—it is clear that rewarding prosperity and exercising adversity are both good. Likewise, since prosperous fortune amends the wicked (as was seen before) and adversity corrects them and justly punishes them, it is clear that this too is good. **"But if it pleases you."** Here he compares this conclusion to the opinion of the common people, showing that it is "unthinkable" to the masses, and he inquires what the common people feel about any given fortune. Secondly, from the opinion of the common people, he concludes something contrary to the common people themselves. There, **"See therefore."** Philosophy says: "If it pleases, let us count that opinion—that all fortune is good—among those opinions which you recently placed as paradoxical." Philosophy says: "What?" that is, "For what reason?" Boethius says: "Because the common speech of men takes up the use of saying that the fortune of some is bad and of others is good." And Philosophy says: "Do you wish, O Boethius, that we approach the speech of the common people for a little while, so that we do not seem to have receded too far from the common usage of men?" Boethius says: "As you please." And Philosophy: "Do you not judge that which is beneficial to be good?" Boethius says: "It is so." And Philosophy: "Fortune which either exercises or corrects is beneficial." Boethius says: "I confess it." And thus Philosophy concludes: "All fortune is good which exercises and corrects." Boethius says: "Why not?" <note>meaning "certainly"</note> and Philosophy adds: "This fortune which exercises is the good of those who are placed in..."

<summary>Lady Philosophy argues that all fortune is inherently good because it serves a divine purpose: rewarding the virtuous, testing the good, or correcting the wicked. Boethius acknowledges the logic but notes that this contradicts the common human perception that "bad luck" exists.</summary>

# Prose 7.

He wages war through virtue against hardships. But the fortune which corrects belongs to those men who, turning away from vices, take up the path of virtue. Boethius says: I cannot deny it. Philosophy asks: What of pleasant fortune, which is granted to the good as a reward? Does the common people <note>original: "vulgus"; referring to the unlearned masses or general public opinion</note> decree—that is, judge—it to be evil? Boethius says: Not at all; they judge it to be the best, just as it is. Philosophy asks further: What of the remaining fortune which punishes, and which—

**"Let us for a little while," she said, "agree with the speech of the common people, lest we seem to have moved too far from the ordinary usage of humanity." Boethius: "As you please," I said. Philosophy: "Do you not then think that which is useful is good?" Boethius: "It is so," I said. Philosophy: "Indeed, that which either exercises or corrects is useful." Boethius: "I confess it," I said. Philosophy: "Therefore, it is good." Boethius: "Why not?" Philosophy: "But this belongs to those who, being placed in virtue, wage war against hardships, or those who, turning from vices, take up the path of virtue." Boethius: "I cannot deny it," I said. Philosophy: "What then of the pleasant fortune which is granted to the good as a reward? Does the common people judge it to be evil?" Boethius: "By no means; but just as it is, they judge it to be the best. What of the rest, which, since it is harsh and restrains the wicked with just punishment? Does the people think it is good?" Boethius: "On the contrary, they judge it to be the most miserable of all things that can be imagined." Philosophy: "Look then, lest by following the opinions of the people, we have concluded something very unexpected—"**

<column-break/>

—though it be harsh and restrains the wicked with just punishment: does the common people think it to be good? Boethius says: On the contrary, they judge it to be the most miserable of all things that can be imagined. It should be noted that all fortune is either for the exercising of the good and the correcting of the wicked, or it is for the rewarding of the good and the punishing of the wicked. The fortune which is for the exercising of the good and the correcting of the wicked is, in both cases, good, even according to the opinion of the common people. This, Philosophy proves: That which is useful is good. But the fortune which exercises good men is useful to the good, and that which corrects the wicked is useful to the wicked. Therefore, both are good. Furthermore, the fortune which exercises belongs to the good who wage war against vices. The fortune which corrects belongs to the wicked who turn toward virtues. However, the fortune which rewards the good is good even according to

---

the commoners. But that which punishes the wicked is the worst of all according to the commoners. And Philosophy touches upon this opinion of the common people regarding both types of fortune in the text. "Look then." Here, Philosophy concludes from the premises of the common people something unexpected and contrary to the common view: namely, that "bad fortune" belongs only to the wicked. This is despite the fact that the common people often think that bad fortune happens to the good. And she says: "Do you see that we, by following the opinion of the common people, have brought together—that is, concluded—something very unexpected among the common people?" "What is it?" says Boethius. For from these things which were granted according to common opinion, it follows that for those who are in the perfect possession of virtue, or in the progress toward it, or in the attainment of it: all fortune is good, whether it be prosperous or adverse. But for those remaining in wickedness, all—

# Book Four

->that fortune is the worst.<- And Boethius says: "It is true according to the common people, because no one would dare to confess according to the truth; for in the reality of the thing, all fortune is good, whether for the good or for the evil, as you have proven." <note>original: "omnis fortuna bona est"</note> It should be noted that all fortune is either **rewarding**, **exercising**, or **correcting**.
*   **Rewarding fortune** belongs to those who are in the possession of virtue.
*   **Exercising fortune** <note>meaning: fortune that tests or trains the soul</note> belongs to those who are making progress in virtue.
*   **Correcting fortune** belongs to those who are beginning to be virtuous.

From which it follows that for those who persist in wickedness, fortune is the worst. And this is true according to common opinions. Note that any fortune can be considered in two ways: in one way, in comparison to the **universal cause** <note>referring to God or Divine Providence</note> which rules and disposes all things, ordering each thing to an end suitable for them. In this way, all fortune is good, as has been proven. Or, fortune can be compared to the person to whom it happens; and in this way, only that is called "good" which confers some benefit to the one it reaches, and that is "bad" which confers nothing good. Therefore, he says: here Philosophy makes a certain exhortation.
Since all fortune is good, a wise man ought not to take it badly whenever he is led into a **contest with fortune**. <note>original: "certamen fortunae"</note> And it does not befit a brave man to be indignant—that is, to be disturbed—whenever the **warlike tumult**—that is, the noise of battle—sounds.

<column-break/>

we confer. **B**oethius: "What," I asked, "do you mean?"
**P**hilosophy: "From these things indeed," she said, "which have been granted, it follows that for those who are either in perfection, or in progress, or in the attainment of **Virtue**, all fortune, whatever it may be, is good; but for those remaining in wickedness, all fortune is the worst."
**B**oethius: "This," I said, "is true, even though no one dares to confess it."
**P**hilosophy: "Therefore," she said, "a wise man ought not to take it badly whenever he is brought into a contest of fortune, just as it does not befit a brave man to be indignant whenever the warlike tumult sounds. For to both of these, the difficulty itself is the very material: to the one, for the sake of spreading his glory; to the other, for the sake of confirming his wisdom.
For this reason is it called **Virtue** <note>The Latin 'virtus' shares a root with 'vir' (man/strength), implying manly strength or courage</note>: because, relying on its own strength, it is not overcome by adversity. For you who are placed in the progress of virtue have not come here to dissolve in delights or to wither away in pleasure. You must engage in a battle against every kind of fortune with great sharpness. Let neither sad fortune oppress you, nor pleasant fortune corrupt you; occupy the middle ground with firm strength."

---

For the very difficulty of fighting and resisting fortune is, for every brave and virtuous man, the material—that is, the cause—of spreading his glory. For warlike exercise is the cause of glory for a brave man. To the other—namely, the virtuous man—the resistance of fortune is the material, or the cause, of confirming wisdom—that is, virtue—from which victory such difficulty is called "virtue." For it is called virtue because, relying on its own strength, it is not overcome by adversities. And she adds: "For you, placed in progress—that is, on the path of virtue—have not come into the world to dissolve..."

It should be noted that virtue consists in the middle between two extreme vices, toward one of which prosperous fortune impels us, and toward the other, adverse fortune. For example: Adversity impels one toward despair and timidity; prosperity, however, impels one toward presumption and audacity. Between these consists the middle of virtue, the excess or defect of which is vicious. Philosophy hints at this in the text. Note that it is in a human's power to make fortune what they will, namely good or bad. Philosophy declares this regarding adverse fortune: because if we accept it with a good soul for the sake of exercise and correction, it is good. If, however, we endure it with a [bitter] soul even as a punishment, it is bad.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Five of Boethius's "The Consolation of Philosophy." It follows the conclusion of Book Four, where the discussion on the nature of good and evil and the governance of the world ended.</meta>

# Book Five

She had spoken, and was turning the course of her speech toward other matters to be treated and explained. Here begins the fifth book of Boethius on the consolation of philosophy, of which this is the first prose. In this section, Philosophy wishes to resolve certain doubts following her determination concerning fate and providence. For it seems from what has been said that "chance" does not exist; because if all things are foreseen so that nothing happens outside the order of divine providence, it seems that nothing happens by chance, since chance implies an unexpected event. Likewise, it seems from what has been said that free will does not exist; because all things are arranged according to the order of fatal necessity, and free will excludes necessity. It seems, therefore, if providence and fate are established, that free will is entirely excluded. Philosophy, therefore, in the present book, inquires whether chance exists and what it is, and inquires whether free will exists, setting forth arguments by which free will does not seem able to stand alongside divine providence.

<column-break/>

## Book Five, Prose One.

SHE HAD SPOKEN, and was turning the course of her speech to treat and explain certain other matters. **Boethius:** Then I said: "Your exhortation is indeed right and most worthy of your authority. But as to what you said a while ago—that the question of providence is entangled with many others—I am now experiencing this in reality. For I ask: do you judge that chance is anything at all, and if so, what is it?" **Philosophy:** Then she replied: "I hasten to fulfill the debt of my promise, and to show you the way by which you may be carried back to your homeland..."

<note>The "homeland" here is a metaphor for the state of spiritual peace and intellectual clarity.</note>

After this, she presents the false solution of certain people which she disapproves of, and provides her own solution which she confirms with reasons; she also determines the nature of eternity and many other things as will become clear. This book is divided into eleven parts: for there are six prose sections and five meters. These parts and what is determined in them will be clear in the progress of the book. In the first prose, she determines the nature of chance. First, Boethius touches upon the actions of Philosophy, commending the exhortation she made, and moves the question concerning chance. Second, Philosophy excuses herself from determining it, and Boethius removes that excuse. Third, Philosophy determines the nature of chance. The second part begins at "Then she: I hasten"; the third at "Then she: The custom." First, he says Philosophy "had spoken" these aforementioned things and "was turning the course of her speech" (that is, her discourse) to treat and explain certain other matters. Then I, Boethius, said: "O Philosophy, your exhortation is right and altogether most worthy of authority. But what you said a while ago in the sixth prose of the fourth book—that the question of providence was entangled with many other questions—I experience in reality. For I ask whether you judge chance to be anything at all in the nature of things, and what you judge chance to be in the nature of things." Note that by saying "she had spoken," Boethius implies that Philosophy had already explained those things pertaining to her speculation, and thus had determined the principal intention of this book. And Philosophy "was turning the course of her speech"—that is, her flowing discourse, for the speech of Philosophy was hindered neither by the ignorance of the teacher nor the slowness of the learner—she was turning this speech to treat certain other matters. What those matters were, Boethius does not express; perhaps because in his opinion they were less desirable, or perhaps they were extraneous to the current purpose.

# Book Five

If there is any [chance]. Because of this, Philosophy, in order to inquire whether chance exists or not, takes the definition of what is signified by the name and says: If some say that chance is a rash event produced without any cause, then I see that the word "chance" is empty, as if nothing in reality corresponds to it. **For who, while [God] constrains.** Here Philosophy disproves that opinion, showing that chance is nothing according to that definition. Secondly, she resolves the question according to the truth of the matter at the point: **My Aristotle.** <note>A reference to Aristotle's *Physics*, where he defines chance as an accidental cause.</note> First, she provides one argument. Second, another at: **For nothing.** The ancients used to say that chance is a "rash event," that is, unforeseen. Philosophy argues against this as follows: Wherever all things are foreseen, there is nothing rash; but all things that exist are foreseen by God; therefore, among the things that exist, nothing is rash. The text briefly hints at this reasoning, saying: **For what place can be left**—that is, abandoned—**to rashness**—that is, lack of foresight—**while God constrains all things into order**, namely, the foreseen order. It is as if she says: none.

<column-break/>

**And if one defines chance as being produced by no connection of causes, I confirm that chance is nothing at all, and I decree that the word is utterly empty beyond the signification of the subject matter. For what place can be left for rashness when God constrains all things in order? For it is a true sentiment that "nothing comes from nothing," which none of the ancients ever opposed, although they applied this not to the operating principle <note>The "operating principle" refers to God as the Creator who acts upon the world.</note> but to the material subject—that is, concerning the nature of all reasons. But if something should arise from no causes, it would seem to have arisen from nothing; if this cannot happen, then it is not possible for chance to be of the kind we defined a moment ago. Boethius.**

---

It should be noted that all things are foreseen by God; the reason for which is: Whatever things God is the cause of, all such things are foreseen by God. But God is the cause of every being; this is evident because the heavens and all of nature depend upon Him, as is clear from the twelfth book of the *Metaphysics*. <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, Book XII (Lambda), which discusses the Unmoved Mover.</note> **For it is a true sentiment that nothing comes from nothing, which no one, etc.** Here he provides another argument proving that chance cannot be produced without any cause, as the ancients said, and he argues thus: That which is from nothing, is nothing. But that which is from no cause is from nothing; therefore, that which is from nothing is nothing. But according to the ancients, chance is from no cause because it is produced without any connection of causes. Therefore, chance is nothing. Whence he says in the text: **It is a true sentiment which none of the ancients ever opposed**—that is, contradicted—namely, that nothing exists out of nothing. Although those ancients made that proposition—"nothing comes from nothing"—as a kind of foundation, they did not mean it regarding the operating principle, namely, regarding God the Creator, because He made something out of nothing. Rather, they understood this regarding the "natural subject," that is, regarding the whole of nature founded in matter. He explains himself saying: **This is concerning the nature of all reasons**—that is, concerning matter, which is the subject of natural forms. But if something arises from no causes, it seems to have arisen from nothing. But this cannot happen—that something arises from nothing. Therefore, it is not possible for chance to be of this sort—that is, such as we defined a moment ago according to the ancients—namely, that it is an event [without cause].

# First Prose

...rash without a connection of causes. What then should be said about chance? Boethius asks: Is there nothing in the nature of things that can rightly be called chance or a fortuitous event? Or is there something, even if it remains hidden from the common people <note>original: "vulgus"</note>, to which these names apply? It should be noted that this proposition—"nothing comes from nothing"—is true in relation to a **particular cause** which requires material for its action; however, in relation to a **universal cause** <note>The "universal cause" refers to God as the primary mover of all existence.</note> which is the cause of all being, it is not true. Hence we say that God created all things from nothing, and we hold this by faith. But the ancients did not speak of this mode of production through creation, but only of the first mode. Thus Aristotle says in the first book of the *Physics*: "It is impossible for anything to be made out of those things which do not exist." For in this opinion, all who perceive nature agree. First, she says "My Aristotle," meaning he who was nourished and instructed by my doctrine, defined chance in the *Physics* (specifically in the second book of the *Physics*) with a brief and near-true reasoning—that is, near to the truth.

**B.** "What then," I said, "Is there nothing which can rightly be called either chance or a fortuitous event? But it is not from nothing. For it has its own proper causes, whose unforeseen and unexpected meeting seems to have produced a 'chance' event. For unless the tiller of the field dug the ground, and unless the depositor had buried his money in that place, the gold would not have been found."

And Boethius asks: "In what way?" Philosophy says: Whenever something is carried out—that is, made—for the sake of some thing, and another thing happens due to certain causes other than what was intended, that is called chance. As if someone, for the purpose of tilling a field, digging the earth, finds a weight of buried gold; this finding of gold is believed to have happened fortuitously—that is, by chance. But such a casual event is not "from nothing"—that is, from no cause, as the definition of the ancients used to say. For a casual event has its own proper causes, whose unexpected and unforeseen meeting (unforeseen, that is, by the one who did something for the sake of another thing) will be seen to have worked the "chance." For unless the tiller of the field dug the earth (which digging is one cause of the finding of the gold) and unless the depositor had buried (that is, hidden) his money in that place (which is the other cause of the finding)...

# Book Five

->gold would not have been found.<- It should be noted that "chance," according to Aristotle <note>referring to Aristotle's *Physics*, Book II</note>, occurs when something is done for a specific purpose—such as digging a field for the purpose of sowing—but something else happens due to certain causes beyond what was intended. This is "chance," just as the discovery of a treasure is accidental because it was not intended by the digger of the field. From this, it is clear that the discovery of treasure is accidental not because it was unforeseen by God, but because it was unforeseen by man. Thus, chance is nothing in relation to God, but it is something in relation to man, occurring beyond his intention and foresight. These, therefore, are the things of chance. Here, Philosophy <note>The personification of Lady Philosophy in Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy*</note> shows that although chance has causes, it does not have "essential" causes <term>per se: causes that directly produce an effect by nature or intent</term>, but rather "accidental" causes <term>per accidens: incidental or secondary causes</term>. She says: These, therefore, are the causes of a fortuitous gain—that is, a chance event—because a fortuitous gain arises from causes that meet and flow together, not from the intention of the person acting. For neither the one who hid the gold nor the one who worked (that is, dug) the field intended for that money to be found; but, as I said, it happened beyond the intention of the actor that this man dug where the other had hidden the money, and so the discovery of the money occurred.

<column-break/>

### These, therefore, are the causes of fortuitous gain, which proceeds from causes meeting and flowing together, and not from the intention of the actor. For neither he who hid the gold, nor he who worked the field, intended that the money should be found; but, as I said, it happened by coincidence that where one hid it, the other dug. We may therefore define chance as an unexpected event resulting from converging causes in those things which are done for some purpose. Moreover, that which makes the causes meet and flow together is that Order, proceeding with an inevitable connection, which, descending from the fountain of Providence, disposes all things in their proper places and times.

---

It should be noted that an efficient cause <term>causa efficiens: the agent or force that brings something into being</term> does not act unless it is moved by a goal. However, a goal only moves the actor insofar as it exists in their intention. Therefore, regarding the effect that is intended, the agent is an "essential" cause; but if something happens during the action beyond the agent's intention, the agent is an "accidental" cause. Thus, because chance happens beyond the intention of the agent, it does not have an essential acting cause, but an accidental one. *We may therefore define.* Here, Philosophy solves the second question by showing what chance is. She concludes its definition from what has already been said, saying: We may therefore define chance as an unexpected event from converging causes in those things which are performed for some other purpose. Then she shows how a chance effect falls under the order of Providence. For it was said that chance arises from converging causes; however, the fact that causes converge arises from the order of Providence. Whence she says: That which makes the causes concur and flow together is that Order—namely, the order of Fate—proceeding with an inevitable connection of causes, which (this Order) descending from the fountain of Providence, disposes all things in their own times and places. It should be noted that this definition of chance is good because it distinguishes chance from other things. By saying "chance is an unexpected event," we exclude effects that happen by necessity or frequently—such as the sun rising or a human being born with five fingers on one hand. Such things do not happen by chance or unexpectedly. By saying "from converging causes"...

It uses the classic Aristotelian example of a farmer finding buried treasure to illustrate that while an event may be accidental to a human, it is part of a divine order.</summary>

# First Meter

The definition of chance is concluded, which was said in the first way to be produced—according to the ancients—from no connection of causes. However, by saying that in these things which are done, they are directed toward something else, "chance-ness" <note>original: *casualitas*</note> in itself is excluded from chance. For chance and fortune are accidental causes and are outside the intention of the agent.

->The first meter of the fifth book.<-

### The first meter of the fifth book.

<margin>
**From the crags of the Achaemenian cliff** This is the first meter of this fifth book, which is called an elegiac meter. The first line is dactylic hexameter; the second is trochaic pentameter or dactylic pentameter. In this, Philosophy shows how a chance event relates to divine providence. The subject matter of the example is that the Tigris and Euphrates are two rivers proceeding from the same source, which afterwards are divided from one another, and if they should meet again
</margin>

**From the crags of the Achaemenian cliff**
**Where the retreating battle fixes turned arrows**
**In the breasts of those following;**
**The Tigris and Euphrates release themselves from one source**
**And soon are separated by disconnected waters:**
**If they should meet in their course and be called back again into one,**
**That which the wave of each channel draws must flow together.**
**Ships and trunks torn by the river would meet,**
**And the mingled water entangles these chance occurrences.**

it is necessary that ships and other things carried by those rivers meet; this meeting happens insofar as they are governed by the downward flow of those rivers, and yet it is outside the intention of those who steer the ships. In the same way, the meeting of chance causes, although it is outside the intention of the agents themselves, nevertheless they meet according to the downward flow of the fatal order resulting from the governance of divine providence. And although to us, who are ignorant of the order of divine providence, something may seem like chance or fortune, nevertheless in comparison to God, all things are ordered and foreseen. Whence it says in the text: The Tigris and Euphrates release themselves from one source from the <term>crags</term> <note>original: *scopulis*, meaning rocky peaks or hollows</note>, that is, the hollows of the Achaemenian cliff, that is, a mountain of Parthia <note>Achaemenia refers to the Persian Empire; the commentator identifies this with Parthia</note> where indeed in Parthia the <term>retreating battle</term> <note>original: *fugax pugna*</note> fixes turned arrows, that is, darts, in the breasts of those following. For it is the custom of the Parthians that they fight by fleeing, shooting arrows backward against those pursuing. And "soon," that is, after a small space, the Tigris and Euphrates are separated by "disconnected waters," supply: by other waters; and if the said rivers meet again, that is, come together, and the course is called back into one, it "flows together," that is, it must flow together, that which the wave of "each channel," that is, of both rivers, "draws," that is, leads with it. And "ships" <note>original: *pupes*, literally the sterns of ships</note> and "trunks torn," that is, uprooted by the river, will meet; and the "mingled" water, that is, the flowing together, "entangles," that is, will entangle "chance occurrences" <note>original: *fortuitos modos*</note> because the wave will make the ships and trunks meet by chance. Yet "the slopes of the earth" themselves—that is, the depression of the earth giving a path to the rivers—and the "downward order of the gliding whirlpool"—that is, of the running water—govern those "wandering chances," that is, the chance events. And so it is regarding a chance event in respect to providence. Whence it says <term>chance</term> <note>original: *fors*</note>, that is, chance or fortune, which seems to float with "loosened reins," that is, without governance, "endures the bit," that is, governance, and "moves," that is, passes through, by the "law itself," that is, through the law of divine providence. <insert>Note what is written in Genesis: The Tigris and Euphrates are rivers whose source is in Paradise. # Second Prose

Therefore, in those beings in whom reason exists, there is also the freedom of willing and not willing. Thus, the argument can be formed in this way:
Everything that can use reason possesses the judgment to recognize what should be avoided and what should be desired. But what anyone judges to be desirable, they pursue; and what they judge should be avoided, they flee from. Therefore, everything that can use reason possesses the freedom of willing and not willing. It should be noted that he says that which uses reason has a judgment by which it may discern each thing. He says this to distinguish it from natural judgment—

**But what anyone judges to be desirable,**
**they seek; but they flee from what they estimate**
**should be avoided. Wherefore, in those in whom**
**reason exists, there is also the freedom of**
**willing and refusing. But I do not establish**
**this freedom to be equal in all beings.**
**For in the celestial and divine substances,**
**there is both a clear-sighted judgment and**
**an incorruptible will, and an effective power**
**to achieve what is desired is ever present.**
**Human souls, however, must necessarily be**
**more free when they preserve themselves in**
**the contemplation of the divine mind; but**
**less so when they slip down into bodies,**
**and even less when they are bound by**
**earthly limbs. But the extreme state is**
**slavery, when, having surrendered to vices,**
**they have fallen from the possession of**
**their own reason. For when from the highest—**

<column-break/>

—which is found in brute animals <note>original: "brutis," referring to non-human animals lacking rational souls</note>, by which each thing to be done is not judged [universally], but only some particular thing. For example, a sheep does not judge regarding everything that should be avoided, but only regarding the wolf. And bees do not have the industry to perform any work except for honeycombs. But the judgment of reason concerns anything that is done. It should be noted that he says one possessing the judgment of reason judges by themselves what is to be pursued or avoided. For although brute animals in a certain way "know" things to be avoided or pursued, they do not do so by themselves, because they are not the cause of the judgment. Man, however, not only knows the end and the things ordered toward the end, but knows universally by way of comparison and by way of a syl-

logism; furthermore, man judges and discerns his own judgment, because the intellect is a power turned back upon itself. *But this [freedom] is not in all.* Here Philosophy shows how free will <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity of a rational agent to choose between different possible courses of action</term> is diversified in different beings, namely in angels and men, saying: I do not establish this freedom of choice to be equal in all. For it is greater in divine substances than in men. For in celestial and divine substances there is "clear-sighted judgment," that is, infallible judgment; and there is in them an "incorruptible will," that is, inflexible toward evil; and there is "at hand," that is, ready, an "effective power" of things desired, because there is no hindrance to their execution. Human souls, however, must be more free when they keep themselves in the contemplation of the divine mind; but they are less free when they "slip down into bodies," that is, into the care of temporal things. And they are even less free when they are "bound by earthly limbs," that is, by affections through which they are less able to resist rising passions. "Extreme," that is, the greatest, is the "slavery" of souls when, given over to vices, they have fallen from the possession of their own reason, by which they ought to be ruled, that is, directed in acting. For when—that is, after—souls have cast down the eyes of reason and intellect from the light of the highest truth to lower and dark things—that is, to earthly and fleshly things—they are soon "blinded," that is, obscured by a "cloud of ignorance" <note>original: "nube nescicie"</note> and are disturbed by "destructive affections," that is, by passions to which they yield.

# Book Five

By selling themselves and consenting, they assist—that is, they increase—the servitude which they have brought upon themselves—that is, introduced—and the souls of the wicked are, in a certain way, captive by their own liberty. It should be noted that **free will** <note>Latin: *liberum arbitrium*</note> is the freedom of judging and executing matters. Or, according to Boethius in his commentary on the first book of *On Interpretation* <note>Latin: *Perihermeneias*, a work by Aristotle commented on by Boethius</note>, free will is the judgment of the mind concerning the will, with no external force either violently compelling or violently hindering it. No one compels one to do what dis-

pleases, and no one hinders one from doing what pleases. It should be noted that free will consists of two things: the freedom of judging and the freedom of executing what has been judged. The first, namely the freedom of judging, is hindered by ignorance; but the freedom of executing is hindered by the inability to perform and the corruption of the will. For sometimes we are able to accomplish good, yet because the will is corrupted by vice, we do not accomplish it. However, in separate substances <note>referring to angels or pure celestial intelligences</note> there is neither ignorance of judgment, nor in-

### When they have cast themselves down from the light of the highest Truth to lower and dark things, they are soon clouded by a mist of ignorance and disturbed by ruinous affections.
### By approaching and consenting to these, they assist the servitude they have brought upon themselves, and are in a certain way captive by their own liberty. Nevertheless, He, looking forth upon all things from eternity, sees with the gaze of His providence <gloss>He sees and hears all things</gloss> and disposes all things predestined according to their merits.

For the Intelligences are deceived in nothing; therefore they have a piercing judgment and never will anything but the good. Therefore, an incorruptible will is in them, and they can perform whatever they desire. Therefore, in them is the effective power of their wishes. It should be noted that some have said it was the intention of **Plato** that human souls were created together in heaven and afterwards descend into bodies and are held in them as if in chains. According to those thinkers, the degrees of freedom of human souls which he <note>Boethius</note> sets down in the text are distinguished thus: namely, that souls, since they are created in heaven, are most free in the contemplation of the divine mind. However, when they are already bound to bodies, they are still less free. But the least freedom is in them when they are subjected to vices. This exposition, however, does not hold according to the truth <note>likely a reference to the orthodox Christian view rejecting the pre-existence of souls</note>. Therefore, it is explained otherwise: that those souls must be freer which serve divine contemplation, such as the souls of the virtuous and contemplative whose "conversation is in heaven." Those, however, are less free which slip away toward bodies—that is, which descend to the care of temporal things, such as practical men who busy themselves with temporal goods to be dispensed for the common utility. Still less free are the souls bound to earthly limbs—that is, those who descend to caring for their own body and their own utility. But the least free are those who, subjected to vices, lose their reason. For a wicked man is the servant not of only one master, but of as many masters as he has vices, according to **Saint Augustine**. *Nevertheless, He...* Here Philosophy shows how the acts of free will fall under divine providence; because, for this reason, the divine knowledge extends to all things, saying...

# Second Meter

All these things said regarding the various degrees of liberty and regarding all acts proceeding from them are discerned by that gaze of divine providence, looking forth upon all things; and it disposes each predestined thing by rendering to its merits: good things to the good and evil things to the evil. And this is confirmed by Greek authority <note>likely a reference to Homer or the Orphic hymns</note> which sounds in Latin as: *God sees all and hears all.* Or according to others it sounds: *God illuminates all things more brightly than the sun.*

<column-break/>

### The Second Meter of the Fifth Book.

**Homer of the honey-sweet mouth sings**
**Of Phoebus <note>The sun god, Apollo</note> clear with pure light**
**Who yet is not strong enough to break through**
**To the innermost depths of the earth or the sea**
**With the weak light of his rays.**
**Not so is the Creator of the great world**
**To Him who looks upon all things from on high:**
**No mass of earth resists Him**
**Night does not obstruct Him with black clouds**
**What things are, what they were, and what may come**
**He discerns in a single stroke of the mind**
**Whom, because He alone beholds all things,**
**You might truly call the Sun.**

From the predominant foot <note>a technical term in poetic meter</note>. In this, Philosophy commends the excellence of divine knowledge in comparison to the material sun, saying: Homer of the honey-sweet mouth (that is, of sweet eloquence) sings (that is, describes) Phoebus (that is, the sun) clear with pure light. For perhaps Homer wrote a book concerning the brightness of the sun—which sun, namely, is not strong enough to break through (that is, penetrate) the innermost depths (that is, the deep parts) of the earth and the sea (that is, the ocean) with the weak (that is, feeble) light of its rays. Not so (that is, it is not thus) with the Creator of the great world, namely God. But He, by His knowledge, penetrates all things since nothing can be hidden from Him. To this Creator, looking upon (that is, beholding) all things from the high heaven, the earth resists Him with no mass (that is, magnitude), just as they stand in the way of the sun's rays. Nor does dark night obstruct Him with black clouds. Rather, in one stroke of the mind (that is, in a single mental gaze) He discerns what things are (regarding the present), what they were (regarding the past), and what are coming (regarding the future). Because this Creator alone beholds all things, you are able to call Him the True Sun.

<column-break/>

It should be noted that although divine providence has looked forth upon all things from eternity, free will is not necessitated because of this to do good or evil. Because according to Aristotle in the third book of the *Ethics*: "Man is the master of his own operations from the beginning until the end." And therefore, according to the merits of the operations of free will, he receives punishment or reward.

### Second Meter
### of the Fifth Book.

->Of Phoebus clear with<-
->pure light.<-

This is the second meter of this fifth book, which is called Archilochian <note>named after the Greek poet Archilochus</note> from its inventor. It is dactylic <note>a poetic rhythm consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones</note>.

<column-break/>

It should be noted that although God, by knowing all things, provides even for those things which happen by free will: He nevertheless willed certain creatures to be of free will. Because this more greatly becomes the divine goodness. For just as a kingdom is better and more noble in which the king is served not only by slaves but also by free men, rather than where he is served only by slaves; so the kingdom of God will be better and more fitting because there are some creatures who are free.

### Prose Three of the Fifth Book.

Then I said, "Behold." Here begins the third prose of this fifth book, in which Boethius objects to the preceding statements, showing that providence and free choice cannot exist together. First, he premises that the statements may hold doubt; second, he sets forth the reasons for the doubt at the phrase "Too much, I say." First, he says: "Then" (meaning at that time), "I," Boethius, "said: 'O Philosophy, I am again confused by a more difficult ambiguity.'" And Philosophy asks, "What is that ambiguity? For I already conjecture" (that is, I judge) "by what things you are troubled" (that is, you are being disturbed). It should be noted that "to conjecture" is to think something based on certain signs. Thus, Philosophy conjectures Boethius's doubt through the "common accidents" <note>A logical term referring to circumstances that usually accompany a situation.</note> because commonly, whoever spoke of providence and free choice doubted their compatibility. "Too much, I say": here Boethius expresses his doubt, showing that providence and free choice are incompatible. First, he does this. Second, he excludes certain ways by which some attempted to defend providence at the phrase "What therefore." To prove the incompatibility of the aforesaid, he posits three reasons. The second is at "To these things." The third is at "Finally." First, he posits the first reason. Second, he excludes a certain solution to it at "For neither [can] any other deed." First, he says: It seems to oppose and conflict "too much" that God foreknows all things and that there is any freedom of choice. He proves that these conflict: For if God foresees all things and cannot be deceived in any way, it is necessary that that which providence has foreseen to be in the future must happen; for if it did not happen, providence would be deceived. Therefore, if from eternity He foreknows not only the deeds of men but even their counsels and wills, there will be no freedom of choice, but all things would happen by necessity. Furthermore, he declares that God foreknows all things by His providence. For no deed or any will could exist except that which He sensed beforehand (that is, foreknew)...

<column-break/>

### Prose Three of the Fifth Book.

**T**hen I said, "Behold, I am again confused by a more difficult ambiguity." **P**hilosophy: "What is that?" she said. "For I already conjecture by what things you are troubled." **B**oethius: "It seems to oppose and conflict too much," I said, "that God foreknows all things and that there is any freedom of choice. For if God foresees all things and cannot be deceived in any way, it is necessary that that which providence has foreseen to be in the future must happen. Therefore, if from eternity He foreknows not only the deeds of men but even their counsels and wills, there will be no freedom of choice. For neither can any other deed or any will whatever exist, except that which the divine providence, which is incapable of being mistaken, has sensed beforehand. For if [things were to happen] otherwise than foreseen..."

<summary>Boethius presents the classic "problem of prescience," arguing that if God foreknows all human thoughts and actions with certainty, then human free will must be an illusion, as all events would occur by necessity.</summary>

# Third Prose

If divine providence has known something, it is unaware <note>original: "nescia" - here meaning it cannot be mistaken or ignorant</note> of error; that is, it is not possible for it to be deceived, nor can things happen otherwise than as they have been foreseen. For if they were able to be turned aside in another direction <note>original: "detorqueri"</note>—namely, so that they happen differently than they were foreseen—then the foreknowledge of God would no longer be firm, but would instead be an uncertain opinion; which I judge to be a wicked thing <note>original: "nephas"</note> to believe concerning God. It should be noted that through the text, the logic is formed thus: Those things which are foreseen happen infallibly by necessity. But all things are foreseen by God infallibly. Therefore,

They are able to be turned aside. Foreknowledge of the future will no longer be firm, but rather an uncertain opinion, which I judge a wicked thing to believe of God. For I do not approve of that reasoning by which some believe they can loosen this knotty question. For they say that a thing is not going to happen because providence has foreseen it as a future event, but rather the opposite: because a thing is going to happen, it cannot be hidden from divine providence. And in that way, it is necessary for this to fall back into the opposite side. For it is not necessary that the things which are foreseen must happen, but it is necessary that the things which are going to happen must be foreseen. As if, indeed, the question were which thing is the cause of the other: whether foreknowledge is the cause of the necessity of future events, or whether the necessity of future events is the cause of foreknowledge.

<column-break/>

all things happen by necessity, and thus the freedom of choice <term>libertas arbitrii: the capacity of a human being to choose between different possible courses of action</term> perishes. It should be noted that the knowledge of God is not "opinion," because opinion concerns those things which can be one way or another <note>referencing Aristotle's Posterior Analytics</note>. Knowledge, however, concerns those things which cannot be otherwise. Therefore, the knowledge of God must not be called opinion. **For I do not approve of that reasoning.** Here, Philosophy <note>The personification of Philosophy in Boethius's dialogue</note> excludes a certain response that could be given to the aforementioned reasoning. First, she presents it; second, she excludes it at the phrase "As if, indeed." First, she says: "For I do not approve"—that is, I do not endorse—that reasoning—that is, the response—by which some believe they can resolve the difficulty of the question. For they say not therefore

---

is a thing going to come, but rather the reverse: because what is going to happen cannot be hidden from divine providence. It is as if one said the outcome of the thing is the cause of the foreknowledge, and not the other way around; and therefore, from the outcome, the necessity of foreknowledge ought to be concluded, not the reverse, according to them. And in this way, it is necessary that what is concluded regarding the outcome falls back into the opposite part—namely, that what is concluded about the outcome should conclude this about the presence of knowledge. For it is not necessary to join the things that are foreseen (according to them), but it is necessary that the things which are future must be foreseen. It should be noted that the prior reasoning claimed that all future things happen by necessity because God perceives future things infallibly. The response of certain people, however, says the opposite. For it says: it is not because God foresees them that future things necessarily happen, but because they are future, God foresees them. **As if, indeed, which thing is the cause of the other.** Here she excludes that response, saying: This response proceeds as if the labor consisted of asking which thing is the cause of the other—whether foreknowledge is the cause of the necessity of future events, or whether the necessity of future events is the cause of providence. But we strive—that is, we labor—to demonstrate this: namely, that the outcome of things foreknown is necessary, in whatever way <note>original: "quoque modo"</note>—that is, in whatever manner it holds itself to be.

# Book Five

The order of causes. Even if, for the sake of the gods, foreknowledge does not seem to impose a necessity of happening upon future things: which he declares by an example, saying: If someone sits, it is necessary that the opinion which conjectures that he sits be true; and conversely, if the opinion about someone is true that he sits, it is necessary that he sit. Therefore, in both—namely, in the opinion and in the sitter—there is necessity; in the latter, namely in the sitter, there is the necessity of sitting; in the other, namely in the opinion, there is the necessity of truth. But no one sits for that reason <insert>add: by chance</insert> because the opinion is true, since the truth of the opinion is not the cause of the sitting; but rather this opinion is true because someone sitting preceded it: and so the cause of truth proceeds from the other side, yet in both there is a common necessity. And in the same way, it happens to argue concerning providence and concerning those things which are foreseen. Whence he says it is evident, that is, it is manifest to reason concerning providence and concerning future things. Especially if something is foreseen for the reason that it is future, yet it does not happen simply because it is foreseen; nevertheless, it is necessary either that things to come be foreseen by God, or that things foreseen happen, so that in both parts there is a necessity, even if in one there is <term>casualitas</term> <note>original: "casualitas" - here referring to the accidental or contingent nature of the event itself</note>. This alone is enough, that is, it suffices to suppress the freedom of choice.

<column-break/>

the necessity of future things should be labored as the cause of providence. And let us not strive to demonstrate that in whatever way the order of causes holds itself. It is necessary that the event of things foreknown occurs, even if foreknowledge does not seem to impose a necessity of happening upon future things. For indeed, if someone sits, it is necessary that the opinion which projects that he sits be true. And conversely, if the opinion about someone is true because he sits, it is necessary that he sit. In both, therefore, necessity is present. In this one, indeed, to the sitter; but in the other, to the truth. But no one sits for the reason that the opinion is true, but rather this is true because someone sitting preceded it. Thus, since the cause of truth proceeds from the other side, a common necessity is nevertheless present in both. It is evident that similar things are reasoned concerning providence and similar matters. For even if they are foreseen because they are future, and do not happen because they are foreseen, it is nevertheless necessary either that things to come be foreseen by God, or that things foreseen happen, which alone is enough to suppress the freedom of choice.

---

It should be noted that this response which he introduces in the text seems to have been that of **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who wrote extensively on free will</note> in his commentary on the *Epistle to the Romans*. He says: "A thing will not be because God knows it is future, but because it is future, it is therefore known by God before it happens." This, however, can be understood in two ways. In one way, that the event of the thing is the cause of foreknowledge according to the logic of consequence, and thus the response is true. In another way, it can be understood that the event of the thing is the cause of foreknowledge according to existence; and in this way it is false, and in this way it is disproved here by **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose work "The Consolation of Philosophy" is being discussed here</note>. First, therefore, Boethius shows that this response is not to the purpose. Second, he shows that it does not include the truth. [There...]

# Third Prose

Now indeed, how preposterous it is. Here philosophy shows that this response includes a falsehood because it posits that something temporal could be the cause of the eternal. For they say that future things are the cause of eternal providence. Whence he says: *Now indeed it is preposterous*, that is, it is perverse, that the outcome of temporal things should be said to be the cause of eternal foreknowledge, which is what is claimed in that response. Whence he adds: *What else is it but to think that God provides for things for this reason...*

**Now indeed, how preposterous it is that the outcome of temporal things should be said to be the cause of eternal foreknowledge. What else is it, moreover, but to think that God foresees future things because they are going to happen, than to think that those things which happened long ago are the cause of that highest providence? To this, just as when I know something is, it is necessary that it be so; likewise, when I know something will be, it is necessary that it will be so. Thus it happens, therefore, that the outcome of a foreknown thing cannot be avoided. Finally, if someone thinks something is otherwise than the thing actually is, that is not only not knowledge, but it is a deceptive opinion far removed from the truth of knowledge. Therefore, if something is to happen in such a way that its outcome is not certain and necessary, how can it be foreknown that it will happen? For just as knowledge itself is unmixed with falsehood, so that which is conceived by it cannot be otherwise than as it is conceived.**

<column-break/>

...future things because they are going to come, than to think that those things which happened long ago—that is, the future things themselves—are the cause of the highest providence. <note>The author is arguing against the idea that human actions "cause" God to know them, as that would make the eternal God dependent on time.</note> As if to say: it is nothing else. It must be noted that no temporal thing is the cause of the eternal, but rather the reverse. For the less worthy is not the cause of the more worthy, because a cause is more worthy than its effect; however, the temporal is less worthy than the eternal, just as the corruptible is less worthy than the incorruptible. Therefore, the point stands. *To this, just as when I know something is.* Here he posits a second response to prove the second conclusion, saying: *to this*—supply "to the aforementioned things"—this reasoning must be added: just as when I know something is, it is necessary that it be so, likewise when I have known something is future, it is necessary that it will be so. Thus it happens, therefore—that is, it results—that the outcome of a foreknown thing cannot be avoided.

---

Note that the argument can be formed thus: as knowledge stands in respect to a present thing known, so foreknowledge stands in respect to a future effect. But when I know in the present that something is, it is necessary that it be so. Therefore, when something is foreknown to be in the future, it is necessary that it will be so. But God foreknows all future things; therefore they happen by necessity, and thus again the freedom of choice <term>libertas arbitrij: the capacity of the human will to choose freely</term> is taken away. *Finally, if someone.* Here he posits a third argument for the same point, saying: If anyone should think something is *otherwise*—that is, different than the thing actually is—that is not only—that is, not merely—not knowledge, but it is a deceptive opinion far removed from the truth of knowledge. Therefore, if something is to happen in such a way that its outcome is not certain and necessary, how can it be foreknown that it will happen? As if to say: in no way. He assigns the reason for this, saying: Just as knowledge itself is unmixed with falsehood, so that which is conceived by it cannot be otherwise than it is conceived. Because if it could be otherwise, then knowledge could be false.

It specifically refutes the idea that temporal events could cause God's eternal knowledge, asserting that the eternal must always be the cause of the temporal.</summary>

# Book Five

From this, it follows that this is the reason why knowledge is free from falsehood: because it is necessary for each thing to be exactly as knowledge perceives it to be. It should be noted that the reasoning intended here is this: whoever thinks a thing is otherwise than it is, their estimation is false; it is not knowledge, but a deceptive opinion. Therefore, if God foreknows that something will happen in the future, and if that thing does not necessarily happen exactly as He foreknew it, then God’s foreknowledge would not be knowledge, but a deceptive opinion. Consequently, future events foreseen by God must happen by necessity, and thus free will <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity of the human will to choose between different possible courses of action</term> is destroyed. What then? Here, Philosophy <note>referring to Lady Philosophy, the personified guide in Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy</note> rejects the methods by which some strive to save the concept of providence. First, she asks how divine providence can be saved while disproving two ways in which some have attempted to save it. Second, she presents a third way, likewise disproving it (beginning at the phrase "But if in the view of..."). First, she says: what then shall we say? In what way can it be said that God foreknows these uncertain future events? The first way is to say that God judges those things which He provides for infallibly, even though they might not happen. But that is improper, because then His providence would be deceived. Whence she says: For if God judges—

<column-break/>

## For that is the cause why knowledge is free from falsehood: because it is necessary for each thing to be exactly as knowledge perceives it to be. What then? In what way does God foreknow these uncertain future events? For if He judges that things will inevitably come to pass which are also possible not to happen, He is deceived—which is not only a wicked thing to believe, but even to speak aloud. But if He decrees that they will be in the future just as they are, so that He knows they are equally able to happen or not to happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this, which grasps nothing certain, nothing stable? Or how does this differ from that ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias: "Whatever I say will either be or will not be"? In what way would divine providence excel human opinion if, like men, it judges as uncertain those things whose outcome is uncertain?

---

—judges, that is, that things will happen infallibly which are also possible not to happen, then God (it follows) is deceived; which is not only—that is, not merely—wicked to think concerning God, but also wicked to utter with the voice. The second way is to say that God provides for future things indeterminately, just as they are future. But in this way, God's providence is not certain. Whence she says: If God discerns that these future things which are provided for are indeterminate, just as they are—so that, namely, He knows them to be equally—that is, in an equal manner—able to happen or not to happen, what is this foreknowledge which grasps nothing certain, nothing stable? (As if to say: such providence is nothing at all). And how does this foreknowledge differ from that other ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias, who used to say, "Whatever I say, this will be or will not be"? In what way—that is, in what respect—would divine providence excel—that is, prevail over—human opinion, if it judges uncertain things just as men do, whose outcomes are uncertain? (As if to say: it differs in nothing). It should be noted that when Tiresias <note>A famous blind prophet of Apollo in Thebes, known for being transformed into a woman for seven years.</note> had seen two snakes mating, he separated them by throwing a staff and was changed into a woman. After seven years, seeing the snakes mating again, he separated them with a staff and was changed back into a man.

### Third Prose

When a disagreement arose between Jupiter and Juno as to whether the pleasure in sexual intercourse was greater for the man or the woman, Tiresias was chosen as the judge because he had experienced the lot of both sexes. When he stated that the pleasure of the woman was greater, Juno, being moved to anger, blinded him. Jupiter, however, taking pity on him, gave him the spirit of prophecy in compensation for his lost sight. Yet his prophecy was such that "whatever I say will either be or will not be." <note>This refers to the mythological figure Tiresias, whose "prophecy" here is a logical tautology, highlighting the difference between vague human prediction and certain divine foreknowledge.</note>

---

**But if, at that most certain fountain of all things, nothing can be uncertain, then the outcome of those things which He has firmly foreknown as future is certain. Therefore, there is no freedom for human counsels and actions, which the divine mind—foreseeing all things without the error of falsehood—binds and constrains to a single outcome. Once this is accepted, it is clear how great a collapse of human affairs follows. For in vain are rewards or punishments proposed for the good and the bad, which no free and voluntary movement of minds has deserved.**

<column-break/>

If, therefore, God did not foreknow future indeterminate things otherwise than that they "will be or will not be," His foreknowledge would not differ from the foreknowledge of Tiresias, which is ridiculous. **But if, at that...** Here the author posits the third way of those attempting to save the concept of providence. And it is this: that we should suppose all things to happen by necessity and take away free will. First, therefore, he sets forth this method. Second, he shows what inconveniences follow from it, at the point: **Once this...** First, then, he concludes this method, saying: **But if...**

---

at that most certain fountain of all things, nothing can be uncertain, the outcome of those things which He Himself has firmly foreknown as future is certain. Therefore, there will be no freedom for human counsels and actions, which the divine mind—foreseeing all things without the error of falsehood—binds and constrains to a single outcome.

<margin>It should be noted that no change falls upon the fountain of all things <note>original: "fontem omnium rerum," referring to God</note> because His knowledge cannot be uncertain. Even if it were uncertain, it would be imperfect and [not] divine. If, therefore, it is certain with respect to future things, it is necessary that all future things foreknown by God happen by necessity.</margin>

**Once this is accepted.** Here he posits the inconveniences that follow if free will is taken away. And first, he shows what inconveniences follow on the part of men; second, those on the part of God; third, those on the part of the union of men to God. The second begins at: **Than which nothing...**; the third at: **Therefore, neither of hoping...** The inconveniences on the part of men, if there is no free will, are that rewards or punishments are proposed to men in vain, and the wicked are punished and the good rewarded unjustly; nor will there be vices or virtues in men, just as there are none in other things that act by the necessity of nature and not by the liberty of the soul. Whence he says: **Once this is posited**—namely, that free will is denied—**it is clear**, that is, it is manifest, **how great a collapse**, that is, how much destruction of human affairs follows. For rewards are proposed to the good and punishments to the bad in vain: thus human statutes and laws will be useless, which establish punishments and rewards that no free and voluntary movement of minds has deserved. And that will seem the most iniquitous of all which is now judged most equitable: namely, that the wicked are punished and the upright rewarded, whom their own will does not send toward the one or the other—that is, toward uprightness or wickedness.

# Book Five

->The cause of the difficulty is that the movement—that is, the act—of human reason cannot be applied to the simplicity of divine providence. It should be noted that the question concerning divine providence and free will is the most difficult of all questions, about which many of the ancients doubted, and not a few moderns have fallen into error because of its difficulty. **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in his book *On Divination*, treating this and being unable to resolve its difficulty, utterly denied providence and the foreknowledge of future events by God in the aforementioned book. **I ask, therefore.** Here, **Philosophy** <note>The personification of Lady Philosophy</note> approaches the solution to the question. First, she discusses the motives of **Boethius**. Second, she solves the doubts or the question itself at the point beginning "Since therefore." Regarding the first, it should be known that there were two principal motives for Boethius concerning this question. First, because it seems necessary that if God foresees future things, they must happen by necessity. The second motive is that future things whose outcome is uncertain—such as contingent future events—cannot be certainly foreseen by God. First, therefore, she treats the first motive. If, therefore, foreknowledge adds no necessity to future things—which you yourself admitted a little while ago—what is the reason that the voluntary outcomes of things are forced into a certain event?

# Fourth Prose

It seems to have been sufficiently shown that causality over future events does not exist, because those things which proceed from free will are not necessary. First, therefore, he sets forth this response by resuming his solution, saying: "For I ask why you think the reasoning of those who solve this is less effective, who think that the freedom of choice is not hindered by foreknowledge because they estimate that foreknowledge is not the cause of necessity in future things." <note>The author is analyzing the argument that knowing something will happen doesn't force it to happen.</note>

**"Indeed, for the sake of the position, so that you may perceive what follows, let us suppose there is no foreknowledge. Therefore, as far as this pertains, are those things which happen from free choice compelled to necessity?" Boethius: "Not at all." Philosophy: "Let us suppose again that it exists, but enjoins no necessity on things; there will remain, as I think, that same intact and absolute liberty of the will. But foreknowledge, you will say, although it is not the cause of the necessity of future events happening, is nevertheless a sign that they are necessarily going to come. Therefore, even if there had been no foreknowledge, it would be certain that the outcomes of future things were necessary. For every sign only shows what is; it does not actually effect what it designates. Wherefore it must first be demonstrated that nothing happens out of necessity, so that foreknowledge [might be seen as a sign of this necessity]."**

<column-break/>

The inference of the necessity of future things is hindered, as is evident from this: that you do not draw any argument for the necessity of future things except that those things which are foreknown cannot not happen. If, therefore, fore-notion—that is, the foreknowledge of future things—imposes no necessity on future things, as the response says and as you also admitted a little while ago, what is it—that is, what could it be—by which voluntary outcomes are compelled to a fixed event? And so, through this response, the necessity of future things is excluded. And he manifests this in an example, saying: "So that you may perceive what follows for the sake of the position"—that is, for the sake of an example—"let us suppose"—that is, let us posit as an impossibility—"that there is no foreknowledge of later things." Therefore, this being posited, as far as this—that is, as far

---

as that inference by which the necessity of future things is concluded from foreknowledge—would those things which come from choice be compelled to necessity? Boethius says: "Not at all." And Philosophy says: "Let us suppose again that there is providence <note>original: "providentia"</note>, but that it enjoins nothing necessary on future things; there will remain, as I think, the same liberty of the will, intact and absolute from all necessity." It should be noted that the prior solution was rejected as being both good and bad. It was good in this: that it posited that foreknowledge is not the cause of the necessity of future things; for it said, "Future things happen not because God foresees them." But it was bad in this: because it posited that future things are the cause of God's foreknowledge; for it said, "Because things are future, therefore God foresees them." <note>The commentator is distinguishing between God's knowledge causing events (which would destroy free will) and events causing God's knowledge (which would make God dependent on time).</note> It is clear, therefore, from the response of the ancients, that foreknowledge is not the cause of necessity for future things.
