# Book Five

If it were established that the outcomes of the future are of necessity—that is, that the events of the future are necessary even if there were no foreknowledge—this is proven from the nature of a sign, saying: For every sign only shows what a thing is, that is, it manifests that of which it is a sign, but it does not cause what it indicates. <note>The author is distinguishing between a sign (which points to a reality) and a cause (which creates a reality).</note> Wherefore, if foreknowledge—that is, providence—appears to be a sign of the necessity of future things, it would first have to be demonstrated that nothing happens except by necessity—that is, that all things happen necessarily. Otherwise, if this necessity of the future

is nothing, then that foreknowledge could not be a sign of a thing that does not exist. And so, it is not valid to argue for the necessity of future things from foreknowledge as if from a sign. It should be noted that a sign is not the cause of that which it signifies, but only manifests that the signified thing exists; just as a wreath <note>original: "circulus" - a traditional hoop or wreath hung outside a tavern to indicate wine is for sale</note> is not the cause of the sale of wine, but is only a sign of the sale. If, therefore, foreknowledge were a sign of the necessity of future things, it would presuppose that they are necessary; and thus, to show that foreknowledge is a sign of the necessity of future things, it is necessary first to show that future things are necessarily going to happen

<column-break/>

**before foreknowledge could be a sign of this necessity. Otherwise, if this necessity is nothing, then foreknowledge cannot even be a sign of a thing that does not exist. But now, it is established that a proof supported by firm reasoning must be drawn not from signs or arguments sought from the outside, but from appropriate and necessary causes. But how can it be that those things do not happen which are foreseen as being about to happen? As if, indeed, we did not believe that those things which providence foreknows as future would happen, and did not rather judge that, although they do happen, they nevertheless had nothing in their own nature of necessity that they should happen.**

->**Which you may easily weigh by this**<-

before foreknowledge could be a sign of the necessity of future things; otherwise, foreknowledge would be a sign of something that does not exist, which is absurd. **But now.** Here he shows that the method of proving from a sign is not effective and says: It is established—that is, it is manifest—that reasoning supported by—that is, strengthened by—demonstration must not be drawn from signs nor from arguments sought—that is, accepted—from the outside. Instead, firm reasoning must be drawn from appropriate—that is, from proper—and necessary causes. Since, therefore, the aforementioned reasoning proceeded from a sign, it is not effective or demonstrative, since it is "from the posterior" <term>a posteriori: reasoning from effects back to causes</term>. However, a demonstration, which is the most powerful of proofs, is "from the prior" <term>a priori: reasoning from causes to effects</term>, since it is from causes that are in themselves immediate, prior, and better known; and for that reason, a demonstration is a syllogism that produces knowledge, effective for proving according to the *Posterior Analytics*. <note>A reference to Aristotle's work on logic and scientific proof.</note> **But how can it be.** Here Philosophy <note>Lady Philosophy, the personified guide in Boethius's text.</note> raises a certain doubt and resolves it. For it seems to follow from what has been said that some things can be foreknown which do not happen by necessity. But if they do not happen by necessity, they might not happen; and thus it follows that something foreknown by God might not happen. First, therefore, Philosophy asks about this in doubt, saying: Since it is the case that those things which are foreknown are not necessary but can not-happen, how can it be that those things which are provided <gloss>foreseen</gloss> as future do not happen? Rather, one must say that they do happen by foreknowledge, but nevertheless they do not happen by necessity. Whence she says **As if, indeed.** As if she were saying: This doubt proceeds as if we did not believe that those things which providence foreknows are going to come, but this is not true; rather, we judge that although the future event happens, it nevertheless has nothing of necessity.

It distinguishes between "a priori" and "a posteriori" reasoning to explain why human events can be certain to happen without being forced by necessity.</summary>

## Fourth Prose

<note>original: "Prosa quarta"</note>

It is inherent in its own nature that it should happen; that is, he demonstrates by an example how something is grasped with certainty which is nevertheless not necessary, saying that something may be known to happen and yet not by necessity. You may consider this from the following example: for we observe many examples with our eyes while they are being done—that is, while they are in the process of happening—such as those things which chariot drivers are seen to do in managing and turning their four-horse chariots, and so on. In the same way, regarding this manner in which things happen—

**For we observe many things with our eyes while they are being subjected to them, such as those things seen to be done by chariot drivers in managing and turning their four-horse chariots, and so on. Does any necessity, therefore, compel any of those things to happen in such a way? Boethius: Not at all. Philosophy: For the effect of art would be in vain if all things moved by compulsion. Therefore, those things which lack the necessity of existing while they are happening, were going to happen without necessity before they happened. Wherefore, there are certain things about to happen whose outcome is released from all necessity. For I think no one would say this: that the things which are happening now were not going to happen before they happened. These things, even though foreknown, therefore have free outcomes.**

<column-break/>

—in other voluntary acts: does any necessity compel any of those things to happen exactly as they appear to your eyes? Boethius says: "Not at all," and assigns a reason: for the effect of art <note>The term "art" here refers to "ars" or technical skill/craftsmanship.</note> would be in vain if all things were moved by compulsion, and the art of steering a chariot would be in vain if it were steered by necessity. Therefore, those things which lack the necessity of existing when they happen are going to be without necessity before they happen. From this, she concludes that there are certain things to come whose exit—that is, the outcome—is released from all necessity. And perhaps someone might say that the things which are happening now were not "going to happen" before they existed. She excludes this, saying: "I think no one would say that the things which—

---

—are happening now were not going to happen." For that would be too irrational. Therefore, it is necessarily concluded that these things, even when foreknown, have free outcomes. Because just as the knowledge of present things imposes no necessity on those things which are in the present (as is clear in the aforementioned example of the steering of the chariot), so the foreknowledge of future things imposes no necessity on those things which are to come. <margin>Note that although future things are necessary by "conditioned necessity" in comparison to divine providence, not all things are necessary by "absolute necessity."</margin> For many things happen freely, such as those things done by art and by will, and the steering of chariots. For if the steering of a chariot happened by necessity, the skill of steering a chariot would be in vain. <margin>It should be noted that just as things actually happen, so they were going to be in the future. But certain things happen freely in act; therefore, they were going to be free in the future. Consequently, not all things are necessarily future, although they are by conditioned necessity insofar as they are compared to divine wisdom; yet, considered in their own nature, they do not happen by absolute necessity, as will be seen later where he distinguishes between the two types of necessity: conditioned and absolute.</margin> But you say this: Here Philosophy discusses Boethius's motive regarding whether uncertain future things (such as contingencies) can be known with certainty beforehand. And first, she raises a doubt about this and touches upon the reason for the doubt. Second, she assigns the cause of the error there: "The cause of this error..."

<summary>This page uses the analogy of a chariot driver to argue that observing an action does not force that action to happen; similarly, God's foreknowledge of the future does not impose necessity on human free will. It introduces the vital distinction between "absolute necessity" (laws of nature) and "conditioned necessity" (things that must be true only because they are happening).</summary>

->**Commentary Text**<-

It is. He says first: But you ask, O Boethius, whether it is even possible for there to be any foreknowledge—that is, prescience—of those things which do not have necessary outcomes, that is, events. For you believe this is in no way possible. For these two things seem to you to be discordant: namely, foreknowledge and the contingency of events <note>contingency: things that may or may not happen, as opposed to things that must happen by necessity</note>. For you think that if contingent things are foreseen, they must necessarily follow; and if necessity is absent, they cannot be foreknown at all. You think nothing can be grasped by divine foreknowledge unless it is certain. And if those things which have uncertain outcomes—that is, events like contingent actions—are foreseen as if they were certain, you think that is the "mist of opinion" <note>original: "caliginem opinionis"</note> rather than the truth of science. 

In this you are deceived, and the cause of your deception is your error regarding the judgment of cognition. For you believe it is a departure from the integrity of science to judge things otherwise than they are, and in this you err. It should be noted that because *we* cannot certainly foreknow future contingent things, we think God likewise cannot. However, a thing remaining the same can be known in different ways by different observers. To know a thing otherwise than it is *on the part of the thing known* is not science; but to know a thing otherwise than it is *on the part of the knower* is indeed science. Thus, although future contingents are uncertain in themselves, they can nevertheless be foreknown by God without the error of falsehood. 

The cause of this error: Here he assigns the cause of the mistake. It should be noted that the cause of the error—why we think uncertain future things cannot be certainly foreknown—is because it is thought that the faculty of cognition depends on the nature of the thing known, rather than on the knower themselves, which is false. First, he sets forth this cause of error. Second, he disproves it at the point beginning "For as this briefly..." He says first: The cause of this error is because it is estimated that everything anyone knows, they know only from the force and nature of the things themselves which are known, and not from the power of the knower. ### Prose 4

If knowledge were based on the capacity of the thing being known, then all things would be known in the same way by everyone. Thus, something would be understood in the same way by both the human and the divine intellect, which is false; for things that are uncertain to human understanding are certain to the divine understanding. Therefore, knowledge is instead measured according to the capacity of the power of the knower. Thus, the more effective and certain the power is, the more certainly and clearly it grasps the object.

<margin>
For as this may be clear from a brief example. Here he proves that the faculty of knowledge is according to the faculty of the power of the knower and not the thing known. First, he declares this with examples. Second, he proves this same thing by reason at the point "Nor is that unjustly." The first part is in two sections according to two examples at "Man himself also." First, he says that knowledge happens according to the faculty of the knower, which is clear by a brief example: for sight knows the same roundness of a body in one way, and touch in another. For sight, remaining at a distance (that is, from far away), beholds the whole.
</margin>

**...is grasped by the capacity. For as this may be clear from a brief example: sight and touch recognize the same roundness of a body in different ways. Sight, remaining at a distance, beholds the whole at once by casting out rays. But touch, clinging and joined to the orb, moving around the circumference itself, grasps the roundness in parts.** <note>Boethius uses the example of a sphere to show that the "object" doesn't change, but the "knower's" method (eyes vs. hands) changes the experience of it.</note> **Man himself is also observed differently by the senses, the imagination, reason, and intelligence. For the senses judge the figure as it is established in the underlying matter; imagination, however, judges the figure alone without the matter. But reason transcends this as well, and considers the species itself which exists in individuals...**

...the body at once by casting out visual rays. Here, add "touch," clinging and joined to the orb (that is, the roundness) and moving around the circumference itself (that is, around the round body), grasps its roundness in parts (that is, through parts). It should be noted that he suggests a double difference between the way sight and touch know things. The first is that sight knows a round body while existing at a distance. Touch, however, does not know it unless joined to it. The second difference is that sight grasps the whole body at once; touch, however, does so through parts. Such a diversity in knowing would not exist if the thing were known from its own nature, since the same thing remains in both types of knowledge.

It should be noted that some have said vision occurs through the emission of visual rays from the eyes to the thing seen. But this opinion is against Aristotle <note>original: "contra Aristotelem"</note>; for vision does not happen by sending something out, but by receiving something within. For "seeing" happens when a sensitive part is acted upon, according to the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's "De Anima"</note>. Here, however, he speaks according to the opinion of the ancients when he says that sight beholds the whole body by casting out rays. "Man himself also." Here he places a second example regarding the subordinate cognitive powers. Second, he shows how these powers relate to one another at "In which that..." First, therefore, he declares how the same thing is grasped in different ways by different powers, saying: the external sense beholds man in one way, imagination another, reason another, and divine intelligence another. For the external sense, such as sight, judges the figure of the man in the underlying matter (that is, in sensible matter), but imagination...

# Book Five

->[The faculty of imagination] discerns the shape alone without the matter, that is, in the absence of the material thing. But Reason transcends this imagination and examines the species itself—that is, the specific nature of man which exists in individuals—discerning it through universal consideration. The eye, however—that is, the consideration of Intelligence—is higher, because divine Intelligence, having surpassed the circuit of the universe which exists in individual things, gazes upon that simple form <note>The "simple form" refers to the Platonic Idea or Archetype.</note> (namely the Idea of Man) which exists in the divine mind, using the sharp vision—that is, the speculation—of the pure mind.<-

It should be noted that the first [example] concerned cognitive powers that were not subordinated to one another, such as sight and touch. This current example, however, concerns subordinated powers, of which there are four: namely, the **exterior sense**, which is in all animals; **imagination**, which is only in perfect <note>In medieval philosophy, "perfect" animals are those with complex sensory systems and memory.</note> animals; **reason**, which is only in humans; and **intelligence**, through which one understands divine knowledge. These powers have different ways of knowing the same thing (namely, man), as is declared in the text; this would not be the case unless

<column-break/>

## [Reason] examines [the species] through universal consideration. But a higher eye exists for Intelligence; for having surpassed the circuit of the universe, it gazes upon that simple form itself with the pure vision of the mind.

In this, there is one thing to be considered above all: for the superior power of comprehension embraces the inferior, but the inferior in no way rises to the superior. For the sense is not able to perceive anything outside of matter, nor does imagination behold universal species, nor does reason grasp the simple form; but Intelligence, looking down as if from above, having conceived the form, judges all things that lie beneath it, but in that same way in which [it knows] the form itself.

---

knowledge occurred according to the capacity of the powers of the knower, and not according to the thing known. **In this, there is one thing to be considered above all.** Here, Philosophy shows how the aforementioned cognitive powers relate to one another, showing that whatever the inferior power can do, the superior can also do, and more besides. And first, she shows this regarding Intelligence in respect to the other powers; second, she shows the same regarding Reason (the second part begins at: *Reason also...*). First, she says: **In this**—that is, in the order of these powers—**it is especially to be considered that the superior power of comprehension embraces the inferior within itself**, because the superior power knows everything that the inferior knows. The inferior, however, does not rise to the superior so as to apprehend what the superior does. She manifests this in an example, saying: **For the sense is not able to apprehend anything outside of matter**, and **imagination beholds universal species**—that is, less particular ones—but **reason grasps the simple**—that is, the universal—**form**. **Intelligence**, however, being divine and looking as if from above (since it is at the highest grade of cognition), having conceived the **ideal form**, judges all things that are subject to that form; for example, by knowing the "Idea of Man," it knows everything that is in man. But it comprehends that form in a way that can be known to no inferior power. For it knows the "universal"—that is, the universal form of reason—and the "shape" of imagination, and the "material sensible" which pertains to the exterior sense, without using reason, nor imagination, nor the senses, but beholding all things with a single stroke of the mind—that is, it knows without a process of reasoning <note>original: "absque discursu" - referring to intuitive knowledge that happens all at once rather than step-by-step.</note> what [is].

# Prose 4

Reason does not do this. It should be noted that because a higher power includes the lower power—just as a square includes a triangle, as is clear in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima* II.3, where he discusses how the powers of the soul are nested like geometric shapes</note>—therefore, whatever the lower power can do, the higher can also do, and more so. This is because it comprehends in a more universal way what the lower power grasps in a more particular way, though the reverse is not true. Therefore, what the human understanding can comprehend, the divine intelligence can also comprehend, though not the reverse. Reason also

**comprehends things that could be known to no other. For it knows the universal of reason, the shape of the imagination, and the material object of the senses, using neither reason, nor imagination, nor the senses, but beholding all things—if I may say so—formally with that single stroke of the mind. Reason also, when it looks upon something universal, comprehends things imaginable or sensible without using imagination or the senses. For it is reason that thus defines the universal of its own conception: "Man is a two-legged rational animal." Although this is a universal notion, no one is ignorant of the fact that the thing is an imaginable and sensible reality, which reason considers not by imagination or sense, but in a rational conception. Imagination also, although it took its beginning from the senses for seeing and forming shapes, yet in the absence of the senses**

<column-break/>

when it looks upon something. Here he shows the same regarding reason: that just as intelligence comprehends the other three lower powers, so reason also comprehends under itself the other two powers, namely imagination and sense. He says that reason conceives of something universal without using imagination or the senses, and it comprehends imaginable things through a universal comprehension. For it is reason that defines the universal of its conception thus: "Man is a two-legged rational animal." <note>original: "Homo est animal bipes rationale"</note> Since this definition is a universal notion (that is, a way of making something known), and since no one is ignorant that the thing explained by this definition is also imaginable and sensible, that reason considers the universal not by using imagination or sense, but by a rational conception. Then he shows that just as

---

reason comprehends imagination and sense, so imagination comprehends sense, saying: imagination also, even if it took its beginning entirely from the senses for seeing and forming shapes, yet when the external sense is absent, imagination surveys—that is, knows—all sensible things, not by a sensible method, but by an imaginary method of judging. And then he concludes, saying: "Do you see, therefore, how all things use their own faculty in knowing, rather than the faculty of the things that are known?" It should be noted that although reason, in comprehending its universal, does not use imagination and sense, yet in its act it presupposes imagination and sense, because "nothing is in the intellect unless it was first in the senses." <note>A fundamental principle of Scholastic empiricism often attributed to Aristotle</note> Similarly, although imagination does not use the senses in its own operation, it presupposes that the sense has been active, because "phantasy" (which he here calls imagination) is a movement produced by the sense in action, according to the second book of *On the Soul*.

Nor is this unjust. Here he confirms his statement by reason, saying: that a thing is known not according to its own nature, but according to the nature of the one who knows it.

# Book Five

Injustice <note>original: "iniuria"; here meaning "without reason" or "improperly"</note> does not occur in this matter. For since every judgment of knowledge is an act and operation of the one judging—that is, of the cognitive power—it is necessary that everyone who knows performs their own work (their own operation of knowing) not from another power, namely from the thing known, but from their own power, which is the strength of the knower. ¶ Note that from the text, the following reasoning is formed: Every act and operation follows the condition of that power to which the act and operation belong. But judging or knowing is an act and operation of the cognitive power and not of the thing known. Therefore, judging and knowing follow the mode and condition of the cognitive power and not the thing known.

### The Fourth Meter of the Fifth Book.

Once the Porch <note>The "Stoa" or "Porch" refers to the Stoic school of philosophy in Athens.</note> brought forth.
¶ This is the fourth meter of this fifth book, which is called Glyconic after its inventor, and Choriambic from its predominant poetic foot. In this meter, he disproves the opinion of the Stoics, from which the opposite of his own words seems to follow. For it was the opinion of the Stoics that intellectual knowledge was perfected solely by the fact that external bodies [impressed] their

<column-break/>

sensible qualities, which [the mind] illuminates not by a sensible but by an imaginary <note>meaning "pertaining to the faculty of imagination"</note> method of judging. Do you see then, how in knowing, all things use their own faculty rather than the faculty of those things which are known? Nor is this an injustice; for since every judgment exists by the act of the one judging, it is necessary that each person performs their work not from an outside will, but from their own will.

->**Upon the mind; just as it was once**<-

likenesses upon the mind, so that the mind behaves only in the manner of a passive receiver <note>original: "patientis"</note> and the external thing in the manner of an active agent. From this it follows—since the passive receiver is drawn to the nature of the agent and not the other way around—that knowledge would follow the nature of the thing known and not the nature of the knower, which is contrary to what has been said. ¶ First, therefore, he sets out the opinion of the Stoics. Second, he disproves it at the point beginning "But the mind." First he says: "Once the Porch brought forth old men"—supply "the Stoics," who were called old men because of the maturity of their character. "Old men," I say, "far too obscure"—supply "in their opinions"—which Stoics believe that senses and images (that is, the forms of sensible things) are imprinted on minds from external bodies. And they proposed that those bodies imprint images on minds in the same way it was once the custom for someone writing with a swift pen to fix pressed letters on the level surface of a page that previously had no marks. It should be noted that the Stoics are named from *stoa* in Greek, which is *porticus* [Porch] in Latin, because they used to dispute in Athens in a very prominent porch and other public places. They proposed that the soul has only the role of a passive receiver in respect to external things; because knowledge seems to follow an active power rather than a passive one, therefore, according to them, knowledge ought to be considered according to the faculty of the thing known (which is active) rather than the soul of the knower (which is passive).

It should be noted that the first inconsistency is this: if intellectual knowledge were made through the mere impression of bodies upon the soul, then there would be no power through which the soul could know incorporeal things, because through the mere impression of bodies it would only know corporeal things. Note that from the text such a reasoning is formed: That soul is not only passive but active which judges, composes, and divides, and refutes false things with true ones. But the intellectual soul is of this kind; therefore, etc. The major premise is noted because to judge, to compose, to divide, and to refute are seen to be active operations. The minor premise is apparent: the soul judges between true and false; it composes the predicate with the subject; sometimes it divides the predicate from the subject and refutes false opinions. *This [mind] is more efficient.* Here Philosophy <note>the personification of Philosophy in Boethius's work</note> posits the truth, saying: This mind is more of an efficient cause <term>efficient cause: the primary source of change or action</term>, which is a cause far more powerful than that which, in the manner of matter—that is, in the likeness of matter—suffers impressed marks. And because someone might believe that there was no passion <note>here meaning "being acted upon" or sensory input</note> in the soul, he therefore adds: a certain passion precedes the operations of the soul in the living body, exciting and moving the strengths of the soul to work, as when light strikes the eyes, then the sight is acted upon.

acted upon. But every passive power necessarily requires an active power to bring it
into action. Such an active force cannot be a bodily thing outside, since the agent is more excellent than the
patient <note>In medieval philosophy, the "agent" is the thing doing the action, and the "patient" is the thing receiving it</note>. Therefore, such an active force on the part of the soul will be the active intellect, whose operation is to make potentially
understood things actually understood. Thus, from things outside, by the power of the active intellect, something is impressed
upon the passive intellect through which it is brought into the act of understanding. It is not, therefore, the intention of Boethius to deny
that the mind is passive by reason of the passive intellect, but he intends that the mind or soul
has more efficiency in understanding than it has passivity from the external bodies themselves. And consequently, the efficiency
of the intellect ought not to be attributed to external things, which was the intention of the Stoics.

---

# Prose V.

They protect the body in such a way that in the act of knowing, the soul follows its own motion, even though external qualities affect—that is, change—the instruments, which are the organs of the senses. The physical suffering <note>original: "passio"; here meaning the passive reception of sensory stimuli</note> of the body precedes the strength of the active mind; this physical experience provokes the act of the mind within itself and awakens the forms resting within. If this occurs in our soul, how much more so in those beings which are absolute and free from all affections—that is, the qualities of bodies—such as the separate intelligences <note>Refers to angelic or non-corporeal beings</note> and especially God.

In discerning, those beings do not follow external objects, but rather they expedite—that is, they perfect—the act of their own mind, which is the intellectual operation according to their own nature. It should be noted that from the text one can argue thus: If a quality exists in a subject where it is less expected to be seen, it certainly exists where it is more expected. But it is less apparent that our soul, in the act of knowing, follows its own motion rather than the motion of the thing known; and yet it follows the faculty of its own cognition. Therefore, much more so does the Divine Intelligence follow its own motion of cognition in knowing, rather than the motion of the thing known itself. **By this reasoning**—here he draws two conclusions from the premises—

<column-break/>

—awakening the forms resting within. If in the soul of a sensing being, the mind is not merely marked by passive experience <note>original: "passione"</note> but by its own power judges the passive experience subjected to the body, how much more do those beings which are free from all bodily affections, in the act of discerning, not follow external objects? Instead, they carry out the act of their own mind. **By this reasoning**, therefore, multiple types of knowledge have fallen to diverse and different substances. For **Sense** alone, destitute of all other types of knowledge, fell to immobile living things, such as the shells of the sea and other things that cling to rocks for nourishment. But **Imagination** belongs to mobile beasts, in whom there is seen to be some effect of fleeing or seeking. **Reason**, however, belongs only to the human race, just as **Intelligence** alone belongs to the Divine—

<column-break/>

—saying: Since knowledge follows the nature of the knower and not the nature of the thing known, and since knowers are diverse according to their nature, it is necessary that different types of knowledge belong to different knowers. Whence he says: **By this reasoning**, because knowledge follows the nature of the knower, multiple types of knowledge have fallen to diverse and different substances. For **Sense** alone, deprived of other knowledges, fell to immobile living things, such as sea shells and whatever things are nourished while adhering to rocks. **Imagination**, however, fell to mobile beasts which move with progressive motion, in whom there is seen to be an affect—that is, an appetite for fleeing evil or seeking good. **Reason**, truly, through which we comprehend the universal, belongs only to the human race, just as **Intelligence** belongs to the Divine race.

Then he poses the second conclusion: that the form of knowledge is better known and more noble which not only apprehends its own object, but also the objects of other types of knowledge. Whence he says: **Whereby it happens** that this notion—that is, knowledge—is superior—that is, more noble—than the others, which by its own nature—that is, its proper nature—not only—that is, not merely—knows its own object, but also knows the subjects of the other notions. Note regarding the first conclusion: since acts and operations are diversified according to the diversity of the agents performing them, it follows that if the agents and workers are diverse, they must have diverse operations.

# Book Five.

...and cognitions, because of which sensation, without other forms of knowledge, was granted to lower animals <note>original: "animalibus ignobilibus"</note>. Here, he takes "sensation" strictly as sensory apprehension, which is only moved by the presence of a sensible object. In this way, it is distinguished from imagination, which does not only apprehend a present thing but also absent ones. It should be noted regarding this conclusion that whichever power knows more things is seen to be more excellent than that which knows fewer. Therefore, if some power knows its own proper object and, along with it, the objects of other inferior powers—just as the divine intelligence <note>original: "intelligētia diuina"</note> does—and not the other way around, it follows that the superior power, knowing more things, is nobler than the inferior. Why then does philosophy show here the insufficiency of those who, based on our mode of knowing, disprove divine providence? Secondly, she exhorts us to consider the mode of divine knowledge, at the point: "Wherefore in that..." First, she demonstrates their insufficiency through a simile. Secondly, she applies that simile to the proposition at the point: "It is similar..." The comparison she intends is this: Sensation and imagination are lower forms of knowledge than reason. If, therefore, sensation and imagination wished to judge the mode of knowing belonging to reason based on their own mode of knowing, and were to say that the "universal" <term>universal: a general concept or essence that applies to many things, as opposed to a single physical object</term> which reason apprehends is nothing...

...or if the judgment of reason were true, or if it were particular and sensible while reason said the opposite. It is manifest that we, who flourish with both forms of knowledge, would rather assent to reason, judging the motive of sense and imagination to be insufficient. He says, therefore: "What then if sense and imagination resist," that is, contradict reason, saying there is no universal which reason thinks it beholds, arguing thus: "That which is sensible or imaginable cannot be universal" according to the judgment of sense and imagination. Either, therefore, the judgment of reason must be true—and consequently nothing would be sensible, which is absurd—or, because it is known to them (namely sense and imagination) that many things are subject to the senses and imagination which must be sensible, you would believe the conception of reason to be empty, which considers that which is sensible and singular as if it were a kind of universal. # Prose 5

Those faculties, namely sense and imagination, are truly unable to aspire—that is, to reach—the knowledge of the universal, because their cognition does not exceed physical shapes. Reason, on the other hand, would say that one ought rather to believe in the firmer and more perfect judgment of things. In a dispute of this kind, therefore—namely between sense and imagination on one side and reason on the other—should we, in whom the power of reasoning exists as much as the power of imagining and sensing, not rather approve the cause of reason?

## Concerning the belief that the knowledge of things rests in a firmer and more perfect judgment. In a dispute of this kind, should we, in whom the power of reasoning, imagining, and sensing exists, not rather approve the cause of reason?

It is a similar case when human reason thinks that the divine intelligence cannot behold future events except in the way that reason itself knows them. For as you argue, if certain things do not seem to have fixed and necessary outcomes, those things cannot be foreknown as certainly about to happen. Therefore, there is no foreknowledge of these things; for if we believe foreknowledge exists even in these matters, there will be nothing that does not happen out of necessity. If, therefore, just as we are sharers in reason, we could likewise possess the judgment of the divine mind—just as we judged that imagination and sense ought to yield to reason—so we would deem it most just for human reason to submit itself to the divine mind. ...of reason. It should be noted that one must stand by the judgment of the nobler power rather than the judgment of the ignoble power. Since reason is a nobler power than sense and imagination—because reason comprehends its own object as well as the objects of sense and imagination, but not vice versa—therefore one must stand by the judgment of reason rather than the inferior powers.

**It is a similar case.** Here he applies that analogy to the proposition and says: That which was said concerning sense and imagination in respect to reason is similar to the fact that human reason thinks the divine intelligence beholds nothing except as reason itself knows it. This is apparent from the very mode of arguing. For you "discourse"—that is, you argue—that if any things seem not to have certain and necessary outcomes, such things cannot be foreknown as certainly about to happen. Therefore, there is no foreknowledge of such things; if we believe this foreknowledge exists in these matters, nothing will happen that does not come from necessity.

If, therefore, just as we are participants in reason, we could also have the judgment of the divine mind: just as we now judge that imagination and sense ought to yield to reason, so we would "deem"—that is, judge—it most just for human reason to submit itself to the divine mind. It should be noted that the relationship is similar between the judgment of sense and imagination in respect to reason, and reason in respect to the divine intelligence. For it seems to sense and imagination that reason cannot comprehend a thing otherwise than as they themselves comprehend it—which is false. In the same way, it seems to human reason that the divine intelligence cannot know uncertain things otherwise than as reason itself knows them—which is false. ## Fifth Meter.

a dactylic meter named after its leading foot. In this, he shows that man is disposed toward the contemplation of heavenly things by the shape of his body. There are other animals in whom there is a "wandering lightness of wings" which "beat the winds" and "float through"—that is, pass through—with "liquid flight" the "spaces of the long ether," which is the air. There are others who "rejoice to have pressed their footprints into the ground"—that is, the earth—with their steps, and to "cross"—that is, pass through—the green fields, and they rejoice to "enter the woods." Although you see all these animals differ in their various forms, nevertheless their "prone faces"—that is, inclined toward the earth—serve to weigh down and dull their senses.

# Prose 6.

It should be noted that Philosophy touches upon three kinds of animals: namely, creeping things, winged things, and walking things. Although they differ in their forms—for some are formed for creeping like serpents, some for flying like birds, and some for walking like beasts—nevertheless they all agree in this: that they have their faces turned down toward the earth. *The human race alone raises its high head loftier.* Here he describes the figure of man, saying:

Though you see that all things differ in various forms, yet the downward-facing countenance serves to dull the heavy senses. The human race alone raises its high head loftier. And light, it stands with upright body and looks down upon the earth; unless you, being earthly, are badly deceived, this figure warns you. You who seek the heavens with an upright face and have lifted up your brow: carry your soul also into the sublime, lest the mind, weighed down, sink lower while the body is raised higher.

<column-break/>

The human race alone raises its high head <note>original: "celsum cacumen"</note>, that is, its head, loftier; and light, it stands with an upright—that is, erect—body and looks down upon the earth with a face raised toward heaven. You, earthly man, who seek heaven with an upright face and have lifted up—that is, you raise—your brow: this upright figure warns you that you are badly deceived unless you also carry—that is, extol—your soul into the sublime, that is, into heavenly things. This is so that the mind, weighed down—that is, depressed by heaviness—does not sink "to the bottom" <note>original: "pessum," an adverb of place meaning toward the feet or underneath</note>. Let that mind not settle lower than the body which has been raised higher. It should be noted that since man has a body shaped erect toward heaven, if the soul were not raised toward the contemplation of heavenly things, the body would seem to be more noble than the soul.

<column-break/>

<margin>Note according to Aristotle in the 16th book of *On Animals*.</margin>
Man, among all animals, has a rectilinear figure. Ovid also speaks of this figure in the book of *Metamorphoses*, saying: *And while other animals look downward at the earth, He gave to man a sublime face and ordered him to see the heavens, and to lift his upright countenance to the stars.*

...of divine knowledge. At the point: *Since therefore every judgment.* First, he [Boethius] premises that eternity must be defined. Second, he defines it, at the point: *Eternity, therefore, is the interminable,* etc. First he says: Since it was shown a little while ago that everything which is known is recognized not from its own nature—that is, from the nature of the thing known—but from the nature of the one knowing, let us now look, as far as is permitted, into what the state of the divine essence or substance is, so that we may recognize what His knowledge is. <margin>It should be noted that "men living by reason" are those who are guided by the light of wisdom. And all these concede that God is eternal. It should be noted that because the eternity of God, the nature of God, and the knowledge of God do not differ in substance, therefore once eternity is known, the nature and knowledge of God are known. *Eternity, therefore, is.* Here he proceeds concerning eternity. First, he provides its definition. Second, he clarifies it, at the point: *Which from a comparison.* First he says: Eternity is the possession of an interminable life, existing as a whole, simultaneously, and perfect. Note that according to Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar</note> in his book *On Causes*: Something is eternal and in eternity, and is eternity itself, such as God. Some things are eternal and are in eternity, but are not eternity itself, such as motion, time, and the world. He says "eternity is a possession"; here they use the word "possession" to designate the immutability and the lack of deficiency in eternity, because it is firmly possessed and quietly held. And he says "of life" to suggest that non-living things are not measured by eternity. And he says "interminable" <note>without end or limit</note> to differentiate it from that life which has a limit on the part before and the part after, such as the life of a human; or a limit on the part before only, such as the life of angels. And he says "whole and simultaneous" to differentiate it from the angelic life; for although the being of an angel according to substance is "whole and simultaneous," it is not so according to operation, since an angel has successive operations and thoughts. And he says "perfect" to designate that nothing is lacking to eternity; for that is "perfect" to which nothing is lacking, according to the first book of *On the Heavens and the Earth* <note>Aristotle's De Caelo</note>. *Which from a comparison.* Here he clarifies the definition. Second, he rebukes certain people who were misusing the word "eternity," at the point: *wherefore not rightly.* First, therefore, he clarifies the definition of eternity in comparison to time, saying: Wherefore it was said that eternity is the whole and simultaneous possession of an interminable life, which is clearer from a "collation"—that is, from a comparison—of temporal things. For whatever lives in time, existing as a present thing, proceeds through succession...

Therefore, that which endures the condition of time—even if, as Aristotle judged regarding the world, it never began to be nor ever ceases, and its life is extended with the infinity of time—it is still not such that it may rightly be believed to be eternal. For it does not comprehend and embrace the whole space of its life at once, even if that life be infinite; rather, it does not yet possess the future, and the past has already flowed away. Therefore, that which encompasses and possesses the entire fullness of boundless life at once, from which nothing of the future is absent and nothing of the past has flowed away, is rightly held to be eternal. This is because it does not comprehend nor embrace the whole space of its life (its duration) at once, even if it lasts for an infinite time. It does not yet have the infinite future, and it no longer has the past that has been traversed. Therefore, whatever comprehends and possesses the whole fullness of boundless life at once, since nothing of the future is absent and nothing of the past has flowed away, that is rightly declared to be eternal. Because that eternal being is in possession of itself,

It should be noted that because we arrive at the knowledge of eternity through the knowledge of time—since opposites shine more clearly when placed beside one another—he therefore declares the nature of eternity to us through the nature and succession of time. For just as the logic of time consists in succession and the grasping of "before" and "after" in a motion where one part passes away and another is yet to come, so the logic of eternity, by contrast, consists in the grasping of the uniformity of that which is entirely outside of motion, comprehending the past and future simultaneously as a "present." # Book Five.

For an endless life, it is necessary that any differences of time be absent, even if a set time is assumed; because it [eternity] assists the differences of time in the same way that it exists in itself. However, the movement by which it exists in itself is ever-present; therefore, it also assists the differences of time through a present movement. **Wherefore some do not rightly think who, when they hear it seemed to Plato that this world neither had a beginning of time nor would have an end, think in this way that the created world is made co-eternal with the Creator. Nor should God be seen as older than created things by a quantity of time, but rather by the property of His simple nature. For that infinite motion of temporal things imitates this ever-present state of an unmoving life.**

Aristotle attributes this same view to him in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>Latin: "De caelo et mundo"</note>, saying that Plato alone "generates" the world. # Book Five

Wisdom teaches how one ought to speak properly concerning God and the world, saying: If we, following Plato, wish to assign names that are worthy—that is, suitable to the things themselves—let us say that God is **eternal**, but let us say the world is **perpetual**. <note>The author distinguishes between "eternal" (outside of time entirely) and "perpetual" (existing forever within time).</note> And this harmonizes with the saying of the author of the *Grecismus*: <note>The *Grecismus* was a popular 13th-century grammatical poem by Eberhard of Béthune.</note> "Eternal truly is without beginning and without end; perpetual is that which has a beginning but shall lack an end." Since, therefore, every judgment—here Philosophy shows the mode of divine knowledge based on what has been said. First, she shows what the nature of divine knowledge is and how it should be named, saying: since every judgment grasps those things subjected to it (that is, its objects) according to its own nature (that is, according to the nature of the knower). Now, the nature of God is such that His state is always eternal and presential; from which it follows that the knowledge of God, having transcended all the motions of time, remains in the simplicity of its presence, and embracing the infinite spaces of past and future time, considers all things in its simple cognition as if they were being carried out "now" (that is, presently). Then she shows how the knowledge of God is to be named, saying: Therefore, if you wish to weigh the "presence" by which He discerns all things, you will not judge divine knowledge to be "foreknowledge" as if of the future, but you will more rightly estimate divine knowledge to be of an "instance" (that is, of a presence) that never fails. This she confirms through the etymology of the name **Providence**, saying: hence divine cognition is not called "pre-vision" <note>original: *preuidentia*</note> because that implies an order toward future things, but it is called **Providence** <note>original: *prouidentia*</note> as if "looking forth" <note>original: *porro*</note> from afar, established far from the lowest things, as if it perceives all things from the high summit of the world. Note that cognition follows the mode of the thing knowing; therefore, the cognition and knowledge of God follow the state and disposition of God. But the state of God is eternal and presential, since the Divine Being is measured by eternity. Therefore, the knowledge of God shall be eternal and presential, so that He knows all things that are past and future as if they were present. It should be noted that someone might say: "Non-being cannot be present to anyone; but the past and the future are non-being; therefore, they cannot be present to divine cognition." It must be said that "non-being" is twofold: one kind is in no way a being nor can it be a being, and such a thing is not really present to anyone even if it is nothing. The other is "non-being" not simply, but because it is not a being *in act* <note>meaning it does not currently exist in the physical world</note>; and although a being of this sort cannot really coexist with "present time," it can nevertheless coexist with **eternity**. Because eternity, since it is infinite, exceeds present time by extending itself to the past and the future. And thus the past and the future are to be coexistent with eternity presentially, because in eternity there is no succession. Hence, it does not follow that if something coexists with eternity, that for that reason...

<column-break/>

Since, therefore, every judgment grasps those things subjected to it according to its own nature, and God’s state is always eternal and presential, His knowledge also, having transcended every motion of time, remains in the simplicity of His presence; and embracing the infinite spaces of the past and future, He considers all things in His simple cognition as if they were even now being carried out. Therefore, if you wish to weigh the "foreknowledge" by which He discerns all things, you will more rightly judge it not to be a "foreknowledge" as if of the future, but a knowledge of a never-failing presence.

# Book Five

->**Why this divine foreknowledge?**<-

Here he shows that regarding contingent events <note>events that may or may not happen</note>, God’s certain knowledge and the uncertain outcome of the event exist simultaneously, saying: Therefore, this divine foreknowledge by which God knows future things does not change the nature of things regarding necessity and contingency. For it does not impose necessity on a thing that is contingent, but views such things as present before itself just as they will one day come to pass in the future. Nor are the judgments of things confused; He does not make the contingent to be non-contingent, but by a single gaze of the mind He knows both necessary and non-necessary future events.

He declares this by an example, saying: Just as you humans, when you see at the same time—that is, in the same instant—a man walking on the earth and the sun rising in the sky, although both are seen at once, you nevertheless discern that the former is voluntary (namely, the man walking on the earth) and the latter is necessary (namely, the sun rising). In a similar way, the divine gaze, looking down upon all things, does not in the least disturb the quality of things—that is, the contingency and necessity of things. I say they are present to Him by reason of eternity, but future in relation to the condition of time. Whereby it happens that God's knowledge of future things as if they were present is not mere opinion, but a knowledge based on truth—

<column-break/>

—and He distinguishes by a single gaze of His mind those things that will come to pass necessarily from those that will not. Just as when you see at the same time a man walking on the earth and the sun rising in the sky, although both are viewed together, you nevertheless discern them and judge the one to be voluntary and the other to be necessary. Thus, therefore, the divine gaze looking down upon all things does not disturb the quality of things; they are indeed present to Him, but future according to the condition of time. Whereby it happens that this is not opinion, but rather a wonderful knowledge based on truth, since He knows that something is about to happen while also knowing that it does not lack the necessity of existing <note>original: "necessitate carere non nesciat" - He is not ignorant that it lacks necessity</note>. At this point, if you should say that what God sees as about to happen cannot fail to happen, and that what cannot fail to happen occurs by necessity, and you bind me to this word "necessity," I shall confess that this is a matter of the most solid truth. But—

---

—confirmed truth, that is, when He knows something is about to come forth—that is, is future—He is not ignorant that the same thing can lack the necessity of existing. 

It should be noted regarding the statement that God knows all things as present (namely, past and future), some propose the example of a staff fixed in a river, which is successively present to the whole river and its parts. Thus eternity is simultaneous with all of time and with all things that flow in time, so that the whole of time and whatever is successive in time is present to eternity. It is as if eternity were placed like a center point and all of time like the circumference; then, although the circumference moves continuously and one part succeeds another, yet in comparison to the center, it remains uniform. Another example is given of someone walking along a road who does not see the people coming behind him; but he who looks down from a high tower would see the whole road and the people passing along it at once.

# Book Five

In the same way, whatever divine providence sees as present, that must necessarily exist—namely, under the condition by which it is foreseen and by which it is placed as present to Him, even though it possesses no necessity of its own nature. But God beholds those future things as present which proceed from the freedom of choice <note>Latin: *libertate arbitrii*</note>. Therefore, these things, when related to the divine gaze, become necessary through the knowledge of the divine mind. Yet in themselves—that is, in their own nature, without respect to the divine knowledge—they do not fall away from the absolute (meaning perfect) freedom of their own nature.

<margin>It should be noted according to the intention of Boethius <note>The author refers to Boethius, the 6th-century philosopher whose "Consolation of Philosophy" is being commented upon here.</note>: This is the reasoning. Whatever is foreseen by God happens by necessity, but by **conditioned necessity** and not by **absolute necessity**. Others solve this differently, saying that the proposition is true in the **composite sense** but false in the **divided sense**. Hence, when it is said: "Whatever is foreseen necessarily happens," it is true in the composite sense, because it is impossible for what is foreseen by God not to happen; however, in the divided sense it is false, because the outcome of a thing, at least a contingent one, is not necessary in itself.</margin>

<column-break/>

**Therefore, in this way, if providence sees anything as present, it is necessary that it be so, even if it has no necessity of nature. But God beholds those future things which proceed from the freedom of choice as present. These things, therefore, when related to the divine gaze, become necessary through the condition of the divine motion. Yet considered in themselves, they do not cease from the absolute freedom of their nature. All things, therefore, which God foreknows will be, will undoubtedly come to pass. But some of them proceed from free choice; although these happen by existing, they do not lose their own nature, because before they happened, they were able not to come to pass.**

---

All things, therefore, will undoubtedly come to pass which... Here the Philosopher <note>Referring to Boethius as the authority.</note> concludes from the preceding points that these two things stand together: that some things are in themselves contingent and uncertain, yet they happen with certainty insofar as they are foreseen by God. Secondly, he objects against this at the point: *What difference does it make then that they are not necessary?* when he first says: "Undoubtedly all future things which God foreknows are to be," otherwise divine providence would be deceived. But some of them "proceed"—that is, they come forth—from free choice, so that although their existence is certain, they could have not happened. Hence he adds that although they happen, they do not lose their own nature of freedom, because before they happened, they could have not occurred.

Note that the whole intention of Boethius is founded upon this: that something which is a free future event, by its own nature in comparison to divine foreknowledge <note>Latin: *prescientiam*</note>, happens necessarily; and such is **conditioned necessity**, because insofar as it is foreseen, it thus necessarily happens, but not **absolutely** if the foreknowledge is set aside.

*What difference does it make then that they are not necessary?* Here he objects against the solution and then solves the objection. Secondly, he objects to that solution again at the point: *But if you say in my...* The objection consists in this: Since a contingent future event that is foreknown happens with certainty and necessity, there does not seem to be a difference between the contingent and the necessary. Hence he says: "What difference does it make then that contingent and free future events are not necessary, since they happen in the likeness of necessity?" Then he solves it, saying that between a necessary and a contingent outcome there is this difference, which appears clearly through the examples I set down a little while ago: namely, the rising sun and the walking man. While these things are happening, they cannot "not happen," and thus both are necessary under the condition of presence. Presence...

->Prose 6.<-

...it is necessary that they exist while they are present; however, one of them—namely, the rising sun—was necessary to exist before it happened. But the other—namely, a man walking—is by no means under a necessity to happen before it actually happens. In the same way, those things which God holds as present undoubtedly exist because of the condition of necessity, since they are foreseen to happen as if they were present. Of those things thus foreseen, one kind descends from the necessity of things (like the sun rising), while the other from the power of those performing the act (like a man walking). From which he concludes: "Therefore..."

# What does it matter then that they are not necessary, since by the condition of divine knowledge they happen in every way like necessity? This is because of those things I proposed a little while ago: the rising sun and the walking man. While they are happening, they cannot *not* happen; yet of these, one was necessary to exist even before it happened, while the other was not at all. So also, the things God has as present undoubtedly exist, but of these, one descends from the necessity of things, the other from the power of those performing the act. Not without cause, therefore, did we say that these things are necessary if referred to divine knowledge, but if considered by themselves, they are free from the bonds of necessity. Just as everything that is open to the senses, if you refer it to reason, is universal; but if you look at it by itself, it is singular <note>The author uses a logical analogy: a specific person is a "singular" individual to our eyes, but to our "reason," they belong to the "universal" category of Humanity.</note>. But you will say: "If it is placed in my power to change my purpose, I shall void providence, since I may perhaps have changed what providence foreknows."

# I respond that your purpose indeed...

<column-break/>

...not without cause have we said this: that those things which happen contingently <note>term: contingent (events that can either happen or not happen, as opposed to necessary events like the sunrise)</note> are necessary if they are referred to divine knowledge—namely, from the condition of divine science. If, however, they are considered by themselves, they are absolute from bonds—that is, from the chains of necessity. This is shown by a simile: just as that which is evident to the senses, if you refer it to reason, is then universal; but if you refer it to the sense, it is then singular. It should be noted that if the same thing, when related to different things, can be both universal and singular, it seems similarly that the same thing compared to different things can be both contingent and necessary. For the particular has the nature of the contingent, and the universal has the nature of the necessary. But we see that human nature, when compared to the *active intellect* <note>term: active intellect (the part of the mind that processes raw data into abstract concepts)</note> which abstracts from individual conditions, and compared to the

*possible intellect* <note>term: possible intellect (the capacity of the mind to receive or become those concepts)</note>, has the nature of the universal; yet human nature compared to the sense (which perceives the particular) has the nature of the singular. For it is universal while it is being understood, and particular while it is being felt. Similarly, it will be so regarding a contingent future: that the event itself, compared to divine foreknowledge, is conditionally necessary; but considered in itself, it remains contingent. "But if you say 'in my [power]'": here he objects against the solution already stated and then solves that objection. Secondly, he moves the doubt there: "What therefore." First he says: You will object against the solution thus: "If it is in my power to change my purpose—that is, by running or not running—I shall void—that is, frustrate—divine providence when I shall have changed those things which He foreknew to be future." He himself solves this, saying: I respond that you are able to bend—that is, change—your purpose; but the truth of providence beholds that very "being able"—namely, that you can change your purpose—and whether you actually do change your purpose; and it beholds to what you turn your purpose. Therefore, know that you are not able to avoid divine foreknowledge, just as someone with free will...

<summary>This page explains the distinction between "simple" and "conditional" necessity, arguing that while God sees all future events as present (and thus "necessary" in his sight), human actions remain free and contingent in their own nature. It uses the analogy of "universal" versus "singular" concepts to show how one thing can be perceived differently by different levels of understanding.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book Five of Boethius's "The Consolation of Philosophy," specifically addressing the compatibility of divine foreknowledge and human free will.</meta>

# Book Five

Even if you turn yourself toward various actions, you cannot escape the gaze of the present eye. <note>The "present eye" refers to God's vision, which sees all things as if they are happening "now" in an eternal present.</note> Note that although a human being can change their purpose, they do not thereby escape divine foreknowledge, because God foreknows that very change. For instance, if God foresaw that you were going to the market tomorrow, even though you are able not to go and might propose not to go, you will nonetheless go; for God sees simultaneously your purpose, your power of not going, the change of your purpose, and the action of going. In no way can one escape His presence. What then will you say? Here a doubt is raised: You will perhaps say, "Will divine knowledge then be changed by my disposition—that is, by my variation—so that when I want now this, now that, divine foreknowledge will seem to alternate its ways of knowing?" He responds: "Not at all." This happens because divine knowledge is not changed; for the divine gaze runs ahead of every future thing and twists it back <note>original: "retorquet"</note> to the presence of His own knowledge, knowing all things simultaneously as present. Nor does He alternate—that is, change—His ways of foreknowing now this and now that successively, as you imagine. Instead, remaining free from change, He anticipates and embraces your changes in a single stroke. God does not obtain this presence of comprehending all things as present from future things, but from His own simplicity. From this is resolved—that is, declared—that which you proposed a little while ago: namely, that it would be unworthy if our future actions were said

<column-break/>

to be able to deflect [His knowledge]. But since the truth of the present providence beholds what you are able to do, what you actually do, and where you turn, you cannot avoid divine foreknowledge, just as you cannot escape the gaze of a present eye, even though you turn yourself toward various actions by your free will. What then, you will say? "Will divine knowledge be changed by my disposition? So that when I want now this, now that, the turns of His knowing would also seem to alternate?" **B.** <note>Boethius</note> Not at all. **P.** <note>Philosophy</note> For the divine gaze runs ahead of every future thing and twists and recalls it back to the presence of its own proper knowledge. Nor does it alternate, as you imagine, the turns of foreknowing now this and now that; but remaining [stable], it anticipates and embraces your changes in a single stroke. God obtains this presence of seeing and comprehending all things not from the outcome of future events, but from His own simplicity. From this is also resolved that which you proposed a little while ago: that it is unworthy if our future events are said to provide the cause for God's knowledge. For this power of knowledge, embracing all things with a notion of presence, [itself provides the measure] to things.

---

to provide the cause of God's knowledge. For the virtue of divine knowledge, embracing all things presently, itself imposes the measure <term>modum: a philosophical term for the limit, boundary, or essential character of a thing</term> upon all things. Because the knowledge of God is the cause of things, it owes nothing to the things themselves; it receives nothing from them as we receive knowledge from things. If God did not simultaneously know those things which happen successively in time, then God's knowledge would be variable, because the knowledge of one thing would succeed the knowledge of another. But because He knows all things simultaneously as present, no variation falls into His knowledge—it is not as if He first does not know a thing exists, and later knows it does not exist, and later that it does. Rather, He knows all things to be simultaneously. Therefore, He knows at once that something "is not" in one distinction of time measuring the thing, and "is" in another distinction of time. Since these things are so... <note>Here the author begins to conclude the argument based on the premises above.</note>

<summary>This page argues that God's foreknowledge does not change based on human choices because God exists in an eternal "now," seeing all past, present, and future events simultaneously through divine simplicity.</summary>
<keywords>Boethius, Philosophy, Providence, Foreknowledge, Book Five, On the Consolation of Philosophy, Knowledge of God, Free Will, Eternity, Simplicity</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the final prose section (Prose 6) of Book V of Boethius's "The Consolation of Philosophy," resolving the tension between divine foreknowledge and human free will.</meta>

# Prose 6

<gloss>
Speaking on the compatibility of free will with divine foreknowledge, saying: Since these things are as previously stated, the freedom of the will remains inviolate <note>original: "intemerata," meaning uncorrupted or pure</note>. Nor do laws propose punishments and rewards for humans unjustly, since our wills are free <note>original: "solutis," meaning released from all necessity</note>. God also remains immovably foreknowing of all things, and the present eternity of His vision runs alongside the future quality of our acts, dispensing <note>meaning distributing</note> rewards to the good and
</gloss>

<margin>
punishments to the wicked. Nor are hopes and prayers placed in God in vain, for they cannot be ineffective when they are righteous. Note that because of free will, things are able to happen otherwise than they do; therefore, rewards for the good and punishments for the evil are not proposed unjustly. Nor are hopes and prayers frustrated. However, all these things would be frustrated if all things were bound by the chain of necessity, as is clear from what has been said. Therefore, turn away from vices. Here, the author <note>likely referring to Boethius or the commentator</note> adds a useful exhortation, saying: Since it is the case that you are not compelled by necessity to do anything, but free will remains in you, therefore turn away from <note>meaning despise</note> vices, lest through them you justly incur punishments. Cultivate <note>meaning practice</note> virtues, through which you may pursue merits. Lift up your mind to righteous hopes which tend toward true happiness.
</margin>

<note>The initial letter 'Q' (from 'Quibus') is omitted, intended for a decorative rubricated initial.</note>
**[To all things] it [eternity] has set a measure; it owes nothing to those things that come after. Since these things are so, the freedom of the will remains inviolate for mortals; nor do laws propose rewards and punishments unjustly for wills that are free from all necessity. There is also a spectator looking down from above, God who foreknows all things, and the ever-present eternity of His vision runs alongside the future quality of our actions, dispensing rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked. Nor are hopes and prayers placed in God in vain; since they are righteous, they cannot be without effect. Therefore, turn away from vices; cultivate virtues. Lift up your mind to righteous hopes; offer humble prayers to the heights. A great necessity of goodness is imposed upon you, if you do not wish to hide from the truth, since you act before the eyes of a Judge who sees all things.**

<gloss>
stretch toward the heights, namely to God, with humble prayers; and you should do this with merit. For if you do not wish to hide by turning your mind away from these things, then a great necessity of probity <note>meaning virtue</note> is imposed upon you. For that which you do cannot be hidden from Him who is the judge of your acts. Whence he adds: Since you act before the eyes, meaning since your actions are in the sight of the Judge who sees all things, namely God. Note that vices are to be despised because they make a person slavish; for he who commits sin is a slave to sin. And Seneca says: "If I knew the gods would forgive sins and men would be ignorant of them, I would still blush to sin because of the vileness of the sin itself." Virtues, however, are to be cultivated, because virtue is that which makes its possessor perfect and renders his work good. Righteous hope and righteous prayers are to be offered to God, because through these we are joined to God and speak to Him. And if we do not hide by neglecting the aforesaid things, we shall pursue the great excellence of virtue and the promises resulting from it. For all things we do are in the sight of God who sees all; for so it is written in Hebrews chapter four: "All things are naked and open to the eyes of Him" <note>Hebrews 4:13</note> who is God, blessed forever and ever. AMEN.
</gloss>

<summary>This concluding passage of Boethius's work argues that because God exists in an eternal "now," His foreknowledge does not impose necessity on human actions, thereby preserving the moral significance of virtue, prayer, and divine justice.</summary>
<keywords>free will, divine foreknowledge, eternity, virtue, providence, Seneca, Hebrews 4:13, Boethius</keywords>
