<meta>This is the opening preface (Prohemium) of a commentary on the Pseudo-Boethian work "On the Discipline of Scholars." It establishes the philosophical justification for education as a means of elevating the human soul above animalistic passions.</meta>

# Preface.

->The commentary on the divine Severinus Boethius’s *On the Discipline of Scholars*<-
->begins auspiciously.<-

Hermes himself, the father of philosophers, writing to Asclepius <note>original: "esclapiũ"; referring to the Hermetic Corpus</note>, long ago testified that man alone is truly the image of God and the world. This is because he possesses within himself a divine intellect through which he may at times be so elevated above the world that even the material of the world follows his conceptions. We see this most powerfully in men of excellent natural character, who act through their souls to transform the bodies of this world so that they are said to perform miracles. Therefore, in that part where man is made in the image of God—by which he is connected to the world—he is not subject to the world but is placed over it as its ruler and governor. David, that just man, knew this in the book of Psalms when he said: *You have made him a little lower than the angels, etc. You have subjected all things under his feet.* <note>Psalm 8:5-6</note> Indeed, it is clear that this occurs most of all when a man is drawn to the summit of the mind through doctrines and disciplines. There, established in the citadel of the mind, he looks back upon, directs, and governs this mortal body which weighs down the soul, as if from a watchtower. For these reasons, it is considered not without merit that men who are naturally vigorous in art and reason more than others should exist as the lords and rulers of others.

Nevertheless, if through choice or the affect of unbridled inclination a man makes himself inferior to the world, he is then as if stripped of the honor of humanity; thus, transforming himself into the backs of other beasts, he takes on the characteristics of a brute. Thus, through lusts he becomes a pig; through anger, a dog; through plunder, a lion; and through various other vices he transforms into the nature of other beasts. Plato himself called this transformation the "second incorporation of souls." <note>A reference to the Platonic idea of metempsychosis or the soul's descent into lower forms.</note> Yet one should not think this alteration of the mind is merely metaphorical; he who makes himself inferior to the world must necessarily be led away from the distinct repetition of human limbs and appearance. From this it follows, as Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, that those laboring in venereal passions and drunkenness are greatly altered according to the body. A sign of this is that animals that mate frequently age quickly, and more die by the throat <note>i.e., gluttony</note> than by the sword.

Therefore, one must labor with all strength and effort so that man—the very image and specimen of his Creator—is not dragged down from the citadel of the mind by these lusts and affects of indignation, becoming inferior to the world. Instead, he should either eradicate and root out those disturbances which the Greeks call *pathe* <note>original: "pate"; Greek: πάθη (passions/suffering)</note>—namely lusts and the affects of inclinations—or at least break, moderate, and rule them. He must restrain them like unbridled horses with the bits of reason, so to speak, so that what was denied to his fragile and falling nature he may attain through study and discipline, following the example of the great Hippocrates. 

Indeed, as Aristotle says and Albert the Great after him, when his disciples were already marvelling at his most holy character and divine wisdom, they once brought an image of Hippocrates to Philemon the physiognomist <note><term>physiognomist</term>: a practitioner of the historical "science" of judging a person's character from their facial features or body type.</note> to judge the man's character. When Philemon had inspected it with his art, compared limb to limb, and cautiously noted the force of the natural signs which clearly signify things concerning the body and soul, he pronounced that the man was a lecher, a deceiver, and a lover of intercourse. While the disciples were indignant and blamed Philemon for pronouncing such insults against the best man nature could produce, they brought the judgment to Hippocrates. Hippocrates, however, being conscious of his own character and inclinations, confessed that Philemon had spoken the truth; but he said that through the love of philosophy and the desire for honesty, he had conquered the lusts of his heart. Thus, what had been denied by nature, he received through philosophy. For Aristotle taught that philosophy is nothing other than victory and abstinence from concupiscence <note><term>concupiscence</term>: strong desire or lust, often used in a theological context to describe the inclination toward sin.</note>.

# Preface.

...moreover, he called it the best gift, for nothing better could be devised for living well and blessedly <note>original: "bene beateque vivendum"</note>. Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> indeed referred to it as a discovery of the gods, and another likewise called it the parent of all disciplines and the foster-child of the guide of life, which one cannot easily reach without that teachability <note>original: "disciplinabilitate"</note> by which man ought to excel all other living creatures. For these reasons, Severinus Boethius, at the request of Marcianus and for the advancement of those to be educated, published this book, by whose instructions—as if by a certain guide, method, and path—anyone may be led more readily from the cradle, as they say, into the most fertile field of philosophy.

But before we come to the sequence of the book, those things must be set forth which elucidate the cause of the undertaken work, declare the title, show the intention of the author, and the part of philosophy to which the book is subordinated. Regarding the first, therefore—since nothing happens, as Plato judged in the *Timaeus*, whose origin is not preceded by a legitimate cause and reason—four causes of the book must be enumerated: namely, the **final** cause, which is placed first in intention; the **formal**; the **efficient**; and the **material**.

The **material cause**, which is also called the subject because the author's intention is occupied with it, is the aptitude for receiving instruction from a teacher. For Boethius's intention is occupied with this: to render the one to be educated fit to receive the teacher's instruction.

The **final cause**, which is also called the utility of the book, is the benefit of the students; namely, that having read through this book, those who were unrefined <note>original: "rudibus"</note> may be led by its instructions to the knowledge of philosophical truth.

The **efficient cause** is twofold: the moving and the moved. The **moving cause**, in the opinion of some, was Marcianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author famous for an encyclopedia on the liberal arts</note>, who also wrote the book *The Marriage of Mercury and Philology*, and whom Boethius is said to have followed in writing *The Consolation of Philosophy*; however, this is thought to have little weight, since Marcianus himself had emerged so learned in such great doctrine and abundance of writing that if he had perceived anything to be written for the utility of scholars, he would not have doubted that he himself, rather than a substitute, would undergo the work. Nevertheless, it is true that a certain Marcianus—whoever he may be, yet dear to Boethius—enjoined this work upon him, as is clearly known from the preface of the book. For he says: *Your intention knows the matter; I will attempt to comply with your petitions, Marcianus.* And this can be the moving cause of the undertaken work. The **moved efficient cause** is Boethius himself, as will be immediately added in the title of the book itself.

But the **formal cause** of this book, as of other books, is twofold: one is the form of treating <note>the method of argument</note>, the other the form of the treatise <note>the physical structure</note>. The **form of treating** consists in the mode of proceeding, and here the mode is definitive, divisive, and positive in examples, as becomes more clearly known to one looking at the process of the book. The **form of the treatise** is the division of the book into chapters, and of chapters into their parts, and of parts into small sections. And let these things suffice concerning the causes of the book.

Now we must dwell longer on the title of the book, where it should be noted: A **title** is a brief annotation of those things which are contained more diffusely in the following work. And it is named from *Titan*, which is the sun or "the illuminating one," as if "of Titan," since it illuminates the book and declares what follows. The title of the book, therefore, is this: *The book of the illustrious man Anicius Manlius Severinus Torquatus, former consul and ordinary patrician, Boethius, on the discipline of scholars begins happily.*

But perhaps someone may ask why so many names are bestowed upon Boethius. To which it must be answered that it was the custom of the Romans to ascribe the names of their ancestors to themselves, or because these are bestowed upon him for honor and praise. He is called **Anicius** either from a certain Roman of that name, or as if "invincible" <note>A folk etymology: "a-" (without) and "nikos" (victory/conquest)</note>, for he could least of all be conquered; for he never knew himself to be puffed up in prosperity nor depressed in adversity. For he always showed himself with an equal mind, like a "four-square" <note>term: <term>tetragonum</term> (a cube or square). A reference to Aristotle's Ethics, describing a virtuous man who stands upright however he is thrown.</note> which stands upright wherever it is cast. So also Boethius could be conquered neither by love nor by hatred, which he himself testified in the first book, fourth prose of the *Consolation of Philosophy* when he said: *No one ever dragged me from right to wrong.* He was called **Manlius** from Manlius, a Roman of his family. **Torquatus** from a Torquatus of the same...

Indeed, he was called Boethius from *boetus*, which sounds like "helper" <note>Greek: boēthos</note> of the public accounts, as the gloss maintains in the law *Boetos* regarding bookkeepers. From this, the name Boethius took its origin, since he was a co-helper in examining public accounts, as John de Platea says in the said law. Therefore, these names, surnames, or family names were attributed to Boethius either by kinship, friendship, or certainly by chance, just as a plurality of names was attributed to other Romans, such as Marcus Tullius Cicero, Publius Virgilius Maro, etc. It is added in the title "On the Discipline of Scholars" so that the intention of the author may be introduced. For when Boethius himself had seen almost innumerable students panting for learning beyond measure, order, and rule—and for that reason emerging as very little learned—he took pity on the common utility of the unrefined. To counter such disorder, he established a method and form of learning in this book. In this work, he decided that the first elements must be provided to the unrefined; he advised that adults be subjected to discipline and the mastership; he restrains the proud; he refreshes those making progress with wise foresight; he renders those provided for venerable to the mastership; and finally, he concludes with the status of the masters themselves toward their subjects. It is added in the title "begins happily." "Happily," I say, as much by that happiness which is the highest good as by that which consists in the goods of fortune. For this book is a step and a ladder by which one arrives at the knowledge of truth, which is wisdom; once attained, all goods—both of fortune and of the soul—are attained along with it, as Solomon himself testifies. Finally, it must be seen to which part of philosophy it is subordinated. It is subordinated to Ethics, because it speaks of the behavior of the student toward the teacher, which is reduced to Ethics. Therefore, these five things have been declared, if you consider rightly, which are frequently recited in the manner of authors at the beginnings of books, and are contained in these verses: *The utility, the title, the intention, the part of wisdom, and the four causes completing the whole matter.* For which reason, let us approach the letter of the text.

# Preface

The Preface <note>original: "Prohemium"</note> is divided into three parts. In the first, the author sets forth his intention and adds the reason for that intention. In the second, he previews the order to be followed in this work. In the third, he establishes the method of proceeding. The second part begins at "First of all"; the third at "This, however." The first part is further divided into two: in the first, he does what was mentioned by stating his intention; in the second, he assigns the cause of the intention at the point beginning "for because of the schools."

<column-break/>

The first part is again divided into two. In the first, he does what was mentioned. In the second, he avoids arrogance at the point "O, would that." And Boethius <note>The text refers to Boethius, the 6th-century philosopher, though modern scholars attribute this specific work to a 13th-century author.</note> says, "O Marcian," and in this he wins his goodwill by calling him by his own name. "Your intention has known how to demand," that is, to ask for, "a compendious treatise," that is, brief

<column-break/>

**ability is available, as well as the decline of my genius and the tenacity of my hardships: I will attempt to comply with your friendly requests, Marcian. And although I am hindered by a double kind of commentary—yet not altogether of different sorts—on certain editions of Aristotle as well as other philosophers**

---

and useful; and this is said in contrast to "wasteful," which is judged to be wordy and useless. In this, he encourages the listener toward docility <note>In a medieval context, "docility" means a readiness or openness to be taught.</note> through the compendium of teaching on the *Discipline of Scholars*, that is, the norm of learning. In this, he makes the listener attentive through the utility of the teaching. And so, in this first part, he does three things: he wins goodwill, he encourages docility, and he arouses the attention of the listeners. 

It follows: "O, would that"—understand "it were requested"—"from the smallness of my spirit," that is, of my genius; for in this, he avoids arrogance. Then Boethius says he accepts the burden of writing. "Notwithstanding the smallness of my genius, I, Boethius, will attempt to comply," that is, to condescend, "to your friendly requests, and this according to," that is, insofar as, "my faculty," that is, my wisdom, "is available," that is, supplies it, "and insofar as the decline," that is, the weakness of my genius—which stands for "and"—"and the tenacity," that is, the hardness or the weight of my hardships, that is, my calamities—understand "are available." 

"Although I am hindered"—understand "so that I cannot easily accomplish it"—"by a double kind," that is, manner, "of commentaries," that is, of certain books explained; "yet not altogether," that is, entirely, "of different commentaries, I say, on certain editions," that is, compilations, "of Aristotle, that Peripatetic, and of other philosophers," by explaining them—understand—and by translating some from Greek into Latin. 

Which stands for "and": "although I am thinned out," that is, exhausted in strength by my own study, so that I can hardly find time for my promises; "and although I am gnawed," that is, thinned out—and he speaks metaphorically, for "to gnaw" properly means to tear with the teeth—"by the torture," that is, the torment, "of the inhuman," that is, cruel, "King of the Goths, namely Theodoric" <note>Theodoric the Great, who imprisoned and eventually executed the historical Boethius.</note>; and this while the *Consolation of Philosophy*—that is, the book he had published concerning the consolation of philosophy—was arriving. 

Which stands for "and": "although I am thoroughly worn down," that is, thinned out, "by the extreme," that is, the highest, "investigation," that is, the subtlety, "of the Trinity," which is "profound," that is, deep to understand. He says this as if to say: "Although I am hindered by all these things beyond my strength, nevertheless, because there is such force of friendship between us that I can deny you none of your requests, I will therefore attempt to comply with your petitions." 

It should be noted that Boethius names his book *On the Discipline of Scholars*. Hence, the difference between "discipline" <term>disciplina: the act of receiving knowledge</term> and "faculty" <term>facultas: the settled mastery of a subject</term> is this: "discipline" is named from "learning," which sounds like receiving knowledge, wherefore discipline is in the student. "Teaching" <note>original: "doctrina"</note>, however, is in the teacher. "Faculty" is the knowledge or profession in both. Discipline and teaching are in motion; faculty is at rest.

-># Prologue<-

It should be noted regarding what is said here, that Boethius, in his double role as a commentator, understood that men were born not merely for themselves, but for their friends, their country, and the common utility of all. Indeed, the divine Plato warned Archytas of Tarentum <note>A Greek mathematician and philosopher, friend of Plato</note> to remember that he was not born for himself alone, but for his country and his kin, so that only a very small part of himself was left for his own use. Foreseeing this, Boethius—wishing to leave behind an eternal memorial for posterity—

exhausted by his own studies and gnawed by the torture of the cruel King of the Goths <note>Theodoric the Great, who imprisoned and eventually executed Boethius</note>, yet softened by the preceding consolation of philosophy and the profound perception of the Trinity. For what is more luminous in the training of the gymnasiums <note>term: gymnasium; here referring to schools of higher learning or philosophical exercise</note> than the proper knowledge of artificial and natural progression, and the gradual exhibition of the powers of the intellect? For of eloquence...

<column-break/>

...he spent his days and nights: now in explaining the books of the philosophers; now in translating Greek manuscripts so that they might speak to us openly in Latin <note>original: "latine"</note>; and now in the tradition of his own works. In this matter, he was held day by day with such great effort and such great nocturnal study <note>term: lucubratio; study or work performed by lamplight at night</note> that it gave material for his accusation. For while he was diligently free for study and for the commentaries of the books to be explained, and for all other things pertaining to these, it became his habit to flee the company of men and retreat into the library which he had established at home,

filled with philosophy. For these reasons, those envious of his character falsely accused him of speaking with demons, in the likeness of the great Socrates—of whom Apuleius also believed, without punishment, that he had a familiar god <note>note: a "daimon" or guiding spirit</note> obedient to him, about which he even published a book entitled *On the God of Socrates*. Excusing himself from this accusation in the first book of the *Consolation of Philosophy*, in the fourth prose, Boethius addresses Philosophy thus: "But you also drove from the seat of our mind the desire for all mortal things, and under your eyes there was no place for sacrilege. For you instilled daily into my ears and thoughts that Pythagorean saying: 'One must serve God, not gods.' <note>original: "Deo nō diis seruiendum"</note> Nor was it fitting for me to seek the protection of the vilest spirits, you who fashioned me into such excellence that you might make me similar to God." Thus he spoke. It should be noted: **Talent** <note>original: "Ingenium"</note> is the interior power of the mind by which we often find what we have not learned from others; it is so called as if "born within," namely from nature. Note **Hardship** <note>original: "erūna"</note>, that is, misery, want, or calamity. It is derived from *e* and *rumen*, as if "outside of food" <note>note: a medieval folk etymology linking misery to a lack of nourishment</note>; hence "wretched." Likewise, a **Commentary** <note>original: "commentum"</note> is a collection into one of things held in the mind by the study or teaching of many; according to this, any book can be called a commentary. But in our usage, a commentary is called an expository book, namely one which serves the explanation of the meaning of some book and not the construction of the literal grammar. According to this, it can be defined thus: A commentary is an explanation of words that does not consider the joining of the words, but the sense. **For what in the gymnasiums.** In this part, Boethius assigns the cause of his intention and of the work undertaken: for first he says that, notwithstanding the impediments of both his studies and his many hardships, he wishes to take up the burden enjoined upon him.

From this, "gymnasium" is the place in which such things formerly happened; and from this, by a metaphor, the study of scholars and masters is called "gymnas," and the place of study is called "gymnasium." And sometimes the study itself is so called, as in the present case; because just as the body is exercised in the wrestling floor, so the soul is exercised in study. <meta>This page continues the introductory preface (Prohemium) of a pedagogical or philosophical treatise, likely from the late medieval period, focusing on the definitions of learning spaces and the psychological faculties of the mind.</meta>

-># Preface<-

An exercise or a place of exercise may be called a **gymnasium**, just as a school is. And as some say, *gymnasium* is the Greek word for what is called *exercitium* <note>original: "exercitium"; meaning exercise or practice</note> in Latin. It should be noted that there is a difference between **understanding**, **intelligence**, and **intelligibility**. For **understanding** <note>original: "intellectus"</note> is properly the power of the soul capable of grasping incorporeal substances stripped of their forms, or the forms surrounding them. **Intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentia"</note>, however, is the power of the soul that aspires to comprehend something concerning the divine substance.

...must be restrained by the commendation of examples, by explaining them distinctly.
**Fourth**, concerning the wise provision for students and their gradual standing. **Fifth**, how the venerable and sincere devotion of students is to be brought toward mastery. **Sixth**, concerning the rule for those becoming masters, its threefold division, their status toward subordinates, and the previously known method of teaching. We have undertaken these things to be carried out for the recognition of intelligence, almost omitting the ancient method of treating them—

<column-break/>

...comprehends. **Intelligibility** <note>original: "intelligibilitas"</note> is a certain power of the soul that enfolds all forms in a kind of simplicity, without natural or temporal order; and in such a way, God alone comprehends things, because He is said to comprehend them all in a single intuition without succession.
**"In the first place, the first [matter] of boys,"** etc. This is the second principal part of this preface, in which, after he has explained his intention and the cause of his intention, he now clearly suggests the order of the work undertaken and whatever must be carried out in the entire process of the book. The second part begins there: "secondly, namely"; the third there: "thirdly, concerning those"; the fourth there: "fourthly, concerning the students"; the fifth there: "fifthly, how"; the sixth there: "sixthly, concerning those becoming masters," etc.
And he says that **in the first place**, i.e., in the first chapter, the delights—otherwise called the "delights," i.e., the light instructions—of boys are to be tasted beforehand, i.e., treated beforehand or put first. And **Albert** <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval philosopher and teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note> provides the reason for this in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle's "Physica"</note> when he says that boys first call all men "fathers," etc., because boys themselves have a brain that is moist and cold, such that they are least able to grasp the differences between sensible things. But when the brain in them becomes drier, then cognition will be better known to them. Therefore, one must begin from the easier and more common things according to the order of teaching itself, and transcend to the more difficult and more specific; for this path is innate to us, according to the first book of the *Physics*.
**Secondly**, it will be seen—that is, in the second chapter—how the elation, i.e., the pride, of adults—that is, those already mature in age—is to be subjected, i.e., placed under a master, and connected, i.e., joined, to discipline. For elation and pride in no way allow a student to study, since the Wise Man says: *The spirit of wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul.* <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note>
And hence in the **third** chapter, he teaches about restraining, i.e., correcting, the elation of those adults, and this by explaining distinctly, i.e., succinctly, a commendation of examples to prove the point.
In the **fourth** chapter, it will be treated (supply: "further") concerning the sagacious, i.e., provident, provision—namely, of external things, without which it is difficult to practice philosophy; for which reason the priests in Egypt, as **Aristotle** testifies in the *Metaphysics*, having acquired the necessary things, were able to...

# Preface

...philosophers first began to wonder. In the fifth chapter, it will be determined how a venerable—that is, honorable—and sincere—that is, pure—devotion—that is, intention—of a student is to be brought forth—that is, displayed or offered—toward the **mastery** <note>The "magisterium" or rank of Master.</note>. In the sixth chapter, the standard of the one acting as master will be treated, as well as the threefold division—that is, partitioning—of masters, and their status regarding those under them, once the method of teaching—that is, informing—has been learned beforehand.

<margin>Note: "Sagacious" of every kind is the same as talented, far-seeing, shrewd, and foreknowing of future things; hence "sagacity." Likewise, "sincere" (sincerus, sincera, sincerum) is used in the same sense as "without wax," namely pure, constant, clean, without vice or stain; the 'e' is pronounced long. Whence **Horace** says in his Epistles, at the end of the second epistle: "Unless the vessel is sincere [clean], whatever you pour in turns sour." Likewise **Virgil** in *The Salad*: "It settles sincerely and is strained through the holes."</margin>

->**...sending forth things never before practiced in a lighter style. Since the execution is for the most part for the sake of informing the unrefined, the translation for the sake of clarifying must be that much lighter.**<-

->The preface ends.<-

->The treatise follows.<-

**"You shall sow cleansed seeds,"** and so forth. This pertains to the recognition of intelligence. This is the third principal part of this preface in which **Boetius** <note>The text attributes this to the 6th-century philosopher Boethius, though modern scholars identify this specific work as a 13th-century pedagogical manual.</note> promises the method of proceeding in this book. It is divided into two parts. In the first, he does what was just said. In the second, he assigns the cause for what was said, beginning at "Since in the greater part," etc. And he speaks thus: "Certainly we, Boetius, have undertaken these aforementioned things to be carried out—that is, perfected—for the commendation of intelligence; we, I say, sending forth almost entirely our former method—that is, the way of treating or writing usually observed by us—having never at any time practiced a lighter—that is, a plainer—style or way of writing." And here he assigns the cause for what was said: because the execution (understand: of the present work) is for the most part for the sake of informing—that is, instructing—the unrefined—that is, the unlearned—by which path they may be able to reach the summit of the sciences. Therefore, this translation (another version says "transaction") for the sake of clarifying—that is, declaring—this path and track will be that much lighter—that is, plainer. **It should be noted** that in the text a rhetorical figure is employed called <term>lepos</term> <note>A term for charm or elegance in speech; here referring to the "royal we."</note>. This is a manner of speaking to a single person using a plural verb for the sake of honor or ornament, as when **Cicero** writes "you [plural] might write." Thus, "We, Boetius, have undertaken these things to be carried out."

**"Since the undiscerning,"** etc. The preface being finished, the treatise consequently begins, in which he now carries out in an orderly fashion those things he promised to do in the preface. The whole treatise is divided into six chapters. In the first, he shows in what manner the unrefined and undiscerning are introduced to learning. In the second, how the students themselves are subjected to the master. In the third, how the pride of the arrogant is restrained. In the fourth, how he might sagaciously provide for those students through external things, as if Fortune were the mistress. In the fifth, how the sincere devotion of a student may be raised to the loftiness of the mastery.

It is established that Boethius <note>The text refers to the Pseudo-Boethius, the presumed author of this medieval educational manual.</note> himself divided it in this order in the prologue, although many exist who think the entire book should be divided into three parts.

### Chapter One.
**W**hen, however, the seven-year infancy of the undiscerning and powerless is led to

first, those things which concern the external aspects of the one being introduced—namely, concerning the body and things adjacent to the body—are treated. In the second, however, those things concerning the mind and those things adorning and nourishing the mind, such as doctrines and sciences, are taught. The second part begins at: *In the first things, therefore.* The first division is further divided into two. In the first, he determines those things which must be observed concerning the body of the one being introduced before he is delivered over to doctrine. In the second, those things which must be observed concerning the body itself after he has been newly delivered to doctrine are discussed. The second part begins at: *Of the librarians, however.* The first of these is again divided into two. In the first, he does what was said. In the second, he confirms this very thing with examples. The second part begins at: *It is read.* The first of these is again in two parts: for first he declares those things which must be avoided concerning the limbs of the body of the one being introduced. Second, those things concerning the time of introduction. The second part begins at: *And lest the intemperance of the time.*

Boethius says first that when infancy—that is, childhood of seven years <note>original: "septennis"</note> (and at this age infancy ends and childhood begins)—of the undiscerning—that is, the untaught—and the powerless—understand "in bodily strength"—is led to be imbued—that is, educated—care must be taken—that is, foreseen—lest the disposition—understand "natural"—of the limbs—supply "of the infantile body"—the integral parts—that is, the integrating parts such as the hands and feet and likewise of the other limbs—be unseemly—that is, disordered, imperfect, disproportionate, or naturally base. And understand that care must be taken when that undiscerning one is led to be imbued lest the intemperance—that is, the disproportion by reason of the quality of the dominant season—such as for instance the bluntness—that is, the hardness of winter <note>original: "hyemis"</note>—constricting because of excessive cold, the nature of which is to shatter things of the same kind; or the depth—that is, the excess of summer—scorched <note>original: "combustis"</note> because of the excellence of heat, generates an increase—that is, an augmentation of danger—understand "to the one being introduced." For these very things, unless they are provided for quite cautiously, bring great increases of danger to childish tenderness.

It should be noted in this that Boethius says "seven-year infancy," etc. He makes it understood that boys themselves are to be delivered <note>original: "mancipandus," a legal term for formal transfer or enslavement, here used for dedication to study.</note> to letters in infancy. For that age is fit for this because it has as yet seen little, wherefore all things are new to it, and it is greedy for new things; and whatever it hears, it wonders at, doubts, and asks about. Thus, after the strength of the mind has been taken up, it may more firmly retain and more clearly understand what the "new jar" <note>A reference to Horace: "The jar will long keep the fragrance of what it was once steeped in when new."</note> had received. Indeed, at this age, as Quintilian touches upon in the first book of the *Institutes*, whatever is conceived takes root more easily. Whence it is said in various proverbs: *The vessels taste of whatever they first received.* So, he says, it is with infants. And Augustine, in the first book of the *Confessions*, lamentably confesses of himself that he always exposed his youth to games and not to studies: "I was put into school," he says, "to learn letters in which I..."

# Chapter

I was ignorant, wretch that I was, of what use it might be, but I delighted in play. And this is **infancy** itself, the first of the ages of man, which lasts for a seven-year period; beginning from this is **boyhood**, which is, as it were, pure and least suited for procreation, extending into the fourteenth year. From that point begins adult **adolescence**, suited for procreation, which is extended to the twenty-eighth year. From there **youth** begins, stretching up to the fiftieth year, and from this the age of the **elder**, which the Greeks call *presbytes* <note>original: "presbite"; referring to the Greek word for elder</note>, <margin>taking its origins, it proceeds into **old age**, which is the seventieth year; this is completed by no set number of years, but after those five ages, whatever of life remains is assigned to labor and sorrow.</margin> It must be noted <insert>for one who is to be educated, care must be taken lest there be an unseemly disposition of the limbs, such as the integral parts, or a sharp intemperance of weather, such as the numbness of a pinching winter or the burning of summer.</insert> that Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher</note> says the greatest care must be taken lest the one to be imbued with letters has a [poor] disposition of the limbs. For it is necessary to judge an unsuitably monstrous arrangement of the limbs as a monster in the soul, as Philemon, Palemon, Loxus, Aristotle, and many others have reported. For souls themselves follow their bodies, and in themselves they are not impassive to the motions of the bodies; and this becomes very manifest in cases of drunkenness and sickness. For they seem to change the mind greatly by bodily passions, from which that common proverb took its origin: *A churl in body is a churl in soul.* <note>original: "Rusticus in corpore rusticus et in anima"</note> For since the figure and habit of the limbs are both generated and nourished from the blood—and similarly the spirits, which are the vehicles of the virtues of the soul, are generated from the moisture of the blood—it follows that the inclinations of the passions may be known from the very habit of the limbs, and the soul itself, being carried, follows the motion of its carrier in many things. Because of this, the wise Ptolemy <note>The famous Greco-Egyptian astronomer and geographer</note> said that a diviner pronounces better and more truly when receiving judgment from the "favorable stars," calling the "favorable stars" the figures and accidents found in physical things which are impressed by the higher [celestial] powers. For we know this is already impressed upon the matter, wherefore we pronounce for certain that the whole is inclined toward those accidents; thus it happens that we say those soft in flesh are fit in mind, and that a distorted face follows a distortion of morals.

It should be noted concerning this that he says: *And lest the intemperance of the time, etc.* Just as Avicenna <note>The Persian physician Ibn Sina, author of the "Canon of Medicine"</note> teaches in the second section of the first Canon, chapter four of the first sum (which is on the judgments of times and their changes), every time that has a healthy complexion is proportional and suitable. But since the complexion of infancy exists in a nearly temperate heat and a nearly superfluous humidity (as in the same Canon, section 1, first doctrine, chapter 2), it is suitable that for his instruction he choose a time proportional to his nature. This, however, among the four seasons of the year, is **Spring**, beginning from the equinoctial point and continuing until it reaches the middle of Taurus, [where] it is exchanged for Summer. For this time is more temperate on earth, because warming things are not so necessary on account of cold that much care must be taken, nor is ventilation [needed] on account of heat. And in this season is the beginning of trees putting forth leaves; and its time among physicians is the "vernal equality," existing either before or after the preparation itself until the sun is in the middle of Taurus, although among astronomers it extends right to the summer tropic, after which time Autumn is closer to temperance. The remaining two times [Winter and Summer] are subject to intemperance, either by excessive cold or abundant heat. Thus it happens that weak infancy should be committed to letters either in Spring or Autumn, but more so in Spring.

# First Part

For it is read that the son of Timothy... In this section, **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval education.</note> corroborates the aforementioned points with examples; namely, how even the slightest neglect of superior factors gives rise to a great increase in danger. ->that the depth of danger generates an increase.<-
**It is read that the son of Timothy, while leprosy was pressing upon him, was castrated, club-footed, and swollen with a hunchback; though devoted to teaching, he became a lowly outcast of the common people and a ridiculous object of disparagement among his companions. Likewise, we have seen the son of a suburban praetor devoted to his letters while the Dog Star was inciting the heat. However, when he did not enjoy his accustomed shade, being destitute of his own strength and crushed by the penalty of jaundice, at last, with his vital spirits thinned, he succumbed to a lymphatic disease. Behold how much difficulty...**

<column-break/>

...in the example, the son of Timothy was castrated, that is, deprived of his testicles, and this while leprosy—that disease—was "incumbent," meaning imminent or pressing upon him. He was "club-footed" <term>loripes: literally 'thong-footed,' referring to someone with twisted or paralyzed legs</term>, that is, lame or with a twisted foot; and "swelling with a hunchback," that is, a tumor or hump on the back. Though "devoted," meaning handed over, to "teaching," he became an "outcast," meaning an object of contempt, of the "common people," and a "ridiculous disparagement"—that is, a mockery—of his own companions. "Likewise"—supply here another example—"we have seen the little son of a praetor," that is, a suburban provost, devoted to "letters" while the "Dog Star" <note>original: "canicula," referring to Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, associated with the sweltering 'dog days' of summer.</note>—that star—was "inciting," that is, raging. "However"—certainly—when that little son of the praetor...

<column-break/>

...did not "enjoy," that is, make use of, his "accustomed shade," meaning his usual umbrella or parasol, he himself, "destitute," meaning abandoned by his own strength, and "crushed," that is, afflicted by the "penalty," meaning the disease, of "jaundice" <note>original: "hictericie," from the Greek 'ikteros,' a yellowing of the skin.</note>, at last—finally—being "thinned," that is, consumed in his "vital spirits," he "succumbed"—closed his life—to a "lymphatic disease," that is, a watery disease which is "dropsy" <term>idropisis: an old medical term for edema or the buildup of fluid in the body</term>. And the rest follows: "Behold," that is, see, how much difficulty the "indisposition of the limbs"—supply in the son of Timothy—and the "intemperance of the air"—understand in the son of the praetor—brought upon "childish tenderness." For the former became an outcast of the common people, while the latter miserably closed the day of his life with infirmities.

Note regarding what is said about the **Dog Star**. There is a double dog in the heavens: the Greater and the Lesser. The Greater is called by another name, **Sirius**, and has 18 stars in its form and 11 outside of it. The Lesser is named **Anticanis** and has 2 stars. When the sun enters the Greater Dog, the heat is doubled and sicknesses are generated in human bodies, by which many perish at their end; from this dog, the "dog days" are named. Regarding this, **Persius** <note>A Roman satirist (34–62 AD).</note> says: "now the dry Dog Star parches the harvests." And by poetic license, it is feigned that Hecuba was transformed into this dog. It should be noted that **leprosy** is a similar disease corrupting the figure, form, and composition of the limbs, and thus finally dissolving the continuity of the body itself, arising from melancholic matter dispersed through the whole body. And this is introduced either from the womb or afterward.

# Chapter.

If [leprosy is contracted] from the womb, this is because the person was conceived during the time of menstruation, or because he is the son of a leper, or because a leper had intercourse with the pregnant woman. If it occurs after the womb, this can be because the air is bad, corrupt, and pestilential, or because he continued to eat melancholic foods <note>In medieval medicine, "melancholic" foods were thought to produce black bile, leading to illness or depression.</note>, namely lentils and other legumes, and melancholic meats such as fox, bear, and wild boar, and so forth. It should be noted that Jaundice <note>original: "Ictericia"</note> is a universal discoloration of the skin, just as

morphea <note>A skin condition involving painless, discolored patches.</note> is a spotted discoloration of the skin. § However, they differ in this: morphea is due to an error of the third digestion <note>The "third digestion" refers to the process where nutrients are assimilated into the tissues.</note>; here, jaundice is due to an error of the second [digestion, occurring in the liver]. And there are three species of it: namely yellow, green, and black. And

<column-break/>

**the unseemly indisposition of the power of the limbs and the intemperance of the air have contributed to the tenderness of childhood. Let there be a moderate supply of food. Let the drink be thin, and let there be a scarcity of the same. Similarly, let there be no lack of clothing.**

<column-break/>

dropsy <note>original: "ydropis"; an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note> frequently follows this disease, which is an error of the uniting power in the whole body following a change in the digestive power in the liver. And thus dropsy is an error of the digestive power in the liver. Likewise, "lozipes" means lame, having a twisted foot like a "lozi" <note>likely referring to a cross-shaped or slanted gait</note> or having a wooden foot bound with straps, of whom Juvenal says: *The upright man laughs at the twisted-foot <note>original: "lozipedem"</note>, the white man at the Ethiopian.* Likewise, "gibbus" means a hump, but there is a difference: for a "struma" <note>a goiter or swelling</note> is on the chest, while a "gibbus" is on the back. Whence Juvenal: *swelling with a goiter and likewise with a humped womb.* Regarding "Of Books" <note>original: "Liborum autem"</note>: In this part, Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher; the text here comments on his "De Disciplina Scholarium".</note> treats those things which must be considered regarding a newly introduced student, namely the proper provision of food, drink, and clothing, and this in general. In the third chapter, he speaks more specifically. And he says that certainly the supply of food should be moderate, namely neither abundant nor deficient. Let the drink be thin—add "and"—and let there be a smallness, that is, a moderation of it, and let a "penuria," that is, a lack of clothing, be absent. It should be noted that nature by itself is not sufficient for contemplation, but it is necessary for food and drink and other service to exist beforehand. But these should in no way be excessive, since nature is content with moderate and very small things, as stated in the second book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose five. Therefore, hunger must be tolerated, as Seneca says in his 15th letter, which certain people tolerated during a siege following the example of our ancestors, who traversed lands and seas not so that honeyed wine and precious food might pass through their throats, but being devoted to contemplation alone, they preferred to eat to live rather than live to eat. For tyrannies and the subversions of cities and wars, whether hostile or civil, as Jerome testifies in his letters, were not stirred up for a simple diet of vegetables and fruits—as Diogenes asserted—but for meats and feasting on delicacies. Let us read the books of our predecessors and the volumes of the ancients: of Dicaearchus, Xenophon, Josephus, Eubulus, and almost all others who write history, and we shall find nothing else but that those ancients, for the sake of study, avoided cheap foods and those only in moderation; they also utterly avoided gluttony and delicacies as impediments to contemplation. For delicacies themselves cast the mind down to the ground and, held back by the sinews of the body, they prevent it from being raised to the peak of contemplation. Moderate living, on the other hand, does the opposite, which is why Juvenal says a hungry jackdaw rises into the sky. Persius Flaccus also says: *The parrot and the magpies attempt to try our words.* Juvenal says of the jackdaw: *The hungry jackdaw, if you bid it, will go to heaven.* And likewise of the others, Persius says: *Who smoothed the way for the parrot's "hello"? Who taught the crows and the magpies to say our words?*

The first again into two: first he does what was said; second, how much time should be spent on this kind of education (at the word "Nor in such laborious"). And Boethius says first that the love of the figures representing the elements—that is, the letters—must be impressed upon the raw students in the first place—that is, in the beginning—because through the joining—that is, the combination—of the letters to be joined (understand: for the purpose of making syllables and words), the joining, I say, is not a little skillful—that is, very much so—and he touches there on the higher things. Then he adds the time which should be spent in this study, saying: nor must one insist—that is, linger—much in such laborious struggle—that is, study—nor must one depart—that is, withdraw—quickly, as it pleases that foolish master and is the case with parents (understand: if the boy seems more prompt—that is, more capable—and by frequent use of the aforesaid things in many ways—that is, much—then he is guided more subtly in other sciences, understand: higher ones). It should be noted that Boethius says the raw students are first to be imbued in grammar, and the reason for this is that, as Al-Farabi <note>original: "Alforabius," referring to the 10th-century philosopher Al-Farabi, known for his work on the classification of the sciences.</note> wishes, grammar itself is the mother of the other arts, which took its name from letters. For grammar is named from *gramma*, which is "letter," and *ricos*, "science" <note>A medieval etymology: "gramma" (Greek for letter) + "ricos" (a corruption of "logos" or "scientia").</note>. For it is through this that human concepts and all doctrines are finally signified more aptly and freely. Necessity invented this; for since before its invention men spoke inordinately and according to their whim and without art, it happened that they expressed their concepts less well; but they were also less able to understand aptly, whereby it happened that they could hand down sciences more slowly and with more difficulty. For which reason the wise took care to remove these inconveniences; and they handed down a skillful, uniform, and congruent way of speaking, so that all human concepts and all doctrines might finally be signified and learned more freely through the same art. It should be noted that Boethius calls all letters "elements," and not incongruously; for just as the elements themselves are the principles of all things composed of elements, so letters are the principles of all words and of the three parts of speech. Whereby it happens that just as from a diverse mixture of elements diverse species of composed things are made, so also from a diverse combination of letters a diverse representation of voices, words, and sentences is made. And we know these letters to be of many kinds: for some are Hebrew, others Chaldean, others Egyptian, others Greek, others Latin. The inventor of the Hebrew letters, which they say were the first, was Moses; and they are twenty-two in number. However, it is believed that Abraham invented the letters of the Syrians and Chaldeans, which agree with the Hebrew letters in number and sound, differing only in their characters. But the letters of the Egyptians...

# First

Queen Isis, the daughter of Inachus, coming from Greece into Egypt, discovered [letters] and handed them down to the Egyptians. <note>Isis was often conflated with the Greek figure Io in medieval mythography.</note> However, the Phoenicians first discovered the use of Greek letters. Whence Lucan says: *The Phoenicians were the first, if rumor is believed, who dared to mark sounds with unpolished figures.* <note>original: "Fenices primi fame si creditur ausi. Mensuram rudibus vocéq; signare figuris." from Lucan's Pharsalia.</note> But Cadmus, the son of Agenor, brought fifteen Greek letters from Phoenicia into Greece; to which Ipomedes <note>Likely a corruption of Palamedes, traditionally credited with adding letters during the Trojan War.</note> added three during the Trojan war. After which Simonides, the inventor of artificial memory, added three others.

As for Latin letters, as Isidore reports (who holds the greatest authority in these matters), the nymph Carmentis first delivered them to the Italians; however, she only provided seventeen letters, which are: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, i, l, m, n, o, p, r, s, t, u. <note>Isidore of Seville was the primary encyclopedist of the Middle Ages.</note> Afterward, the letter "h" was added as a mark of aspiration. In the process of time, the Latins also invented the letter "q," in place of which the ancients used to write "c." Furthermore, Salustius the schoolmaster first devised "k" to be used where the ancients wrote "c" and "q."

<column-break/>

## [The student] must persist and not depart quickly, as Servius suggests; for if he is seen to be more prompt in many things, he is then found to be even more capable in others. The second building-block of this laborious struggle stands upon the traditions of Probus and Didymus, as well as other philosophers whom venerable authority commends. It must be noted, however, that in this way the Latin tradition should be subject to a faithful resolution, and the native language of the learner should be explained word-for-word. For the tenacity of the foundation...

Furthermore, from the time of Augustus, the letter "x" was added. And finally, in the time of the same Augustus, the Latins borrowed two letters from the Greeks: namely "y" and "z," for the sake of better writing Greek names. When all these are joined together, it is manifest that the Latin language is completed with twenty-three letters. 

**The second [building-block] of the laborious [struggle].** In this part, he shows how the unrefined <term>rudes: beginners or uneducated students</term> ought to be instructed after the first elements of grammar and the combinations of those elements. And he does two things: first, he does what has been said; second, he determines the manner and time of this kind of instruction, where he says "it must be noted." And he calls it the "second building-block"—indeed, "building-block" is said by a certain metaphor. For just as a wise architect completes a house to be built in an orderly way from the smallest and most fundamental parts, so also the master himself ought to complete the student with individual particles of doctrine as a foundation and base. 

Therefore, that "second building-block of the laborious struggle" (that is, of this study) "stands" (that is, is strengthened) in the "traditions" (namely, the writings) of "Probus and Didymus" (these grammarians) and of others whom "venerable authority commends." Then he shows the method to be observed in these traditions, saying: "Certainly it must be noted" (that is, considered) in these traditions just mentioned, that the "Latin tradition should be subject to" (that is, correspond to) a "faithful resolution" (that is, exposition and declaration); so that, for instance, unknown things are not interpreted through things even more unknown, or one thing for another. And it must be noted that the <term>idioma: the property of speaking or native tongue</term> of the learner should be "explained word-for-word" (that is, from word to word). "For" (meaning because) it is "necessary" (that is, opportune) for the "tenacity" (that is, the firmness) of the "foundation" (namely, of grammar, and consequently of all other arts) to consist in these aforementioned traditions. It is as if he says: since these things are so, it is opportune that these things be faithfully [taught].

# Chapter
<margin>B</margin>

...and they should teach how to give. It should be noted that there were many principal writers of our grammar, such as Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, a 4th-century grammarian whose work was a staple of medieval education.</note>, whose teacher is said to have been Didymus, as placed in the text. Also Priscian, Varro, and Quintilian, and many others besides. Among these may be numbered Ennius, who was the first to compose meters, succeeded by Anathero, Sappho, Archilochus, Simonides of Colophon, Asclepius, and many others whom it would be tedious to recount. Their writings—if not all, then at least some of the lighter ones—should be examined after the first elements of study.

In these matters, one must dwell diligently. One must not depart with the "monthly leap of Phoebe" <note>original: "menstruoso saltu phebes"; referring to the moon's quick cycle</note>, nor should one be confirmed by the "solar course" alone. Rather, one must linger diligently for the completed interval of Mercury, and that same interval nearly doubled. For by diligence, the bluntness of any work is softened.

<column-break/>

**"Nor with the monthly."** Here he adds how much time one should linger in this second order of learning. He says one must not depart—that is, withdraw—from the study and struggle of the aforementioned traditions with a "monthly"—that is, defective—"leap," meaning the course of the moon which is completed in a month. Nor should one linger only for a "solar course," which is a year, for the movement of the sun is completed through a year. Rather, one must linger diligently

for the "completed"—that is, whole—"interval," meaning the movement of that planet Mercury; and not just once, but with that same interval "nearly doubled." And because Mercury completes its course in two years <note>In medieval geocentric astronomy, Mercury's cycle was often calculated differently than modern orbital periods; here the author suggests a two-year cycle</note>, which when doubled makes four, it is clear that one should linger diligently in the traditions of the superior teachers for four years. I say "diligently" because the "bluntness"—that is, the dullness—of performing any work is "softened"—that is, made easy—by diligence. It should be noted that although according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the eighth book of the *Politics*, it is useful and commendable to participate sometimes in the liberal and mathematical arts (the use of which is ordained for the exercise of excellent doctrines up to a certain limit), nevertheless, to exercise oneself in them continuously and assiduously unto any kind of perfection is sometimes harmful. This is because continuous consideration of them withdraws a person, either entirely or in part, from the practice of moral virtue. Therefore, a limit is established for how long one should linger in them and in each of them. It should be noted, as has already been proven many times in philosophical and mathematical matters, that the sidereal bodies themselves—both of the planets' orbs and of the eighth heaven, which Aristotle judged to be the "first movable"—receive their brightness from the sun. For the sun itself is the source of light, as witnessed by the vastness of its body, which, as Ptolemy taught, exceeds the earth one hundred and sixty-six times. Similarly, there is a most unified power in it, which the density of its body proves. Likewise, light is diffused in it, which its situation in the middle of the orbs demonstrates. However, there is a difference among bodies in the manner of receiving this kind of light. For some receive it in their depths, such as transparent and <term>diaphanous</term> <note>transparent or translucent</note> bodies, as are the bodies of almost all stars. Others receive it only on the surface, such as opaque bodies, of which number the moon is one. In whatever way they receive it, however, it is necessary that they be positioned against the projection of the light rays. And the more they are distanced from the projection of such rays, the more they fail in that light...

# Second

It thus happens that we consider the moon alone among the celestial bodies to be "monthly," that is, failing or deficient, both in relation to us and in the truth of the matter. In terms of the truth, this is because the interposition of the earth’s diameter prevents it from being illuminated by the rays of light, which clouds it over—as is manifest in an eclipse. In relation to us, however, it occurs when it is renewed for us. The ancients also named the time of this revolution a "month" <note>Latin: *mensem*</note> from *mene* <note>Greek: *mēnē*, meaning moon</note>, which sounds like "failure" or "defect." Hence we call the moon "menstrual" <note>The author uses *menstruam* here in its etymological sense of "monthly" or "failing/waning."</note> as if it were failing in any given month. Therefore, **Boethius**, wishing to establish a fixed limit for learning the rudiments of grammar, said that one should not depart from this study within a lunar revolution—which he called "menstrual," namely a month—nor in a solar course, which is a year. For as has long since been demonstrated by astrological considerations, the sun travels through the zodiac on any given day by approximately 59 minutes and 8 seconds. When these are gathered over 365 days and reduced to whole degrees, the 360 degrees of the zodiac are established, and by these, the twelve signs are completed. For this reason, it is manifest that the sun undoubtedly traverses the entire zodiac in 365 days, which make a year. Boethius determined that one should not depart from this struggle even in that space of time, but rather one must remain for four years, which he explained through the motion of Mercury.

**The tradition of Seneca; the incompleteness of Lucan.** In this part, Boethius shows by which traditions of the teachers the unrefined students themselves are to be imbued after the aforementioned doctrines. And it is divided into two parts. In the first, he says that after the above-mentioned things, they should be educated in the traditions of the poets, in which the greater part of grammar is established. In the second, he shows to what extent they shall afterwards be imbued with the institutes of rhetoric, which are known to be most closely joined to poetry; there he says: *But of the others...* And he says that from here—that is, after the aforementioned—these things are to be investigated, that is, searched out: namely, the **tradition of Seneca**, that is, his published work; the **incompleteness of Lucan**, since he was prevented by death before he could finish his book; the **prolixity of Virgil**, namely in his writing; the **urbanity of Statius**, that is, his curiosity <note>In a medieval context, *curiositas* often refers to careful attention to detail or elaborate care.</note>, for he always stood forth as a writer of sophisticated matters; also the **harsh translation of Flaccus** (namely Horace), which is also reproving of vices; the **harsher edition of Persius Flaccus** (understand: harsher than Horace) both in style and in the reproof of vices; the **not unworthy—indeed worthy—injury of Martianus** <note>Likely referring to Martianus Capella's satirical or critical style.</note>; and finally the **discretion of Naso** <insert>supply: Ovid</insert>. All these are to be investigated and commended—that is, imprinted—upon the **cell of memory**, that is, the faculty of remembering. It should be noted...

<column-break/>

**The tradition of Seneca; the incompleteness of Lucan; the prolixity of Virgil; and the urbanity of Statius; the harsh translation of Flaccus; the harsher edition of Persius; the not unworthy injury of Martianus; the discretion of Naso are to be investigated and commended to the cell of memory. And as the capacity of the genius of other philosophers is available, their morality is not to be passed over in silence, so that the serenity of sententious composition may flourish and the delight of meters may bloom. Which the venerable eloquence of Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> with the highest desire...**

## [The Study of Rhetoric]

is to be placed. However, care must be taken in such matters lest it happen as it did to Jotarius <note>likely a corruption of a name like Joannes or a specific contemporary reference</note>. For he himself for thirty years handed over his ignorance of the aforementioned philosophers in the gymnasiums to be imbued. But when the day arrived for him to excel among the mediocre, whose wife was Ene— <note>The text here appears to break or contain a fragmented anecdote</note>

<column-break/>

commends him in the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. Nevertheless, poetry is useful if it is imitated in the proper way and practiced with lawful use. Indeed, very useful words are learned in it. As Augustine testifies in the first book of his *Confessions*, it is filled with the weightiest opinions.

These studies also drive the youth; they delight old age; they adorn prosperity and provide a refuge and solace in adversity; they delight at home; they do not hinder abroad; they stay awake with us through the night, they travel with us, and they go with us to the countryside <note>This is a famous paraphrase of Cicero’s *Pro Archia Poeta*</note>. Nor is it a wonder, since even Democritus taught that good poets are inflamed by a certain divine spirit, of which Ovid sang:
> *There is a god within us: and we have commerce with heaven. From ethereal seats that spirit comes.* <note>original: "Est deus in nobis: sunt et commercia celi. Sedibus ethereis spiritus ille venit." from Ovid's Fasti/Ars Amatoria</note>

Poetry itself also

---

provides the greatest addition to rhetorical eloquence. For this reason, it is most closely joined to rhetoric and is almost its sister. For, as Cicero says, the poet is a neighbor to orators, a little more restricted in rhythm, but freer in the license of words; in many kinds of ornament, however, he is an ally and almost an equal. Therefore, since Boethius himself recognized that poetry brings all these things, he urges that those who are unrefined, following the footsteps of their ancestors, should embrace the poets with the greatest effort, and especially those whom he commemorates in the text, among whom the Mantuan prophet Virgil so excelled that he deserved to be called the best of poets.

**Of the other philosophers.** In this part, Boethius shows how, after grammar and poetry, the unrefined are to be instructed in rhetoric. And it is divided into two parts: for first he does what has been said; second, he determines that one must dwell upon the eloquence of Marcus Tullius Cicero by way of antonomasia <note>The use of a title or epithet instead of a proper name, e.g., calling Cicero "The Orator"</note> at the point: *O how much*. And he says: Also the morality of the other philosophers must not be passed over in silence; rather, it must be embraced with all efforts. And this is to be done as much as the capacity—that is, the power of the intellect—of the one being instructed allows, so that the serenity—that is, the splendor of the composition <note>term: "dictaminis" - the art of formal writing or prose composition</note>—may flourish, full of the weight of the philosophers' thoughts, and the pleasantness of the meters may bloom.

And then he adds: *O how much* the venerable eloquence of Tullius <note>Cicero</note> is to be esteemed with the highest desires. For just as Aristotle is among the philosophers, and Virgil among the poets, so also Marcus Cicero himself excelled among the orators. It should be noted regarding what he says, "so that the composition be full of thought," etc., that Cicero himself and the others who taught rhetoric confessed that eloquence without wisdom is very harmful and never profitable, while wisdom without eloquence has been very profitable. Judging it unfair that eloquence should be judged and praised by the splendor of words alone, but rather according to the weightiest thoughts wisely drawn from true wisdom. Therefore, there is little substance or virtue or solid beauty—

# First

It seems that a certain dullness is brought to speech by one who devotes himself solely to rhetoric and eloquence, much like one who binds words together using bare, foreign, or merely "precious" material. Concerning this matter, Marcus Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator.</note> in that book which he published *On the Orator* addressed to his brother Quintus, and Quintilian himself when treating the *Education of the Orator*, confess that a perfect orator is rare or non-existent in that age. They assert a cause for this that is not without wit: for an orator ought to be persuasive in every kind of wisdom <note>original: "sapientie"</note>, so that he may bring forth what he has learned elsewhere with the splendor of speech, and indeed do so well. For in what way shall he persuade others in **Sacred Scripture** who has never read it? Or who shall persuade in **Natural Philosophy** who has not seen Aristotle and the rest of the philosophers? Certainly, in no way. Therefore, wisdom must be joined with formal writing <note>original: "dictamie," referring to the Ars Dictaminis or the art of composition.</note> so that what is conceived in other doctrines may be brought forth under rhetorical beauty.

However, one must be careful, etc. In this section, Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 CE), whose works on logic and music were foundational to medieval education.</note> adds a caution regarding all the aforementioned things, suggesting

> he had found in the serenity of the half-lines of Virgil.

And he does three things: first, he shows that impropriety itself must be guarded against; second, he summarizes the aforementioned by concluding at the point: "Behold how much," etc. And he says "one must be careful" in the higher traditions and in attaining them, lest that happen to someone which happened to—that is, befell—**Iotarius**, so named. For this Iotarius surrendered his ignorance to be imbued—that is, educated—in the gymnasiums (meaning the studies of the aforementioned philosophers, understood to be both the grammarians, the poets, and the rhetoricians) for thirty years (that is, the space of thirty years). 

But when the day arrived for him to preside over average scholars (meaning to instruct them), namely after the completion of thirty years of study, he asserted (that is, affirmed) that he had doubted for a long time whose wife **Aeneas** was—whom (Aeneas) he had found in the "serenity of the song," by which I mean the hemistichs <note>original: "emistigiorum," meaning half-lines of poetry.</note> (that is, the imperfect verses) of **Virgil**. And again, the same Iotarius, when requested (that is, questioned) by one of his disciples how (that is, by what measure) he could "turn in a verse" (meaning in a poetic line) the first syllable of this word *Magister* <note>Teacher/Master</note>, he (Iotarius) replied that it would be absurd (that is, unfitting) for the first syllable of so great a name to be abbreviated (that is, shortened in meter). Instead, he thought it should be pronounced with an acute accent (that is, a long delivery); for he estimated that, for the sake of honor, it was far too absurd for its first syllable to be shortened. 

Then, concluding by way of summary, he says: "Behold how much time" (because thirty years) "and how much expense the dullness" (that is, the stupidity) "of a stiff neck has wasted." It should be noted that since all knowledge, according to the testimony of Cicero in his *Dialogue to Hortensius*, is obstructed by many difficulties. For there is both obscurity in the things themselves and weakness in our judgments. For which reason **Socrates** himself used to say he knew nothing. Therefore, one must keep watch over study without laziness, just as the ancients studied wisdom itself, so that as much as the weak mind and the "dullness of the neck" excludes, so much may constant and diligent vigilance bring in. Thus Socrates...

# Chapter

studies were delayed. For as Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a Roman author known for his collection of historical anecdotes.</note> says in book eight, he never ceased to learn every day. It is also said of Pythagoras that he was constantly intent upon his teachings. Whence also Eunodius says: "The master of arts is persistence; the stepmother of learning is negligence." Hence the moral Cato <note>Referring to the *Distichs of Cato*, a popular medieval textbook for teaching Latin and ethics.</note> advised: "Instruct your mind with precepts, lest you cease to learn. For without learning, life is but an image of death." Not so was Iotarius, whose habits Boethius asserts must be guarded against.

### [words should not] be shortened, but rather pronounced with a sharp accent. Behold how much time and expense the dullness of a "hard neck" <note>A metaphor for stubbornness or stupidity; see the translator's note below regarding "dure ceruicis."</note> has wasted. However, having completed—not unworthily—the rudiments of this type of gymnasium <note>term: gymnasium (a place of study or school)</note>, one must proceed to the thresholds of a science of greater inquiry. A science, I say, which we know to be the sole investigator of truth and falsehood.

<column-break/>

Indeed, although he <note>Iotarius</note> had applied himself to study for thirty years, he nevertheless grew strong in no knowledge, since a harmony did not unite him as a recipient with his teacher as was fitting. It should be noted that Virgil, after many and diverse works, finally attempted the *Aeneid*. He left behind a book common to Greek and Latin names and things, but, being prevented by death, he left certain parts imperfect; for that reason, he ordered it to be burned in the fire. But this was not done.

Augustus, however, ordered Tucca and Varus—men excelling in that age—to correct it under this law: that they should remove superfluous things but add nothing. Whence we find his verses half-full, which they call "hemistichs" <note>term: hemistich (a half-line of verse)</note>. Concerning this matter, these verses of Sulpicius of Carthage survive: "Virgil ordered these songs, which sang of the Phrygian leader, to be abolished by rapid flames. Tucca and Varus forbid it, as do you, greatest Caesar. You do not allow the history of the Latin consul to perish," etc. And in these hemistichs, the same Iotarius, finding "Aeneas" with a weak mind, thought he was someone's wife, not knowing that Aeneas was the leader of Phrygia, fathered by Anchises and born of the mother Venus. Note that "neck" (*cervix*) is properly the back part of the neck, and is sometimes taken for pride, and sometimes for the whole head; and in this way it can be understood here when it is said "of a hard neck," that is, of a head hard for receiving the deep things of teachings. "Having completed—not unworthily": this is the second part of the second principal part of this first chapter, in which, after Boethius shows with what things youths must first be imbued from infancy, he now declares in what they are to be instructed second: namely, in the very first principles of the art of logic. And this part is divided into two parts. In the first of these, connecting himself to the previous points so that he may make the students attentive and ready to be taught, he aptly commends logic. In the second, he demonstrates the order and manner of proceeding in logic, at the point: "To this..." The first part is in two: for first he continues the things to be said; second, he commends logic at the point: "A science, I say." And he says that having completed and passed through—not unworthily (meaning not fruitlessly like Iotarius, but diligently)—the rudiment, that is, the new instruction of this gymnasium (that is, the study of grammar, poetry, and rhetoric), one must proceed to the thresholds (that is, the entrances) of a science which is of greater inquiry (that is, investigation). Then he approaches the commendation of logic itself, at that point.
