<meta>This page introduces a commentary on Logic, likely focusing on the "Isagoge" of Porphyry, as evidenced by the discussion of the five universals. It establishes Logic as the foundational "science of sciences."</meta>

# First

Of science, I say. And it is divided: for first he commends it as a whole; second, as to a specific part, where he says: *But what is the knowledge...* First he commends it in one way, and second in another way, where he says: *This is, I say...* And he says that after the aforementioned things, one must approach the thresholds of science for greater inquiry. Of science, I say, which we know alone to be the investigator of the true and the false; and this is logic itself, since the true and the false are not investigated except by means of argumentation. Logic alone, however, teaches how to argue. Wherefore we find it alone to be the **science of sciences** <note>original: "scientiam scientiarum"</note> by way of antonomasia <note>A rhetorical term for substituting a title for a proper name, e.g., calling Logic "The Science."</note> by reason of its universality and its administration. For it indeed assists all sciences, and for that reason the Commentator <note>Likely referring to Averroes or Aristotle himself</note> calls it the "method of knowing" when he says: *It is impossible to seek the sciences and the method of knowing at the same time.* Although some understand this only regarding applied logic. Of the science of sciences, I say, obtaining—

<column-break/>

### —the subjects of the sciences by the title of its subtlety. This is, I say, the mistress of the ladder, which, by the nature of the "garments," provides to the one penetrating to the heights of any sciences the increases of the Virtues. But what is clearer than the knowledge of the five universals, which is the mistress of the trivial sciences, the power of the quadrivial sciences, and the fullness of the collateral sciences?

---

—by the title, that is, by the honor of its subtlety, the subjects (that is, the objects) of other sciences are placed under it. After this, he commends it in another way and says: this logic, I say, is the "mistress of the ladder," that is, gradual; for through it one ascends to the summits of all other sciences, since it has a path to the principles of all methods. And this is what he adds: namely, that logic provides to the one "penetrating" (that is, searching out) the "heights" (that is, the summits) of any sciences the "increases of the virtues" (that is, the arguments of the power) of reaching them. And this is by the "nature of the garments," that is, of the premises, namely by the mediation of the major and minor [premises]. And he calls these premises—the major and the minor—the "extremities" or "garments" by way of a simile. For just as garments surround and cover the body itself, so also the premises include the conclusion itself. For which reason it is said that once the premises are positioned and granted, it is necessary for something else—namely the conclusion—to result from those things which were positioned and granted.

Then he commends it as to its part. And he says: *But what is clearer than the knowledge of the universals?*—that is, that part of logic which concerns the universals <note>Referring to the five predicables: genus, species, difference, property, and accident</note>—which knowledge is the "mistress" (that is, holding the magistracy) of the **trivium** <note>The three introductory liberal arts: Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric</note> and the "power" (that is, the force) of the **quadrivium** <note>The four mathematical liberal arts: Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy, and Music</note>. For they themselves are sterile, mute, and powerless without logic; and it is the "fullness" of the collateral arts (that is, all the others). It should be noted that logic is placed second among the liberal arts, although Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher</note> advises it should be learned after rhetoric. And it is called "rational" [philosophy]; for it teaches how to define and divide, and how to discern the true from the false. It is certainly a necessary and useful art, because according to Hugh [of Saint Victor] in the *Didascalicon* <note>A famous 12th-century guide to the arts and study</note>, through it the hidden truth is found by subtle objections. The most wise Solomon in Proverbs admonishes that this should be learned when he exhorts us to understand...

<margin>B 4</margin>

...admonishes the wisdom and the craftiness of words, as well as parables and obscure speech, the sayings of the wise and their riddles—all of which, as Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> says to the Great Orator, are **dialectic** <note>original: "dyalectica"; here meaning the art of logical discussion and investigation of truth.</note>. Augustine also commends logic among the other arts because it renders minds more practiced and powerful. Indeed, this discipline, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), author of the Etymologies.</note> says in Book II, was invented for discerning the causes of things; for which reason it is the "science of sciences."

**To climb to the peak of this imperial mistress, however, one must follow this order: First, an internal knowledge of terms must be applied, then their connection in a proposition (which is not hidden), and finally the worthy joining of those propositions. Furthermore, the definitions of terms which we call syncategoremata <term>syncategoremata: words like "all," "none," or "some" that do not have a meaning on their own but modify other terms</term> must be committed to memory.**

<column-break/>

...without which none of the other sciences can be perfectly mastered. It must be noted that a **universal** is that which is "one turned toward many" <note>original: "vnum versum in multis"; a classic definition of a universal concept.</note>. This is understood in two ways: namely, the physical and the logical. In the **physical** sense, it is the common nature itself, naturally fit to be found in many and able to be shared equally by them—such as "humanity," according to which it is said that by participating in the species, many men are

one man by the nature of the thing. In that same place: A **genus** <term>genus: a general category, like "animal"</term> contains many species within itself potentially, but none actually. In the **logical** sense, it is the very intention of universality as it is formed by the intellect, such as genus, species, etc., and according to this it is said: *It is the intellect which creates universality in things.* There are five kinds of these universal intentions: one is **genus**, another **species**, the third **difference**, the fourth **property**, and the fifth **accident** <note>These are the "Five Universals" of Porphyry, essential to medieval logic.</note>. Nothing exists more useful than the certain knowledge of these, and nothing is clearer. I say "more useful" both for the teaching of Aristotle's *Categories*—since nothing is established in that categorical arrangement unless it is a genus or a species, etc. For Plato commands that one who descends from the most general genus to the most specific species should rest there. Similarly, it is useful for assigning **definitions**, since a definition indicates what the "being" of a thing is. The "being" of a thing is nothing other than its **quiddity** <term>quiddity: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, which is certainly constituted by the "difference" added to the "genus." From these, a definition is integrated, and again for those things which are useful in demonstration, namely definition and the rest. In the text where it says *rudimento* [rudiment], it means a new judgment or new instruction (derived from *rudio* [to instruct]). Also, where it says *limina* [thresholds], a threshold is the boundary of a house or building, whereas a *limes* is a boundary of regions; hence Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine, a Christian writer.</note> says: "High virtue seeks the narrow boundary." Also, where it says *fastigia*, it means heights or summits. There is also a "summit of goods." Regarding the phrase "To this imperial [mistress]": In this part, after Boethius <note>Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), whose commentaries were the standard logic textbooks of the Middle Ages.</note> had offered praise of logic, he now manifests how one is to be educated in it. It is divided into two parts: In the first, he demonstrates the order of proceeding in it. In the second, he adds the manner of proceeding regarding that order. The second part begins at "To these and the others." The first part is in two: first he does what was said regarding "positive logic," and second regarding "sophistical" or "privative" logic. The first is in two: for first he does this regarding categorical terms...

# First

...regarding categorematic terms <note>original: "reumaticos," likely referring to terms with independent meaning like nouns or verbs</note>. Second, regarding syncategorematic terms <note>words like "all," "some," "not," or "if" that only have meaning when used with other terms</note>. At that point, the text discusses the nature of terms. This first part is divided into three sections according to three orders to be observed. It says first that one must climb, that is, ascend step-by-step to the peak—the summit—of this imperial mistress, namely Logic, in the following order: since the intrinsic knowledge of terms—namely "incomplex" terms such as the noun and the verb, the subject and the predicate—is required. And this pertains to the first order. Because the joining

<margin>and coupling—that is, the visible union—of these aforementioned terms in a proposition; and this pertains to the second order. Because the connection—that is, the worthy joining—of propositions, namely in a syllogism <note>a formal argument consisting of two premises and a conclusion</note>; and this pertains to the third order. All these aforementioned things must be applied in the introduction of logic for the unlearned.</margin>

->**These things must be impressed upon the mind, as they serve the "sophistical fantasy" <note>the deceptive appearance of truth in a false argument</note> in no small way. We remember Trebatius <note>likely a reference to Gaius Trebatius Testa, a Roman jurist often cited in medieval logic texts as an example of a learned man who initially ignored logical subtleties</note>, a most prudent man, but unskilled in this matter, who passed over this knowledge in silence as if it were unworthy of being reported. But when the day of conflict arrived, we saw him most miserably held back by these things, with sophistry winning the day.**<-

---

It should be noted that the intrinsic knowledge of terms mentioned in the text is nothing other than knowing what a "noun" is and what a "verb" is according to logicians, and in what manner they can enter into a proposition; which term is common and which is singular, and what a "genus" is—these we call "incomplex terms." The coupling of these is nothing other than their proper placement in a proposition, and then they enter into a "complexion" <note>a compound statement</note>. Furthermore, the connection of propositions is a syllogism, whether it be categorical or hypothetical, or simply called demonstrative, probable, or sophistical. All of these are treated abundantly in the books of Aristotle, Porphyry, and Boethius. 

However, because the diverse and varied connections of these propositions can hardly be made without knowledge of **syncategorematics**, which diversify propositions in both quality and quantity—and which sometimes amplify, sometimes restrict, and sometimes narrow the **categorematic** terms themselves, and perform other functions established in logic—Boethius advises that knowledge of these should by no means be bypassed, confirming his words with both reason and example. For he says that the determinations—that is, the signs, both universal and particular, as well as the remaining parts of terms which we call "syncategorematic" (meaning "co-signifying")—must be impressed upon the memory. 

He adds the reason, saying: because they serve the "sophistical fantasy" not a little, but a great deal—that is, that part of logic—and it is understood not just for sophistry, but for every part of logic. Then he confirms the above with an example, saying: certainly we knew Trebatius, a prudent man but unskilled in this, who passed over—that is, skipped—in silence, making no mention of the knowledge of these terms, as if it were a science unworthy of report. But what happened when the day of conflict—that is, of disputation—arrived? We saw him held back—that is, led to the point of being refuted—most miserably by these syncategorematics, with the sophistical art winning. And we saw him unseemly—that is, reproachfully—sequestered, divided from the college of his associates. What happened further is understood: the same Trebatius, confused by distress—that is, troubled—begged, or rather obtained by begging through his associates, that which he previously judged—that is, reputed—unworthy of speech: namely, the knowledge of syncategorematic terms.

It emphasizes the vital importance of "syncategorematic" words (logical connectors) through the cautionary tale of Trebatius, who lost a debate because he neglected them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues a commentary on the nature of logic, specifically transitioning from positive logic to the study of sophistry (deceptive reasoning). It references Boethius and Aristotle.</meta>

# Chapter

It should be noted that a <term>syncategorema</term> <note>original: "sincathegoreuma"</note> is a "con-signifying" word, derived from *syn* (with) and *categorema* (predicate). According to logicians, all parts of speech other than the noun and the verb are called syncategoremata. It should also be noted that a **fantasy** <note>original: "fantasia"</note> is a mental image formed from things already known, whereas a **phantasm** <note>original: "fantasma"</note> concerns things unknown. From this distinction, the term "sophistical fallacy" is derived.

And indecently sequestered from the company of its own. What further? Confused by the narrowness of shame, that which it previously judged unworthy of speech, it afterwards begged for in groups. Moreover, the **sophistical art**, endowed by the fringes of this imperial lady <note>referring to Philosophy or Logic personified</note>, confused by an insolent mind and consumed by the fame of trifling loquacity, drenched in the rouge of a woman's face, looked upon the barbarian nations with a sideways glance.

<column-break/>

...fantasy, since it appears to be something other than what it is. For there are **sophistical refutations** <note>original: "elenchi"</note>, which are not true refutations although they seem so, but are rather <term>paralogisms</term> <note>false arguments</note>, as stated in the first book of the *Refutations*. **Of this imperial lady.** After **Boethius** showed in the preceding part the method of proceeding regarding positive logic, he now does the same regarding **sophistical logic** itself. And it is certainly called the "sophistical art"—that is, the art which

is concerned with sophistical refutations—endowed, that is, decorated with "fringes," meaning the extremities which are called the fringes of the premises. This is quite consistent with what he had just said: "which by the penetrating nature of the garments," etc. **Of this lady**, meaning imperial Logic, also **confused**, that is, more **insolent**, meaning proud, bold, wanton, and importunately powerful in mind. All these terms are well-placed to suggest the "cautions" or tricks of the sophists. For a sophist ought to have a confused and long-winded manner in disputing, so that no one is able to repeat his intricate arguments. Similarly, he should be insolent and bold, as **Aristotle** wishes in the *Refutations*. And it follows: **consumed**, meaning perfectly seen, by the **eulogy**, meaning the testimony, of **trifling**, meaning feigned, **loquacity**, meaning talkativeness. It is also a trick of the sophists to speak in multiple ways so that they appear learned to those standing around. And **drenched**, meaning irrigated, in the **face**, meaning the ostentation, of a **woman’s rouge**, meaning the appearance of true wisdom although it is not. It looked back at the **barbarian**, meaning ignorant, **nations** with a **glance**, meaning with a sideways eye. We have known this art to be decorated in the commentaries of **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, the "Peripatetic" commentator on Aristotle</note> and in our own commentaries; and we have known it to be perfected, meaning completed, in this translation by which we turned it from Greek into Latin, and it must be cared for **exceedingly**, that is, diligently. 

It should be noted that the sophistical art is twofold. One is **teaching**, the other is **using**. The teaching part is that which teaches one to recognize a sophistical <term>syllogism</term> and its principles, causes, and properties. This is true science and a true habit acquired by demonstration. The other is the "using" part, through which we employ the sophistical syllogism in disputes. This is what is being discussed here. However, Boethius by no means advises using this, but persuades us to acquire it exceedingly in order to avoid sophistical snares and deceptions. For it is not wisdom at all, but a deception in speaking, an entanglement of words, appearing to be wisdom but not being so. **Gregory** <note>likely Pope Gregory the Great</note> speaks of this when he says: "What else is a syllogistic dispute than to contend with words and subvert the listeners?" And in it, as **Augustine** pleases, one seeks the "victory of words and ambitious ostentation." It deceives not only the slow-witted but often the ingenious. Therefore, in the book *On Christian Doctrine*, he calls the use of sophistical disputation an "execrable lust for quarreling." Nevertheless, these tricks must be studied—not so that one may practice them, but so that one may be able to take great precaution against them.

It cites authorities like Boethius, Aristotle, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Gregory, and Augustine to warn against the "womanly rouge" of false wisdom.</summary>

<header>First</header>

Likewise, a "fringe" <note>original: "fimbria"</note> is said to be the edge of a garment or a thread that is attached for the decoration of clothing. Here, however, it is understood either as the "extremities" of a syllogism <note>the concluding parts of a logical argument</note> by way of metaphor, or as the logical appendages which a sophist <note>a philosopher who uses clever but fallacious arguments</note> uses in his arguments.
Likewise, an "eulogy" <note>original: "eulogium"</note> is said to be wisdom, or a good reputation, or a testimony. Likewise, "fucus" <note>original: "fucus"</note> is a counterfeit color; hence "fucata" (as Papias <note>an 11th-century lexicographer</note> says) means painted, tinted with a counterfeit color, contaminated, feigned, and not a true appearance.

**To these and others.** In this part, Boethius, after he has shown the order of proceeding in the very beginnings of logic, now adds the method and the rule to be observed regarding that order. And it is divided into two parts. For first, he does what has been said; second, he responds to a certain unspoken question, at the point: **If indeed.** The first part is divided into two: for first, he sets down the method which must be used in acquiring the institutions of logic; second, he shows three effects proceeding from this, at the point: **vocal.**

<column-break/>

# ...he was looking back upon, which we know to be decorated and made perfect in translation in the commentaries of Alexander <note>likely Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> and our own, and which must be cared for with the greatest effort. For the perfection of these and others, we are accustomed to use a threefold recollection: the first of which is vocal; the second, mental; and the third, common. Vocal [recollection makes] the sophistical...

And he says that we are accustomed to use a threefold recollection <note>original: "recordatio," referring to the way information is stored or recalled in the mind</note> for the perfection of these (namely, the aforementioned things) and others (namely, those yet to be said). He means to say that in acquiring every science, we use a threefold recollection: the first is **vocal**, that is, the bare retention of words; the second is **mental**, that is, the recollection of the meaning of the words; the third is **common**, consisting of both the word and the meaning. And he adds the effects of these three recollections, doing three things in order. For first, he sets down the first three effects; second, he adds the second three effects; third, he confirms the third recollection above the others. The second part begins at: **Vocal [generates] blindness**; the third at: **For just as.** He says, therefore, that **vocal recollection** makes one a **sophist**, that is, one who has the appearance of knowledge, because it fills the ears with the bare voice while remaining ignorant of the definition of the name. **Mental [recollection]** makes **judgment**, that is, certainty (another version of the text has "unrefined"), because it makes the intellect discern between the true and the false, although it may be unable to express this distinction with the voice. But the **common [recollection]**, which belongs to both words and meanings, if it is continued—namely, by comparing the thing to the word—makes one **perfect** (understand: in the art). For just as he had conceived it by mental recollection, so he expresses it by the voice compared to the vocal [recollection]. From there, he sets down the second three effects of the aforementioned recollections. And he says **vocal recollection** generates **blindness**, that is, an ignorant man. For who can know the words themselves if he does not at all remember the power <note>the underlying meaning or logical force</note> of those words? On account of which, he is easily deceived by a false argument <note>original: "paralogizatur," to be led into a paralogism</note> as in the first book of the *Sophistical Refutations* <note>original: "elencorum," referring to Aristotle's work</note>. **Mental [recollection]** generates **knowledge**, that is, it renders a man knowledgeable, but powerless since he cannot explain with the word those things which he knew in the mind.

<meta>This page continues a pedagogical discussion on the acquisition of knowledge, specifically focusing on the relationship between theory (science) and practice (use/experience).</meta>

# Chapter

Indeed, common recollection generates **use** <note>original: "vsum"; here meaning practice or experience</note> because it makes one capable. For just as nature makes one able and art makes one easy, so too—as it seemed to Victorinus <note>likely Gaius Marius Victorinus, a 4th-century grammarian</note>—**use** renders one powerful. Moreover, use hastens—that is, it accelerates the journey toward mastery. Therefore, from the first to the last, common recollection hastens toward the mastership. He confirms this by adding a comparison: for just as prudence profits little or nothing without justice, while justice without

<column-break/>

**produces mental judgment. Common [recollection], if continued, produces perfection. Vocal [recollection produces] blindness; mental [recollection produces] knowledge; common [recollection produces] use. Moreover, use hastens to hurry toward mastery. For just as prudence without justice profits little or nothing, while justice without prudence profits much, so knowledge without use profits little. Use, however, without knowledge, profits much. If indeed a young recruit <note>original: "tirunculus"; a beginner or novice</note> of good character is unable to grasp the whole of knowledge in succession...**

<column-break/>

prudence profits much, so knowledge without use profits little, but use without knowledge profits much. It should be noted regarding the statement that "prudence without justice profits little or nothing" that the reason is this: justice is the container of all other virtues and the destroyer of all evils. Therefore, it is more necessary to the world than the others. First, this is found in the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, where he says: "Justice is, in a way, every virtue." Adding the reason, he says: "Because it includes within itself the acts

---

of all virtues." And Tully <note>Cicero</note> in the second book of *On Duties* says: "Justice is the one mistress and queen of all virtues." The second point is clear because justice itself is the inhibitor of all evils. Therefore, by the law of opposites, injustice is the permitter of evils; wherefore it is a perfect evil. But a perfect evil destroys itself, according to the fourth book of the *Ethics*. The third point is declared thus: through justice, innocence is protected, malice is punished, audacity is restrained, pride is worn down, and all things are rendered secure. For this reason, this virtue—according to Isidore in the fifth book of *Etymologies*—is not undeservedly called "Queen." Wherefore Augustine, in the second book of *The City of God*, chapter 18, treating most fully of justice itself, says in conclusion: "It is most true that a republic cannot be governed without justice." For this reason, Tully asserted that nothing is so friendly to a city or kingdom as justice. Because of these things, the other virtues without it profit little or nothing. And it is similar regarding **use** and **knowledge**. For as Seneca says, nothing is more hateful than knowledge where it stands alone, understanding that it profits little or nothing without its use. Well-adding to this, the same Seneca says: "For what does it profit those who know to consume their days in things that profit neither at home, nor in military service, nor in the forum, nor in care, nor anywhere else, except only in the schools?" Knowledge, therefore, without use, profits nothing and is unfruitful. For it takes its increase from use and exercise, just like any art (as noted in the *Digest* regarding legacies). If knowledge were separated from use, certainly use devoid of art is more useful than an art which does not have its use, as Polycrates reports in his fifth book. *If indeed [a recruit] of good [knowledge]*: Here, Boethius, responding by anticipation <note>original: "antipophorizando"; a rhetorical device of answering a silent objection</note>, answers a certain silent question. For someone might say: "O Boethius, it is well and fitting for one wishing to learn to grasp in the mind every single thing you have advised; but what if one cannot grasp all those things in the order you have arranged?"

<summary>This page argues that practical experience (use) is superior to theoretical knowledge (science) when they are separated, drawing a parallel to how justice is the essential "queen" of all virtues. It cites classical authorities like Aristotle, Cicero, Seneca, and Augustine to emphasize that knowledge is only fruitful when applied to the common good.</summary>

They will be unable to be retained, partly due to the smallness of their talent and partly due to any other occasion.
To which he, responding, says: certainly if a young recruit <note>original: "tirunculus," a diminutive of "tiro"</note>—that is, a new scholar—is unable to comprehend <gloss>that is, usefully, intently, and diligently</gloss> the whole speech <gloss>that is, the lesson</gloss> of good knowledge, let him seize it <gloss>that is, powerfully capture it</gloss> at least <gloss>that is, at the minimum</gloss> at the first pronunciation. Now, having seen the sciences of light matters, concerning the Porphyrian speculation of the five universals—which are called "monsters" by Aristotle—attention must be turned to his necessary categories, which in the light of exposition...

---

...as was seen in Aristotle's second book *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>. The soul is made like a blank tablet <note>original: "tabula nuda"</note> on which nothing is depicted, yet it is born fit to be depicted upon. However, this fitness for being depicted must not be brought into reality from the beginning with a tumultuous noise nor with a great and confused mass of forms, but it must be adorned here and there in a gradual order with the little flowers of the sciences. For the intellect is refreshed, and finally the memory—the faithful preserver of things conceived—is strengthened, and the greatest part of the labor is removed if the things heard, read, and conceived are committed to memory bit by bit rather than in one single breath; otherwise, the mind and spirit will be worn out by long and enduring labor. For those things which have been conceived vanish like fluid and falling things unless they are repeated.
<note>Note:</note> "Tiro" is the word for "strong" in Greek and Latin; hence "this recruit" <note>original: "tiro, -nis"</note> means a new soldier newly chosen for military service, because a strong man is usually chosen for this. By similarity, anyone ignorant and unrefined is called a "recruit" when they set out to practice something; hence "young recruit" <note>original: "tirunculus"</note> is the diminutive. Likewise, "at least" <note>original: "saltem"</note> is an adversative conjunction with a sense of lessening; it is derived from "captives" who, being unable to speak for fear, said "saltem" <note>a play on "salutem" or "safety"</note> as if they were asking that they might not lose their life and safety.
"Having seen the sciences of light matters": This is the third part of the second principal part of this first chapter, in which Boethius, after he showed in what things boys must first be imbued and in what things secondly, now shows in what things they must be instructed thirdly. And he intends that after the aforementioned things, which are all like the rudiments of the sciences, the scholars themselves are to be educated in the sciences that require greater inquiry, namely in the science of universals and the categories <note>original: "predicamentorum"</note>, etc.
And this part is divided into two parts: first, he sets down the mode and order by which one must insist upon the more speculative part of logic; second, he repeats a certain thing said earlier so that he may add to the preceding things (at the point: "Nor from where these"). The first part has three orders of books necessary for this part: namely, the Universals and the Categories on one side, and the Divisions and *Topics* of Boethius on the other; and after this, all the remaining books of the "New Logic" of Aristotle, namely the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics*, etc. The second starts at "To ours also," the third at "Aristotle also." The first is in two parts: first, he advises education in the books of the *Isagoge* <note>original: "predicabiliũ"</note> by Porphyry; second, he recommends those same universals based on their utility (at the point: "O how much"). And he says: "Having seen the sciences of light matters" <gloss>that is, of the lightest teachings, understand those which lead lightly into the knowledge of logic</gloss>, attention must be paid to the "Porphyrian speculation" <gloss>that is, the speculative consideration by Porphyry</gloss> of the five universals <gloss>namely: genus, species, etc.</gloss> concerning which are all the sciences of the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics*, which are called universals.

# Chapter

Aristotle, specifically in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, calls "monsters"—that is, things existing outside of nature—those universals I call necessary, which are useful for the *categories* <note>original: "cathegorias"</note>—that is, the predicaments of Aristotle—which we, Boethius, have made clear <note>original: "patefecimus"</note>, that is, declared twice in our commentaries. And this was done by the light of exposition, that is, by an explanatory declaration. Next, he commends the science of universals based on its utility. And he does two things: for first he does—

**—what was said in our commentaries twice. Oh, how much utility is contained in these if an intrinsic knowledge is held. Is not the literal faculty of Sophroniscus <note>Sophroniscus was the father of Socrates; here used to refer to a specific school or style of teaching</note> to be marked as a vice, I say? Our own volumes, decorated with a beauty of style, are also not to be omitted.**

<column-break/>

—what was said. Second, he removes errors from the same; there, where it says: "Is not the literal." And he says: Oh, how much utility is held in these, namely the universals, if they are known by intrinsic notice, that is, internal knowledge. Afterwards, removing error, he says: "Is not," that is, "Is it not the case that the literal faculty—

---

—that is, the vocal teaching alone of that master Sophroniscus, is to be marked with vice, that is, to be reprehended, I say? That is, I say that the teaching of Sophroniscus, since it taught only the chatter of words which make men sophists and seemingly wise, must be utterly abolished in the teaching of these universals, and the force of the words must be attended to. It should be noted, as Aristotle relates in many passages, that the opinion of Plato was that universals themselves were essences existing by themselves and separated from singular things according to their being, yet giving a name and a definition <note>original: "rationem"</note> to those singular things. Aristotle himself, in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics*, attacks this opinion of Plato with many arguments as being erroneous and truly discordant with philosophy. Therefore, holding it in ridicule in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, he says in this manner: "Let the genera and species rejoice," for if they exist in the way Plato proposed, "they are monsters." Wherefore, in the introduction to *On the Soul*, he says: a universal—namely the Platonic kind—is nothing, or it is posterior to its singulars. And Boethius spoke to this purpose when he said "those which are called monsters by Aristotle," implying "in the version of Plato." Likewise, a *category* <note>original: "cathegoria"</note> is a predicament, or a predication, or a signification; hence the predicaments of Aristotle are called categories. "And our volumes": In this part, he touches upon the second order of books to be learned in this area. And he says "and our volumes," namely those made by us, such as the *Book of Divisions* and the *Book of Topics*, decorated with a scheme of style—that is, nobility of style—are not to be omitted after the reading of the universals. This is to say that in these, great profit consists. Whence *Schema* <note>original: "Scema"</note>, a neuter noun, signifies noble honor, dignity, a crown, or an ornament; whence Juvenal says: "What do the schemes <note>referring to ancestral busts or decorations</note> do," etc. "The succinct [works] of Aristotle also": In this part, Boethius places the third order of books to be learned in this area. And it is divided into two parts: for first he does what was said; in the second, he commends the books themselves by the nobility of the author, there: "For what of Aristotle the Peripatetic." The first part is in two: for first he does what was said; second, he responds to a certain silent question which could be drawn from the aforementioned, there: "I preferred truly." And he says also "brevity"—another version has "succinct truth"—implying that he abounded more in meaning than in words, although with a "tedious voice," that is, generating boredom because of the hardness of the translation, yet not unfruitful—implying "in the richness of meanings"—it is not to be omitted. From these words, however, someone might take the opportunity to ask why he translated the words of such a great philosopher in such a harsh and uncultivated style, rather than with an equal scheme and lively style...

# Second

...those things which lie in the Greek, he by no means transferred. To which Boethius [replies]: "Certainly I preferred," that is, I wished more (understand: I, Boethius), "to serve a faithful translation" so that I might exchange word for word, rather than "be rebuked by the rashness," that is, the presumption of arrogance, that is, pride. From there he commends the teaching of Aristotle. "For," because "what is more serene," that is, more tranquil, than the "lucid truth of Aristotle?" (Answer: nothing).

<margin>
It should be noted, as Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers</note> reports, that Aristotle, the disciple of Plato, wrote many books: both in logic, in physics, and also in mathematics and others, so that the number of books reaches three hundred; and elsewhere it is said that he published a thousand treatises.
</margin>

<column-break/>

> Also the succinct brevity of Aristotle, although tedious in voice, is nevertheless not unfruitful. For I preferred rather to serve a faithful translation than to be rebuked by the rashness of arrogance. For what is more serene than the lucid truth of Aristotle? And while these things are being done, the fruitfulness of grammar is by no means to be neglected. For through it, the possession of any commendable art is rendered a pleasant return. And the charm of rhetoric...

---

...of which, however, either through the lack of translators or some other occasion, we do not have the full abundance. Nevertheless, of those which have come down to us from the works of logic, there are the *Book of Categories*, *On Interpretation* <note>original: "peri hermenias"</note>, the *Priors* <note>Prior Analytics</note>, *Analytics* <note>Posterior Analytics</note>, *Topics*, and *Sophistical Refutations* <note>original: "elencorum"</note>. Although the translator of these may have been harsh, they exist as most refreshed in truth, because it has been said of this matter: "He who departs from Aristotle departs from the truth." Averroes <note>The influential 12th-century Islamic philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> says the same: "Nature generated that man for us so that through him the secrets of philosophy might be revealed to us." Therefore, it is not without merit that one is right to call him the "Rule of Nature." Concerning this useful Aristotle, we read that Plato, the "secretary of divinity," more often condemned [him]; yet when understanding is not present to the reader, the audience is deaf. Therefore, his doctrine must by no means be omitted.

"And while these things are being done." In this part, Boethius repeats a certain saying of his for the sake of the aforementioned, so that he may add it to the preceding things. And he does two things: first, he does what was said; second, he removes a certain doubt at the point: "Of the quadrivials." He says, therefore, that when all the aforementioned things pertaining to logic are being done (namely, in the mind), the fruitfulness of grammar is not to be left behind in any way. And he gives the reason for this, saying: "since the possession of any commendable," that is, praiseworthy, "art is rendered pleasant through it." For grammar itself, as was seen above, is the mother of all arts, without which all other sciences are utterly mute. And for this reason, the "charm of rhetoric," that is, the ornament of rhetoric (understand: must by no means be left behind) for the reason stated above.

Next, since it could be doubted—because all these things shown concern the "trivial" arts <note>The Trivium: Grammar, Logic, and Rhetoric</note>—what should be thought of the "quadrivial" arts <note>The Quadrivium: Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy, and Music</note>. Solving this doubt, he says: "Also the good," that is, the dignity of the quadrivial arts, namely arithmetic, geometry, astrology <note>In this period, "astrologia" often referred to both astronomy and astrology</note>, and music, "acquired by the comparison," that is, the gathering of study, "must not be omitted." And giving the reason, he says: "since the boldness," that is, the furious curiosity of study in these mathematical sciences, "generates the flower" (understand: of the sciences), which also "brings forth fruit." And add this: if the boldness of this study is mixed with doubt, "since doubt provides a great increase to knowledge."

# Chapter

From this comes that saying of the philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle</note>: "To doubt individual things is not entirely useless," and one should also understand that it bears flower and fruit if it is timely—that is, appropriate to its own time. For just as a proper and extended occupation with the uncertain boundaries in mathematics provides a great foundation for the sciences, so on the contrary, a constant persistence in them brings about a cursed detriment. For, as was said above, a continuous focus on them—

<columns>2</columns>

The honor of the studies of the <term>Quadrivium</term> <note>The four "mathematical" subjects of the seven liberal arts: Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note> acquired through comparison should not be neglected as far as possible. In these matters, the boldness of study generates a flower and bears fruit if it is mixed with doubt and is timely.

### Chapter Two

This concerns the basic instructions for scholars and the growth of virtues. Now, concerning their submission toward their teachers, briefly—

<column-break/>

—consideration, especially either simply or in part, withdraws one from the practice of virtue. It should be noted that **Plato**, in the seventh book of *The Republic*, said that the mathematical disciplines—which we designate by the name of the **Quadrivium**—are primarily necessary for the knowledge of truth and for demonstrations. For they are in the first grade of certainty; he said that they are like steps for knowing higher things. For in all these disciplines, he says, the instrument of the soul—which was lost, so to speak, and blinded by other exercises—is purified and better uplifted. **Aristotle** compared these to **Metaphysics**, and although they agree, they do so differently. For the metaphysician considers all quantities insofar as they are beings (as in the fourth book of *Metaphysics*), but the mathematician deals with quantity as his subject. There are four mathematical disciplines, which is why they are called "Quadrivial": because all four are concerned with quantity. Among these, by the nobility of its subject, **Astrology** <note>In this period, "astrologia" often encompassed both astronomy and astrology.</note> is first, which **Polycrates** says nature introduced, reason proves, and the experience of utility approves. It is indeed the law which, traversing with searchable reason the courses, figures, and relationships of the celestial bodies around themselves and the earth, demonstrates their truths and how they act upon all things below the sphere of the moon. After this is **Music**, which reconciles the sounding multitude of its proportions into a certain equality of voices. **Plato** names this the most powerful of the arts. For in the *Timaeus*, he says the power of harmony is for mitigating the pains of human souls and making them joyful. **Socrates** learned this as an old man and ordered that youths be instructed in it. This is followed by **Arithmetic**, which the writers of doctrines decreed to be the first. For, as it is, it needs no other discipline, as **Boethius** says. It is certainly an art of great virtue, since it renders its practitioners sharper for all disciplines, as **Plato** said in the seventh book of *The Republic*. For you have noticed, **Socrates** said, that those who are by nature arithmeticians appear to be sharper in all disciplines. Those who are duller in intellect, if they are instructed in this—even if they gain no further utility—usually become more ingenious than they were. The last among these is called **Geometry**, first discovered by the Egyptians. For when the [Nile] flooded, as **Strabo** [says] in the book—

# Second [Book]

<note>The header "Secundum" refers to the second book or major division of the treatise.</note>

...the book discusses the layout of the world in part 15. With the Nile River and all its territories having been covered, the beginning of dividing land by lines and measurements gave a name to the art <note>Geometry</note>, which was thereafter expanded more broadly by the sharp insight of wise men.

### Chapter Two

With these scholarly basics established—this is the second chapter of this book on the *Discipline of Scholars* <note>original: "De disciplina scholarium," a famous medieval textbook long attributed to Boethius but likely written in the 13th century</note>. In this chapter, after [the author] has taught concerning the fitness a scholar ought to have regarding the delights of the sciences to be impressed upon himself—which consists of an orderly process toward the sciences themselves—he now consequently determines in this second chapter the fitness required in respect to the one administering knowledge to the scholars. This consists of the submission of the scholars toward the master.

<column-break/>

One must begin briefly: for he who does not know how to be a subject cannot know how to be a master. For it is a wretched thing for one to be a master who never knew himself to be a disciple. Moreover, the submission of the disciple ought to consist of three things: namely, attention, goodwill, and teachability <term>docilitas: the capacity and willingness to be taught</term>. Attentive, I say, in practice; teachable in intellect; well-disposed in spirit. Attentive for hearing; teachable for understanding...

---

And this entire chapter is divided into two principal parts. In the first, he does what has been said. In the second, however, he sets forth certain impediments that can occur to remove the submission of scholars, at the point: "Let the disciple not be..." The first part is divided into two: for first, he connects what has been said to what is to be said; second, he pursues his intent, at the point: "The submission of the disciple ought..." The first of these is further divided into two: for first, he connects the previous words to the following; second, he gives the reason for this continuation, at the point: "Because he who does not know..." And he speaks first thus: With these "basics"—that is, the lighter teachings and the "growth of virtues"—that is, the perfections of the other sciences of the scholars themselves, understood as they were explained in the previous chapter—"now," that is, in this second chapter, it "must be arranged"—that is, taught in an orderly fashion. Another version of the text has "must be begun"—that is, started briefly concerning the "submission"—that is, the humble yielding of the scholars toward the master. And adding the reason for this, he says: "because he who does not know how to be a subject"—that is, to have been submissive—it is necessary that he "does not know how to be a master." Confirming this, he says: "But if it happens that the same person who did not know himself to be a disciple becomes a master, this is nevertheless wretched"—that is, detestable. It should be noted, as Hugh reports in the *Didascalicon*, book two <note>Hugh of St. Victor (c. 1096–1141), a leading mystical theologian and educator</note>: among those things which are most beneficial for studying, a humble and submissive mind is especially necessary for a disciple. This is nothing other than a just and close harmony between the giver and the receiver. Speaking of this, Quintilian <note>A Roman educator and rhetorician</note> says in the first book of his *Institutes*: "Just as it is the duty of teachers to teach, so it is for disciples to show themselves teachable." For knowledge cannot grow strong unless the harmony of the giver and receiver is joined. Thus Socrates was under Diogenes—who, as Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> reports in the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, called Philosophy down from heaven and placed it in the cities—and thus Plato, the secretary of divinity, was under Socrates; and Aristotle, the leader of the Peripatetics, was under Plato. Thus, finally, the rest remained well-disposed and submissive in mind under their elders, so that they deserved to be called the most abundant fountains of philosophy.

# Chapter

The submission of the student is necessary. After Boethius <note>referring to the author of 'The Consolation of Philosophy' or here, likely the 'De Disciplina Scholarium' formerly attributed to him</note> connected what has been said with what is to be said, he now pursues his intent regarding the submission of the student toward the teacher. And it is divided into two parts: for first, he posits in what that submission consists; second, he declares this more clearly at the point "so that he may be attentive." And he says first that the submission of the student ought to consist in these three things: namely, in **attention**, **benevolence**, and **docility** <note>teachability or readiness to be taught</note>. And declaring this, he adds: namely, that he should be sub-

**-missive, benevolent for the sake of retaining. These three indeed concur interchangeably for perfection. Let the scholar not be "discolus" <note>wayward or rebellious</note>. He is called "ediscolus" as if divided from the school.**

<margin>
The scholar should be attentive in exercise, that is, in the labor of study, by studiously applying the mind to the words of the teacher; for this exercise makes any work easier for those performing it. Let him also be benevolent in mind and docile in talent. Declaring which, he adds: I...
</margin>

-mitting that the student be attentive to hearing the words of the teacher, not merely to grasp the matter from the words, but to arrive at the sequence of things within the words. And I say that the student should be benevolent for the sake of retaining—supply "the things heard." And this benevolence is the love of learning by which doctrine is more strongly impressed; and I say let him be docile for the sake of understanding. But truly these three—namely, attention, benevolence, and docility—concur; that is, they come together for the perfection (understand "of the student") interchangeably, that is, in a diverse and permuted order. So that, for instance, now he is attentive, now docile, now however benevolent, without regard for which of them is established first. It should be noted that these three—attention, benevolence, and docility—submit one most greatly to the teacher and the doctrine; however, the greatest of these is the love of learning, by which the hearts of those to be instructed are more strongly enticed to grasp the doctrine. And this love is said to consist of three things: namely, affection for the instructor, the attainment of the refreshing fruit by the one being renewed, and the fulfillment of the natural appetite for knowledge. For by the intimate affection for the instructor, the things heard are rendered more credible in the recipient; and this affection is situated in the fear and reverence for the one delivering [the teaching], concerning which it is said in Hebrews 13: *We had fathers of our flesh as instructors of this sort, and we revered them* <note>original: "Patres carnis nostre huius eruditores et reuerebātur eos"</note>, that is, they feared them reverently. And hence Cato says: *Fear the teacher* <note>original: "Magistrū metue"</note>. We clearly see examples of this in Trajan and Alexander. For the Emperor Trajan, as it is read, revered his teacher Plutarch most highly. So also Alexander revered Socrates <note>The text likely confuses the historical tutor Aristotle with Socrates here</note>, whom, when he had once met him, leaping down from his chariot, he received him reverently. The second thing by which the love of the learner is established is the attainment of fruit by the recipient, by which the student is enticed toward discipline. For the fruit of wisdom is a gift of God, as Augustine says in the 12th book of *The City of God*, to which nothing encountered is to be preferred and it can be compared to no price. Concerning which Tully <note>Cicero</note> says in the second book of *On Duties*: *For what is more desirable after the gods? What is more excellent, what better, what altogether more worthy than wisdom?* To which the answer is: nothing. The third thing by which the love of learning is established is the fulfillment of the natural appetite for knowledge. Concerning this appetite, it is said in the first book of the *Metaphysics*: *All men by nature desire to know.* The end and fulfillment of an appetite of this kind is nothing unless it be to understand, the perfection of which consists in the knowledge of truth alone, not in the comprehension of the surface alone. For it does not suffice for the learner to read superficially unless he understands and turns over the things latent within and renders them to memory. And to this end, that which Jerome writes figuratively in the canon against Marcion and Basilides (1. q. 1) serves best, where it is said: *nor should we think the Gospel lies in the words of the Scriptures...*

<sig>C</sig>

# Second

not in the sound but in the sense; nor on the surface but in the marrow; not in the leaves of words but in the root of reason. For then a disciple makes progress when he pays attention carefully, understands what is heard with a teachable spirit, and recommends what is understood to the scrutiny of the heart with goodwill. **But let him not be a "discolus" <note>original: "discolus"; a Latinized Greek term meaning unruly or wayward, here interpreted as "separated from school"</note>.** This is the second principal part of this chapter in which **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval education</note> posits certain impediments that could occur regarding this aptitude, namely the submission of the disciple toward the master. And it is divided into three parts according to how he posits three impediments: namely, waywardness, violence, and luxury. The second part begins at "But let him not be violent," and the third at "of luxury." The first part is further divided into two: first, he does what was said; second, he declares what it is to be wayward, at the words "A wayward person, however." And he says first: a scholar desiring to reach the heights of the sciences should not be wayward, that is, turned away or diverted from school. And adding this explanation, he says: "Discolus" is said as if "divided from school" <note>original: "a scola diuisus"</note>, for "school" in Greek is called "vacation" <note>original: "vacatio"; meaning leisure or freedom from labor for the sake of study</note> in Latin. Hence, "discolus" is as if divided from school. Then, so that the vice of waywardness may be more clearly shown to be avoided, he says: A wayward person is he who runs about through the alleys and streets and taverns and the cells of harlots, and through public spectacles, that is, public places where games are performed. For spectacles are places where formerly comedies and tragedies were played, as the Greeks say. And they are held in the "Authentica" <note>A reference to the "Authenticum," a collection of Justinian's legal decrees</note> concerning consuls, in the law regarding those who go through processions, that is, public displays; through dances, that is, ritual trippings; through carousings, that is, banquets; through dinners, that is, late-night feastings; and public ones, that is, open ones. And this is drawn from the ancients who dined in the open. And this with wandering eyes, that is, looking here and there with a disordered face, that is, ill-mannered and distorted, and with an unbridled and dissolute tongue. For for all these things, school is postponed. It should be noted, as **Azo** <note>A highly influential medieval jurist from Bologna (c. 1150–1230)</note> says, that <term>study</term> <note>original: "studium"; defined here as intense mental application</note> is a vehement and assiduous application of the mind toward doing something with the highest will, from which will labor is brought into the work, and it loses the weariness of labor, turning it into delight. However, if this assiduous vehemence is interrupted, it will certainly bring no benefit. It is interrupted, however, by many things which **Boethius** enumerates: namely, the frequency of alleys and streets, the tavern, the dance, and every public spectacle. For in all these things the mind is restless, which only by being quiet becomes wise, and it is removed further from that which it had begun. Our ancestors, foreseeing this, chose solitary places as most fit for study and contemplation. Whence **Agelius** <note>Aulus Gellius (c. 125–180 AD), author of "Attic Nights"</note> in the first book of *Attic Nights* says: **Socrates** remained motionless from sunrise until sunset, vacant for study, and with eyes raised to heaven, he insisted on contemplation alone, caring nothing for the anxieties of the world. And **Horace** says of **Aristippus** <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates</note> thus: "Aristippus would be unwilling if he could make use of kings." For the ancients, as **Jerome** reports in his letters, left the crowds everywhere for the sake of study and gardens...

<column-break/>

# Book Two

->**On the Unrefined**<-

Lest through luxury and an abundance of resources the strength of the mind should soften and its modesty be stifled. ...we recall. This is a parenthesis: we perceived with our own eyes many unruly students in the city of Julius Caesar, which was called Paris, and we saw many successful men begging—that is, seeking the arts by begging—yet with no masters administering to them the cups, which is to say the teachings, of philosophy; understand this to be because they were held back by the vice of unruliness. It should be noted that Gaul is a province of Europe, as Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose encyclopedia was a standard reference in the Middle Ages.</note> reports in Book 15. Gaul is named for the whiteness of its people, for *gala* in Greek means milk <note>original: "gela enim grece lac dicitur"</note>. And hence the Sibyl calls the Gauls white-skinned: "then their milky necks are moistened with gold." And a large part of it is France, named after the Franks who first inhabited that part, or after Francus the executioner who succeeded to the kingship in Paris. Although this land has many noble cities, Paris nevertheless holds the leadership. It was formerly called Lucotecia <note>Lutetia</note> and the city of Julius—not because he founded it, but because he enlarged it.

<column-break/>

**...begging, and we deeply grieved that many successful Slavs and Britons, traveling to Rome for the sake of study, were provided with no cups of philosophy for them. For they were not fed even by the smallest sparks of the Athenians. At last, however, they began to speak Greek in the French tongue. But if anything other than the twisted volumes...**

For just as the city of Athens once adorned Greece as the mother of the liberal arts and the fountain of all sciences, so Paris in our times has exalted not only France, but indeed the remaining part of all Europe in science and morals. In praise of which Architrenius <note>A satirical poem written by John of Hauville in 1184.</note> speaks thus at the end of his second book: "At last a place is reached, a second palace of Phoebus <note>Apollo, god of wisdom and light.</note>. Paris is a Cirrha in virtue, a Chrysa in metals, Greek in books, Indian in studies, Roman in poets, Attic in philosophers; the rose of the world, the balsam of the earth, with the adornment of Sidon. She has her own food and her own drink. Rich in fields, fertile in wine, gentle to her inhabitants. She bears honey for herself, is uncovered by brambles, and her woods are full of clusters of grapes. Full of wild game, fish-filled in her lakes, bird-filled in her streams. Abundant in housing, strong in her lord, pious to kings, her air is sweet, pleasant in her site, good in every way—everything is beautiful, everything is good, if only fortune would favor the good."

But in our judgment—that is, with us judging—not so much time was lost...

For the Romans had been corrupted not only by this vice of unruliness, but by every other vice as well, so that they could hardly attempt anything new in the way of vice. Hence, Junius Juvenal, crying out against the vices of the Romans, addresses the Romans in this manner: "Every vice stands at a precipice; posterity has nothing it can add to our manners." <note>Juvenal, Satire 1.147-149</note> It is as if the poet said: every vice that can be devised is already being entirely perpetrated.

# Second Book

Since he who has been violent toward his master shall in no way be a true possessor of knowledge, it must be noted that Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval education.</note> greatly warns scholars not to inflict violence upon their teacher, so that they do not blaspheme him in word nor offend him in deed. However, so that these things may be more easily avoided, those things which are most likely to lead to this must be driven away: such as rash presumption of oneself, the ambition for one's own excellence, and the failure to consider one's own fragility. The first must be avoided especially because it withdraws the help of God.

<margin>Judith 6: "O Lord, show that you do not abandon those who trust in you, and you humble those who glory in themselves and their own strength." <note>original: "domine ostende qz non dimittis gloriantes in te..."</note> The ambition for one's own excellence must also be avoided because it is a sin against God and neighbor. For with God there is no partiality toward persons, but only toward merits, since he created all men from one and the same father. As Boethius attests in *The Consolation of Philosophy*: "The whole race of men on earth descends from a similar origin," etc. Furthermore, it must be avoided with the greatest effort...</margin>

**...he was not a son of love, but rather a messenger of unhappiness; he once laid wicked hands upon his master, William, who was stammering, and he defiled his venerable white hair with the foul touch of his feet. What was the cause of such a great crime? Because at the first impression of the air <note>meaning: the first hearing of the spoken word</note> he was unable to comprehend the entire instruction. Oh, the shame! Oh, the approach of the unhappy disciple becomes an attack upon the head of happiness. Let Nero rejoice in such a wicked heir.**

...consideration. By the counsel of the Savior in Matthew 7: "First cast the beam out of your own eye, then you shall cast the splinter out of your brother's eye." Whence it is commonly said: "He ceases to rebuke the blemish in another's eye who is accustomed to carry a beam in his own light." When these things have been avoided, certainly no violence is allowed to be committed. Regarding violence, Albinus: In this part, Boethius introduces a certain example of the aforementioned things, namely of violence, and he does two things. The first part is further divided into two: for first he does what was said, and second he subjoins the cause of this crime at the point: "What was the cause of such a great crime." And he says let Albinus, the "son of white" <note>A play on the name Albinus, from 'albus' (white).</note>, come forward as an example of violence. This Albinus, since he was not a son of love because he did not love his master at all, but was rather a precursor—that is, a messenger—of unhappiness, once laid wicked hands (this is said of the effect) upon his master William <note>likely referring to William of Conches, a 12th-century grammarian and teacher</note> who was "stammering," that is, faltering; and he defiled the "white hair," that is, the venerable old age of this his master, with the "foul," that is, shameful, "touch of his feet." And subjoining the cause of this crime, he asks: "What is the cause of such a great crime?" as if to say: for what reason did he perpetrate such a great crime against his master? And responding to this, he says because Albinus himself was unable to comprehend the "entire instruction," that is, the lesson, at the "first impression of the air," that is, at the first pronunciation of his said master. After this, inveighing against him, he says: "Oh, the shame," which is an interjection of one grieving and blaming. And he says this out of great indignation...

<margin>He had many disciples, of whom Anytus, as it is said, was one of the leaders of the Athenians. And concerning this, Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> in the book of *Tusculan Disputations* says: "Hemlock killed the great Socrates." Moreover, Nero himself, looking one day upon Seneca his master and calling to memory the lashings he had inflicted upon him in his boyhood, growled; and as if desiring vengeance for these injuries, he commanded that he should choose whatever kind of death he wished. Seneca, therefore, thinking it a pleasant kind of death to die in a bath, chose the cutting of both arms. Wherefore, by a certain omen, his name was well-called 'Seneca'—that is, 'killing himself' <note>A medieval folk etymology: "se necans"</note>. Well, therefore, does Boethius say: "Let Nero rejoice in such a wicked heir; let Anytus rejoice in such a defiled successor," because just as Nero and Anytus, so also Albinus himself was plunged into Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. But let Grillus rejoice with Socrates in Seneca's appetite, because he had chosen the better part, since he is numbered in the catalog of saints. Note that 'stammering' <note>balbutiens</note> and 'stuttering' <note>balbus</note> are the same as 'faltering,' one who does not express words but breaks them, named from 'to stammer'; but 'lisping' <note>blesus</note> is one who brings forth letters imperfectly. The first is in two parts: for first, he proposes that luxury in general must be fled; second, dividing it, he follows one of its species, at "Which the triple..." And he says that the disciple should strive to alienate himself from the heat of luxury. It should be noted that "luxury" in this context is taken as a broad term, covering superfluity in intercourse, in food, and in clothing. And according to this, the satirists posited a triple luxury, as he will immediately set forth. # Second [Book/Chapter]

...weakens, and finally abandons each of one's strengths. Therefore, Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind, a 4th-century theologian</note> said to Alexander: "It is our custom," he says, "among the Brahmans <note>original: *bragmani*; referring to the Indian sages often cited in medieval texts as models of asceticism</note>, that we do not give our limbs over to lust." That [lust] which is found in feasting must also be diligently avoided, because it entices the soul toward depravity and, in the manner of a serpent, spreads its hidden poisons. This is according to that passage of Virgil in the *Bucolics*: *Each is drawn by his own pleasure*, and it follows: *You who gather flowers and strawberries growing on the ground, flee from here, boys, a cold snake lies hidden in the grass.* <note>Virgil, Eclogue 3.63 and 3.92-93. The "snake in the grass" is a metaphor for hidden danger in worldly pleasures.</note>

Indeed, [the third type] is the assistant to gluttony. We have frequently known subjects to suffer from the foul madness of any [of these lusts]. All of Rome wept for the blood-related son of Lucretius, a disciple of Zeno, who was ensnared by a shameful appetite for intercourse; he was nevertheless born of the most illustrious lineage, of tall stature and a sanguine temperament, and indeed of marvelous eloquence and sharp intellect. But he rejoiced in daily marriages beyond what was right, while his father bore the penalty; for he illicitly consumed his patrimony and his parents' wealth, and he was notorious among all jealous men. He was always gaping after alleys and the small rooms of harlots.

<column-break/>

...for in a delicate and gluttonous life, poisons lie hidden which drown the soul itself in Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Again, that [luxury] which is placed in clothing is no less to be fled, because one should glory not in exterior appearance but in the interior. Whence Seneca says: "No one indeed says a sword is good if its belt is gilded or its scabbard is distinct with gems, but a sword is called 'good' because it cuts well and has a good edge." <note>Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, 76.11</note> Whence there are these verses: *If golden nobility clothes a clay pot, it does not therefore follow that the pot is any less clay.* Regarding this threefold [division] of the satirist: In this part, Boethius <note>The text attributes these divisions to Boethius, likely referring to the "Consolation of Philosophy" or a commentary thereon</note>, in the manner of the Satirists, dividing luxury itself...

...into parts, he proceeds to argue against it. And he does two things: first, he divides luxury itself into three species; second, he demonstrates that its first species is utterly to be abhorred by means of an example, at the point [beginning] "With a shameful..." And he says the satirists—understand "poets who are rebukers of crimes and vices"—divided this luxury by a threefold partition, i.e., into three species, saying that one luxury consists in adornment (supply: "of clothes"), another in intercourse, and the third they said was the "assistant," i.e., the companion to gluttony, that vice of excessive drinking. And we, Boethius, know that subjects, i.e., scholars, frequently suffer from a foul madness, i.e., a stinking fury of any [kind] of lusts. Some poets are called lyric, some comic, others tragic; others are called satirists from "satire," which is a poem of rebuke or a corrective reprimand, because it rebukes in order to correct. And hence a satirist is a writer of satires. And these satirists divided luxury into three species, as is evident in the text. Likewise, "foul" (*feculentus*) means full of dregs and stinking. "With a shameful appetite for intercourse": In this part, Boethius, dissuading from the foulness of the first species of luxury (i.e., intercourse), provides an example. And he does two things: first, he does what has been said; second, from the proposed example, he concludes that this species is to be detested above all, at the point "Behold how much..." The first part is further divided into two: first he does what has been said; second, he adds a certain notable point concerning this, at "son, father." And he says: the first species of luxury, which consists in intercourse, is to be entirely spurned. And this is so that it does not happen to us as it did to the blood-related son of Lucretius, the disciple of Zeno, whom all of Rome wept for as "ensnared," i.e., captured and held by a shameful appetite for intercourse; and here "Rome" is used for the Roman people. He was indeed born of the most illustrious lineage...

As in: "Why did I not obey the teachings of my master? And why did I despise my companions (understand: by not imitating them in good things)?" As if to say: if I had done all these things, I certainly would not have been adjudged to this abominable gibbet of the cross.

From this example, having been set forth, he draws out a certain notable point or a general sentiment, saying: He who wishes to beware lest the aforesaid things happen, it is necessary that the father himself indulge, that is, that the father should grant or give labor to the chastising, that is, the correction of the son; and this is said on the part of the father. Similarly, it is necessary that the master himself inform, that is, that the master should inform or teach the disciple in morals; and this is said on the part of the master.

It is to be noted, as **Fulgentius** <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Latin writer of the late 5th/early 6th century known for his mythological allegories.</note> relates in the second book of his *Mythologies*: "Although in all things the love of lust is base, it is yet baser in honorable men; for that injury is contrary to majesty." Therefore, the lust of the sanguine man is most base, which he brings into the argument: though he excelled in the most illustrious origins of birth and wonderful gifts of nature, yet because he [indulged] in sexual intercourse beyond what was due...

It followed that whoever used such things would enter the path of perdition. For that vicious and foul love accords with such danger; and when one is vacant only for that which he loves, he never sees what is expedient, because the love of luxury <note>original: "luxurie"; here meaning lechery or excess</note> is blind. Wherefore the ancients despised lust as the enemy of honor. Thus Scipio Nasica prohibited theaters and places of prostitution, as Augustine relates in his book *The City of God*. Likewise, "zealous" <note>original: "zelotipus"</note> means full of zeal, that is, envious or suspicious.

### Why did I not obey the teachings of my masters, and why did I despise my companions? It is necessary for a son to yield to a father’s correction, and for a master to shape the character of a pupil. Behold how detestable is the assault of harlots. For a harlot is a "nine-hour woman" <note>original: "nonaria"; a Roman term for prostitutes who were legally allowed to begin work only after the ninth hour (3 PM)</note>, the gate of hell, the way of iniquity, the sting of the scorpion, the snare of crimes, the pit of destruction. —picious. It is used in both an active and a passive sense, of which there are five names contained in this verse: *Guest, jealous, spouse, carrier, foster-child; these names can signify either acting or suffering.* It is also spoken of as "jealousy" for adultery, and "jealous" for an adulterer, and it is taken in this way in the present context. Likewise, "itching" <note>original: "pruritus"</note>, that is, a scabies; it means a heat or burning of the flesh compelling one to scratch; here it is used for lust, and not inaptly. Likewise, "to indulge" <note>original: "indulgeo"</note> signifies various things. For to indulge

For they expose their own flesh for sale and, under the pretext of life, acquire their food through fornication; they neither love nor seek to love, but serve their execrable greed from the foulest part of luxury. Of these, Theodolus says: *The robust mind of a man falls by womanly levity,* because surely an unchaste woman is a snare for a man. And therefore they add: *The Assyrians wept because they believed a woman.* And furthermore, someone said: *Woman pollutes the body, annihilates wealth, kills the soul, snatches away strength, bereaves the eyes, and embitters voices.* And elsewhere: *Brothels [destroy] the body, wealth, and soul.*

She said: "A thousand denarii." <note>A significant sum of silver coins</note>
To which Demosthenes replied: "I do not buy regret at such a price." And rightly so, for it is foolish to buy at a price that which is followed by pain. Likewise, a *nonaria* is a prostitute, and she is so named from the "ninth hour" <note>roughly 3:00 PM</note>, because before the ninth hour she was not permitted to leave the brothel. For before that hour, it was the ancient custom to debate the welfare of the republic; therefore, it was forbidden for prostitutes to be seen until then, lest they incline the young men toward foul pleasures. Likewise, *viscarium* <note>a snare or birdlime</note> comes from *viscus*, which is the glue by which birds are caught. Hence, a snare. Likewise, ignominy is infamy, as if "against the name." Therefore, let intoxication be far from scholarly men; for we read that the ancients lived with parsimony. Socrates stood out as most temperate and was content with a single evening meal, knowing that nature is satisfied with few and very small things, and judging nothing more suitable for that man than sobriety, by which the prosperity of body and mind is strengthened. Hence Ennodius says: "Let sobriety always be related to honest studies. No faith is whole in joyful times nor in doubtful ones. I embrace the healthy branches that give good seeds. After faults, the burnt offerings of God are the soul."
