# Chapter

In this section, Boethius, after having detested the first two types of luxury <note>Latin: *luxuria*, here meaning excess or debauchery</note>, shows that this third type must also be shunned. This part is divided into two: first, he teaches to flee this third species; second, he verifies his words with examples, beginning at the phrase *When once...* The first part is further divided into two: first, showing it must be fled, he demonstrates those whom it principally concerns; second, he declares in what things it consists, at the phrase *This however joys...*

<columns>2</columns>

**unconquered. This [luxury] however joys in the frequent variety of garments and in their decoration <note>Latin: *sigillatione*, referring to seal-like patterns or embroidery</note> limb by limb; and by the benefit of the comb to polish the hair <note>Latin: *cesariem*, specifically the hair of the head</note> and with the twisting of the curling iron; and to wanton in a row of diverse flowers; and to drench one's throat <note>the face</note> with rouge; and to gape at the frequent discipline of the razor; to fill the bosom with aromatics; to show to the common people a neck with jeweled necklaces and a belly restrained by Parthian belts; and to walk like a queen in beaked and patterned shoes with the neck**

<column-break/>

joys. And he says first that this third species of luxury is concupiscence, that is, a certain desire which gapes at—that is, intends toward—ornaments and consists in—that is, is married or joined to—the lineage of the powerful, that is, of nobles and the wealthy. I say ornaments to which a safe estate—that is, the status of poverty—gives way, being unconquered—that is, not surpassed—by their vanity. It should be noted that this third species of luxury which gapes at ornaments is nothing other than the extolling of the body or of

<columns>1</columns>

ornaments, and those things which belong to the body, or finally of clothing. Whatever it may be, it is a certain pride and vainglory. As it appears to Sallust in the *Jugurthine War*, and is also proven by experience, this evil is more common to nobility than to the humble. For poverty inhabits humble huts, but "lightnings strike the highest mountains." <note>A reference to Horace, Odes 2.10</note> Poverty is therefore safe, for it does not seek the clothing of the body but the abundance of the soul, concerning which it was said by the poet: *O truly safe estate of the poor and of the narrow hearth! O gifts of the gods not yet understood!* <note>Lucan, Pharsalia 5.527</note>

**This however joys.** In this part, Boethius shows in what things this third species of luxury is mostly placed. And he says that this third species of luxury joys in the frequent variety of clothes and their "sealing"—that is, their decoration limb by limb, from one limb to another. For this Polemo, as Valerius relates in Book 6, Chapter "On the Change of Manners," stood out as so given to allurements that he rejoiced in his very infamy. And when he had once risen from a banquet after sunrise, heavy with wine and smeared with the best ointments, clad in a transparent garment and with wreaths binding his head, and saw the open schools of Xenocrates <note>A Greek philosopher and head of the Platonic Academy</note> before which he happened to pass, he entered so that he might mock the most wise precepts with the wantonness of his drunkenness. And while all those sitting by were indignant, Xenocrates, with a mature expression, set aside the matter he was discussing and began to speak of modesty and temperance. Hearing the gravity of his speech, Polemo first cast away the crown taken from his head; afterwards he laid aside his cloak and cast off his convivial hilarity. At last, he laid aside all luxury. Thus, healed by the medicine of a single speech, he escaped from infamy thereafter. # Third

He introduces inconstancy itself as the handmaid of arrogance and pride, joined to it as if a close sister, so that by utterly despising and refuting it, one may long for **constancy** itself. And he divides this chapter into two principal parts: first, he sets forth his intent; second, he introduces the example of inconstancy itself, at the point: *When in the gymnasia...* <note>original: "Cum in gymnasijs." Referring to places of study or schools.</note> The first part is divided into two: first, he shows that constancy is to be embraced above all else; second, he compares it to inconstancy, at the point:

What indeed is more radiant? And he says: Since the student himself is known to strive toward perfection, he must therefore impress upon his mind the effective cause of perfection—namely, **constancy of continuity** in study. For it is this which completes a work begun and leads it to the desired end. Whence that common proverb is taken: *Continued things flourish; discontinued things shall perish.* <note>original: "Continuata vigent: discontiuata peribunt." A medieval scholastic maxim emphasizing persistence.</note> It should be noted

<column-break/>

that he is known to impress constancy upon the mind as far as his ability allows. For what is more radiant in a work of love than **constancy**? What is more wicked than **inconstancy**? The first gives birth; the second dissolves what has been born. The first moves forward; the second moves backward. The first gathers; the second scatters what has been gathered. Moreover, when we had decided to toil in the schools and thought it worthy to take the place of the master, [we encountered] the son of inconstancy—or rather, to speak more truly, inconstancy itself in

because no laudable work or anything to be counted among "crowned merits" <note>A reference to spiritual or academic rewards/honors.</note> is thought to exist if the constancy of continuity and **perseverance** are known to be absent. For where one remains constant, he deserves to receive the reward of his labor. Indeed, the crown shall be given to the one who strives lawfully and perseveres until the end. For a <term>habit</term> <note>Latin: "habitus." In Aristotelian philosophy, a stable disposition of the mind or character acquired through repeated action.</note> is not generated from bare acts in this way unless the perseverance of the work is present. One must therefore study perseveringly, since among human occupations nothing is more delightful than to continually meditate upon the sciences, to contemplate varieties, and to take pleasure in the arts. 

But perhaps you will say that you cannot always intend to study, since it is necessary to interrupt it for other things. Responding to this doubt, I say that a <term>measure</term> <note>Latin: "modus." The golden mean or moderation.</note> must be applied in all things to be done. For in order to persevere, it is not necessary that you assist in labors incessantly; it suffices if, while you are unable to intend to study continuously, you at least persevere for a long time while you *are* intending, so that the habit may indeed take root in your soul. According to that saying of **Seneca** in *Oedipus*: *What cannot be done often, let it be done for a long time.* And this is what **Quintilian** says in the fourth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*: *One must at least persevere, because even if strengths fail the mind, one must nevertheless intend more often.* 

For nothing, as **Boethius** adds in the text, is more radiant in a small work of love than constancy itself—that is, perseverance. And conversely, nothing is more wicked than inconstancy. Because the first gives birth—that is, it acquires perfection for the student; the second, namely inconstancy, dissolves what has been born—that is, what was acquired. The first proceeds toward perfection; the second recedes from it. The first gathers—that is, accumulates perfection; the second scatters what has been gathered, according to this common saying: *Continued things flourish; discontinued things shall perish.* 

*Moreover, when in the gymnasia...* This is the second principal part of this third chapter, in which Boethius now confirms by example what he had previously said concerning inconstancy in comparison to constancy. And this part is divided into two parts: in the first, he does what has been said; in the second, from the example...

**Fortune assigned Inconstancy to be imbued by our precepts.** <note>original: "constantia fortuna nostris assignabat preceptis imbuendum"</note> **He who gaped at satiric inks monthly; for these historians, very often daily; for elegiac poets, yearly. But by reason of disputation, he lamented over Aristotle nightly; in philosophical editions, monthly...**

...to be imbued, that is, to be educated by our precepts, which are our teachings. Namely, this son of inconstancy gaped at the precepts—the lessons—of the satirists, that is, of the satiric poets who rebuke vices, for a month. And he gaped at the historiographers, that is, the writers of histories (so called from *historia* and *graphos*, meaning writing); "very often" is a prepositional phrase meaning most frequently, and he did this daily. For the Elegiacs, that is, the writers of elegies, he stayed for a year. But he lamented—that is, he gaped and followed while lamenting—Aristotle nightly, meaning only at night, and this only because the "reason of disputing" (that is, arguing) compelled him. Also, in philosophical editions—that is, in the books of philosophy and in the compilations of the Twelve Tables <note>The Twelve Tables were the foundation of ancient Roman law.</note>—he was engaged almost instantaneously. Whence this Law of the Twelve Tables was the origin of all law, according to the Gloss on the *Institutes* regarding natural law <note>original: "Instituta de iure naturali"</note> and the *Digest* on the origin of law. It is called a written law in twelve tables, ten of which were brought from the cities of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians by the "Ten Men" <note>The Decemviri, a commission of ten men appointed to draw up a code of laws in Rome.</note>, and two were added later by the same men for their clarification. 

However, in a short time, he became disgusted with all of them. It should be noted that this son of inconstancy, who is introduced into the argument by Boethius, was like those who celebrate the vows of fasting one day and spend their time in study the next; they permit themselves to pray now, and pre-ordain themselves to be continent later. Of such people, Horace says in his Epistles: *What he sought, he scorns; he seeks again what he recently lost. He seethes, and his whole order of life is inconsistent.* <note>original: "Quos petijt spernit repetit quos nuper amisit. Estuat et vite discōvenit ordine toto." From Horace, Epistles 1.1.98-99.</note> It would be more profitable for the lives of such men if they studied to keep their minds constant in good undertakings rather than rolling through desires for novelty. For as the common proverb says: *A rolling stone gathers no moss.* <note>original: "Non fuit insutus lapis per loca volutus." Literally: "A stone rolled through places is not covered [in moss]."</note> So too, a mind turning now to these things, now to those, is not said to blossom with the flowers of many diverse doctrines.

*At length he began to be a merchant.* In this part, Boethius shows the turns of the second kind of diversion and mutability of the son of inconstancy. This same son of inconstancy, when he had become disgusted with all the aforementioned things, finally transferring himself to secular business, began to be a merchant by sea-voyage. But what happened? In the space of the first night, he was provoked to gaping by nausea—that is, vomiting—and this was compelled by the bilge-water, that place in which the ship's filth is collected. And finally, terrified by the leaping of the unfaithful sea, he desired to be...

### On the Studies of Crato
In this part, **Boethius** <note>likely referring to the author of the 'De Disciplina Scholarium', formerly attributed to Boethius</note> shows the third kind of diversion and changeability of the "Son of Inconstancy." He says that when this Son of Inconstancy grew weary of the previous pursuits, he turned himself afterward to the studies of that philosopher **Crato**. The capacity of Crato’s "semicircle"—meaning his teaching chair—was feared because of its many questions. For this Crato had a certain chair arched above in the manner of a semicircle, in which arching many types of questions were inscribed in a triple space.

This section is divided into three parts according to the triple location of the questions described on Crato’s seat. The second part begins at: *The map of the second circle.* The third begins at: *The final surface of the semicircle.*

The first of these contains seven parts, according to the seven questions described on the first surface of the semicircle. As the text says: *The width of the upper circle, formed*—that is, arranged—*as a flat surface*—that is, according to the plane of the **Zodiac**—*smiled upon* (meaning it invited those looking) *with drachmas*—that is, with sevenfold questions of seven different kinds. It should be noted that the author says this semicircle on Crato’s seat was wide and arranged in the form of the Zodiac to avoid a logical inconsistency: namely, that a "circle" is a line, and a line is length without width or depth. Therefore, to exclude this, he says the semicircular width was formed in the manner of the Zodiac, which extends twelve degrees in width, so that "circle" is understood as a circular surface and not just a circumference.

**The First Literal Proposition:** Here he places the first question described in the upper part of the semicircle of Crato’s seat. He says: *The first literal proposition on this seat asked whether the Divinity*—that is, God, on whom the heavens and all nature depend (referring to the 12th book of **Metaphysics**) —*of the Empyrean heaven itself could be darkened*—that is, overshadowed—*by any nature participating in "earthliness"*—that is, corruptibility.

Note that there is a double exposition of this question's title: one is the unsuitable assertion of the philosophers; the other is close to theological truth. The mind of the philosophical assertion is: *Whether God himself can know base things...*

<column-break/>

Indeed, he became weary of all things in a short time. If he indulged even slightly in the inspection of books or their writing, he would look at many within an hour, yet he would lay his hands on none of them to finish them, even for the shortest time. To the first part of this, the response is clear, which is as follows: for the stronger an active power <note>original: "virtus activa"</note> is, the further it extends its action into more remote things, as is apparent even in the actions of the senses. Now, the power of the divine intellect in knowing things is likened to an active power. **Terrified by the assault of the flooding, the gardener** <note>original: "ortolanus"</note> **desired to be. But when the pulse of military service failed, he transferred himself to the army. Having seen the incursions of the enemy, he committed his back to flight. And he gaped at the study of Crato** <note>Crato was a legendary philosopher often associated with the education of youth in medieval lore</note> **whose semicircle's capacity was dreaded for its many questions. <column-break/>

it is necessary that his knowledge extends even to the most remote things. But the grade of nobility or vileness in all beings is measured according to their proximity to or distance from God, who is of infinite nobility. Therefore, no matter how vile things may be among beings, God knows them on account of the greatest power of his intellect. Nor is this truth repugnant to the sayings of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the eleventh book of the *Metaphysics*.

For there he intends to show that the divine intellect does not understand anything other than itself that would be the perfection of its intellect as a primary thing known. And according to this, he says that vile things are better ignored than known—namely, when there is one knowledge of vile things and another of noble things, and the consideration of the vile hinders the consideration of the noble. Nevertheless, the vileness of the things known does not redound upon the knower by itself. For it is of the nature of knowledge that the knower contains the species of the thing known according to his own mode. By accident, however, the vileness of the things known can redound upon the knower, either because while he considers vile things he is distracted from thinking of nobler things, or because from the consideration of vile things he inclines toward certain undue affections. All of which certainly cannot be in God, wherefore etc. And this accords with what is said in *Wisdom* 7 <note>The Book of Wisdom in the Vulgate</note> concerning divine wisdom: that it reaches everywhere because of its purity, and nothing defiled enters into it. The title of the question can also be understood to ask whether God could assume humanity for himself. And to this, a sufficient answer is given in the first chapter of John: *And the Word was made flesh*, where "flesh" is taken for "man" according to Augustine. Therefore, this affirmative part of the question is to be assumed among the faithful as the primary foundation of the Christian faith.

**Second [Question]**
**Whether the vital service of spirits.** This is the second question of the first part of the semicircle of Crato’s chair. Its title, like the first, receives a double interpretation; wherefore it is resolved with two responses according to the first exposition of the total meaning of the question. **Whether separate substances, such as angels and demons, can assume human bodies.** As far as the second exposition is concerned, it seems only to mean: **Whether the intellectual soul itself can be united to a human body as its form.** Regarding the first exposition of the question, the text is to be supplied in this way: The second of the questions placed in the upper part of the semicircle is this: **Whether the service** <gloss>that is, the ministry</gloss> **of the vital spirit** <gloss>that is, of the angels serving God or of the demons</gloss> **or rather the spirit itself can be blackened** <gloss>that is, obscured or uncovered</gloss> **or surrounded by the circuit** <gloss>that is, the compass and clothing</gloss> **of earthly dregs** <gloss>that is, of the body</gloss> **and by this subsidy** <gloss>that is, the help of nature</gloss>. And to this it must be answered that by divine permission both good and evil spirits can assume earthly bodies. Concerning the good ones, indeed, it is manifest in history...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological inquiry into the nature of spirits and the union of soul and body, following the previous discussion on the hierarchy of beings.</meta>

# Third

In the book of Tobit, and especially in chapter 12, it is said that the angel Raphael himself ate, which is certainly a physical act. <note>original: "angelum ipsum raphaelem comedisse"</note> Regarding evil spirits, it is similarly evident in the case of Incubi and Succubi, whom some call "hairy ones" <note>original: "pilosos"; likely a reference to satyrs or forest demons in medieval lore</note>. These are most lustful demons who, by God's permission, assume bodies to oppress women or place themselves under men. Just as with these, so with others, it is undoubtedly permitted for them to assume bodies either to tempt the good or to punish the wicked. For the entire intention of demons is either the exhaustion of the good or the retention of the wicked. For this reason, they often disturb the elements, frequently stirring up storms at sea and in the air; they corrupt and devastate the fruits of the earth, as seen in Revelation chapter 7. They always crave the afflictions of the righteous, but if they do not receive power from God, their strength for the moment of temptation avails them nothing.

As for the second exposition of the title, the text reads: *Whether the vital service*—that is, the life-giving spirit, namely the soul—*can be blackened*—that is, united and clothed as a form—*by the surrounding of earthly dregs*—that is, in the body itself—*by the help of nature*—that is, naturally.

Regarding the solution to this, it should be noted that various opinions exist among philosophers on this matter. For Aristotle reports in the first book of *On the Soul* and the seventh book of *Metaphysics* that Plato posited the intellect is united to the body not as a form is to matter, but as a mover to the thing moved, in the same way a sailor is united to a ship, or an intelligence to a celestial sphere—not by way of informing it, but by a contact of power. <note>Plato's "sailor in a ship" analogy suggests the soul is a separate entity merely directing the body.</note> Since by this contact the indivisible can touch the divisible, Plato says that man himself is not a single being composed of a body and an intellective soul, but is the intellective soul itself using a body, just as a man uses a garment. The Commentator <note>Averroes, the 12th-century Islamic philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, however, in the third book of *On the Soul*, says that the intellect is joined to us through the continuation of the understood intention, because the same intention informs both the intellect and the imaginative power.

But these positions are irrelevant, as is evident. The first is irrelevant because a moved object does not receive its formal being from its mover; therefore, the moved object is naturally in act before it is moved. For that which is moved is already in act, according to the fifth book of *Physics*. But man has his formal being through the intellect, as is clear; therefore, the intellective soul is not united to the body merely as a mover, as Plato wished. Nor is it united to it through understood phantasms <note>mental images</note> as the Commentator wished.

This is proved: an understood species is related to a phantasm just as a visible species is to colors, according to the Commentator in the second book of *On the Soul*. Therefore, the continuation of the "possible intellect" through an intelligible species with a phantasm in us is similar to the continuation of the visual power through a visible species with the color in a stone. But this continuation does not make the stone see; therefore, the continuation of the possible intellect in us with a phantasm does not make us understand.

Therefore, it must be said with Aristotle that the intellective soul is united to the body substantially through "information" <note>the process of a form giving shape and essence to matter</note>, so that it is the substantial form of the human body, not only giving it the ability to operate (as an intelligence does to a sphere), but also giving it its specific and essential being. It is clear that the specific difference constituting any species is taken from the form of that species. This is clear from the mind of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *Metaphysics*, saying that contraries following matter do not make a difference in species, but contraries following form do. Now, the proper difference of man is "rational"; therefore, it is taken from the human form. But "rational" is taken from that which is intellective and reasoning; therefore, the intellect is the form of the human body. Wherefore, as said in the text, it is a "vital service"—that is, giving life. For the soul itself is the "act" of an organic physical body having life in potentiality.

Thirdly, according to the Jewish threefold division, this is the third question in the upper part.

<column-break/>

...the level surface smiled upon the sevenfold drachmas.

The first literal extension asked whether the dominion of the Empyrean heaven could be obscured by any princely nature of earthliness.

The second asked whether the vital service of spirits could be blackened by the surrounding of earthly dregs through the aid of nature.

->placed upon the chair of Crato<- <note>Likely referring to a specific academic chair or a set of philosophical propositions attributed to a scholar named Crato.</note>. And it is as follows: Whether one should rather acquiesce—that is, obey—the threefold Jewish division of the poles (that is, the heavens), or rather the simple Aristotelian partition (that is, division). It should be noted that where the Hebrew tradition holds that beyond the orbits of the planets there consist three heavens: namely, the **Starry Heaven**, the **Aqueous** or **Crystalline Heaven**, and the **Empyrean Heaven**. Our theologians maintain that above all these is the High One Himself <note>original: "celsi ipsm"</note>, who is the same in substance with God, though differing in our reasoning. For it is nothing

<margin>
other than the excellence of the power of God, by which He contains and encompasses all created things. After this, the Empyrean heaven is the most noble among all simple bodies, and therefore it is called "fiery" by the saints—
</margin>

**The third question, however, is whether one should acquiesce to the Jewish threefold division of the poles or to the simple Aristotelian partition. The fourth is, if the Jewish division is accepted, whether the boundaries are from them, or in them, or** yet not because of heat, but on account of the bodily light diffused within it. No philosopher attained an understanding of this, except perhaps—according to the opinion of John of Damascus <note>original: "damasceni"</note>—those alone to whom the nations attributed these dogmas as their own. This heaven is uniform, because just as it is necessary for the One to exist before the many, so also it is necessary for a uniform nature to exist before a multiform one. And it is itself immobile, because it participates in uniform goodness. But perhaps you will say: "Every body has a motion natural to itself." I respond: this is true of a body ordained for generation. The Empyrean heaven, however, is elevated above this kind of order.

The third heaven is the **Aqueous** or **Crystalline**, which Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar</note> concedes as an opinion; for among the doctors there is much diversity concerning it. It exists out of light as if from its fulfillment, and out of transparency as if from its material disposition. And this is the first to be subject to motion, which is why it was fittingly named the **First Mover** <note>term: "primum mobile" - the outermost moving sphere in classical astronomy</note> among the astrologers. The philosophers, speaking only according to the senses, scrutinized it according to the suitability of reason, both on the part of the mover and the motion, as well as its uniformity. After this heaven is the **Firmament**, which Aristotle falsely thought was the First Mover. And it is no wonder he was wrong, for as Ambrose says, that philosopher erred in many things that are above the moon; therefore it is no surprise if he erred in this heaven by calling it the First Mover.

Regarding this matter, we say in conclusion that one should acquiesce not to the Aristotelian but to the Jewish assertion concerning these heavens, and especially to the tradition of the theologians. The reason is that all spheres and heavens have a certain goodness proportioned to the First. Therefore, they either have this proportion without motion—and such would be the most noble, which is the Empyrean heaven—or they have this goodness proportioned to the First through motion. This is either through diverse motion—and this will be the Firmament, which is moved by a double motion—or it is necessary that there be something that has goodness proportioned to the First through a *single* motion. This cannot be the Empyrean heaven, which is immobile, nor the Firmament, which contains two motions. Therefore, there will be something prior to the Firmament and posterior to the Empyrean; and this is the Aqueous or Crystalline heaven itself, of which it is said: *And He divided the waters from the waters* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:7</note>.

**The fourth question: If the Jewish division is accepted.** This is the fourth of the questions placed on the upper part of the chair of Crato, which is elicited as a certain corollary from the third. It asks: if the Jewish assertion is to be accepted (which distinguishes a threefold heaven), then are the boundaries—that is, the extremities or surfaces of those heavens—"from them" (that is, continuous), or are they "in them" (that is, contiguous), or at least is each of these boundaries distinct (that is, following one after another)? If, however, one should acquiesce to the Aristotelian tradition, which places only the eighth circle after the orbits of the planets, then while the parts of the heaven move totally, the whole heaven itself does not move locally at the same time. Whence, to the first of these questions, it must be said briefly that the heavens themselves are contiguous; and not only the things of the upper heavens, but also the orbits of the planets. For the diverse motion of the spheres itself brings this about, and God the Greatest so disposed it to be. For just as a mobile thing cannot be continuous with an immobile thing, so neither can it...

# Third

The **prime mover** <note>original: *primum mobile*; the outermost moving sphere in the Ptolemaic system</note> can be made solid with the **empyrean heaven** <note>the highest heaven, believed to be the abode of God and the angels</note>. Nor is the eighth circle <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, which resists the daily motion, connected in any way to the prime mover itself; this is certainly prevented by the diversity of its motion from the first, and the multitude of its motions. The same reasoning can be applied to the orbits of the planets, both because of the diversity of their motions and the **eccentricity** <note>the off-center positioning of planetary orbits</note> of their spheres, all of which in no way permit a continuous connection.

Regarding the rest of the question, the answer is easily seen. For the heaven itself can be understood to move to another place in two ways: either by **circular motion**—and I say the whole moves together and at once from East to West every natural day—or by **rectilinear motion** <note>motion in a straight line</note>. And I say that in no way, because of the supreme perfection of the celestial body,

<column-break/>

each one individually. And if, according to **Aristotle**, when the parts of a whole are moved locally, why is the whole not moved? 

**Fifth:** Why is there a continuous transformation of the elements, and are the elements the same as they were at first, or do others exist?

**Sixth:** Since one of the contrary elements...

<column-break/>

can perfection fall into the heaven, since it would have a contrary. It would also follow from that absurdity that there would be a place outside the heaven and a **vacuum**, which is false, since outside it there is nothing: neither place, nor time, nor vacuum. Instead, there are the best beings leading a life which they complete in all eternity.

Note the word **individually** <note>original: *sigillatim*</note>: that is, singularly, through each one separated. It is said to be "in the singular." **Priscian** <note>a famous 6th-century Latin grammarian</note> takes it from "individuals" just as from "doorkeepers." Commonly, therefore, *sigillatim* is said for *singulatim*. Hence the Prophet says: *He who fashioned their hearts individually* <note>Psalm 33:15</note>, etc.

**Fifth:** Why is the transformation of the elements continuous? Because they are born fit for transformation. This appears in the second part of the treatise where it is asked: *Why is the transformation of the elements continuous?* To solve this question, it must be noted that some elements are **symbolic** <note>sharing a quality</note> and some are **dissymbolic** <note>sharing no qualities</note>. Symbolic elements are those that agree in another primary quality, such as fire and air in "heat." Dissymbolic elements are those that do not agree, such as fire and water. 

In answering the question, I say that the elements are transformed continuously because they are born fit for transformation. This fitness comes either from their agreement in primary qualities or from the inherent contrariety that always exists between the **active** and **passive**. Therefore, it is said that in symbolic elements, transformation is easier—not indeed by reason of speed, but by reason of the fewness of things corrupted. For dissymbolic elements, because of their inherent contrariety, enter into transformation more quickly. But I say the transformation is easier by reason of the fewness of things corrupted: for in symbolic elements, only one quality is corrupted—as when air is generated from fire, only the "dryness" of the fire is corrupted. If, however, water is made from fire, two are corrupted, namely "heat" and "dryness." Nature, therefore, does not labor as much in the transformation of symbolic elements as in dissymbolic ones. Although in dissymbolic ones it is faster because of the inherent contrarieties, as has been said.

Since, therefore, the elements are continuously transformed, do they **consist**—that is, remain numerically the same as they were before, or not? Here it is appropriate to note that something being the "same" as it was before is understood in three ways:
1. **Most strictly:** because it is varied neither in its whole nor in its substantial part; in this way, God or the **intelligences** <note>angelic beings that move the spheres</note> are numerically the same as they were before.
2. **Strictly:** because it is varied neither in its whole nor in its substantial part regarding its principal components; in this way, a man is that which he was before.
3. **Broadly:** because the accidental dispositions are not notably or sensibly varied; in this way, a person is said to be the same as before.

Having seen this, I say that just as no inanimate beings remain numerically the same in the second way through their whole duration, neither do the elements. But they do in the third way. It is clear because a new partial **form** and new partial **matter** are acquired and similarly lost by any such thing; yet a similar multitude of accidental dispositions remains. Therefore, although no...

# Chapter

...of these elements existing before a thousand years: if these elements are said to have been continuous because a similar arrangement of accidental dispositions <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accidental" quality is a property (like heat) that can change without changing the essential nature of the thing itself.</note> has continually appeared in them. **Note:** an element is so called as if it were "ilemetus," from *hyle* <note>original: "ile," from the Greek "hyle" (ὕλη), meaning primordial matter</note>, that is, primordial matter. For God first created *hyle* and from *hyle* separated the four elements. **The Sixth** concerning one of the elements. This is the sixth of the questions from the previous part of Crato’s chair <note>Likely a reference to a specific curriculum or "cathedra" (professor's chair) at a university</note>, the theme of which is B. Whether any of the contrary elements, such as water, can take on...

# Whether water may take on an accidental quality, such as heat; and why fire does not take on an accidental coldness.

# The Seventh: whether any zone other than ours is habitable. What was the first birth of those living there, what is their arrival, and what sort of departure is exchanged?

<column-break/>

...an accidental heat, and why, if this is so, fire cannot receive an accidental coldness. And to this it must be said that fire, among all the elements, possesses the greatest activity <note>The power to act upon other things</note> because of the abundance of its "form." Thus it happens that all other things—in which such great activity is not found, but rather a "passibility" <note>The capacity to be acted upon or changed</note> due to the abundance of matter which is the subject of transmutation and passibility—can be easily led into its own nature. It is easier, however, to change them toward their appropriate properties because of their inherent contrariety, although as a consequence it can also transform those properties themselves. Yet, on the other hand, other elements are not able to act so strongly upon fire as to reduce its heat to coldness, as the insufficiency of their activity prevents this.

**The Seventh: whether any zone other than ours [is habitable].** This is the seventh and last of the questions of the upper circle of Crato’s seat, which asks whether there is any habitable zone in the hemisphere other than our own—that is, in our hemisphere—and if so, what was the first birth of those living there, since it is clear that Adam, the first-formed <note>original: "prothoplautum" (protoplast), a traditional term for Adam as the first molded human</note>, did not decline toward those parts at all; and furthermore, how there is an arrival at those parts and a departure from them. It should be noted that this question is moved specifically because of the **Antipodes** <note>Literally "those with feet opposite"; people living on the other side of the Earth</note>. For the Antipodes are underground peoples who are against us, having their feet turned toward ours, as some think. **Papias** <note>A 11th-century lexicographer</note> says they are called Antipodes because they are thought to be contrary to our footsteps. 

Therefore, for the solution of the question, it must be known that their existence is understood in two ways: either that they live in the lower hemisphere, or with us in our own. Regarding the first understanding, I say that the Antipodes cannot live in that manner, since that which we call the lower hemisphere is totally submerged in water; for which reason the earth is called "enclosed" because it is inhabited-around by the Ocean. It is also called the **Island of Atlantis**. So says **Marcus Cicero** in the *Dream of Scipio*: "All the earth which is inhabited by you is a small island, narrow at the top and broader at the sides, surrounded by that sea which you call the Atlantic, the Great Sea, or the Ocean, etc." Since, therefore, that part is submerged, it is clear that only that part which floats above the waters, which we inhabit, is traversed by habitation. 

As for the second understanding—that these Antipodes live in our hemisphere, or at least could live there—it is not dissonant with reason. However, according to the latitudes of the regions which extend from the south to the north at most to the 80th degree according to the opinion of **Ptolemy**, the brevity of the earth's latitude would prevent direct opposite positions in the middle. But according to the longitudes of the regions, which extend from the east all the way to the Western **Fortunate Islands** <note>The Canary Islands, then considered the western edge of the world</note> for 180 degrees (which is half the circle), it is not impossible for Antipodes to be located. For those existing in the furthest ends of the east have their meridian 90 degrees distant from the equinoctial, and similarly for those in the furthest western places. Thus it happens, since the meridian is a circle cutting the sphere into two quarters, that the heads and feet of both extend from opposite parts. It is clear, therefore, that the Westerners are positioned diametrically opposite to the Easterners. And these are called Antipodes or "Antigenoi" <note>Those of an opposite origin</note>. 

Nor is it an obstacle if one were to say: "The nature of contraries is such that if one is suitable, the other will be unsuitable." Therefore, if the habitation of the east is suitable and healthy for living creatures, then the one diametrically opposite to it would be unsuitable. It is replied that this verse applies to things formally opposite that do not have the same situational relationship as in this proposal. Thus, the solution to the question asking about their first birth is easily brought forward: I say it was from Adam, just as with others. And similarly for the other point: what is the arrival and what sort of departure from them? I say it is the same as for the rest, unless the barbarity of nations and the unknown spaces of the journeys should hinder those wandering through.

# The Third Part

### The Map of the Circle
In this section, Boethius <note>Likely referring to the author of the commentary or a specific textual authority</note> sets forth the second order of questions depicted on the Chair of Crato, toward which the "son of inconstancy" <note>A metaphorical figure representing the student or seeker of knowledge</note> turns after the first set. This section is divided into nine parts according to nine types of questions, which will become clear as we proceed. He states first that the **map**—that is, the plain, form, or arrangement of the second circle of Crato’s seat—held the eyes of those looking upon it with a **ninefold inspection**, meaning an examination of nine questions.

The **first question** contained the width of the **Zodiac** <note>The belt of the heavens extending about 8 degrees on either side of the ecliptic</note>, that celestial circle which modifies—that is, measures—the quality of the other circles. Understand here the other spiral circles, such as the two tropics, the two polar circles, and the one in the middle of them all which they call the **equator** or the **equinoctial**. I say "modifying" in an **inspective** sense (according to appearance), and "modifying" in a **definitive** sense (by showing the essences of those **colures** <note>Two principal meridians of the celestial sphere</note>, which are semicircles), and "modifying" in a **progressive** sense (following the logic of the quantity of the entire world-form).

<column-break/>

->**The map of the second circle held the eyes of the observers with a ninefold inspection. The first of these contained the width of the zodiac, modifying the quality of the circles and the colures.**<-

It should be noted that the intent of this entire text is to seek a description of the circles of the **universal machine of the world** <note>original: "universalis mundi machine"; a common medieval metaphor for the cosmos as a divine mechanism</note> from this second part of the semicircle of Crato’s chair, and finally to find the measurement of the quantity of its form. For the resolution of all these matters, it must be noted that in the world-machine itself, some circles are imagined to be **greater** and others **lesser**. The **greater** circles are those which cut the sphere into two equal halves. The **lesser** circles divide it into two unequal parts. Among the greater circles is the **Zodiac**, which they call the "circle of life" or "of animals" (from *zoes*, which means animal <note>original: "a zoes quod est animal"; a medieval etymology linking the Greek 'zoon' to the zodiac</note>), because in it are figured the twelve signs named after animals. This circle, in its length, contains 360 degrees by astronomical division, just like any spherical circle. In its width, however, it contains twelve degrees, which a certain line cuts through the middle lengthwise; this line is properly called the **ecliptic**. This circle is also divided according to portions of length into twelve parts which we call **signs**, beginning from **Aries** and passing through **Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn,** and **Aquarius**, until it reaches the end of **Pisces** and finally returns to the head of Aries.

Therefore, it must be understood that by the rotation of the firmament, these zodiacal parts undoubtedly designate certain circles—not indeed real ones depicted with color or other industry, but purely **intellectual and mathematical** circles. The greatest of these, equidistant from both poles and extending from east to west and back to the east through the heads of Aries and Libra, is called the **equator**. Just as this circle is marked by the heads of Aries and Libra through the daily revolution, no less are the two **tropics** described through the circumferences of Cancer and Capricorn. They are called "tropics" as if to say "turning points" <note>original: "quasi conversivi"</note>, because when the sun reaches those circles, it either returns toward us or at least recedes from us in its own proper motion. Yet these circles are not among the "greater" circles, since they cut the sphere into unequal parts. Furthermore, just as we grant that the two tropics are described by the extreme parts of the zodiac, so too—since the zodiac circle is oblique and has its own poles different from the poles of the world—we must admit that an **arctic** circle (near the "Bears" <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Minor</note>) and an **antarctic** circle (opposite the Bears) are described by the daily revolution of the poles of the zodiac. Their distance from the poles of the world is found to be equal to the distance of the tropics from the equator.

<summary>This page explains the astronomical geometry of the "Chair of Crato," focusing on the Zodiac and how its movement defines the equator, tropics, and polar circles. It emphasizes that these celestial circles are mathematical constructs used to measure the "machine of the world."</summary>
<keywords>Zodiac, Equator, Ecliptic, Tropics, Arctic Circle, Antarctic Circle, World-Machine, Crato, Astronomy, Geometry</keywords>

## Again, because through the sun’s own motion it happens that now the equinoxes <note>original: "equinoctia"</note> and now indeed the solstices <note>original: "solsticia"</note> occur: it is necessary to imagine certain arcs distinguishing both the equinoxes and the solstices. Likewise, it is called a map <note>original: "mappa"</note>, a picture, or a form: thus we also speak of a map of the world <note>original: "mappam mundi"</note>. It is also called a *togilla* from the hand, because it is a *manupia*, that is, purifying the hand. From this comes *mappella*, the diminutive. Second, whether the stars are

---

fixed. This is the second of the nine questions in the other part of the semicircle of the chair of Crato <note>likely a reference to a specific diagram or classroom seating arrangement in the original manuscript's context</note>. And it asks whether the stars—namely those which were ordained in the eighth heaven by the will of God—are fixed, that is, located immovably so that they are moved in no way except by the motion of their own heaven in its superior place (namely the eighth heaven); or at least whether they are discerned to wander about, that is, to be moved in the likeness of the planets. This is to ask whether they are moved by a motion other than the motion of the firmament itself. For the solution of this question, it should be noted how, through astrological demonstrations, God himself—the maker and father of every universal creature, by whom justice is assigned to them, as Plato judged in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "Thimeo"</note>—wishing to make nothing but a beautiful world-machine, adorned it for the universal generation and life of lower things with diverse and innumerable stars. He established some as fixed and some indeed as wandering. Fixed, indeed, not because they are moved in no way, but because they consist in their heaven as if nailed and firm, so that they are carried around by no motion other than that of their own heaven. Beneath these, in a diversity of orbs, he located the wandering stars, that is, the planets—called *planets* as if from *planytas*, which sounds like "striking with error." For that thing "errs" which is diversified every day and moment, not by its own motion, but by a motion different from both the first mover and the firmament; which diversity indeed seems to strike mortals with error. Each of these planets is carried around in its own orb—an "orb," I say, in its aggregate as one, but with several circles according to the diversity of each motion. Consider that all these things have been demonstrated in the astrological observations of Ptolemy, Alfraganus, Thabit <note>original: "Thebith"</note>, Battani <note>original: "Albategni"</note>, and others. Therefore, when these things are collected as noted before and each weighed one by one, that which was asked is easily resolved: whether the fixed stars are moved by their own motion or at least by the motion of the planets. Between a "star" <note>original: "stella"</note> and a "constellation" <note>original: "sidus"</note> there is this difference: a star is said to be any single one, while a constellation is a collection of many stars. Nevertheless, these names are frequently confused among authors, who take "star" for "constellation" and "constellation" for "star." And "star" is said to come from "standing" <note>original: "stella a stando"</note> because they are at rest, and they are properly stars which are situated in the firmament. Third, whether comets are red, etc. This is the third of the nine questions of the second part of the semicircle of the chair of Crato, which asks whether comets—that is, "haired stars," glowing redly as omens for the significance of some great future event—run through, that is, are moved around the arc in a circular motion with the other planets and in their likeness; or whether the comets themselves, being destructive or annihilative, return into their chaos, that is, into their matter from which they were generated, having been born by the promise of the nature of the Maker, that is, of glorious God. Note that although others ask whether comets are stars or generated in the air itself, to this I say that among the ancients and in common there has been great diversity. For the Pythagoreans said a comet was one of the seven wandering stars; Anaxagoras and Democritus, however, said they were of the nature of the heavens. But since all...

# Third Part

The third part <note>referring to a previous logical division in the argument</note> argues that if a part of the heaven were permanent, it would follow that comets would be permanent; which is false. Therefore, one must say with Aristotle in the first book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "pmo metheoroz"</note> that a comet is an ignited exhalation of an elementary nature. This is evident because a comet is neither fire nor air, since it is an imperfect mixture, nor is it a vapor, since it does not ascend to such a height. Therefore, it is an exhalation. The conclusion follows because it does not appear to be anything else. The second part is evident because a comet is either of a heavenly nature or of an elementary nature. But it is not of a heavenly nature; therefore, it is of an elementary nature. The logical consequence is clear with the major premise, and the minor premise is declared: because no part of heaven is generated or corrupted, according to the first book of *On the Heavens* <note>original: "pmo celi"</note>. But

<column-break/>

**every comet is generated and corrupted, therefore etc. From these points, the question is easily answered: comets are not stars but exhalations. And if it is said that a comet moves with a circular motion, while no elements move with this kind of motion, etc., it is answered that although the elements do not move except by one motion derived from an internal drive to flee their contrary—namely, straight motion—nevertheless they can be moved naturally from an external source in a circle through the influence of the heaven. By this same influence, the comet is moved similarly along with the air in the upper region in a circle.**

**Next, regarding the text where it says "prodigiously": a prodigy is a foul monster prepared for devastation; and similarly regarding the word "destructively." Note that the appearance of a comet always signifies great and evil effects. For as Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous Arab astrologer</note> maintains in his commentary on the last proposition of the *Centiloquium* of Ptolemy and also Aristotle in the first book of the *Meteorology*: they signify great droughts of the earth's produce, sterility, earthquakes and an abundance of vices, floods of waters, death and plague, battles, the overthrow of kingdoms, and the changing of laws or the novelty of sects. And all these things happen according to the diverse magnitude, figure, color, motion, place, and duration of the comets.**

**Hence Seneca, in his book *Natural Questions*, says that two islands were announced as submerged by a comet. And as Justin relates, in the year that Mithridates was born, a comet was seen for four hours, filling the sky with such brightness that it seemed as if it were on fire and the rays of the sun were overshadowed. This Mithridates waged atrocious wars with the Romans for forty-six years, as Valerius Maximus says concerning study and industry, and as Solinus asserts in his book *On the Wonders of the World*. Furthermore, during the reign of Nero, a comet appeared for six months, and Seneca reports the same above. But what could be worse in those times than to live under such a curious master, of whom John of Salisbury <note>original: "Johãnes solobriensis"</note> speaks in the *Policraticus*, book one? In such a mass of empire, he cast aside all dignity, so that pursuing philosophy as if it were a threat to the majesty of the empire, and fearing more noble characters, he subjected himself to the counsels of actors.**

**The fourth question: whether it is of an inferior nature. This is the fourth question of the second part of the semicircle, which asks whether complexioned things—that is, all those things generated here below of an inferior nature (meaning of the elements)—contract their virtue (that is, their existence) or their eclipse (that is, their defect) from the planets (meaning from celestial influence) or from their primary progenitors (meaning their parents). For if it is from the planets, it is either according to necessity or at least according to the event (that is, by chance). If truly from the progenitors, since one progenitor is sometimes white and another black and vice versa, why is the one born from them not both white and black? And similarly, if so, why does the one born sometimes resemble the parent in the extremities of the body, such as the hands, feet, and the rest, and similarly why in speech and other behaviors does it resemble the one giving birth? Sometimes, however, it resembles neither of the parents (this is understood). For the absolute resolution of this question and any of its parts, it must be noted that in the generation and production of things into being, a triple formal principle must be assigned: namely, the first and principal principle itself, which is the First Cause itself <note>God</note>.**

This principle, however, is a power consisting in the seed of living beings, just as the craftsman exists in the crafted object; this is called by some physicians the "formative power" <note>term: formative power (virtus formativa) — the biological force believed to shape an embryo</note>, by others the "life-giving power," and by some the "image of the world." These three principles relate to each other in the production of living beings such that the lower is influenced by the higher and not the reverse. Therefore, to satisfy the question here, it must be said that all generated things receive their power, their lifespan <note>original: "periodum"</note>, and their decline from that very seed-principle, as if from a principle immediately moved by the influence of the celestial bodies at the nod and will of the First Cause. 

Yet, it must not be thought that these things happen by some forced necessity unless the First Cause itself has so disposed it; for the impressions of natural causes are received in their effects according to the mode of the receiver. Lower things, however, are fluid and do not always remain in the same state because of matter itself, which is in potentiality for many forms. And this is as **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar</note> reports in the first book of *Minerals*: that **Plato** intended this when he said that forms themselves are received according to the merits of the matter. Hence **Ptolemy** <note>The famous Greco-Egyptian astronomer</note> says in the *Alarba* <note>The Tetrabiblos</note> that the effects of the stars are uncertain and diverse because in lower things they arrive through "the other" and "by accident." Through "the other" because of the elementary powers which they first inform; "by accident" because they do not reach lower things except through a universal existence which is confused and of uncertain dispositions. 

And the same **Ptolemy** in the *Quadripartitum* says again: we ought not to believe that higher things proceed inevitably like those things which happen by divine disposition and which are by no means to be avoided, nor those which happen truly and out of necessity. In the *Centiloquium* <note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note> it is also said: "These judgments which I hand to you are midway between the necessary and the possible." Therefore, this part of the question is resolved: whether complexioned beings receive their powers and lifespan from the planets or from the first parents, since they receive them from both, though by different reasoning. Similarly, if from the planets, whether by necessity or by chance. It remains, therefore, to explain how the diverse resemblance of offspring toward parents is resolved. It must be said that the cause of this resemblance or dissimilarity is confirmed both by the influence of the celestial body and by the matter receiving these impressions, as well as by many concomitant causes and the connections of the higher powers. 

And hence **Hippocrates** says, as **Galen** reports, that every substance is bound and perfected in the planets, the signs, and the connections of the four elements. And for this reason **Nectanebus**, the natural father of **Alexander** <note>referring to the legend of Alexander the Great's birth</note>, observing the time with Alexander's mother **Olympias**, waited for the conjunction of the Sun entering Leo and Saturn in Taurus, from which planets he wished his son to receive his form and power.

# Third Section

**Fifth: What is the proportion of motion?** This is the fifth question of the second part of the *Semicircle of the Seat of Craton* <note>A likely reference to a specific medieval or Renaissance diagram or philosophical teaching attributed to a figure named Craton</note>, in which it is asked what the proportion—that is, the relationship—of motion is among the planets. This means: in what relationship does the motion of one planet stand to the motion of another, and what is their connection—that is, their ordering—namely, which of them is ordered higher or lower within the celestial body. For the solution to this question, it must be noted that the motion of the planets is diverse,

<insert>
of the generators. Fifth: what is the proportion of motion to motion among the planets and what is their connection? Sixth: since Saturn is the most cruel among the planets and Venus the most kind, whether the kindness of one retards the malice [of the other].
</insert>

just as their diverse spheres demonstrate. For from the diversity of motions, it is necessarily seen that one arrives at a diversity of spheres. Among all the planets, **Saturn** is the slowest of all; for this reason, he is called "the Old Man" <note>original: "senem"</note> because of the slowness of his motion, since he completes his course in thirty years alone. **Jupiter**, truly a benevolent planet, completes his motion after him in twelve years. **Mars** in three. The **Sun**, truly the middle of all, in one year. Similarly **Venus**. **Mercury** likewise, the most industrious among them all, in a year. The **Moon**, truly the highest purity <note>likely referring to its proximity to the sublunary realm</note> and the lowest [sphere], in only a month. Therefore, it must be concluded briefly when it is asked what the proportion of motion of one planet is to the motion of another: it is the same proportion as that of any number to any other. For the one investigating this more curiously, one must return to the books of the arithmeticians and geometers; for in these, the proportion not only of the voice <note>original: "box" (vox), referring to musical intervals</note> but of any things whatsoever is most abundantly taught. Moreover, the order of the planets beneath the eighth circle <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> is commonly remembered by these verses:

->There are eight spheres which you can thus remember:<-
->High is the starry one, then Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars,<-
->The Sun, Venus, and Mercury; the Moon lies last below.<-

Also note: proportion is nothing other than a certain relationship of one to another of two quantities, of whatever size, provided they are of the same kind. And they are said to be "of the same kind" as number to number, straight line to straight line, surface to surface, or body to body. For a line is not proportioned to a surface or a body; for which reason no proportion of the diameter to the side is found to be reachable, as Aristotle [says] <note>A reference to the mathematical incommensurability of the diagonal of a square, a classic problem in Aristotelian logic and geometry</note>.

**Sixth: Since Saturn is among the planets...** This is the sixth question of this second part of the *Semicircle of the Seat of Craton*, in which it is asked: since it is the case that Saturn is the most cruel <note>original: "sevissimus"</note> among the planets and Venus the most kind, whether the kindness of one—namely Venus—coming from an opposite aspect <note><term>aspect</term>: the angular distance between planets in the sky, believed to determine their influence</note> (which is across the diameter of the circle), retards—that is, tempers and restrains—the malice of the other—namely Saturn. For the solution of this question, it must be said: among the planets, some are called malevolent and some benevolent according to the traditions of the wise. The malevolent are like **Saturn**, who is depicted armed with a scythe as an enemy of living nature, and **Mars**, whom they place as the god of war; and because of their malice, they are called "the infortunes" <note>original: "infortunas"</note> because they plot misfortune for a birth or any beginning. The benevolent are **Jupiter**, whom they call the significator of heroes and great men, and similarly **Venus**, the significator of all kindness; for which reason they call them "the fortunes." Regarding these, the present question is only about Saturn and Venus, to which it must be answered that Venus in no way diminishes the malice of Saturn from an opposite aspect. For it is a rule among the wise that when the "fortunes" look upon the "evils," they diminish their hindrance, but only if they look from an **amicable aspect**. An amicable aspect is only the trine or the sextile <note>Trine (120°) and Sextile (60°) were considered harmonious; Opposition (180°) and Square (90°) were considered harsh or conflicting</note>. But when the "evils" look upon the "goods" from a fourth [square] or opposite aspect, they strongly impede the benevolence of the "goods," because it is an aspect of the wicked and from a wicked perspective. And so much for this question.

### Seventh: Why the South Wind, though naturally cold, appears otherwise.
This is the seventh question of the second part of the aforementioned semicircle, in which it is asked why the South Wind <note>original: "nothus", a Latin term for the South Wind</note>—and more truly that wind is the southern one—is naturally cold and dry since it comes from the southern part and the Antarctic pole, yet appears to us to be the opposite, namely moist and hot. For the solution to this question, it must be noted that there are two winds according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book of *Meteorology* and

<margin>
This is according to the two signs of heaven under which the sun, running its course, stirs up or causes the winds to cease. These are commonly recited in these verses: "The East Wind, the South-East, and the East-South-East are of the dawn. The North-West, the West, and the West-South-West blow at sunset. At midday, the South Wind, the South-South-West, and the South-West are with the South. And the North, the North-North-East come, and the North-West from on high." And of all these winds...
</margin>

## Eighth: Of the other coming from the opposite side.
## Seventh: Since the North-West wind <note>original: "chorus"</note> is naturally cold and dry, why does it appear contrary to us?
## Eighth: What is the proportional connection of the elements?
## Ninth: What is the path and effect of the sun and moon?

...the matter is a hot and dry exhalation, wherefore none are said to be cold and moist by their own substance, but only by reason of their mixing with the air. The text speaks to this proposition of mixing when it says: although the South Wind is naturally cold regarding its primordial mixing with cold air—since it rises in the coldest zone near the Antarctic pole, which is said to be uninhabitable due to its excessive cold—why then does it appear hot to us? I say that while it blows through the torrid zone which is under the equator, it takes heat unto itself; and because it comes toward the south where there is a greater abundance of water and places full of vapor and dew, it contracts and acquires a foreign moisture. Whence among us it is found to be hot and moist, and while it is blowing, the air, filled with the aforementioned vapor, is more frequently resolved into rains.

**The eighth question: What is the connection of the elements?** This is the eighth question of the second part of the often-mentioned semicircle of the Chair of Crato <note>A mnemonic or physical teaching device used in medieval universities</note>, which asks what the connection—that is, the proportional joining—of the elements is. For the solution to this question, it should be observed that the elements themselves are bound together and ordered by certain numerical proportions, as Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works were fundamental to medieval science</note> testifies in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book 3, Meter 9, when he says: "You bind the elements by numbers, so that cold things may agree with flames, and dry things with liquids; lest the purer fire fly away, or weights pull down the submerged earth." For just as two numbers agree in one proportional middle number, so two contrary elements in two qualities agree in one proportional middle element. For example, in square numbers: two times two are four; three times three are nine. Take therefore a number that exceeds four (the first square) just as the second (namely nine) exceeds the found number, and that is six, according to the same proportion. And it is called a *sesquialter* <term>a ratio of 3:2</term> or *hemiola* <term>the Greek term for the same 3:2 ratio</term> proportion. For just as six contains four and half of four, so nine contains six and half of six. The proportion of the elements is the same: for fire and water are in two contrary qualities, and these are bound by one middle, namely air, which just as it agrees with water in moisture, so also it agrees with fire in heat; wherefore it follows that the proposed question is satisfied.

**The ninth question: Concerning the sun, etc.** This is the ninth and last of the questions of the second part of the semicircle of the Chair of Crato, which investigates the path of the sun and moon and their wonderful effects.

# Third Part

For the explanation of this matter, I believe we must rely most heavily on the assertion of the wise astronomers <note>original: "astrologorum" - in this period, astrology and astronomy were considered the same science</note> who, deviating not at all from the path of truth, maintain that God, the Best and Greatest, set two great lights—namely the sun and the moon—over the world above all other stars. This is attested by both sacred and ancient authority and is proven by daily experience. He granted them a motion that differs between them, just as He did for the other five planets under the belt of the zodiac signs.

Sometimes they are far from the earth and from each other; sometimes they approach; sometimes they align with themselves; sometimes they move apart and turn toward other paths by their motion, as has long since been most certainly demonstrated in the theorems of the astronomers, and especially of Ptolemy. Furthermore, He gave them power over all things to be generated and those already generated, as well as over their decay. For this reason, it was not absurdly said by Aristotle when he remarked: "According to the approach and retreat of the sun in the eighth sphere, generations and corruptions <note>The cycle of birth and decay</note> occur in these lower realms." For the work of the sun's substance is greatest, both because of the magnitude of its body—which exceeds the earth one hundred and sixty-six times, as we also said above—and likewise because of the nature of its light. For it is certain that the other stars borrow their light from it as if from an inexhaustible fountain. Desiring to embrace these and other matters in a few small verses, Martianus Capella addresses the sun thus: "O high power of the unknown Father, first offspring, sense-giving fuel of the mind, source of light, origin, God of nature's kingdom and witness of the gods, eye of the world and brightness of shining Olympus," etc. Wherefore, according to the Pythagoreans, it was called the "heart of heaven." The moon, however, is established as the mistress and moderator of the sea and waters and of all things that come from them, which is accepted through many experiments both in the sea and rivers as well as in plants. For their moisture is greatest, as in gourds and the marrow of human bones and all living things. The wise men of the stars have experienced many things in their powers, just as they left to posterity in their writings. Similarly, physicians certify that all illnesses are terminated either for good or for ill according to the sixteen locations of the circle through which the moon passes; in which spirit Hippocrates says in the first of his *Prognostics*: "There is something celestial which the physician himself must foresee." If his prudence is so great, it is indeed wonderful and stupendous.

Now, having understood all these things as they were set forth, I judge it follows that the last questions of this second part, and likewise all others, have been resolved. Therefore, we must proceed to the third and final part of the semicircle.

<column-break/>

### The last level of the semicircle proposed:
### Why is there trembling in the lands?
### Why does the lightning burn the air?

<column-break/>

In this part, Boethius shows the third order of questions inscribed on the chair of Craton. Just as the "Son of Inconstancy" turned himself to seize the second questions after the first, so at last he has devolved to these, having grown weary of both the first and the second.

And this part is divided according to the number of questions described in this last part of the semicircle; the parts will become clear in the process. And it says "the last level," that is, the surface of the semicircle, "proposed"—understand here the questions that follow.

It should be noted that these questions are almost identical to those recorded by Virgil in these verses: "Whence the trembling in the lands; by what force the deep seas swell, and having burst their barriers, sink back into themselves again. The various eclipses of the sun and the labors of the moon. Whence the race of men and cattle; whence the rain and fire. Arcturus, the Pleiades, the Hyades, and the twin Bears. Why the winter suns hasten so much to dip themselves in the Ocean, and what delay hinders the slow nights." And the first part of our text can be read in meter thus:

# Chapter

Why does the earth tremble? Why does lightning burn the air? Why does the fury of the sea overflow, and its malignant motion? etc. **Why does the earth tremble?** This is the first question of this final part, in which the causes of earthquakes are investigated. And it must be said that when we speak of an earthquake, it is not to be understood that an ascent or descent of the entire earthly element occurs; nor should it be thought that the earth itself moves in a circle while the heavens remain still, as some have thought of individual cases. For such an earthquake 
<margin>is entirely impossible: because, as Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher</note> holds in his mind, even if all the gods descended, they could not move the earth in this manner</margin>

> **Why the fury of the sea overflows:**
> **And its malignant motion.**

But it must be considered that an earthquake itself is a collapse, a trembling, a staggering, a thrusting, a piercing, a splitting, and an overturning—as Albertus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a dominant figure in medieval science</note> further explains—arising from a hot and dry exhalation <term>exhalation: a vaporous gas thought to be trapped underground</term> shut up within the earth and seeking an exit. Whence it must be considered that the sun and stars, by their heating, generate many exhalations from the earth which, sometimes not having an easy exit by reason of cold or rains closing or constricting the pores, flee from one another and are gathered together. Then, strengthened by <term>antiparistasis: the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat intensifying when trapped by cold</term>, they exit violently with great force, causing the earthquake. An earthquake can also be caused by windy exhalations entering the earth at night because of the flight from their opposite <note>the cold of the night</note>, which produce a similar motion when the pores of the earth are closed by the cold of the night. **Why does lightning burn the air?** This is the second question of this final part, and by it, it is asked why lightning burns the air by its effect. To ask this is simply to ask what the cause of the generation of lightning and flashing is. Whence note, according to Aristotle in the *Meteorology*, that "flashing" <note>original: *choruscatio*</note> encompasses both lightning and the thunderbolt. For properly speaking, a "flash" is the sudden appearance of a subtle, inflamed vapor vanishing in the air without descending to the earth. "Lightning" <note>original: *fulgur*</note>, however, is a subtle fire, yet thicker than a flash, descending to the earth and penetrating plants and soft things, as is reported in the third book of the *Physics* by Algazel <note>Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a Persian philosopher</note>. A "thunderbolt" <note>original: *fulmen*</note> is indeed an ignited vapor, compacted and solid, falling impetuously with greater force than lightning; for it strikes what it touches, penetrates and burns, divides and splits, and no physical body resists it. Wherefore Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636)</note> says that "to flash" <note>original: *fulgere*</note> is the same as "to strike" <note>original: *ferire*</note>. These three, however, do not differ essentially since they are of the same material species and from the same effective cause, namely heat and cold. They differ only accidentally, as was said above; therefore, when the cause of the generation of one is expressed, the generation of all is revealed. Thus it must be said with Aristotle that all these are caused by vapor gathered in the clouds and rubbed and inflamed by their vehement collision. And according to the diversity of this vapor—due to the different admixture of earthiness or lack thereof—they are distinguished only accidentally, as has been said. **Why the fury of the sea overflows.** This is the third question of this part, by which it is asked why the "fury," that is, the heat of the sea, overflows abundantly, increasing and decreasing. He wishes to say: what is the cause of the ebb and flow <note>the tides</note> of the sea? And it should be noted that the sea is understood to flow and ebb in three ways: first, from the north to the south and vice versa; second, by the agitation of the winds; third, naturally and regularly every natural day twice. The first flow and ebb is because of the abundance and elevation of the waters in those places; and therefore, since water naturally flows to a lower place, it is necessary for the water to flow toward the south. Conversely, it flows from the south to the north because the water there is greatly swollen and consequently greatly elevated by the power of the sun. The second flow is violent and moves toward every direction. The third flow, however, is from the influence of the moon, which by its light as well as its influence causes the ebb and flow. And because...

This becomes true regarding the light [of the moon], because the rarefaction <note>The thinning or expansion of a substance</note> and swelling of the sea appear to happen by reason of the moon's light, since all light is heating and rarefying. As for the "influence" <note>term: influence (influentia); in medieval science, this referred to an invisible power flowing from the stars to the Earth, distinct from visible light</note>, it is similarly evident, because the moon could not cause this flow by its light alone. This is proven because if it were so, then the flow and ebb would be greater during the quadratures <note>The moon's first and third quarters</note> than during the conjunction <note>The new moon</note>, which experience shows to be false. It is necessary, therefore, for an influence to act together with the light, so that the light and the influence are the causes of this flow and ebb. It must therefore be said that just as the soul

alters food through heat and attracts it through another power, so the flow signifies the swelling and alteration of the moon by means of light,
