which swells the sea, and through a hidden power attracts it—just as a magnet attracts iron—from the east to the south and from the west to the "angle of the night" <note>The north, or the lowest point of the heavens below the horizon</note>. From the south to the west, however, and from the angle of the night to the east, it flows back because the moon no longer looks directly upon the sea with its powers; and thus, in a privative sense, it is called the cause of the ebb. 

The fourth question asks about the saltiness of the sea and where it is caused. According to the opinion of Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotelis sententiam"</note>, as he notes in his book *On Sense and the Sensible*, flavor is an affection of the moist by the terrestrial dry, such that from different mixtures of the terrestrial dry with the moist, different flavors result. Since saltiness is a flavor, it necessarily arises from the mixing of the terrestrial dry with the moist—but not simply the dry, rather the *burnt* dry. This is evident in lye, which does not become exceedingly salty unless there is strong heating and burning of the ashes; and similarly regarding urine, as is well-proven among physicians. Therefore, if we assume the eternity of the world, it is necessary that the sea be salty. For in it there is much burnt terrestrial matter left behind by hot and dry exhalations, and there is also pure water mixed in, with the heat of the sun cooking it and causing the moisture to rise, as is clear to experience. And he rightly said "assuming the eternity of the world," because if the world were created, the sea would not have been salty for a long time afterward.

What is the nature of winged creatures? This fifth question asks about those birds that leave us in winter and return in summer. To this it must be said that among these birds are commonly the hoopoe <note>original: "upupa"</note> and the stork <note>original: "ciconia"</note> and that kind; they are birds possessing little natural heat and can least protect themselves from the cold. Led by nature, they depart at the onset of winter to warmer regions where they can be preserved by both food and the healthfulness of the air.

What is the roundness of hail? To this sixth question, it must be said that hail always tends toward roundness because it is generated from a cloud divided into drops which, fleeing their opposite <note>Cold fleeing heat, or vice versa</note>, tend toward roundness, which is the first and most perfect shape, as is declared elsewhere. It is an "impression" <note>A meteorological phenomenon</note> that is only generated in the middle region of the air; not in the highest region because of excessive heat, nor in the lowest because of the diminished cold caused by the reflection of the sun's rays. For much and thick matter cannot be frozen except by excessive cold; therefore it is generated only in the middle region of the air.

The length of snow: that is, why it does not tend toward roundness like hail. To this seventh question, I say that snow is generated from vapor raised up to the beginning of the second region of the air, and there that vapor freezes because of the cold (though not excessive cold) and because of the lack of the sun, which is not strong enough to attract it to the upper or middle part of the second region. Therefore it falls to the earth so weakly frozen, spongy, and thin.

## Whether the virtue of stones arises from their temperament or from their matter. Whether the magnetic attraction arises from the components together or from the influence of one alone.

<margin>
On the virtue of stones. This question asks concerning the virtue of stones, namely, whether the virtue of stones arises from the temperament <note>The "complexio" or balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> of the stones or from the matter itself. For the solution of this question, it must first be set forth what has long been shown by the most skilled philosophers: that all
</margin>

matter of stone is either a species of a certain earth or a certain species of water. For one of these two prevails in stones, and according to the different victory, different stones are generated when the mineral virtue of stones—which they call the "formative power"—encounters them. For just as in the seed of an animal, which is a surplus of nourishment, there descends from the seminal vessels a formative power of the animal which forms and produces the animal (and is in the seed in the same way that a craftsman is in the thing crafted), so it is also in the matter itself prepared for stones: forming and producing the stones and leading them to the forms of this or that stone. Moreover, this formative virtue is generated in the matter of the stone itself and is caused by the virtue of the stars infused into that specific place. And all these things are found in the making and mixing of stones. Therefore, to satisfy the question, we say that since the elementary virtue itself (which is the matter of the stone) leaves behind very few operations—and those almost "deaf" <note>Meaning dull or lacking significant effect.</note>—and yet there are almost infinite and most noble virtues in stones, such as driving away poisons, expelling carbuncles <note>A type of skin infection or boil.</note>, and similar things which cannot exist from elementary virtue alone, it is clearly and necessarily concluded that the virtue of stones comes from the substantial form itself first intended by nature, and from that formative virtue introduced into the elementary matter by a celestial virtue infused in that place. It does not come from the elements, as was the opinion of Alexander the Greek Peripatetic <note>Referring to Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle.</note>, because elements cannot operate except through the primary qualities <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>. However, the virtues of stones cannot be reduced to primary qualities. Nor does the virtue of stones come from the Ideas themselves, as Plato wished, who says all lower things modeled on Ideas are from higher Ideas, which he said were separate and of marvelous power. For those are what generate whatever is generated, as he asserts (though falsely, as has been disputed at length elsewhere). But as it is agreed, and as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>, the father of philosophers, and many of the Indians also wished, the virtue of stones comes primarily from the virtue of the stars and their images, according to the manner already described through the infusion of the higher circle <note>The celestial spheres.</note>. And this virtue descends into the things of nature nobly and ignobly. Nobly, when the matters receiving these virtues are more similar to the higher things in light and transparency. Ignobly, when the matters are confused and dreg-filled, in which the celestial virtue is, as it were, oppressed. Thus, according to the diversity of the influence of those higher bodies, it is established that there are diverse virtues of stones. Thus the sapphire works its own virtue, the diamond its own, the carbuncle <note>A red gemstone, often a garnet or ruby.</note> also, and the magnet <note>The lodestone.</note> each work their own virtues. Wherefore it must also be said that the diamond-like <note>Or "adamantine."</note> virtue consists of this higher virtue; it does not arise merely from the proximity of iron to it, although that proximity may be required so that the virtue may operate. And so much for this question.

**Why rain is sweet.** This question seeks the cause of the sweetness of rainwater. To this, it should be said that the heat of the sun, drawing up the water and the vapors themselves, heats and digests <note>original: "digerit"; in medieval science, "digestion" referred to the refinement or ripening of a substance through heat</note> them. From this digestion, sweetness is generated in those waters thus drawn up, which we call rainwaters. **The warmth of a well in winter.** In answering this question according to the opinion of Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval philosopher and scientist</note>—though it is somewhat at odds with the opinion of Aristotle—it must be noted that the element

<margin>

than in winter. And the reason is that in summer, the exterior crust of the earth is very cold due to a double *antiparistasis* <note>original: "antiparistasim"; a Greek physical concept where one quality strengthens its opposite, such as cold intensifying internal heat</note>, namely, the external heat of the air and the internal heat of the interior crust. In winter, however, it is warm because of the heat driven toward it by the coldness of the surrounding air; because of this, the water existing there and emerging from there is rendered lukewarm in winter, whereas in summer it is exceedingly cold. And a similar reason can be given for well water. And this is the opinion of Albert.

**The triple emission of sight.** This question asks what the triple emission of sight is. This refers to the fact that there are three kinds of seers: for some see sharply, others more sharply, and a third group most sharply. What cause renders sight so diverse? To answer this, it must be notably observed that in the organ of sight there is a certain nerve which they call the "optic" <note>original: "opticum"</note> nerve, in which the visual power consists. This is not to say that if the eyes were plucked out, the eyes would still see—for the eyes of a man are the instruments of seeing—but because the strength of vision is in that nerve, just as in other parts of the body the physical nerves are the support and strength of the body. Therefore, it should be said that those who have eyes on the surface of the head, stretched furthest from this nerve—as if distanced from their source of strength—see "sharply," not meaning an excellence of sharpness, but that the vision itself is impaired. However, those who have eyes somewhat fixed see "more sharply," as they are closer to the optic nerve. But those who have eyes well-fixed and almost recessed in the head see "most sharply," because they reach the line and the optic nerve, which is the primary fortification of vision. Or it could be answered otherwise: that this diversity arises from the diversity of the visual organs in size and smallness. Indeed, large and protruding eyes see more weakly than small ones because of the dilation and diffusion of the visual rays themselves, since all vision occurs through rays, as is declared in the study of perspective <note>original: "perspectiva"; the medieval science of optics</note>. Therefore, the gathering or the diffusion of visual rays generates either strength or weakness of vision, since it is certain that every power is stronger when united than when dispersed. etc.

**And the composition of colors.** That is, the inspection, if the noun is derived from the verb "to discern" <note>original: "cerno"</note>. <column-break/>

Because the things explained above are themselves innate, that is, given and spoken for the instruction of scholars. Now, however, since nature by itself is not sufficient for contemplation unless secondary things are present—of which Fortune is the mistress—therefore we must treat briefly the sagacious provision for scholars, so that they are not

---

by any means withdrawn from doctrine and study by penury and want. But since the complexion of the human body consists and is supported—that is, fortified—by phlegm, blood, choler, and melancholy <note>original: "flegmate sanguine colera et melancolia"</note>; I say these four bodily humors, it is necessary for every person to "draw out," that is, to extract from these four humors a certain "preeminence," meaning a certain dominance by which they are named. He means to say: since the human body is composed of these four humors, it is necessary—since these humors are contrary to one another—that some quality be unified in the body itself to give it a name, such as being melancholic, phlegmatic, choleric, or sanguine. 

It should be noted that a "humor" is the material principle of sensible bodies. And there are four in the human body, as has been said, which Joannitius <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873), a famous physician and translator whose work was central to medieval medical education.</note> says are called the "children of the elements" because each of them originally consists of their qualities. These four humors, when observing a due equality and proportion in quantity and quality, perfect, nourish, and preserve all blood-bearing bodies in a proper state of health. Conversely, from their inequality or infection, they generate and induce sickness. For these humors were necessary, as Galen <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire.</note> says in his commentary on the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, calling them "Chymes" <note>original: "Chimos"</note>; they are very necessary for the constitution of the body, for its governance and preservation, and for the restoration of things lost from the body's substance. Yet they do not exist in the body with simply equal powers, since they are opposites; therefore they cannot stand together except in a proportional equality, so that one of them maintains dominance. This is why it is said in the text: "it is necessary for each to draw out a preeminence," etc., meaning to have one humor dominating more than the others. 

"For the melancholic, [subject to] laziness," etc. In this part, Boethius <note>The author of the source text being commented upon, likely the "De Disciplina Scholarium" formerly attributed to Boethius.</note> shows specifically how provision should be made for disciples and scholars according to their complexions regarding study, food, clothing, and the place for those who are known to have the humor of melancholy prevailing more than the others. And he says it is "appropriate"—that is, fitting—for a melancholic subject to laziness to study in "secret and cornered places"—that is, full of corners—because they are naturally fearful. Therefore, if they were to occupy themselves with study in wide and spacious houses and see shadows from afar, they might be led into fear and [distraction].

## shall have required for dryness;
## to be comforted by a full reception of drink
## according to measure, lest too much study
## generate a gasping consumption <note>original: "tisim"</note>
## and a tightness of the chest.

It is necessary for him to enjoy moderate drinks so that <gloss>namely</gloss> they do not have sharpness or fumosity, such as smoky wine which is entirely contrary to his nature as well as to anyone's. For it, as has already been taught in the preceding sections, clouds study and contemplation and leads one entirely away from the path of learning. But nonetheless, it is well for him to be comforted <gloss>that is, nourished</gloss> by a full <gloss>that is, copious</gloss> reception of drink, and this according as the dryness of study requires; lest the persistence <gloss>that is, the curiosity</gloss> of excessive study—supply: which dries out the radical humor—just as any care might generate this gasping <gloss>that is, panting</gloss> consumption <term>tisis: a wasting disease of the lungs, often associated with tuberculosis</term> and a tightness of the thorax <gloss>that is, the chest</gloss>. **It is to be noted** that the Melancholic is named from melancholy, which is a mixture of black blood with gall; and it is the worst of the constitutions. It is indeed named from *melan* which is "black" and *chole* "gall," because it is from the dregs of black blood with an added abundance of gall. Hence the melancholic, whose properties, manners, and nature are commonly recited in these verses: > **Envious and sad, deceitful and of a yellowish color; Not without fraud, timid, and of a tenacious right hand** <note>meaning he is stingy or miserly</note>. And this constitution is likened to the earthly constitution, which is cold and dry; so also is melancholy. And although this constitution may be most foul, as was said before, it is nonetheless to be affirmed that almost all famous men who have left anything worthy of praise to posterity have abounded in this constitution, since this constitution provides a good memory on account of water and earth, as **Ramon Llull** <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and polymath</note> proves from his mind in his work on astrology. For water, as he says, is restrictive, greedy, and receptive of impressions, and earth is a thick subject in which the impression of the species <note>mental images or forms</note> which are remembered endures. Therefore, melancholic men are most disposed to acquiring great sciences, and this because of the multiplication of many species; hence it is not absurdly thought that the greater part of philosophers were melancholics. Attending to which, the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle</note> in his book of *Problems* says: > **Whoever have been excellent men, whether in philosophy or politics or poetry or the arts, are called melancholics**. For even Hercules was of this nature; and they are occupied by illnesses which are from black bile; therefore the ancients called the illness of epileptics the "sacred disease" and the "Herculean disease." **Note**: <term>tisis</term> is an ulceration of the lung with a consumption of the whole body; for this ulceration constricts the pipe of the lung by which the inspiration and respiration of air occurs, and this is fittingly called a gasping <gloss>that is, panting</gloss> consumption, as in the text; hence "phthisic." Likewise, the <term>thorax</term> is the chest, or that part of the chest which is from the neck down to the stomach, which we call the "ark" <note>Latin: "archa"</note> because the secret <gloss>that is, the hidden place</gloss> is there, by which other things are fended off. It is also called the *thorax loxica* elsewhere; whence Job 41.

# Fourth Section
->from nature<-

Note therefore that the **sanguine** person <note>Latin: *sanguineus*; the personality type dominated by blood, characterized by cheerfulness</note> continually desires hilarity and joy because of the goodness of his **complexion** <note>term: *complexion* (the specific balance of the four humors in an individual)</note> which is hot and moist. Since human life consists most of this heat and moisture, it is fitting for him to be adapted to all pleasant, joyful, and clean places. 

Furthermore, it is not absurd to say that the sanguine person profits more by playing than by meditating. Indeed, the vivacity of his talent makes this so, being rooted in the soft substance of his **imagination** <note>Latin: *ymaginatio*</note>; yet he does not retain things understood and grasped as stably as the **melancholic** <note>the personality dominated by black bile</note> because of the moisture mixed into his complexion, which is the mother of forgetfulness rather than memory. However, he retains more than the **phlegmatic** <note>the personality dominated by phlegm</note> because of the heat mixed with his moisture.

The condition, nature, and character of these sanguine people are easily denoted by these verses:
*Generous, loving, cheerful, laughing, and of a ruddy color.*
*Constant, fleshy, bold enough, and curious.*
<margin>Another version has: *singing, fleshy, etc.*</margin>

It should be noted, as **Suetonius** <note>Roman historian</note> reports, that the *hirquus* is the corner of the eyes where matter collects. And because some, out of excessive lewdness, are accustomed to twist their eyes like goats <note>Latin: *hircos*</note>, it is called *hircus* from the he-goat, a lewd animal whose eyes look askance with lust and are twisted like goats. 

Likewise, regarding "cheerful" <note>Latin: *hilaro*</note>, that is, "making joyful," whence **Macrobius** says: *Words no less than wine cheer the banquet.* And the syllable "la" is shortened, as **Horace** says in his *Epistles*: *The gloomy hate the cheerful man, and the playful hate the gloomy,* etc.

The **choleric** <note>the personality dominated by yellow bile, associated with fire and anger</note> person, however, is pale. In this part, **Boethius** <note>Christian philosopher</note> shows what place of study and what arrangement of nourishment is suitable for the choleric. He says: Let the choleric, who is usually of a pale appearance <note>Latin: *effigiei*, meaning face</note>, be always submitted to solitude—that is, a solitary place—lest he, being moved by the hearing of too much noise, pour out his bile <note>that is, his anger</note> upon the whole company <note>Latin: *cohortem*, meaning his social circle</note> and thus hurt or offend the venerable majesty of the master. And exclaiming against the injury of the master's office, he says: *Oh, how that injury to the master is to be avoided!* 

These things were said concerning the place; next he deals with nourishment, saying: *And we have known him to be sustained by a larger dinner and soothed—that is, nourished—by a stronger drink.* And regarding this, he shows a caution to be observed, saying: *But yet care must be taken* (supply: in the providing of such food and drink) *lest there be drawn out—that is, excited—from their rabid or furious minds the heat of choler and the error of strife.* This means it must be foreseen with the greatest care lest an excessive display of drink stir up and kindle his choler too much, lest strife and war be raised among his companions on these occasions. 

Note, as **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African, a medieval translator of medical texts</note> says in the *Pantegni* <note>term: *Pantegni* (a major medieval medical encyclopedia)</note>, Book II, Chapter 2: *If choler rules the body, the skin will be grayish-blue or lemon-yellow.* And this is what the text says: *the choleric is of a pale appearance,* etc. And they are the ones who [prefer] leisure...

<column-break/>

...We have known them to be more often comforted by a very serious question than if he were to blink alone at the walls with squinting eyes. However, this is not always to be trusted. It is fitting for this man to be cheered with lighter foods and very pleasant drinks.

Oh, how the injury of the master is to be avoided! We have known this man to be sustained by a larger dinner and by drink...

### On Washerwomen and Old Women
In this part, Boethius, after the aforementioned points, shows in what manner provision should be made for the scholars regarding the persons serving them. He does two things: first, he addresses what was said regarding old washerwomen; second, regarding the assisting servants at the section beginning "The lodging, etc."

First, he says: the removal—that is, the keeping at a distance—of old washerwomen <note>original: "lotricum"; women who wash clothes</note> is to be highly valued, because their approach and access is healthier the rarer (that is, the slower) it is. Giving the reason, he says: lest, while she is present, she might suggest—that is, secretly whisper into the scholar's ear—something defiled (that is, polluted), by which the scholar's mind might be turned from study; or even lest she herself should extract something from the "softened" servant <note>original: "mancipio"; here meaning a domestic slave or servant</note>—that is, one inclined toward the old woman's words—taken from the master's property.

And this is because the "mercy" of servants is rarely found, and in an *agon* <note>term: agon; Greek for a struggle or contest, here meaning a time of great necessity or trial where a friend is tested</note> the constancy of servants is found even more rarely. "Ah!" is the interjection of one speaking a curse. "Ah, I say, to the seductive servant"—that is, the deceiving one—in whom the affection of the master trusts fully. Inveighing against such a person, he says: "What is more foul—that is, more detestable—than such a person?" Since, as Seneca reports, nothing is found more effective for harming a master than a "familiar enemy" <note>A common medieval proverb: there is no pestilence more capable of doing harm than a domestic foe.</note>. What is even heavier than such a crime? He implies: nothing. Note that *agon* is called the "struggle of death," whence we sing "In the triumphal struggle, etc." <note>A reference to liturgical hymns for martyrs.</note> but here it is taken to mean "necessity."

# Fourth [Book/Chapter]

The servant Elimax, a slave to unfaithfulness, himself suggested—that is, he whispered into his master's ears—that all the meat provisions, all the fish supplies, and all other goods for sale had been valued—that is, purchased—at more than double their worth. Indeed, with such madness of unfaithfulness did he persist that he "drained"—that is, converted to his own use—the growth of the master's entire substance—that is, his resources. Furthermore, he dragged Nicostratus himself into extreme—that is, utter—poverty and the long-lasting—that is, daily—shouting and harassment of creditors. By this shouting and molestation, nothing is more bitterly impressed upon the mind—namely, the debtor's mind. Woe, therefore, to the insanity—that is, the fury—of the creditor. When Nicostratus had fallen into all these things, both extreme poverty and the furies of creditors, his own lack finally led him to the recognition of his error—that is, the crime of Elimax. <note>The text uses "error" here in the legal or moral sense of a transgression or crime.</note> But Nicostratus himself "convened"—that is, summoned to legal action—Elimax regarding his error—that is, his crime. ...by counting out borrowed money. Generally, however, anyone who follows the faith of another for any cause whatsoever is called a **creditor**: one who trusts the debtor. one who is false or depraved by the mark of flattery. To this companion, the scholar can reveal (that is, open) his foreknowledge (that is, his private mind). This companion should assist (that is, succor) the scholar when fortune is cloudy (that is, adverse). And this companion should show (that is, offer) himself attentive (that is, diligent) with aid for the scholar when some illness is pressing (that is, weighing upon him). These things are said regarding adverse health. And let them be able to rejoice in little questions (that is, in doctrinal doubts and inquiries arising between them for the sake of learning) by way of competition—now by arguing, now by replying, and performing other such things which are known to be useful in scholarly debate. And let them rejoice step by step (that is, in an orderly fashion) in commendable recollection (about which enough was said in the first chapter when the triple method of memory was taught). And I say let them rejoice mutually and alternately in the happiness of correction (that is, happy discipline), so that they may charitably correct, discipline, and rebuke one another in their errors. > Interpose joys sometimes among your cares. <note>A famous maxim from the "Distichs of Cato," a standard medieval schoolbook.</note>

So that the mind may be refreshed alternately by pleasantries and places of joy, and so that the integrity of mutual love (that is, social bond) may be preserved.

# Chapter

The nature of love should remain—that is, endure—between them in such a way that the dew, meaning the love of the earliest time <note>original: "primevi temporis"</note>, is instilling—that is, continually pouring in or dropping. In the middle of time, it should be inundating—that is, flowing over. But in the end, that social love should exist as inebriating—that is, making joyful and filling. Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher; the text here interprets his views on the stages of affection.</note> means to say that love between them should be like dew, which first drops, secondly cleanses, and thirdly intoxicates; thus also their love increases day by day.

<margin>
It should be noted that the companion <note>original: "socius"</note> of whom Boethius speaks in the text ought not to be unruly, nor double-tongued, nor cruel; but rather he of whom Seneca speaks when he says: "The possession of no good thing is pleasant without a companion." <note>A famous quote from Seneca’s Letters to Lucilius regarding the necessity of shared joy.</note> He certainly possesses the conditions and properties which a faithful friend ought to have in himself. The first of these is that his and his partner's "refusing" and "willing" should be the same, as is clear in the 8th book of the *Politics* <note>Referring to Aristotle's Politics, though the sentiment is also famously Ciceronian.</note>: "To friends, the same things are to be refused and willed." And Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> against Sallust says: "It is the mark of friends, if they be true friends, to will the same and refuse the same."
</margin>

**by sweetly obeying. And so, let the integrity of mutual affection remain between them, so that the dew of the earliest time is instilling, in the middle inundating, and in the end truly inebriating. What is sweeter, what is more illustrious, what is certainly better? For no adoption of favor provides an end to an outstanding love. Envy, indeed, if it should happen "according to something"—namely in the process of learning—is gracious; but simple envy, which is characteristic of a consumed author, is destructive. Moreover, the light of my parent, his providence, as is customary in conversation...**

<column-break/>

The second property is to die for a companion, of which Varro says in *On Old Age*: "It often happens that one dies for a friend." The third is to adhere inseparably to the companion, of which Sextus the Pythagorean says: "He was least a friend who is ever separated from a friend unless death intervenes." The fourth is to guard against harm, of which Apuleius the Platonist says in his book *On the Politician and the Citizen*: "A foxy companion is one who does not guard his companion from danger and fault." A perfect companion, therefore, is one who applies circumspection and cautions to his companion.

It should be noted that Boethius calls Fortune "cloudy"—that is, dark or blind. For Fortune was depicted by the ancients as blind because she approaches and recedes unexpectedly, or because she makes a person blind by extolling him in prosperity and depressing him in adversity. Almost the same words are found in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book 1, Meter 1, when he says: "Now that cloudy Fortune has changed her deceptive face," etc. Note that "teter, tra, trum" means black or fierce; thus in the song: "A foul [tetrum] chaos falls." 

"What is sweeter?" In this part, Boethius sets forth the utilities that arise from the acquisition of a faithful companion, saying: "For what is sweeter"—that is, more pleasant—"or what is more illustrious"—that is, more bright—"or what is better" (understand: than this social love and partnership)? He implies: nothing. And joining the reason for this, he says that no "adoption"—that is, a feigning of love—provides an end to "outstanding"—that is, true and perfect—favor, but it is destined to endure in him. And then, by anticipating an objection <note>original: "antipophorizando"</note> and responding to a silent question, he says: someone might say above that there ought to be a little "dispute of questions" between companions; but if this dispute brings in a certain envy, will this social bond be dissolved? Responding to this, he says that if envy happens "according to something" <note>A scholastic term meaning "in a certain respect" rather than absolutely.</note>—namely in learning—this is certainly "gracious" because it sharpens the intellect, and therefore is in no way destructive to such a partnership. But if "simple"—that is, absolute—envy should creep in, it is never permitted to happen in true partnership.

# Chapter

The proven divinity—that is, the divine wisdom—of **Plato** flourishes here. Indeed, this Plato had taught so much concerning divinity that he deserved to be called "divine." Here, in another place, flourishes the "concretion"—that is, the compilation of arguments—of that philosopher **Zeno**, in which he strove to prove the squaring of the circle. <note>original: "quadraturā circuli"</note> Also the "delight"—that is, the doctrine which he had prescribed concerning love—of that master **Peribonius** flourishes here. In another place flourishes the "promise" of this **Pythagoras**.

<margin>
The Italian philosopher who first discovered that souls would be immortal and pass from one body to others. He used to promise, saying that he was first **Euphorbus**, second **Thalides**, third **Hermotimus**, fourth **Pyrrhus**, and finally **Pythagoras**. **Ovid** followed this opinion in the 15th book of the *Metamorphoses*, saying of Pythagoras: "I myself remember that at the time of the Trojan War, I was Euphorbus, son of Panthous, in whose breast once stuck the heavy spear of the younger son of Atreus <note>Menelaus</note>." And **Horace** in his *Odes*: "And the realms of Tartarus hold the son of Panthous, sent down once more," etc. And wanting to show this, **Boethius** says: "the promise of Pythagoras."
</margin>

...after three days, by showing the names of the streets and the ruggedness of the alleys, saying: "Here flourish the presages of the **Chaldeans**; the not-hidden glory of **Ptolemy**; the sincere truth of **Aristotle**; the proven divinity of **Plato**; the concretion of **Zeno**; the delight of **Peribonius**; the promise of **Pythagoras**; the *Iliad* and the labor of **Homer**; the theorems of **Euclid**; the 'porisms' <note>deductions or corollaries</note> of **Dares**; the examinations of **Hippocrates**. Here flourishes the efficacy of the **Areopagus** and skill in the laws; the confused glory of the **Hippodrome**; the victory of the **Circus**; the power of the **Gymnasium**; the flashing of the **Cestus** <note>a weighted leather boxing glove</note>; the loftiness of missiles; the shouting of sailors; the wandering of youth; the gathering of the dance."

->Therefore this light and many other things of Favonius<-

The *Iliad* flourishes here—that is, the doctrine of **Homer** which he had composed concerning the Trojan War. Here also flourish the "theorems"—that is, the rules and geometrical propositions—of this philosopher and geometer **Euclid**. Wherefore a "theorem" is a diligent and fit description of words or a rule. From this, the rules of geometry are called theorems, as if they were "fittings," such as this: "Every whole is greater than its part," or similarly, "If equals be taken from equals, the remainders will be equal." Here indeed flourish the "Axioms"—that is, the sophisms of this philosopher **Michalus** <note>likely a corruption of a name like Nicomachus</note> which he had published concerning music. Wherefore an "axiom," according to **Huguccio**, is called a concatenation of speaking, just as sophisms are. **Papias**, however, says they are eloquent utterances and especially propositions in the *Topics*. Here, moreover, flourish the "aporisms"—another letter has "porisms," which is more correct—that is, fit proofs. And it is said from *porus*, which is a certain opening, of that **Dares**, the writer of the Trojan histories, who asserted that the soul, after being snatched from the body, would be a mere shadow. Here also flourish the "examinations"—that is, the investigations—of that physician **Hippocrates**. And he rightly names the documents of Hippocrates "investigations," because through many investigations and experiments, the operative art of medicine was reached. Here—that is, in this place—flourishes the "efficacy"—that is, the vigor—of the **Areopagus**, which is the street where the schools of the philosophers were located. From which street Saint **Dionysius the Areopagite** was also named. And it is called from *Ares*, which is "virtue" <note>or Mars/valor</note>, and *pagos*, which is "village," because in that street the science of nature was learned through virtue. And "skill in the laws" flourishes here—that is, properly called legal expertise and the legal expert. After these things, turning himself to the public spectacles by showing him each thing in order...

It should be noted that Boethius, perceiving that prodigality is exceedingly damaging to scholars as well as to anyone else, leading to the ruin of misery and want, and finally bringing shame and becoming a proverb to both friends and strangers, warns that thriftiness—that is, the liberality which stands in modesty and temperance—must be embraced. And what you have, save, always thinking it to be lacking to you.* It should be noted regarding this part where it says "first diligently inspect," etc.: To turn over or read books for study is not enough, but it is fitting to hear suitable teachers. If anyone, therefore, desires to become learned, let him choose a learned man, since the insufficiency of teachers closes the way of discipline. Choose that learned man, consulting Varro, whom you might admire more in his own works than in those of others. For he will teach nothing magnificent who has learned nothing from himself; which Boethius himself, attesting in the lower parts, says: *It is indeed the mark of a most abject mind to use things already found and not things to be found.* Note regarding this which says: "I prefer indeed [the teaching] of a stammerer," etc. No one, according to the exterior appearance which nature has bestowed upon him, is to be despised when his internal virtue is unknown, by the authority of Ecclesiastes 11: *Praise not a man for his beauty, neither despise a man for his appearance.* And the moral Cato: *Do not despise the strength of a small body; he prevails in counsel to whom nature denied strength.* For sometimes the vessels of a small body are more precious, as gems and small stones bear witness. So also, what a sagacious nature had withdrawn through the vice of a stammering tongue, they sometimes repair with more abundant counsel and intelligence. Hence this common saying: *Better are the wounds of a friend than the deceitful words of a flatterer.* Note that "stammering" was explained in the upper parts, chapter 4, in that part when violence was discussed. # Fourth

A **stepmother** <note>Latin: *noverca*</note> is she who has married a husband who already has a son or daughter by another wife; we generally call such women "unjust." Whence a certain poet says: *A stepmother’s power rejoices in venting its rage upon the afflicted.*

**The detestable [tenacity] of parents, etc.** In this section, Boethius <note>The author refers to the "Pseudo-Boethius," the supposed author of *De Disciplina Scholarium*, a 13th-century guide for students</note>, after describing those things by which poverty is most often inflicted upon students, now adds the appropriate remedies for each case. He divides this into six parts according to the six remedies applied to the six causes inducing poverty. The second begins at: *The overflowing...* The third at: *By service...* The fourth at: *Of the hastening German...* The fifth at: *For marriageable sisters...* The sixth at: *Of industrious thrift.* Therefore, he first posits the remedy against the first cause, which is the **stinginess of parents** <note>Latin: *parentum tenacitas*</note>, which sometimes exists to such a degree that, unless it were bent by artifice and service, it would permit the children to fall into extreme want. Of this—

<column-break/>

### The detestable and hooked stinginess of parents is softened by the persistence of prayers; it is often dissolved by tedious speeches; it is soothed by timely weeping; it is often stirred by false promises; it is dissolved by affectionate little gifts; it is pierced by flattery if it be timely; if less so, it is hardened; even if it be as hard as adamant, it is stripped away by the warning of examples; and it is stirred by the requests of others.

Boethius, providing a guide for students regarding this stinginess, says in these words: **Detestable**, that is, hateful, and **hooked** <note>Latin: *adunca*</note>, meaning greedy. It is well-said to be "hooked" by way of a metaphor, for "hooked" sounds like something curved. Whence the saying: *That which must grow hooked shows itself curved.* **Greed** <note>Latin: *avaricia*</note>, because of its excessive inflexibility and tenacity, is deservedly called "curved." Therefore, the **hooked stinginess**—that is, the greedy parsimony of parents—is **softened**, meaning it becomes sweet and is bent, by **persistence** (understand: much persistence) of **prayers**, that is, of supplications. For it both becomes sweet and is softened by **tedious words** (understand: pleading words frequently doubled and consequently causing boredom by excessive repetition). And **often** (that is, frequently) that stinginess of parents is **dissolved** by **speeches**, meaning the ornate and polished persuasions of the children. It is also **soothed** (softened) by **timely weeping** (at the right place and time). And sometimes that stinginess is **stirred** by **false promises**. Similarly, it is sometimes **dissolved** by **affectionate little gifts** (gifts given with affection). It is also **pierced** (entered into) frequently by **flattery** (blandishments), and this if it be **timely** (at the right place, time, and in a suitable manner). But if it be **less so** (understand: if the flattery is not timely), certainly that stinginess is **hardened** <note>Latin: *consolidatur*</note> to the student's detriment. Furthermore, that stinginess of parents is utterly **stripped away** by **exemplary warning** (persuasion that brings forward examples), even though it may have been **adamantine** <note>Latin: *adamantina*</note>, meaning most greedy. This is said by way of a comparison: for just as a diamond <note>The word *adamas* referred to both diamonds and magnets in medieval lore</note> attracts iron, so also the stingy and greedy person continually insists on things they do not have. Similarly, the stinginess of parents is **stirred** (urged) frequently by the **requests** (intercessions) of **others**, namely, friends.

It should be noted that students, regarding parents and friends who are stingy and parsimonious and can only be bent with difficulty, ought to behave like a **drop of water** upon the hardest stones. Let them consider that it is not by the force of its fall or its weight that the drop hollows the stone, but by its **assiduity and persistence**. So also the parsimony of parents, though it cannot be bent and soothed by a single instance, may at least be soothed when doubled ten times, or rather, many times. If **skill** <note>Latin: *ars*</note> is added to this assiduity and persistence, certainly the work will prosper for the better. For as **Pamphilus** <note>A reference to the 12th-century comedic poem *Pamphilus de Amore*</note> says:

<meta>catchword: skill</meta>

# Chapter

Art breaks the spirit and destroys strong cities. By art towers fall, and by art the burden is lightened. <note>original: "Ars animos frangit..."</note> And likewise Ovid, in *The Art of Love*: By art the ships are guided with sail and oar; by art the light chariot is driven; by art love must be ruled. <note>original: "Arte cite velo..."</note> It should be noted, according to Thomas <insert>Aquinas</insert> in the *Summa Theologica* (Second Part of the Second Part, Question 115), that there is this difference between a "pleaser," an "adulator," and a "flatterer." A pleaser is one who speaks with the sole intention of being delightful. But a flatterer speaks with the intention of acquiring gain. An adulator, however, <margin>is commonly attributed to both; however, the verse is sometimes found used for the other among authors quite often.</margin>

**One must obey the flooding storm of poverty through the increase of labor: by writing, by gathering the threshing, by cleaning the floor-spaces, and by serving for a time. If, however, the ingenious faculty of writing should compel a voluntary motion, we have deemed it worthy to restrain the sting of necessity.**

<margin>
The flooding storm of poverty. In this part, Boethius <note>The author refers to Boethius, likely commenting on "The Consolation of Philosophy" or a related medieval pedagogical text.</note> posits a second remedy against the second evil, which is the lack and poverty of parents. He does two things: first, he posits the remedy; second, he helpfully subjoins a certain note regarding this, at the point beginning "If however..."
</margin>

One must take care; and he says that if the poverty of parents causes distress, one must obey—that is, provide for—the "penury," meaning the misery of the "flooding" (abounding or perilous and fluctuating) "storm," through the "increments," meaning the increases, of "labor." Specifically, by "writing" <note>original: "scripturando," a medieval term for professional scribal work</note>—another version of the text has "continual writing"—and by gathering the "threshing," that is, the harvests. "Threshing" <note>term: tritura - the act of beating grain from husks</note> is derived from "to rub" because it rubs against the floor. "Floor-spaces" <note>term: area - an open level space, often a threshing floor</note> means the flat surfaces of houses and other places, by cleaning them; similarly by serving for a time. But nevertheless, among all these, we have "deemed it worthy to restrain"—that is, to check and reserve—the "sting," meaning the prick, of "necessity" (indigence), namely in writing, if the "ingenious faculty" (the art) should "compel" (drive) a "voluntary motion" (the will itself) to do this.

It should be noted that poverty of this kind, which he intends in this second remedy, even if it is stretched beyond one's strength, must nevertheless be endured with patience. This is following the example of our ancestors, who cultivated a peaceful and accepted poverty daily for the love of integrity. Thus Diogenes the Cynic, as Seneca reports, wished to rejoice in poverty and to overcome the powers of the age through poverty. Indeed, he was more powerful than Alexander, who possessed all things, since there was more that Diogenes refused to accept than Alexander was able to give. His only habit, as Jerome reports against Jovinian, was to use a double cloak on account of the cold; he had a pouch for a larder and a staff to support the frailty of old age.

Nevertheless, since nature itself requires certain things by which it may be more strongly sustained for philosophizing, it is fitting that what fortune had taken away from exterior things should be acquired through labor and industry. Thus, just as nature does not abound in superfluities, so also it should be known not to fail in necessities. The labors and industries by which this necessity is repressed are those which the text enumerates; if you use them to remedy want, you will see that the comforts of nature will never be lacking to you. Likewise, a "floor" <note>original: "area"</note> is a place fit for shaking out grain, or it is called an equality of boards, or the breadth of houses; hence "areola" is the diminutive. However it is taken, it is well applied to the purpose.

"One must take care, however, lest a delicious..." Here Boethius subjoins a certain noble observation regarding the first-mentioned remedy, and it is divided into two parts: first, he does what was said; second, he explains the sayings by an example, at the point "The wickedness of Glebeo." And Boethius says that in these aforementioned things, and especially in writing, one must take the greatest care lest a "delicious" appetite—that is, a voluptuous and luxurious one—[take hold], whether in that luxury which consists in ornaments or that which consists in feasting and intercourse, according to the proclamations of the satirists.

<meta>This page continues a pedagogical or moral commentary on the life of a scholar, likely referencing the Pseudo-Boethian "De Disciplina Scholarium." It focuses on the dangers of greed, flattery, and the specific hardships faced by the author under a figure named Glebeo.</meta>

# Fourth [Chapter]

Whoever he may be, one must take care lest he excite the mind of the scholar—that is, to warn him—toward committing any base act, and thus enervate—that is, utterly uproot and eradicate—**siren-like gain**, <note>original: "lucrum sirenosum"</note> meaning that which is attractive yet deceptive. One must also beware lest **prodigal flattery**—that is, lavish praise that goes to excess—which is rarely faithful, defraud the mind of the scholar. For if one is conquered by flattery and the false delights of writings, he may be rendered inferior in his studies. Therefore, one must especially beware lest the **sinister left hand**—meaning a treacherous familiar or friend—drink up, that is, withdraw from sight or hearing, whatever the **right hand**—meaning the labor and faithfulness of the writer—has softened or earned.

It should be noted regarding the text that there are three evils which should principally terrify scholars, as well as anyone else, away from the abuse of acquired goods. The **first** is the contempt for spiritual goods which follows this abuse, as is clear regarding Esau in **Genesis 25**, who sold all his birthright for a meal. The **second** is poverty even unto beggary; this is clear in the **Prodigal Son** in **Luke 15**, who, after wasting his substance, came to such penury that he desired to fill his belly with the husks of swine, but no one gave to him. The **third** is the sin of robbery, and **Cato** touches on this when he says: *Use what you have acquired, but do not seem to abuse it; those who consume their own goods seek the goods of others when their own are gone.* <note>A common medieval citation from the Distichs of Cato.</note> It should be noted regarding the phrase **siren-like gain**: a Siren is a sea monster that draws sailors to itself by the sweetness of its song and causes them to drown; hence it is named from *siren*, meaning "to draw." In this way, gain attracts men to itself by its sweetness and finally leads those it has attracted into Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Therefore, it is well called siren-like gain, meaning attractive and deceitful.

<column-break/>

-> Yet one must beware lest a luxurious appetite excite the mind and enervate gain; the siren-like flattery of those who commonly write is prodigal and rarely faithful, and a sinister familiar drinks up by sight or hearing whatever the right hand of the writer produces. Despite the wickedness of Glebeo, and notwithstanding the favor of my kindred, how much disadvantage in learning and decrease in virtue he brought upon me while I was serving under Herodianus. Since the small fire of my paternal wealth was mostly failing, we endured to mitigate our sorrow more cautiously through the aforementioned means, thinking it safer to choose to be in need than to endure the paths of long labor. <-

Then Boethius, enumerating the disadvantages brought upon him by the aforementioned Glebeo, says: "But what, while we, Boethius, were earning our life by the labor of our hands as is preferred, the wickedness and sinister depravity..."

...what is to be thought of a son. Rather, it evaporated toward the good—that is, it vanished and exhaled—by an internal fire, that is, by a kindled anger instigated by the aforementioned Glebeo. Because of this, the parent's affection, having evaporated and as if exhaled, deprived me of my accustomed support. For these reasons, the wise man warns in Ecclesiasticus 22 <note>A book of the Apocrypha/Deuterocanon</note> that we should not show ourselves as companions to this vice, lest perhaps we be found disgraced by its persistence. Likewise, "two-year period" <note>original: "bimatus"</note> means the space of two years. It is derived from *bimus*, which is composed of *bis* (twice) and *annus* (year). And he says that if the scholar's means cannot be comforted—that is, helped by the aid or support of a stepfather or grandfathers—I say what must be done: that their stinginess should be diminished by threats, just as was promised, by a timely movement or a "playful transaction" of that master of voices. Likewise, *derogo* (to derogate) means to speak ill of, to detract, or to diminish in part, not in whole. *The neglect of a hurrying brother.* In this part, Boethius places a third remedy against a third impediment which also frequently brings penury upon scholars. Mitigate the neglect, that is, the negligence, of a "hurrying" brother—that is, one who prodigally celebrates daily feasts—with a "eulogy," that is, a persuasive, mild, and sweet speech. In this speech, which is full of examples, let the cunning, that is, the shrewd wickedness of the aforementioned brother, be corrected by a nearby admonition, or let the madness of his neglect (negligence) be suppressed.

# Fourth

It should be noted that a father is the cause of his son's existence, nourishment, and discipline. Among all things that seem to benefit and profit the correction and instruction of sons, the only truly effective method is paternal correction and instruction from a tender age. For those who are well-instructed in their tender years are easily inclined toward good when they reach maturity. However, the rule of correction must not involve excessive ferocity; for although it is good to correct sons, it is not permitted to destroy them.

Paternal discipline is only <margin>Paternal discipline is useful when mercy is present.</margin> useful when mercy is present. But, alas, in this present time, they are corrected with neither discipline nor mercy. Thus it happens that when fathers hope to rejoice in the works of their sons, they are instead desolated in every way. If correction is applied late and tardily, it should be administered not with harshness, but only with mild <term>eulogy<note>original: "eulogio"; here meaning a kind or fair speech rather than a funeral oration</note></term>.

Likewise, "germans" <note>siblings</note> are properly so called when they have the same mother but different fathers, as if coming from the same womb <note>original: "genitrice"</note>.

<column-break/>

## If the means to provide comfort are lacking, let the resources be diminished; let them be reduced by timely management,
## as the pleasant transaction of Proculus teaches.
## Let the neglect of a feasting sibling be mitigated by an exemplary speech. Let him be corrected by the reminder of his kinship. Let craftiness or madness be repressed. A sister in her marriageable years must be complied with by her kinsman as quickly as possible, lest through the fault of neglect the first rose be plucked by an unworthy thumb.
## How commendable is the sister's modesty!

However, those who have the same father and mother are also called siblings. Likewise, the term "eulogy" was explained above where "sophistry" was discussed. *To the sister in her marriageable years by her kinsman.* In this section, Boethius <note>The text refers to the "De disciplina scholarium," formerly attributed to Boethius but now known to be by a 13th-century author.</note> provides another remedy against the fifth impediment that leads to scholarly poverty, which is the marriageability of a sister. It is divided into three parts: first, he provides the remedy with the underlying cause; second, he inveighs against those who, through neglect, do not indulge the modesty of chastity (at the mark ¶ *How*); third, he adds an example concerning the aforesaid (at the mark *to be complied with*).

He says first: That if a scholar exists in poverty and the time of the "nobility" <note>meaning marriageable status</note> of his sibling (that is, his sister) is near, he ought to pause his studies for her sake so that a marriage may be provided for the sister. For the "german" (the sister) who is a kinswoman and in her first marriageable years (the years of puberty, which are the years fit for marrying) must be "complied with" (that is, succored) as quickly as possible (very fast).

Giving the reason, he says: and this is done so that the "first rose" (which is virginity itself) is not "plucked" (taken away). He uses the metaphor of the "unworthy thumb" to mean an unworthy hand or an unworthy lover, through the "fault of neglect" (negligence). It should be noted regarding the phrase "first rose" that virginity itself is an honorable name, and therefore it is not undeservedly compared to a rose—not simply, but honorably, if it is illustrated by good works. For in the Gospel, we read of five foolish virgins; therefore, it is not believed that they earned entry to the celestial gate by their virginity alone. It is a beautiful thing to be a virgin, but much more beautiful if, along with virginity, they flourish with sacred works, diligently exposing the mind now to prayer, now to meditation. Jerome, in his witness to Eustochium <note>Refers to St. Jerome's famous Letter 22 to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity.</note>, says that virgins ought to be occupied in these things.

¶ *How commendable is the sister's modesty, etc.* In this part, he inveighs against those who do not provide for chastity due to negligence. He says that the profession (the observance) of a sister's modesty is commendable, and the loss of its opposite (unchastity) is to be desired, just like the "resection" (the cutting away) of that superfluous flesh which defiles the face of modesty...

It should be noted that God has naturally placed a sense of shame in women so that they might dread being called back to sin and immodesty. Observing this, many women of old desired to live in the flesh in such a way that they preferred to die rather than stain the flower of their virginity with a foul approach. Not only is the glory of Christians filled with examples of these women, but also that of the pagans who were utterly ignorant of Christ. ...a profession and a painful commission of the opposite, full of shame as if disfiguring the face with a cutting of the flesh. The marks of brotherly affection to be observed in Simacus, the steward <term>oeconomus: a household manager or steward</term> of the second Theophrastus, must not be passed over in silence. # Fourth [Book/Chapter]

After the bitterness of her sister's—namely Belisia's—[loss] was snatched away from the shipwreck, Belisia follows; that is, she follows her brother Simachus everywhere, serving him in many ways. Belisia herself ministered to her brother Simachus, who had been reduced as if to extreme want, providing all necessities in the "likeness of merits"—that is, in recompense for the dowry he had provided. For when the means were lacking so that she could no longer provide for her brother, she, Belisia, secretly exposed the "flower of her own flesh" to allurements—that is, to lusts and Venusian delights <note>original: "delectationibus venereis"; a euphemism for entering prostitution to support her brother</note>—specifically so that she might gain a life for her brother. She indeed preferred—that is, she wished more—to succumb to the vice of "neglect"—that is, luxury—than to destroy the "covenant," which is the love of fraternal constancy, while she, Belisia, remained alive. Nor did Belisia remain "retrograde" from what she had begun—namely her promises—until she finished what she had started "without a suitable [end]" <note>original: "sine ydoneo"; implying she persisted even through unseemly means</note>. In short, Belisia performed these and similar acts to such an extent and persisted in all of them until she completely freed her brother from his miseries. It should be noted regarding this that he calls Simachus a "steward" <term>iconomus: from the Greek 'oikonomos', a household manager or treasurer</term>. Perhaps this was his actual name, or because he acted as a dispenser of goods. For an *iconomus* or *economus* is one who is the dispenser of money, grain, and all things possessed; hence "economus." **Xenophon** has a beautiful book <note>referring to Xenophon's *Oeconomicus*</note> which, as **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, who translated Xenophon into Latin</note> interprets it, designates the management of a villa or the administration of an entire household.

### On the Industry of Tenacity
In this section, **Boethius** introduces the sixth and final remedy against the sixth impediment of scholars: poverty. It is divided into two parts according to two remedies. The second part begins at "Whatever under these," etc. First, he says that if there is a domestic consumption of resources and imminent penury, one must help; he says one must succor this "domestic burning"—that is, poverty—with the "element of industry"—that is, with the cunning and caution of "tenacity," meaning thriftiness. Understand this to mean: lest one should lend money to anyone. And this is so that the "diligence of lent money"—that is, money provided—does not "infuse bile"—that is, anger. For "bile" is often used for anger, as was explained above. Or, supply: lest that diligence provide a cause for "conflict"—that is, the tribulation of a fight or a disagreement over another matter. Then, adding the second remedy, he says that if a scholar is unable to avoid lending his money when it is necessary, it must be cautiously considered "under these"—that is, in these provisions—lest a "puny"—that is, small and modest—tenacity of things should in the future "daze"—that is, bow the face—with the "judgment of redness"—that is, the sign of shame. I say "redness" because just as death is characterized by paleness, so shame is characterized by redness.

<column-break/>

...to succumb rather than to break the covenant of fraternal constancy while she lived. Nor did she remain retrograde from her undertakings until she finished what she had started without a suitable [end]. One must succor the domestic burning with the element of industrious tenacity, lest the diligence of lent money infuse bile, or provide a fall into the affliction of another matter. Whatever is done under these circumstances must be weighed cautiously, lest a puny tenacity of things should in the future daze the face with the judgment of redness. For strong floorboards are often known to be ruined in the countryside by the injury of a single little spark.

# Chapter

Boethius <note>Original: "Boe." refers to Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, though here used in the context of the *Scholar's Discipline*, a medieval text formerly attributed to him.</note> wishes to say that since the scholar himself is necessarily compelled to lend his money, he should nevertheless take care for his property so that he remains secure either by a guarantor or a pledge. And notwithstanding that the amount of the loan might be small <note>original: <term>cto</term>, likely a contraction for *cito* or *contracto*</note>, for very often—that is, quite frequently—stronger structures <note>original: *tabulata*, meaning floors or timbered buildings</note>, namely edifices, are known to collapse from the damage of a single little spark. It is no wonder then if small things [are lost].
<margin>It should be noted that Boethius in this part especially advises against the lending of money.</margin>

<column-break/>

...and the giving of a loan, although we are bound to this by both divine and human law. Wherefore even by Cato <note>Dionysius Cato, author of the *Disticha Catonis*</note> it has already been advised by law: "Give a loan." But Boethius, why then do we laugh? He responds that although things are such that we are bound by both divine and natural laws to provide a loan to one in need, so that by these means we may charitably provide for their necessities.

Boethius, however, seeing that for the most part lawsuits and discords arise from this kind of lending—according to that common proverb: *If you grant a thing, you will not get it back; if you get it back, not so quickly; if so quickly, not so dear; if so dear, you truly lose a friend*—hence Boethius warns that this lending of money should be especially denied, lest by the occasion of a benefit, a harm is inflicted, as is clearly seen in the first following example. <margin>What of the bald soldier endowed with the light of wisdom, etc. <term>tc.</term></margin> In this part, Boethius, concerning this last remedy for poverty itself which sometimes happens from the giving of a loan, adds an example to corroborate his teaching concerning the Bald Soldier, saying: Let it be known, for example, what antiquity <note>original: *canicies*, literally "gray hair," used here for ancient authority</note> felt concerning the bald soldier endowed with—that is, ennobled by—the light of wisdom. This bald soldier, making a passage—supply "on a certain expedition"—in the first flower of military service—that is, while his military career was still flourishing—carried with him secretly—that is, hidden—under his cloak <note>original: *birro*</note> a certain jar <note>original: *amphoram*</note>, a silver one as some think, others a lucrative one, and more truly as follows: regarding an earthen pot found by chance or luck, or perhaps if any necessity should press, he might provide for his convenience by its means. Which jar he entrusted—that is, handed over—to the grace—that is, the kindness—of a servant <note>original: *mancipii*</note>. But when, after a slight change of status—that is, a small time having passed—the bald man himself chose the place of another cohort—that is, company—and he addressed—supply "with friendly words"—the cook concerning the earthen pot so that he might restore it. But the restraint of resentment and strife being loosened—that is, rising between the bald soldier and the cook—the cook himself, feeling resentment, struck the "gray hair"—supply "of the soldier"—with the earthenware—that is, with the earthen jar—and so shamefully struck the head of the soldier. Which gray hair, although it was afterwards decorated—that is, adorned—on account of the glory of triumphal military service with ivy (this evergreen herb), nevertheless the soldier himself could not thereafter revoke—that is, bring back—the injury—that is, the blow—done to him to its pristine state—that is, as it had been before—so that no scar would remain. He could not revoke it, I say, by any nerve—that is, connection—or by the medicine of any juice—that is, of herbs—nothing less than the shame—that is, the disgrace—to himself and his lineage <note>original: *stirpi*</note> resulting from the attack and the striking of the earthen jar.

# Fifth Section

It should be noted regarding the passage where it is said "the ivy was decorated," etc. Among the ancients, it was the custom that famous poets, by merit of their dignity and the sharpness of their genius, were crowned with ivy as a sign of the greenness <note>original: "virentis," implying both physical vitality and lasting memory</note> of their memory and intellect. As previously stated, this was done for the merit of their dignity, or at least to prevent vapors from ascending to the head; for it is the nature of this herb that it by no means allows smoky humors bubbling up from the stomach to reach the head. Thus we read in Virgil: *Pastors, decorate the growing poet with ivy.* <note>Virgil, Eclogues 7.25</note> And in Persius: *Whose images the clinging ivy licks.* <note>Persius, Prologue to Satires, 5</note> This was observed not only toward poets, but also toward soldiers when they performed something worthy of glory in war, for which they earned crowns of either ivy or laurel. Note that a **birrhus** <term>birrhus: a thick, hooded cloak or overcoat</term> is a coarse garment, and the name comes from the Greek *birrhos*. Also—

<column-break/>

—although the ivy was decorated afterward, no strength of sap could thereafter restore the injury to its former state, due to the impact of the earthenware <note>likely referring to a broken vessel or a metaphorical "clay" obstacle</note> and the shame brought upon the branch. Therefore, let the resources of poverty be safe and clean, content with little, manfully enduring attacks, always panting <note>original: "anhelans," meaning to strive or long for</note> toward the highest things, and obedient to all. And let it be ready for service.

---

The nature of labor was explained in the preceding sections. "Therefore let it be safe," etc. In this part, Boethius <note>The commentator attributes the text to Boethius, though modern scholars identify the author as Pseudo-Boethius</note>, after all the things mentioned above regarding the destitution of scholars, finally concludes from all these points the manner and rule by which poverty itself must be endured, saying: "Therefore," that is, because of what has been said, let the safe resources of poverty be "clean," meaning infected by no evil envy; "panting," meaning always reaching for the highest; and let it be "content with little," that is, with the modest amount that suffices for nature; and let it be "enduring," that is, suffering manfully with an equal mind, in the manner of a wise man who holds himself like a **tetragon** <term>tetragon: a square or four-sided figure, used here as a metaphor for stability and moral perfection</term> without reproach against the "attacks," that is, the insults of Fortune; and let it be "obedient to all," meaning rebellious in nothing; and let it be "prompt," that is, ready for "service," meaning ministry. Let it be slow to speak, for in much talking, falsehood is rarely absent; and let it be faithful in "compliance," that is, service; and let it be "integral," meaning not damaged but full of love; "sweet," that is, affable to a colleague; and let it be lacking in "tumorosity," that is, pride and the swelling of the heart; for the opposite of this and all the aforementioned things is not valued when found with a poor man. Then, by addressing the reader, he answers a silent question. For someone might say: "But when the poor man has all these qualities in himself, what reward for his labors should be expected?" Answering this, he says: "Although the retribution," that is, the compensation for labor, is withheld by many, nevertheless the "adoption of love and favor" will be earned by the virtue of the labors. Confirming this by a comparison, he says: "Does it not happen," that is, does it not frequently occur in a small lapse of time, that which could not be produced in a "yearly circle," that is, the space of a year? And I say this as one "driven out," that is, expelled from a place and business by the office of a flatterer as much as by the "consort," that is, the society of a "delator," meaning an informer or accuser. For where such people exist, they are the procurers of all evil. It should be noted regarding the phrase "let poverty be clean," that it means not infected by the desires of our earth, for nothing is enough for this greed. From the second book of *The Consolation of Philosophy*: since, as Seneca says in his seventy-third epistle, "this greed believes nothing is its own because it always distrusts." For this reason, poverty does not pant after the goods of Fortune, but always after the **Highest Good**; for in that alone is all fullness and the fulfillment of our desire. Therefore let it be...

lest, however, total trust be placed in these, he dissuades them by an example at the point: "nor entirely." And he says first: secondly, it is necessary for a scholar striving for the height of the mastership that he acquire, that is, procure for his exercise, that is, for his study.

## Having dismissed his company, he flocked to his papers, inquiring into the knot of the proposed question. Secondly, that he should acquire a supply of books for his exercise so that when there is need, he may consult them. Nor should he believe in them entirely, like Jugio <note>A character used as a cautionary tale of a student who relied solely on his notebooks</note> who [followed] his master Montanus.

A supply of books, and this for the reason that, namely, when there is need, he may consult them, specifically for solving questions. And then, dissuading excessive confidence in them by an example, he says: "nor yet should the scholar himself believe entirely," that is, totally, in them—namely, the books—so that he commits nothing at all to memory. Just like that scholar Jugio, who trusted so much in the warnings, that is, the teachings of his master named Montanus, that every word uttered from his mouth—that is, the master's—he would engrave, that is, write down in quires <term>quaternus: a gathering of four sheets of parchment</term>, that is, books, committing absolutely nothing to memory. And he valued this very thing received from the master's mouth as if it were something sacred. And eventually, when he took the turn, that is, the place of the master, he preached nothing else in the schools except that which he had written in his little notebooks while his master was teaching. Wherefore—that is, because of this—he himself often went away confounded by shame, that is, embarrassment, because he preached to the scholars nothing other than what the book contained.

From this, he adds a certain notable point concerning this: "Indeed, for certain, to always use things already found and not things yet to be found is the mark of a most miserable intellect." And it is for fools to trust entirely in the orations, that is, the teachings of the mastership, that is, the master. But yet, one must believe at first until it is seen what he—the master—thinks. Afterward, one must imagine that he—the scholar—has erred, or that the master erred in teaching. And this is so that if by chance the disciple is able to find something to object to in the committed diligence, that is, the doctrine. For it is the opinion of Aristotle <note>A reference to the Aristotelian principle that a learner must first believe what they are told before they can judge it</note> that the learner must believe until he perceives better, etc.

It should be noted that although a supply of books distracts much, as Seneca reports in his second letter to Lucilius <note>Seneca the Younger, "Moral Letters to Lucilius," Letter 2, which warns against reading too many different authors</note>, since a supply of them only brings honor and does not instruct. For "there is no end to the making of books" (Ecclesiastes 12). Although these things are so, it does not matter how many books one has if they are good and filled with good instructions. We read that the ancients, attending only to this manner, stored them up like treasures in books. Thus, we read that in Egypt, one library had forty thousand volumes of books, all of which, however, after five thousand one hundred thirty-four years had passed from the beginning of the world, in the year 95 of Christ's birth, were consumed by a single fire. This was at the time when Virgil, Horace, Sallust, historians, Plotinus, Posidonius the Stoic, and other men worthy of memory flourished at Rome. Therefore, the examples of the elders are to be imitated in these things, who did not buy books for the sake of honor but procured them for the sake of instruction.

Note that a *quaternus* <note>quire</note> is named from "four." For a *codex* is collected from four sheets of paper; a *quinternus* from five; a *sexternus* from six; a *triternus* from three. Likewise, there is a difference between *estimo* and *extimo*: for *estimare* is to think or suppose, but *extimare* is to tax or value, etc.

# Fifth

Thirdly, he should have certain people whom he may teach in private. In this section, Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), though this specific text, "De Disciplina Scholarium," is a 13th-century pseudo-Boethian work used as a pedagogical manual in medieval universities.</note> sets forth the third instruction most necessary for a prospective master. It is divided into two parts: first, he states what has been said; second, he adds the reason for his statement, beginning at "For others, etc." And he says, thirdly, it is necessary for the prospective master to have certain people—namely scholars—whom he may teach in private, read books to them, and shape them with other instructions. In this way, he may know what has been understood by rooting it more firmly, and he may learn to express what is known in words—supplementing what was explained in the first instruction. Thus, he acquires for himself the practice of his art through frequent expression; this practice (as was said above regarding the triple recollection) provides—that is, administers—mastery. Adding the reason for these things, he says: because to teach others is to indulge—that is, to devote effort—to one's own faculty, which is to say, to knowledge, according to the saying: *He who teaches another instructs himself.* It should be noted that in the text a "gradation" is omitted, which is a rhetorical figure <term>gradatio: a ladder-like rhetorical device where the last word of one clause becomes the first of the next</term> formed when the following word is shaped from the preceding one, as if by steps of voices, as in this meter: *What is lighter than smoke? A breeze. What than a breeze? The wind. What than the wind? A woman. What than a woman? Nothing.* <note>original: "Quid leuius fumo flamen . qđ flamine ventus . qđ vento mulier . qđ muliere nihil ." This was a common medieval misogynistic trope used to demonstrate rhetorical structure.</note> Fourthly, it must be arranged. Here Boethius sets forth the fourth instruction necessary for prospective masters. He does two things: first, he states what has been said; second, he confirms the statements with an example, at "as Flavus, etc." And he says: fourthly, it must be arranged—that is, provided for—that the prospective master himself should allure—that is, by his good character and goodwill he should attract, not buy with a price as Flavus himself had done—I say he should allure those mentioned in the previous instruction, and as many others as possible. And let him see to it that when the opportunity for the time of his inception as a master arrives, he may rejoice in their intrinsic sight—that is, their presence. For what is more shameful than to be deserted—that is, to be left alone without the company of listeners at the first time of your inception—that is, of your masterly honor. And setting forth the example of Flavus, he says: To be left behind, I say, like that scholar Flavus, who at the time of his "exodus" <note>The "exodus" or "inception" refers to the formal ceremony where a student became a Master.</note> and his new beginning believed that everyone would be subject to him because of the command—that is, the power—of his lineage and his opulence—that is, the abundance of his ruling wealth—that is, his treasure. **he trusted so much in the warnings of the master**
**that every word proceeding from his mouth**
**he would scratch into his notebooks and regard as sacred.**
**Doing nothing else than taking the place of the master in**

**Indeed, it is the mark of a most wretched mind to always use**

**But first, one must believe until it is**
**seen what he thinks; afterwards, one must pretend**

**Thirdly, that he should have certain people**
