**than those he shapes with basic rudiments, so that he may thus know**
**what is understood, and learn to express what is known, and having expressed it...**

# Fifth <note>original: "Quitum"</note>

Plato. These men, doubting individual things, affirmed nothing as certain; an opinion which **Heraclitus** also seems to confirm. There was another sect of the **Epicureans**, named after Epicurus the Athenian, who placed the highest good in pleasure, as **Aulus Gellius** says in book 13. He also posits two goods, namely: a body without pain and a soul without disturbance, as **Seneca** reports in letter 66 to Lucilius. If this is founded in the pleasure of the flesh, it is to be rejected; if in the pleasure of the mind, it is to be supported. And Seneca attests that Epicurus posited it thus

<columns>2</columns>

in his book *On the Firmness of the Wise*. There is also another sect of philosophers which is that of the **Peripatetics**, which **Aristotle** founded, so named from *peri*, which is "around," and *patos*, "treading," as if "treading around" or walking about. For the philosophers of this sect, and especially Aristotle among them, used to dispute while walking, or even by walking from school to school

<column-break/>

**...walk about in a peripatetic fashion and oppose courteously, and let him bite back sharply against those who are being insolent, and let him respond more diligently according to the time, lest if his will be silent, it be imputed to the ignorance of blindness or the arrogance of rashness. Indeed, we have seen many of those observing—though unwillingly—enjoy a downfall because of the insolence of their response. For it is not in the interest of the learner to incite the ruler <note>the teacher</note> with shameful speeches and insulting remarks. Nor is it permitted [to seek] the highest...**

<columns>1</columns>

and they inquired what better things they could acquire and add to their opinion. And the text speaks to such a purpose when it says "let him walk about the schools of those in a peripatetic fashion," etc. "Indeed, many because of the response." In this part, **Boethius** <note>The author refers to Boethius, likely the "De Disciplina Scholarium" formerly attributed to him</note> moves that insolence and rashness must be avoided above all in the aforementioned matters. And first he does this; secondly, he adds the cause there: "For it is not," etc. And Boethius says: we have seen many of those observing "enjoy a downfall," that is, a falling from the grade of magisterial dignity, because of the "insolence of the response." For it is not in the interest of the learner to "incite," that is, to provoke the "ruler," that is, the master, with "insulting" and "shameful" remarks, that is, those bringing reproaches. For just as God and a parent, so also a master is to be held in honor and reverence, since no equivalent recompense can be paid to them for what has been received. According to that saying: *To God, parents, and masters, no equivalent is returned.* It should be noted that "insolence" <term>proteruitas: specifically a bold, rude, or cruel behavior</term> is properly cruelty and terribleness in both word and deed. Hence a "forward person" <note>original: "pternus"</note> is noted by Boethius; whence the *Grecismus* <note>A popular 13th-century grammatical poem by Eberhard of Béthune</note> says: "Someone is wicked who is insolent in words and deeds." And it is derived from *pro* or *pros* and *tonus*. Therefore, just as it is not permitted to rise up against a master in deeds (as was taught in the second chapter on violence), so also it is not permitted to be insolent toward him in words. For he is not worthy of knowledge who rises up against the teacher of knowledge. In the same place: "Wherefore," etc. "Nor is it permitted [to seek] the highest familiarity." Here Boethius, after the instruction declared above, adds a certain notable point, saying: the scholar himself ought not to gape at secrets, namely books, chests, and the bedchamber, even if he has been joined to his master with the "highest familiarity"—and this unless ordered; and if ordered, yet as if unwilling. And bringing in a certain **Frontinus**, a disciple of **Xenocrates**, who, looking into the secrets of his master, thought he had acquired the total doctrine of Xenocrates from these things, he says: "Did not" (that is, "surely") the "insolence of that scholar Frontinus" open the "scrutinies," that is, the secret records of his master Xenocrates, and inspect things previously taught publicly (namely in the schools), and believed himself to be mastered <note>made a master</note> from this "theft-like and insolent inspection..."

# Fifth Section

...to students, and this only if one’s means allow. Or, understand this to mean: if resources are not sufficient for everyone, then at least at one’s pleasure—that is, according to one’s own will—to the masters and students, or solely to the masters of his own profession (that is, his sect or faculty). It should be noted regarding this passage that a gathering of colleagues is praised in a brief speech; for we truly praise when we extol the greatness of a matter with few words. Indeed, in much speaking, falsehood is rarely absent, and flattery is rarely lacking. Hence Cato says: *Be sparing in praise.* <note>original: "Parce laudato." Referring to the Distichs of Cato, a common medieval schoolbook.</note>

It is well to be sparing, because there is no virtue so lofty that it is not touched by the sweetness of glory, as reported by Seneca and Ovid in the *Tristia*: "Finally, glory gives no small strength to the soul, and the love of praise makes the heart fertile." <note>original: "Deniqꝫ non paruas animo dat gloria vires. Et fecūda facit pectora laudis amor." Ovid, Tristia, 5.12.37-38.</note> For this reason, Jerome, writing to Sabinianus, says: "We are led by a natural evil, and we willingly favor our flatterers. And although we may answer that we are unworthy, and a hot blush may pour over our faces, yet the soul rejoices inwardly at its own praise." <note>original: "Naturali ducimur malo..." Jerome, Letter 147.</note> Thence Claudian—

<column-break/>

**...must be provided with decent adornment and festive preparation, if means allow, for all; or at the pleasure of the individual, at least for those of the same profession, splendidly provided. Nevertheless, it must be elegantly considered and more cautiously investigated before the elevation to the Mastership, whether he might be able to be sustained by his own resources during the course of the first year, if need be. For it is shameful, out of reverence for so great a name, to beg at the very first appearance; like Strictonius, who, having venerably carried out everything pertaining to the Mastership, began to beg on the third day. He soon repented of such great daring. What wonder—**

<column-break/>

—less; for virtue rejoices to join the Muses to itself as witnesses. "Whoever does things worthy of a poem loves a poem." <note>original: "gaudet enim virtus testes sibi iungere musas..." Claudian, De Consulatu Stilichonis.</note> Therefore, praise must be given sparingly, supported by the dignity of the one praising, the merit of the one praised, and the magnitude of the thing for which he is praised. If these are not present, it is manifest that it is not praise but flattery.

Furthermore, what a "stema" <note>term: stema (stemma). Usually a lineage or garland; here likely referring to a formal academic heading or coat of arms discussed previously.</note> is has already been shown in the preceding chapters; therefore look for it there. *Nevertheless, it must be elegantly considered, etc.* This part is usually assigned by many as a "caution" regarding the preceding instruction. In my view, however, it would be more appropriately assigned as the **Seventh Instruction**. But whatever the case may be, I leave it to the shrewdness of the reader. This much must be said: when the text serves as a caution for the previous instruction, the letter reads *Nevertheless elegantly*; if it is a new instruction, the letter reads *Also elegantly*.

And according to the first reading, it says: it must be considered cautiously, that is, wisely (understand: in these matters and concerning those things taught in the above instruction). It must be more cautiously investigated before the "elevation"—that is, the promotion to the Mastership—so that during the "course"—that is, the curriculum of the first year (understand: the first year following the attainment of the Master's rank)—the new Master himself might be sustained by his own means if necessary. "For" stands for "because" it is shameful to "beg"—that is, to be in want—at the "first front"—that is, immediately—on account of the reverence due to so great a name (namely, the Mastership). He means to say: it is exceedingly shameful that a student to be promoted spends so much in the acquisition of the Master’s dignity that as soon as he has obtained the rank, he is forced to beg. And he adds the example of a certain **Strictonius**, who, after all things pertaining to the Mastership had been completed and executed venerably, splendidly, and honorably...

## Chapter Six.

**Having set forth those things which were arranged**
**for the instruction of scholars, while observing**
**a moderation of clarity. We do not care to burden**
**the reader with brevity of speech,**
**nor to confuse with delay. Never more clear—**

<column-break/>

—the heights of such great honor. And from this, noting a certain point, he exclaims saying: ¶ Because the venerable, that is, the reverend, commendation is of a happy end, meaning a happy finish. For he himself is the one toward whom all things must be ordered. If, therefore, the end is good, the whole is praiseworthy and approved. For which reason it is not unsuitably said: *The outcome proves the acts.* <note>original: "Exitus acta probat," a famous Ovidian proverb.</note> And likewise: *The end crowns the work.* And furthermore, all things are named from their end. Chapter 6 and the last.

---

*Having set forth those things which pertain to the instruction of scholars, etc.* This is the sixth and final chapter of this entire treatise, which is on the *Discipline of Scholars*. <note>A medieval textbook long attributed to Boethius, though actually written in the 13th century.</note> In which, after those things he taught in the previous chapters—and specifically after he determined in the first preceding chapter certain documents regarding the masterly dignity, <term>masterly dignity: the status and rights of a Master of Arts</term> both those contributing to it and those required as necessary—now consequently in this last chapter he proceeds principally concerning the masterly dignity itself and the things that surround and accompany it. 

And this whole chapter is divided into three principal parts according to the three kinds of masters. In the first part, indeed, he determines the first species of masters and the things that regulate them—and not only those first ones, but also others of whatever kind they may be. In the second part, at the words: *The extremes of the present volume.* In the third, at: *Since because of the sweetness, etc.* 

The first part is further divided into two parts: for first he continues what was said to what is to be said; second, he determines the status, norm, and rule of the masters at the words: *Such is the masters', etc.* Likewise, first he places his intention with respect to the preceding things; second, with respect to the following at: *Now to...* First he does what was said; second, he shows the mode of proceeding to be observed at: *Nor to increase...*; third, he adds the reason for his process at: *Since not only...* 

Say, therefore, first: *having set forth* those things which are *arranged*, i.e., delivered separately in the previous parts for the *instruction*, i.e., the information of scholars; and this while *observing a moderation*, i.e., modesty, of *clarity*, i.e., determination. And because we, **Boethius**, <note>The commentator identifies the author as Boethius, though modern scholars disagree.</note> do not care to *burden*, i.e., constrain the reader with the *brevity* (supply: of our edition), nor even to offend with *delay*, i.e., prolixity; sometimes having used a *lighter style*, i.e., matter, and a *clearer lineage*, i.e., ornament of words. And this is because the style (understand: of our whole treatise) is *commended*, i.e., delivered, not only to the *discreet*, i.e., the learned, but also for the *rude*, i.e., the unlearned; and this with the *series of enigma*, i.e., obscurity, *postponed*, i.e., left behind. Since, however, these things are so, one must *hasten*, i.e., accelerate now, namely in this place, to the *venerable majesty of the masters* (understand: by determining their status).

and a rule to regulate themselves toward others. Likewise, a **riddle** <note>original: "enigma"</note> is a figurative speech or an obscure expression, or a likeness, or a hidden or dark question that is difficult to understand unless it is opened up. As in that passage from Judges: *Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness* <note>Judges 14:14, referring to Samson's riddle</note>, signifying that the honeycomb was extracted from the mouth of the lion.

The division of the masters, however, is held to be such. In this part, Boethius, after he has connected himself to the preceding sections, now pursues his intention. And he does two things: for first, he sets forth certain divisions of the masters; second, he demonstrates the rule and the mode that regulates them, at the point beginning: *Of such indeed...* The first part is in two; for first he sets forth the first distinction of the masters, and second he joins the second distinctions, at the point: *As much of those as...* etc. And he says first that the division of the masters is held to be such (supply: as follows).

<column-break/>

**...with a sharp style and a lighter lineage: since it is commended not only to the discerning but also to the unrefined, the series of riddles having been set aside. Now we must hasten toward the venerable majesty of the masters. The division of the masters, however, shall be held as such. Certain of such great men dwell in two cities more radiant than the rest, namely Rome and Athens: proceeding nowhere further except as far as their fortune succeeds...**

---

For certain of the masters dwell in two more excellent cities, that is, more famous than the others, namely Rome and Athens, never proceeding further unless perhaps insofar as fortune succeeds, that is, smiles upon them so that they are elevated higher, that is, to higher things. Or thus: never proceeding further, namely from these cities, and this insofar as (that is, as long as) fortune succeeds for them so that they may be elevated higher. And he means to say that there are certain masters who only have their dwelling in the Roman and Athenian city. But there are other masters who, omitting the heights (that is, the summits) of the aforesaid cities, namely Rome and Athens, seek the emoluments (that is, the profits) of the towns (that is, the fortified camps) and villages—so that "town" <note>term: "oppidum" - usually a fortified town or settlement</note> may be taken in a broad sense—of the towns, I say, adjacent to the aforesaid cities (understand: either distant from afar or from nearby). And I say they seek them first because of poverty (supply: to be remedied); I call poverty a "stepmother," that is, contrary to discipline. For as has been said quite often: Nature is not sufficient to contemplate by itself without exterior things. Then also (that is, secondly) they seek the emoluments of other towns because of the shining sweetness of their native country, that is, their paternal soil. He means to say that after those masters who dwell in the cities of Rome and Athens, there are other masters who are in towns, and some of these in the towns of their native soil, while others are in towns entirely foreign. And concerning all of these, it will be treated in their own order and place in the following. <margin>It should be noted that just as there were many sects of philosophers, so also there were many receptacles of studies.</margin> Therefore, commemorating the more celebrated assemblies of doctrines by the opinion of historians, the studies of Athens stood out as more brilliant than the rest; which Jerome himself commends, saying: *Athens would be the most fit for study.* For first it handed down the laws of study to others and transmitted the rights; in it flourished almost all the lights of philosophy, just as the fame has gone out and been spread so far. After the study of Athens, the Roman study flourished, crowded with Italian philosophers, in which Julius Caesar flourished, in the first book on the life of Caesar, there...

# Chapter

Cato flourished, as Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler</note> says in his first book; there Virgil, Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>, Seneca, and many others were highly esteemed. And literature commends these two centers of study. There is also another, the University of Paris, which was sufficiently praised in the preceding sections. Even the modern age has almost innumerable universal schools of learning, which I know not whether to praise or blame, since virtue stands on its own and does not require an outside preacher. Likewise, the profit <margin><term>Profit</term> <note>original: "emolumentum"</note> properly refers to the gain from a mill, but it is used here for any kind of gain or advantage. Thus in Malachi chapter three: "And what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances?" <note>Malachi 3:14</note>. Of both these and those, some by reason of a beautiful, etc. Here he posits another distinction among masters, saying: Of the masters indeed dwelling in the aforementioned cities and surrounding towns, some are masters who assume authority—that is, the master’s rank and title—by reason of a "beautiful denomination," which is to say, for the sake of fame, so that they may be honored by men. And these</margin> proceeds to them so that they may be more deeply venerated. Others of the aforementioned, leaving behind the heights of the adjacent towns, seek profits, partly because of poverty (the "stepmother of discipline") and partly because of the resisting sweetness of their native land. Of both these and the others, some assume authority by reason of a "beautiful denomination" <note>A prestigious title or name</note> so that they may be honored. Others do so by reason of understanding, lest they be confounded by their own ignorance. A third group, observing more subtly, take up the master’s cloaks <note>original: "paludamenta"</note> for the sake of the advancement of both parts. Of such

<column-break/>

are those who seek only the glory of a name. Others, however, assume the master’s rank for the sake of understanding, and this specifically so they are not put to shame by ignorance. But the third group are those who, observing more subtly than the former, take up the "cloaks"—that is, the honor which properly consists in these garments—which are "magisterial," meaning they show one to be a master. He means to say that the third group are those who assume the magisterial dignity for the sake of the advancement of both aforementioned parts: namely, both to appear and be celebrated with honor, and also for the sake of understanding. It should be noted that while knowing is good and delightful above all else, since knowledge itself embraces all things and permits nothing to be unknown, the act of knowing is not entirely praiseworthy if it is acquired solely for the glory of fame. For although it is a "fine thing to be pointed out with a finger and have it said: 'That’s him!'"—according to the opinion of Persius Flaccus <note>A Roman satirist; the quote is from Satire 1.28</note>—it is nevertheless not holy. Therefore, that kind of knowing is to be chosen which accompanies a virtuous life, not a desire for glory. Thus, of these types of masters, only that one is praiseworthy which receives the increments of knowledge in order to dispel the cloud of ignorance. Likewise, the "cloak" <note>original: "paludamentum"</note> is a type of royal garment which they used to wear to openly show a future war. It is named from "openly" <note>Latin: "palam"</note> because then the war was shown openly to all. It is also the magisterial garment in which those about to become masters are dressed to show the title of their future merits. For whoever of such, having assumed the due beauties... In this part, Boethius, after the previous two-part division of masters, now concerning any of...

# Sixth Part

The author joins together the norm and the method regulating teachers, both within themselves and in relation to others. This part is divided into two sections: first, **Boethius** sets down certain precepts regulating masters absolutely and in regard to themselves; second, by comparison in regard to others. The second part begins at "But these things..." The first part is further divided into two: first, he does what was said; second, he adds the reason for his statement at "For no thing..." The first of these is again divided into two: first, he does what was said; second, he provides an excuse for the aforementioned precepts at "If indeed anything contrary..." And first, setting down the instructions regulating the status of a master, he says that whatever master he may be, if he wishes to pursue the rewards of his assumed beauty—that is, of magisterial honor—and of his due office, it is necessary—that is, opportune—that he should be powerful—that is, shine forth more brightly—in a universal honesty of character. Namely, that he—

<column-break/>

**For whoever wishes to pursue the rewards of the beauty he has assumed and of his due office: it is necessary that he shine forth more brightly in a universal honesty of character. So that he may be, in every way, truthful in speech, just in judgment, prudent in counsel, and faithful in what is entrusted to him; constant in countenance, kind in speech, distinguished by virtues, and may stand out as praiseworthy in goodness.**
**If, however, anything contrary should happen, it usually happens through the appetite of human frailty. Let him also be good in his social conduct. For no thing—**

<column-break/>

—should be truthful in speech, just in judgment, etc. The text is plain. And "if anything contrary should happen" <note>original: "si quid contrarium accidat"</note>—understand this to mean contrary to the above—this usually happens through the "appetite of human frailty," that is, through sensuality itself. For that is weak and prone to evil. And because it is weak, a weakness of character very often follows it. For a weakness of the temperament <note>The "complexion" or balance of bodily humors</note>, as is often seen by physicians <term>medicis</term>, is followed by a weakness of character. It should be noted that although a master may possess all those things in himself which the form of teaching contains—such as the consideration of teaching, conformity to examples, and again, a copious eloquence—these nevertheless are by no means sufficient unless he instructs by his work those things which he teaches by his word. For this is the best way of wisdom: to conform one's works to sound doctrines. Whence **Prosper** says in his **Book of Epigrams**:
> It is not enough to unroll the Lord's precepts with the tongue. He remembers the law who is mindful of the work.

For it is a shameful thing, as **Lactantius** says in his **Book on False Wisdom**, to proceed toward philosophy and not to perform the works of philosophy. For such a life is not true, but "cloaked" <note>original: "palliata," meaning a life that wears the philosopher's cloak without the reality of the virtue</note>. Now, the works of philosophy are the morals and the divine institutes, in which the master should so shine that he is not only an example to the disciple, but also an ornament. The reason for all these good things is consequently annexed here when it is said: "since no thing is more ruinous—that is, harmful—to a disciple than the shameful life of a master." For as we—**Boethius**—have seen, things poured from a stinking—that is, contaminated—vessel are very often confounded—that is, corrupted. Since a stinking vessel corrupts the waters, so it is said that just as waters are corrupted by a stinking vessel, so is knowledge by a shameful teacher. Regarding which it should be noted that there are many "wise men" of the present day who, although they intend sound doctrines, nevertheless lead a brutal life, just as **Aristotle** touches upon in the **first book of the Ethics**. These are certainly to be held in hatred, following the example of **Pacuvius**, who rejected all such people with such loathing that he did not think it worthy to communicate with them in word or deed, as **Aulus Gellius** and **Helinandus** record in their chronicles. Of whom **Lactantius**, in his book on False Wisdom, says: "Certain people, hiding their vices under the pretext of philosophy, as are the sophists <term>sophiste</term> at home..."

# Chapter
## Section b

They do those things which they argue against in the schools. Thus they only teach and do not act; they themselves strip the weight from their own precepts. This type of behavior is most shameful, as Seneca witnesses in his 24th letter to Lucilius <note>original: "Seneca ad Lucillum epistola xxiiij"</note>. For he says it is shameful to say one thing and feel another. And again in the 44th letter: This is most shameful, which is often cast against us, that we handle the words of philosophy but not the works. Hence Cato says: *It is shameful for a teacher when his own fault refutes him.*

A teacher's shameful life is a more ruinous thing for a student. For things poured in are very often seen to be tainted by a stinking vessel, because a stinking vessel corrupts the waters poured into it. These things have been arranged for the formation of the teacher's soul. Now we must discuss the other primary matters—I do not say the "first-primary" matters, but the "second-primary" ones. A teacher is also required to be learned, gentle, firm, "ancient" (not in years), not negligent, and not arrogant.

<column-break/>

Therefore, when anyone's life is looked down upon, it is necessary that his teaching also be looked down upon, as Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> wishes in his 6th Homily, Book 2. Let prudent men learn from these words the form of teaching, and let them persuade their students to become studious not only by turning the pages of books but also by composing their own character. Likewise, "ruin" <term>pernicies: death or destruction</term> is death or destruction. That is, he should impose punishment upon those who do wrong and dissolve the disputes of the sophists <note>original: "sophistaz"</note>, that is, those engaged in disputations, and he should bite back at <note>original: "remordeat"</note>, that is, punish, those who bark <note>original: "oblatrantes"</note>, which refers to those who are constantly snarling against others, a term taken from dogs. ## **So that he may impose punishment on those who err. He should dissolve the disputes of the sophists. He should bite back at those who bark. He should restrain those who speak ill. He should chastise the insolent. And he should make the entire determination dialectical. Let him be ancient, not in years, but in perpetual knowledge. If indeed both are present, his condition will be the healthier. Not negligent. Since just as in every...**

Rigidity is to be imputed to fault. Indeed, only light chastisement is permitted to masters, as found in the section "On Homicide" in the chapter *Ad audientiam* and in the twenty-third question, sixth chapter, first part <note>References to Canon Law: the Decretals of Gregory IX and Gratian's Decretum</note>. And hence it is that if, by a light striking, a scholar should die, the master is not held responsible, as Vincentius <note>likely Vincentius Hispanus, a 13th-century legal scholar</note> maintains. And this applies if the boy is healthy and robust; it is otherwise if he is tender, because then it is no longer a "light striking." See the Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*, the law *Qua actione*, paragraph *Si quis* <note>Reference to Roman Civil Law regarding liability for damages</note>. This is also noted in the Decretals, the chapter *In magistrā*, under the section on elections.

**Let him be ancient, not in years.** This is the fourth instruction <note>original: "documentū"</note>, which concerns the long experience and perpetual knowledge of masters. And the author says the master should also be "ancient," that is, supported by experience. And he says this well: ancient indeed not in years, but in perpetual knowledge, that is, knowledge firmly rooted in him. But nevertheless, if both should be present—namely, old age along with knowledge—his condition will be healthier. It should be noted by this requirement for the master to be "ancient" that he wishes him to be practiced through long experience in doctrines and in the form of teaching. In doctrines, as was taught in the first instruction. In the form of teaching, however, so that he may teach rightly and skillfully <note>original: "artificialiter"</note> to each person according to their capacity and according to the requirements of each art.

And Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century writer on agriculture</note> touches upon this form of teaching best in the first book of *On Agriculture* when he says: "The first part of prudence is that you consider the person of the one you are about to instruct. For it is foolish to address rustics in the style of the most learned men." Thus, so that one may teach well, it is expedient that he seek out a method useful to the listener and consider his capacity, age, and perception. Nor should he begin to instruct in the "arts" <note>the Liberal Arts</note> until he has first shared the "parts" <note>the basic components or elements</note>. And from this is taken that common proverb: **"The old masters learned the arts after the parts."**

**Not negligent.** This is the fifth instruction, which is about the perseverance of masters. And it says: Let the master by no means be negligent, but persevering. Since just as in every work constancy and diligence are found to be like a mother, so also, conversely, negligence is the stepmother—that is, the enemy—of all doctrine and discipline. Thus it happens that it is more fitting to serve a mechanical science <note>manual trades or crafts</note> than to be burdened by the yoke of negligence. It should be noted that a lazy man is unworthy of good things, and he who has no diligence deserves to be endowed with no benefit. For man was born to this end: that he should labor with his body for food, and with his mind for...

-># Sixth<-

...virtues. And not only for himself, but as **Plato** says to **Archytas**, for his country and his friends. <note>original: "ad Architam patrie atqȝ amicis" - referring to Plato's Ninth Letter, where he argues we are not born for ourselves alone.</note> For laziness makes many people idle because it dreads continuing healthy undertakings. And these people alone are "soft," as **Aristotle** himself wishes in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, where he says: "Softness is the fleeing of laborious things." <note>Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IV.</note> This must be avoided by teachers above all else; likewise, perseverance must be firmly embraced with a calm mind. Once embraced and retained,

honors, virtues, sciences, and riches are usually acquired. For virtue is not easily entrusted to slow minds, as **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> testifies in the third book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. And **Virgil** says in the *Bucolics*: "The cowherds came slowly." <note>Virgil, Eclogues (Bucolics) 10.19.</note> Truly, every slow person lacks the prize. **Let him not be arrogant.** This is the sixth instruction, by which it is advised that arrogance must be avoided by teachers. And **Boethius** does two things regarding this instruction: first, he shows that arrogance must be avoided at all costs; second, he demonstrates who those teachers are who foster arrogance (at the point beginning "These are..."). And he says that a teacher should in no way be arrogant, since arrogance works absolutely no good toward students; he shows this regarding both the poor and the rich. He says that the "lively little spark"—that is, the love of knowing—in a poor man is extinguished by the arrogance of the teacher. This is said regarding the poor. Furthermore, the "will to learn is sequestered"—that is, separated—from the rich (understand this as being caused by arrogance itself), because the "assiduity"—that is, the diligence—of an arrogant teacher never instructs a man faithfully. Likewise, the arrogant, the proud, the boaster, the elated, and the puffed-up are the same; however, arrogance differs from pride. For pride is empty glory concerning what one actually possesses, but arrogance concerns what one does not possess—as when someone believes they know things they do not know, or have qualities they do not have. Often, however, these two terms are confused by authors. **These are they who disdain to teach what they know with humility.** In this part, he shows which teachers are marked by this vice of arrogance. He does this according to two types of arrogance: one in teaching, the second in outward display (at the point "These also are..."). And he says these arrogant teachers are those who disdain to teach humbly the things they know, and refuse to show correctly the things they understand; because, "placed on a summit"—that is, in pride and haughtiness—they "despise the minds of those deserving"—that is, those desiring instruction—by "feeling disgust," which is to say, acting as if the students cause them loathing. These arrogant ones also do not refer the cause of their knowledge back to the Giver of knowledge—that is, the glorious God from whom "every best gift and every perfect gift" is given, according to **John** <note>James 1:17; the text attributes this to John, likely a common medieval slip or referring to the general Johannine circle/Gospel themes of light and truth.</note>—for He attributes all things fluently and does not reproach; He gives more than is asked. I say they do not refer the cause of their knowledge to Him, but rather look to their own excellence, estimating in themselves alone that the things they know, they know by their own excellence. And then he follows with the second type of arrogant people, saying "these also are..."

<column-break/>

**...constancy is found to be the mother of work! Just so, negligence is the stepmother of all doctrine and discipline. For it would be more fitting to serve a mechanical art than to be burdened by the yoke of negligence. Let him not be arrogant. Since the lively little spark of the poor man is extinguished by the arrogance of the teacher, and the will to learn is sequestered from the rich. Because the assiduity of an arrogant teacher never instructs a man faithfully. These are they who disdain to teach what they know with humility, and are unable to correctly show the things they understand by reason; because, placed on a summit, they despise the minds of those who are deserving.**

# Sixth Section

## On the Necessity of Divine Aid and Punctuality

One should wait for no one unless the greatest necessity urges—that is, weighs upon them. It must be noted concerning this instruction from Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose "Consolation of Philosophy" was a foundational textbook in medieval education.</note> that it is of the utmost importance to consider that before the beginning of such a task, the imploring of divine help must not be omitted. For God alone is He who pours the riches of His wisdom into the souls of the wise. And He grants to students the grace of understanding, to whom nothing is difficult and without whom nothing is possible to be possessed, as is said in the prologue of *The Government of Princes*.

And "every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights," <note>original: "omne datum optimum... a patre luminum descendens"; a quote from the Biblical Book of James 1:17.</note> as the Scripture says. And Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> says: "No one is so learned, no one so taught, who does not stand in need of heavenly illumination." And Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> says: "Unless He be within who teaches, the tongue of the teacher labors in vain." Therefore Philosophy, wishing to show in what true happiness exists, in Boethius's third book, ninth prose of *The Consolation*, warns to invoke divine help, for certainly if this is bypassed, no beginning is rightly established. Our ancestors, observing this,

<column-break/>

will banish themselves once [the opportunity] is taken away. However, when the recruit <term>recruit: "tyro," a beginner or student soldier of learning</term> of good inquiry has entered the schools for the sake of reading, having assumed a rigor within, it must be considered that at the time of dawn <note>original: "aurore tempore"</note> he should begin continually with a low voice, with a "round mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo"; a classical idiom for eloquent, well-formed speech</note> ascending moderately, unless a great necessity urges waiting.

Because if the diligence of the master presumes to wait for some beyond the space of the due time, the delay of laziness confounds them and promotes anger through resentment. For when the disciple of laziness, that craftsman of sleepiness, recognizes the diligence of the master, he will either hasten more maturely or, confounded by shame, will sleep to his own disgrace.

always implored divine aid when undertaking arduous tasks. Thus Plato, about to begin the "generation of the sensible world," says: "Truly, my Socrates: since it is the custom for all that a certain religion should pray for the help of divinity," etc. <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> Therefore, let there be a preface to my prayers to Mary, so that those things may be said by us which please God, etc. And Haly Abenragel <note>An 11th-century Arab astrologer and physician, known in Latin as Haly Abenragel.</note> says: "Graces to the living God," etc. So also Ovid in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*: "Gods, breathe upon my undertakings, for you have changed even those," etc. And so almost all the rest.

Let the master therefore take heed that before he performs those things taught by this precept, he should supplicate God as the illuminator of all hearts. Likewise, "Recruit" was declared in the upper chapters. "Dawn" is said to be the beginning of the brightening day or the first splendor of the air, which in Greek is called *eous*. Whence Virgil says of the roses: "The tighter dawn <note>original: "eous"</note> had preceded the yoked horses," etc.

"Because if the diligence of the master..." In this part, Boethius adds the causes of his saying. And it is divided into two parts: for first he does what was said; second, he confirms the sayings by example. The first is further divided into two, as he assigns two causes. He says that if the diligence of the master presumes to wait for some beyond the space of the due time, these two evils might perhaps happen: namely, that perhaps the master himself will confound those whom he awaits by the delay of laziness. That is to say, when the master waits for them, they can pull this laziness into a habit for themselves, thinking the masters will wait for them continually just as they did once. And this is the first evil to come from such waiting. The second is truly because perhaps by such waiting the master [arouses] anger...

->**And in the schools, lest the matter be finished, he would say to his arriving companions: "The redness of the light, the gold of the day's dawn, is not yet confounded." He behaved this way around midday. <column-break/>

...was harmful to him while he sought to "imprison" (that is, to swallow) the food, because sleep had so oppressed him that whatever he had begun was pulled back by a dream. Wherefore, addressing Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, the famous Roman philosopher.</note> and Marcianus <note>Likely referring to Martianus Capella, author of 'The Marriage of Philology and Mercury'.</note>, he says: "O Marcianus, dearest of companions, if indeed—for certainly—your intention knows to what fruit of maturity and labor you believe this Dromon will arrive." He says this because, in fact, he knows that he will never be able to reach any fruit.

It should be noted regarding this example that although moderate sleep is good, moderate laziness is the worst, because the lazy neglect themselves and their affairs and, like beasts, roll around in the dregs of their own sins. For drowsiness is the fuel of all vices. Whence Cato <note>Dionysius Cato, reputed author of the 'Distichs', a popular medieval schoolbook.</note> says: "For long rest provides nourishment for vices." Wherefore Ovid also, rebuking the drowsy in his second book <note>original: "li. ij. siue titulo" - referring to the Amores.</note>, breaks out into these words: "Unhappy is whoever sustains rest through the whole night and calls sleep a great reward." And likewise: "Rest is poorly present to a heart always devoted to sleep; O how many ruins you lie open to, yourself naked of good. He whom night alone holds knows not how to watch for danger."

Persius <note>A Roman satirist known for his difficult, moralizing style.</note> rouses these drowsy ones in his fifth Satire with these words: "In the morning, lazy one, you snore. 'Rise,' says Avarice, 'hey, rise!' You refuse; she insists: 'Rise!' she says. 'I cannot.' 'Rise!' 'And what shall I do?' you ask. 'Fetch hemp from the sea, castor oil, flax, ebony, incense, and slippery Coan silk. Be the first to take the fresh pepper from the camel's back. Turn a profit, swear an oath.'" It is as if the poet were saying: "Rise, lazy one, rise, for the reason for rising is urgent."

Gaufredus <note>Geoffrey of Vinsauf, a medieval rhetorician, author of the 'Poetria Nova'.</note> in his *Poetria* also most aptly described the habit of the drowsy, conforming to the example set forth. For he says: "Do you know the delay of the lazy man? If he is called in the morning, he ignores it. If he is summoned again with a loud, repeated voice, he snores with a 'watchful nose.' At last, forced by the shouting, he moves his tongue with a slow mouth and says, 'What do you want?' You say, 'Rise, come!' He says, 'No, let me rest.' 'Nay, it is day, rise!' 'My God, look, I am rising. Go, I will follow.' But he does not follow the one he neglects, and you say, 'Will you not come?' 'A moment ago...'"

And he should take care not to be moved by "foul"—that is, obscure—difficulties. Rather, armed with studious premeditation—that is, with pre-planned study—among the "strifes"—that is, the disputations which are scholastic strifes—he should intrepidly settle them—that is, declare them—with an agile mind. This means he should harmonize opinions with ease and take care to arrange in his memory what anyone has objected to him (namely, while disputing) in such a way that at the time of "uncovering"—that is, solving and untying the knot—he does not withdraw from the path of reason. Instead, having accepted moderation—that is, modesty in clarifying—he should resolve—that is, declare explicitly and clearly—the enigmas—that is, the obscurities and sophisms proposed to him—in a fitting order, just as they were proposed and objected, and not later.

# Sixth

->First and foremost, by resolving what comes after.<- It should be noted that Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a philosopher whose works on logic were foundational to medieval education.</note> strongly warns that the master of sophistry <term>sophistria: the use of fallacious arguments, usually for the sake of showing off cleverness rather than finding truth</term> must be avoided in scholastic debates. And the reason is—as was also sent before in the previous sections—that it is nothing but an ambitious display of words. For it fills one with a confidence based solely on words to be proven; for which reason Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), influential Christian theologian.</note> in *On Christian Doctrine* calls it the "lust for quarreling" and the "science of impiety." See also above in the first chapter on the study of logic. Likewise, the term "foul"—that is, black and obscure—and the rest were discussed in the previous sections.

If, however, a very great doubt arises in the minds of discerning men, as is accustomed to happen. Here he presents the second instruction regarding the aforesaid matters. And he does two things: for first he presents the instruction, and second, regarding what was previously assumed, he says another thing there: "in the same way." And he says that if in a disputation <term>disputatio: a formal academic debate used as a teaching method</term> a very great doubt occurs, as usually happens to the minds of the discerning, one must use the efforts of deliberation in deciding what should be answered. That which the "stirred up" mind—that is, moved by the natural motions of the conscience—shall have dictated, understand that after such deliberation, it must be brought forward—that is, it must be determined publicly "on the morrow"—that is, on the following day and lesson. 

And then, regarding the previously assumed instruction, he does two things in placing another: first he places the instruction, and second he confirms it there: "For more easily..." And he says "in the same way"—namely, in the manner previously mentioned—it must be done if a master has premeditated something very difficult, because it is also to be commended to "discretion." Another version of the text has "to the disputation," and this is more true as appears from what follows. And adding the reasons, he says: "for" (meaning "because") a small spark of difficulty is often found more easily by "deferring"—that is, by debating—than if it were committed to the private observation of study. Confirming this, he says that, as Aristotle <note>Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose "Topics" deals with the art of dialectic and probability.</note> says (understand: in the *Topics*), truth itself is found not only in "the other"—that is, in one person—but is found in several or in many.

It should be noted regarding this statement, "for more easily by deferring," etc., that a disputation is a scholastic act by which anyone shows their intention to seek the truth through reason and asserts it with their strength. Indeed, among other acts, nothing is proven clearer or more healthy for the student than this: for it is this which shells the truth <note>original: "enucleat" - to remove the kernel from the husk; to clarify</note>, makes manifest the riddles, and condemns errors and wanderings. Therefore, it is not absurdly said that truth is found more easily by debating than by studying alone.

<column-break/>

But in a fitting order, having assumed a moderation of clarifying riddles, he should explicitly dissolve them. If, however, a very great doubt happens to the minds of the discerning in debating, as is accustomed to happen, one must use efforts in deliberating; and what the mind, stirred up by natural motions, has dictated to the conscience, must be brought forward on the morrow. In the same way, if anyone has premeditated something very difficult, it is to be commended to discretion. For more often a small spark of difficulty is found more easily by discerning <note>original: "disscerendo" - likely a variant of "disceptando" (debating) or "discernendo" (distinguishing)</note> than if it were committed to the observation of study. Because the truth of knowledge is not found in one person alone, as Aristotle says. It must also be noticed that in three ways...

A great [benefit]...

<column-break/>

shown how the master ought to conduct himself in a <term>disputation</term> <note>a formal academic debate used as a teaching method</note>. But it still remains hidden what reasons he ought to produce so that the debate arising between the disputants may be resolved with fitting arguments. And responding to this, he says that the knowledge of discerning masters is accustomed to use three modes in traditions and disputations. And this is according to three kinds of masters. For there are some who are subtle, some more subtle, and some most subtle. For some are accustomed to boast—that is, to use gloriously—traditions, which are new and unusual reasons and teachings. And this

was said regarding the third kind of masters. Others are also accustomed to cloak the minds of students with old—that is, ancient—and foul—that is, obscure—reasons; and this is said regarding the first [kind of] masters. And there are a third group who are accustomed to rouse—that is, to move—the understandings of the believing scholars with the most ancient—that is, very old—editions and reasons, but renewed; and they use them as if flowing from their own streams—that is, from their own sciences. And these are those who embrace the second kind, namely the moderately subtle. It should be noted among all kinds of masters, those are certainly known to be the most subtle who do not always use the books of the ancients and those almost obliterated, or even those renewed. For those [who do so] are begging and snatching the things of others and ascribing them to their own genius as if devised by themselves. But the most acute are those who long for new institutes. For it is the mark of a most miserable genius, as was also shown before, to always use things already found and not things yet to be found. Wherefore [etc]. Likewise "foul" means "obscure," as was explained above. *If any of these students*. Here he presents the second incidental point, which is such: Someone might perhaps say, if the boys and scholars are unable to fully understand the questions and reasons brought forward by the masters, what is to be done? Responding to which he says: that if the scholars assisting at the disputation are unable to understand the reasons of the master brought into the midst, and yet the reasons themselves delight them, then those scholars are to be joined—that is, associated—with the <term>head-scholar</term>—that is, the <term>bachelor</term> <note>original: "baccalario," a student who has earned his first degree and assists the master</note>—so that he may faithfully impress upon them the sequence of memory—that is, the manner of remembering and also of understanding. Or also the same head-scholar may recommend—that is, inform and show—to those scholars the diligence of "plowing"—that is, of writing. Since a great <term>nourishment</term> <note>original: "fomentum," meaning an incentive or increase</note>—that is, an increase of utility—will be gathered from these, namely from private instructions.

# Sixth

It should be noted that the "recollection" mentioned above in the first chapter is commonly called such; indeed, it is of great use to the student because, as is said there, it generates "use" <note>original: *vsum*; here meaning practice or habitual application</note>. Use, moreover, hastens toward mastery. The reason for this is given in the same place: just as prudence without justice is known to be of little or no benefit, while justice without prudence is of much benefit, so science <note>original: *scientia*; systematic knowledge or skill</note> without use is of little value, but use without science is of much value, just as and in the same manner these and other things are explained at greater length in the previously cited passage; see there. Likewise, "foment" <note>original: *fomentum*</note> means nourishment, like food, and is sometimes used for the effect of growth. It is derived from the verb *foveo* [to cherish or warm]. Likewise, "series" means order or tenor. It is derived from *sero* [to join or weave]. So that he may arrive at the peak of the magistracy <note>the status or office of a Master</note> in due time. Here Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval education</note> begins his division: that

<column-break/>

**indeed in these things the nourishment of utility will be gathered. But so that the student may arrive at the peak of the magistracy in due time, he must dwell in the study of continuity, and he must persist in a more secret retreat—even if he is of a sanguine temperament—lest the noise of those standing by dull his mind or the brawling of those passing by confound his intellect, with no chains hindering his vital spirits. It is also agreeable to honor that the secrets**

---

One might ask: after the master has already performed all those things as taught in the preceding sections, should he from then on abandon study and intend only for scholastic exercise? To this Boethius says no. And he does two things: first, he says the master himself must adhere to continuous study; second, he shows in what places, where he says *In a more secret retreat*. And he says first that just as one must dwell—that is, be at leisure—in the study of continuity so that the student may reach the peak of the magistracy, so also the master must continually study so that he may preserve that very peak of mastery. And showing the place of study, he says that one must persist—that is, for the sake of study one must dwell—in a "retreat," meaning a more secret place, even though the master himself may be "sanguine" <note>referring to the 'sanguine' temperament in medieval humorism, associated with being social and active</note>. For those of a sanguine nature, as has already been demonstrated above, are to be instructed in open, pleasant, and joyful places; nevertheless, despite this, the master ought to study in secret places. This is lest the noise of those standing by dull him in his study, and similarly lest the noise of those passing by confound his intellect; rather, he should be in a quiet, clean place, purged of all chains hindering the master's vital spirits. And giving the reason for these sayings, he says: for it is agreeable to the honor of masters that the master, in searching out—that is, inquiring into—secrets, should be solitary, so that he may present his findings to all by "drawing out"—that is, expounding—his books into the open. For would not a "son of detraction" <note>a critic or slanderer</note>—whoever he may be—looking upon the diligence of the master in drawing out—that is, putting into public—his books for the sake of study, consider it defiled? That is, he would certainly think something evil. Since it is so that perhaps a "wicked eye" would imagine evil from this public display, it is more honorable for any master who studies to betake himself to a solitary place. It should be noted regarding what is said about the continuity of study: just as "one warm day does not make a summer, nor one swallow a spring" <note>original: *vna yrundover*; a Latinized Greek proverb</note>, as Aristotle says in the first book of the *Ethics*, so also not a single studious and scientific act makes one studious and scientific. For, as was also declared in the preceding sections, the continuation of study is required for the perfection of mastery. Indeed, study is like a "dripping drop" that hollows a stone, which hollows the stone not by one fall, but by various falls now multiplied a thousand times. So also a master of good character [does not succeed] by the first titles...

# Chapter

Having attained their course of study, one should not abandon their zeal, but should adhere to study and exercise continuously even unto the end. And this should be done in a solitary place; for a soul occupied by earthly assaults is by no means able to reach the attainment of the sciences. For study requires a freedom of the mind that utterly rejects earthly things, since the soul itself was created apart from the world. Wherefore it is necessary that the soul delight only in things clean and pure, and not in those that are impure and wrapped in earthly mass.

<margin>Wherefore, etc. Also "to probe" <note>Latin: *rimari*</note>, that is, to scrutinize and investigate. The term is drawn from pigs, who search for husks and roots through a "rift" <note>Latin: *rimam*</note> in the earth. Whence Prosper says: "The right hand of salvation probes the secrets of the heart." *If indeed in the early days:* This is the fourth incidental point occurring regarding the aforesaid. And it is such: someone could certainly say that all these things are well and excellently arranged regarding those masters who have an abundance of scholars; but what of those whose lecture hall is not full? Whose presence is ignored and whose company is utterly cut off? Responding to these, he speaks as in the text. And he does two things according to two modes in the text.</margin>

**By probing <note>Latin: *rimando*</note> in this way, let the master exist in solitude rather than exhibiting his presence to all by dragging out his books. For would not a son of detraction <note>A person prone to slander or gossip.</note>, seeing a master diligently bringing out his books, meditate on what he might defile? If indeed in the early days of his mastership his diligence does not have an abundance of learners, let him not grow lukewarm for that reason, nor let him vanish having cast away hope; but let him press on with his studies all the more sharply and offer himself strenuously in the conflict <note>The "conflict" refers to the academic debate or disputation.</note>, so that in this way he may attain honors, albeit with few followers. ¶ For we have frequently seen many men, distinguished by a flourishing zeal for depth, be strenuously titled <note>Given a formal degree or honor.</note> through the company of only a few. ¶ Was not Theophrastus, that craftsman of subtlety, supported by the adornment of only a few, cheated of his hope and cast aside the care of governing because...**

...placed. The second part begins there: ¶ *With gifts, however.* ¶ The first part is in two sections: for first he posits a certain instruction or mode regarding the incident; secondly, he adds the cause for it there: **For of the few.** And he says first that if the diligence of the master has not had an abundance of learners (that is, scholars) in the early days, he should not grow lukewarm (that is, he should not desist from what he has begun) for that reason (that is, because of that). And this is so that he does not vanish (that is, withdraw) having cast away hope. But by how much rarer his audience is, by so much more sharply should he press on with his studies and offer (that is, exhibit) himself in the conflict (that is, the scholastic struggle, which is the disputation) strenuously (that is, ardently), so that in this way he may attain honor, albeit with few. And giving the reason for the aforesaid, he does two things. For first he posits the reason; secondly, he attaches a certain example regarding this there: **Was not... And** he says "for" because we, Boethius, have seen many distinguished (that is, marked out) by a zeal for depth be titled (that is, praised) while the company of a few disciples was flourishing. And he posits an example regarding what he had said, lest often etc., concerning Theophrastus, saying: was not that Theophrastus, being a master and a craftsman of subtlety and supported by the adornment of a few, did he not himself cast aside the care of governing, and this because he was cheated of the hope of future governance? As if he were to say: "Indeed." Which thing, however (namely, to cast aside the care of governing), he did unwisely; but certainly he would have acted more wisely if he had exhibited himself...

# Sixth

->**The Sixth Section**<-

One should maintain a commendable zeal for observance. It should be noted, as the text says, that one must not despair because of a scarcity of listeners. For even if the abundance of scholars were very small, one must not, for that reason, cease from exercise and study. In these matters, worldly glory is not what should be considered, but rather the goal of study and exercise, which is wisdom; for it is the nature of wisdom to make one blessed (as stated in the first book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>) and to make life happy, as Seneca says to Lucilius. By this wisdom, Solomon obtained sovereignty and the honor of the Proverbs, in the second chapter: "It is better." <gloss>For its acquisition is better than that of gold and silver (from the same source).</gloss> For when wisdom is possessed, all good things come along with it. Therefore, let the recruit of the sciences not grow lukewarm <note>original: "tepescat"</note> if he lacks a crowd of students, since a more generous reward for his labors has been established for him.

<column-break/>

However, he acted imprudently. For he would have acted more prudently if he had shown himself commendable in the study of observance. Nevertheless, through the gifts of the master Leontinus, his discernment acquired for him the fellowship of many. For he judged it more beautiful to live in this way than to be deprived of a gathering of learners. Indeed, by the circuit of piety, the leaders of scholars...

---

Likewise, "I grow lukewarm" <note>original: "tepesco"</note> is an inchoative verb from "to be lukewarm" <note>original: "tepeo, tepere"</note>, that is, to become tepid. And to be lukewarm is to be nearly between heat and cold. "Nevertheless, through the gifts of Leontinus": Here is the second incidental lesson to be observed concerning the aforesaid. It does two things: first, it sets down the method by which a master can obtain scholars; second, it raises an objection <term>antipophora: a figure of speech where one anticipates and answers an objection</term> or at least places a certain noteworthy point about this, starting at "Indeed, by piety." And he says that if a master does not have an abundance of listening scholars, the method is to purchase and hire them for himself with gifts, following the example of Leontinus, whose discernment acquired for him a fellowship of many through "gifts," that is, presents. For he "judged," that is, estimated, it would be more beautiful to "live," that is, to apply himself to poverty, than to be deprived of a "gathering of learners," namely scholars. It should be noted that if it is certain that even the gods above are appeased by gifts and presents, according to Ovid in his tradition *On the Art of Love*:

> By a gift the gods above are appeased; by a song, the spirits of the dead, etc.

It is no wonder, then, if men were appeased by them. Indeed, we strive for all things through gifts, so that if something is difficult to obtain by prayer, it may be made easy by a gift. Wherefore Ovid well said in the same place:

> Songs are praised, but great gifts are sought.

And likewise:

> Though you come yourself, Homer, accompanied by the Muses, if you bring nothing, Homer, you will go out the door.

Using this counsel, Leontinus prepared with gifts those whom fortune had taken away from him. "Indeed, by the circuit of piety": Here Boethius places a certain noteworthy point concerning the aforesaid, by which he advises that the distribution of alms should be made to the poor. And this is if the master has a sufficient supply of resources. He does two things: first, he does what has been said; second, he highly commends this distribution at the point "Which is more noble." And he says the leader of scholars, "soothed," that is, protected or distinguished by the "circuit of piety," that is, by piety itself, is bound by the law of charity to "soothe," that is, to cherish the hearts of the disciples "living," that is, existing in poverty. And this applies to those learning studiously and diligently, not indeed to the "unruly" <note>original: "discolis," referring to difficult or wayward students</note>. I say "soothe" them with food and "shoes" and "clothing"—and if not new, at least "worn," that is, torn and old. And I say this if his means are sufficient; for God does not require anything to be sought beyond a man's power. And let the master himself assist them with "other things given," that is, with gifts other than those mentioned; similarly, let him assist them with "encouraging counsel," that is, let him advise and stir them up so that before they abandon their study, they might rather come to receive alms from him or from others. It should be noted that although Boethius [mentions] only...

# Chapter

The author admonishes the rectors of scholars to embrace piety; yet it is something to be sought by all with all their strength. For this is the virtue of brotherly charity which nature urges and reason approves. For we are all of one nature. For which reason, works of piety must be shown toward all. Hence Seneca in *Thyestes*: "No force is greater than true piety." <note>original: "Nulla vis maior pietate vera est." From Seneca's tragedy *Thyestes*, line 549.</note> For whomever true love has held, piety will continue to hold. By these words, then, it is concluded that the work of charity is piety, and that nature seeks piety.

It should be noted regarding point B, where he says "if the means are available," <note>original: "si facultas suppetit"</note> that one should not give so much that in the course of time the things to be bestowed fail. Therefore, a prudent man should look to what might happen to him. For as Socrates testifies: "It is better to be cautious than to be afraid." <note>original: "Melius est cavere quam pavere."</note> Thus, all things are to be bestowed in such a way that they are not prevented from being asked for again in the passage of time.

**Piety**—that is, mercy, kindness, propitiation.
**I soothe** [Mulceo]—to soften, to cherish, to charm.

The hearts of disciples living in poverty and learning studiously are held soothed and charmed. Namely, let him assist them with food, shoes, and at least worn-out clothes—if the means are available—and other gifts, and with encouraging counsel as is fitting. For what distribution <term>erogatio: the act of giving out or distributing funds/alms</term> of nature is more noble or sweeter than that given to true scholars? For it is more noble to cherish a scholar with those things in which there is the smallest display from the giver, but the greatest readiness from the poor recipient, than to cherish actors and prostitutes.

<column-break/>

**What is more noble?** In this part, he recommends the distribution made to poor scholars, saying: "For what distribution"—that is, alms—"is more noble"—that is, more honorable or sweeter—"than that which is made to true scholars?" It is as if he were saying "none." Since to cherish—that is, to soothe—scholars with these distributions in which the display of the giver is minimal and the readiness—that is, the reception—of the recipient is maximal, is more noble—that is, more blessed and honorable—than to be charmed—that is, to foster—the detestable—that is, hateful—attacks of actors and prostitutes.

It should be noted that among all distributions that can be made, that one is more noble which is shown to disciples by a master; because in that act a double distribution is committed: namely, bodily and spiritual. For the **bodily** is that which is shown through food, clothing, and other external service. But the **spiritual** is that by which the ignorance of the disciples is healed and the one who doubts is counseled. Since, therefore, there is a double distribution in these cases, while in others it is usually single, it is certain that nothing exists more noble or sweet.

Also, note regarding what is said, "which is made to true scholars," etc. Although everyone should be helped, a choice must nevertheless be made; in which the character of the one to whom it is given must be observed, as well as their spirit and the sanctity of their life. For one should not give to the unruly, nor to the ungrateful, nor to squanderers, nor to those who love God very little. And therefore it was well said by Cato: "See to whom you give." <note>original: "Cui des videto." A maxim from the *Distichs of Cato*, a popular medieval schoolbook.</note>

Also, an **actor** [histrio] is a performer or jester who knows how to represent the various gestures and habits of men. And it is derived from *historia*, which is to gesticulate. Hence, the presenters of comedies were formerly called actors.

**Though fortune may be cloudy.** This is the fifth and final incident that could happen regarding the aforesaid: namely, the adversity of fortune. And he does two things in this part: first, he places a teaching regarding this incident; second, he confirms the teaching itself with an example. And he says: "though fortune itself may sometimes be cloudy"—that is, adverse.

It contrasts the noble act of supporting scholars with the "hateful" practice of funding entertainers and warns that charity should be discerning and prudent.</summary>

# Sixth

Nevertheless, the care—that is, the vigilance and the anxiety of study—of the teacher <note>original: "magistrantis," referring to one acting as a master or teacher</note> should not despair because of this. Instead, by governing himself, he should always endure well—that is, with equanimity—and suffer manfully—that is, with a brave soul—the incursions—that is, the adversities—of fortune, always looking forward to a sweeter and better outcome. He should not act like that teacher Loriandus <note>A likely reference to a contemporary or local figure used as a negative example of despair</note> who, when fortune did not always smile upon him, dismissed his schools and fell into despair. And therefore, Proch says: the destruction of one who gives up is detestable.

<margin>
Proch <note>Possibly a shortened reference to Proclus or a similar commentator</note> says the transaction—that is, the constancy—of this teacher Loriandus is shameful—that is, to be rejected. It should be noted that although every virtue consists of the highest equanimity, that constancy of mind (as it may be called) is most to be praised. Macrobius, in Book I, describes it thus: "It is the soul raising itself above danger, fearing nothing except what is base, bravely enduring adversity and humbly enduring prosperity." This belongs to a constant mind, as Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says.
</margin>

## Although detestable incursions of fortune may arise everywhere, the care of the teacher should not despair; rather, by always governing himself in a courtly manner, he should manfully endure these incursions while waiting for a sweeter outcome.

## ¶ The shameful transaction of Proch’s Loriandus.

## ¶ If, however, due to the impulse of a festive season, it pleases him to visit places of delight, the discretion of the teacher should always have with him the more noble members of his assembly, as well as those more eminent in appearance, lest he seem to many to be destitute of comfort, or lest he be driven into danger.

In Book I of *On Duties* <note>Cicero's "De Officiis"</note>, he says one should be least perturbed in harsh circumstances. He who lacks this virtue will obtain no prosperity in his works. Therefore, when fortune shows a cloudy face to a nobleman, it must be endured with equanimity and hope must be placed in the Lord; because, as the Prophet witnesses: "those who hope in the Lord shall not be confounded." For this reason, fortune was formerly depicted as cloudy, as was sufficiently taught above. "If, however, due to the impulse of a festive season..." After Boethius <note>The author of the source text being commented upon, likely the "Pseudo-Boethius" in "De Disciplina Scholarium"</note> has established in the preceding sections the rule and manner regulating teachers themselves, both regarding themselves and their disciples, and this both in morals and in the administration of sciences; here, consequently, he sets down the manner and rule regulating teachers in relation to others besides their disciples. And this part is divided into two parts according to the two lessons he provides. The second begins at: "It is permitted, however, in schools, etc." The first is in two parts: for first he provides the lesson, second he adds the cause, and third he corroborates it with an example. The second begins at: "Lest as if..." and the third at: "The forest of Maro..." And reading all of this up to the second lesson, he says first: when it pleases a master to visit places of delight due to the impulse of a festive time, the discretion of the teacher should always have with him the more noble of his assembly—that is, of his scholars—and also those eminent in form. For an eminent form of body is commonly held to represent also the excellence of the soul. And let this be done so that the master himself does not appear to many to be destitute of solace—that is, comfort—or also lest he be driven—that is, moved—into danger. For "woe to the man who is alone, for when he falls he will have no one to lift him up." And showing the evils that can happen if the aforesaid things are not observed, he says by example: "For the solitary passage <note>original: "saltus," meaning a forest clearing or a leap/passage</note> of Maro"—perhaps he means Virgil <note>Publius Vergilius Maro</note> or another—grieved—that is, he sorrowed greatly—to be deprived—that is, destitute—of the assembly—that is, the society—of happy scholars...

<summary>This page advises teachers to maintain emotional constancy during hardships and suggests that when traveling during holidays, they should be accompanied by their best students to maintain their social standing and safety.</summary>

# Chapter.

The solitary passage of Aaron <note>original: "solitario suo transitu Aaroni"; likely a reference to a specific passage or metaphorical "leap" in the text being commented upon</note> occurred: the nature of which Boethius did not express here. Although he may be rigid in the schools. This is the second instruction by which he informs teachers how they ought to conduct themselves toward others outside of their students. And he says: the master of students himself, although he ought to be rigid in the schools—understand this as expressed above in the same chapter where it was said "rigid" etc.—nevertheless, the master ought to be devout in

> **The leap of Aaron grieved to be deprived of the assembly of happy disciples. Although he ought to be rigid in the schools: nevertheless, let him remain devout in his gait when offering greetings: pleasant in speech to those passing by: a companion to those playing along: faithful in admonition to those staying with him: cautious in chastity toward his neighbors: lest a friendly intimacy drink in the stench of a sighing nose, should any be present. The final compilation of the present volume stands concerning the masterships of those whom poverty—the stepmother to the liberal arts—has compelled to invade foreign borders. And concerning those whom the sweetness of their native land calls back, [to say] something briefly—**

<column-break/>

his gait, that is, in his passage before the people; and I say this regarding greeting anyone according to their status. He ought also to be pleasant in speech to those "transmigrating," that is, those passing him by, and a comrade and companion to those "playing along," that is, those harmonizing with him. And let him be faithful in "admonition," that is, in wholesome advice, to those "staying," that is, those living with him. And also let him be "cautious," that is, shrewd, in "chastity" toward his "neighbors," that is, those nearby. It is as if he were saying: if he cannot live chastely, let him at least act before his neighbors so that if he does anything sinister, it does not become known to them; so that what cannot be done chastely

may at least be carried out cautiously. And adding the reason for this, he says: And this ought to be done for the reason stated, lest "friendly intimacy," that is, a friendly neighborhood, "drink in," that is, take away, the "stench of a sighing nose" <note>A metaphorical expression meaning the detection of a hidden vice or foul reputation</note>. This is a metaphorical expression. "The final compilation of the present volume stands." This is the second principal part of this last chapter. In which, after Boethius has determined and set down the various divisions of teachers and regulated the morals of those who live in the principal places of study—namely Athens and Rome—with instructions, he now intends in this second principal part of the chapter to show how those who have the care of ruling schools in camps or in villages surrounding the aforementioned places of study ought to behave, being hemmed in by poverty. And this part is divided into two parts. In the first part, he sets forth his intention; in the second, he pursues it, at the point: "When for the sake of poverty." And he says: the "final," that is, the last compilation of the present volume "stands," that is, exists, so that I may speak "briefly," that is, with brevity, concerning those "masters" whom "poverty"—existing as a "stepmother," that is, something contrary and hostile to the "liberal arts"—has compelled to "invade foreign borders," that is, foreign regions; and similarly also concerning those whom the "sweetness of their native land" has called back—understand this to mean to stay there. And concerning these in the third principal part. It should be noted regarding what he says about the "liberal arts": by these liberal arts he understands the seven liberal arts. I call them "liberal" because they are everywhere distinct from other "illiberal" [mechanical] arts. For the former pertain to the soul, while the latter pertain to the body.
