->Sixth.<-

Indeed, those arts ordered toward the body are called liberal: also because through them a person is disposed by the intellect toward the highest end, such as the use of moral and intellectual virtues, or toward the use of perfect happiness, which is speculative. Those who consider such things are naturally free and not servile, since they flourish in intellect. Therefore, these are rightly called the "liberal arts." <note>The term "liberal" comes from the Latin *liber*, meaning free; these were the studies suitable for a free person rather than a slave.</note> And again, they are called liberal because they require free, unencumbered, and exercised minds, because they

dispute subtly concerning the causes of things, and concerning many of those things which are removed from the senses. And furthermore, they are called liberal because in ancient times only the free—that is, the noble and high-born—were accustomed to study them. The common people, however, worked in the "mechanical" arts <note>The mechanical arts included crafts like weaving, smithing, and agriculture, viewed as manual labor.</note> because of their skill in labor, which indeed is a skill and work more suited to the commoners.

<column-break/>

Leisure and study belong to the noble, according to Hugh <note>Likely referring to Hugh of Saint Victor, a famous 12th-century theologian and educator.</note>. Likewise, the word "end" (*finis*) is of uncertain gender <note>original: "incerti generis"</note>, that is, a boundary; it is derived from "rope" (*funis*) because the boundaries of fields were divided by small ropes. Whence the prophet says: "The lines [ropes] have fallen for me in goodly places." <note>A quote from Psalm 16:6.</note> And "end" can mean a boundary, a consummation, death, or the fatherland; whence the verse: "The end is fatherland, death, consummation, and goal." It is commonly of uncertain gender, either masculine or feminine. **When, however, for the sake of poverty.** After Boethius <note>The text refers to the "De disciplina scholarium," attributed in the Middle Ages to Boethius, though now known to be by a later author.</note> set forth his intent, he now pursues it here. He does two things: first, Boethius shows how those masters living outside their own fatherland, in the places mentioned above (whether near or far), ought to conduct themselves toward their scholars. Second, how they should act toward those other than scholars, at the point: "When, however, the meal..." The first part is divided into two: first, he addresses what was said regarding himself; second, regarding the vice-teacher, at the point: "And it must be noted." The first of these is again divided: first, he sets down general instructions; second, he adds special instructions at the point: "And to the boys." And he says first that when any of the masters, for the sake of repelling poverty—that is, driven by poverty itself—seeks the "sweetest scent of profit" (understand: in foreign parts), then it must be considered that the master himself should persist—that is, intend—as much as he can in frugality. And I say this "while preserving honor," because he should also see to it that he "desires moderate clothing" (understand: yet worthy of the magisterial honor according to the previous precepts) and "devotes himself"—that is, applies himself—especially to the governance of scholars. Note that all these general precepts were essentially derived in the earlier parts of this same chapter: namely, the master's frugality, the respectability of his garments, and the due attention toward his scholars; therefore, it would be superfluous to treat them again here. Look for them there. Likewise, first he shows how he should behave before the young and small; second, how before the adults, at: "And to those same ones when somewhat grown..." And first he says that when a master has undertaken the care of governance in foreign parts, he ought to show, first and principally...

# The Sixth Part

->The proud man should find.<- Here **Boethius** <note>original: "Boe." referring to the author of the text being commented upon, likely Pseudo-Boethius in 'De Disciplina Scholarium'</note> shows how a teacher ought to behave toward rebels. He says that if a teacher finds someone who is defiant or proud, he should punish him sweetly; that is, he should correct and rebuke him with sweet words and exhortations toward the good. He should set before him examples by which he might be restrained from his defiance and pride. But if he cannot be corrected at all by words and charitable, sweet warnings or examples, let him be afflicted—that is, let him be corrected with rods and

flogging. And I say this only if it is done with the consent of the parents. Giving the reason, he says: so that the defiant one might emerge "punished to the fingernail" <note>term: "ad unguem" - a Latin idiom meaning to perfection or highly polished, like a sculptor checking a seam with a fingernail</note>, that is, to perfection, lest he fall entirely into ignominy, which is infamy, as one who is despaired of. Note that a teacher ought to act toward defiant disciples in the manner of a prudent physician. For a **Physician**, in curing diseases, first administers mild medicines 
<column-break/>
so that he does not conform to the rigor of justice alone. Thus, he should be suitable not only in teaching but also in pleasantness. He should grant time for play at the proper season, and the benefits of teaching should be withdrawn under no circumstances. If, however, he finds the defiant and the proud: let him punish them sweetly and set forth examples of character by which they may be restrained. Otherwise, with the consent of the parents, let them be afflicted with rods, so that they may emerge punished to perfection, lest they fall into despair and ignominy. But when the affection of the teacher [finds those] chilled by age

for the good, and so that through the lightness of the medicine the patient becomes accustomed to healthy drinks. In the same way, a teacher should first deal with rebels using sweet words, so that, enticed by the sweetness of the correction, they may cease from the disease of rebellion. But if they cannot be pulled back by these means, a sharper medicine must be used: namely, the striking of rods. This should be chosen so that one rotting limb, if not cut, does not hinder the health of the whole body. Likewise, the rebellion of a defiant scholar should not provide an occasion for the despair of ignominy. **But when the affection of the teacher has.** In this part, **Boethius**, after he had promised instructions on how a teacher should behave toward those disciples who are subject to correction, here does the same regarding those who are placed entirely outside the "moon of correction" <note>interpretive: likely meaning outside the normal age or sphere of physical discipline</note>, such as the "statue-like" elders, the "wanderers," and others. And he sets down several brief instructions according to the plurality and diversity of all these disciples. He says when the affection of the teacher encounters those chilled by age—that is, the "statue-like" elders, who are beastly and crude in natural talent, or the "wanderers" <note>original: "planeticos" - referring to students who lack focus or wander mentally</note>, and I say this of all who share in the scholastic entrance—what should be done? I say if the teacher cannot use the most useful means—that is, the rigor of correction—among them, he must act in the following way. For he must smile upon—that is, favor—those worn out by their senses (the elderly); and he must groan with—that is, feel pity for—the statue-like ones (the unrefined) on account of the crudeness of their talent. For the wanderers, he should rejoice with them through imagery—that is, through similarities and the bringing forth of examples. And if any are accustomed to luxury, such as those with curled hair, the refined, and the soft: then he should "burn"—that is, he should punish their vice by thoroughly burning away those with curled hair who have shaggy locks—that is, crimped hair—and he should trust that those overflowing with "fucus" <note>term: "fuco" - a Roman term for rouge or false dye/pretense</note>, that false color, will have their throats irrigated by tears. And he should punish them so much that, being provoked to tears, they wash away the dye from their throats.

In whatever way they have conducted themselves, the end of the work will show it. Wherefore he says, "For what..." as in Isaiah. <note>A reference to the Prophet Isaiah, likely regarding vanity or the revealing of secrets.</note> It should be noted concerning this that he says "lest a familiar [voice]," because benefits which are often given for free and bestowed under the pretext of piety are often changed into insults and reproach. For there are those who receive benefits and attribute them to the neediness of those bestowing them. For they say to themselves: "He gave this because he needs me or will need me; for he knows either that I can be of use to him in some way or he hopes for the service of my family." He also says many benefits and payments are made to them under the pretext of fraud. Again, others, when they have received gifts, acknowledge them very little. Nevertheless, a wise and good man commends a gift, however small it may have been, and delights in its constant remembrance. For which reason, one must look out especially to whom it is paid. Therefore, let it be paid to members of the household rather than to familiar neighbors, lest through external benefits, internal want be rolled out into the public.

Also, an old woman <term>anus: a woman of many years</term> is called "ancient" as if having many years (*annos*). Or it is said to be from *a* and *nus*, that is, "sense," as if "without sense" <note>A common medieval folk etymology: a- (without) + nous (mind/sense)</note>; and the 'a' is shortened. Whence: "Pamphilus, take away your hands and now the old woman (*ănus*) will return." It is also called the posterior part of the body, and then the 'a' is lengthened (*ānus*), as in the verse: "While the old woman (*ănus*) bends herself, the anus (*ānus*) hisses behind her." <note>A crude grammatical mnemonic used in medieval schools to distinguish vowel length.</note> Likewise, "futile" is that which flows down quickly and easily, and it is said because it can retain nothing; and from this, by a metaphor, a man is called "futile" who is vain, superfluous, and talkative, who can veil or conceal nothing. Whence: "That vessel is futile which no receiving-hole closes; so a futile man is one divulging everything he hears."

"Let bold [rapacity] in the smallest things be far away." Here he places another instruction which dissuades the master from avarice and tenacity. And he says "rapacity," that is, paternal <insert>cruel</insert> avarice, should be far away in the smallest things—supply "matters." He says this because if it is absent in the small, it should be even more so in the greatest, through that <term>topic: a logical rule</term> "If that which is less, then that which is more." And this concerns avarice. And it follows: let "hooked"—that is, curved and almost inflexible—"tenacity" also be absent, being the "stepmother"—that is, the enemy—of reputation. Likewise, just as in anyone, so also by a teacher, among other evils, this vice of rapacity must be fled. For illicit gain is [not] justly possessed, and because it was [not] justly acquired, it is therefore justly lost. Here Cicero says in the *Second Philippic*: "Ill-gotten gains come to a bad end." <note>original: "Male parta male dilabuntur"</note> Indeed, it is difficult for anyone to prosper from rapacity. For if anyone should seem to rejoice in his days in what he has snatched, nevertheless his prosperity either will not be long-lasting or will not endure in his successors, according to that saying of Seneca to Lucilius: "To no one," he says, "for whom rapine has turned out happily, does the joy of the stolen thing last in their posterity." Nor is it a wonder: because nothing violent is perpetual. Therefore, let it be far away...

while the scholar is incumbent, care must also be taken lest the master himself, living outside his own fatherland, play in the "dust"—that is, secular labor—which is full of "dregs"—that is, the filth of those things mentioned, namely the scholarly governance—and he should not play at it for more than three years, notwithstanding that...
</margin>

->**he plays in that same place. Although the greatest abundance of wealth or companions may be present, joined with an opulence of affection, unless a promotion of honor flourishes in that love, or an elevation of means in that honor. However, when on account of the delights of the sweetness of the fatherland and of parents...**<-

...an abundance—that is, a greatest plenty—of wealth <note>original: "gaze," a Persian-derived term for treasure</note> and profit, and an abundance of companions—that is, of scholars—is present, joined—that is, coupled—with opulence. That is, with an abundance of love (another manuscript has "confederated by love," but it comes to the same thing), unless—that is, except if—a promotion to a greater status flourishes; that is, unless he hopes to be promoted to greater things. Or certainly, if an elevation of means—that is, of riches and profit—flourishes in honor. It is as if he says: for then one should stay longer when greater rewards are expected. Likewise, it is called "dust" <note>original: "pulvis"</note> because it is taken from the living. Hence, we often take "dust" to mean "labor." Wherefore Virgil says in a certain Eclogue: *What does it profit to be away, weary from the summer dust, rather than to have reclined on a thirsty couch?* <note>original: "Quid iuvat estivo fessum pulvere abesse..."</note> and Horace: *There are those whom it delights to have gathered Olympic dust in the chariot race* <note>original: "Sunt quos curriculo pulverem olimpicum collegisse iuvat"</note>, although perhaps it is interpreted in another way there. Likewise, "dreg-filled" <note>original: "feculentus"</note> is said from "dregs" <note>original: "fece"</note>; that is, stinking or full of dregs. For the suffix "-lentus" often signifies fullness, just as "-osus" does.

**However, when on account of the delights of the sweetness of the fatherland.** After Boethius <note>The author of the source text being commented upon, likely the 'De Disciplina Scholarium' formerly attributed to Boethius</note> has shown in this last chapter how masters governing schools in the two most solemn cities, such as Athens and Rome, and similarly in places adjacent to them yet outside their own fatherland, ought to conduct themselves both toward themselves and toward their scholars and others distinct from their scholars; now, consequently, in this final part of the entire work, he determines how masters undertaking the care of teaching students in their own fatherland ought to govern themselves. 

And this part is divided into two parts: for first, he sets down certain lessons regulating the master himself as to the composing of his morals; second, as to the vices to be avoided (the second part begins at "Of Jests"). The first is further divided into two: for first he does what has been said; second, he subjoins the cause of the lessons at "Since the many-threaded..." And first, setting down the lesson, he says: when any of the masters has undertaken the care of governing schools in the borders of his native soil—that is, in his own territory—both on account of the delights of the sweetness of the fatherland and also on account of the venerable sight of parents, he must apply himself—that is, give his time—(it is understood: the master himself) to "pompous"—that is, proud, not with that pride which is stained by vice, but pompous, meaning full of "philosophical pomp"—speech—that is, to conversation and discourse—and similarly, he must smile upon a "cautious and splendid procurement"—understand this as the providing of food and other provisions; and I say this "in turn," not indeed...

# Chapter

On each individual day, or when the time demands or means permit, one should enjoy a variety of clothing—namely, using other decent ornaments such as rings, the *birrus* <note>original: "birrum"; a hooded cloak or cape worn by officials and academics</note>, and similar items which magisterial honor requires. And adding the reason for this variety of clothing, he says: and this is because the beauty—that is, the decency—of many-colored <note>original: "polimite"; referring to embroidered or multi-colored fabric</note> clothing, and the glorious ornaments of rings and other headbands—

**Whoever has accepted the care of ruling venerable appearances must insist on a stately manner of speech within the borders of their native soil. One must, in turn, smile upon elegant and splendid management and rejoice in a variety of garments, because the beauty of many-colored clothing and the insignia of rings compel many to obtain a reputation other than what truth demands. The favor of ornament and the charm of speech compel very many people—provided with an erroneous sense—to see one as exceeding Homer, provided the order of teaching has been diligently observed. Also, let the damaging desire for jokes be carefully removed, so that (as rarely happens) provincial honor may carry fame into the commendation of the title. Indeed, the more the title of beauty has arisen, the more one must insist on the favor of subjects, so that what cannot be carried by one's own mouth...**

<column-break/>

...of headbands, they compel many to obtain something other than what the intrinsic truth itself demands and requires. For a man well-dressed is believed by a thousand to be skilled in his garments. Therefore, let him be that man. And attaching another cause, he says this very thing: that ornament and favor—and the charm (that is, the wit) of speech and conversation—compel many to exceed (that is, to excel) in sight and appearance. I say that many such people, distinguished in this way by clothing, favor, and wit of conversation, are compared by an erroneous sense—understand this as being due to a feigned decency—to that Greek poet Homer. He says that the ornament of garments and the other things mentioned above often cause a master to be esteemed as wiser and more skilled than Homer, even if he is not so in the reality of the matter.

It must be noted that to anyone, their own fatherland is sweet, because the place of birth is the preservative principle for everyone, just as a father exists as the productive principle. This is attested by Porphyry the Isagogic <note>referring to Porphyry of Tyre, whose "Isagoge" was a standard medieval textbook on logic</note> when he says: "For the fatherland is the principle of generation, just as the father is." Indeed, in that place, celestial virtue flows vigor into the one born and preserves him in being, just as a place preserves that which is placed within it. Therefore, one's fatherland is sweet to everyone because of the preservation of the place of birth. Similarly, it is also sweet because of the reverence for parents, which was the first commandment given with a promise, as is clear from Exodus 20 when it is said: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may be well with you." For reverence for parents brings longevity of life and an abundance of temporal goods. Also, "many-colored" <note>original: "polimit[a]"; from the Greek 'polymitos'</note> is used as an adjective; a many-colored garment is of many colors and is named from...

It also provides a philosophical and biblical defense of the love for one's fatherland (patria) and the duty to honor parents.</summary>

# The Garland

->**Column 1**<-

...roundness, which is the pole, because that garment is round. In this context, it can be understood in both senses. Likewise, **charming** <note>Latin: *venustus*</note> means decent, and is derived from Venus. Papias <note>A famous 11th-century lexicographer</note> however says that "charming" means wise, adorned, modest, witty, and beautiful; hence, "charm" <note>Latin: *venustas*</note> is wit and beauty. **The damaging lust for games, etc.** In this section, Boethius, after the aforementioned points, sets down instructions regulating teachers regarding the flight from vices.

And this part is divided into two sections according to the two instructions he provides. The second begins at: **When, however...** First, he provides one instruction concerning the avoidance of illicit games; second, he adds the reason for the instruction at: **But because of the mouth, etc.** And he says first that **damaging lust**, that is, the desire for games, should be taken away—understand this as applying to the teacher—so that...

<column-break/>

...from their own [the students'] commotions, it may be bestowed through timely speeches. So that he may be seen as commendable not only in the sweetness of his character but also in the sharpness of his own faculty <note>meaning his intellectual skill or academic discipline</note>. When, however, the commendation of both character and faculty has come into public view, care must be taken lest unchastity dull the head or adultery confound the speech, and illicitly...

<column-break/>

...evil. And this is so that the provincial honor—that is, the honor of the people of the province and the fatherland—might be extolled; that is, it should lift up the fame (supply: of the teacher) toward the commendation of his title, which is his honor. This, however, rarely happens, since "no one is accepted in his own country, nor is a prophet," as is said in the Gospel <note>A reference to Luke 4:24</note>. And it follows: the more the title—that is, the praise and honor of charm and nobility—has arisen (that is, increased), the more one must insist upon (that is, devote oneself to) the favor of his subjects, namely the scholars <note>students</note>. 

And assigning the cause of the instruction, he says: it is fitting that all these things be done so that the praise which cannot be brought forth (understand: because of the speaker's modesty, since self-praise is loathsome) amidst the commotions (that is, the tumultuous words) of one's own mouth, might at least be bestowed and made known by the timely speeches of those subordinates. Thus, the master himself may be looked upon and admired not only for the sweetness of his character but also for the sharpness (that is, the excellence) of his faculty (that is, his sciences). 

It should be noted that teachers staying in their places of birth ought especially to abstain from the company of players <note>gamblers</note> on account of the many most vile conditions by which any player is bound. 
1. The first is the **desire for winning**, which proceeds from greed, which is "the root of all evils" (First Timothy 6). 
2. The second is **despoiling the first**, which is robbery. 
3. The third is **blaspheming God**, which is most foul. 
4. The fourth is **perjury**, by which the Church is despised. 
5. The fifth is **strong lying**, by which the neighbor is scandalized. 
6. The sixth is **stealing**, which leads to hanging. 
7. The seventh is **becoming angry**, which often leads to homicide. 
8. The eighth is **not observing holy days**, for which players deserve to be stoned just like those who gathered wood on the Sabbath. 
9. The ninth is the **loss of all goods**. 

For these reasons, a teacher of good inquiry who desires to spread his good fame and honors should avoid the dishonesty and madness of games, since nothing dishonors a man as much as the dishonesty of games. For the game of dice <note>Latin: *alea*</note>, as is written in the first book of the *Policraticus* <note>A work on government and ethics by John of Salisbury, 1159 AD</note>, is the mother of all evils. Therefore, the enormity of dice and other games should be avoided, following the example of Chilo the Lacedaemonian <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>. He, having been sent to Corinth to form an alliance, found the leaders and elders of the people playing at dice. His business being thus unaccomplished, he returned, saying...

# Chapter

->He said<- he was unwilling to stain the glory of the Spartans—whose architecture was famous in Byzantium—with such infamy that he should be said to have entered into a partnership with gamblers. It is also excellently reported that Themistocles <note>original: "Temistodes"; likely referring to the Athenian statesman Themistocles</note> maintained that magistrates should be kept away from games and all lighter pursuits, lest the Republic appear to be "playing," and lest, having abandoned its gravity, it announce its own defect. Thus he spoke. Furthermore, since the good reputation of both one's character and one's ability

<margin>The good reputation of both character and ability</margin>

is blackened by the stench of vices, [one must take care] lest the roses emitting a spring scent seem to die out, and the lilies sought through the sweat of chastity seem to wither. **The image of the venerable Crato** <note>Crato of Thebes, a Cynic philosopher known for his virtue</note> [is presented] to his other companions of the same profession, and even to those who had been moved to sorrow by a single glance at him...

<column-break/>

Here is placed the second lesson by which Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, the Roman philosopher</note> urges the masters themselves to embrace the flight from luxury <note>term: "luxury" (Latin: luxuria); in this medieval context, it specifically refers to lust or lewdness rather than material wealth</note> with all their might. This part is divided into three sections: first, he sets down the lesson; second, he provides the reason for the lesson; third, he confirms all these things with an example. The second part begins at "Lest the roses"; the third at "The venerable Crato." And first, in setting down the lesson, he says with commendation—

---

that is, praise and honor—that when the reputation of both the character and the ability of a master has gone out into the public—that is, into public fame—it must be considered and more firmly guarded against, lest unchastity <note>original: "incestus"; here meaning general impurity or lust</note>—that is, luxury or fornication—should bow his head—that is, surround and bend it—and also lest adultery should confound his face (this is a synecdoche, a part used to represent the whole). And he adds: lest the vice of stinking and illicit malice blacken and darken a reputation—it is understood—acquired through great labors. And giving the reason for these things, he says these must be considered lest the roses—that is, good reputation itself—emitting a spring scent—that is, vernal and sweet—should seem to die out; and also lest the lilies of chastity—that is, chastity itself, which is rightly compared to lilies—sought by sweat—that is, by labor—should seem to decrease—supply: from their beauty. It is as if he were saying: lest that good reputation cease to smell sweet.

Note that Boethius, observing among other vices that tend to destroy and even blacken a good reputation, identifies luxury <insert>lust</insert> as the primary one. Therefore, through this lesson, he teaches the master of true wisdom to avoid this vice and retain a good reputation, which he will easily be able to fulfill if he wishes to adhere to the counsel of wisdom. Whence Wisdom herself says against this vice and the remaining vices in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 7: "All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable honors through her hands." <note>A quote from the Biblical Book of Wisdom 7:11</note> Cato, observing this, said: **"Flee luxury"** etc., and it follows at the end of the second verse: "for they are contrary to reputation." I say "contrary" because it is most clear not only in words but by example. For was not the most famous city of the Volscians, wealthy and ordered by laws and customs—as Valerius reports in Book 9, Chapter 1—after it fell into luxury, did it not fall into injury and baseness so that it was subjected to the most insolent domination of slaves? So too the Roman Empire, as Polycrates <note>likely referring to John of Salisbury’s "Policraticus"</note> reports in Book 6, Chapter 12, was exhausted by luxury and lust during the reign of Nero. What, therefore, is more foul than this vice? What is more damaging? By it, virtue is worn away, victories grow weak, dormant glory is turned into infamy, and the face of honesty is blackened.

Likewise, "incestuous" means "unchaste," referring to one who lies with a nun, a blood relative, or a virgin; for it is illicit intercourse. But "adultery" is, as it were, "access to another's bed" <note>a common medieval etymology: ad-alterius-thorum</note>; for as the Master says in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, it is illicit intercourse with a married woman. But "debauchery" <note>original: "stuprum"</note> is the illicit deflowering of a virgin. "Fornication" is a general term for all these, but specifically refers to intercourse with an unmarried widow or a prostitute.

# Sixth Section

In this section, Boethius confirms the things said above by means of an example. He does two things: first, he sets forth the example; second, he adds a certain notable point concerning it at the phrase *For although.* In proposing the example, he describes what and how many reproaches, mockeries, and blasphemies were incurred because of the vice of adultery. The venerable likeness—that is, the image and the outcome—of that master, Crato, provided a cause for sorrow and an increase of sadness, not only for his own professional standing <note>original: "proprie facultatis id est artis"</note>

and his accomplices—that is, his associates—but even for others who were connected to him in a single regard. Specifically, this Crato, while he was sleeping at a certain time in the lodging <note>original: "diuersorio," meaning an inn or guest house</note>—that is, the house—of that man Lastor (whoever he may have been), and this for the sake of the delights—that is, the adultery—of his wife Eufrasia <note>The text alternates between Eufragia and Eufrasia; I have standardized to Eufrasia</note>, he was discovered—that is, caught—in the act of embracing. What followed? Crato himself was dragged by his hair, punished with a whip, torn—that is, mangled—with wounds, and then rubbed with salt; and afterwards, to increase his punishments, he was drenched in the urine of slaves. And again, he was cast out into the corners—supply "of the house"—

<column-break/>

**...provided [a cause for sorrow] and an increase [of sadness], who, while sleeping in the lodging of Lastor for the sake of the delights of his wife Eufrasia, was discovered in an embrace. He was dragged by the hair. Punished with a whip. Mangled with wounds. Rubbed with salt. Drenched in the urine of slaves. Cast out into the corners. Lifted up on the beams. At last, when the torturers were exhausted, he was deprived of his genitals. Placed upon a dunghill. Exposed to those passing by. He became the outcast of the common people, the desolation of his disciples, the reproach of his fellow soldiers; he stood as a raw and cruel, wretched and most miserable spectacle of grief to all: for the sake of his affinity and the glory of his kindred profited him in nothing.**

---

...lifted up on the beams. But at last, when the torturers who were agonizing him (as is permitted) were weary and exhausted, he was deprived of his genitals and placed upon a dunghill <note>original: "sterquilinio"</note>, exposed to those passing by—understand this as "to become a laughingstock." When all these things had been carried out, he became the outcast of the common people—that is, their derision, etc.—as the text follows more clearly. Indeed, the literal text needs no further explanation. It should be noted that although many evils accompany adulterers and likewise other fornicators of whatever condition by the just judgment of God, nevertheless these things which the text enumerates in this example, though they do not frequently happen exactly as they are narrated to have happened to Crato, are nonetheless among those punishments which are more readily inflicted when an adulterer is caught in the vice than others. Similar are the things which Horace enumerates in the first book of his *Sermones*, in the second Satire. For he says in this manner: *This one threw himself headlong from the roof; that one was beaten with lashes. This one, fleeing, fell into a band of robbers; this one paid money to save his body. The stable-boys debased this man; and even that: It happened that a certain man mowed off the testicles and the lecherous tail with a blade; all said it was by right,* etc. Thus says Horace. Also, "sorrow" <note>original: "meror"</note> is nearly "grief with silence," and it comes from the verb *mereo, -es* [to deserve or grieve]. Also, "lodging" <note>original: "diuersorium"</note> is a "diversity of ways" where a traveler turns aside from the path, or a place remote from others, or a receptacle—namely, an inn or a hospital. And it is named from *diuerto* [to turn aside]; hence in Luke: *there was no room for him in the inn.* And as the Gloss says, it is a place between two walls having two gates, so that it is accessible from different ways.

# Chapter.

<note>original: "Capitulum"</note>
...he should receive those who arrive. For although the first signs may sometimes be sound. In this final small section of this entire book on the discipline of scholars, regarding what was said just before, he adds a certain notable point by which he warns all teachers that whatever they have done, whether in morals or in the administration of teachings, they should at least carry these out in such an order and manner that just as the middle stages prevail over the first, so also the final stages should surpass the middle and the first. **For although the first signs may sometimes be sound: the final ones, however, will remain as stains of a different flavor, etc.**

stains—that is, shameful and wicked things—of a different flavor, meaning of a different sort than the first. It should be noted that just as it is of little use to act well if the mind is unstable—since a habit is formed from no acts unless the perseverance of good work coexists—so also it profits little, or rather nothing, for one who begins with good things, is lukewarm in the middle, and confounds the end with horror. Whence it is well said in the proverbs of the wise: "It profits nothing to do well if you stop." For it is shameful to desert good works once begun and to decline into evil. Therefore, having begun with a good purpose, one must persevere continually. Moreover, he perseveres who continues the good things he has started. He also continues who closes each thing with the highest end of creation. Who is God, glorious and blessed forever. Amen.

I was deliberating likewise to loosen the song of the sons.
With a slanting face, I am carried away deaf from the heights:
Let it not be a shame to have constructed deceits from the mound of fate
While the ample harvest moves the rumor-bearing sounds
Sometimes a madness bordering the sea was present
While I speak from the fourth head, compare the work.
I pray these things, O youths, by whom youth must be celebrated,
May my lyre now suggest innocent melodies.
